The authors show the hope fails. They construct two sets whose degrees sit directly adjacent, one forming a minimal cover of the other with nothing in between. Both sets can even be built inside the same enumeration degree, a related ranking. The result settles the density question for several connected degree systems at once. All of them are now known to have gaps.
arxiv-2412-19791:
Shaoshuai Chu, Alexander Kurganov, Mingye Na, Bao Shan Wang, and Ruixiao Xin make numerical methods for conservation laws better in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Hyperbolic systems of balance laws model flows with sources, from shallow water to gas dynamics. High-order schemes rebuild solution values from cell averages with polynomials. Plain rebuilding swings near shocks, though rebuilding characteristic variables in its place fixes that. Well-balanced schemes must keep steady states in an exact way. That takes a balance among flux, source, and nonconservative terms.

The team brings in a characteristic decomposition applied to equilibrium variables, values that stay constant at steady states. That choice keeps rebuilds free of swings and steady-state preserving too, in a fifth-order A-WENO interpolation inside a well-balanced frame. Examples show the scheme is exact and stable, and the decomposition acts as designed on problems where past rebuilds do poorly.
arxiv-2501-01291:
Yu-Han Huang, Argyrios Gerogiannis, Subhonmesh Bose, and Venugopal Veeravalli organize, in a 2025 preprint, the design of bandit algorithms for worlds that change in jumps. A multi-armed bandit learner picks among options whose payoffs it must learn by trying. In piecewise stationary worlds, some payoffs shift suddenly at unknown times, then hold steady. Practical fixes bolt a change detector onto a standard learner. The authors ask what each part must guarantee for the combo to work. Their aim is a modular theory, not one more bespoke algorithm.

They first sharpen the known lower bounds on regret for such worlds. Then they state the conditions a detector and a base learner must meet. Under those conditions, regret bounds follow in one unified way for many pairings. New pairings built on the rules come out order-optimal. Experiments confirm the approach tracks rivals in regret while catching changes well.
arxiv-2501-03991:
Yuxi Xia and co-authors study what shapes calibration in large language models, in this 2025 paper. Calibration means a model's stated confidence matches how often it is right, which matters for safe use. The team sets a controlled test bed with twelve models and four prompt styles. They ask whether pooling answers from several models, and choosing the right training loss, can sharpen confidence estimates.

Their framework trains a helper model that reads the agreement among several models' answers. Agreement plus a focal loss both improved calibration over baselines. Few-shot prompts suited the helper approach best. Helpers stayed reliable as accuracy shifted, beating the models' own stated confidence. The authors map these factors to guide safer deployment of language models.
arxiv-2501-04391: Bagheri, Roy, and Pöschel ran computer tests in twenty twenty-five on wet grains to check three ways to model the pull of liquid bridges between grains. The tests sheared the grains in a split-base cell, with each bridge model run in turn. The bulk grip of the mass grew in a straight line with the pull of the liquid skin in all three runs. The rub rate of the mass changed only a little with that pull.
arxiv-2501-04491:
Yanan Zhao, Qiaoli Dong, Yufei Zhao, and Chunlin Wu present a fast algorithm for sparse data recovery in a 2025 paper. The task is to find solutions where whole groups of values are zero, using a harsh penalty that favors such grouping. Their algorithm mixes threshold steps, a linear shortcut, and momentum tricks to move quickly.

A key gain is that the method never needs to solve a large equation system. For two common cases it needs only basic matrix work and soft thresholding, which suits very large problems. The authors prove the method settles to a solution under stated conditions. In tests it matched rival accuracy at about half the computing time of the next fastest method.
arxiv-2501-05891:
Raimondi, Giallorenzo, and Gabbrielli ask in twenty twenty-five if small language models can answer course questions well. They test models on quiz items from a class on programming languages. The set has one hundred sixty-two multiple choice questions, and the team shares it in public.

They try three sizes of the LLaMA-2 model, from small to large. They tune the small models on parts of the course textbook. They also shrink the models to use less memory and power. The tuned small models beat the large generic ones on the quiz. The result suggests teachers can get good answers with cheap tools and their own course text.
arxiv-2501-07591:
Sun, Wu, Xu, and Zhu explore in twenty twenty-five a way to catch light dark matter that supernova bursts have kicked to high speed. When a star collapses, it floods space with neutrinos, and some may strike dark matter particles and boost them. Most boosted particles carry modest energy, in the range where special chip detectors can register a shared shiver of electrons rather than a single hit.

The team computed how often such collective excitation signals would appear in these detectors. The limits they derive beat standard neutrino and dark matter searches for very light dark matter. The authors present the channel as a strong new window on particles below the usual detection floor.
arxiv-2501-08891:
Sebastiano Cocchi and co-authors send quantum keys through open air with a time bin code, in work from twenty twenty-five. Quantum key sharing can secure messages over long range, but air links and fiber links use unlike light and codes. That gap makes it hard to join the two into one network.

The team used infrared light in the band that fiber likes best, with time bin coding that fiber needs. Keys crossed fifty metre and five hundred metre air links in day and night hours. Rates stayed high for hours, far higher on the short link. The result backs a hybrid network that could link ground users to satellites one day.
arxiv-2501-09391:
Guangyuan Liu and four co-authors pay edge devices to make good images for the metaverse. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Diffusion models create rich, realistic scenes, but they are heavy to run. Phones and edge nodes have limited power and shifting wireless links. Quality image generation at the edge is thus a resource puzzle. The authors answer with incentives.

Their framework blends contract-inspired contest theory with deep reinforcement learning. Edge devices compete to send high-quality semantic data. Contracts reward efficient, faithful transmission. The learning layer adapts choices as network conditions change. Resource allocation and data quality are handled together. Immersive worlds could draw on nearby devices without draining them. The scheme fits mobile edge computing more broadly.
arxiv-2501-09991: Donald Stanley and Masahiro Takeda wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on an old question posed by Steenrod: which rings can be the cohomology ring of a space? The team defines a ring-side version of a known task, coloring the vertices of a graph so no linked pair shares a color. Their new form is a span coloring, set for Stanley-Reisner rings. These rings are built from a graph by a known rule: a plain polynomial ring divided by a set of square-free terms.
arxiv-2501-10391:
Tytti Rintamäki and Harshvardhan Pandit build a machine-readable form for a new EU rights check, in work published in 2024. The EU AI Act asks groups that deploy AI to weigh risks to health, safety, and basic rights. That check is called a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment. The law also calls for a form and an auto tool to aid the task.

Their ontology spells out the check's parts in web-standard code. It builds on a known privacy vocabulary used for data checks under GDPR. The form lets teams create and run the check with software help, and lets more compliance tools grow on top.
arxiv-2501-12391:
Ziming Liu and co-authors ask, in a 2025 paper, whether the way neural networks pick up skills can be studied the way physicists study matter. They start from an observation they call the Domino effect: skills are learned one after another, and finishing one skill often triggers the start of the next, like falling dominoes. To explain it, they build three toy models of rising realism.

The Geometry model reproduces the domino pattern and yields fresh readings of scaling laws and optimizers; a famous set of scaling rules falls out of it. The Resource model reframes the picture in terms of shared capacity and illuminates tasks built from parts. The Domino model strips the idea to its bones and shows why modular designs help. The toys are not just theory: changes they suggested sped up real training runs.
arxiv-2501-12691:
Uzi Harush, Ravid Straussman, and Baruch Barzel wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It warns that judging a treatment by how a mixed cell population reacts at first can mislead, since cells in a tumor or infection do not all act alike.

The usual plan watches the early response and stretches it forward, as if all cells were the same. Fresh tests show cancer cell groups are in fact mixed, which breaks that plan. The authors build a stochastic frame to forecast the full course of a mixed group. Often the average cell traits that rule the early phase fail to foretell the end. Spread in the group, by contrast, marks the stats that do foretell it, and the odds and time scale of remission.
arxiv-2501-13491:
Munachiso Nwadike and Zangir Iklassov lead a team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, whose byline lists a slightly shifted author set. It names a trick, the self-referencing causal cycle, by which language models can beat the so-called reversal curse.

Models learn facts in one token order, so they often fail to give the line that comes before a known line. The authors find loops in the training text, which they call cycle tokens, that link far parts of a text. Those loops let a model reach back to what came before. With a firm probability frame and set tests, they show how the cycles steer what a model can recall. Code and full test notes are shared.
arxiv-2501-14891:
Muhammad Muzammil and Viqar Husain study a chaotic early-universe model with quantum matter in a 2025 paper. The Mixmaster universe bounces between shapes as it evolves, a classic example of chaos in cosmology. The authors couple it to a massive scalar field and treat parts of the system quantum mechanically.

They compare three setups: classical space with quantum field, and corrected discrete space with classical or quantum field. In the corrected versions, the universe bounces several times before expanding, and field excitations grow through each bounce. Anisotropy rises and falls around the bounces. Chaos measures show the quantum-corrected systems are less chaotic than the classical one, hinting discreteness tames early-universe chaos.
arxiv-2501-15891:
Hailong Guo and five co-authors present Any2AnyTryon, a virtual try-on system that follows text instructions instead of rigid inputs. Shoppers want to see a garment on a model, a model wearing a different garment, and other combinations. Paired training data are scarce, and most systems handle only one fixed task, often needing masks or poses.

The team first built LAION-Garment, described as the largest open garment try-on dataset. Their model adds adaptive position embeddings so inputs of varied sizes and categories can be handled in one framework. That design supports mask-free generation with better control. The authors aim at a single tool for the many directions try-on requests take.
arxiv-2501-16291:
Abhishek Ninad Kulkarni, Jie Fu, and Ufuk Topcu study how an AI system should act when it faces a foe and its likes are not fully ranked. In step-by-step clashes, the world is random. Some results are left unranked. Safe systems still need plans that fit the likes that are stated.

The team models two-player stochastic games on graphs. Goals are stated in linear temporal logic over finite traces. That form lets goals overlap and leaves some pairs unranked, which fits how human likes work. They bring in an idea called non-dominated almost-sure winning. It aims at a most liked result while staying robust against the foe. Plans built on it turn out to be Nash equilibria when players are risk-averse. A drone delivery case shows the frame in use.
arxiv-2501-17191:
Miao Li and co-authors made review summarization inspectable by breaking it into checked steps organized around aspects, the features reviewers praise or pan, such as cleanliness in hotel reviews. Their system first finds the aspects in a pile of reviews, then consolidates opinions for each one, then writes the final summary. Each stage produces outputs a human can audit, unlike a single black-box pass.

Across scientific, business, and product review sets, the summaries stayed closer to what reviewers actually said than strong baselines, in both automated scores and human judgment. The aspect-based middle steps also carried more useful information than rival decompositions. Tests showed the intermediate outputs genuinely help people summarize large review volumes themselves.
arxiv-2501-17891:
Vittorio Lippi presents statistical tools for posture control experiments in a paper from two thousand twenty-five, written alone. Such experiments summarize body sway with a frequency response function, a set of values across frequencies. Researchers may want to know how likely a new result is to come from a known group.

Lippi sums up a recent method that builds confidence bands for these functions by resampling. On that base, he proposes ways to score the likelihood that a single result belongs to a given set. He also gives a test for comparing two groups of unpaired samples. The tools could help diagnose conditions or judge how human-like a robot or wearable device moves.
arxiv-2501-17991:
Laurie Boveroux, Damien Ernst, and Quentin Louveaux wrote a research paper in two thousand twenty-five on scheduling work in factories. The problem asks how to order jobs on machines so the weighted sum of finish times stays low. The authors test Monte Carlo Tree Search, a search method linked to learning from trial and reward.

Inside, they set up several ways to frame the task for the method, including cases where jobs loop back to machines. They also build a new test set from real factory data, with large shapes that are not simple grids. Tests show the method gave good plans for large cases and beat their constraint programming approach.
arxiv-2501-18191:
Abubeker Abdurahman, Abrar Hossain, Kevin Brown, Kazutomo Yoshii, and Kishwar Ahmed add job scheduling tools to a large simulation toolkit, in a paper from 2025. Supercomputers must queue thousands of jobs and hand out machines with care. Bad scheduling wastes costly hardware and makes users wait. Their toolkit mimics such systems cycle by cycle, in parallel.

The new part packs modern scheduling methods and resource rules. It also models workflows where tasks depend on each other and claim resources in chains. Checks show the simulator matches real systems on wait times and machine use. It also scales well when split across many processors. Labs can use it to test a scheduling idea before touching a real machine. That saves both time and risk in system design.
arxiv-2502-00091: Arthur and Kemp propose a LiDAR method for positioning spacecraft above the atmosphere in twenty twenty-five. Their system has a transmitter and a receiver, both based on the craft itself. It uses intensity modulated direct detection. A constellation of orbital reflectors returns the signals. The paper discusses how precise the method can be and how much power it needs. It also weighs the method against GPS and other navigation satellite systems now in use. It ends by setting out where such a method could be put to work.
arxiv-2502-00191:
Armando Castañeda and Gilde Valeria Rodríguez wrote this theory paper in 2025 on checking software that runs across many machines. Runtime checks watch a running system and flag breaks from a set rule. That is easy on one machine, but hard when no single watcher sees the whole run, messages lag, and some machines fail.

The authors set up a shared frame for this task. Each watcher holds just a slice of the record of events and must judge the whole. They give several grades of what it could mean to judge rightly, show how the grades relate, and prove what can and cannot be done. A key result: only rules that do not hinge on the true order of events can be judged in such a loose net. They then give a weaker setup where some time-based rules can still be checked in a forward-looking way.
arxiv-2502-00791:
Ling Xing and co-authors present Vist, a method that shrinks the text fed into large language models without losing accuracy. Their paper appeared in 2025. Long prompts cost heavy computing time and memory. Vist mimics human reading with two paths. A fast path turns distant parts of the prompt into images, which a small vision model skims. A slow path gives the nearby text to the main model in full.

A special training goal teaches the skimming part to focus on rich content and skip filler words. On eleven tests of learning from context, Vist matched full-text accuracy with 2.3 times fewer tokens. It also cut computing work by 16 percent and memory by half. The authors report it beat the strongest rival compressor by a clear margin.
arxiv-2502-00891:
David Kalaj proves an isoperimetric result in complex geometry in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. The isoperimetric question asks how the volume of a region relates to the size of its boundary. Here the setting is the Bergman ball, a unit ball in complex space with its own Bergman geometry.

Kalaj looks at nearly spherical domains, sets that sit close to a ball in shape. He proves a quantitative form of the inequality for them: the gap in the inequality is controlled by how far the set strays from a true ball. He also proves a Fuglede-type theorem for these sets. The paper is the first on this phenomenon in the Bergman ball, matching a known result for the hyperbolic ball.
arxiv-2502-01991:
Tunazzina Islam and Dan Goldwasser test whether language models can help people label moral framing in social media posts in a 2025 paper. In vaccination debates, moral viewpoints shape opinions, but spotting morality frames by hand is slow, costly, and inconsistent because the task is mentally heavy.

Their process has two steps: the model first generates concepts and explanations, then human annotators evaluate them using a think aloud tool. With model help, annotators became more accurate, found the task easier, and felt less cognitive load. The authors present the result as evidence that pairing humans with language models can improve complex labeling work where meaning depends on psychology and language together.
arxiv-2502-03191:
Vasellini and four co-authors use computer agents to test how an old African polity held together, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The Aksum polity is often seen as ruled from the top by strong kings. New digs hint its early leaders may have been ritual heads, not rulers with force. The team tests if joint work can thrive with no forced rule.

They build agents that play a shared-goods game based on Aksum data. Joint work did emerge with no forced rule, at least at first. Over long spans, it faded without a central power to hold it. The result hints that shared norms can start a complex society. Lasting growth, though, may need some central rule to stay stable.
arxiv-2502-04491:
Ziheng Cheng, Tianyu Xie, Shiyue Zhang, and Cheng Zhang give transfer learning for diffusion models a theoretical footing in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models generate impressive content but need huge data to train from scratch, which many tasks lack. Borrowing from related tasks helps in practice, yet nobody had proved why for conditional diffusion models.

The authors assume all tasks share a low dimensional representation of their conditions, echoing real training recipes. They show that a good representation learned from source tasks cuts the data the target task needs by a lot. Real world application checks and numerical experiments support the math. The paper is a first step toward principled data saving for generative models.
arxiv-2502-07291:
Fanhui Meng and nine colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on how information spreads through online social networks. Social media can carry a message to millions within hours, but researchers have disagreed about the mechanism behind the spread. Human behavior and the sheer variety of messages make the pattern hard to pin down.

The team analyzed data from WeChat, Weibo, and Twitter, covering 7.45 billion users in total. They found one mechanism everywhere: spreading is driven by social reinforcement, where repeated exposure encourages sharing, working against social weakening, where interest fades. They build a model on this interplay. A shared mechanism could help predict which messages will take off and which will die out.
arxiv-2502-09091:
Uniqueness theorems say exactly when two number-theory functions must be the same function. Jun Wang, Qiongyan Wang and Xiao Yao study functions in the extended Selberg class, a broad family that includes many prized examples. Instead of comparing the functions at fixed target values, they subtract a moving target: a flexible third function that itself varies. They ask when the two shifted functions having the same zeros forces them to be identical.

Under a stated limit on how fast the moving target may grow, they prove the two functions must indeed coincide, zeros counted with multiplicity. They also build examples showing the growth limit cannot simply be dropped. Their proof uses a fresh strategy borrowed from complex dynamics, based on special directions first used to study Julia sets. The authors suggest the method may serve other problems in value-distribution theory.
arxiv-2502-09191:
Yuto Ohki and Masahito Mochizuki write, in a 2025 article, a systematic theory of how electric currents push magnetic skyrmions around. Skyrmions are nanoscale whirlpools of magnetization, stable enough to be candidate bits for future memory. Currents move them, but the motion splinters into many behaviors depending on the skyrmion's type, the drive mechanism, the device shape, and the magnet itself. That variety has made the field rich and confusing at once.

Using the Thiele equation, the compact law of skyrmion motion, the authors work through the grid of cases. Swirl handedness and type, thin plates against narrow tracks, current along or across, both spin torques, ferro- against antiferromagnets: each gets its chart. Simulations confirm the analysis case by case, with direction and speed charted for each. The article aims to be the reference a device designer consults before choosing a geometry.
arxiv-2502-09591:
Chuanhui Liu and Xiao Wang rethink variational inference for survival analysis in a two thousand twenty-five statistics paper. Survival models predict time-to-event curves, and censored cases, where the event has not yet come, are the norm.

The authors show a subtle flaw: a badly built variational distribution can undo the whole analysis. The best variational distribution, oddly,, the one that bounds the log-likelihood perfectly, can depend on how censoring itself works. Their fix, censor-dependent variational inference, builds that link in. A variational autoencoder version, CD-CVAE, makes it scalable, and tests show greatly better estimates of each person's survival curves.
arxiv-2502-10591:
Jake Postiglione and four co-authors model what happens when a supermassive black hole bends the gravitational waves of a smaller binary orbiting nearby. Such binaries are expected to form and merge inside active galactic nuclei, deep in the giant's gravity well. The future space detector LISA would hear their low-frequency signal.

For a GW150914-like binary near a hundred-million-solar-mass black hole, the lensed signal drifts in and out of LISA's detectable band in a predictable pattern. Unmodeled, these signatures could confuse global fits of the LISA data stream. If recognized, they offer independent measures of the galaxy's tilt, inner disk warping, and the giant black hole's spin.
arxiv-2502-12191:
Ruoxuan Feng and co-authors presented AnyTouch in 2025, a way to teach robots touch across many sensor kinds. Camera-based touch sensors mimic human skin, but each brand speaks its own data dialect, which blocks a shared touch brain. The team first built TacQuad, a data set that lines up readings from four sensor types on the same touches.

AnyTouch then learns one code for touch from both still frames and moving clips. Fine detail comes from masked modeling at the pixel level. Broader meaning comes from lining touch up with other senses and matching across sensors. The shared code beat prior methods on touch tests and passed skills from one sensor to another. A real pouring task checked the system on a live robot.
arxiv-2502-12491:
Fuyuki Kitagawa, Ryo Nishimaki, and Nikhil Pappu develop encryption schemes whose leased keys stay secure even against collusion. Secure key leasing lets a holder lend a quantum decryption key that stops working once returned or certified deleted. Earlier work assumed an adversary receives at most one such key, which poorly matches real use.

The authors define collusion-resistant security, where an adversary can adaptively obtain many leased keys and query a verification oracle. Public key and ciphertext sizes must not grow with the number of keys. They construct a public key scheme from the learning with errors assumption. They also give attribute-based variants, one using classical deletion certificates.
arxiv-2502-12691:
Timon Winter, Stanislav Frolov, Brian Bernhard Moser, and Andreas Dengel work on making panoramas from text in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Text-to-image models have weak grip on layout and on panoramas, which need spherical distortion and edges that join with no seam. Dense methods grip layouts well and spherical methods grip panoramas, but no one had joined the two. A plain prompt to a model for a panorama gives broken shapes.

The team joins training-free dense methods with fine-tuned panorama models in systems, MultiStitchDiffusion and MultiPanFusion. No benchmark had been there for the joined task. So they built Dense-Synthetic-View, a data set with layouts. MultiStitchDiffusion won on image quality. It won on prompt and layout grip. MultiPanFusion made more varied images but flawed foreground objects. The paper puts forth fixes: bootstrap coupling, and turning off one attention route in the foreground.
arxiv-2502-14191:
Michihiro Yasunaga, Luke Zettlemoyer, and Marjan Ghazvininejad released a benchmark in twenty twenty-five for judging reward models of image-aware AI. Reward models grade AI answers and steer training toward answers people prefer. For models that see images as well as text, no broad public test of these graders existed.

Their Multimodal RewardBench holds over five thousand expert-checked items. Each item gives a prompt, a chosen answer, and a rejected one, across six areas from plain correctness to safety. Even the best judges, two top commercial models, reached only seventy-two percent accuracy. Most judges did worst on reasoning and safety items. The authors share the data openly as a hard test for improving reward models.
arxiv-2502-14591:
Ziqin He and co-authors design control methods that learn from data for systems whose state is a tensor. Their 2025 paper deals with multi-linear systems, where the state needs more than a flat table of numbers. Data-driven control can shape a strategy without first naming the system's rules.

Existing data-driven tools were built for standard linear systems, not this tensor kind. The authors give a framework where system change is set by a product between two third-order tensors. They state firm conditions for when data is enough to identify the system, steady it with feedback, and tune it well. Worked examples test the framework. The paper extends a popular control style to a richer class of systems used in signal and image work.
arxiv-2502-14891:
Zhe Huang, Shuo Wang, Yongcai Wang, and Lei Wang present CoDiff, in a 2025 preprint, a system that lets self-driving cars see together without being fooled by noise. Cars that share sensor findings spot more than one car alone. In practice, position errors and delays smear the shared features, and detection suffers. Diffusion models are natural cleaners of noisy data. The authors use one to realign the fused features from several cars. The work is, they say, the first to bring diffusion models to joint perception.

Features are first compressed into the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder. Each car's data then guides a diffusion sampling that scrubs the shared map. Step by step, the fused features grow clearer and fuller. On simulated and real road data, CoDiff beat prior methods. It held up especially well when position and timing noise ran high.
arxiv-2502-18891:
Ziyuan Zhong and Junyang Zhou propose a dynamic classification method that aims for zero missed cases with few false alarms. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets safety-critical fields like medical diagnosis. A missed case there can be grave. Their method first splits the data by a self-supervised grouping that learns the data's own shape.

Each split zone holds train and test parts with near-matching borders. One model type then serves each zone, working on a narrow range. Border rules refine the outputs and drop weak calls, with no extra model needed. Tests show no missed detections and slight false alarm counts when split errors stay small. Top ensemble rivals were beaten in those runs. With larger split errors, scores stayed on par with leading models. Tuning and speed remain open work.
arxiv-2502-19991:
Leimin Tian, Shiyu Xu, Kerry He, Rachel Love, Akansel Cosgun, and Dana Kulić teach a robot to hand objects to a person the way people do. Handovers pepper collaborative work, from restaurants to assembly lines. Safe, efficient transfers need the robot to read human context, not just positions. The team collected teleoperation data in a naturalistic crafting task.

A model trained on that human-guided data then ran the handovers itself. Cross-validation on the data set came first. A user study in the same crafting task followed, comparing autonomous and teleoperated episodes. Users' perceptions were measured alongside task success. The autonomous policy achieved genuinely collaborative handovers. Yet the comparison with human control exposed clear avenues for improvement. The paper maps both the competence reached and the social polish still missing.
arxiv-2502-20891:
Hong-Hao Ma, Zheng-Kui Tao, and Juan-Juan Niu compute how often exotic four-charm particles could be born indirectly at colliders, in a 2025 paper. The fully charmed tetraquark is a rare beast of four heavy quarks. Their route is indirect: a Higgs, W, or Z boson decays to a charm quark, which then fragments into the tetraquark. Two calculation frameworks, a standard factorization and the Suzuki approach, were run side by side.

Despite different assumptions about sideways momentum, the two methods agreed. The W decay channel at the LHC looks most generous. A future circular collider running on Z decays should make enough events to detect. The authors also chart how the charm quark's mass and energy share shift the predictions.
arxiv-2503-00391:
Ruiwu Liu builds macroeconomic models linking economic development, health investment, and fertility. The working paper treats health as an intermediate good rather than a final consumption item. Households invest in health defensively, and that choice feeds back into population dynamics and growth.

This framing produces non-monotonic effects: better health can raise or lower growth and population depending on the stage of development. The models aim to explain how growth, population, and health interacted during the early stages of human development. Liu presents the suite as a new interpretation of long-run socio-economic patterns, where environmental adversity shapes defensive health spending. The paper is theoretical, developing the model family rather than testing it on data.
arxiv-2503-01991:
Xiangdong Ji and Chen Yang trace how momentum flows inside the nucleon in a 2025 nuclear physics study. A proton or neutron holds together quarks and gluons whose motions and forces must balance so total momentum is conserved. Momentum current density gives a picture of that flow, fed by quark motion and by gluon interactions.

Quark flow turns out to encode the color-Lorentz force pressing on the quarks. Conservation lets the authors trace that force back to the gluon stress and a scalar anomaly term acting like negative pressure. Lattice calculations supply state-of-the-art numbers for the pieces. The picture clarifies how the nucleon's mass and spin budgets fit together.
arxiv-2503-02691:
Barusco and co-authors study step-wise learn for spot-the-flaw sight tools on edge gear. Sight flaw tools flag odd bits in shots for plant and street use. Edge gear has tight chip and store room for such tools. Live data shifts shift too, so tools must keep pace as feeds change. The team tests STFPM, a tool with a small store mark on edge gear. A play-back trick, called Replay, pairs with it in tests.

A fresh tool, PaSTe, gets its first step-wise test in this work. PaSTe proves both leaner and more sharp than its peer. Its pixel score rose 10 percent with Replay switched on. Its shape also suits squeezed play-back tricks in the tests. Those tricks cut store load by up to 91.5 percent.
arxiv-2503-05291:
Fernando Moreno presents a software tool that paints pictures of comet dust tails before comparing them with the sky. A comet's tail brightness encodes the dust it sheds: grain sizes, speeds, and loss rates. Fitting real images by hand is slow and unsure. His code, COMTAILS, runs the physics forward instead.

The tool fires virtual dust grains along paths set by the comet's orbit, drawn from a NASA ephemeris service. A Monte Carlo routine builds the glow that telescopes would see. An optional star field lets users check how the tail dims background stars. Moreno shows the code matching recent images of two bright long-period comets. It also suits active asteroids. The tool stands ready for targets of a planned European comet mission.
arxiv-2503-05991:
Zixuan Liu and a team of co-authors present GrInAdapt, a method to map blood vessels in images of the eye. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with scans of the fundus, the back of the eye, taken by a method called OCTA. Vessel maps help doctors spot eye disease, but models trained in one clinic often fail on scans from other devices or sites.

GrInAdapt works in three steps. It grounds all images in one shared space, merges guesses from many views into agreed labels, and adapts the model to each new domain, with no labeled target data. It can also borrow cues from color photos of the fundus. Tests across devices and sites beat past methods.
arxiv-2503-06991:
Yongwoo Kim, Sungmin Cha, and Donghyun Kim question how machine unlearning is graded, in this 2025 paper. Unlearning should erase chosen data from a trained model while keeping the rest intact, for privacy or legal reasons. Most checks read only the model's output scores on small test sets. The authors warn that such grades can give a false sense of security.

Their wider audit inspects the model's inner representations at large scale. Leading methods either wrecked the representation quality wholesale or merely relabeled outputs while keeping the erased data's imprint inside. They add a tougher test where forgotten classes resemble later task classes, forcing real representational change. The authors offer their protocol as a stricter standard for the field.
arxiv-2503-07891:
Lee and a large team of co-authors introduced an embedding model in this report from twenty twenty-five. Embeddings turn text into numbers that capture meaning for search and ranking. The model draws on Gemini, Google's flagship system, inheriting its feel for many languages and code. One unified model serves classification, similarity, clustering, and retrieval alike.

On a massive multilingual benchmark of over one hundred tasks, it beat all prior models substantially. The lead held across the multilingual, English-only, and code leaderboards. Specialized models built for single domains were also surpassed. The report argues generality no longer costs accuracy. Precomputed vectors can be dropped into downstream systems directly.
arxiv-2503-10191:
Brian Pulfer, Yury Belousov, and Slava Voloshynovskiy harden vision transformers against adversarial attacks by tuning a few secret tokens. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Public foundation models are shared widely, so attackers can craft attacks on the very backbone a defender uses.

Instead of retraining the whole model, their method adds a handful of private tokens and tunes only those. The cost is tiny compared with classic adversarial training. In white-box tests, where the attacker knows the model, robustness rose sharply. Normal task accuracy stayed intact. The trick exploits the transformer design itself: extra tokens steer attention away from attack patterns. The authors pitch it as cheap insurance for anyone building on public models.
arxiv-2503-11591:
Srikar Yellapragada and co-authors squeeze pathology images with borrowed autoencoders in two thousand twenty-five. Whole slide images are huge, straining storage and transfer in digital pathology. Standard squeezing like JPEG saves space but blurs the fine traits that later tasks read.

Their trick: reuse autoencoders built for image generation models as learned squeezers. Three models at varied squeeze levels were rebuilt and scored by pathology foundation models. A fine-tuning step, guided by a pathology-tuned sense of likeness, sharpened the rebuilds. On sorting, segmentation, and case-level tasks, swapped-in reconstructions lost little accuracy. A clustering step shrinks the stored codes further, and the tuned weights are shared in public.
arxiv-2503-12991:
Sam Albin and nine co-authors describe tuning a particle physics analysis facility for a speed challenge in a 2025 paper. The challenge: process two hundred terabytes of collider data in twenty minutes using notebook style analysis. Their facility was set up with over two thousand computing cores for fast turnaround.

The team compared ways to scale work across two job systems and two schedulers, and compared two services for managing analysis clusters. A set of cache servers on fast drives, coordinated by a redirector, kept data local and cut wide area traffic. Token based authentication stayed invisible to users. Network monitoring let them verify the total data rate stack by stack, confirming the facility met the challenge conditions.
arxiv-2503-14991:
Stefan Arnold inspects, in a 2025 preprint, what privacy protection does to the shape of text inside a model's representation space. A common privacy recipe paraphrases text with a language model, adding randomness for safety. How that warps the text's geometry was unstudied. Arnold estimates the intrinsic dimension of the paraphrases' representation manifold at several privacy levels. Word-level methods, he finds, inflate that manifold badly. Sentence-level methods keep its shape much closer to human paraphrases.

Among sentence methods, masked paraphrasing preserves structure best. Causal paraphrasing, which writes left to right, fares worse. Arnold blames a cascade: one unnatural word choice bends the next, and the distortion compounds. The result gives privacy engineers a new gauge to watch. Budgets alone do not tell how much a paraphrase has been bent out of shape. Geometry checks could join standard utility tests.
arxiv-2503-15191:
Kim, Song, Seo, and Kim tune how a finance question tool finds the right pages before it writes its answers, in work from twenty twenty-five. Finance files, like yearly firm reports, use trade words and tables set inside tables. How well the tool finds pages caps how well it can answer. Their chain of steps tunes the hunt before, during, and after the search.

Prep work adds detail to both the asks and the file text before the hunt starts. Tuned embeddings, plus a mixed dense and sparse search, pull in more of the right pages. Preference optimization and a pick of the best files then polish the last set. Seven finance benchmarks show large gains in how well the hunt works. Answers hit the mark more and fit the ask, thanks to the sharper hunt. The full chain is shared on GitHub for others to rerun.
arxiv-2503-15891:
Rui Wang, Yiming Jiao, Xiaowei Zhao, and Chong Huang wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about heating the Sun's outer air, called the corona. The corona is far hotter than the surface below it, and why is still an open puzzle. Energy for the heating is thought to come from churning motions under the surface.

The team combined views from two space missions, Solar Orbiter and SDO, with a method that extends surface magnetic fields upward. They estimated the stored magnetic energy of release events at many sizes in the quiet Sun. That energy tracked closely with bright emission from hot gas. The authors check whether such events could supply a useful share of the heat.
arxiv-2503-16091:
Abdullah Mamun, Diane Cook, and Hassan Ghasemzadeh built a forecaster for missed medication in a 2025 paper. People with chronic disease who skip doses face costly harm, and timely nudges could help if risk were known in advance. Phones and wearables now make such forecasting practical.

Their system, AIMI, combines phone sensor data with each person's medication history to estimate the chance of forgetting a dose. In a study with 27 heart patients, their best network reached about 93 percent accuracy. Tests stripping parts away showed that two ingredients matter: using what is known about the future schedule, and training tuned to the person. The authors release the code for others to build on.
arxiv-2503-17091:
Marcin Markiewicz and Konrad Schlichtholz widen a tool from quantum theory, in work from 2025. Unitary designs let a small finite set stand in for endless spins of a quantum state. The pair asks whether like finite sets can average states over far broader classes of change, drawn from Lie groups.

They build such sets for any reductive group, as long as the average runs evenly over the compact part. Their sets mix small unitary designs that act on set subspaces. The sets rival known builds in size and can run well on quantum circuits. The work broadens a core trick used to tame quantum noise and tests.
arxiv-2503-17191:
Chris Purdy and Stefania Damato settle in 2025 when two composable data types can be combined into one. In their setting, a container describes a data type by its shapes and positions. Some containers carry a monad structure, a standard pattern for sequencing computations, but two such containers usually refuse to compose.

A distributive law is the extra rule that lets two monads merge. The authors characterize exactly which laws exist between monadic containers. They also handle the mixed cases with the dual, comonad side, completing a small zoo of characterizations. Most of the theory was proven inside the Cubical Agda proof assistant, so the results are machine-checked.
arxiv-2503-17491:
Emanuele Giacomini, Luca Di Giammarino, Lorenzo De Rebotti, Giorgio Grisetti, and Martin Oswald build LiDAR odometry and mapping purely from Gaussian primitives. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents Splat-LOAM. LiDAR gives exact geometry, but light, sharp maps of a scene stay hard to keep. Classic and NeRF-style maps trade accuracy against memory and time. Their pipeline keeps the scene as Gaussians alone.

Spherical projection steers how the primitives refine, driven only by LiDAR returns. No camera data enters the loop. Motion tracking matches current registration scores in their tests. Mapping quality hits the top tier while GPU needs stay minimal. That thrift suits live robots with small computers. The authors offer the method as a base for real-time estimation stacks.
arxiv-2503-17691:
Murray Stokely, Jim Winget, Ed Keyes, Carrie Grimes, and Benjamin Yolken describe a market system for sharing computing power in a 2025 study. Large organizations run clusters of machines on several continents, and teams compete for capacity. Instead of handing out fixed shares, the authors let users bid for long-term resource bundles.

A simulated clock auction turns bids into uniform prices that balance supply and demand. Reserve prices follow current use, nudging users toward idle resources. Auctions repeat at set intervals, so prices move like those in a real economy. Because the system handles provisioning, users can adjust long-term plans as prices change.
arxiv-2503-17991:
Valentina Beorchia and Rosa Miró-Roig prove the weak Lefschetz property for equigenerated Artinian complete intersections across a stated degree range. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works with ideals built from equal-degree forms in polynomial rings. The property asks that multiplication by a general linear form have full rank between graded pieces. The bound they reach ties the safe degrees to the form degree and the number of variables.

One consequence settles a live question. The Jacobian ideal of a smooth threefold of degree at least seven in four-dimensional projective space satisfies the property in the critical degree, answering Beauville. Lefschetz properties govern how algebra mirrors geometry, so range results like this one get used widely.
arxiv-2503-18791:
Rupali Chandar and colleagues present the PHANGS-HST-Halpha survey, Hubble Space Telescope imaging of warm ionized gas in nearby galaxies. The PHANGS project is assembling a comprehensive multi-wavelength dataset of nearby massive star-forming galaxies to investigate star formation across scales. Companion programs have supplied molecular gas maps from ALMA, optical spectroscopy from the Very Large Telescope, broad-band Hubble imaging, and infrared imaging from the James Webb Space Telescope.

The new component adds high-resolution narrow-band imaging, at scales of a few parsecs, in hydrogen-alpha filters with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. It covers the warm ionized gas in the first nineteen galaxies observed in common by all four PHANGS programs. Combined with the molecular, stellar, and infrared views of the same galaxies, these maps let astronomers follow the full cycle from cold gas to stars to feedback in matched detail.
arxiv-2503-19091:
Yuchen Fang, Javad Lavaei, and Sen Na bound the work a stochastic optimizer needs when its noise has heavy tails. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies problems with a random goal and fixed equality rules. Their method wraps sequential quadratic programming in a trust region. True values, slopes, and curves are not at hand; noisy oracles stand in.

Past studies assumed tame, light-tailed noise and first-order targets. This work allows biased, heavy-tailed noise in the value oracle. It also reaches second-order targets, points that pass a curvature test too. Rates match the light-tailed case for first-order points. Second-order points cost more steps, as theory expects. A floor on the target gap is set by the bias size. Tests on the CUTEst set check the method in practice.
arxiv-2503-20491:
Jiale Cheng and a large team optimize the prompts fed to text-to-video generators, judging the rewrite by the video it produces. Generators are trained on polished, detailed descriptions, but users type terse, vague requests. Off-the-shelf prompt polishers can distort intent, drop details, or add risks. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's framework follows three principles: harmlessness, accuracy, and helpfulness. First they build and refine a supervised data set embodying those principles. Then preference learning adds two feedback channels, one on the rewritten text and one on the generated video itself.

Experiments showed clear gains in safety, alignment with intent, and video quality over baseline polishers. Closing the loop at the video level is the distinctive step. The prompt is treated as a control knob for the final artifact, not as prose to prettify.
arxiv-2503-22391:
Md Fazle Rabbi, Rajshakhar Paul, Arifa Islam Champa, and Minhaz Zibran dissect security flaws in the Maven ecosystem, the library hub behind much Java software. Reused components carry risk when flaws linger, so the team ran a large-scale analysis of vulnerability types, documentation delays, and fix timelines.

They counted over seventy-seven thousand vulnerable releases tied to two hundred twenty-six weakness types. On average, a flaw waited nearly five years just to be documented, and four point four years to be resolved; some stayed open past a decade. The authors warn that these delays leave library users exposed and call for faster, more careful vulnerability handling across the ecosystem.
arxiv-2503-22791:
Erin Kara and Javier Garcia review what X-rays reveal about supermassive black holes in a 2025 astronomy survey. X-rays come from the inner accretion flow, the last stretch before gas crosses the event horizon, where energy release drives black hole growth. That same region launches the outflows and jets that shape whole galaxies.

The review covers steady accretion in active galactic nuclei and violent transients such as stars torn apart by tides. Changing-look events, where a galaxy's core transforms, also feature. By gathering the X-ray view in one place, the authors show how the smallest scales govern the largest feedback loops in galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2503-24291:
Sergio Barrera Cabodevila, Xiaojian Du, Carlos Salgado, and Bin Wu ask whether making quarks changes how the fireball of a heavy-ion collision settles into thermal equilibrium. Their paper came out in 2025. In the standard picture, a pure glue system thermalizes in three stages, called bottom-up, before quarks fully join in.

Their calculation extends the classic estimates to include quark production from the start. The three-stage picture survives unchanged in character, and they derive how the quark population grows at each stage. Numerical solutions of the transport equation approach the predicted picture as the coupling weakens. A second, fuller quantum chromodynamics simulation agreed remarkably well at middling coupling. Quarks, they conclude, ride along with the glue's schedule rather than rewriting it.
arxiv-2504-01891:
Sedykh and co-authors present a hybrid quantum-classical network in two thousand twenty-five for solving fluid flow equations. The Navier-Stokes equations govern fluids, but classic solvers and physics-informed networks both miss parts of the frequency range in a solution. Accuracy and speed suffer together.

Their design splits the solution by frequency, giving each band its own parallel hybrid network that mixes quantum and classical layers. Training simplifies because each stream handles a narrower job. On the classic Kovasznay flow problem, the hybrid beat a matching classical network. Velocity error fell by about thirty-six percent and pressure error by about forty-one percent, with roughly a quarter fewer parameters. Tests covered both data-driven and physics-driven training.
arxiv-2504-02491:
Maximilian Mahlein and six co-authors present a fuller model of how light nuclei form when particles fly out of a high-energy collision. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Three loose particles can stick into one nucleus, like those of helium's light form. Getting that sticking right matters for nuclear physics and for the hunt for rare antimatter in space.

Their model, ToMCCA-3, tracks the three-body dance with realistic force laws. Those laws are pinned by scattering data and by close-pair measures from real collisions. They fed the model with simulated proton collisions at top collider energy. The predicted spectra for light nuclei and their antimatter twins were checked against ALICE data. The yields proved sensitive to the chosen wave patterns. The work sets up wider studies across collision types.
arxiv-2504-03891:
Angela Cratere led a team putting neural networks on small satellites in a 2025 paper. Their task is spotting clouds in Earth images aboard CubeSats, where computing power is tight. Four network models were sped up on a programmable chip using a vendor AI framework. Two models judge single pixels or patches, and two judge whole images.

Trimming channels cut model size and math sharply with minimal accuracy loss. Shrinking numbers to eight-bit form kept accuracy nearly intact on the chip. The two whole-image models ran in real time at low power, beating prior onboard cloud detectors. The authors see chip accelerators widening what small satellites can do.
arxiv-2504-07191:
Barbosa, Santos, Zamperlini, and da Silva study a quantum particle moving in a space-time scarred by two topological defects at once, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The defects are a cosmic string, which cuts a wedge out of space, and a global monopole, which removes a solid angle around a point.

Using a metric that combines both defects, they solve the Klein-Gordon equation by separating variables. They then place the scalar particle in external potentials, focusing on the Cornell potential, which mixes a Coulomb-like pull with a linearly growing term. A side-by-side comparison with the pure Coulomb case isolates what the linear term changes. The defects deform the radial wave equation, shifting bound-state energies and scattering phase shifts. The work deepens the theory of spin-zero particles in curved, defect-ridden geometries.
arxiv-2504-08691:
Laura Borgongino and co-authors make a superconducting diode with a two-tone drive instead of exotic matter or magnets, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such diodes pass supercurrent one way, a prize for cold computing. Past builds leaned on rare traits that block scale-up.

The mixed-tone signal breaks time and space balance inside a plain junction. A wireless antenna flips the diode's pole and strength from afar. Peak yield hit the ideal full mark across a wide tone range. The effect held to near one degree above zero on the Kelvin scale's low end. Rectified signals came out clean. Readers get a platform-free diode for future cold logic.
arxiv-2504-10491:
Berthier, Prencipe, and Provenzi rebuild in twenty twenty-five the basic terms of colour perception on a quantum-like frame. Everyday terms such as brightness, lightness, and hue rest on informal definitions. Standard colour models describe light well, but they leave how people judge colour on shaky ground, the authors argue.

Their frame borrows tools from quantum information, such as states, effects, and a measure of how alike two states are. With those tools they give strict definitions for six colour traits, from brightness to hue. As a test, they derive a known effect where a surface keeps its judged lightness under changed lighting. The work aims to put colour science on firmer math.
arxiv-2504-11391:
Stefan Dittmaier, Tim Engel, José Luis Hernando Ariza, and Mathieu Pellen sharpen the theory behind a planned measurement of the tau lepton's magnetic moment, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The tau's moment is poorly known compared with those of its lighter cousins, the electron and the muon.

A promising route uses grazing collisions of lead ions at the LHC, where the ions miss each other but their light fields create tau pairs. The authors give a state-of-the-art prediction for that production, including the decays of the taus themselves. They weigh how spin links between the two taus change the outcome. They also assess the effect of the final leptons' masses, of next-order electroweak corrections, and of how the photon flow from each ion is modeled. The result is a firmer yardstick for future measurements.
arxiv-2504-11791:
Hammad and Jueid reviewed progress in twenty twenty-five on measuring the top-Higgs coupling at the Large Hadron Collider. The coupling describes how the top quark interacts with the Higgs boson. A precise measure could reveal new physics, especially CP violation, an imbalance between matter and antimatter behavior.

That imbalance is a key ingredient in explaining why the universe holds more matter than antimatter. The review surveys recent studies and the machine learning tools they use to bound the coupling's CP phase. It highlights newer methods beyond the traditional ones, including transformers and heterogeneous graphs, which mix different node types. The authors weigh the future promise of these tools for sharper measurements at the collider.
arxiv-2504-11891:
Muhammad Rehman and Sven Heinemeyer refine predictions for Higgs boson masses in a supersymmetric model, in a 2025 paper. Supersymmetry partners every known particle with a heavier twin, and its minimal version can be stretched with extra symmetry-breaking terms that ignore the usual holomorphic rules. Two such terms are their focus.

One term reshapes the bottom quark's partner masses and Higgs couplings; the other shifts the masses of the charged and neutral partner particles. Parts of the parameter space fall to a consistency check forbidding charge- and color-breaking ground states. In what survives, the extra terms lift the light Higgs mass by up to about one and a half giga-electronvolts, and the heavy Higgs masses by over forty in favorable corners. Precision matters because the measured Higgs mass is a strict test of such models.
arxiv-2504-12491:
Hansi Zeng and co-authors ask whether signs seen during the first training of a language model can predict how well it will do after fine-tuning, in a paper from 2025. A common sign, called perplexity, tracks how surprised a model is by text. It works well in studies of model size, but its value at a fixed size was unclear.

The team built fifty variants of a billion-parameter model, each trained with different settings or data. All were then fine-tuned and tested on a range of tasks. The task was framed as picking which of two models would do better. Perplexity proved to be a poor guide. New signs drawn from the training stage cut the error rate of such picks by more than half. The authors show the signs help in real model choices.
arxiv-2504-14391:
Rahul Thapa and ten co-authors ask whether videos can teach AI medicine in twenty twenty-five. Public biomedical videos on platforms like YouTube are made for human students. They mix medical imagery with narration, diagrams, and context. That pedagogical richness makes them messy by machine learning standards.

The team built a video instruction data set of over a thousand hours. Video-caption and question-answer pairs were curated through a multi-step pipeline with humans in the loop. Diverse biomedical video data is rare, so the set fills a real gap. General vision-language models were then tuned on it and tested for biomedical knowledge. Readers learn how far teaching material made for people can carry a model toward medical competence.
arxiv-2504-14691:
D. Bazeia and colleagues studied a toy ecosystem in 2025 where three species chase each other in a circle, like rock-paper-scissors. In the spatial May-Leonard version of this game, species invade each other's territory and form moving patterns of clusters and spirals. The authors asked how mobility, the rate at which individuals move, controls the scale-free features of those patterns.

They measured several quantities that follow power laws, including the number of clusters, a characteristic pattern length, individual lifespans, and how far individuals travel in a lifetime. Mobility turned out to organize all of them, giving researchers a single dial that tunes the model's statistics. Such measures matter beyond the toy model, because real ecosystems also show patchiness and long-tailed distributions. Quantifying how movement shapes them speaks to biodiversity theory and conservation alike.
arxiv-2504-14891:
Aoran Gan and co-authors published a 2025 survey on how to judge systems that answer questions using retrieved documents. Such systems, called RAG, pair a language model with a search step over outside sources. The mix promises answers that are current and checkable. Judging them is hard, because both the searching and the writing can fail, and the sources keep changing.

The survey gathers the ways researchers measure these systems. It covers checks of raw performance, factual accuracy, safety, and computing cost. It also catalogues the test datasets and scoring frameworks built just for this purpose. A review of highly cited studies shows how evaluation is actually done in practice. The authors claim the survey is the most complete of its kind. It bridges older judging methods and new ones built for the language model era. Newcomers and veterans alike can use it to pick sound tests.
arxiv-2504-15791:
Raquel Fernandez-Peralta, Javier Fumanal-Idocin, and Javier Andreu-Perez turn fuzzy classifiers into crisp ones in two thousand twenty-five. Rule based systems are a prized form of explainable AI. Fuzzy rules serve control and classification well inside their own field. Outside it, fuzzy splits of the feature space can be hard to read.

Their method reduces a fuzzy rule base to a crisp rule base. They weigh distinct crisp forms and give an algorithm to build them. They also gauge the complexity of the crisp result. That gauge can help users pick among fuzzy models. The work builds a two way bridge between the camps.
arxiv-2504-18591:
Giovanni Catalani and four co-authors present a neural field method that predicts steady physics fields while respecting the shape of the part studied. Fast stand in models for physics equations are in demand, but many handle odd shapes poorly. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The method, called enf2enf, stores shape traits at set points in space, so local detail stays in place through the network. Local traits merge with global settings, then decode into smooth fields that can be read at any point. Tests on air flow and strength benchmarks matched or beat graph based and operator based rivals. It also runs in real time and scales to fine meshes.
arxiv-2504-20191:
Daniel Bäumer and Rupert Klein merge two atmospheric models into one boundary layer theory. Their twenty twenty-five paper joins a precipitating flow model with a three-layer boundary scheme. Most reduced weather models long ignored moisture and phase changes. Recent work finally added rain physics to simplified flow models.

The new theory keeps an added middle layer where heating occurs. Detailed treatment covers how water vapour saturates and condenses. Simple bulk rain closures enter the derivation step by step. The authors solve a symmetric special case exactly. Numerical examples then show how the bulk flow behaves. Weather modellers gain a cleaner theory for moist air near the ground.
arxiv-2504-21091:
Rongmon Bordoloi, Andrew Fox, and Felix Lockman find cold gas clouds riding the Milky Way's nuclear wind far above the disk. Eleven high-velocity hydrogen clouds sit at latitudes of twenty-five to thirty degrees, inside the northern Fermi Bubble. Deep twenty-one centimeter observations with the Green Bank Telescope reached more than twice the sensitivity of earlier bubble surveys. The clouds race toward us at ninety to one hundred eighty kilometers per second.

Eight are spatially resolved, spanning four to twenty-eight parsecs, with masses up to about fifteen hundred suns. Several show internal velocity gradients, coherent structures rather than static blobs. Their survival so high is puzzling: clouds expelled from the galactic center should shred quickly in the hot wind. The authors suggest these are fragments of a larger cloud torn apart by the surrounding gas. The find constrains how galactic winds carry cold material.
arxiv-2504-21591:
Tang and Tsuda study time periodic solutions of the compressible Euler equations with damping in twenty twenty-five. These equations model gas flow without viscosity. Long time behaviour is delicate, since there is no viscous smoothing to rely on. Damping helps global solutions exist, but ones that repeat in time are harder to get. The force that drives them must repeat in time as well, and it must stay small.

For space dimension three or higher, they prove that such a solution does exist. It stays stable when the start is nudged by a small amount. The size of that nudge shrinks to zero as time goes on and on. Low frequency parts are handled with the help of potential based estimates. A new weighted energy estimate avoids loss of derivatives at high frequencies. The work extends what is known about damped gas dynamics as a whole.
arxiv-2504-21691:
Valentín Reparaz and four co-authors study a driven superconducting circuit in a 2025 paper. The circuit is a fluxonium, a type of qubit, shaken by a strong periodic drive far from its natural frequency. Such driving produces Landau-Zener-Stückelberg patterns, interference fingerprints that reveal the circuit's energy structure.

The team simulated the full multi-level circuit rather than a cut-down two-level version, to stay close to real devices. The spectra show resonances that arise when interference favors jumps to higher levels. For the simple case they give a plain reading of the pattern, and for the full case they derive an effective two-level model. The work should help predict lab outcomes and design fast qubit gates.
arxiv-2504-21791:
Chen marks the path form of the two-part chance heat form at its edge point. Edge point here is where the form's acts turn most frail. Chief claims give a full, path-wise tale of its split parts. Those parts are the marks that name a chance path's drift and sway. Sharp, true forms for the co-sway count cap the chief claims. The proof builds a growth form for co-sway counts of smoothed kin.

Those kin are near forms that stand in for the true path. Math from quantum-solved tools feeds the chance sums in the proof. That feed lets the growth form land in clean, closed terms. The work thus pins how paths act at the frail edge. It does so with no loose ends in the co-sway tale.
arxiv-2505-00191:
Yuyan Ge and three co-authors build a chest report classifier whose reasoning a doctor can read. Their system appeared in twenty twenty-five. Artificial intelligence could speed up diagnosis from radiology reports, but black-box answers are hard to trust in clinics.

The method first pulls a set of key facts from many reports. For a new report, it asks whether a few chosen facts follow from the text. The answers to those questions drive the diagnosis. By design, the questions and answers are the explanation. A guide called Information Pursuit picks the most useful questions, and a language model checks each fact against the report. Tests on a large chest imaging data set showed the approach works well.
arxiv-2505-01791:
Shafeequdheen, Nayak, and Rowthu proposed this image method in twenty twenty-five for finding the edges of objects in pictures. The task, called segmentation, splits an image into regions that differ in brightness or texture. A classic energy model, named after Mumford and Shah, guides the split. Most methods carry the moving border as a level set, a kind of contour map.

The authors drop the level set entirely. They track the border as a polygon of points and move it by following the shape gradient of the energy. Each step of gradient descent nudges the points toward a better fit. Tests on varied images showed the method catches fine and narrow borders well, even in textured scenes. The approach offers a simpler route to the same goal.
arxiv-2505-02291:
Suh, Pang, Zhao, and Tedrake put forth a new zone rule in twenty twenty-five for planning hand moves that lean on touch. Touch acts do not bend both ways, so a round trust zone fits them poorly. Their zone rule keeps that one-way trait while it stays cheap to run.

A plan tool built on the rule makes short touch plans that hold in their zone. Those short plans are then sewn to one long world plan. On a two-arm rig and a three-view hand rig it beat learned tools on cost by a lot. The hand plan map built in minutes on a plain laptop.
arxiv-2505-02391:
Jiarui Yao and co-authors present, in a 2025 machine learning paper, a smarter way to train models that reason step by step. Training samples each prompt the same number of times, which wastes effort on easy prompts and starves hard ones. The team instead shifts the sampling budget toward where it cuts error the most.

Their method tracks how often each prompt yields a good answer and how large its error signal is, then assigns samples to keep total error low under a fixed budget. Theory shows faster progress under stated conditions. On math tasks, training ran two to four times faster with better scores, and the same trick improved a second training method too.
arxiv-2505-03991:
Hao Xu and co-authors wrote a survey in two thousand twenty-five on deep learning for finding events in sports video. Such tools power automatic performance review, highlight clips, and tactical choices. Three close tasks cause confusion: locating long action segments, spotting a moment that marks an event, and pinpointing the exact frame.

The survey separates those tasks and maps the main methods for each, including ways to model time, fuse sound and image, and learn from little data. It reviews benchmark sets and scoring rules, noting a bias toward broadcast-quality footage of elite sport. Everyday players are largely missed by past surveys. The authors close with open problems for the field to tackle next.
arxiv-2505-06691:
Victor Hugo Pereira Rodrigues, Tiago Roux Oliveira, Miroslav Krstic, and Tamer Basar design algorithms that steer competing players to equilibrium without models, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. In noncooperative games each player pursues its own payoff, and a Nash equilibrium is where nobody gains by deviating alone. The players here do not know their quadratic payoff functions. Sinusoidal perturbations let each estimate its pseudo-gradient from observed payoffs, an extremum seeking trick.

Communication is event-triggered to save bandwidth: each player broadcasts only when its current gradient estimate has drifted enough from the last sent value, and tunes its own trigger threshold. The authors prove local convergence, quantify the small residual set around the equilibrium, and establish a minimum dwell time ruling out infinitely fast switching, the Zeno behavior. Stability analysis uses Lyapunov methods and averaging for discontinuous systems. An oligopoly example illustrates the theory numerically.
arxiv-2505-06791:
Jiaming Hu, Jiawei Wang, and Henrik Christensen sped up robot motion planning on graphics chips. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with finding a clear path for a robot. Sampling based planners are fast in plain scenes but lag when joint limits bind. Past chip based work used a tracking compiler that strained on complex robots or scenes. The team used a run time compiler from a chip maker instead.

Their frame, cpRRTC, plans paths with bounds in place and still runs in near real time. Tests showed strength where past chip planners failed. Readers in robotics get a planner that keeps speed as scenes get hard. Fast bound aware plans matter for arms that work near people.
arxiv-2505-09591:
Tobias Jan Wieczorek and co-authors make visual question answering models know when to stay silent in this 2025 paper. Vision language models often answer confidently and wrongly. Selective prediction lets a model answer only when sure enough. Bayesian methods promise that awareness but can be costly on large models.

Their method, Variational VQA, adapts recent variational training tools. It improves calibration and selective prediction on question answering and visual reasoning tasks. Gains were largest when allowed error rates were very low. Often a single posterior sample beat standard training for reliability. A new risk averse selector uses prediction spread to beat plain averaging. Cheaper uncertainty tools could make deployed vision models safer.
arxiv-2505-10291:
Miguel Barroso Varela and Orfeu Bertolami wrote this cosmology paper, published in 2025. It shows that a quiet bookkeeping choice in a modified gravity theory, how to write the matter term in the action, changes how cosmic structure grows.

The theory couples matter directly to curvature, and for a perfect fluid two writings of the matter term compete. The authors compare their effects on the effective strength of gravity as density ripples evolve. One choice, reviewed under a simplifying approximation, can drive that strength to a wild divergence in late-time models. Full equations avoid the blow-up but squeeze the allowed size of modifications hard. The other choice dodges both problems at late times, because ordinary matter then has almost no pressure. Predictions follow for sample models, sharpening how such theories can be tested.
arxiv-2505-12891:
Shaohang Wei and co-authors build in 2025 a hard test of how well language models reason about time. Real life piles up dates, fast changes, and tangled social timelines, which older tests simplify away. Their benchmark, TIME, holds 38,522 questions across three levels and eleven task types.

The questions draw on encyclopedia entries, news, and dialogue, each stressing a different real-world challenge. The team ran both reasoning-tuned and standard models and studied how extra thinking time at test changed scores. A small human-checked subset, TIME-Lite, is included for careful follow-up work. The authors release the data and code to standardize time-reasoning research.
arxiv-2505-13091:
Yuanbo Wang and six co-authors present Touch2Shape, a model that rebuilds 3D shapes from touch rather than sight. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that image-based diffusion models grasp global shape well. They miss fine local detail, and they suffer under blocked views and poor light. Touch sensors read local surface form directly, with no such limits.

A touch embedding module feeds tactile images into the diffusion model as a compact code. A fusion module then sharpens the rebuilt shape with that code. For active search, reinforcement learning trains a policy that picks where to touch next. The diffusion code guides that policy through a novel reward. Tests in look and in numbers back the rebuild quality. The touch policy lifts scores further. The work suits robots that must handle objects they cannot fully see.
arxiv-2505-13691:
Finch and five colleagues fold high density theory into neutron star matter models in one smooth frame in twenty twenty-five. The equation of state links pressure and density inside these dead stars. Hard core theory only holds far above star densities, yet it can still bound the model. Past work bolted it on at one chosen density, which split the treatment.

Their unified model runs from crust to theory densities with full freedom between. The theory data then act as part of the prior. Softening of the core matter held up in their tests. The top star mass did not drop, though. Sound speed in the densest cores seems to fall already, they find.
arxiv-2505-13991:
Jared Lichtman explains a classical counting result showing a famous number theory conjecture holds for almost every case, in a 2025 note. The abc conjecture ties a sum's size to the primes inside it. Lichtman revisits an old estimate by de Bruijn with an elementary, self-contained proof. Among all coprime triples in a large cube that satisfy the sum, only a thin slice can possibly break the conjecture's bound.

The note then points forward: Browning, Lichtman, and Teräväinen recently sharpened that slice's count, the first power-saving since 1962. The exposition doubles as a bridge to the new work. Lichtman presents the old argument for its own beauty and for the door it reopens.
arxiv-2505-14491:
Abdughani and co-authors study dark stuff that kills off mostly to ghost grains. Dark stuff can wipe out fast near tight peaks or by the Sommerfeld boost. When both boosts join, the wipe can grow past the norm by far. In such cases, heat ties may break well before the stock split. That break shifts the left mass of dark stuff left in space. Wipes to stock grains are capped by dawn-sky reads, save for ghost grains.

Ghost-grain outs slip that cap, so the team homes in on them. They solve linked heat sums to find the left mass left. Test data then bound the free traits of the model. Next-wave tests get a reach sketch from the same sums.
arxiv-2505-14691:
Caroline Lemke and Benjamin Bisping give one general method for solving energy games, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Energy games are contests used to check that a system can reach a goal without running dry. Classic versions track energy as a list of numbers. Those numbers only grow or shrink by fixed steps. Many real problems need richer rules than that.

Their framework asks only that energies form a well-founded lattice with joins. It also asks that each move's energy change can be undone through a paired function. Under those mild demands, one algorithm decides the winner. The authors show the method covers standard energy games, declining variants, and shortest path problems. They back it with a machine-checked formalization and two working programs.
arxiv-2505-15991:
Derek Frydel wrote a physics paper in 2025 on run-and-tumble particles confined in a harmonic trap, using integral equations. Run-and-tumble particles are self-propelled specks that move in runs, then stop and reorient; they are a standard toy model for microscopic swimmers. Such models are typically easy in one dimension, harder in two, and unsolvable in three.

Frydel reformulates the motion as a jump process. Each run becomes a jump, and a transition operator gives the distribution of landings. Their resting spread then follows from an integral equation built on that operator. In two dimensions, the operator turns out to be reversible. That reversibility implies detailed balance, from which that spread follows at once, without solving the main equation. The particles are still not in true equilibrium; the balance is a property of the jump viewpoint. Changing the waiting time spread kills that trait.
arxiv-2505-16091:
Jinpei Guo and colleagues build an image compression system that rebuilds pictures in a single diffusion step at any chosen file size. Diffusion models restore images superbly but usually need many slow passes from pure noise, and a separate model per bit rate. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team reframes the job. A compressed image code is treated as a partly noised version of the original code, with the noise level set by the chosen bit rate. One trained model then maps that state back to a clean image in one pass.
