Linking bit rate to a matching step on the diffusion path lets one model serve all rates. Because the compressed code keeps much of the picture structure, a single cleanup pass is enough. In extensive tests the system led on both measured quality and visual quality, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-16791:
Tillmann Rheude, Roland Eils, and Benjamin Wild introduced Cohort-based Active Modality Acquisition in twenty twenty-five. In multimodal learning, some data types for a sample may be missing, and acquiring them costs money. The question is which samples in a whole cohort deserve the extra measurement under a fixed budget — a test-time, group-level problem earlier work largely skipped.

Their strategies estimate each candidate's expected gain by imputing the missing modality, judging what it would add before paying for it. Upper-bound heuristics benchmark the choices. On data sets with up to fifteen modalities, imputation-guided picks beat entropy-based, pre-acquisition, and random selection. A demonstration on the UK Biobank cohort showed the method guiding proteomics purchases for disease prediction at scale.
arxiv-2505-16991:
Abdul Hannan, Alessio Brutti, Shah Nawaz, and Mubashir Noman present a training plan for small speech recognition models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Large models score well but are too heavy for small devices with tight memory and power. Past ways to shrink them lose much of their skill, or need long training to win it back.

Their two-step plan learns shared representations from one large model, then makes several small ones from it. Each small model trains in few rounds, yet keeps strong scores. On standard speech test sets, training runs about three times as fast. Word error rates also drop by a clear margin next to past routes.
arxiv-2505-17191:
William Sands, Jing-Mei Qiu, Daniel Hayes, and Nanyi Zheng proposed a faster simulation method in 2025 for multi-scale BGK equations, which model gases through colliding particles. Such simulations store a large solution matrix, and low-rank methods cut the cost by tracking only the most important rows and columns. The authors extend their earlier adaptive-rank framework from a collisionless plasma system to these nonlinear collisional equations.

Their greedy sampling strategy picks the important rows and columns directly, then updates them with a local solver and rebuilds the full solution by cross approximation. That avoids taking apart nonlinear terms such as the local equilibrium distribution. A conservative correction step keeps mass, momentum, and energy exactly accounted for, and the authors show through asymptotic analysis that the method keeps the right behavior in limiting regimes.
arxiv-2505-17291:
Linus Bleistein, Aurélien Bellet, and Julie Josse studied optimal transport with missing data in twenty twenty-five. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to morph one distribution into another, but real data sets have holes, with missing rates that vary by feature and by sample. Their setting assumes values are missing completely at random, at uneven rates.

For Gaussian data they show the Wasserstein distance and linear transport maps can be debiased with little cost in sample needs. For the entropy-regularized problem they give an efficient, consistent estimator based on repeated singular value thresholding. Its tuning parameter can be picked without a validation set, using their debiased distance — a trick of wider use in matrix completion. Numerical tests back the theory across applications.
arxiv-2505-18191:
Jonathan Dan, Amirhossein Shahbazinia, Christodoulos Kechris, and David Atienza wrote this report in two thousand twenty-five. It sums up a contest on finding seizures in brain wave records, run under the SzCORE frame at a meeting on AI in epilepsy care.

Hand review of long EEG records is still the norm, and models that shine in print often fail on new patients. The contest scored many top methods on a held-back set of records from dozens of subjects, with expert marks as truth. The best score was low, and top scorers were not the most steady across subjects. The gap between claimed and held-back results shows why shared, strict tests matter. The test base now stays open for future work.
arxiv-2505-20591:
Sairam Gurajada, Eser Kandogan, and Sajjadur Rahman study how to tune prompts for systems that turn plain questions into database queries in a 2025 paper. Large language models can do this translation when given the right context, such as table details and example pairs. Picking that context per question is costly at run time.

The authors argue that production systems need precision and speed, not just good-looking queries. A fixed, well-chosen set of examples may matter more than examples picked by similarity. Their framework searches for such a set while balancing accuracy against how fast the generated queries run. Early results support the approach. The work speaks to teams deploying these systems where slow or wrong queries carry real costs.
arxiv-2505-20691:
Shenkai Zhao and four co-authors built an active learner that knows how unsure it is, in a paper published in 2025. Partly labeled classification gains when the learner picks which new cases to label. Earlier picks often skip the confidence grade of each prediction, so the wrong cases get picked. Their method grades doubt for labeled and unlabeled cases in one framework, built on evidence-based deep learning.

A balancing method stops the doubt grade from warping when class counts shift. The selection rule takes the most doubtful case when loss turns up late in training. On photo classification sets it beat both partly labeled and fully labeled active rivals. The authors say doubt-aware selection makes each label buy more.
arxiv-2505-20791:
S. M. Rafi-Ul-Islam, Zhuo Bin Siu, and colleagues study tunable defect states in electric circuits that mimic topological materials in a 2025 physics study. Their chain follows a classic two-band pattern with gain and loss added, making the system non-Hermitian. In that regime a skin effect piles most states against one edge, competing with the parity-time symmetry and with topological states bound to defects.

Reconfigurable defect states, modes that can be moved or switched by design, are the prize. Circuit platforms let such exotic physics be built on a bench and measured directly, guiding later material versions.
arxiv-2505-21791:
Julia Nakhleh and Robert Nowak wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It proves that training a ReLU network with a sparsity-driving penalty, pushed to its global best, yields the sparsest network that fits the data.

Wide nets can fit a set in many ways, so which fit to pick is a real ask. Pruning after the fact is the usual tack. The authors give a smooth training goal based on small-power norms of the weights. Its global minima are shown to be exactly the sparsest one-hidden-layer ReLU nets that match the data. The combinatorial hunt for the sparsest fit thus turns into a smooth climb that gradient methods can walk.
arxiv-2505-22491:
Moritz Haas, Sebastian Bordt, Ulrike von Luxburg, and Leena Chennuru Vankadara explain why very large learning rates can train wide networks well. Their 2025 paper confronts a theory-practice gap: standard theory predicts instability at big rates and no feature learning at stable ones. Real networks, though, train stably at large rates and learn real features even when very wide.

The authors split the supposedly unstable regime in two. In one part, training truly blows up. In the other, outputs grow without bound while gradients and activations stay calm, a controlled divergence. At the edge of that calmer regime, a clean infinite-width limit exists under the standard loss. The finer map reconciles practice with theory and guides rate choices for large models.
arxiv-2505-22791:
Francesco Libbi, Lorenzo Monacelli, and Boris Kozinsky show that laser pulses can force strontium titanate into a ferroelectric state it never reaches on its own, in a two thousand twenty-five physics paper. The material's ferroelectric mode softens on cooling, yet quantum fluctuations keep it paraelectric down to absolute zero.

Resonant mid-infrared pulses drive the system far from equilibrium and quench those fluctuations. A metastable ferroelectric state appears, distinct from the conventional ground state. Using a first-principles machine-learned potential energy surface, the authors predict when the induced state stays long-lived and explain recent experimental observations. The result suggests a general light-based route to ferroelectric order in related oxide perovskites.
arxiv-2505-23091:
Zeyu Liu leads a team of twelve authors unlocking reasoning in small multimodal language models through a staged curriculum. Text-only models learned to reason with rule-based reinforcement learning, but small models that also see images start from weaker reasoning and can lose ground when vision is added. Good multimodal reasoning data are also scarce.

Their Infi-MMR framework runs three phases, beginning with foundational reasoning activation on high-quality text data. Later phases add the visual side gradually, guarding against the failure mode where reinforcement learning produces elaborate but wrong reasoning. The resulting three-billion-parameter model is the demonstration vehicle. The authors present the phased design as the key to transferring reasoning skill into small multimodal systems.
arxiv-2505-23491:
Sándor Lökös finds the shape of counts of charged bits from one rule: make entropy as large as it can be. Crash labs count how many charged bits fly out of each crash. The counts trace a curve known as a negative binomial. New work ties the curve's Shannon entropy to how the inner parts are linked in a quantum sense.

Lökös shows the counts found in labs flow from that one rule on its own. No prior guess about the crash is put in. With the set bounds, the least biased curve is the one nature shows. The famed shape thus gets a plain cause, not just a fit. The paper casts a law of crash counts as a fact of pure stats. What looked like force at work may at root be chance and bounds.
arxiv-2505-24591:
Sherelyn Alejandro Merchan, Jacqueline Faherty, and a team of astronomers build a portrait of a cold alien world in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their target is a T8 brown dwarf, a substellar object too small to fuse hydrogen, catalogued as 2MASS J04151954-0935066. They built a spectral energy distribution spanning optical to mid-infrared wavelengths. New JWST and Magellan spectra anchor it. Mid-infrared photometry and past spectra and photometry from many telescopes and surveys join it.

The spectra show strong molecular absorption from ammonia, methane, hydrogen sulfide, carbon dioxide, and water at set wavelengths, plus a carbon monoxide feature. No potassium doublet absorption showed in the high-resolution near-infrared data. A possible new carbon dioxide feature was found in the mid-infrared. The full distribution lets the team bound the brown dwarf's luminosity, temperature, mass, and radius from data. That feeds the study of cold substellar atmospheres.
arxiv-2505-24791:
Zhang and four co-authors speed stepwise flow tools with side-by-side word picks in this twenty twenty-five paper. Flow tools build clean draws yet must cast each bit in strict turn. That turn-lock makes draws slow and bars real use in the field.

Inside, the team finds late bits need not wait on all past bits for good draws. Loose ties in deep coats let many bits be cast at once in their build. A Jacobi loop casts bits in banks and trues them round by round. Proofs give fast close rates and cap rounds at the turn count. Tests hit near five times the pace at the same draw grade.
arxiv-2506-01591:
Yuan Gan, Jiaxu Miao, Yunze Wang, and Yi Yang build a shield for portrait photos against a new kind of fake video, in a 2025 paper. Modern tools can animate a still face so it mouths along to any audio track, well enough to fool viewers. Such fakes feed scams and false news. Earlier shields added noise patterns to portraits, but they could not stop the audio from driving the face, and cleaning tools could wash the noise away.

Their method, Silencer, works in two stages. First, a training goal teaches the pattern to make the generator ignore the audio track, leaving the face still. Second, a further goal hardens the pattern against the cleaning steps an attacker would use. Tests show the shield holds where earlier ones failed. The authors frame the work as a privacy defense and a warning about talking-head tools.
arxiv-2506-03491:
Brenda Murillo and Fabio Sanchez review two decades of math models of bulimia nervosa, in a paper from 2025. Bulimia is an eating disorder marked by binge and purge cycles. Its spread is shaped not only by inner strain but also by social and digital life. Older models often treated it as a purely personal illness.

The review gathers group-based, random, and delay-based models. A key line of work treats the disorder as socially transmissible, passed through norms and peer pressure. The authors find the largest gap around social media, whose role has grown fast. They call for models with feedback loops and content-driven influence. Network effects that shift over time belong in the frame too. Better models, they argue, can steer public health steps in the online age.
arxiv-2506-03791:
Nowak and co-authors built a theory model of electron flow at a special oxide interface where a thin sheet of electrons behaves like a two-dimensional gas. At this interface the allowed energies form a strongly non-circular pattern, so electrons do not spread evenly in all directions. The team used a tight-binding model, which tracks electrons hopping between atomic sites, and simulated what a scanning gate microscope would see near a narrow constriction.

The direction of the electron stream and the spacing of interference fringes both depend on how the constriction is aligned with the crystal. When the gates sit off the natural axes, trajectories skew sideways, and electrons from different orbitals separate. The results guide future microscope experiments on this material.
arxiv-2506-04891:
Viacheslav Kuzmin and co-authors build a faster simulator for quantum machine learning in a 2025 paper. Quantum learning circuits are often built from repeating layers of the same gates applied across all qubits. Simulating them on a normal computer is the main way to develop the field, so simulator speed sets the pace of research.

The team benchmarked general and gate-specific tricks for applying a layer of gates to a state vector. The best trick depended on how many qubits the layer touches. Mixing tricks by layer sped up both the forward pass and the backward pass used in training. Their TQml Simulator switches method layer by layer on that basis. The work gives quantum learning researchers a sharper tool for testing circuit designs before hardware runs.
arxiv-2506-04991:
Eric Gottlieb, Matjaz Krnc, and Peter Mursic define two variants of the game Nim in this 2025 paper. In classic Nim, players remove tokens from piles. PNim replaces piles with integer partitions drawn as Young diagrams. A move removes rows or columns from one diagram. RNim replaces piles with hyperrectangles, and a move shortens one side.

For PNim the authors bound the Sprague-Grundy values tightly. They also characterize exactly which partitions have value one, the key case for winning play. For RNim they give a full formula for the value of any position. Both games are placed in the Conway-Gurvich-Ho hierarchy of game types. Combinatorial game fans get complete tools for these variants.
arxiv-2506-06591:
Shijing He and colleagues interview the people who build smart home products in China about how they handle privacy. Past research asked owners, users, and bystanders; the makers' own views stayed largely unstudied, especially outside the West. Twenty-seven semi-structured interviews cover managers, engineers, designers, legal experts, and marketers. The team probes their perspectives, daily practices, and risk fixes.

Compliance with Chinese data law dominated the answers. That legal frame, participants said, typically puts national security above individual privacy rights. Cultural and social factors shaped how they weighed privacy against security and convenience. The findings feed recommendations for product teams. The authors also propose socio-technical and legal interventions, with special care for at-risk groups in multi-user homes. The study gives privacy research a view from the factory floor of a huge market.
arxiv-2506-07891:
Simone Facchiano and colleagues removed unsafe concepts from video generators without retraining in a 2025 paper. Video models trained on web data can produce harmful content, and unlearning methods either filter outputs, which can be bypassed, or fine-tune weights at high cost. Their method needs only five paired prompts, safe and unsafe versions of one idea, to estimate a refusal vector in the model's internal space.

That vector is folded into the weights in closed form, and a low-rank contrastive step keeps the edit focused on the target concept so unrelated quality survives. On two open video models and two safety benchmarks, unsafe generations fell by large average margins while prompt fidelity held. Cheap, surgical edits suit fast-moving model releases.
arxiv-2506-08691:
Congzhi Zhang and seven co-authors present VReST, a plan that boosts thought in large vision and language models with tree search and self scoring. Such models do well on many tasks but can stall on hard visual thought tasks. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

VReST needs no extra training. It grows a search tree where each node is one thought step and each path is a full chain. A self reward scores each step by how useful its sub questions are, if the answer looks right, and how well image and text clues match. No extra model is needed for the scores. The method beat current prompt tricks on three math based visual test sets.
arxiv-2506-09391:
Haoran Zhao and Robert Hawkins compare how people and language models write politely in a 2025 study. Polite speech balances two goals: sharing information and protecting social standing. People switch between warm strategies, such as compliments, and cautious ones, such as hedging and indirect requests, depending on context.

The authors test humans and models in both constrained and free production tasks. Larger models, at the top size range studied, reproduce key human preferences for matching strategy to situation. Smaller models show flatter patterns. The comparison matters because assistants that sound rude, or oddly blunt, can damage trust even when their facts are right.
arxiv-2506-11291:
Sarnighausen, Hohage, Burger, Hauptmann, and Wald set out regularization methods for inverse problems that change with time, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such problems work back from what is seen over time to a function that keeps changing. Lebesgue-Bochner spaces treat time and space in unlike ways, which fits this task well. Two methods are given: Tikhonov regularization in Banach spaces, and a method that penalizes change over time.

The authors work out duality mappings and show that these spaces are smooth of power type. That shape lets Tikhonov regularization run in practice, with split rules for time and for space. The second method instead puts a cost on change over time itself. Both methods are tested on dynamic CT scans, which rebuild a body part as it moves. The frame suits medical imaging and other tasks where the thing rebuilt keeps changing.
arxiv-2506-11491:
Zahedi and six co-authors build a graph net that sorts tissue zones from space gene reads in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such reads map gene work by spot, which shows how a tissue is built and split. Noise, scale, and cell ties all trip past tools in that task.

Inside, three graphs catch space nearness, gene likeness, and zone build in one frame. Each graph gets its own code, and a focus step fuses the three codes well. A group-cut loss keeps the codes true when reads run thin in a zone. Batch drills let the tool scale to half a score of ten thousand cells. Tests on four rigs beat top tools by wide score gaps in the run.
arxiv-2506-12091:
Harry Amad, Nicolas Astorga, and Mihaela van der Schaar present CALM-DT, a way to keep digital twins up to date. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a pain point: a digital twin mirrors a real system, but real systems change. New variables appear, and old twins must be rebuilt or retrained to cope.

The team recasts the twin as a language model task. The model learns in context, from examples fed to it at run time, so updates need no new training. Tuned encoders fetch the most apt past cases to guide each guess. Tests show CALM-DT matches older twin methods and adapts to shifts they cannot handle.
arxiv-2506-12891:
Zeki Doruk Erden and Boi Faltings (2025) propose a new design philosophy for artificial intelligence borrowed from evolutionary developmental biology. Modern machine learning, they argue, mirrors the old Modern Synthesis in evolution: both assume simple building blocks, weak structure, and gradual tuning. That view was overturned in biology by evo-devo, which showed how development organizes adaptation. AI still patches its weaknesses one heuristic at a time. The authors map the analogy in detail.

From developmental principles they sketch two learning systems. Regulatory connections let parts switch each other on and off. Somatic variation with selection generates candidate changes inside the system, and weak linkage keeps parts loosely coupled. The authors claim these designs dissolve several standing limits of neural networks at once, rather than trading one against another. The paper is a manifesto with worked examples: biology's revised theory of evolution, they argue, should become AI's theory of learning machines.
arxiv-2506-12991:
Yuanhe Tian, Xu Li, and four colleagues plug grammar knowledge into large language models to sharpen aspect-based sentiment analysis, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The task is judging feelings toward specific aspects of a product or service, which demands tracking which words attach to which aspect through the sentence's syntax.

Fine-tuning big models for this is expensive, and data is often too scarce anyway. The authors instead build plug-and-play components that inject syntactic knowledge into a frozen model. The components can carry constituent structure, word dependencies, and other grammar signals in extendable form. No heavy training is required. The language model gains the structural hints it needs to link opinions to their targets. Aspect sentiment is where generic fluency fails quietly, praising the camera when the complaint was about the battery. Syntax, the authors argue, is the missing scaffold.
arxiv-2506-13491:
Tobias Gurtler and Benjamin Lucien Kaminski lay foundations for programming when the world is random and only partly visible in a 2025 computer science study. A robot or controller in such a setting cannot know the exact state, so it must act on a belief: a probability distribution over possible states. Their language keeps that belief as a first-class object the program manipulates symbolically.

Programs can model the environment, interact with it, and condition their beliefs on observations. Formal groundwork matters because belief-guided code is easy to write subtly wrong. A language with proved semantics lets safety claims about such systems be checked.
arxiv-2506-16291:
Fang, Moreira, Wang, and Zhang present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on fast Lyapunov spectra for a class of interval maps. The maps have countably many branches and may hold a parabolic fixed point. No distortion assumptions are made in their work. They study the multifractal behavior of growth rates along orbits. A geometric approach replaces the usual thermodynamic machinery. The fast spectrum turns out to be piecewise constant. A jump at infinity may appear in that spectrum.

Upper and lower versions of the spectrum are also pinned down. The results extend earlier work on the Gauss map to this whole map family. Sharp contrasts with the classical spectrum are highlighted. The paper refines how growth at infinity is measured.
arxiv-2506-16791:
Erickson and six co-authors launched a living benchmark for table-shaped data in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Machine learning on tables is booming, but its test sets sit frozen while models change. Flaws found later never get fixed. TabArena instead updates continuously, with a public leaderboard and named maintainers.

The launch curated datasets and well-built models, then ran a large comparison. How models were validated, and whether settings were ensembled, proved decisive. Gradient-boosted trees still led on practical data under tight budgets. Deep learning caught up given time and ensembling, while foundation models shone on small sets. Mixing models pushed scores highest, though some gains traced to validation overfitting.
arxiv-2506-17891:
Jiahao Lu and Jiacheng Deng present a method in two thousand twenty-five for three-dimensional instance segmentation. The task is to pick out each object in a point cloud scene, with a mask and a class label for each one. Transformer methods do this well, but they focus on links between scene and query features.

Their method, Relation3D, also models links inside the scene features and among the queries. An aggregation module groups points into superpoints, and a refinement module uses contrastive learning to improve them. A relation-aware attention step adds position and geometry into how queries interact. Tests on four standard data sets, including ScanNet and S3DIS, showed top performance, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-21291:
Guillaume Carrière and Frédéric Cazals rethought how clustering methods pick their starting seeds in a 2025 paper. K-means and its Gaussian mixture cousin both live or die by initialization, and classic seedings sample points with probabilities tied to distance. The authors dissect seeding into three choices: which metric samples the seeds, how many options compete, and which metric judges them. They then exploit a lookahead rule, judging seeds by coherence with the final scoring metric rather than a proxy.

Multipass runs tame the luck of random draws. Across tests the new seedings improved final scores by a consistent constant factor over strong rivals. That includes a recent multi-swap method, at modest extra cost. Subtle lessons include how poorly seed quality predicts final quality.
arxiv-2506-22491:
Oliver Warke, Joemon Jose, Faegheh Hasibi, and Jan Breitsohl introduce PromptAug, a data augmentation method for classifying conflict on social media, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Good classifiers need quality labeled data, which is scarce and expensive for nuanced harmful behavior.

Augmenting conflict data is tricky because language model guardrails resist generating offensive content. PromptAug works around that problem and delivered statistically significant gains of about two percent in accuracy and F1 score on conflict and emotion datasets. Evaluation covered extreme data scarcity, diversity analysis, and a thematic review. The authors flag four recurring flaws in augmented text, including humor ambiguity and misinterpretation, and frame the work as interdisciplinary.
arxiv-2506-22991:
Mehdi Bennis and co-authors lay out a vision for wireless networks built to bounce back, in a 2025 paper. Networks now rank with power and water as core infrastructure, yet storms and attacks keep disrupting them. The authors argue the next generation must plan for disruption as a certainty, not a surprise.

They first separate resilience from its cousins, reliability and robustness. Resilience comes in two flavors: elastic systems that snap back, and plastic ones that reshape themselves around damage. Math foundations follow, built on abstraction and composition. The paper then surveys enabling tools, from self-aware agents that rehearse failures to reconfigurable radios. Applications close the tour. The piece serves as a manifesto for resilience as a design native, not a patch.
arxiv-2506-23191:
Gabriel Iturra-Bocaz, Danny Vo, and Petra Galuščáková study, in twenty twenty-five, how the depth of relevance judgments affects search ranking models. Search systems learn from judged data sets. Shallow sets have many queries but few judgments per query. Deep sets have fewer queries but many judgments each. The team trained BERT-based rerankers, models that reorder search results, on both types. Tests ran on two known collections, MS MARCO and LongEval.

Shallow-judged data generally gave better generalization and effectiveness. The broader range of contexts likely helps. Deep-judged data lagged, though the gap could be softened by adding more negative training examples, results the model must learn to rank low.
arxiv-2506-23491:
ZongHan Hsieh, Tzer-Jen Wei, and ShengJing Yang present ZonUI-3B, a 2025 vision-language model that points at screen elements for automated control. Grounding, naming the exact spot of a button or field, must work across phones, desktops, and web pages at many resolutions. Their model is small enough to train fully on one consumer graphics card, yet it rivals far larger systems.

Three choices carry the design. A mixed data set of twenty-four thousand examples spans platforms and resolutions, with care for scarce high-resolution desktop shots. Training runs in two stages, broad first and then focused on fine screens. Trimming repeated data helped as much as adding more. On standard grounding benchmarks the model scored about eighty-five percent, best among models under four billion parameters. Ablations back each design choice.
arxiv-2507-01391:
Pooja Devi, Rositsa Miteva, and colleagues run a broad statistical study of solar radio bursts and space weather in a 2025 study. Type II bursts signal shock waves racing from the Sun, and they may arrive alone at metric wavelengths or extend to much longer waves. The team links each burst type with flares, sunspot layouts, filament eruptions, and mass ejections.

Interplanetary counterparts, shocks, particles detected in place, and geomagnetic storms are also tracked. Comparing the two burst families across so many partners shows which solar events travel outward to disturb Earth. Such statistics support forecasting of space weather that threatens satellites and power grids.
arxiv-2507-02991:
Steven Yang, Michal Levin, Govinda Anantha Padmanabha, and six co-authors study 3D printed digital materials in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Polymer jetting mixes soft and stiff photopolymers at tiny scale in one build. The mix makes composites with stiffness that can be tuned. The team tested five mixes under pull and twist at three rates. The response was not a straight line. It changed with rate. It was shaped much by what the mix held.

To model this, they built a neural network with physics built in. One part learns a hyperelastic energy rule that shifts with the mix and keeps convexity in the strain terms. A next part gives viscoelastic relaxation parameters from the mix. A sparse form keeps the learned laws clear. The model matched pull and twist, even for mixes between those tested. Such laws could cut design time for printed multi-material parts.
arxiv-2507-03991:
Ashutosh Marwah and Frédéric Dupuis prove the safety of a quantum key method run in parallel. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, covers device-free key sharing. In this setup, users need not trust their own devices. Many rounds of a quantum game run at once to build the key.

The proof leans on tools for repeated games with an anchor. Answers on a small random slice of rounds mimic a single-round plan. A new entropy theorem then gives the needed bound on secret bits. The result is a broader, more basic proof than past ones. It backs key sharing that stays safe even against the device makers.
arxiv-2507-04791:
Dionis Totsila and four co-authors add voice-guided collision avoidance to two-armed robot control in a 2025 paper. Steering a bimanual mobile robot through clutter by headset is hard: depth is elusive and distances deceive. Their system pairs immersive virtual reality control with spoken safety commands.

An operator drives the robot with hand controllers and can say, for example, avoid the yellow tool. The system grounds the phrase in the camera view, segments the named object, builds a 3D mesh, and feeds it to a whole-body controller that steers the robot clear. In static cluttered scenes, experiments showed safety improved without slowing the work. The authors present language as a natural safety channel for teleoperation.
arxiv-2507-04891:
Mingxin Liu and colleagues present MurreNet, a network that predicts cancer survival by fusing tissue images with genomic profiles. To predict survival needs both whole slide pathology images and genomics. But the two modes are deeply unlike each other. Plain fusion misses how they act within and between modes. That limits what the model can learn.

MurreNet first splits paired inputs into parts that are specific to one mode and parts that are shared. That cuts redundancy between them. A training rule then refines those parts. It constrains how alike they are, how distinct they are, and how well they stand for the data. Last, a deep fusion step joins the boosted traits into one form for prediction. Broad tests on six cancer cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas show the design's worth.
arxiv-2507-06191:
De Blas and five co-authors globally fit effective new-physics interactions across particle data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. If new physics is heavy, its effects compress into effective coefficients. Electroweak, Higgs, top, Drell-Yan, and flavor data constrain them jointly. Coefficient running between energy scales is included consistently.

Two flavor symmetry assumptions for the operator set are compared. Single-coefficient fits are reported alongside the global one. The HEPfit framework implements the analysis with current data. State-of-the-art theory predictions back every observable. The bounds guide where new physics could still hide.
arxiv-2507-07391:
Inyoung Ryu and Tian Yang wrote a math paper in 2025 on maps from surfaces into a matrix group. A punctured surface is a sheet with points removed, and its loops form a group. The paper studies maps of that group that keep a set type for each loop. It asks how many separate pieces the space of such maps has.

The authors finish a full sorting of those pieces. The pieces are counted by two kinds of labels: a class number for each rim loop and a sign for each rim image. A classic bound links the labels that can occur. When the surface is a punctured sphere, extra pieces appear with no curved maps at all. The paper ends with an exact count of all the pieces.
arxiv-2507-09291:
Yuval Grader and Hadar Averbuch-Elor improve indoor localization from floorplans in a 2025 paper. A floorplan is a compact map of a building, rich with meaning: doors, windows, and room shapes. Most localization methods match only depth cues from a sensor, discarding that meaning.

Their framework estimates both depth rays and semantic rays from the input, then merges them into a probability map over positions. The map is built coarse to fine: a sparse pass finds promising areas, then denser sampling sharpens them. The system finally predicts a 2D position and facing direction. On two standard benchmarks it beat prior methods clearly on recall, showing semantics carry real locating power.
arxiv-2507-10291:
Kristine Ung and three co-authors measured a key energy level in diamond with fine care. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the nitrogen-vacancy center, a defect used in quantum sensing. Much is still not known about its energy steps. The team sought the exact energy to free an electron from one singlet state. Past work had placed it in a rough range.

They varied laser tone and diamond heat, and watched light output drop at the point of freeing. A magnet based trick let them read only the spin linked light. Readers who build quantum sensors get a sharper value for a state that shapes how this defect works.
arxiv-2507-10791:
M. Bordag and D. N. Voskresensky study how a vortex of condensed scalar particles can form in a rapidly rotating cylinder when a magnetic field is present. Without the field, rotation alone struggles to trigger Bose condensation of the charged field; the field opens the way. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors treat two field layouts: a uniform field filling the whole cylinder, and a thin flux tube along the axis. They solve the governing equation numerically for the condensate and compare with linearized and approximate analytic treatments, extracting threshold rotation speeds, sizes, and energies.

For the same settings, the flux tube condensate sits at lower energy than the uniform field one, making it the favored state. Work of this kind connects to pion condensation debates in neutron stars and heavy ion collisions, where rotation and magnetism are extreme.
arxiv-2507-11191:
Tire making wastes time and rubber every time a line starts up, and Eider Garate-Perez, Kerman López de Calle-Etxabe, and Susana Ferreiro attack that waste with data alone. No formula describes their extrusion process, so they train learning models on past production records to stand in for the real line. An evolution-style search then hunts the stand-in for the best start-up settings, with penalties that keep it inside safe ground.

The settings it found beat the best the plant had ever run. Start-up and setup time fell by sixty-five percent, and scrap rubber dropped a great deal as well. The team offers the recipe for other factories whose processes defy tidy equations.
arxiv-2507-11291:
Benjamin Berendsohn studies pattern hunting in a stream of numbers in a 2025 paper. The input is a permutation revealed one element at a time, and the question is whether it contains a given smaller pattern in relative order. Because the input is a permutation, the future is partly predictable, which changes what streaming algorithms can do.

The paper maps the memory needed for every pattern type. Rising and falling patterns need only a small, logarithmic memory. Two families of length-three patterns need roughly the square root of the input size. Every other pattern forces memory that grows almost linearly. If the stream is an arbitrary sequence instead, nearly all patterns become expensive. The results draw a sharp line by pattern shape.
arxiv-2507-11491:
Suyog Mahulkar and Jaywant Arakeri wrote this fluid mechanics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on clapping as a way to swim. Two flat plates snap shut like hands, squeeze out a jet, and push the body forward; some sea creatures move this way.

The pair simulate two thin plates set at a sixty-degree angle, using motion copied from lab tests. One case lets the body move, and the other holds it fixed. The fixed case builds higher pressure between the plates and leaves unlike swirls behind: triangle and omega loops versus a simple oval loop. After the clap, they audit the energy. Part of the work hides in the vortex cores as a stored form they call core potential energy. Side tests on plain vortex rings confirm the split, backing an old guess in the field.
arxiv-2507-12691:
Avi Parrack, Carlo Leonardo Attubato, and Stefan Heimersheim weigh tools made to catch false acts by language models. Straight sort tools called probes read a model's in side acts. They tell false acts from true ones. Their worth in use is not clear. A false bot might learn to dodge them.

The team says to gauge probes by a black to white gain. That is how much a watch with probe reach beats one with no such reach. This frame takes the probe's plus worth in true watch states. Used on probes that live now, the gains were weak but gave hope. The text gives a stick to judge if act based watch earns trust when put to use.
arxiv-2507-12891:
Marco Piccininni, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Mats Stensrud refine the no anticipation notion in difference in differences in two thousand twenty-five. The method is a workhorse of empirical work in economics. Its no anticipation rule says treatment cannot act before it starts. In standard causal time order that sounds automatic, though.

The team argues the muddle lies in which intervention is meant. Current statements of the rule stay ambiguous on that point. They propose fresh definitions to pin the idea down. New identification results follow from the sharper forms. Subject matter sense is restored to the assumption.
arxiv-2507-13391:
Abiodun Oketunji builds an expectile based risk framework for the FTSE index in two thousand twenty-five. Value at Risk, the classic gauge, failed badly in market stress. The crisis of two thousand eight exposed those flaws in full. Expectiles offer a tail aware swap for quantile based gauges.

Two decades of FTSE returns span crashes and recoveries alike. New expectile regression forms and threshold rules drive the method. Backtests check the gauges across market states and confidence levels. Expectile Value at Risk beat classic gauges in those tests. Gains held in volatile spans, with less model risk. Practice and policy guides close the work.
arxiv-2507-13691:
Jana, Solanki, and Ojha compute gluon Wigner distributions inside a dressed quark in this 2025 physics paper, published in Physics Letters B. Wigner distributions give the fullest picture of how particles are spread in position and momentum. The authors work at non-zero skewness, where the proton hands over unequal momentum shares.

Their model treats the target as a quark dressed with one gluon, using light-front wave functions. They derive formulas for cases where the gluon, the target, or both spin sideways. In the lengthwise boost-invariant coordinate the distributions oscillate like a diffraction pattern. Similar patterns were known for other polarization choices. The results extend the map of gluon structure used to interpret collider data.
arxiv-2507-14391:
Sahil Loomba and Dean Eckles ask which causal measures in networks actually serve policy choice, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. When one person's treatment affects others, many effect measures compete. Two virtues matter: reading as a summary of unit-level effects, and guiding which policy to pick.

Many measures average first over units, then over assignments, or the reverse. The common order often fails policy choice, since even uniform policies yield uneven exposures. The other order can lose the unit-level reading. The expected average outcome keeps both virtues, the authors argue, and deserves more use.
arxiv-2507-14491:
Bing-Ze Lu and Richard Tsai wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, whose text calls it a study of artifacts of numerical integration in learning dynamical systems. It shows the solver picked to fit data can twist the system that learning finds.

To grade a candidate law, one must run it with a numeric integrator and match its path to the data. The authors show a damped swing can be learned as anti-damped, with its swing flipped, while still fitting the points. The solver's stability zone warps the learned law. Smaller steps or higher order do not fix it in general. One named midpoint method can keep the true flavor, be it energy-keeping or fading.
arxiv-2507-16191:
Zeng and six co-authors built a video tracker in twenty twenty-five that reasons out loud about a target's state across frames, with checks on that reasoning. Stock trackers stack past frames with no watch on the link step, so drift creeps in. Their tracker turns those links into a step-by-step state forecast.

True target traits anchor each step and keep the forecast on course. A squeeze step strips spare facts so links stay sharp. On known test sets it set top marks while still running in real time. Watched reasoning beats blind stacking for frame links, they show.
arxiv-2507-17691:
Jiang, Kovuri, Tao, and Tan present CASCADE in twenty twenty-five, a tool built at Google to clean up scrambled code. Coders sometimes hide what their code does by renaming parts and shuffling its form. That blocks testing, safety checks, and the hunt for harmful code. Older tools need hundreds of hand written rules to undo the tricks.

CASCADE pairs a large AI model with a strict code rewriter. The AI finds the key helper blocks that most tricks rest on. The rewriter then restores real names and shows what the code truly does. The tool is already in use at Google and has cut the work of reading hidden code.
arxiv-2507-19091:
Xuanpeng Xiao and co-workers foretold alpha decay lifetimes of superheavy nuclei with a Bayesian neural network in a 2025 paper. Alpha decay half-lives guide the hunt for new elements, and the coupled-channels model with a nonlocal twist supplies the physics usual test. Adding a Bayesian network on top, the authors find nonlocal effects shift the math work materially. The network sharpens accuracy and extrapolates confidently beyond known nuclei.

An account tool ranks the inputs: the decay energy dominates the half-life, as physics expects. Applied to element chains beyond the current table's edge. The model flags a strong shell effect at a neutron count long foretold to be magic. Its forecasts obey the classic Geiger-Nuttall relation, a consistency check the authors highlight.
arxiv-2507-22291:
Christopher Brown and a large team introduce a model that maps the whole Earth from sparse labels. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called AlphaEarth Foundations. Satellites gather huge amounts of data, but ground truth labels are rare. Each mapping task has so far needed its own custom model.

Their model blends place, time, and measure type from many data sources into one code per spot. That code beat other known methods on many mapping tests without new training. The team has released a global yearly data set built from these codes. It aims to make maps and land watch tools faster to build at any scale.
arxiv-2507-23191:
When a database plus background knowledge answers a question, responsibility scores say how much each fact contributed. Meghyn Bienvenu, Diego Figueira and Pierre Lafourcade study how hard those scores are to compute in this knowledge-backed setting. They focus on new Shapley-inspired scores, built as weighted sums over the smallest fact sets that still yield the answer. Building on database results, they show the scores stay computable in reasonable time for queries rewritable as simple database queries.

The picture flips when the knowledge can express reachability. In the harder combined view, the problem is already intractable for simple questions when the language allows joining facts. The same holds for unions of well-behaved joined questions, even without any background knowledge. On the bright side, for common lightweight languages they carve out neatly structured question classes where the scores stay efficiently computable.
arxiv-2508-00291:
Haibin Zhang and co-authors report a joint hunt, with two Subaru-based instruments, for the flash of light from a candidate black hole merger, in a 2025 paper. Gravitational-wave detectors flagged the event, S250328ae, as a likely binary black hole merger some 500 million parsecs away, localized to a patch of sky. A wide-field camera, the Dark Energy Camera, swept the region and, after heavy filtering, kept thirty-six promising transient candidates.

A spectrograph then took spectra of those candidates, of X-ray picks from another satellite, and of possible host galaxies, nearly 3,900 targets in all. Fitting sorted the haul into a dozen supernovae, hundreds of quasars and galaxies, and assorted stars. Watching which sources changed over time narrowed the field further. The paper presents the search as a working template for camera-plus-spectrograph teamwork in multi-messenger astronomy.
arxiv-2508-01591:
Hanxi Li and six co-authors present a framework for spotting defects in industrial images in a 2025 paper. Standard detectors compare test images only against stored examples of normal products, which can miss subtle flaws. Their method also uses the test image itself as a source of reference material.

First, patches of the test image are compared with a bank of normal features, and patches that look most normal become self references. Comparing other patches against those references sharpens the defect signal. Both sets of difference features feed a sequence model whose attention heads steer toward suspect regions. On three standard benchmarks the method reached state of the art scores across detection and localization measures.
arxiv-2508-02091:
Xiaoya Li and four co-authors let a learning system write faster nearest-neighbor search code by treating speed itself as the reward. Approximate nearest-neighbor search underpins retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems, and hand-tuning its algorithms is slow expert work. Their framework, CRINN, reframes the tuning as reinforcement learning with contrastive signals.

The system generates candidate implementations and keeps the ones that run faster while holding accuracy. Across six standard benchmark datasets it took first place on three and tied for first on two more. The authors argue the lesson extends beyond search: language models with reinforcement learning can automate sophisticated algorithmic optimization. Code is released publicly.
arxiv-2508-02991:
Bangzheng Li and Yichen Xiao wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on localization for quantales. A quantale blends a complete lattice, a grid-like order of elements, with a way to multiply them. Localization is a classic trick that zooms in on part of an algebraic structure.

The authors copy the idea of a filter from lattice theory to build multiplicative filters for quantales. Zooming in at such a filter gives a localized quantale. They prove results shaped like the classic theorem that the spectrum of a ring forms a sheaf. Payoffs include the Baire Category Theorem and broader versions of it. They also state an algebraic form of that theorem they believe is new.
arxiv-2508-03791:
Abdelaali Boudjemaa wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It studies ultracold atomic gases with quadrupolar interactions, frozen into Bose-Einstein condensates, after a sudden change in their interaction strength, in the presence of random disorder.

Using an established approximation scheme, the author first maps the gas at rest: how disorder, interactions, and excitations reshape its density and energy, and where the math can be trusted. Then the interaction is quenched, jumped to a new value. In the long run, the gas settles with more quantum depletion and more disorder-driven deformation than at rest. The deformation rings with damped oscillations on the way, whose size depends on the disorder's grain size and the strength of the quadrupolar force. The work speaks to lab studies of dirty, interacting quantum gases.
arxiv-2508-05591:
Natalia Emelianova, Carlos Kamienski, and Ronaldo Prati test a new kind of neural network as a guard for Internet of Things networks. Connected devices are multiplying fast and have become prime targets for cyberattacks. The candidate networks, called Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, differ from standard ones by learning their activation curves instead of fixing them.

In intrusion detection tests, these networks beat classic multilayer perceptrons and matched strong tree-based systems such as Random Forest and XGBoost on accuracy. They also offered clearer insight into why an alert fired, a trait security teams value. The authors present the approach as a competitive, more readable option for spotting attacks on device networks.
arxiv-2508-06091:
Hauke and Wałęga settle an open ask about the power of graph nets in this twenty twenty-five paper. Graph nets learn from linked data, and past work tied one plain type to a known logic tongue. The open ask was if a type with a final read-out step could say more than that tongue can.

Inside, the pair proves the read-out type can in fact say strictly more than the whole tongue. The proof holds for graphs with one-way links and for graphs with two-way links alike. Their work also yields fresh facts on how strong a class of boundless logic tongues can be. The result caps a line of work that had stalled on this ask for years.
arxiv-2508-07291:
Minling Li, Chao Wang, and Zhifei Zhang prove that a simple shear flow stays stable even when a fluid barely resists motion, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The flow is Couette flow, where fluid layers slide past each other at a steady rate.

They work with the compressible Navier-Stokes equations in two dimensions at high Reynolds number. If the starting state sits close enough to the pure shear, with the gap shrinking as the Reynolds number grows, the flow exists for all time and stays close. Formal estimates suggest this closeness demand cannot be eased. The proof uses a Fourier multiplier method and new variables that untangle the system. It captures faster decay from mixing while taming the lift-up effect that can stretch disturbances.
arxiv-2508-07491:
Oleg Udalov sets out a 2025 method for building quantum circuits whose final state lands, with high chance, on one chosen string of bits. The circuits use random gates laid out in a brick-wall pattern. Midway through, the qubits can be strongly linked, yet the end state is a fixed pure string that the builder picks in advance.

Udalov also gives a way to hide that final string inside the circuit's structure, and to set how strong the peak should be. A changed version of the method can make circuits with two peaks or more. He then tests a standard way of simulating such circuits on a normal computer. The test shows it works well for shallow circuits but gives no real gain for deeper ones.
arxiv-2508-11891:
Gonzalo Herrera and Shunsaku Horiuchi calculate a new source of high-energy neutrinos: cosmic rays bouncing off supernova neutrinos. A supernova floods space with neutrinos at modest energies. A fast cosmic ray proton can strike one and hand it a huge boost. Crowded places like active galaxy cores hold plenty of both ingredients.

The team works out the flux this process would send to Earth. Under plausible conditions, today's giant neutrino telescopes could see it. The collisions reach energies where new physics might fatten the interaction rate. A fatter rate would raise the signal at both birth and detection. That double effect lets telescopes set fresh limits on the ultra-high-energy proton-neutrino cross section. The work turns a background process into a probe of physics beyond the standard model.
arxiv-2508-12091:
Muhammad Tayyab and Jahanzeb Tariq show that a deterministic map and a stochastic gas share deep correlation structure in their super-diffusive regimes. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies the slicer map, a deterministic system whose diffusion turns anomalous by tuning one parameter. Its position moments and low-order autocorrelations already shadow the Lévy-Lorentz gas closely. Low-order matches alone, though, cannot prove kinship of the underlying dynamics.

Higher-order correlations are the stricter test. The authors derive the slicer map's generalized autocorrelation analytically, including scaling forms for three-point functions across time orderings. Power-law tails from simulated gas data match those scalings. The map stands certified as a deterministic analog of the gas, enabling cheap prediction of multi-time correlations.
arxiv-2508-13291:
Foley, Mocz, Burkhart, Hernquist, and Goodman wrote in twenty twenty-five about turbulence behind shock waves in space gas. The gas between stars often moves faster than sound and churns in complex ways. The team ran sharp computer simulations of single shocks moving through such churning gas. They tracked how swirling energy grew before and after each shock passed. Their code models fluid motion on a moving grid.

Shocks boosted swirling energy behind them and gave the swirls a preferred direction. Energy and its loss also spiked near the shock front itself. Scaled to real superbubbles, such shocks could drive large flows of cold gas. The findings match related fluid studies. They help explain how shocks reshape the gas between stars.
arxiv-2508-13691:
Yuki Uematsu works out a theory of electric double layers in mixed liquids in this two thousand twenty-five paper. When a charged surface meets a liquid, ions gather in a diffuse layer near it. The layer's capacitance matters for devices like supercapacitors. Most theory treats a single pure liquid. Real systems often mix two liquids, and ions may prefer one over the other.

Uematsu derives the capacitance at the point of zero charge in closed form. The answer differs from the single-liquid shortcut unless both ion types share the same solvation preference. Near a surface instability line in the phase diagram, the capacitance blows up and strays far from the simple estimate. The results guide the design of energy storage that uses mixed electrolytes.
arxiv-2508-14191:
Alireza Khalilian and five co-authors build a flat-lens camera for plant health checks in a 2025 paper. Imaging that reads light polarization reveals tissue structure that plain brightness images miss, but the optics are bulky. Their array of tiny lenses, made from a silicon-rich material, captures two polarization directions at once at the exact color where chlorophyll absorbs. Chips are made with standard chip-factory processes.

Fused and difference maps showed structure direction and pigment variation in healthy and stressed leaves. The lenses reach high sharpness and light throughput while staying compact. The team presents the device as a scalable route to early, label-free detection of plant stress.
arxiv-2508-15491:
Bogdan-Vasile Matioc and Christoph Walker use a math tool for chance fields on the Hele-Shaw task. That task models fluid held tight in a thin gap. Skin pull drives the edge as it moves in this slow flow. The bulk flow is ruled by a set of math laws with fixed terms, set in bound shapes.

In this frame the team proves that a fix lasts for a short time and that the flow smooths out. They prove this in near best spaces for such tasks. They also set a broad rule for when a fixed fix stays firm, for a class of hard tasks. When they use it, the fixed fixes for Hele-Shaw prove firm and fade at a fast rate. The work shows this tool as a strong route into free edge fluid tasks.
arxiv-2508-15791:
Xiaolei Diao and six co-authors build InteChar, a unified character list that lets computers model ancient Chinese oracle bone script. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The earliest Chinese writing resists digitization because many of its characters were never encoded.

InteChar folds unencoded oracle bone glyphs together with traditional and modern characters in one extensible scheme. A companion corpus pairs expert-annotated inscriptions with model-assisted additions. Models trained on that corpus with the new encoding improved across many ancient-language tasks. Provenance studies and cultural history both depend on reading these bones at scale. The authors present the pair as foundation work for computational study of early Chinese.
arxiv-2508-16691:
Valle and Rizzuti, two authors listed by initials and surnames, rebuild a famous math link in 2025 from the physics of quantum states. The link ties the group of rotations in space to a larger group that drives two-level quantum systems. Each rotation matches two of the quantum operations, a two-to-one pairing.

Their route starts with how a lab prepares and changes a quantum state. They model each change as a process that must keep the state pure and be fully reversible. From those plain demands, the pairing between rotations and quantum operations falls out on its own. The authors offer the build-up as a clear teaching path into quantum symmetry, grounded in steps a lab can really carry out.
arxiv-2508-16791:
Quoc Tran-Dinh and Nghia Nguyen-Trung build methods that speed up like Nesterov's scheme and cut noise with variance reduction, for generalized equations whose operators may not behave in the usual way. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Such equations cover many data driven problems, past plain minimization. Operators that are not monotone break the rules that most fast methods rely on.

Their past-extragradient frame mixes old steps into each new step. Mini-batching and control-variate tricks keep the random estimates in line. Three well known tools for variance reduction fit the frame as variants. The rate of convergence in expectation beats non-accelerated rivals by a full order. The step sequence itself settles to a solution almost surely. Tests with numbers back the theory. Better oracle complexity is part of the gain, and the frame covers biased estimators too.
arxiv-2508-18291:
Alireza Khalilian and Hima Nikafshan Rad design a chip-scale biosensor tuned by a genetic algorithm. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The device senses changes in refractive index, a label-free way to spot chemicals. A metal-insulator-metal waveguide feeds a silicon ring resonator. Light coupling between them creates a sharp resonance. Small index changes shift that resonance measurably.

Finite-difference time-domain simulations drive the design search. The algorithm maximizes sensitivity and figure of merit while narrowing the line. The final device posts strong numbers on all three counts. Precise discrimination of tiny index changes follows. The design is compatible with standard CMOS fabrication. Medical and biochemical diagnostics are the aimed uses.
arxiv-2508-18391:
Nitin Nagesh Kulkarni, Bryson Wilcox, Max Sawa, and Jason Thom ground preference tuning in physics knowledge graphs. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets AI advice in fields like metal joining. Language models often cannot tell sound physics from slick nonsense. In joining, a wrong call can scrap parts, break gear, or hurt people. Their PKG-DPO frame welds a physics graph to direct preference optimization.

The graph encodes cross-domain links, conservation laws, and heat rules in ranked layers. A reasoning engine uses it to sort valid replies from invalid ones. A test suite scores rule compliance. Against a plain knowledge-graph variant, violations fell and physics scores rose. Parameter accuracy and reasoning alignment gained as well. Metal joining is the test bed, but the frame claims wider reach.
arxiv-2508-20291:
Heather Johnston and co-authors model how a young star's changing light shapes the birth of giant planets in a 2025 paper. Before a star settles onto the main sequence, its brightness shifts over the very years when its planet-forming disk is alive. That shifting light heats the disk, and stars of different masses shift in different ways. Most planet formation models leave this effect out.

The team ran pebble-driven core growth models for stars from one to somewhat above two solar masses. Giant planet formation proved sensitive to the light history: where and when a giant can form moves with it. Brighter light puffs up the gas and pebble layers, which can slow pebble capture and make giant growth harder. The work argues that a star's youth cannot be treated as a steady lamp.
arxiv-2508-20591:
Jose Puente and Carlos Puente explored in twenty twenty-five whether Bitcoin could serve as a shared monetary standard between Earth and Mars. The obstacles are physical: signals take minutes to cross the gap, links drop, and clocks cannot be casually trusted. Their answer centers on a new primitive, Proof-of-Transit Timestamping, which creates tamper-evident audit trails for Bitcoin data crossing those slow, intermittent links.

The proposed architecture replicates block headers first over delay-tolerant networks and low-orbit optical meshes, runs long-lived Lightning channels guarded by planetary watchtowers, and settles locally through federated sidechains. Mars would hold one-to-one pegged assets while Earth's base layer stays untouched. The authors are candid about limits: if both time-beacon regimes fall, the timestamping degrades to administrative assertion.
arxiv-2508-20891:
Luis Pena-Monino and Miguel Perez-Torres model radio signals from planets close to small red stars in two thousand twenty-five. A planet that moves inside its star's magnetic reach can stir radio emission from the star. Spotting that signal would offer a new way to find planets and probe their magnetic fields.

Their public code, SIRIO, is tested on three known systems where such signals have been claimed. The models say all three planets likely sit in the regime where the effect should work. One model of the signal predicts very faint emission, while a second, based on magnetic reconnection, gives better hopes. Gas absorption may also dim the signal in one system.
arxiv-2508-20991:
Patryk Będkowski and five co-authors present ExpertSim, a learning-based tool that simulates particle detector responses far faster than standard methods, in this 2025 arXiv paper. At CERN's Large Hadron Collider, simulating how detectors react to collisions eats huge computing time. Generative models could help, but detector data vary so much across cases that generic models struggle.

ExpertSim uses a team of generative experts, each trained on a slice of the data, aimed at the Zero Degree Calorimeter in the ALICE experiment. With each expert focused on its own kind of response, the system generates results that are both sharper and much quicker than the classic random-sampling approach. The authors share their code in public for other teams to build on.
arxiv-2508-21191:
Ali Rahimi Khojasteh and Dominique Heitz offered a physics-based forecaster in 2025 for the paths of particles carried by turbulent flow. Predicting where a drifting particle will go is hard because readings catch only snapshots in time. Their insight is that the flow's coherent motions, the set up forms that nearby particles share, carry enough information to reconstruct a likely path even from sparse findings.

The clue leans on Lagrangian coherent forms, the moving barriers that set up transport, and uses a finite-time Lyapunov exponent field to segment coherent paths locally. A new cost function then balances fidelity to the particle's logged place history against actual consistency with the surrounding coherent speed and acceleration fields. Tests on 3D synthetic data and on test readings of a cylinder wake showed the method can recover highly probable paths.
arxiv-2509-00091:
Ephraiem Sarabamoun, working alone, tests whether groups of local language models that debate each other reason better about alignment in 2025. Alignment means making AI act in line with human values, a key need as models take on high-stakes choices. Reliance on closed commercial services limits who can repeat or join such work.

Across one hundred fifty debates in fifteen scenarios and five group setups, groups beat single models on a seven-point rubric. Gains are largest for depth of reasoning and for argument quality. Truthfulness and human enhancement show the strongest jumps of all. Code, prompts, and the debate set are shared in public. Open local debates could widen who can study and test alignment methods.
arxiv-2509-00391:
Yuting Tan, Xuying Li, Zhuo Li, Huizhen Shu, and Peikang Hu appraise GCG adversarial attacks on large language models in 2025. GCG, Greedy Coordinate Gradient, crafts prompt suffixes that jailbreak a model's safety rules. An annealing-augmented variant, T-GCG, extends the method. The study tests both across open models of varied scale.

Three findings stand out. Attack success falls as model size grows, reflecting harder loss landscapes. Prefix-based heuristics greatly overstate success compared with strict semantic judgments by GPT-4o. Coding prompts prove far more vulnerable than safety prompts in the tests. The appraisal urges stricter, semantic evaluation before claims about jailbreak strength are trusted.
arxiv-2509-00591:
Lang Xiong leads seven authors in total, with Nishant Bhargava, Jianhang Hong, Jeremy Chang, Haihao Liu, Vasu Sharma, and Kevin Zhu, on evaluation awareness. Large language models may act differently when prompts feel like a test rather than real use, so benchmark scores may not show true safety or honesty.

Xiong and his co-authors build a probe that scores prompts from test-like to deploy-like, then rewrite prompts toward a natural style while keeping the task. Rewritten prompts raise honest replies, lower deceptive replies, and raise refusals across models. Their workflow, Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate, shows evaluation awareness can be measured and shifted, and argues for more realistic tests before deployment.
arxiv-2509-00691:
Alex Gulko, with two co-authors, introduces CE-Bench for sparse autoencoders. Sparse autoencoders try to uncover readable features inside large language models. Most automated checks of such tools rely on an outside model as judge. CE-Bench is built to avoid that judge. It is lightweight and contrastive in design.

The benchmark rests on curated pairs of stories. Each pair differs in a controlled way. Broad studies show CE-Bench measures interpretability in a reliable way. Its results align well with existing benchmarks. The team reports strong rank agreement with SAEBench results. No external language model judge is needed at any step. Code and data for the benchmark are open-sourced.
arxiv-2509-00791:
Michele De Solda leads a team of eight authors on cleaning seismic catalogues. Dense sensor networks now produce huge automated catalogs of earthquakes. Many are released without systematic quality control. They can contain false detections or events placed in the wrong spot. The team aims to clean such catalogs with computer vision.

Their workflow joins waveform-based location methods with deep learning image classification. It works on coherence matrices, grids formed by stacking waveforms. Real events show a single focused peak in that grid. Noise looks blurred and incoherent by contrast. Cleaning thus becomes a binary image classification problem. Waveform location also raises the resolution of event positions. Validation uses the public COSEISMIQ dataset.
arxiv-2509-01091:
Estimates in Bayesian work, where beliefs are updated with data, can jump around more than users would like. Minh-Long Nguyen, Christopher Drovandi, and Leah F. South study control variates, add-on terms that cut that spread. Many such terms rely on gradient data from the sampling method itself.

The team builds these terms by averaging many simple fits, an ensemble approach. They focus on a popular family called zero-variance control variates, which can overfit when a problem has many dimensions. The usual fix, penalized fitting, can be very slow. Their averaged version aims to keep the gains in precision without that cost. The work offers a faster way to get steadier estimates from the same samples.
arxiv-2509-01391:
Text-to-speech systems usually convert written characters into sounds through a step called grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, which needs costly hand-made phonetic records. Joonyong Park, Daisuke Saito, and Nobuaki Minematsu present a method that skips that step for mixed-script texts, such as Japanese writing that joins Kanji and Kana characters. A pre-trained speech model supplies discrete tokens learned from speech itself.

They train a T5 encoder to produce pseudo-language labels directly from such mixed text, using labels drawn from the speech model's tokens. The approach cuts the need for manual transcription and scales to large untranscribed audio sets. In tests, the system matched the performance of standard conversion-based speech synthesis. It also kept natural traits of speech, such as accents and intonation, pointing to cheaper voice building for complex scripts.
arxiv-2509-01691:
Filip Karpowicz, Wiktor Kepinski, Bartosz Staszynski, and Grzegorz Sarwas test whether shrinking image data helps sort photos that carry many labels at once. Their images hold many light bands, which makes them rich but heavy to process. The shrink step, called principal component analysis, squeezes the data down to three parts. Those parts then feed a small classifier built on two deep image networks.

How much the shrink step helps turns out to hinge on which network is used and how it is trained. In some setups it aids the task, and in others it does not. The authors point to self taught pre-training and other shrink methods as next steps. The study gives a clear map of when the simple shrink step is worth using.
arxiv-2509-02191:
Pieter Smet builds fake model scores to grade predict then optimize flows prior to real model work. Such flows feed model forecasts into an optimizer to back choices when key inputs are not known. Good forecasts do not always mean good choices, so the link needs checks in advance. Past fake based checks took just two class cases and forced many costly optimizer runs.

His way fakes multi class scores at set skill levels for inputs with class type doubt. Those fakes build a map from forecast error to choice regret for the flow. A first order shortcut from single class slip regret cuts the work by a lot. Tests show the faker hits its aimed skill and the shortcut tracks the full map. Truth fades when slips at the same time start to clash.
arxiv-2509-02291:
Isabel Rendell wrote a 2025 solo number theory paper on a step inside quadratic Chabauty, a method for finding rational points on curves. The test objects are Atkin-Lehner quotients of modular curves at prime level, with genus at least two.

Quadratic Chabauty needs a p-adic height, and that height needs a Hodge filtration for a certain vector bundle with connection. Rendell's algorithm computes that filtration from weakly holomorphic modular forms rather than from a plane equation for the curve, which speeds the computation. She runs it on a genus seven curve at level 193. The run also uncovers congruences linking iterated integrals of cusp forms across the two eigenspaces of the Atkin-Lehner involution, a symmetry of the curve.
arxiv-2509-02491:
Charles Pert, Dalal Alrajeh, and Alessandra Russo present a 2025 computer science paper testing whether recurrent neural networks can learn omega-regular languages, the infinite-word languages used to specify reactive system behaviour. Such languages are usually handled by Büchi automata, which face scaling problems.

Networks were trained on eventually repeating infinite words to mimic target automata built from temporal logic formulas. Test automata ranged from a handful of states to over a hundred. Networks were then judged on sequences far longer than any training example. Most tasks reached perfect or near-perfect generalisation at eight times the training length. The authors present this as the first such study, supporting neural components inside verification tools that mix learning with logic.
arxiv-2509-02791:
Skyler Degenkolb and five co-authors wrote a 2025 nuclear physics paper. It simulates ultracold neutron experiments. Those experiments hunt for a permanent electric dipole moment. That is a tiny charge split that would signal new physics. Reading such data demands faithful models of stored neutron ensembles.

The authors show stored and transported ultracold neutron traits can be simulated reliably. Those simulations then drive simulation-based inference. The method extracts parameters of neutron capture and beta decay. It matches simulated and measured behaviour to do so. The demo tackles a longstanding difficulty. Counts are very low, and the apparatus is complex. Reliable forward simulation plus modern inference offers a route to more physics from scarce neutron data.
arxiv-2509-03091:
A. A. Lagutin extended a 2025 theory of how shock waves in space accelerate cosmic rays. Cosmic rays are fast particles from beyond Earth, and a leading idea says shock fronts boost them by bouncing them back and forth. The standard theory assumes normal diffusion, where spread grows in a simple, steady way.

Lagutin allows stranger transport built on Lévy flights, occasional very long jumps, and Lévy traps, long pauses between moves. With that change, the spreading pattern gains heavy power-law tails instead of the classic bell shape. He derives a new formula for the slope of the particles' energy spectrum. It reduces to the standard slope under normal diffusion. It also recovers earlier results for the slower and faster spreading regimes.
arxiv-2509-03191:
Taiga Saito, Yu Otake, and Stephen Wu applied a tabular foundation model to geotechnical benchmark problems in 2025. Site characterization estimates soil properties, such as shear strength, from borehole data to guide construction. The benchmark, tied to an airport soil dataset, poses two tasks with real engineering stakes.

The model, TabPFN, is a transformer pretrained to handle small tables by learning from context examples at run time, with no tuning. One task predicts how undrained shear strength varies with depth; the other fills in missing mechanical parameters. Both drew extra context from a large indirect database of past sites. TabPFN beat a conventional hierarchical Bayesian model on accuracy and gave well-calibrated uncertainty. It was also far faster on the first task.
arxiv-2509-03291:
Krisztina Perger, Judit Fogasy, and Sándor Frey asked in 2025 whether little red dots could be stars being torn apart. Little red dots are compact early galaxies spotted by the James Webb Space Telescope, and their nature is unresolved. Leading ideas involve active black holes or dusty star formation, but neither explains the whole population.

Tidal disruption events, where a black hole shreds a passing star, offer an alternative. The authors test that idea against radio observations, which so far give only upper limits from stacking many dots. Radio-quiet disruptions fit those limits in any case they checked. Radio-loud ones fit only under special conditions. Weighing event rates, delayed radio flares, and the stretching of time in the early universe, they find the idea plausible from the radio side.
arxiv-2509-03391:
Trent D. Buskirk and 3 co-authors reviewed literature in 2025 on large language models inside survey research. Survey science has long been human-powered while eagerly adopting new technology for collecting and processing data. Language models promise help at every stage but bring new prerequisites and pitfalls.

The review, described as a working paper, searches several large databases and citation networks for documented uses. Findings are organized by the survey process: before data collection, during it, and after it. Examples show models drafting materials, assisting collection, and aiding analysis. Pitfalls drawn from the literature are discussed alongside the use cases. The authors argue that survey research's hard-won knowledge about data quality can guide how language models develop next.
arxiv-2509-03491:
Kanchan Shaikh and seven co-authors report a 2025 research paper on second-harmonic generation in a stacked two-layer material. One layer is tungsten disulfide and the other is rhenium diselenide, held together by weak van der Waals forces. Such stacking lets researchers tune how materials handle light.
