Historical revisionism, propaganda, and manipulation were the weakest spots. Models were most fragile for prompts set in this century or in history. Prompts tied to Latin America, the United States, and Britain drew refusals. The pattern shows safeguards tuned on harm do not travel to political terrain. The authors warn that refusals mirror systematic biases in the models.
arxiv-2510-05091:
Le Zhuo and ten co-authors confront a blind spot of image generators in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modern models paint beautiful natural images with ease. They stumble on structured visuals such as charts, diagrams, and math figures. Those images demand exact text, careful layout, and factual fidelity.

The team built a dataset of 1.3 million structured image pairs from executable drawing programs. They trained a unified model that couples a vision-language model with an image generator. A new benchmark, StructBench, tests over 1,700 hard cases with a question-based scoring method. Even leading closed models scored far from satisfactory in their tests. The authors' model edited strongly, and extra reasoning at inference helped every architecture.
arxiv-2510-05291:
Tarek Naous and twenty co-authors measure cultural bias in AI across Asian languages in this 2025 arXiv paper. Language models often favor Western-associated entities, as earlier Arabic studies showed. Whether the same bias appears across Asia was unknown for lack of benchmarks. Their benchmark, Camellia, covers nine Asian languages and six cultures.

Camellia contains 19,530 entities hand-labeled as Asian- or Western-associated. It adds 2,173 natural masked contexts drawn from social media posts. Four multilingual model families were tested on adaptation, sentiment, and extraction tasks. All models struggled to adapt culturally in every Asian language tested. Different families showed distinct sentiment biases of their own. Extraction quality also lagged for Asian entities, though gaps shrank when tests ran in English.
arxiv-2510-05491:
Li and colleagues improve the optimizer, the rule that updates a model during training. The standard optimizer, Adam, adjusts each weight on its own and ignores layer structure. A newer method, Muon, reshapes whole update matrices and often trains models faster. Their 2025 paper, NorMuon, tries to keep the strengths of both methods.

The team found a flaw in Muon, since some neurons receive far larger updates than others. NorMuon fixes that imbalance by tracking statistics for each neuron and scaling its updates evenly. The method keeps Muon's cleaner update geometry while adding Adam-style balance. In tests, NorMuon beat both rivals on training efficiency at a billion-parameter scale. Gains reached about one fifth over Adam and about one tenth over Muon. The authors also built a distributed version that spreads the heavy math across devices. Memory use stayed close to Muon's own footprint.
arxiv-2510-05991:
Cattaneo, Jansson, and Nagasawa make inference robust for pairwise difference estimators. Such estimators weigh pairs of data points that look alike in key traits. Older bell-curve results demand tight limits on the bandwidth. Their 2025 paper gives sound inference under far weaker demands.

Small bandwidth asymptotics stretch to the convex pairwise setting. Gaussian fits stay sound even with smaller-than-standard bandwidths. A jackknife debiasing method opens the door to larger bandwidths instead. That method keeps the goal's convex shape intact throughout. A new bootstrap corrects bandwidth-driven variance warps at the source. Three leading examples show the theory at work. Convexity is used with care throughout the proofs. Sound inference then holds across a wide range of bandwidth choices. Picking bandwidth from finer expansions is a planned next step. Built regressors pose an open problem the authors flag.
arxiv-2510-06191:
Mamajiwala and five co-authors speed up calibration of heart models for atrial fibrillation in a 2025 statistics paper. Fibrillation is a common arrhythmia of disordered atrial electrical activity, and standard catheter ablation is invasive and irreversible. Patient-specific digital twins could guide treatment, but only if calibration from routine measurements runs fast enough.

They frame calibration as a static inverse problem: infer tissue-level electrical parameters from observations. They replace the costly physics simulator with cheap Gaussian process emulators. Then they adapt the ensemble Kalman filter, normally a tracking tool, to this static nonlinear setting. The filter returns samples matching the best Gaussian approximation of the posterior. Benchmarked against Markov chain Monte Carlo, the approach held up while running far faster. Near-real-time calibration could let doctors predict ablation outcomes within clinical timescales. The recipe applies to static inverse problems across science and engineering.
arxiv-2510-06291:
Zhang and six co-authors generate real-looking GPS trajectories with a transformer-based diffusion model in a 2025 machine learning paper. Synthetic movement data helps researchers facing high collection costs and strict privacy limits. Earlier generators used convolutional UNet backbones, which drifted off route and lost street-level detail.

Their Trajectory Transformer uses a plain backbone for conditioning and noise prediction. They test two GPS embedding schemes: learned place embeddings and direct longitude–latitude embeddings. They also analyze performance across model scales. On two real-world datasets, the model clearly improved generation quality. The drift problems of convolutional generators were largely fixed. Generated paths kept street-level structure instead of cutting corners. The scale analysis also tells practitioners how large such a generator needs to be. Better synthetic trajectories let city teams train models and test policies without exposing real movements.
arxiv-2510-06391:
Elle examines whose opinions reward models actually reward in a 2025 computational linguistics paper. Reward models act as proxies for human preference during language model alignment. Yet their baked-in perspectives are poorly understood and may not represent everyone equally.

The paper formalizes a framework for measuring captured opinions. Controversial topics let the author quantify each model's attitudes and values. Sociodemographic bias is then measured group by group. The results are uncomfortable. Reward models align poorly with several demographic groups. They can even systematically reward harmful stereotypes. Prompting to steer toward a target group's preferences helps only partly. Steering alone cannot overcome the built-in misalignment. The findings argue for auditing reward models directly during preference learning. Without such care, alignment propagates the biases of whoever the reward model favors.
arxiv-2510-06691:
Jing-Zong Zhang and four colleagues use machine learning to read the debris of nuclear collisions. Their 2025 paper studies heavy-ion collisions, where nuclei smash together at high energy. The final-state data are rich but very high-dimensional. Hand-picked observables can miss subtle patterns in that data.

Their tool is a transformer-based autoencoder trained in two stages. First it learns from unlabeled collision data on its own. Then it is fine-tuned for specific physics tasks. As a test, the system sorted collisions into large and small system types. It reached much higher accuracy than PointNet, a standard baseline. Analysis with principal components and SHAP values showed what it had learned. The encoder captures tangled, nonlinear links between particles rather than single obvious measures. That makes its features both discriminative and open to interpretation. The approach could support many later analyses of collision data.
arxiv-2510-06791:
Changlin Song and four co-authors teach computers to find faces that are not even in the picture. Their 2025 paper defines a new vision task called extreme amodal face detection. Ordinary detection finds faces that are visible or partly hidden inside the frame. This task asks where faces sit outside the frame, within a wider view.

Such awareness helps privacy tools avoid capturing bystanders and helps robots plan around people. Older approaches needed video sequences or costly generative models to guess completions. The authors instead read context cues from a single image. Their detector predicts a heatmap of likely face locations beyond the edges. A selective coarse-to-fine decoder keeps the computation light. They built a dataset, EXAFace, to train and test systems on this task. Their method beat all compared approaches while using less computing power. It even outperformed the generative methods it was designed to replace.
arxiv-2510-07591:
Taguchi and Sproat present IASC, an interactive system that uses language models to invent constructed languages. Their 2025 paper serves two audiences: hobbyist worldbuilders and linguists testing how language designs hang together. The pipeline is modular and conversational. First an agent designs a target phonology, refining its attempt step by step against commentary feedback. Next, English sentences are translated into a morphosyntactic markup encoding the desired word order and feature specifications, with affixes represented as bundles of grammatical features.

Finally the system writes a short grammatical handbook, complete with sample sentences, and names the language itself. It can translate further sentences on demand. Configurations can mimic real typological profiles, such as a Welsh-like feature set detailed in the paper's tables.
arxiv-2510-07891:
Bermudez wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper asking why spacetime has a Lorentzian signature, . General relativity usually assumes that split. Bermudez builds a covariant theory where the signature emerges on its own. An internal tensor field defines the metric, and its eigenvalues set the signature. Two potentials shape the dynamics of that field.

A curvature potential drives geometry toward flatness. A signature potential has wells for every possible stable signature, . Our universe, in this picture, is a condensate that settled into the Lorentzian well. That phase is the only one supporting the wave-like equations that observable dynamics needs. Small ripples around it reproduce general relativity at low energies. Jumps between signatures are exponentially rare. The theory offers a simple origin story for both the flatness and the causal shape of spacetime. Signature change has a long history in quantum cosmology.
arxiv-2510-08091:
Palta and Rankel wrote this 2025 paper testing whether language-model arguments can move human judgments of plausibility. Commonsense benchmarks ask which answer sounds most plausible, and such answers are rarely provable. The authors collected three thousand human judgments and over thirteen thousand from language models. Each answer appeared with a model-written argument for it, against it, both, or neither.

Human ratings rose when a supporting rationale appeared and fell when an opposing one did. People found the model arguments convincing overall. Language models showed the same pattern, with even higher sensitivity. The findings cut two ways. Persuasive rationales could help people stress-test arguments. They could also steer beliefs in domains where humans feel expert, quietly undermining independent judgment. The authors argue safeguards matter as model explanations spread.
arxiv-2510-08191:
Yuzheng Cai and a team at Tencent Youtu Lab present a 2025 arXiv paper on teaching large language models new skills without retraining them. Their method, called Training-Free GRPO, targets AI agents that lose skill in niche fields. Such agents often struggle to use tools well or to follow the right prompts. Standard fixes retrain the model, which costs a lot and needs much data.

Instead of changing model weights, the team stores lessons from past tries as text guidance. The system runs each task in groups, judges which tries worked best in words, and saves that know-how. It then feeds the saved lessons back during later calls to steer the model. Tests on math problems and web search used DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus, a very large model. With just a few dozen training examples, the method beat small models that had been fine-tuned in the usual costly way.
arxiv-2510-08391:
Yue Yu and Myung-Joong Hwang describe a surprising symmetry effect in quantum phase transitions in a 2025 arXiv paper. When a system breaks a discrete two-fold symmetry, its low-energy excitations usually share that same discrete symmetry. Their theory studies systems with anisotropic long-range interactions, where distant parts interact unevenly. An order parameter measures how strongly the symmetry is broken.

In their model, the order parameter rescales two competing kinds of interaction terms. When one rescaled interaction vanishes, a new conservation law appears that the original Hamiltonian lacked. That law amounts to an emergent continuous symmetry in the broken phase. A striking effect follows: quantum correlations in the ground state are forced to zero. The ground state factorizes, splitting into independent parts, despite strong interactions. The authors call this a universal feature of fully connected systems and their lattice versions.
arxiv-2510-08791:
Zou and Yin build a system that answers questions about medical images, in this 2025 arXiv paper on visual question answering. A doctor or student might show the system a scan and ask what it shows. Good answers require the model to line up image content with question wording at several levels. Earlier systems aligned the two in piecemeal ways and often absorbed irrelevant outside knowledge.

Their framework unifies alignment across levels, views, and training stages, using contrastive learning and a transport method that matches distributions. It also mines hard negatives, meaning look-alike wrong answers, and forces the model to tell them apart using soft labels. A gated attention step then pulls in only the useful parts of a ready-made answer vocabulary. The system beat prior best results on four public test sets for medical image questions.
arxiv-2510-08891:
Wang and colleagues build a virtual clinic where future health professionals learn to work as a team, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Students in pharmacy, medicine, nursing, and social work must practice collaboration before real patients depend on it. The traditional stand-ins, case studies and hired actors, are costly and cannot reproduce the shifting complexity of real care. The team's system, AIMS, replaces the actor with an AI patient inside a three-dimensional virtual space.

A large language model drives the patient's speech, while a game engine renders the scene and a character pipeline shapes the patient's appearance. In a formal usability session, students took their professional roles and mixed scripted exchanges with free conversation, probing symptoms, home context, and care needs. Testers found the conversations realistic and suited to each profession. Glitches in audio routing and reply speed were logged and fed into the next round of fixes.
arxiv-2510-08991:
Jiang, Zhang, and Findlater explore how AI image descriptions could open visual workplace tasks to blind and low vision professionals, in this 2025 arXiv workshop paper. Many jobs quietly demand visual work: building slide decks, editing photos, reviewing a colleague's design. Traditional aids supply bare access to images but stop short of supporting full participation, which feeds both exclusion and stigma. Generative AI can now describe images with context and personalization.

The authors organize professional needs into creating, critiquing, and consuming visual content, and give design suggestions for each. Good descriptions, they argue, should carry the specialized insight a task needs, such as design principles, spatial layout, and aesthetic quality. They develop the point through cases including a blind video creator who films and edits content. Their closing argument is that well-contextualized descriptions can build autonomy, inclusion, and skills over a career, not merely access in the moment.
arxiv-2510-09091:
Yu and colleagues review what the lowest radio frequencies reveal about pulsars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A pulsar's radio spectrum, its brightness across frequencies, carries fingerprints of the emission engine, the star's magnetosphere, and the thin gas the signal crosses on its way to Earth. New telescopes in the Netherlands, the United States, and Australia have opened the band below three hundred fifty megahertz in recent years. Pulsars there behave in strikingly varied ways.

The review maps the shapes those spectra take and the progress made in modeling them. It explains the physical processes that bend the low-frequency end, including absorption and the scattering that smears pulses in interstellar gas. Several outstanding puzzles about the emission mechanism remain open. The authors look to SKA-Low, the coming Australian array with unprecedented sensitivity, to resolve them. They frame such spectra as a precision probe of extreme physics around neutron stars.
arxiv-2510-09491:
Siddhartha Mangamuri, Lénaïc Couëdel, and Surabhi Jaiswal study a two-layer plasma crystal in a 2025 arXiv paper. A dusty plasma holds tiny particles that arrange into ordered crystals, and a bilayer crystal has two stacked layers. The authors formed a stable hexagonal bilayer of melamine formaldehyde particles inside a confinement ring in an argon discharge, then varied the ring's voltage.

Adjusting the voltage produced a clear coexistence: a melted, fluid-like core surrounded by a solid crystalline edge. Sound wave spectra of the crystal shifted in ways that the classic single-layer mode-coupling instability theory does not predict. Further analysis tied the melting to particles pairing dynamically across the layers, which strengthens non-reciprocal interactions between them. The findings highlight interlayer coupling and confinement as underappreciated drivers of melting in layered plasmas.
arxiv-2510-09791:
Sneha Gathani and seven co-authors, among them Peter Haas and Zhicheng Liu, write a grammar for what-if analysis in a 2025 arXiv paper. Analysts use what-if questions to explore hypothetical scenarios and alternative paths to a goal. Tools support the practice under scattered terminologies with incompatible techniques, which limits expressiveness, reuse, and integration with AI.

From recurring patterns across one hundred forty-one publications in visual analytics and human-computer interaction, the authors derive PRAXA, a compositional grammar. It has three primitives: the data under analysis, the predictive model, and interaction operations pairing user actions with system responses. They encode the grammar in a declarative specification language. Reconstructing earlier workflows as PRAXA compositions exposed a bias toward single-step rather than multi-step reasoning. Capabilities described with different terms turned out to share one structure under different settings, and genuinely new multi-step workflows emerged by composition.
arxiv-2510-10191:
Dong and co-authors mitigate bias in face gender classification in this 2025 arXiv paper on fair machine learning. Face gender models often mirror the demographic biases of their training data, performing unevenly across gender and racial subgroups. The usual fix needs labeled demographic data, which is often unavailable.

The authors introduce pseudo-balancing, a strategy for semi-supervised learning that works without such labels. It balances the training mix using the model's own predicted structure rather than true demographic tags. The approach aims to even out subgroup performance while respecting privacy limits on collecting sensitive attributes. Fairness without labels matters because the settings that most need debiasing are often those where labels cannot be gathered.
arxiv-2510-10291:
Barbieri, Blot, Sablik, and Salo give a geometric barrier to self-simulation for groups in this 2025 arXiv paper in symbolic dynamics. A subshift is a set of patterns on a group, like tilings with local rules. Self-simulation asks whether a system can reproduce its own behavior at a larger scale.

The authors introduce a new invariant for finitely generated groups, unchanged by quasi-isometry, that is, by rough geometric distortion. They show every group with this property carries a subshift that is effectively closed by patterns yet cannot be realized as a factor of any subshift of finite type. That is a concrete obstruction: some pattern systems provably cannot be simulated by the simplest rule-based ones.
arxiv-2510-10391:
Roche and co-authors show a breakdown of the Wiedemann-Franz law in this 2025 arXiv paper in mesoscopic physics. The law ties a material's heat conduction to its charge conduction, and it holds widely for electrons in ballistic channels under the standard Landauer-Büttiker framework. Strong Coulomb interactions break that framework.

The authors study a chain of small metallic dots, connected by ballistic channels, where charge cannot pile up on the dots. They show theoretically that this interacting quantum Hall metamaterial conducts heat better than charge, violating the law's fixed ratio. The result identifies a clean setting where interaction effects rewrite a textbook transport rule, with implications for heat management in quantum devices.
arxiv-2510-10591:
Zachary Selk proves a transformation formula for a generalized probability density, in this short 2025 arXiv note. The setting is a metric measure space: a set equipped with both a distance and a measure. On such spaces, the Onsager-Machlup functional plays the role of a density, assigning relative likelihoods to points. Researchers had studied what happens when the measure is reweighted, meaning some regions count more than others. The matching question for the metric was open.

Selk settles both at once. For geodesic metric measure spaces, where shortest paths exist between points, he proves how the Onsager-Machlup functional changes when the metric and the measure are reweighted together. The formula tells exactly how the density-like values transform under such reweightings. This closes a gap in the theory of these functionals, used for most likely paths of random processes on very general spaces.
arxiv-2510-10791:
Dale Zhou and six co-authors argue that memory tells similar things apart by throwing information away, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The standard view says discrimination works by expanding neural codes so similar stimuli get maximally distinct representations. The rival compression hypothesis says the brain instead applies lossy compression, discarding seemingly irrelevant detail. The team tests the two ideas by predicting performance on the mnemonic similarity task, a standard test of telling lures from studied items.

They train neural networks to compress perceptual and semantic factors, and measure lossiness with a mathematical framework. Greater lossiness predicted easier and better lure discrimination, matching compression and not expansion, especially in deeper network layers tied to higher visual areas. They confirm this across two image sets and four behavioral datasets. Brain imaging then found signatures of compression in visual regions V4 and IT and in hippocampal subfields, linked to discrimination.
arxiv-2510-10891:
Jinxin Xiong and six co-authors speed up a core power grid optimization by fixing variables step by step, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Security constrained unit commitment decides which generators run, subject to contingencies. Its bottleneck is solving huge linear programming relaxations inside branch and cut solvers. Classical methods need costly matrix factorizations at this scale. First order methods avoid those, but they converge to non vertex solutions that standard machinery cannot use.

Their successive fixing framework bridges the gap. A customized, GPU accelerated first order solver guides a logic driven strategy that fixes variables. Each round yields a smaller mixed integer problem, tightened further by presolving. The cycle of relaxing, fixing, and presolving progressively shrinks the problem into a tractable final model. On public benchmarks exceeding 13,000 buses, the approach achieved a tenfold speedup over state of the art methods, without compromising solution quality.
arxiv-2510-11291:
Scheduling radio resources in future 6G networks means granting airtime under interference limits, fast fading, and strict compute budgets. Muhammad Bilal and Xiaolong Xu propose a spiking neural network scheduler for open radio access networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their NOS scheduler borrows its dynamics from neurons: an excitability state stands in for buffer pressure, and a recovery state suppresses repeated grants.

A small-signal analysis compresses topology, controller gain, and control delay into one design number, a spectral margin that the authors use to prove stability results. When the margin is positive, the system is geometrically ergodic and the backlog and delay tails decay in a controlled sub-Gaussian way. In numerical studies sweeping control delays from 5 to 20 milliseconds, the scheduler sustained higher utilization and smaller extreme delays than proportional-fair and backpressure baselines. Every grant stayed feasible on integer resource blocks.
arxiv-2510-11791:
Afif Omar and Adam Ritz use the universe's first minutes to test light dark matter. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies thermal relic candidates lighter than one giga-electronvolt. Such particles keep annihilating faintly even after their abundance freezes out. If those late annihilations spray pions and kaons into the young universe, they can shift the balance of protons and neutrons. That shift would spoil the predicted amounts of light elements forged in big bang nucleosynthesis.

Omar and Ritz focus on candidates whose annihilation is p-wave, meaning it slows as particles move slower, which hides them from many other tests. They show the injected hadrons interact before the deuterium bottleneck, the step that gates all later element building. This makes nucleosynthesis a sharper probe than the cosmic microwave background or present-day searches in the galaxy. Whole classes of light dark matter models, long considered safe, face exclusion by this argument.
arxiv-2510-12191:
Raz studies how much a polynomial in three variables can expand finite sets of real numbers, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. An expanding polynomial takes inputs from three sets and produces many more distinct output values than the inputs contain. Raz extends a method called the proximity technique, first developed by Solymosi and Zahl, from the two variable case to three variables.

She works with a specific polynomial built from a squared difference and a second squared term involving a further polynomial of degree at least three. For input sets that each contain the same number of points, she proves the output set grows with an exponent of five thirds, up to a small loss. This improves the earlier exponent of three halves proved by Raz, Sharir, and De Zeeuw. No three variable polynomial was previously known to expand this strongly.
arxiv-2510-12491:
Arendt, Yusef-Zadeh, and Heywood catalogue the radio filaments threading the innermost region of the Milky Way, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The central molecular zone, the dense gas ring around the galactic center, hosts many thin thread like structures. The authors imaged the innermost two hundred parsecs with the MeerKAT radio telescope, working near one point three gigahertz.

The catalogue was generated by repurposing software built to detect filaments in solar coronal loops. It has two parts. A main catalogue lists places and basic properties point by point along each filament. A summary catalogue gives mean, median, or total values per filament. Tabulated values include length, position, curvature, brightness, and spectral index. The contents mix nonthermal radio filaments, parts of supernova remnants, and heat emitting regions. The authors discuss how to select useful subsamples and flag details to watch for when examining filaments.
arxiv-2510-12591:
Brevidelli raises the lower bound on the size of any faithful linear representation of a surface's mapping class group, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The mapping class group collects the distinct ways to deform a surface. A faithful representation realizes it as matrices without collapsing distinct elements. Korkmaz had shown any such representation of a genus g surface needs dimension at least a linear bound in g.

Brevidelli improves that bound greatly for genus at least seven. A new element is a finer study of commutation relations, using a specific pants decomposition of the surface. He shows any representation below the new threshold must kill one natural subgroup of the Torelli group. Lower bounds for related groups follow, from the Johnson group to pure braid groups, all growing linearly in genus or strand count. He also gives evidence that better low genus bounds would lift the result.
arxiv-2510-13091:
Zheng and Shan investigate hiring bias on online freelance marketplaces in this 2025 arXiv paper. These platforms promise a fair arena where skills decide hiring, yet profile details such as gender and region may still sway decisions. Earlier studies mostly mined existing platform data, where confounding factors make bias hard to isolate cleanly.

The authors generate realistic artificial freelancer profiles with a retrieval-augmented language model. This lets them vary one trait at a time in controlled experiments. They pair this with statistical analysis of real post-project data. On gender, initial hiring decisions showed no significant preference, but female freelancers were substantially more likely to receive imperfect ratings after projects ended. Regional bias was strong and consistent: United States-based freelancers were chosen more often in simulations, perceived as more leader-like, and rated higher on the live platform.
arxiv-2510-13391:
Kempinski and Kachman use graph neural networks to estimate Banzhaf values in network flow games. Their 2025 arXiv paper measures how much influence each agent holds in a shared network. Exact computation explodes in cost beyond about twenty agents, which blocks large systems. Sampling methods give rough estimates but cannot reuse knowledge across networks.

The authors frame the task as predicting one value for a whole graph from its structure. They train three network designs on synthetic data covering 200,000 graphs per configuration. The graphs vary in size, agent count, and link density, which broadens the training range. Trained models match exact values closely while running far faster than exact or sampling methods. Most strikingly, they predict values for entirely new network shapes with no retraining. This zero-shot transfer makes the method practical for large, changing systems.
arxiv-2510-13691:
Di Florio, Dong, and Rotolo build a modal logic for verifying machine learning classifiers that reason about legal cases. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets classifiers which predict case outcomes from past decisions, mimicking case-based reasoning. In common law, precedent binds future rulings, yet earlier logic models assumed case bases never conflict. Real courts face clashing precedents head-on.

Their logic adds two dimensions that real legal systems use to settle such clashes. One is time: newer decisions can outweigh older ones. The other is court hierarchy: higher courts outrank lower ones. Together they encode the temporal-hierarchical rule for resolving conflicts between precedents. The logic formally captures legal case-based reasoning with these principles built in. That gives verification tools a way to check classifier outputs against precedential constraint. The work bridges symbolic logic, law, and machine learning assurance.
arxiv-2510-13891:
Yao and co-authors select keyframes for long videos by predicting whole meaningful clips instead of scattered stills. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces K-frames for multimodal models whose context windows choke on full videos. Uniform sampling throws away crucial moments in hour-long footage. Retrieval or reinforcement methods return sparse frames that break scene continuity.

K-frames first predicts semantically coherent, query-relevant clips from the video. Any number of keyframes can then be drawn from those clips to fit a user's budget. A new dataset, PeakClips, supplies two hundred thousand query-conditioned video highlights for training. Learning proceeds through two supervised stages, then a reinforcement stage tuning the policy directly. The stages teach temporal grounding first, then key-clip perception, then end-task performance. Major long-video benchmarks show the approach works at many frame budgets. The authors release the dataset and model as a plug-and-play tool.
arxiv-2510-14291:
Shoichi Oshino and co-authors classify the glitch noise plaguing Japan's KAGRA gravitational-wave detector using machine learning that needs no labeled examples, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Glitches are bursts of nonstationary noise that mimic or mask real signals, and sorting them into types is essential for improving detector reliability and sensitivity.

Working with data from the O3GK observing run, the team trained a variational autoencoder, a network that compresses images into a compact latent code, on glitch images. They reduced the latent variables to three dimensions for visualization. They grouped them with spectral clustering. The procedure identified eight distinct glitch categories, revealing the characteristic noise families of KAGRA during that run. The authors argue unsupervised classification of this kind can guide interferometer upgrades and will matter even more for third-generation observatories, where data volumes make manual glitch hunting impossible.
arxiv-2510-14391:
Jaehoon Ahn, Tae Gum Hwang, and Moon-Ryul Jung redesign beat tracking, the detection of beats and downbeats in music, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their model can learn from data sets that label only beats. Conventional trackers use two binary classifiers for beats and downbeats because one multi-class head cannot use beat-only annotations, and the heads can disagree, forcing post-processing.

Their model, AlignBeat, predicts a set of grid points. Each carries an event time and a probability distribution over downbeat, beat, and no event. A downbeat is automatically also a beat, and no reconciliation is needed. The alignment between grid points and events is a latent variable fitted by expectation-maximization, with unrecorded downbeat labels marginalized out. Across eighteen data sets, keeping beat-only data raised tracking scores, and downbeat accuracy beat the Beat This system with no post-processing.
arxiv-2510-14591:
Lam and co-authors argue, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that language models give bland results when nobody states what the user actually wants right now. Asked to help with a draft, a model with no specific objective falls back on clichés. The authors propose inferring what the user wants in the moment, then optimizing hard for that single goal. They call these just-in-time objectives.

Their architecture watches user behavior passively to guess the current objective. It then steers generation and evaluation against that objective. A guessed goal like clarifying a paper's contribution can trigger custom tools, for example one that critiques a draft using field-specific methods. In experiments with participants working on their own tasks, outputs guided this way won 66 to 86 percent of comparisons against ordinary model output, depending on the study. In-person sessions confirmed that each participant received tools shaped to their own work.
arxiv-2510-14691:
Nunes, Borges, Cruz, and Darin argue, in a 2025 arXiv workshop paper, that game audio deserves a central place in designing play that helps rather than harms. Escapism in games can aid recovery after stress, or slide into harmful avoidance. What separates the two, the authors suggest, is self-regulation: the player's autonomy combined with good outcomes. Sound, usually treated as decoration, shapes that regulation in concrete ways.

Audio can raise or lower arousal, signal that a session or scene is ending, and give a sense of closure. Despite this, its contribution to player well-being is barely studied. The authors identify gaps in methods and in accessibility that keep audio's role invisible. They outline ways to close those gaps, so researchers measure sound's effects properly and developers design for listeners with different needs. Their aim is to move audio from an afterthought to a deliberate tool for healthier escapist play.
arxiv-2510-14791:
Jian and a large team of co-authors measure, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how much phosphorus stars of different ages carry. Phosphorus traces the Milky Way's chemical history, but observations are scarce, so its evolution is poorly mapped. The team took high-resolution near-infrared spectra of 102 giant stars: eighty-two in twenty-four open clusters, plus twenty Cepheid variables, using the GIANO-B instrument.

They confirm that the ratio of phosphorus to iron declines as iron grows, around the Sun's composition, matching earlier work. Among clusters older than a billion years, the phosphorus ratio also varies with age, a time-dependent enrichment pattern. The authors explain it by each cluster's parent gas: older clusters formed where star formation ran more efficiently. Younger clusters and Cepheids show a flat trend, hinting that earlier generations of low-mass stars supplied their phosphorus.
arxiv-2510-15691:
Stock picking uses number-based factors, but news text may carry signals those factors miss. Tian Guo and Emmanuel Hauptmann test combining both sources in this 2025 arXiv finance paper. A large language model turns newsflow into vector representations alongside classic quantitative factors. Their fusion framework merges the two representation sets into one input for return prediction. They compare three fusion designs of increasing complexity, from simple combination to attentive merging.

The simplest method, representation combination, generally beats the more complex fusion designs. A mixture model that blends single-source and fused predictions performs comparably or better. Fine-tuning the language model during training does not consistently help across investment universes.
arxiv-2510-15991:
Huiming Yang leads ten co-authors in a sparse detector that finds objects in three dimensions from camera and LiDAR together. Sparse detectors beat bird's-eye-view designs on adaptability and cost. Yet they often waste tokens on weak foreground features. Geometry kept in the tokens is one key, the team argues. Balance across classes is the other key to strong results.

Their Sparse Selector adds ray-aware supervision. It preserves rich geometry through the training stage. Class-balanced supervision reweights rare classes, so tokens for small objects survive sampling. A ray positional encoding handles the gap in distribution between LiDAR and image inputs. The full detector, CrossRay3D, leads on the nuScenes benchmark on both accuracy scores the authors use. It runs faster than leading rivals. It also stays robust when one sensor feed is partly or wholly missing.
arxiv-2510-16191:
Salvador E Ayala-Raggi and Manuel Rendón-Marín chase a neater formula for the perimeter of an ellipse. No exact formula exists in simple functions, so mathematicians since the seventeen hundreds have traded accuracy against ease of use. Ramanujan's second formula is the classic short one, and this work aims to sharpen it without making it long.

Their fix divides Ramanujan's formula by one minus a small pair of exponential terms, using just four constants. Across ellipse shapes from a circle down to a near-flat sliver, the error stays under about six parts in ten million. That is twenty-five times tighter than the Cantrell formula, a leading rival. The result is a rare mix: a one-line formula that is nearly exact at both extremes.
arxiv-2510-16391:
Renzhi He, Haowen Zhou, Yubei Chen, and Yi Xue present a 2025 method for building 3D views of living cells. Old tools need hundreds of flat images to build one solid view. That is too slow for cells that change fast. Their method, called NVP, learns from just a few views taken through a microscope.

NVP blends two kinds of learned shape models and adds rules from how light bends. Tests on fake and real cell images show sharp results with far fewer views. The team reports about fifty times fewer images and three times less wait. Fast cell views could help track life as it moves.
arxiv-2510-16591:
Cassidy Ashworth, Pietro Liò, and Francesco Caso probe how symmetry shapes learning in a 2025 paper. Their test task is a renormalisation step, a way to zoom out on a system. Symmetry means parts of a model can swap with no change in act. Past work hints that breaks and fixes of such symmetry drive layered learning. They use a sum rule from stats as a clean test map.

They train plain layered nets and graph nets with varied symmetry and maths forms. Too much symmetry or too much free form both hurt new-case scores. Proofs show why some tight nets fail to spread their sums well. Tests extend the same lens to graph nets and their inner steps. The work flags a sweet spot between strict form and free form.
arxiv-2510-16691:
Maksym Mohorian and six co-authors measure chemical abundances in dying stars that orbit a companion and hold a stable disc of gas and dust. These post-AGB and post-RGB binaries often show a strange pattern: heat-resistant elements are scarce in the star while volatile ones remain. The pattern comes from the star taking in volatile-rich gas from its disc.

The team picked systems with faint discs and read high-resolution spectra from two telescope instruments for six targets in our galaxy and two in the Large Magellanic Cloud. They derived abundances for twenty-nine elements, with corrections for effects beyond local equilibrium. All targets showed saturated depletion patterns, which the authors link to how their discs evolve.
arxiv-2510-16791:
Chengxuan Zhu and six co-authors teach a system to copy the photographic style of reference images and apply it to new photos. Style here means the bundle of choices behind a photographer's look, from color to contrast. Earlier tools either failed to learn clear style concepts or damaged the content of the photo being restyled.

Their Personalized Image Filter builds on a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model. The model first learns the average look of named photographic concepts and how text prompts adjust them. Textual inversion then fits prompts to a set of reference photos. Tests show strong extraction and transfer of many styles while keeping the subject of each photo intact.
arxiv-2510-16891:
Ramon Dalmau, Gabriel Jarry, and Philippe Very match airplane contrails seen by ground cameras to the flights that made them. Contrails can grow into thin cirrus clouds that warm the climate, with an effect that may rival aviation's carbon dioxide. Models of that growth need ground truth linking each trail to its flight.

Satellites often catch contrails too late, after wind has bent them out of shape. Ground cameras instead record trails soon after formation, while they are still thin and straight. Using a public camera data set plus aircraft surveillance and weather data, the team builds a modular attribution framework. It compares observed trails with predicted trails from known flights.
arxiv-2510-16991:
Yahli Hecht and Muli Safra prove firm hardness results for lattice problems in a 2025 paper. The Shortest Vector Problem asks for the shortest nonzero vector in a lattice. A lattice is a regular grid of points in high dimensions. The unique variant promises one shortest vector stands apart.

Earlier hardness results relied on randomized arguments, except one norm. The authors now prove deterministic hardness for every relevant norm family. No efficient algorithm can approximate these problems within set ratios. That conclusion rests on standard assumptions about hard logic problems. For some norms, the forbidden approximation ratios grow huge. The results improve on earlier randomized work by Haviv and Regev. They matter because lattice problems underpin proposed post-quantum cryptography.
arxiv-2510-17391:
Reinforcement learning agents that judge success by average reward, rather than by a discounted total, are common in ongoing tasks like traffic control. Jongmin Lee and Ernest K Ryu give the first firm sample bounds for learning such policies offline, from fixed data, while using function approximation to generalise. Earlier work in this setting leaned on strong assumptions about how the system moves between states.

Lee and Ryu add an anchor mechanism to a standard method called fitted Q-iteration, which repeatedly refits a value estimate from the stored data. The anchor acts much like weight decay and turns out to be the key piece that makes a finite time analysis possible. Their results also cover data gathered as one long trajectory instead of independent samples.
arxiv-2510-17691:
Bama Srinivasan borrows from an old Indian school of thought to order AI agent instructions in a 2025 arXiv paper. The school is Mimamsa, which long studied how ritual steps should be sequenced. Srinivasan states its rules in formal terms using action object pairs. Three patterns cover time order from direct claims, task order from purpose, and repeated tasks run in line or side by side.

The framework defines a logic for action object commands with clear rules for drawing conclusions. It extends an earlier system called MIRA, built with Parthasarathi in 2021. A proven theorem ties correct order to how objects depend on each other across steps. Proofs of soundness and completeness back the system. Sound sequencing matters for task planning, robotics, and time based reasoning in agents.
arxiv-2510-17791:
Roberto Hernandez computes all rational points on certain genus three hyperelliptic curves. These curves are defined by a polynomial equation with a parameter. Rational points are solutions where both coordinates are ordinary fractions. Finding all of them is a classic hard number theory task.

Hernandez uses a method first built by Dem'yanenko and extended by Manin. A rival method, Chabauty-Coleman, applies to some family members but runs slower here. He adapts an approach by Kulesz and adds root number checks. Those checks narrow the possible ranks of related elliptic curves. The Jacobian of each curve splits into those simpler pieces.
arxiv-2510-18091:
Rohan Choudhury, with five co-authors, speeds up vision transformers by cutting images into patches of mixed sizes. Standard models use one patch size everywhere, so sharp high-resolution pictures create very long token lists. Their adaptive method gives big patches to plain regions and small patches to busy regions of the same image.

Throughput rose sharply on large models while task scores held steady. The scheme can be added to an already trained model and settles in about one extra pass. It also cut time on dense tasks like detection and segmentation. Vision teams get faster models without retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2510-18291:
Tuan Pham, with Thanh-Tung Le and two co-authors, presents GeoDiff in a 2025 paper on depth estimation. Depth estimation means judging how far each point in a photo sits from the camera. Single photos give relative depth well, but absolute distance stays ambiguous without a scale cue.

GeoDiff treats depth recovery as an inverse problem, meaning it works backward from images to the hidden scene. It pairs a pretrained diffusion model, which generates images by gradual denoising, with stereo geometry constraints. The method needs no retraining and plugs into existing depth frameworks. Tests show it matches or beats leading methods, even on shiny and translucent surfaces.
arxiv-2510-18591:
Chia-Hsuan Lu, together with Tony Tan and Michael Benedikt, works on checking whether a graph neural network can be fooled by tiny changes to its input graph. An attacker who can rewire a few links or alter a few values might flip the network's answer, and deciding whether such an attack exists is called robustness verification. Leading tools translate the question into hard constraint problems and hand them to powerful general solvers.

The authors show that lighter solvers can do better. Their partial solvers always finish quickly, in polynomial time, though they may sometimes leave a case undecided. Trading completeness for speed improved on the state of the art for structural attacks. Their tool, RobLight, was evaluated across a varied set of network designs and data sets, making a case that robustness checking need not rely on the heaviest machinery available.
arxiv-2510-18691:
Feras AlMannaa, with Talia Tseriotou, Jenny Chim, and Maria Liakata, runs the first study of how language models handle long medical records when answering clinical questions, going beyond multiple-choice tests. Real care involves a patient's full context, which can be long and partly irrelevant. The team varied the size and relevance of included content, used models of different strengths, and tested several data sets with different question styles.

Their analysis exposes effects of model size, signs of memorization, and benefits from reasoning-style models, alongside the value and the difficulty of using a patient's complete history. Retrieval-augmented generation, which fetches documents on demand, helped most in some single-document settings yet still stumbled where answers needed reasoning over time. The authors also flag weaknesses in common evaluation metrics for judging such long-context medical answers.
arxiv-2510-18791:
Sasha Allegrini, Antonio Iovino, and Hardi Veermäe test a family of inflation models. The models manufacture primordial black holes. Such holes would have formed in the early universe. A popular family makes them in an ultra-slow-roll phase. Fresh data come from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope. The data prefer a slight upward running of the fluctuation spectrum. That preference squeezes the model family hard.

The tension grows with black hole mass. It threatens hopes of detection by gravitational-wave observatories. Present and planned detectors are both affected. Asteroid-mass holes escape the squeeze. They could still make up all of the dark matter. The authors scanned a six-dimensional parameter space. A Markov chain method did the scanning. One family fit the microwave background best at an inflection point. There, second-order approximations are needed for precise predictions.
arxiv-2510-18891:
Benoit Cloitre, writing alone, studies a prime-generating recurrence he introduced in 2008. It is an analogue of a classic greatest-common-divisor construction. This one is built on least common multiples. The jumps of the sequence are conjectured to be one or prime. A full proof needs a stronger form of a famous theorem. That theorem concerns the least prime in an arithmetic progression. The needed strength lies beyond current reach.

Cloitre attacks the conjecture sideways. His Companion-Sieve framework reduces it to a distribution question for primes in one progression. A classic theorem of analytic number theory then applies. He proves the conjecture holds for a set of integers of full asymptotic density. That proof is unconditional. Any counterexample past a computable bound must involve only large prime factors. A related recurrence encodes twin prime pairs in its jumps. The analysis also yields three new conjectures.
arxiv-2510-19491:
Jonas Gebele and three co-authors design a sealed-bid auction protocol that runs across blockchains without a central operator. Sealed bids keep offers secret until the deadline, but public blockchains expose everything, which clashes with that secrecy. Earlier designs leaned on trusted middlemen, multi-round protocols, or heavy cryptography.

Their protocol moves the sensitive bidding logic onto a confidential compute blockchain backed by trusted execution hardware, while settlement stays on a public chain. Bidders lock funds at escrow addresses generated inside the secure enclave. After the deadline, anyone can trigger a verifiable off-chain computation that names the winner and issues signed settlement transactions. The team built the system on SUAVE with Ethereum settlement and tested its scaling.
arxiv-2510-19591:
Marius Potfer and Vianney Perchet compare two formats for selling many identical items at once. In uniform-price auctions everyone pays one price. In discriminatory ones, each winner pays their own bid. Such sales run again and again in electricity and treasury markets. The pair studies one bidder who learns to bid against rivals he cannot predict.

Both formats look equally hard in the worst case, measured by regret, the gap between the bidder's take and what perfect play would earn. That holds under full feedback and under bandit feedback alike. Yet a closer look shows uniform-price auctions can allow strictly faster learning in some settings. A special case with symmetric rivals who each want one unit shows the same split, so the formats differ more than worst-case bounds suggest.
arxiv-2510-19691:
R. González-Ibáñez, J. Macías-Cáceres, and M. Villalta-Paucar propose LifeSync-Games, a framework that ties video game play to real-life activity in order to support healthy development. Nearly three billion people play games, and research shows both harms like addiction and benefits like sharper problem-solving, yet public debate leans toward the risks. The framework uses simplified digital twins to link the two worlds in both directions.

Playing is designed to encourage self-regulation and growth across physical, mental, and social domains, with real activity feeding back into the game. The authors lay out the theory, the technology components, design guidelines, and evaluation approaches. Early applications in new and bestselling games illustrate how the framework adapts to different titles.
arxiv-2510-20091:
Zhaoyi Joey Hou and eleven co-authors present CreativityPrism, a framework for judging how creative large language models are. Earlier checks were split across fields, leaned heavily on human raters, or used conflicting ideas of what creativity means. Their 2025 work brings those scattered checks into one shared system that can scale across many tasks and models.

CreativityPrism groups eight tasks from three areas: divergent thinking, creative writing, and logical reasoning. It grades outputs on quality, novelty, and diversity, using automatic judges checked against human ratings. In tests of seventeen leading models, larger frontier models led on writing and reasoning but not on divergent thinking. Scores in one area rarely carried over to another, which supports the need for a broad test.
arxiv-2510-20191:
Mingxuan Ge and Dae Woong Ham study a common practice in causal inference: matching treated and control units before running a difference-in-differences estimate when parallel trends may fail. Matching is meant to make the two groups evolve more alike without treatment, and earlier work judged the practice only by the bias it creates. The authors also analyze variance and mean squared error under weaker assumptions than before.

Working with a linear model that includes unobserved time-varying confounders, they find the variance story cuts against the bias story. Matching on observed covariates is not always better than plain difference-in-differences, because of a sample size trade-off. Matching on pre-treatment outcomes, by contrast, is always beneficial, and the authors give practical guidelines with guarantees.
arxiv-2510-20491:
Nitay Hurvitz, Gleb Finkelstein, and Eran Sela study a one-dimensional chain of metallic islands, each Coulomb-blockaded and coupled to quantum Hall edge channels. A single such island already shows rich physics, including charge fractionalization and multi-channel impurity behavior. The authors ask what qualitatively new effects emerge when many islands form an array, focusing on thermodynamic signatures such as entropy and thermal conductance.

For energy scales below the island charging energy, universal and robust behavior appears. At bulk filling factor one the array can support a finite heat flow with no temperature difference between islands. Pinching the array with a quantum point contact produces an entropy change that grows logarithmically with the number of islands, measurable by charge detection and suggesting novel excitations.
arxiv-2510-20591:
Ali Rajaei, Peter Palensky, and Jochen L. Cremer use graph learning to speed up transmission congestion management through busbar splitting, a topology change that can cut redispatch costs. Solving the underlying mixed-integer nonlinear problem for large grids in near-real time is beyond current solvers, and earlier machine learning approaches generalize poorly to unseen topologies and systems. Their formulation uses linearized AC power flow.

A heterogeneous, edge-aware message passing graph neural network predicts which nodes are effective candidates for busbar splitting actions. The network captures local flow patterns and transfers across systems and topology changes. Case studies show speedups of up to four orders of magnitude, delivering AC-feasible solutions within one minute with a small optimality gap on a two-thousand-bus system.
arxiv-2510-20791:
Zhonghao Tu and Ang Li explore whether the sudden spin jumps called glitches in neutron stars can reveal the dense matter law inside them. A glitch fires when stored spin passes abruptly from a superfluid part to the crust that telescopes observe.

Within a simplified three part model, the pair compute glitch rise shapes from self consistent microphysics for pinning and friction across several unified matter laws. Fits to the twenty sixteen Vela glitch favor crust coupling on a scale near one hundred seconds and strong central friction linked to core overshoot. Rise times also respect the observed upper limit, and a sampling study maps which settings stay compatible with the timing record.
arxiv-2510-20991:
Ward Struyve, working alone, tests whether certain semi classical gravity theories can create entanglement between massive systems, a proposed witness for quantum gravity. The Bose and Marletto Vedral proposals argue that gravity induced entanglement would prove gravity itself is quantum.

A class of models that keep gravity classical, entering as a potential in the Schrödinger equation, is shown to generate no entanglement at all. The class covers the Newton Schrödinger model, its Bohmian analogue sourced by real particles, and an interpolating model. The negative result sharpens what a positive experiment would rule out.
arxiv-2510-21091:
Kunwoong Kim leads four co-authors on subgroup fairness in machine learning when several sensitive traits, such as gender, race, and age, combine into many subgroups. Subgroup counts explode as traits multiply, creating heavy computation and tiny groups with too little data to judge.

Their doubly regressing algorithm focuses on subgroups with sufficient sample sizes while also enforcing marginal fairness for each single trait. The balance aims at meaningful protection without chasing noise in sparse cells. Fairness that survives real data limits is essential for hiring, lending, and health tools used at population scale.
arxiv-2510-21391:
Datao Tang and seven co-authors build TerraGen, a generator that creates labeled satellite-style imagery for several vision tasks at once. Remote sensing work needs large labeled collections, yet older generators train a separate model per task and ignore geography, so their fake scenes can break real spatial rules.

TerraGen takes a layout, given as boxes or masks. Renders a matching image, guided by an encoder that unifies both layout kinds and by training signals that stress spatial fit at every scale. The team also built a shared data set of forty-five thousand images and a standard scoring protocol for this multi-task setting. Their generator earns the best image quality across tasks and, used to augment training data, lifts downstream results in both full-data and few-example regimes.
arxiv-2510-21491:
Khaled Hallak and Oudom Kem benchmark methods that fight catastrophic forgetting in federated forecasting, where many sites train a shared model without pooling their data. Forgetting, where new lessons erase old ones, hits hard when each site's time series follows its own pattern, as in air quality monitoring across a city.

Their framework is the first built for this setting, since most forgetting research targets image classification. Twelve sites holding Beijing air quality data act as separate clients, and four remedies compete. Replaying stored examples, penalizing changes to important weights in two different ways, and distilling an older model's answers. The study compares the strategies head to head and releases a reproducible open-source framework, giving builders of edge forecasting systems a practical guide to what actually limits forgetting.
arxiv-2510-21691:
Edward Berman and three co-authors ask whether symmetry-respecting models know what they don't know. Equivariant networks shine where data are scarce, from robot hands to molecules to galaxy shapes. Honest uncertainty estimates guard against their overconfidence, yet the link between built-in symmetry and calibration had never been charted.

Their theory brackets the calibration error of equivariant models from both sides under several symmetry conditions, for classification and regression alike. The bounds expose a failure mode: when the model's assumed symmetry mismatches the data's true symmetry, confidence systematically skews, and the size of the group tunes the effect. Experiments on real and simulated data confirm the predicted patterns, including how random and systematic uncertainties interact with the mismatch, giving practitioners a map of when to trust an equivariant model's self-assessment.
arxiv-2510-21991:
Mateo Clemente leads an eight-author team making robot control policies faster. Diffusion policies, which steer robots by gradually refining a noisy action plan, lead the field at learning manipulation from demonstrations. They were borrowed from image generation and usually need many refinement steps before the robot can move.

Robotic actions are structured and low-dimensional compared with images, so the team tailors the cleanup process to that fact and shows five evaluation steps can suffice. Their genetic denoising strategy keeps a population of candidate cleanups and favors paths that stay close to familiar territory, cutting risk. Across fourteen manipulation tasks the method matched or beat standard policies while sometimes needing only two steps, a change that matters when a robot must react in real time.
arxiv-2510-22291:
Petar Orlić classifies a family of modular curves by how cheaply they can be drawn as coverings of a line. The curves start from X_0(N), the standard modular curve of level N. Quotient it by its full group of Atkin-Lehner involutions, the sign-flip symmetries indexed by divisors of N that split it cleanly, producing the curve X_0-star of N.

The measure is gonality, the smallest degree of a map from the curve to the projective line, computed over the complex numbers and over the rationals separately. Orlić determines every level where the complex gonality equals four. Every level where the rational gonality equals four with a single exception, level three hundred seventy-eight, which the paper leaves unresolved. Complete lists of this kind feed the arithmetic study of modular curves and their rational points.
arxiv-2510-22391:
Jusheng Zhang and five co-authors reframe image captioning as step by step planning rather than one single pass of writing. Large vision language models write fluently at once, but that habit can miss global coherence and fine detail. Their framework, Top-Down Semantic Refinement, treats caption building as a decision process that refines meaning from the top down.

A search method tailored to these models does the planning while calling the costly model far less often. Parallel expansion guided by the image, a light value network, and adaptive stopping keep costs down. On several benchmarks, the plug in module improved caption quality.
arxiv-2510-22691:
Instruction tuned language models generalize well, yet often trail on plain text classification benchmarks. Ruslan Berdichevsky, Shai Nahum-Gefen, and Elad Ben Zaken introduce SALSA in 2025, a pipeline that turns classification into a single token prediction task for such models.

Each class label maps to its own distinct output token, and prompts ask for that one token as the answer. At inference, scores are read only over the class tokens, giving a decision in one forward pass. Light fine tuning avoids training from scratch. SALSA reports leading results across diverse benchmarks, showing the approach is robust and scalable.
arxiv-2510-22891:
Some gamma ray bursts brighten again long after they fade. Jia Ren leads a team with seven co-authors. In 2025 they fit three such events across many wavelengths. The bursts span local to very distant universe. Their late rebrightening has steep rises and fast decays.

Structured jets in stellar wind bubbles fit all three well. The environment shifts from free wind to shocked wind. That shift shapes the afterglow light curves. Derived transition radii are small, under half a parsec. Similar events suggest a median near a tenth of a parsec. Jet structure shows a narrow core. Energy falls steeply with angle. Results hint at highly magnetized jets.
arxiv-2510-23091:
Wansheng Wang, Jiangtao Pan, Jie Wang, and Zaijun Ye propose a deep learning algorithm for high-dimensional equations with jumps. Such equations model systems where values evolve smoothly but also leap, in finance and physics. Classic grids fail in high dimensions, so neural methods are needed.

Their scheme extends a dynamic programming method and a forward-backward approach to integro-differential equations and jump equations at once. Two networks learn the solution and the integral kernel together, at each time step. The design aims for accurate solutions where older deep schemes for simpler equations no longer apply.
arxiv-2510-23291:
Alexandros Konstantinou, the sole author, studies how Selmer ranks change when an elliptic curve is twisted in a quadratic way. Selmer ranks measure hard arithmetic facts about a curve and bound the size of its rational point group. In this 2025 work, he uses only twists that meet the Heegner hypothesis, a named condition in number theory.

He starts from a rational curve with partial two-torsion and a common relaxed Selmer group shared across the twists. From there, he derives clear formulas that show the effect of each twist on the rank. The formulas use matrices whose entries lie in the field with two elements. As a check, he shows the formulas agree with what the parity conjecture predicts. That match supports both the formulas and the picture of how ranks should behave under twisting.
arxiv-2510-23491:
Peter A. Fisher, Johannes Autenrieb, and Anuradha M. Annaswamy design a controller that adapts to unknown machine behavior while never breaking safety limits. Their setting covers a class of systems that can be reshaped by feedback into a simpler form, with unknown parameters and full state readings. Safety limits on the state arise in many real machines, and the barrier rules that enforce them can have any relative degree here.

The design merges adaptive control with control barrier functions in one real-time scheme. The authors prove it stays stable, tracks the control goal, and keeps the system safe despite the unknown parameters, with almost no extra caution built in. Two cases are handled, differing in how the uncertainty behaves. Notably, the proof needs no special excitation in the command signal, and simulations confirm the low conservatism the theory predicts.
arxiv-2510-23891:
Jiaqi Xue and six co-authors present PRO, a method for watermarking text from open-source language models so owners can prove the text came from their model. Watermarking closed models is fairly mature, but open models are copied and run anywhere, so owners cannot control decoding. Baking the watermark into the weights is the natural fix, yet learned patterns often mismatch the detector or wash out after fine-tuning.

PRO trains a small watermark policy model together with the language model. The patterns it produces are easy for the model to learn and match what the detector expects. A regularization term simulates downstream edits like fine-tuning and model merging during training, punishing any drop in detectability. Tests on LLaMA and Phi models show stronger detection and better survival under modification than prior approaches. The authors frame PRO as a practical ownership tool for the open-model ecosystem.
arxiv-2510-23991:
Dor Minzer and a co-author prove near-optimal hardness for approximating constraint satisfaction problems with many variables per constraint. A k-CSP asks for an assignment satisfying as many constraints as possible. A trivial algorithm satisfies a one-over-R-to-the-k-minus-one fraction by guessing, where R is the alphabet size. The question is whether anything smarter is possible.

The answer, for large alphabets, is no. It is NP-hard to distinguish instances where every constraint can be satisfied from instances where nothing beats the trivial fraction by more than a hair. This sharpens the result of Chan, whose soundness bound was weaker by a factor of k over R. The proof extends the authors' two-variable argument, and its new tool is a counting lemma for hyperedges between pseudo-random sets in Grassmann graphs. They note the lemma may serve other problems too.
arxiv-2510-24291:
Vladimir U. Nazarov and two co-authors show that the thickness of electron flow has a huge effect on a tiny motor. The motor is driven by an alternating current. New work has found that electrons in very small wires can flow like a thick liquid. The test motor is a two atom unit placed in that liquid. The current pushes on the unit, while drag from the liquid holds it back. Its motion comes from the balance of the two.

The team ran first principles time based computer trials of the setup. The unit spins in a steady circle when the strength and rate of the current are in the right range. The thickness of the flow changes whether the motor runs at all, and how well it runs. The result ties this new view of electron flow to the design of tiny machines.
arxiv-2510-24491:
Philipp Dorau and Albert Much argue that the semiclassical Einstein equations follow from quantum relative entropy on a horizon. Using modular theory, they show the relative entropy between the vacuum and coherent excitations of a scalar field on a bifurcate Killing horizon equals the energy flux across the horizon. The Bekenstein-Hawking formula then ties that flux to a change in horizon area.

From this identification, the semiclassical Einstein equations follow automatically. The approach generalizes Jacobson's thermodynamic derivation of gravity to a quantum field theoretic setting. It supports the view that spacetime dynamics can emerge from entropy and information principles near horizons.
arxiv-2510-24591:
Christine Ye and twelve co-authors introduce ReplicationBench, a benchmark testing whether AI agents can replicate entire astrophysics research papers. Frontier agents show promise as research assistants, but novel research use requires first proving their faithfulness and correctness on known work. Astrophysics suits this test because it relies on archival data and computation, with little physical experimentation.

Each paper is split into tasks that an agent must complete to reproduce the paper's results. Scoring then measures how faithfully the agent recreated the analysis and conclusions. The framework gives a concrete standard for trusting agents in extended, open ended scientific workflows.
arxiv-2510-24691:
Alexandr Grebennikov and Matthew Kwan push past a known bound on how often a set edge count can show in large graphs. For sets of a fixed size, past work capped the share with a set count near a known constant. They ask when that cap can be cut if the edge count avoids a few tight cases.

For most edge counts, they show a strict smaller cap will do. When the edge count sits far from a whole count times the set size, their cap is much stronger and close to best. The work builds on past bounds and a kin result on graph form counts.
arxiv-2510-25791:
Zihan Pengmei led five co-authors studying thinking kinetics. Costas Mavromatis, Zhengyuan Shen, and Yunyi Zhang helped. Vassilis N Ioannidis and Huzefa Rangwala complete six. Their 2025 paper asks how chain-of-thought shapes transformer learning. Chain-of-thought supervision can improve transformer results largely. Mechanisms by which models benefit remain poorly understood. They study learning changes through grokking phenomena.

Transformers were pretrained on symbolic thinking tasks. Algorithmic hardness was tunable in their setup. Data composition was controllable for systematic study. Two settings compare final answers versus explicit traces. Chain-of-thought generally improves task results, they find. Benefits depend on task hardness systematically. A three-setting logistic curve models quality growth. Learning speed and shape vary with hardness. A transient trace unfaithfulness phase is uncovered. Early models answer correctly while contradicting steps. Later, traces align with answers. Chain-of-thought accelerates generalization but not hardest tasks.
arxiv-2510-25991:
Simon Dirckx, Anna Yesypenko, and Per-Gunnar Martinsson describe a method to solve elliptic boundary value problems by splitting a domain into overlapping slabs or shells. Elliptic problems model steady states, such as heat or potential, with values fixed on the boundary. Their method represents the full solution through its traces, its values on internal interfaces, linked by local solution transfer maps on overlapping double slabs.

A key point is that these interface maps act between separated interfaces, so they have smooth kernels and compress well with low rank methods. The global system has a well behaved Fredholm form and avoids singular interface maps that plague non overlapping schemes. At the discrete level it matches a preconditioned Schur complement system.
arxiv-2510-26191:
Tim Browning and Will Sawin study how often a random large Diophantine equation has a rational solution. A Diophantine equation asks for solutions in whole or rational numbers. They consider high surfaces, higher dimensional surfaces cut out by one uniform formula in powers whose weights are each plus or minus one. They ask for the chance that such a surface contains a rational point.

Browning and Sawin let both the degree of the formula in powers and the dimension of the surface tend to infinity, and study how the chance behaves in that limit. The problem sits at the meeting point of number theory and chance, since the equation is random but the being of a rational point is a rigid number based property. Their work addresses the large degree regime for these sign coefficient high surfaces.
arxiv-2510-26291:
Marc Chamberland and Karl Dilcher evaluate a curious alternating sum involving square roots and the floor function, which rounds a number down to the nearest integer. The sum adds and subtracts the floors of square roots of multiples of n, with the index running up to n itself. Unlike related non alternating sums, which are known only for a class of primes, their sum has an easy closed evaluation for every odd integer n of at least one.

Chamberland and Dilcher give an elementary proof, and they note that the proof was suggested by an AI model. To set the result in perspective, they also prove an asymptotic expression for the analogous sum without the floor function, where square roots appear directly rather than rounded.
arxiv-2510-26391:
Igor Abramov and Ilya Makarov try to rebuild the picture a person is seeing from that person's brain waves. Electrodes on the scalp record weak signals, called EEG, while a person looks at images. Past methods often ignored where the eyes focus, so their rebuilt images could blur or mix up details.

Abramov and Makarov add maps of visual focus, called saliency maps, to guide the rebuilding. A tool reads the brain signal, a tuned image generator turns it into a picture, and a second branch keeps the layout in line with the focus map. Tested on the THINGS-EEG data set, their method beat older ones on both fine detail and broad content. Uses could include medical checks and interfaces that respond to the brain.
arxiv-2510-26591:
A Chaika, with six co-authors, studies how vortices move between two coupled rings of superfluid. Superfluids are fluids that flow without friction, and atomtronic sensors use their trapped motion for precise measures of rotation and force. Vortices, small whirlpools in the fluid, can serve as sensitive probes.

Chaika and the team analyse persistent current oscillations between two density-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate rings. They show the vortex motion is governed by low-energy sound waves running through the bulk of the fluid. A simple fluid model predicts the oscillation rate and damping, matching heavier calculations and simulations. They find the critical damping that splits steady oscillation from stuck vortices. Modulating the barrier between the rings at set frequencies can move vortices across even when the rings are well separated.
arxiv-2510-26691:
Andrea Crespi, with eight co-authors, presents Flinch, a framework for reading cosmological parameters straight from sky maps. Field-level inference works with the full map rather than summary statistics, but it needs gradients to flow from pixels to parameters. Flinch is built to be fully differentiable and fast.

Crespi and the team link Flinch to differentiable cosmology tools, so a map can be used directly without stating a likelihood for summaries. On simulated, masked microwave background temperature maps, it rebuilt both maps and power spectra and inferred parameters with competitive precision. Against the standard pseudo-spectrum approach, error bars shrank by up to forty percent. Among samplers, one called MicroCanonical Langevin Monte Carlo beat the usual Hamiltonian method by orders of magnitude in efficiency.
arxiv-2510-26891:
Martin Loebl, Anetta Jedličková, and Jakub Černý study whether buying rights can keep scarce goods fairly shared. In distribution crises, demand and supply stay misaligned, and scarce resources drift toward the wealthy. Full central distribution may be impractical or politically impossible, while buying rights can be issued digitally and traded on platforms.

Loebl and his two co-authors embed buying rights in a repeated Arrow-Debreu market model. A regulator periodically hands out rights, which are then traded alongside the resource itself.
