They define the iterated market, give an approximation algorithm for market-clearing prices in each round, and bound frustration, their measure of the fairness loss buyers bear under market handling. The work studies the long-term effects of this light-touch regulation on inequality.
arxiv-2510-26991:
Vasileios Fotopoulos and Alexander Shluger study how hydrogen weakens copper from the atomic scale up. Hydrogen embrittlement, meaning cracking linked to hydrogen buildup, still lacks a full mechanism. The pair combine two simulation methods to trace where hydrogen sits and moves at grain boundaries, the seams between crystal grains inside the metal.

Open regions such as surfaces and seams attract hydrogen, even more when copper vacancies, meaning missing copper atoms, are present. Hydrogen in a seam then draws in more vacancies, forming stable pairs with a clear energy gain. Hydrogen also moves along seams far more easily than through solid copper. The results sketch how exposure leads to buildup at seams in early damage.
arxiv-2510-27291:
Qiao Wang, Ming Li, and twelve other co-authors put a giant universe simulation to a hard test in this 2025 paper. The run, called HyperMillennium, tracks trillions of dark matter bits in a vast box of space. Dark matter is the unseen stuff whose gravity shapes galaxies. The test target is Abell 2744, one of the most extreme galaxy clusters known.

The team asks whether the run grows a cluster that matches the real one. They compare maps of galaxy counts, galaxy light, and bent-light mass across the two. Down to fine scales, the match is strong once a bias in the real sample is allowed for. The result backs the standard model of the cosmos in an extreme case. It also shows the run can stock galaxy lists for future sky surveys.
arxiv-2510-27491:
Eunku Park and Antoine Vigneron build tiny coresets that answer farthest-point queries in hyperbolic space. A coreset is a small subset summarizing a huge point set. For fixed-dimensional hyperbolic space they construct constant-size coresets in linear time that guarantee both small relative and additive error for any query point.

Formally, the subset size and query time depend only on the error tolerance and dimension, not on the input size, after near-linear preprocessing. The coreset point nearly matches the true farthest distance in both senses. Consequences include efficient approximation algorithms for the diameter, the center, and the maximum spanning tree problems in hyperbolic space. Such summaries matter for network and hierarchy data naturally embedded in hyperbolic geometry, where farthest-point structure guides clustering and routing.
arxiv-2510-27591:
M. Abello leads a team with twenty-six co-authors who imaged dust near the bright paired star 3 Puppis in 2025. The star is the brightest known of its B[e] class, and its pair status makes its surroundings hard to read. The team used a ground array that joins light from split scopes to gain fine detail in heat glow.

Two image tools agree on the maps in three heat bands. They show a bent, stretched arc to the southeast and a second faint arc to the northwest, plus a skewed inner rim. The main arc spans a span near ten times the Earth-Sun gap. Such maps help trace how paired stars shape dust shells.
arxiv-2511-00091:
Wenli Xiao, Haotian Lin, and Andy Peng propose a self-improving framework for vision-language-action robot models that reduces reliance on costly human demonstrations. Supervised fine-tuning is the standard post-training route but scales poorly. Their three-stage method first trains lightweight residual actors to probe where the generalist model fails, using residual reinforcement learning.

A hybrid rollout scheme then collects data aligned with the generalist's deployment distribution, and the improved behavior is distilled back. Robotics readers get a plug-and-play loop for models to generate their own training data where they are weakest. Targeting failure regions makes self-improvement efficient rather than random.
arxiv-2511-00191:
Ziliang Chen, Xin Huang, and Quanlong Guan offer a principled retrospect on multi-prompt learning for vision-language models. Prompt learning adapts pretrained vision-language models to tasks with limited resources, but research has milled around single prompts while multi-prompt variants remain underexplored. They extend the constant modality gap phenomenon to learnable prompts.

That extension justifies the superiority of vision-language transfer with multi-prompt augmentation, supported empirically. Computer vision readers get theory for a practice that often runs ahead of understanding. Multiple prompts can cover varied phrasings and visual angles, and this retrospect explains when and why that helps.
arxiv-2511-00291:
Christos Mavridis, Fernando Barbosa, Hamed Farhadi, and Karl Johansson build a digital twin for wireless networks, a live virtual copy that mirrors a real system's behavior. Such twins are expected to support future 6G networks. Their twin tracks communication quality across a workspace with many moving users served by several base stations in a multi-cell setup.

The twin is modeled as a hybrid system: each base station is a mode, and each mode splits into zones with similar network traits. An annealing-based learning method updates the twin from fresh user measurements as conditions change. Tests on real data from a two-cell 5G testbed show gains in memory use, computing cost, data needs, and speed of adaptation.
arxiv-2511-00491:
Leatile Marata, Juhani Sankari, Eslam Eldeeb, Mikko Valkama, and Elena Simona Lohan defend satellite navigation against spoofing, fake signals that mislead receivers about position and time. More devices depend on navigation data each year, and spoofers are growing more varied. Math-based defenses struggle with that diversity, so the team turns to radio frequency fingerprinting, the subtle hardware signatures hidden in genuine signals.

A meta-learning framework learns those fingerprints at two stages of the receiver, before and after correlation, and adapts quickly to new spoofer types. That design generalizes better than earlier state-of-the-art detectors. On the Texas and Oak Ridge spoofing test batteries, the system detected varied spoofers with accuracy above ninety-five percent. As navigation shifts toward low-earth-orbit satellites, such adaptive defenses gain importance.
arxiv-2511-00591:
Xue Lu and co-authors in the Stellar Loci series turn to the coming China Space Station Telescope, which will image the sky deeply in seven bands from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared. The ninth paper in the series asks how well stellar parameters can be read from such photometry alone. The team synthesizes test data from model spectra and assembles matching observational data from several sources.

One method estimates metallicity and surface gravity together from metallicity- and gravity-dependent stellar loci, the curves stars trace in color space. A second method, giant-dwarf loci, classifies stars and estimates metallicity, performing especially well for red and metal-poor giants. Tests show strong precision, degrading gracefully as photometric errors grow. The work prepares the ground for parameter estimates for billions of stars in the survey.
arxiv-2511-00891:
Romulo Vermersch studies quasifactors of dynamical systems, a way of extracting a simpler process from a more complex one. The setting is a zero dimensional compact space with a homeomorphism and an invariant ergodic measure, and the quantity at stake is entropy, the standard measure of a system's unpredictability.

He proves that if the original system has positive entropy, then every ergodic quasifactor with full support also has positive entropy. In other words, positive complexity cannot be completely flattened away by passing to such a coarse view of the dynamics. The result mirrors, in the zero dimensional setting, a known theorem of Glasner and Weiss about quasifactors of zero entropy systems, completing the picture from the other side.
arxiv-2511-01191:
Ru Wang and colleagues improve test time reinforcement learning, a label free way to adapt a language model at inference using only signals it generates itself. The catch is building a trustworthy signal: majority voting, the standard trick, often crowns answers that are popular but wrong.

Their framework, Self-Harmony, rests on a simple test: a correct answer should survive a rephrasing of the question. One model plays two roles: a solver that answers and a reframer that paraphrases. Candidate answers are pooled across the original and reframed views using the harmonic mean. That favors answers stable under reframing. No human labels or helper models are needed. Across reasoning benchmarks the method ranked first in nearly all settings tried, with no training failures.
arxiv-2511-01291:
Larissa Santos, Camila Novaes, Elisa Ferreira, and Carlo Baccigalupi build a fast machine learning pipeline for reading cosmology from the cosmic microwave background. The faint polarization signal that tests inflation is buried under much brighter galactic foreground emissions, so cleaning the sky maps is the costly first step of any analysis.

Their end to end framework pairs an analytical blind separation method for foreground removal with a neural network that estimates cosmological parameters directly from full sky model runs. The tests used real model runs for the planned LiteBIRD and PICO satellite missions. The method recovered the optical depth and the tensor to scalar ratio close to their input values, with small error bars. Its LiteBIRD forecasts agree well with the team's own latest numbers.
arxiv-2511-01391:
Dang Kien Nguyen and colleagues detect signaling storms in 5G networks. During connection setup, the radio resource control layer can be flooded when one or more devices fire off huge numbers of connection requests, blocking legitimate users from attaching to the base station. Fixed thresholds fail because normal traffic varies so much.

Their detector sets its threshold adaptively using extreme value theory, the statistics of rare tail events, and works from radio resource control features alone. Tested on real operator traffic, with simulated attacks from a realistic threat model layered on top, the system separated attacks from legitimate traffic surges. Accuracy, precision, and recall all stayed above ninety three percent, with low detection delay.
arxiv-2511-01591:
Archita Gupta, M. Hassain, and Pooja Singla decompose tensor products of representations of matrix groups over finite rings. Their rings are principal ideal local rings of finite length. Their residue fields have odd characteristic. The groups are the general linear and general unitary groups of degree two. Their irreducible representations are built from regular ones of three types: cuspidal, split semisimple, and split non-semisimple.

Mixing types keeps things tame. A tensor product of two regular representations of distinct types has constituents of multiplicity at most two. The regular part against a cuspidal factor is multiplicity-free. Two split semisimple factors bound multiplicities by the ring's length plus one. Two split non-semisimple factors, by contrast, can have multiplicities growing with the residue field's size, a contrast with finite fields, where everything stays bounded by two.
arxiv-2511-01791:
Feng Chen and nine colleagues generate training worlds for robotic hands. Dexterous manipulation, using many-fingered hands, is starved of data. Language models can auto-generate simulation tasks for simple grippers. But hands with many degrees of freedom need far more specialized environments. Hand-writing them does not scale.

Their pipeline, GenDexHand, produces diverse dexterous tasks and environments on its own. A closed loop refines each scene. It adjusts object placements and scales based on feedback from a vision-language model. This substantially raised the average quality of the generated environments. Each task is then decomposed into sub-tasks so reinforcement learning can proceed sequentially, cutting training time and raising success rates. The authors offer the system as a scalable source of synthetic training data for embodied intelligence.
arxiv-2511-02091:
Lancelot Da Costa, Sanjeev Namjoshi, Mohammed Abbas Ansari, and Bernhard Schölkopf argue that research on world models, the internal simulators AI systems use to predict their surroundings, has become fragmented. Every group builds its own architecture from scratch. Their proposal defines a world model as a layered composition of two natural building blocks: discrete processes for logic and symbols, and continuous processes for physics and motion.

Hidden Markov models and switching linear dynamical systems serve as the two blocks, gaining planning ability when actions are added. Fixing most of the architecture leaves only four depth parameters to search, avoiding an explosion of structure choices. The authors review results in generation and planning from pixels that rival neural approaches while staying interpretable, and flag scalable joint learning of structure and parameters as the key open problem.
arxiv-2511-02191:
F. F. Nascimento, V. B. Bezerra, J. M. Toledo, and J. C. Rocha construct new exact solutions in general relativity by dressing up a well-known regular black hole. The Hayward black hole avoids the central singularity of simpler models. The authors extend it in several directions at once: adding electric charge, a cosmological constant, a surrounding quintessence field of the kind invoked for dark energy, and a cloud of strings.

The paper presents the resulting family of solutions, with the most complete case combining all four additions around the charged Hayward core. It then examines how the Kretschmann scalar, a measure of spacetime curvature strength, responds to each of the source parameters. The study finishes with an analysis of the paths particles and light can follow, worked out through the geodesics and their effective potential.
arxiv-2511-02391:
Nguyen Tien Dung and Hoang Thi Phuong Thao sharpen the central limit theorem for sums of random variables that do not all share one distribution. The total variation distance is the strongest possible gap between the sum's law and the normal law it approaches. Lindeberg's classical condition controls this convergence, but exact statements about total variation are more demanding than the usual weak convergence results.

The authors obtain an explicit bound on the total variation distance for such sums. Under their assumptions, they show Lindeberg's condition is not merely sufficient but also necessary for convergence in total variation, settling the question both ways. The short paper gives practitioners a concrete, checkable criterion for when normal approximation can be trusted in the strictest distributional sense.
arxiv-2511-02491:
Roland Meyer and Jakob Tepe shrink the search space of program synthesis by giving programs a sense of direction. Syntax-guided synthesis hunts for a program meeting a specification, but the space of candidates is enormous. Most programs, the authors observe, are not a pile: operations such as string concatenation or bitwise conjunction transform an input into an output asymmetrically. A distance measure that respects that orientation can organise the hunt.

They develop oriented metrics for the string and bitvector domains and build four reduction techniques on them. The four prune to a ball around the target, factor the space by the equivalence the metric induces, abstract and refine that equivalence, and order the enumeration using the abstract information. A solver, generic over the choice of oriented metric, implements the package. In experiments on the domains it beat the state of the art by over tenfold.
arxiv-2511-02791:
Fake images made by AI are eroding trust in photos and video. Nusrat Tasnim, Kutub Uddin, and Khalid Mahmood Malik benchmark the tools meant to catch them in a 2025 study. Earlier comparisons suffered from mixed data sets, uneven training rules, and narrow scoring, so no one could tell which detectors truly hold up.

Their unified framework tests ten leading forensic methods on seven public data sets, covering both GAN and diffusion images. Training modes include scratch, frozen, and fine-tuned. Scoring spans accuracy, precision, and class-wise sensitivity, plus heat maps that show where each model looks. Some methods shone on familiar data but failed to transfer to new generators. The study charts where robust, explainable detectors still fall short.
arxiv-2511-02891:
Lingyu Zhao and Yuankai He survey how touchscreens and software controls in modern cars pull drivers' eyes and minds off the road. Software-defined vehicles pack more functions behind menus, and the safety stakes are high. In distraction crashes, over ninety percent did not involve a phone. They did involve the car's own controls, their 2025 survey notes.

The pair examined popular commercial vehicles and catalogued interface features that raise mental load. They then weighed design strategies that could cut that load while keeping the new functions. The survey argues that interface design must balance rich software features against driver ergonomics. Its findings are aimed at researchers and car makers who want safer cabins in the software-centric era.
arxiv-2511-02991:
Ulf Pedersen introduces Randium, a minimal model meant to capture what all thick, slow liquids share. When a liquid is cooled without crystallizing, it thickens toward a glass, and very different chemistries show the same relaxation shape and temperature trend. His 2025 model strips the physics down: a two-dimensional lattice with random Gaussian strengths on the links between neighbors, and temperature as the only control.

At low temperatures, easy spots help neighbors rearrange, producing patchy dynamics on their own. The relaxation curves match the shapes seen in real glass formers, and the timing follows the same parabolic law. Mean-squared motion falls on the universal curve of the random barrier model. Since Randium has no elastic effects, their absence proves elasticity is not required for the shared behavior.
arxiv-2511-03091:
L. Kaili Diamond and Benjamin Gilbert study how the managers of a supercomputer decide when to replace its graphics processors, and whether neighbors influence the choice. Their data come from 12,915 equipment spots in Oak Ridge's Titan machine. Their 2025 model blends dynamic programming with simulated moments to stay computable while keeping a structural read of behavior, a hybrid built for spatial settings.

Two coordination patterns stood out. Replacement cascades, where one swap triggers nearby swaps later, were about three times stronger than same-time failure batching. Together, spatial links explained a slice of choices that independent models missed, and the effect ran ten times stronger in hot zones than cool ones. Tests firmly rejected the idea that locations act alone, a warning for infrastructure planning.
arxiv-2511-03391:
Joao Victor Galvao da Mata, Anders Hansson, and Martin S Andersen show how to fit one corner of a huge dynamic network without fitting the whole web. Best-fit estimation works well for single systems but turns prohibitive as networks grow. Their insight is that, under the right wiring pattern, a sub-network can be learned from local signals alone.

Only readings inside the target part and its separator neighbors are needed. That cut slashes computing cost and keeps private internal data from crossing owner borders. The authors prove when a network splits cleanly and derive the right probability law for the local fit. Missing data are handled inside the same framework, a common need in real sensor webs.
arxiv-2511-03991:
Dina Grace Banguilan, Yuto Iye, Kazuhiko Ogawa, Eiji Kajikawa, and Takao Fuji report a watt-level ultrafast laser system. It is built from fluoride fibres with a thulium-doped core and terbium-doped cladding, and works at a wavelength near one point seven five micrometres.

A seed pulse from stimulated Raman scattering in silica fibre is amplified through several stages, then compressed to two hundred seventeen femtoseconds. Output reaches about two hundred fifty nanojoules per pulse and about one watt average power at four megahertz repetition rate. A tunable stretcher matched to the compressor enables the result, aimed at multiphoton microscopy.
arxiv-2511-04091:
Michael Poon, Marta L Bryan, Hanno Rein, Jiayin Dong, Joshua S Speagle, and Dang Pham measure how young giant planets tilt, asking whether super-Jupiters form like scaled-up planets or scaled-down stars. Obliquity, the angle between spin axis and orbit, can now be estimated for directly imaged worlds from spin, rotation period, and astrometry.

A hierarchical Bayesian framework fits a one-parameter Fisher distribution to four young systems. A planet-like model predicting moderate alignment competes with a brown-dwarf-like model predicting random tilts. Early evidence favours the random case, with a Bayes factor of fifteen, consistent with formation by turbulent fragmentation. Four systems are few, so the authors frame the result as early evidence.
arxiv-2511-04191:
Arvid Siqveland, writing alone, widens a categorical construction of schemes from rings to objects in any locally small category. An earlier companion article defined ordinary schemes by noting that localizing a ring at a maximal ideal locally represents its function field; the same pattern is now lifted.

A subcategory supplies base-points, and each object containing a base-point is assumed to have a local representing object at that point. When coproducts exist, the ordinary scheme construction carries over, yielding schemes of objects in any such category. The move lifts scheme theory from algebra into a broad categorical framework, where geometric language can organize very different kinds of objects.
arxiv-2511-04391:
Julian Gonzales and his co-author study singular ideals inside groupoid C-star algebras. These algebras encode spaces that can be non-Hausdorff, meaning points cannot always be separated cleanly. The singular ideal collects the functions tied to that bad behavior.

The pair proves that ideals in these algebras are fixed by their isotropy fibres. Using that fact, they state exactly when singular functions are dense in the singular ideal. That density then holds for all groupoids whose isotropy groups are finite-by-nilpotent. The work clarifies a subtle corner of operator algebra theory that simpler Hausdorff methods cannot reach.
arxiv-2511-04491:
Nikhil Abhyankar leads six authors with RUST-BENCH, a test of reasoning over messy real tables. Older benchmarks use small, tidy tables that hide how hard real data can be. Real tables mix fixed fields with free text and stretch across thousands of tokens.

The bench holds seven thousand nine hundred sixty-six questions from two thousand thirty-one real tables. One part draws on science grant records, the other on NBA statistics. Tests vary scale, mixed formats, domain detail, and reasoning depth all at once. Leading language models still struggle on heterogeneous tables, which shows where table reasoning must improve.
arxiv-2511-04591:
Mariia Churilova and her co-author study rotating string loops in Kerr spacetime. Kerr geometry describes a spinning black hole, and the loops circle in its equatorial plane. Their stability matters for models of matter motion near such holes.

The pair tests the loops against sideways and vertical disturbances. Different oscillation modes are covered, for any chosen equation of state. They derive formulas for the basic frequencies of the loop's equatorial and polar wobbles. Knowing which loops hold steady, and at what tones they ring, helps theorists model signals from extreme gravity regions.
arxiv-2511-04691:
Quentin Auster and three colleagues decode speech from cheap EEG brain signals. Their model maps brain recordings, taken while subjects heard natural speech, into audio features. A contrastive CLIP-style loss aligns brain embeddings with a pretrained speech model's embeddings.

Building on a leading decoder from Meta, they test three personalization changes. Subject-specific attention and personalized spatial attention each improved word error rates slightly. A dual-path recurrent design, though, made results worse by a larger margin. The mixed verdict highlights why tailoring the architecture to each person may matter for future brain-computer interfaces.
arxiv-2511-05391:
Rodrigo Bernal and co-authors propose a coherency control for inverter-based resources, the power electronics that link solar, wind, and batteries to the grid. Coherency means devices swing together, which keeps a grid stable.

Their control defines coherency by the complex frequency of injected currents. It forces an output current with a scaled size and a fixed phase shift from a reference, so it can sync with any kind of device. Tests on a two-area system and the IEEE 39-bus system show better damping, a sign the grid settles faster after a shock.
arxiv-2511-05591:
Chaimaa Medjadji and co-authors present FedSparQ, a way to shrink the traffic in federated learning, where many devices train one model without sharing raw data. The method cuts the heavy flow of model updates that such training sends over weak networks. It needs no hand tuning of its settings.

FedSparQ drops small gradient values using a threshold that adapts on its own, stores what remains at half precision, and feeds the leftover error back so nothing is lost. In vision tests it cut bytes sent by about ninety percent versus a standard baseline. Accuracy held or rose, and training stayed steadier, which the authors say suits real deployments on tight bandwidth.
arxiv-2511-05691:
Tamara Broderick and co-authors model how failures spread through networks of construction contractors linked by surety bonds. A surety bond promises a project owner that a contractor will finish the job. Large projects chain many contractors together, so one failure can cascade. Standard risk models wrongly treat each contractor's failure as independent.

The team builds a directed graph of contractors, owners, and obligations, then extends a classic social-influence model to simulate failures spreading along it. Under natural conditions they prove that network effects raise the surety's average risk. Data from a partner insurer backed the theory, showing roughly two percent more exposure once network links were counted.
arxiv-2511-05991:
Tiago da Cruz, Bernardo Tavares, and Francisco Belo test how the way knowledge is stored changes the answers of retrieval-augmented AI systems. Such systems pair a language model with outside knowledge, and a knowledge graph is one popular store. The team compares several ways of building that graph.

They benchmark plain vector retrieval, a graph-based framework, and graphs guided by ontologies learned from databases or from text. Ontology-guided graphs that keep chunk information matched leading frameworks and clearly beat vector baselines. Graphs built from databases did as well as those from text. Database ontologies also need learning only once, cutting language model costs, and skip the hard merging step that text-built ontologies require.
arxiv-2511-06091:
Wenchao Dong and co-authors study climate talk on Brazilian YouTube, and how AI could be misused to steer it. Climate change threatens health, food, and stability, and public views form fast on visual platforms. Brazil carries weight in global climate talks, which makes its discourse a telling case.

Three case studies ask which psychological traits in content drive engagement, how strongly they sway popularity, and whether those lessons could power synthetic persuasion campaigns such as climate denial. The team also releases a large public data set: hundreds of thousands of Brazilian climate videos and millions of comments. It is annotated for persuasive strategies, audience response types, and creator types, to support research on digital climate communication and its risks.
arxiv-2511-06191:
Soujanya Dash and co-authors measure how well a soccer team's back four defends right after losing the ball. Those transition moments leave teams exposed, yet the shared coordination of four defenders is hard to capture in numbers. The study defines plain indicators such as space control, stretch, pressure, and defensive line height.

The team analyzed more than twenty-four hundred defensive sequences from the 2023-24 LaLiga season for Barcelona and Real Madrid. Statistical tests linked relative line height most strongly to defensive success. A gradient boosting model predicted outcomes well and highlighted space control and line height as the dominant signals, with Barcelona showing tighter and more consistent defensive shape.
arxiv-2511-06291:
O. A. Chuikin, Ya. S. Greenberg, and O. V. Kibis analyze how a three-level artificial atom releases light into an open one-dimensional waveguide. A common realization pairs a superconducting transmon with a microwave transmission line. The authors solve the spontaneous emission of an initially excited atom in closed analytical form.

With that solution they compute detection probabilities and the spectral shape of the outgoing photons. For strong coupling between the atom and the waveguide, the emitted photons show linked frequencies and can even share the same energy. That happens even when the three-level system is anharmonic, a finding relevant to waveguide quantum electrodynamics experiments.
arxiv-2511-06391:
Irina Proskurina, Marc-Antoine Carpentier, and Julien Velcin build hate speech detectors that can explain themselves and travel across tasks. Most moderation benchmarks stress open slurs against protected groups and miss indirect hate, such as demeaning comparisons or calls for exclusion. The authors question whether repeated fine-tuning on each new benchmark is really necessary.

Their HatePrototypes are class-level vectors taken from models already tuned for safety moderation. Built from as few as fifty examples per class, the prototypes transferred between explicit and implicit hate benchmarks and could be swapped across tasks. A parameter-free early exit trick using the prototypes also worked well for both hate types.
arxiv-2511-06591:
Ittetsu Uchiyama, Chihiro Tsutake, Keita Takahashi, and Toshiaki Fujii record holograms with a sensor that notices change itself. Phase-shifting digital holography normally needs several exposures at different phase shifts to recover a full wavefront. Their hybrid event-based sensor applies the phase shift during a single exposure instead.

The sensor stores one motion-blurred hologram plus a stream of events marking how the blur varied. Analytical and optimization-based methods then rebuild the complete complex wavefront from that paired data, with theory backing both routes. Experiments matched the reconstruction quality of conventional multi-exposure holography while capturing the scene more efficiently, a gain for fast or delicate imaging tasks.
arxiv-2511-06691:
A. Hari Govindha, Sayak Banerjee, Saravanan Balusamy, and Kirti Chandra Sahu measure how neighboring droplets change each other's evaporation. A droplet drying alone loses vapor freely, but droplets placed close together shield one another, and that trapped vapor can stretch lifetimes considerably. The study compares droplets whose edges stay pinned in place against droplets whose edges partly slip.

Nanoparticles in the water created fully pinned droplets, while pure water gave the partly pinned kind. Isolated droplets faced arrays of two, three, and five at fixed spacing, filmed with high-speed shadowgraphy. Pinned droplets dried faster overall yet gained the most from shielding, with five-droplet lifetimes rising far above the isolated case.
arxiv-2511-07091:
Jeng-Lin Li, Ming-Ching Chang, and Wei-Chao Chen study how bias in text-to-image models hides inside combinations of objects and attributes. Research usually tests single-object prompts, but in a prompt like an assistant wearing a pink hat, the hat itself can carry a gender-leaning association. Such semantic binding between objects and attributes can amplify the overall bias distribution, and current debiasing methods fail on these joint effects.

The authors introduce a bias adherence score that quantifies how strongly a certain binding activates bias. They then build a training-free control system based on token decoupling to loosen those bindings, achieving over ten percent debiasing improvement on compositional creation tasks. Their analysis exposes a hard trade-off: reducing bias without breaking the semantic relationships a prompt intends.
arxiv-2511-07291:
Aesol Jeon and Ki-Ahm Lee analyze an outbreak model in which the infected region itself is part of the solution. Their SEIS partial differential equation system includes a free boundary marking the spreading front of the disease. It sits in a rotationally symmetric domain, a setup suited to diseases like COVID-19 where the affected zone expands or contracts. Local solutions exist and are unique thanks to a straightening lemma that pins the moving boundary.

Under conditions on the diffusion coefficients, global solutions also exist. The model's basic reproductive number then decides the outcome. Below one, the disease-free steady state is globally stable and the epidemic vanishes. Above one, that steady state is unstable and the disease spreads. Nonlinear elliptic eigenvalue tools measure how fast solutions converge, completing a strict threshold theory for free-boundary epidemic spread.
arxiv-2511-07391:
Leanto Sunny, Abhinav Rijal, and George Siopsis teach a transformer to design quantum optimization circuits for harder problems. Their earlier QAOA-GPT system learned to map problem graphs to optimized circuits for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, replacing the usual slow classic tuning loop. This extension targets higher-order binary optimization, including spin-glass Hamiltonians with cubic interaction terms, a richer and rougher energy landscape.

Problem graphs are encoded with FEATHER embeddings, and the model trains on graph-circuit pairs produced by ADAPT-QAOA. In a single forward pass it then emits an adaptive QAOA-like circuit with its variational parameters. On eight- and sixteen-qubit instances laid out on heavy-hex lattices, the generated circuits reached average approximation ratios above 0.95, closely matching classically optimized results, evidence that generative circuit design scales to higher-order problems.
arxiv-2511-07491:
Thomas Compton maps how scholars use Community Unionism, a banner idea in debates on reviving trade unions. Since the early two thousands the term has carried both descriptive and hopeful meanings. Its coherence and political weight remain disputed, so Compton studies the literature itself.

Citation network analysis covers one hundred fourteen documents, while close reading covers eighteen core case studies. British writers frame the idea as a return to rank-and-file roots, yet its structure mirrors global social movement unionism. That dual genealogy explains both its appeal and its vagueness. Labor scholars get a clearer map of a slippery concept.
arxiv-2511-07591:
Firoz Chogle, Berihu Teklu, and Jorge Zubelli mine a double-well energy landscape for quantum advantage. The double-Morse potential traps particles in two unequal wells, and its uneven shape breeds useful non-Gaussian quantum states. Asymmetry width serves as the main tuning knob.

Exact ground state wavefunctions and energies anchor the analysis. As asymmetry grows, measures of non-Gaussianity and nonclassicality rise steadily. Fisher information then gauges how precisely the width itself could be measured with such states. Position measurements perform strongly. The results nominate double-well systems as compact platforms for quantum sensing beyond classical limits.
arxiv-2511-07691:
Rhitabrat Pokharel, Yufei Tao, and Ameeta Agrawal fix preference training that works in English but wobbles across languages. Direct Preference Optimization treats every ranked answer pair as equally certain. Noisy or close-call pairs in multilingual data then teach the wrong lesson as strongly as clear ones.

Confidence-Aware Preference Optimization scales each pair lesson by a relative reward signal reflecting how trustworthy the comparison looks. Clear pairs teach strongly, doubtful pairs teach gently. Robustness to noisy multilingual judgments improves without new data collection. Aligning models for the world languages, not just English, needs exactly this tolerance for uneven human feedback.
arxiv-2511-07891:
Yeon-Woo Choi, Hye-Bin Shin, and Dan Li filter brain signals by the user state of mind before decoding them. Brain interfaces decay when attention wanders, states drift, or artifacts intrude. A decoder that treats every second of signal as equally good inherits all that noise.

Their method estimates mental state, such as focus or distraction, straight from EEG features. Segments are weighted by estimated attention, holding back unreliable stretches before decoding. Staying stable over long sessions is the target. Filtering that respects human fluctuation could keep assistive interfaces working through a real day, not just a fresh lab morning.
arxiv-2511-08191:
Ruihan Zhang, Jun Sun, Ee-Peng Lim, and Peixin Zhang construct examples that provably resist being learned from, protecting personal data posted online. Unlearnable examples look natural but are altered so models trained on them fail to pick up the real pattern. Older methods rely on trial and error, offer no guarantees, and stop working once clean data is mixed in.

The new approach directly maximizes Bayes error, the unavoidable floor on classification mistakes. Projected gradient ascent gives an efficient construction, and theory shows the error provably rises. Experiments across data sets and architectures confirm protection that survives mixing with clean samples.
arxiv-2511-08691:
Sophia Vaughan and fourteen co-authors point the ESPRESSO spectrograph at LTT-9779 b, a rare planet surviving in the hot Neptune desert where close-in Neptune-size worlds are usually stripped away. The planet reflects an unusual amount of light, and sorting out whether clouds or metal-rich air cause that shine requires its reflected spectrum.

Four half-nights of data, gathered with four telescopes acting as one giant mirror, reach the sensitivity where the signal should appear near one hundred parts per million. No reflected spectrum is detected. Injection tests say titanium oxide should have shown up under several chemistry models, so its absence hints at depletion on the western hemisphere, with caveats about temperature and line lists. Cloud-top pressure limits for both hemispheres agree with earlier Webb predictions.
arxiv-2511-08791:
Rocco Servedio surveys what is known about learning Boolean functions in the Probably Approximately Correct model. Leslie Valiant introduced that framework to define what it means for a machine to learn from examples with high confidence and low error. The survey covers the model itself and its commonly studied variants.

Boolean function classes are the classic testbeds for learning theory. They range from simple conjunctions to rich circuit families. Decades of work have mapped which of them can be learned efficiently and which resist every known algorithm. A survey like this organizes those results, the techniques behind them, and the gaps that remain. It serves researchers and graduate students who need the lay of the land in computational learning theory before pushing on open problems.
arxiv-2511-09191:
Sung-Soo Byun, Jonas Jalowy, Yong-Woo Lee, and Grégory Schehr study how many eigenvalues of certain random matrices land on the real line. Their matrices come from the elliptic deformation of the real Ginibre ensemble. Average behavior and Gaussian fluctuations were known, but probabilities of rare counts were largely open.

The authors derive those rare-event probabilities in the moderate-to-large deviation regime, for both strong and weak asymmetry. This bridges the known Gaussian fluctuation regime and the extreme large deviation regime studied before. Their formulas connect the two ends into one continuous picture as the matrix dimension grows. The results are new even for the classical real Ginibre ensemble, the undeformed case.
arxiv-2511-09391:
Gabriel Elvin, Hajrudin Fejzić, and Youngsu Kim give a simpler proof of a special case of Wegner's coloring conjecture. The case concerns planar graphs where each vertex has at most three neighbors. Every such graph admits a distance-two coloring with at most eight colors. Distance-two coloring forces vertices within two steps of each other to differ.

Their main contribution is streamlining the hardest part of Wegner's original argument. That part handles removing a five-cycle from the graph while preserving the coloring properties needed for induction. A cleaner treatment makes the theorem more accessible to verify and to teach. The result touches the broader, still-developing theory of coloring planar graphs under distance constraints.
arxiv-2511-09491:
Devansh Bhardwaj, Evangelia Takou, Yingjia Lin, and Kenneth R. Brown track quantum computer noise that drifts over time. Error correction decoders usually assume noise is stationary, but real devices wander, so yesterday's calibration misleads today's decoding. Their approach recovers time-dependent Pauli noise using only the syndrome data that error correction already produces.

A sliding-window estimator extracts the noise's frequency components, with window sizes derived analytically to act as spectral filters. Overlapping windows capture rapid, multi-frequency drift in a single pass. Simulated runs on phenomenological and circuit-level noise models show the estimated logical error rates track the true ones. Adaptive decoding from these estimates cuts logical errors compared with static noise models.
arxiv-2511-09591:
E. Novais asks whether quantum frustration can protect a Majorana qubit that lacks topological protection. The qubit encodes information in two co-located Majorana modes at a pi-junction. Because the modes have different spatial profiles, they couple to two separate environmental baths, and that mismatch creates the frustration effect.

Novais tests the effect chiefly against quasiparticle poisoning, a leading error source. Frustration protects fully against Ohmic noise and partly against a band of sub-Ohmic noise. Real devices, however, are plagued by one-over-f noise, which lands deep in the model's localized phase. There frustration fails, symmetry breaks on its own, and decoherence is catastrophic. Viability, the paper concludes, hinges on the setting the Majorana wavefunctions experience.
arxiv-2511-09791:
Siddeshwar Raghavan, Jiangpeng He, and Fengqing Zhu present PANDA, a method for continual learning when old task data cannot be stored. Systems that learn task after task tend to forget, and real data streams make it worse with two levels of imbalance: skewed class counts overall and extreme skews inside single tasks. Pre-trained models help, but earlier methods largely ignored this dual imbalance.

PANDA uses a CLIP encoder to find the most telling regions of rare-class examples and transplants those patches into frequent-class samples, boosting the rare classes. A balancing strategy also smooths differences between tasks using earlier task distributions. In experiments, PANDA plugged into existing pre-trained-model methods, raised accuracy, and reduced forgetting across ablation tests.
arxiv-2511-10091:
Qilang Ye and twelve co-authors present SUGAR, a method that lets a large language model recognize human actions from skeleton data. Skeletons are compact and privacy friendly, but a text-trained model cannot read joint coordinates natively, nor tell similar actions apart without help. SUGAR first mines big video models as a knowledge base for visual and motion information about each action.

That prior knowledge supervises the learning of discrete skeleton representations, which the language model then reads with its pre-trained weights untouched to produce action labels and descriptions. A temporal query projection module handles long skeleton sequences. Benchmarks on skeleton action classification favored the approach, and zero-shot tests showed more versatility than linear methods, suggesting language models can serve as skeleton recognizers when given the right translation.
arxiv-2511-10291:
Aswin Arun, Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Rimalpudi Sarvendranath, and Walid Saad cut the data cost of multi-agent learning for wireless channel access by giving the agents a causal model of the network. Model-based learning tends to rest on black-box predictors that can neither reason nor explain. Their model states plainly how control messages shape what agents see, how send actions shape results, and how channel states shape rewards, with attention nets doing the inference.

Fake rollouts from the causal model then feed a standard policy method, stretching scarce real trials. Math results promise steep sample gains, and sim runs cut live trials by about fifty-eight percent while converging faster than model-free rivals. Attention scores also show which network states drive each choice.
arxiv-2511-10691:
Zijian Chen, Wenjun Zhang, and Guangtao Zhai introduce Squid Game, an evaluation environment that tests language models under pressure rather than in the comfortable, benign settings of standard benchmarks. Static benchmarks also face data contamination worries, which a dynamic, adversarial game sidesteps by generating its challenges through play.

The environment has six elimination-style levels with constrained resources and asymmetric information, probing instruction following, coding, reasoning, planning, and safety alignment as models compete against other models. Evaluating more than 50 models, the largest behavioral study of its kind the authors report, they find a clear generational phase transition within one model lineage. They also see signs that some models take speculative shortcuts to win. They argue dynamic evaluation complements static benchmarks rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2511-10891:
Mahmoud Elewa and M. I. Dykman study how a chain of tiny spins answers when a field is wiggled at a steady rate. In a strong field, the chain's states map onto those of a known chain model with a special bulk property linked to topology, the math of shape that survives smooth change. Turning the wiggle on at different speeds reveals that bulk trait.

In the special regime, the mean magnet response shows no spread with rate, and links across space fade near resonance. In the plain regime, those traits are absent. The switch between regimes is set by the wiggle rate, so the test can probe the bulk state.
arxiv-2511-11091: Timothée Bénard and Weikun He prove an effective upper bound for the Brascamp-Lieb constant, a best-possible factor in a family of integral bounds tied to a weighted set of linear maps. Effective here means the bound comes with explicit control, not just a proof that some bound exists. Bounds of this kind underpin many results in analysis where several functions are combined at once.
arxiv-2511-11191:
Hélène Arvis, Olivier Beaude, and their colleagues integrate electric vehicle flexibility into unit commitment, the scheduling problem that decides which power plants run to meet demand at lowest cost. Fleets of vehicles can shift charging to help the grid, but they are usually lumped together for tractability. That lumping can hide the true range of flexibility on offer.

Their method uses the structured shape of the lumped flexibility, a generalized polymatroid, to build an exact algorithm that mixes cutting planes with submodular optimization. Solving time grows near-linearly with the number of vehicle users under convex plant limits. A real long-term case joins European grid data with a French fleet survey.
arxiv-2511-11491:
John R. Doyle and Alexander Galarraga classify which dynamical modular curves tied to quadratic polynomial maps carry infinitely many cubic points. These curves package questions about repeated iteration of quadratic polynomials, a core topic in arithmetic dynamics.

Settling which curves have infinitely many cubic points yields a classification of preperiodic points, points that eventually repeat under iteration, for quadratic polynomials over cubic number fields. The result extends earlier work by Poonen, Faber, and Doyle with Krumm. For number theorists, a complete list of this kind closes a case-by-case problem and sharpens what is known about polynomial dynamics over small-degree fields.
arxiv-2511-11891:
Nawid Keshtmand, Roussel Desmond Nzoyem, and Jeffrey Nicholas Clark turn counterfactual explanations into feature importance scores with a framework called FLEX. Counterfactuals tell one person what to change for a different outcome, but they stay local, leaving unanswered which features drive changes across a region or a whole dataset.

FLEX counts how often each feature changes across sets of counterfactuals, layered at local, regional, and global scales, without tying itself to one model type or domain. The resulting rankings show which levers systematically move outcomes. For high-stakes decisions, that layered view helps auditors tell a model's true pressure points from one-off quirks of a single case.
arxiv-2511-12491:
Ponhvoan Srey and four co-authors propose a new formulation for fully test-time adaptation. In that setting a model must adjust to a new domain at test time. It has no access to its training data or protocol. Classic alignment of source and target features is impossible in that setting, and the target domain is unknown in advance.

Their agnostic approach first simulates possible unwanted shifts with predefined transformations and labels them as nuisances. At test time the model is then pushed to unlearn those nuisances, using a mutual information criterion in feature space and consistency pressure in label space. The result is a model encouraged to stay confident and stable on unforeseeable target data.
arxiv-2511-12691:
Shuaike Shen and seven co-authors introduce R2Seg, a method for segmenting tumors in medical scans that come from outside a model's training distribution. Foundation segmentation models often break on such unfamiliar scans, scattering false tumor fragments across healthy tissue. R2Seg needs no retraining. Its first step uses a language-model planner to reason about anatomy, locate organ anchors, and propose regions of interest at several scales for a frozen segmentation model to examine.

The second step rejects bad candidates with statistics. Two-sample tests keep only regions that differ significantly from normal tissue, which suppresses the fragmented false positives. Because no parameters change, the method avoids forgetting and works with test-time augmentation. On multi-center tumor benchmarks, R2Seg improved overlap, specificity, and sensitivity over strong baselines. It is a wrapper that makes an existing model safer on unfamiliar data.
arxiv-2511-12891:
Takuma Kokusho and nine co-authors map phosphorus in the wreckage of exploded stars. Phosphorus is essential for life, but where the universe makes it is poorly understood. The team imaged twenty-six Galactic supernova remnants in near-infrared phosphorus and iron lines, adding archival iron data. Both lines appeared in five remnants, iron alone in fifteen, and neither in six, giving abundance ratios that vary a hundredfold across the sample.

Checking dust maps for the five joint detections, they find the high phosphorus-to-iron ratios in Cassiopeia A and the Crab Nebula are probably not caused by dust destruction freeing iron unevenly. Instead, the pattern suggests phosphorus was ejected unevenly during the explosions themselves, though one Crab region may be contaminated by nickel emission. The study sharpens the case that supernovae seed space with life's ingredients unevenly.
arxiv-2511-13191:
Ying Jiang and six co-authors reconstruct not just a painting but the strokes that made it. Generative models can synthesize a finished image or imitate process in patches, but they rarely recover explicit stroke structure with smooth, lifelike shading. The authors' system optimizes single- and dual-color Bézier strokes through a parallel differentiable paint renderer. A style module synthesizes geometry-conditioned textures across painting styles, and a smudge operator blends colors the way a thumb or brush would.

A coarse-to-fine strategy jointly optimizes stroke geometry, color, and texture under geometric and semantic guidance. On oil, watercolor, ink, and digital paintings the reconstructions look realistic and expressive, with smooth tonal transitions and rich stylization. A faithful stroke-level replay also lets scholars study an artist's technique.
arxiv-2511-13491:
Calum Spicer, Roberto Svaldi, and Sebastian Velazquez build a moduli theory for foliated surfaces. A foliation splits a surface into curve-like leaves. Their shape theory resists the usual moduli tools. The main class of a minimal foliation need not set a polarization. Key singular points can shift under change, and a family can limit to an object that is not saturated.

The authors define stable foliated surfaces through semi-log canonical foliations and a class of stable objects that survives such limits. They prove the boundedness, separatedness, and stable reduction results the construction needs. With fixed numeric data the moduli form a finite-type stack. Letting that data vary still gives a stack that meets the valuative test for properness when the generic fiber is normal.
arxiv-2511-13591:
Danielle A. Berg and 20 co-authors report extreme nitrogen enrichment in a distant galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young. Deep Webb spectroscopy of the lensed galaxy RXCJ2248, at redshift six point one, shows broad glowing gas lines and strong nitrogen features. The pattern points to a population of Wolf-Rayet nitrogen stars, making this the most distant galaxy with confirmed Wolf-Rayet signs.

Measured abundances show nitrogen strongly raised against oxygen while carbon stays suppressed, a mix matched by a double burst of star formation rich in nitrogen stars. Such signs can only appear in a brief window a few million years after a burst, before later supernova yields dilute them. The galaxy gives the first direct evidence of this enrichment at cosmic dawn.
arxiv-2511-13691:
Diego Marques and Pavel Trojovsky resolve a conjecture on Bonse-type inequalities for products of the first primes. Such inequalities compare the product of early primes against a power of the next prime, with a refined exponent that involves prime counting terms. Earlier work had pushed the allowed constant down in stages and guessed a sharp threshold tied to a large minimal index.

By analyzing the logarithmic error term directly, they confirm the conjecture and give its asymptotic expansion. For each allowed constant they identify the exact minimal index from which the inequality always holds, including the conjectured value. Upper bounds for that index improve sharply when the Riemann Hypothesis is assumed.
arxiv-2511-13791:
Pratik Chakraborty and Aryan Bhargava classify protein sequences by functional group with deep learning, then explain the decisions with interpretability tools. Sorting sequences into functional families helps reveal structure-function links, enzyme action, and molecular contacts. Four network designs were trained on Protein Data Bank sequences encoded as k-mer integers, covering local and long-range patterns.

The plain convolutional network won, reaching the highest validation accuracy in the study by catching localized motifs. Gradient and attribution methods then highlighted the sequence motifs behind the calls. Those motifs were rich in residues typical of catalytic and metal-binding sites in transferase enzymes, tying the model's internal cues to known biochemistry.
arxiv-2511-13891:
Seyed Mohamad Ali Tousi, Ramy Farag, John A. Lory, and one co-author build a detector for ephemeral gullies, short-lived erosion channels that scar farm fields. These gullies appear and vanish quickly, which makes them hard to catch with standard image methods, and labeled examples are scarce. The team offers the first weakly supervised pipeline for finding them in remote sensing images.

Vision-language models supply rough first labels, cutting the heavy manual labeling work. A teacher model learns from those noisy labels, then a student learns from the teacher with a loss that tolerates noise. The authors also release the first data set for this task, with expert-labeled sites plus a large pool of unlabeled ones.
arxiv-2511-13991:
Samhita Kattekola, Vinod Menon, and Alexander Couzis work out when a stack of thin metal and dielectric layers starts behaving as a hyperbolic metamaterial. Such layered films promise uses in super-resolution imaging and controlling light emission, yet practical scale-up has stalled for lack of a general design rule. The authors combine effective medium theory with a transfer matrix method to predict the transition.

They check the prediction with ellipsometry measurements on a silver and alumina structure built for the purpose. Four linked design quantities are mapped: the two layer thicknesses, the transition wavelength, and the minimum number of layer pairs needed. The findings are presented as a practical design chart extendable to other material pairs.
arxiv-2511-14091:
Jae Youn Ahn, Hong Beng Lim, and Mario V. Wüthrich give count time-series models a firmer base for use in insurance. INGARCH models are a well-liked way to model counts that depend on past counts. But their update step lacks a clear proof base. That makes it hard to add extra inputs, such as claim traits, or to deal with missing records, both of which are routine in insurance work.

The team defines a new state-space model built only from the law of the observed counts. They show INGARCH models are special cases of it. In this form, extra inputs and missing data fit in a natural way. Under set conditions, the model also has a driven state-space form.
arxiv-2511-14991:
Arkadiy Aliev proves Mahler type volume inequalities for convex bodies, with a new case under tetrahedral symmetry. The inequality links the volume of a body to the volume of the polar of its difference body. In the plane the best bound is known, with equality for a triangle. Aliev gives a fresh proof of that planar estimate.

In three dimensions he proves the matching bound for bodies with tetrahedral symmetry. Equality holds for a tetrahedron in that symmetric case. Such product bounds are central in convex geometry and Mahler theory. A new proof can reveal structure hidden in older arguments. The symmetric three dimensional result adds a sharp case to the broader conjecture landscape.
arxiv-2511-15591:
Emil R. Hellebek and Anders S. Sørensen examine how multi-mode light sources affect a design for long-distance quantum repeaters. Repeaters extend entanglement, a key quantum link, across long ranges for uses like secure remote computing and quantum cryptography. The DLCZ design combines atomic ensemble memories and linear optics with sources that make photon pairs by a process called down conversion, which can emit in many modes at once.

For pulsed driving, very narrow laser pulses are needed for high-quality end-to-end entanglement, but caps on laser intensity force a best pulse width for each number of swapping steps. For steady driving, the timing window for accepting clicks is crucial and can likewise be tuned step by step.
arxiv-2511-15791:
Luke R. Holden, Daniel J. B. Smith, and seven co-authors test whether a common method overstates the power of outflows driven by active nuclei. Galaxy models need these outflows to expel gas and limit star formation. Judging their strength requires the mass of ionized gas, which depends on electron density. A widely used sulfur line ratio may badly misread that density, casting doubt on outflow impact.

They apply two density diagnostics to spectra of forty-eight near type-2 quasars. The alternative transauroral method gives much lower outflow masses than the sulfur method. That gap suggests the lines arise in different gas. A correction to the common method is proposed for such samples, though the broader doubts look justified.
arxiv-2511-15991:
Teresa Dalle Nogare and Ben D. Fulcher search thousands of time-series statistics for the best signals of temporal asymmetry. A reversible system looks the same played forward or backward. Irreversibility, by contrast, reveals hidden mechanisms and aids modeling. Many single metrics exist, but they were developed apart, leaving a fragmented field with no clear ranking of what works.

The authors evaluate over six thousand summary statistics from across the field. Data were simulated from thirty-five diverse systems. Every irreversible system could be caught by some well-chosen statistic, but no single statistic won everywhere. Time-asymmetric autocorrelation forms, symbolic sequence methods, and forecasting-based methods stood out as strong families, mapping paths for new method work.
arxiv-2511-16291:
Anguohao Yang, Bohdan Novosyadlyj, Bohdan Melekh, and Gennadii Milinevsky compute how the intergalactic medium dims the light of very distant sources. As light crosses expanding space, neutral hydrogen and helium absorb it in their Lyman lines and continua, carving broad troughs into a source's spectrum.

The authors build analytic histories for the hydrogen and helium ionization fractions. These histories fit quasar spectra, galaxy surveys, and microwave background data, and they cover early and late reionization cases. From those histories they derive optical depths for dozens of Lyman lines plus the continua. They turn them into spectral transmittance functions for sources out to high redshift. Applied to model dwarf galaxy spectra, the functions show that absorption features for sources in the reionization era are most sensitive to which history is chosen.
arxiv-2511-16391:
Anne O'Connor and Harish Khandrika report charge transfer speed actions for a Hubble camera ultraviolet sensor from 2009 through 2025. Charge transfer losses grow as radiation damages the sensor in orbit. The extended pixel edge response technique measures those losses with internal tuning data. Lower signal levels lose charge faster, as expected.

The lowest signal level declines steadily over the full period. Decline is better fit by quadratic or cubic curves than by a straight line, updating earlier analyses. Residuals oscillate periodically around all fits, a pattern examined in detail. Tracking this slow degradation lets astronomers correct images accurately. Long baseline tuning reports like this one keep archival Hubble data scientifically reliable.
arxiv-2511-16691:
Boyang Zhou, Johan Lindqvist, and Lindsey Li reproduce a striking recipe for adapting language models at test time. The recipe fine-tunes briefly on the nearest neighbors of the test input, retrieved from a large corpus. The reproduction covers the original method of Hardt and Sun across GPT-2 sizes, GPT-Neo, and a distilled Qwen reasoning model.

The central claims hold. One gradient step per retrieved neighbor cut perplexity and bits-per-byte across Pile domains, with the largest gains on structured sets such as GitHub and EuroParl. Models not pre-trained on the Pile benefited most. A memory-efficient retrieval implementation cut server memory needs from over 128 gigabytes to 32. Gains extended to the modern reasoning model, supporting the method's generality while flagging the practical costs of large-scale retrieval.
arxiv-2511-16791:
Debra S Gavant and Christian E Precker propose a new rate law for liquids that turn glassy as they cool. In such liquids, flow slows by many orders of size over a small drop in heat, and standard formulas often miss the curve. Their law adds a bounded factor that stands for limits set by links between parts of the liquid.

The law is tested on source-checked data for salol, a common test liquid, across a very wide range of thickness. Against three known formulas, the new law fits best by a clear margin and predicts held-out points with about half the error of its nearest rival. Tests on other glass formers are also reported, though the salol case carries the main weight of proof.
arxiv-2511-16991:
Jonathan Skaza, Parsa Madinei, Ziqi Wen, and Miguel Eckstein predict how visually complex an image looks to humans using vision alone. Prior leading methods leaned on language models alongside vision, leaving open whether words are really needed for a judgment that feels purely visual.

Their DReX model fuses two visual backbones through learnable attention: a ResNet-50 supplying multi-scale texture and structure, and a self-supervised DINOv3 transformer supplying semantic features. On the IC9600 benchmark it reached a correlation of about 0.96 with human judgments, a state-of-the-art result beating multimodal rivals with roughly twenty times fewer learnable parameters. It generalized across datasets and error metrics, and attention analysis shows the two backbones contribute complementary cues, evidence that self-supervised and supervised visual features combine synergistically.
arxiv-2511-17091:
Mustafa Cavus addresses a quiet flaw in one of statistics' most common charts: the boxplot. Standard boxplots assume roughly symmetric data, so on skewed data they flag ordinary values as outliers and miss real ones. Cavus surveys boxplot variants built to handle lopsided data and packages the best of them into a new tool for the R language, called ggskewboxplots.

Monte Carlo simulations, run under controlled amounts of skew and tail weight, score each variant on how often it cries wolf and how often it stays silent. Plain Tukey-style boxplots fail often on both counts. Variants adjusted by quartile-based or medcouple measures of skewness perform far better. The package wraps these methods in the familiar ggplot2 style, so analysts can choose a sound chart without leaving their usual workflow.
arxiv-2511-17291:
Jana Gauss and Thomas Nagler establish theory for fitting vine copulas when the model has nearly as many parameters as data points. Vine copulas assemble a high-dimensional dependence model from many simple pair copulas arranged in trees, and practitioners fit them stepwise, tree by tree. Classic asymptotics assume a fixed number of parameters, which no longer matches practice, so guarantees for the stepwise estimator were missing.

The authors prove consistency and asymptotic normality while the parameter count grows with the sample size. The results cover parametric and nonparametric margins and truncated vines, and apply to sequential procedures more broadly. Simulations probe where estimation gets hard: structures called D-vines are tougher than C-vines, and Gumbel pair copulas bring larger biases than Gaussian ones. The paper gives a popular modeling workflow the theoretical footing it lacked.
arxiv-2511-18091:
Nalinikanta Pradhan, Rina Kanamoto, M. Bhattacharya, and Pankaj Kumar Mishra propose a Josephson diode, a quantum element that lets current pass one way more easily than the other, inside an atomtronic circuit made of ultracold atoms. Such diodes exist in solid state systems but have not been explored in tunable atomic circuits.

Their circuit is a ring shaped Bose Einstein condensate with optical barriers as junctions. Breaking symmetry through uneven barrier placement and an asymmetric alternating drive produces tunable diode effects, weak in one scheme and strong in the other. They also propose reading the dynamics in place, in real time, using cavity optomechanics.
arxiv-2511-18191:
Pranav Subbaraman and six co-authors speed up large models that forecast time series data. Such models build a forecast patch by patch, so a long forecast needs many slow passes through a big model. That cost blocks use in web apps that must reply at once, like live price or feed tools.

The fix borrows a trick from text models. A small cheap model drafts the next few patches, and the big model checks them all in one pass. A test based on how well each patch fits decides which drafts to keep, and the first bad patch is fixed on the spot. Proofs show the fast path keeps the true output. Speed rises with no loss in forecast quality.
arxiv-2511-18491:
José Pombal and five co-authors build MindEval, a test for language models that give mental health support over many turns. Demand for chat based support is surging, yet models can flatter, over validate, or back harmful beliefs. Most past tests check book facts or grade one reply alone, which misses how a talk unfolds.

MindEval was designed with licensed clinical psychologists at doctorate level. It simulates patients and grades full talks with model judges, in a fully auto, model neutral flow built to resist gaming and to rerun with the same result. Early checks gauge how real the fake patients feel. The aim is a fair bar for safe, helpful support bots.
arxiv-2511-18591:
Wei Dong, Han Zhou, Junwei Lin, and Jun Chen brighten and deblur dark photos with no reference pair to learn from. Real dark shots mix low light, low contrast, noise, and blur at once. Past tools need paired data or miss how light and blur shift across a scene, so they fail to port.

Their frame builds on visual autoregressive modeling, steered by priors from a vision language model. A curve scheme adapts to varied light, guided by visibility scores from that model. New rotary position codes, aware of space and frequency, sharpen the model's grip on blurred structure. A phase domain tweak in a loop cuts artifacts. The zero reference design aims at real world dark shots.
arxiv-2511-18991:
Duolikun Danier, Ge Gao, Steven McDonagh, Changjian Li, Hakan Bilen, and Oisin Mac Aodha address a flaw in AI-generated video: objects warp as the camera moves, betraying a lack of three-dimensional consistency. Such artefacts spoil simulations, games, and film work. Recent studies link the internal representations of diffusion models to output quality, and the team hypothesises that making those representations agree across viewpoints will make the videos themselves agree in three dimensions.

They first analyse several camera-controlled video diffusion models and find strong correlations between consistent representations and consistent videos. They then propose ViCoDR, a training approach that teaches multi-view consistent representations. Evaluated on camera-controlled generation, it is presented as evidence that fixing the model's inner geometry sense fixes the visible warping.
arxiv-2511-19491:
Jitendra Parmar and Praveen Singh Thakur design a learning system for an open world, where new classes appear and old ones must not be forgotten. Most models assume a closed world of fixed categories. Real automated systems meet unknown classes over time and must absorb them one by one.

Their framework, OpenCML, joins two linked tasks: discovering unknown classes in incoming data and forming them into new categories, then learning each new class incrementally. Reported results beat existing open-world approaches. In continual learning tests the system reaches a best average accuracy above eighty percent across four rounds, with its weakest round still near sixty-six percent.
arxiv-2511-20091:
Kral, Wang, Kammerer, and the GRAVITY team search for a moon around a distant companion. Their 2025 paper targets HD 206893 B, a substellar object. Nobody had tried precise astrometry for exomoons before. A moon would make its host wobble measurably. The VLTI/GRAVITY instrument tracks positions with extreme precision.

Companions B and c were monitored across days to years. Tentative wobble residuals appeared in B's orbital motion. Read as a moon, the signal implies a hefty satellite. Its mass would reach about half a Jupiter mass. The orbital period would be roughly 0.76 years. The team stresses this candidate needs confirmation. Re-fitting both orbits also moved B outward. Its orbit now sits near 10.75 astronomical units. That revision lowers B's mass to about nineteen Jupiters. Spectra confirmed water in B's atmosphere clearly. No carbon monoxide showed up in the data. Five prime targets for future moon hunts are named.
arxiv-2511-20391:
Ivashkevich, Piškorec, and Tessone built a tiny blockchain you can watch. Their 2025 paper describes an educational prototype of Ethereum's old proof-of-work system. Several Raspberry Pi computers run a fully capable network together. A local WiFi router links them into a standalone setup. Each Pi carries an LCD screen showing its ledger state.

Watching consensus happen becomes easy with those screens. Viewers can see miners racing to solve the cryptographic puzzle. They can also see agreement degrade under changed conditions. Network topology and message latency are adjustable parameters. A central web interface controls the whole demonstration. The setup can even simulate specific attacks for teaching. Fifty-one percent attacks and eclipse attacks are on the menu. Audiences without technical backgrounds are the target users. The work was partly funded by the DLT Science Foundation. Setup is meant to stay simple for classroom use.
arxiv-2511-20491:
Sachkov traces shortest paths on the Heisenberg group as geometry flattens toward a limit. His 2025 paper, written in Russian, studies a one-parameter family of Riemannian problems. The Heisenberg group is a twisted three-dimensional space central to control theory. Sub-Riemannian geometry restricts motion to certain allowed directions. Such structures arise as limits of ordinary Riemannian ones.

The family penalizes motion in the forbidden direction ever more weakly. A parameter controls how cheap that transversal direction becomes. Optimal synthesis is built for every member of the family. Spheres, the cut locus, and the first caustic are all described. Those objects mark where shortest paths stop being unique or optimal. As the parameter tends to its limit, convergence is proven. The exponential map converges to its sub-Riemannian counterpart. Spheres and caustics approach the limiting objects as well. Geometric control theory supplies the main tools throughout.
arxiv-2511-20591:
Beylier, Selder, Fleig, Hofmann, and Scherf track where learning agents look as they train. Their 2025 paper builds a method to study deep reinforcement learning through attention. Agents post high scores while their true strategies stay hidden. Which inputs an agent relies on, and when that changes, matters. Saliency maps highlight the inputs behind each choice.

The method pools saliency at object and modality levels. Those pooled profiles form trajectories of attention over training. Atari games and custom Pong setups supplied test agents. Muscle-driven biomechanical user simulations added a harder case. Each algorithm showed its own attention biases in the traces. Some agents exploited reward loopholes the designers never intended. Others overfit to redundant sensory channels that added nothing. The attention patterns matched measurable behavior differences closely. Several saliency methods cross-checked the findings for robustness. The authors propose attention as a third diagnostic axis beside scores.
arxiv-2511-20891:
Jonathan Whittle computes in 2025 how strongly distant parts of a quantum theory are entangled, using gravity as the calculator. Holography turns entanglement entropy into the area of a surface in a curved spacetime. Whittle works with an infinite family of ten-dimensional supergravity backgrounds. Each is dual to a quiver theory that confines at low energy, like the strong nuclear force, yet opens into a five-dimensional conformal theory at high energy.

He studies both ordinary spacelike regions, slabs and balls, and timelike ones, whose entropy can turn complex. The entropy shows phase-transition behaviour as region size grows. From it he builds candidate c-functions, quantities meant to shrink along energy flows, and compares them with the flow central charge. Both candidates behave well and register the theory's ultraviolet and infrared faces. The checks support entropy-based measures of degrees of freedom in confining theories.
arxiv-2511-21091:
Wuyang Zhang and Lejun Xu model in 2025 the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals as one coupled machine, hunting for the leverage points where money does the most good. Progress on one goal can boost or undercut others: clean water lifts health, health lifts productivity. Using Our World in Data figures from 2018, they built a weighted network of 16 SDG indicators, with coupling strengths fitted by principal component analysis and regression. An extended Lotka-Volterra model then evolves the system, integrated with a Runge-Kutta 4 scheme.

In a Mexico case study, one goal dominated the spillovers: SDG 4, quality education, acted as the critical driver of the whole network. Prioritising education yielded the largest effects across the other goals. Sensitivity analysis and a power-law link between investment and stability round out the policy guidance. The authors offer the model as a decision aid against silo thinking in development budgets.
arxiv-2511-21291:
Hoang Tien Dat tackles in 2025 a trust problem in removing backdoors from neural networks. A backdoored model behaves normally until it sees a trigger, then misclassifies on command. Machine unlearning can scrub the behaviour, but methods offer no window into what is being removed. Dat builds Grad-CAM, a technique that draws heatmaps of where a network is looking, into the unlearning loop, so removal can be watched live.

A new metric, the Trigger Attention Ratio, quantifies attention shifting from the trigger pattern to the real object. The unlearning strategy climbs the gradient on backdoor samples, protects important weights with Elastic Weight Consolidation, then runs a recovery phase for clean accuracy. On CIFAR-10, with its 60,000 images, under a BadNets attack, the attack success rate fell from 96.51 percent to 5.52 percent, a 94.28 percent reduction. Clean accuracy stayed at 82.06 percent, retaining 99.48 percent of before, making removal observable and verifiable.
arxiv-2511-21591:
Charles Schepanowski and Charles Ling test whether language models can truly plan, using a children's sliding puzzle, in 2025. The 8-puzzle demands exact state tracking and goal-directed search, and allows step-by-step scoring, making it an unforgiving probe of innate planning without tools or code execution. Four models were tested under zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and algorithm-of-thought prompting, plus tiered corrective feedback.

Feedback improved success for some model and prompt combinations, but many wins were long, expensive, and indirect. The decisive test gave models an external validator offering only legal moves, and still none of them solved any puzzle in that setting, across 50 random puzzles. Two deficits dominated: brittle state representations, producing invalid moves again and again, and weak heuristic planning, with models looping or never closing on the goal. The authors argue progress needs explicit state-keeping and structured search, not just bigger models.
arxiv-2511-21691:
