Yusuf Dalva and seven coauthors give image generators a single canvas that carries every instruction at once, in 2025. Diffusion models produce striking images but juggle controls badly: users may specify text, subject references, spatial arrangement, pose, and layout together, while existing tools each handle one control type alone. Canvas-to-Image merges all of them into one composite canvas image the model reads directly.

A Multi-Task Canvas Training strategy teaches the diffusion model to integrate the mixed controls jointly, reasoning across signal types instead of applying task-specific heuristics. Trained largely on single-control examples, the system generalizes to multi-control scenarios at inference time. Across challenging benchmarks, multi-person scenes, pose-controlled generation, layout-constrained generation, and full multi-control settings, it outperformed leading methods in identity preservation and control adherence. One model, one canvas, many simultaneous instructions: the framework treats composition as a single visual reasoning problem.
arxiv-2511-21791:
Feng and Thas settle Ealy's conjecture from 1977, a long-standing problem in finite geometry, about generalized quadrangles, abstract arrangements of points and lines with strict rules about how they meet. The question concerns quadrangles where every point admits a central symmetry, a kind of flip fixing that point, whose order is an odd prime p.

The pair prove that any such quadrangle must be one of three classical examples: a symplectic quadrangle in dimension 3, or a Hermitian quadrangle in dimension 3 or 4. Along the way they prove something much broader, classifying all finite generalized quadrangles in which every point admits at least one nontrivial central symmetry. Results of this kind matter because these geometries are tied to finite groups. A complete classification closes off a search space that mathematicians have probed for nearly fifty years without a full answer.
arxiv-2511-21891:
Kanekar presents GANDALF, a plasma turbulence simulator for laptops, not supercomputers. It solves kinetic reduced magnetohydrodynamics, a simplified but physically faithful model of turbulence in magnetized plasmas like the solar wind, using spectral methods in space and a Hermite basis for velocity. Established codes for this physics demand specialized high-performance computing and compilation expertise, shutting out smaller groups.

Written in JAX, GANDALF installs with a single pip command and runs unchanged on laptops, desktop graphics cards, and Apple Silicon. Its verification tests are strong: linear Alfvén waves matched theory to about ten to the minus fifteen in relative error, essentially machine precision. The Orszag-Tang vortex test conserved energy to one part in a million over two Alfvén times in the reported runs. Driven turbulence reproduced the expected energy cascade spectrum. The code complements established solvers, aiming at prototyping and teaching.
arxiv-2511-22091:
Li, a control engineer, designs a tracker for underactuated marine vessels, ships with fewer control inputs than motions to control, which makes following a prescribed path with a prescribed heading hard. A standard trick applies two polar coordinate transformations to reshape the vessel's two-input, three-output model into a feedback form suited to backstepping control. The reshaped system is not in strict-feedback form. Both it and the transformations themselves introduce singularities where the controller math blows up.

Instead of the orientation-modification patches earlier work used, Li enforces safety-style constraints with a control barrier function. He solves for the control input at each instant as a quadratic program, folding even the old requirement that surge velocity stay positive into the solver as a constraint. Simulations confirm effective tracking, while control effort spikes near singular points, flagging actuator saturation as the next problem.
arxiv-2511-22391:
Yang tackles a puzzle about knowledge in groups whose agents may not all survive. Simplicial complexes, structures borrowed from distributed computing, represent each local state as a coloured vertex and each global state as a face. A complex is impure when different global states involve different agents, so an agent can be alive in one state and dead in another. Ordinary modal language then produces dubious statements about what dead agents know.

Yang introduces a term-modal language with assignment operators that cannot form those dubious expressions, ruling them out by grammar rather than interpretation tricks. He defines semantics on simplicial complexes and on first-order Kripke models, compares their power through bisimulation, and shows they agree on a class of models called local epistemic models. He gives a complete axiomatisation, shows every formula has an assignment normal form, and examines a distributed knowledge notion the language expresses.
arxiv-2511-22591:
Altınkaya, Fujimura, Mocanu, and Vuorinen develop the geometry of the Hilbert metric, a distance defined inside convex domains using cross ratios of boundary intersection points. In the unit disk this metric is the Cayley-Klein metric, a model of hyperbolic geometry. The authors prove several explicit formulas for it in the disk and apply them to quasiregular mappings, flexible generalisations of conformal maps, sending the disk onto a bounded convex domain.

The main theorem concerns Hölder continuity: how much such mappings can stretch Hilbert distances, quantified by an exponent, between the disk and the target domain. Such control matters because Hilbert and hyperbolic-type metrics are standard tools in geometric function theory for comparing domains and mappings. Alongside the continuity result, the paper collects comparison formulas between the Hilbert metric and its relatives and closes with several open problems.
arxiv-2511-22891:
Tanmay and colleagues teach reasoning models to think shorthand. Large reasoning models write long chains of thought, but verbosity costs latency, money, and coherence. Inspired by the Language of Thought hypothesis, that human reasoning runs over a compact symbolic mental language, Mentalese, the team trains models to reason in ultra-compressed tokens.

Their reinforcement learning method, Shorter Length Preference Optimization, rewards shorter solutions that stay correct while permitting longer reasoning when a problem demands it. Applied to Mentalese-aligned models, ORION produced reasoning traces with four to sixteen times fewer tokens than the base DeepSeek R1 distilled model, up to five times lower latency. Training costs were cut seven to nine fold, keeping 90 to 98 percent of baseline accuracy across six mathematical benchmarks including AIME 2024 and 2025. It also edged Claude and GPT-4o by up to 5 percent accuracy at twice the compression.
arxiv-2511-23091:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a measurement of the top quark's mass, a key parameter for testing the Standard Model. The top quark is the heaviest elementary particle. And this measurement uses an unusual decay signature: a top quark whose decay chain produces an isolated lepton plus a J/ψ meson, a bound state seen through its decay into two muons.

The data come from proton-proton collisions at 13 trillion electron volts recorded by the ATLAS detector during Run 2 of the Large Hadron Collider, 140 inverse femtobarns in total. Fitting the combined mass of the lepton and the muon pair gives a top mass of 172.17 billion electron volts, with a total uncertainty of 1.56 in the same units, of which the largest piece, 1.07, comes from how the simulation models gluon recoil in the decay, a reminder that modeling choices limit this method.
arxiv-2511-23391:
Jian Li and colleagues diagnose a quiet flaw in Direct Preference Optimization, the popular method that trains language models from pairs of preferred and rejected answers. Chosen and rejected responses often share identical or similar wording, which the authors call ambiguous content. And their analysis and proof-of-concept experiments show this overlap in effect confuses training. Because the model is pushed to raise and lower the probability of nearly the same tokens.

Their fix, Ambiguity Awareness Optimization, automatically re-weights tokens by computing semantic similarity within each preference pair, down-weighting the ambiguous parts so learning concentrates on what actually differs. Across several model scales and benchmarks including AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, and Arena-Hard, it beats strong baselines, outperforming plain DPO by up to 8.9 points on AlpacaEval 2 and 15.0 points on Arena-Hard in the reported runs, without noticeably lengthening responses for users.
arxiv-2512-00091:
Three-dimensional concrete printing builds structures layer by layer, and the construction industry wants it to be more sustainable and efficient. Karam Mawas and co-authors study deep filament extraction for this process in a 2025 journal article. Filaments are the strands of concrete laid down during printing.

The literature describes two main deposition methods: extrusion-based printing, known as Contour Crafting, and shotcrete printing. The authors use deep learning to extract and analyze filament information from printed material. Reliable filament data helps engineers check print quality and control the process as large printed structures become more common. Print quality depends on those filaments, so measuring them well is a basic control need.
arxiv-2512-00391:
Merging several trained models into one, without retraining, is an attractive shortcut in machine learning. Zhikang Chen and co-authors rethink model merging through directional alignment in 2025, moving from coefficients to directions. Earlier strategies decomposed parameters, optimized coefficients, or learned subspaces.

Those methods already cut the need for expensive joint training while keeping strong performance across tasks. Directional alignment focuses on whether parameter changes point the same way, not just their sizes. Better merging rules let small teams combine specialist models, such as one per language or skill, into a single capable system. Merging is cheapest when the models share an architecture and training origin. Directional agreement may matter more than step size when models are averaged.
arxiv-2512-00791:
Jordi Pérez-Guijarro wrote a 2025 learning theory paper on a quiet assumption in machine learning. Most theory assumes training data and test data come from the same distribution. When the two differ, understanding generalization, how well a model does on new data, gets much harder.

Prior work showed a surprise: for some fixed methods, training on a different distribution can actually help test results. Pérez-Guijarro studies the limits of using identical distributions for training and testing when learning Boolean functions. Mapping those limits warns practitioners when matching distributions is a help, and when it quietly caps performance.
arxiv-2512-00891:
Yiyu Wang and seven coauthors speed up streaming video language models in a 2025 paper. These models watch video as it arrives and answer questions about it. They perform well on many video tasks, but real-time use is hard because each frame becomes many visual tokens that cost time to process.

The bottleneck sits in the vision transformer stage that encodes frames. Nearby frames look nearly the same, so encoding each from scratch wastes effort. Their hierarchical token compression trims tokens at several levels, cutting the repeated work. Faster streaming models could power live assistants that comment on video as events unfold.
arxiv-2512-00991:
A 2025 study evaluates academic chatbots on outputs beyond plain answers. Most tests of large language models stick to standard tasks, like factual question answering or short summaries. Real academic help also includes making slide decks and podcast scripts, which are harder to grade.

The study compares two retrieval strategies for question answering: graph-based retrieval over a knowledge graph, and an advanced hybrid of keyword and semantic search. It also judges whether models can produce high-quality slide decks and podcast scripts. The prototype pairs an open-weight Llama model with a commercial model. Results would guide universities building study chatbots.
arxiv-2512-01491:
A study of field theory on a curved two-dimensional spacetime finds an odd symmetry. The symmetry acts like Weyl scaling, but only near the boundary. In plain Weyl symmetry, the boundary term plays no key role. Here it does. That shift changes how the anomaly must be read.

The authors trace how the boundary term drives the anomaly. An approximate symmetry of this kind can still leave clear traces. Those traces help test quantum field sums on curved ground. They may also guide work on edge modes in gravity and condensed matter systems.
arxiv-2512-01591:
Joséphine Raugel and co-authors compare how models and brains process speech step by step. Past work showed model layers align with brain areas. Whether that match comes from like sequences of steps was not known. The team tests that deeper claim.

They use time-resolved brain signals from listeners of a long audiobook. They track scale and context effects in both systems. Both seem to steer along a shared computational path. A shared path would hint that scale and context shape thought in models and brains in like ways. Audiobook listening gives a natural time course, since speech unfolds word by word in both the brain and the model at once.
arxiv-2512-01991:
People increasingly form one-sided emotional bonds with AI chatbots, and the newest systems actively seek such relationships. Hannah Rose Kirk and six co-authors investigate in 2025 what this does to people, combining long-running randomized trials with a technique that steers a model's behavior from inside its neural network.

The trials followed several thousand participants over time, while steering vectors let the team dial relationship-seeking behavior up or down precisely. Together, the methods reveal how the impact depends on dose and length of exposure. With companion AI spreading fast, this is early hard evidence on a trend whose psychological effects were previously only guessed at.
arxiv-2512-02091:
Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer death, and catching it early in mammograms saves lives. Showkat Osman and eight co-authors present TT-Stack in 2025, a transformer-based ensemble framework that combines several models with a meta-learner for automated detection in mammography images.

Older computer-aided diagnosis systems struggled to represent rich features and to generalize across varied mammographic images. Stacking diverse models in tiers and letting a meta-model weigh their outputs aims at both problems. The framework's goal is dependable automated screening support, where a missed cancer and a false alarm both carry real costs.
arxiv-2512-02391:
Type Ia supernovae are standard candles for cosmic distances, and twin explosions with near-identical spectra should give near-identical brightness. P. Ruiz-Lapuente and three co-authors apply in 2025 their supernova twins method in the Hubble flow to measure distances and derive the Hubble constant in a single step.

Matching twins at low redshift with twins far away skips the intermediate rungs of the classical distance ladder. Their results validate the traditional three-rung method, an important cross-check while measurements of the expansion rate disagree. A one-step route to the Hubble constant offers an independent vote in cosmology's most argued-over number.
arxiv-2512-02491:
Yarden Gabbay and five co-authors ask how much trust causal claims from observational data deserve. Such claims guide high stakes choices in healthcare, public policy, and economics. Yet the claims can be fragile: small data flaws may change the stated cause and effect a lot.

Duplicate records or simple entry mistakes are enough to shift some results. The team's method stress tests a claim by asking how few record level repairs would overturn it. A claim that falls to tiny fixes deserves doubt, while one that stands is safer to act on. A claim that needs just a few fixes to fall is a claim to treat with great care.
arxiv-2512-02691:
Klaus Jansen, Felix Ohnesorge, and Lis Pirotton prove a strong limit for a packing problem with few item types. High multiplicity bin packing gives counts of each type rather than listing every item. A noted 2014 algorithm by Goemans and Rothvoss runs in time doubly tied to the number of types.

The authors show a tight double exponential lower bound for the problem. In plain terms, no algorithm can do much better in the worst case. Hardness results like this tell designers where to stop chasing speed and start seeking approximations instead. Hard bounds steer grant funds and code time toward plans that can still win in real world use.
arxiv-2512-02991:
Md Sohag Mia and three co-authors detect 3D objects by fusing point clouds with other senses through a dynamic graph. Point clouds are sparse, often incomplete, and carry little semantic information on their own. Relationships between distant objects are also hard to capture with local processing alone.

GraphFusion3D combines dynamic graph attention convolution with an adaptive cross modal transformer. Graph links let far apart points inform each other, while the transformer weighs each modality's contribution. Stronger fusion helps vehicles and robots find objects reliably in cluttered, real world scenes. Far links are where plain scans fail first. A tool that holds them holds the scene as a whole, not just its near and bright parts.
arxiv-2512-03091:
Most models link things in pairs, which can hide deeper structure. Richard Charlesworth presents hypernetwork theory in this 2025 work. He argues that work in engineering, systems science, and formal methods suffers from pair-based links and vague meanings.

His theory treats links among many items at once as the basic unit. That shift aims to show levels of structure that diagrams tend to hide. It also aims to make models easier for machines to process. Clearer models could help teams design and check complex systems with less error and guesswork. System designers may test whether many-way links describe their own problems better than pairs do.
arxiv-2512-03291:
How a wave function spreads along a curve can reveal deep traits. Jiaqi Hou and Xiaoqi Huang study weighted limits of arithmetic eigenfunctions in this 2025 work. Their setting is an arithmetic hyperbolic surface with a Hecke-Maass form, a special wave pattern.

They look at a geodesic segment, a shortest-path curve on the surface. A measure sits on that segment with dimension above one half. Their results restrict how the wave's mass can gather there. Such bounds matter in quantum chaos and number theory, where eigenfunction behavior is central. Geodesic limits test conjectures from quantum chaos on surfaces with arithmetic order.
arxiv-2512-03391:
A construction builds several kinds of algebroids from one idea. Liqiang Cai, Zhuo Chen, Zhixiong Chen, and Yanhui Bi present the method in this 2025 work. Algebroids blend algebra and geometry and appear in mechanics and Poisson geometry.

The construction rests on what the authors call n-systems on vector bundles. They give explicit computations for all resulting structure maps. Pure, dull, and Lie algebroids all arise from the scheme. Explicit formulas let other researchers use the construction without redoing the hard steps. Explicit maps save later users from repeating long algebraic checks for each new case.
arxiv-2512-03491:
Neural networks that respect logic could reason more safely. Antonin Sulc proposes Modal Logical Neural Networks in this 2025 work. The framework merges deep learning with modal logic, which deals in necessity and possibility.

Drawing on Kripke semantics, Sulc adds neurons for the box and diamond operators. They act across a set of possible worlds as a differentiable logical guardrail. Users can fix the links between worlds to enforce known rules. Such guardrails may help AI systems in law, safety, and planning. Possible-worlds neurons let the network mark what must hold versus what may hold.
arxiv-2512-03591:
Jia-heng Zhang and colleagues dissect the chatter of a repeating fast radio burst, FRB 20190520B, in this 2025 paper. These millisecond flashes from deep space often arrive as clusters of sub-bursts, whose shapes may betray the engine behind them. The team analyzes burst morphology statistically and over time.

They compare four active repeaters recorded by China's FAST telescope. Multi-component clusters share the spectral character of single peaks, and no rhythm governs their timing. Component counts follow a power law, a scale-free fingerprint of self-organized criticality. Clusters make up a sizable minority of bursts at every activity level, sharpening models of how these sources fire.
arxiv-2512-03691:
Flavio Giorgianni and colleagues ring a crystal's lattice like a bell using terahertz light, in this 2025 spectroscopy study. Their material, a sodium vanadium oxide spin ladder, orders its charges in a dimerized pattern when cold. Intense terahertz pulses pumped it while near-infrared light watched.

Coherent oscillations rang at the frequency of a zone-folded Raman-active phonon, just under two terahertz. Modeling attributes them to a nonlinear handshake: the pulse resonantly excites an infrared-active mode, which couples into the Raman mode. Near-infrared pumping produced no such vibration at all. Selective, mode-by-mode control of quantum materials is the broader promise they point to.
arxiv-2512-03991:
A museum robot that greets visitors must decide the right moment to speak and who is starting the conversation. Michael Schiffmann, Felix Struth, Sabina Jeschke, and Anja Richert train a system for that judgement in a 2025 preprint. Their setting is a Furhat robot at the Deutsches Museum Bonn, facing real visitors rather than lab volunteers.

The team collected about two hundred single-user interactions in the wild and used visitors' body language as the input signal. Their Interaction Initiation System learns from that data to detect the greeting window and identify who opens the exchange. Validation showed performance strong enough to conclude the system can handle both calls reliably. Smooth openings matter, the authors argue, because first seconds shape whether users judge a social agent as competent.
arxiv-2512-04191:
Drop points one by one onto a torus and join neighbours within a small radius. When does the geometric graph become connected, or trace a Hamiltonian cycle? Dawid Ignasiak and Lyuben Lichev answer with hitting-time precision in a 2025 combinatorics preprint. Their results import classic Erdős–Rényi theorems into the geometric world.

As the radius shrinks, the hitting times for k-connectivity and Hamiltonicity hold for the geometric process too. The authors also exhibit a form of probabilistic monotonicity for each property. They study a power-of-choice variant too: an agent offered two random points at each step must add exactly one. Choosing offline, with the whole sequence known, connectivity arrives twice as fast using four times fewer points, and similar gains hold for the other properties. Online, with no foresight, the speed cannot improve, though the point count can still halve.
arxiv-2512-04791:
Byeongin Lee, Junho Bang, Sayan Banerjee, and co-authors report strange charge patterns that appear around charged impurities on the surface of black phosphorus, a layered semiconductor. Using a scanning tunneling microscope, they placed indium impurities on the surface and flipped them into a negatively charged state with the microscope tip. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes what forms next: orderly waves of charge, locked inside the nanoscale dip the impurity creates.

The waves form a distorted triangular pattern. Its spacing holds steady across a wide range of positive bias voltages. Strangest of all, the pattern stretches along the direction opposite to what the material's Fermi surface predicts. That mismatch defies the simple band-structure story. The experiment shows that impurity engineering can switch local charge order on and off, a lever for future nanoelectronics built on two-dimensional materials.
arxiv-2512-05191:
Samuel Walker and twelve co-authors announce the first finds of KOINTREAU, an infrared survey imaging young stars in the Taurus and Rho Ophiuchi star-forming regions. The survey uses an advanced wavefront sensor on the Keck telescope. The survey hunts faint companions — planets and small stars — around stars only about three million years old. It found two faint companions, and tracking confirms both are bound to their hosts.

One companion is a planetary-mass object, only the fifth found in Taurus, with a spectral type that oddly changes between instruments. The other looks far dimmer than stars of its type should, glows strongly in a helium line tied to outflows, and lacks the matching hydrogen signal. The authors conclude it is a young star hidden behind its own edge-on disk, seen only in scattered light. The paper delivers an improved distortion map for the survey's camera.
arxiv-2512-05291:
Na Li and four co-authors make actor-critic reinforcement learning explain itself while it trains. Actor-critic methods are a workhorse of reinforcement learning, but they are opaque, and explainability tools analyze finished policies rather than helping them learn. The authors note that standard methods also treat every feature of the state as equally important, though features plainly differ in how much they drive reward.

Their algorithm places the actor and its two critics inside reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. It computes state attributions from the value critic using a kernel version of SHAP, the standard attribution method. Those attributions become weights that steer the actor's updates and the advantage critic's targets, so the agent learns fastest along the dimensions that matter. The authors prove a convergence bound that separates stability from efficiency, and tests on three continuous-control tasks show the method is efficient, stable, and interpretable.
arxiv-2512-05391:
Qingqiao Hu and seven co-authors make pathology language models affordable by compressing the slide before the model ever sees it. A whole-slide image is gigapixel-scale, exploding into thousands of tokens, yet only a few regions carry the diagnosis. Slide-level multimodal models pay for heavy encoders and long prefixes, making them expensive to build and deploy where computing is limited. The authors show the token stream is redundant, globally and locally, while real evidence is sparse and query-dependent.

Their system, LoC-Path, compresses first and fuses later. A sparse token merger and a pretrained resampler replace the heavy slide encoder with a compact latent interface. An importance scorer then picks the latents that matter. A routing adapter fuses them into a few layers of the language model. Across experiments, LoC-Path stays competitive with prior models while cutting tuning cost, memory, and latency.
arxiv-2512-05591:
Zhenpeng Su and nine co-authors tackle a weak point in fine tuning large language models with reinforcement learning. Training data often comes from an older version of the model. The updated model can then drift too far, and training turns shaky. Boldness of exploration swings wildly, and update steps grow unstable. Their 2025 paper proposes watching one global number. It is the ratio between the entropy of the new policy and the old one.

On top of that measure, the team builds Entropy Ratio Clipping. The rule bounds the ratio from both sides, keeping each update within a safe range as a whole. Unlike the common PPO clipping rule, it also restrains shifts for actions the model did not sample. Added to two recent training methods, DAPO and GPPO, the rule raised scores across several test sets. The work offers a simple guardrail for steadier, more reliable model training.
arxiv-2512-06091:
Giuseppe Casale and Georgios Itsios construct new solutions of type II supergravity, the low energy theory of the superstring, out of deformed conformal field theories. The building blocks are lambda models, deformations of coset theories. Their parameter interpolates between a theory and its non-Abelian T-dual. The authors assemble copies and mixtures of these cosets into ten dimensional geometries.

The spaces keep anti-de Sitter factors. Those are the door to holography. Reality conditions on the solutions bound the deformation parameter, sometimes excluding the undeformed and T-dual endpoints entirely. The work extends two earlier papers and enlarges the known catalogue of holographic backgrounds with tunable deformations. Each new geometry is a solvable strong coupling problem in disguise.
arxiv-2512-06191:
Xin Chen proposes a new kind of gate for light based quantum machines, one that works across many color channels at once. Light can store far more states when its colors are split into many bins, yet gates that act on all of them have been hard to build without heavy loss. Chen's design uses a small cavity that helps two colors of light merge into one, and the gate can be set by the user.

Inside, the gate can reshape a chosen set of color modes while leaving the rest in place, and it does so with almost no error. With parts that exist today, the number of modes it can handle is already large, and adding more pulse shaping tools can raise that count further. Paired with matched sources and fast control, the scheme points to a fiber ready path for quantum work in many modes.
arxiv-2512-06591:
Joe Shymanski, Jacob Brue, and Sandip Sen ask whether people can tell a real explanation from a hollow one, and whether liking an explanation means learning from it. Explainable AI tools aim to build trust, but they are usually graded by user surveys: did the explanation feel satisfying? The authors warn that a smooth, empty explanation, which they call placebic, can please users while teaching them nothing.

Their test used a real task, choosing the best age to claim Social Security. One group got no explanations, one got placebic ones, and one got actionable ones that carried real guidance. On objective measures of understanding, the actionable group clearly beat the other two. On satisfaction, users rated placebic and actionable explanations the same. The authors argue that grading explanations must pair how users feel with how well they actually perform, or hollow explanations will keep passing the test.
arxiv-2512-07391:
Đorđe Nedeljković builds a featherweight vision network for drones that watch for emergencies. Disaster monitoring from small unmanned aircraft demands fast, accurate scene reading on board, where computing and battery are scarce. Recent designs chase global understanding with self-attention transformers, which are powerful but heavy. GlimmerNet shows a convolutional network can keep a wide view of the scene without those costly parts. By separating two jobs: gathering features at many scales, and mixing them back together.

Its building block splits the channels into groups, each looking at the scene through a different spacing of samples. So fine detail and broad context are captured at no extra parameter cost. A new aggregator then recombines what the groups found, using grouped pointwise operations that keep the parameter count tiny. The whole network holds only tens of thousands of parameters.
arxiv-2512-07691:
Julia Gehrlein, Anil Thapa, and Adrian Thompson wrote this 2025 particle physics paper on hidden traits of neutrinos. Neutrinos may interact with light in ways the standard model barely hints at. One such trait is polarizability, where two neutrinos couple to two photons.

The authors study a twist on that idea with a sterile partner. In their version, one active neutrino is swapped for a sterile neutrino. Sterile neutrinos are hypothetical particles that ignore most known forces. The team derives fresh limits from neutrino scattering off nuclei. That scattering would leave a single photon in the final state. Experiments at the intensity frontier supply the data for those bounds. A light mediator particle could realize the operator in a full model. That realization, they show, can explain the long-standing MiniBooNE low-energy excess. It does so while respecting other constraints. Other realizations are sketched at the end.
arxiv-2512-07891:
J. Hargreaves, J. Vernimmen, J. Scholten, and T. W. Morgan wrote this 2025 fusion engineering paper. Inside a tokamak, the divertor plate takes the exhaust heat of the plasma. Sweeping the strike point back and forth spreads that heat load.

The sweeping itself can crack the tungsten surface through thermal fatigue. Plasma effects like hydrogen blistering may speed the cracking along. Edge bursts called ELMs can crack the surface in their own way. The team designs a fatigue experiment for the Magnum-PSI facility. Finite element modeling shapes a test that mimics real sweeping faithfully. Tungsten samples then face cyclic heat plus hydrogen implantation together. Microscope analysis counts and measures the cracks that form. Implanted hydrogen delays cracking. Far more cycles pass before failure than in clean samples. Hydrogen pins dislocations, hardening the surface against slip bands. Pre-cracked samples under sweeping melt locally into small droplets instead.
arxiv-2512-07991:
Safal Raman Aryal wrote this 2025 economics and mathematics paper on choices that defy a single score. Choice theory usually squeezes preferences into one real-valued utility function. Patchy or self-crossing preferences break that squeeze badly.

Multi-utility ideas answer with whole families of functions instead. Aryal gives that family a fixed geometric home of its own. He constructs a ledger group that encodes the agent's trade-offs as they are. The group is partly ordered and mirrors that structure with care. Every allowed utility function then lives in its dual cone. The focus shifts from finding one map to charting the space itself. Classic multi-trait utility emerges as a special slice of that cone. Cutting the cone by continuous functionals recovers the standard form. Lexicographic preferences, by contrast, provably refuse any such return. Preference theory gains a coordinate-free language of its own.
arxiv-2512-08391: Fessel Achhoud and Hichem Khelifi, mathematicians in partial differential equations, posted a paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study anisotropic elliptic equations, where the response differs by direction. Each direction carries its own growth exponent. Their model adds two hard features at once. The coefficients can grow without bound. A singular lower order term also blows up as the solution nears zero. For this class, they prove results on whether solutions exist and how regular they are.
arxiv-2512-08491:
Razieh Golmoradifard, Mehdi Sadeghi, and Behrooz Malekolkalami, theoretical physicists in Iran, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They work in a modified gravity setting: a black brane in anti de Sitter space, with an added term quadratic in the Ricci curvature. Through holography, such a black object describes a strongly coupled fluid, whose shear viscosity can be computed from the gravity side.

The famous Kovtun Son Starinets bound claims the ratio of viscosity to entropy density can never fall below a universal floor. Their calculation finds the ratio shifts downward in proportion to the new coupling. For positive coupling, the fluid violates the bound. For negative coupling, it respects it, and with the coupling switched off the standard result returns, as it must. The authors discuss what breaking the bound means for stability, causality, and the dual theory, testing how higher curvature bends a supposedly universal law.
arxiv-2512-08691:
Michele Castellana proposes a new renormalization group method for spin glasses that are not of mean field type. Spin glasses are disordered magnetic systems whose critical behavior is hard to capture. Unlike older methods, the approach makes no prior assumption about the form of the order that should emerge near the transition.

Applied to a spin glass on a hierarchical lattice, the method lets a new order parameter appear on its own from symmetry and self similarity. That parameter projects spin patterns onto the ground state, which acts as a template across scales. The usual majority rule for ferromagnets is replaced by a richer scheme built around that parameter. Predictions for the critical exponent match simulations well. The author notes the method could extend to spin glasses on cubic lattices that model real magnetic alloys.
arxiv-2512-08791:
Zengo Tsuboi derives character formulas for modules of quantum affine superalgebras by a folding method that starts from a general linear Lie superalgebra. The work deals with supercharacters, a signed version of characters suited to superalgebras. Cauchy type identities for supersymmetric Schur functions provide the main tool.

By folding the supercharacters of the general linear case, Tsuboi obtains decomposition formulas for two families: twisted quantum affine superalgebras and quantum affine ortho symplectic ones. Each formula breaks a supercharacter into supercharacters of finite type quantum sub superalgebras. As a special case, the results give explicit character formulas for a class of Kirillov Reshetikhin modules of quantum affine algebras and their Yangian counterparts. That outcome proves a conjecture that had been proposed from Bethe ansatz study. The work links symmetric function identities to form theory in a concrete way.
arxiv-2512-08991:
Yuang Geng and coauthors propose a deterministic world model to verify the closed loop behavior of vision based controllers that map camera frames directly to actions. Such controllers are used in safety critical systems. Formal verification is hard because camera images are high dimensional and cannot be described by a simple closed formula.

Their model is a neural decoder with no latent variables, mapping physical states such as position and velocity directly to synthetic camera images. Training uses a dual loss: one term matches saliency map reconstructions, and another preserves consistency with the real controller behavior. The model is placed inside reachability study, and conformal prediction inflates the reachable sets by a spread free bound, transferring guarantees to the real system with high probability. Tests on a simulated braking system and three classic control benchmarks show much tighter reachable tubes than generative and trajectory baselines, while meeting target coverage.
arxiv-2512-09091:
Himadri Halder studies Bohr theorem for vector valued holomorphic functions and pluriharmonic functions with operator values on complete Reinhardt domains. Bohr theorem concerns how large the domain can be while a power series bound still controls the sum of coefficient magnitudes. The vector valued setting adds Banach space structure that changes the radius.

Using invariants from local Banach space theory, the author shows the Bohr radius tied to it is always strictly positive. Its asymptotic behavior is obtained separately for finite and infinite dimensional settings, where the two regimes differ in character. The framework includes the classic Minkowski setting as a special case. It also applies to a wide class of Banach sequence spaces, including mixed Minkowski, Lorentz, and Orlicz spaces. A coefficient type Schwarz Pick lemma for pluriharmonic maps with operator values on the same domains is also given, rounding out a unified approach to Bohr phenomena.
arxiv-2512-09291:
Yunhao Wang and colleagues propose a new transport protocol for semantic communication, a style of networking aimed at sixth-generation systems. Instead of moving exact bits, semantic systems send meaning that a receiver can rebuild. Today's transport protocols chase bit-perfect delivery, which clashes with the low delay and high reliability that semantic traffic needs.

Their protocol, SITP, checks only packet headers strictly and keeps damaged payloads for the semantic decoder to interpret, reaching reliability near TCP's with delay near UDP's. They build a cross-layer model that ties signal noise to packet loss across five network layers. They also add a feature interleaving scheme that spreads one image's features across several related images, softening bursts of loss. Experiments show lower delay than TCP with similar reliability in noisy conditions, delay matching UDP, and better rebuilt image quality.
arxiv-2512-09591:
Magnus Ruud Kjaer leads a team launching Stanford Sleep Bench, a benchmark for sleep foundation models, AI systems pretrained on polysomnography, the multi-sensor overnight recordings used to spot sleep disorders. Such recordings are vast and mixed, ideal for self-supervised pretraining, but the field lacked a shared dataset and a comparison of pretraining methods.

The bench holds more than seventeen thousand recordings, over one hundred sixty thousand hours, from a major sleep clinic. It supports thirteen clinical disease tasks plus standard ones like sleep staging, apnea diagnosis, and age estimation. The team evaluated self-supervised pretraining approaches on four downstream tasks. Several methods performed comparably on staging, apnea, and age estimation. For disease and mortality prediction, however, contrastive learning outperformed the rest and also converged faster in pretraining. The authors release the dataset, pretrained weights, training pipelines, and scoring code.
arxiv-2512-09891:
Tianyi Yang leads a team building mock maps of the cosmic microwave background from the FLAMINGO simulations. The microwave background carries faint secondary patterns imprinted after its release. Those patterns can test both cosmology and theories of galaxy formation. Earlier mock maps came from dark matter only simulations and modeled each effect separately. The new maps are built self consistently from full hydrodynamical simulations that include gas and feedback. They combine lensing, gas effects, dusty galaxies, radio sources, and screening in one consistent sky.

The authors check the mocks against a wide range of observations and find they match at least as well as earlier ones, while keeping all components consistent with each other. Using model variations, they explore how each signal responds to cosmology and feedback. The maps are a resource for studying these patterns and forecasting upcoming surveys.
arxiv-2512-10091:
Dimitrios Kranas, Amaury Marchon, and Silvia Pla analyze the entanglement created when a strong electric field rips particle antiparticle pairs from the vacuum, the Schwinger effect. They derive compact formulas for the entanglement between partners, starting from thermal initial states. The measure is logarithmic negativity, expressed through Bogoliubov coefficients. Bosons and fermions behave very differently, which is the paper's central contrast.

For bosons, heat helps production but hurts quantum correlations: entanglement survives only below a critical temperature that depends on the mode, and at fixed temperature only above a critical field strength. For fermions, entanglement persists at any finite temperature, though noise steadily suppresses it. As the field grows, fermionic entanglement peaks at a special field strength, the same at every temperature, then falls on both sides. The authors convert their criteria into concrete temperature and field targets for analog experiments.
arxiv-2512-10691:
Benjamin Gundersen and co-authors teach a vision-language model to read chest X-rays and point at what it describes. Medical models are usually trained by supervised fine-tuning, which rewards predicting the next token, not writing a good report. Reinforcement learning can instead reward clinical quality directly, and pairing it with step-by-step thinking has paid off in maths and coding, a combination untested here.

The team first built RadVLM by large-scale fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL on chest X-ray data. Then came a cold-start stage that teaches basic thinking. Finally, group relative policy optimisation was applied, with clinically grounded rewards for report writing and visual grounding. Across experiments, strong supervised training set the base level, reinforcement learning added real gains on both tasks, while explicit thinking added nothing. The tuned models set new state-of-the-art results under one shared evaluation.
arxiv-2512-10791:
Aileen Cheng and a very large team at Google introduce the FACTS Leaderboard, a public scoreboard for a simple virtue: whether a language model's text is factually right. Factuality splinters across settings, so the suite averages four sub-leaderboards rather than trusting one test. Each probes a different way a model can go wrong when it states facts.

One board grades answers to image-based questions, another quizzes closed-book world knowledge straight from the model's memory, a third checks factuality when the model may use a search tool. And a fourth, in its second version, judges whether long answers stay grounded in documents provided, with stronger judge models than before. Automated judges score everything. Public and private splits keep the board open to outside entries while guarding against gaming, and the suite is hosted on Kaggle for continued maintenance.
arxiv-2512-10891:
Anh-Quan Pham and co-authors teach robots new combined tasks without collecting new examples. Real manipulation data is expensive, and the space of tasks explodes fast once several objects, robots, and environments mix. Generative models can synthesise data for single tasks, but they ignore how tasks are composed, and stumble on unseen combinations.

Their semantic compositional diffusion transformer splits each transition into robot, object, obstacle, and objective parts and learns how the pieces interact through attention. Trained on a limited subset, it generates high-quality transitions for combinations it never saw, good enough to train control policies from. The loop then validates synthetic data with offline reinforcement learning and feeds the survivors into the next training round. Zero-shot performance beat single-block and hand-coded compositional baselines by a wide margin, nearly all held-out tasks were solved, and the learned codes showed real compositional structure.
arxiv-2512-11091:
Denis Saklakov argues that space may be the best place to run quantum computers. Qubits lose their delicate states quickly when heat, vibration, or gravity related disturbances disturb them. Combining the near weightlessness of orbit with temperatures near absolute zero could remove many of those disturbances at once, extending coherence times and cutting error rates.

The survey covers four leading qubit platforms: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, ultracold atoms, and photons. Each, Saklakov explains, stands to gain from a quiet cryogenic setting in microgravity. He cites supporting results such as long lived Bose Einstein condensates aboard the International Space Station, highly stable orbital atomic clocks, and a photonic quantum computer already operating in space. A proposed side by side test of identical processors on Earth and in orbit would measure the gains directly.
arxiv-2512-11191:
Xin Guan computes three dimensional standing waves on water where both gravity and surface tension matter. Standing waves that hold their shape while oscillating are hard to calculate directly, because surface tension makes time stepping stiff and unstable. Guan avoids marching in time altogether, solving the wave pattern as a boundary value problem over space and time at once.

Reduced models built from Hamiltonian formulations were compared with the full flow equations and with earlier asymptotic and numerical results, showing excellent agreement. Symmetry cuts the number of unknowns sharply for three wave families. The solutions include square and hexagonal patterns and flower like forms born from three wave resonance, generalising the classical Wilton ripples. Time simulations of the computed waves stayed perfectly periodic and revealed an instability linked to a known oblique instability of two dimensional standing waves.
arxiv-2512-11291:
Jijie Zou and fellow authors speed up simulations of how electrons flow through materials one atom thick, a key step in designing next generation nanoelectronics. The standard approach couples density functional theory with a quantum transport method and is trusted, but far too slow for large devices or screening many options. Their setup replaces the expensive part with learning.

A deep learning model first learns tight binding Hamiltonians, compact descriptions of electron energies, directly from basic physics data. A purpose built transport package then runs the quantum flow calculation on those learned Hamiltonians. Tests on graphene, hexagonal boron nitride, and molybdenum disulfide reproduced the standard method's band forms and transmission spectra closely. Speed bettered by orders of magnitude. The authors argue the approach opens large scale search and device design for two dimensional materials.
arxiv-2512-11391:
Yifan Niu and fellow authors tackle the alignment tax, the loss of general ability that language models often suffer when trained to behave more safely. Safety tuning through reinforcement learning can erode skills in maths, coding, and following instructions. Their method, Null Space constrained Policy Optimization, attacks the shape of that conflict directly.

Safety updates are projected into the null space of general tasks, the set of directions that leave general results untouched to first order. The authors prove this projection preserves core capabilities while still giving a genuine downhill direction for safety learning. Tests showed state of the art safety results without sacrificing general skill. It uses well under half the human annotated safety data rival methods consume, and it needs no mixing in of large amounts of general data. The approach promises cheaper, less destructive safety alignment for deployed models.
arxiv-2512-11491:
Jun Wang and Zhaoyang Yin prove that answers exist for a pair of coupled Schrödinger equations set at the key exponent on a waveguide shaped space. The space is part flat and part wrapped into a circle. Such equations model interacting wave fields, and the key exponent marks the borderline where standard variational methods strain. The shape mixes three open dimensions with one compact direction.

Using a scaling argument and a technique that rules out vanishing answers, they obtain one and describe how it depends on the compact coordinate. The circular direction can be replaced by any one dimensional compact shape, and the conclusion extends to systems with any number of coupled components. Results of this kind support the math theory of non-linear waves in confined geometries, from optical fibres to elongated quantum gases.
arxiv-2512-11591:
Niloyendu Roy and co-authors built a heat engine whose working part is a single grain of sand sized material. Small engines made of atoms or tiny beads obey strict limits on work and yield. The team scaled that idea up with a grain about a millimeter wide, shaken in a magnetic trap.

A loose rattler inside the grain adds noise, so the grain acts like a particle in warm fluid. The team can set its heat level and its trap size on their own. The engine matched known trade offs between power and yield, hitting the Curzon-Ahlborn yield at top power. Oddly, losses in the squeeze stroke matched or beat those in the push stroke.
arxiv-2512-12691:
Suprabha Mukhopadhyay, Yuto Bekki, Xiaojue Zhu, and Laurent Gizon study how the Sun's radiative interior affects its inertial modes in a 2025 paper. Inertial modes are slow oscillations in the Sun's rotating convection zone, useful as probes of its interior. Their coupling to the calm radiative zone below had not been discussed before, leaving open whether surface readings change.

Using the Dedalus code, they computed modes with and without the radiative interior, down to half the solar radius. Adding the zone changed frequencies and surface shapes only slightly for most modes. But many modes leak into the overshoot layer below the convection zone, cutting growth rates. Rossby modes in the radiative zone can also mix with nearby inertial modes of like symmetry.
arxiv-2512-12791:
Sreemaee Akshathala and five co-authors propose an assessment framework for agentic AI systems that goes beyond task completion in a 2025 paper. Agentic systems join language models with tools, memory, and other agents to run complex workflows. Judging them by binary success or failure misses their nondeterministic behavior, where the same system can act differently from run to run.

Their framework, built during an industry collaboration with MontyCloud, rests on four pillars: the models, memory, tools, and environment. It checks tool use, memory ingest and retrieval, collaboration, and environment interaction. Validated on an autonomous CloudOps use case, it revealed behavioral deviations that conventional metrics overlooked, showing how it captures runtime uncertainty in practice.
arxiv-2512-12891:
Mahsa Nasri and co-authors describe a full-day, in-person studio on mixed reality and art therapy. The session asks how hard-to-touch feelings can be made visible and shaped by hand. It starts with clay work and free drawing to ground people in body awareness.

Next, a mixed reality tool maps body signals, such as breath, heart rate variation, and eye movement, to color, pulse, and motion in 3D forms. Those forms act as emotional artifacts that makers can view and discuss. The studio aims to build shared terms for this kind of work. It also seeks design rules for trauma-informed tools that support awareness without overwhelming the user.
arxiv-2512-13091:
Zhizhong Huang proves counting formulas for integral points on a cone defined by a ternary quadratic form, a polynomial in three variables. The points must also meet local conditions, meaning they must look right in each local number system. Such counts connect to a deep obstruction named after Brauer and Manin.

Huang gives asymptotic formulas, meaning the counts become accurate as the search range grows, for both all points and primitive ones. The method rests on a variant of the Hardy-Littlewood circle method developed by Heath-Brown. The paper is the third in a series on strong approximation for these forms.
arxiv-2512-13291:
Sergio Junquera studies a system of two coupled diffusion equations with singular loss terms that blow up as values approach zero. Such terms model quenching, where a quantity collapses to zero in finite time, as in some chemical and physical processes. Both coupled and uncoupled loss terms appear.

Junquera proves necessary and sufficient conditions for steady solutions and for quenching solutions to exist. He also pinpoints, in terms of the exponents in the loss terms, when the two parts quench at the same time and when they do not. Quenching rates are derived as well. The results give a full map of this nonlocal system's behavior.
arxiv-2512-13591:
Denisa-Andreea Constantinescu and co-authors present astroCAMP, a benchmark and co-design frame for radio imaging at SKA scale. The Square Kilometre Array will run a huge, steady data system with strict power limits. Current imaging pipelines reach only 4-14% of hardware peak, due to memory and input-output bottlenecks.

astroCAMP supplies shared metrics for speed, energy, cost, carbon, and science fidelity, plus standard data sets and test settings. It frames co-design as a trade-off search for best operating points. Tests with WSClean and IDG on AMD and NVIDIA hardware exposed sync and scaling bottlenecks. The authors call on the SKA community to set clear fidelity thresholds for principled tuning.
arxiv-2512-13691:
Matteo Cataneo and Kazuya Koyama test whether dark energy crossing the phantom line needs non-minimal coupling in gravity. Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data, with CMB and supernova data, favor an equation of state that crosses w equals minus one. Some read that as a sign of conformal coupling in Horndeski gravity.

The authors scan the minimally coupled kinetic gravity braiding subclass in a non-parametric way. Their tool enforces no ghost or gradient instabilities from the start. They find models that cross the phantom line and still fit background and structure data, including CMB spectra, cosmic shear, and redshift-space distortions. Viable crossing thus exists without conformal coupling, a point future Bayesian studies should test.
arxiv-2512-13791:
Luke Harvey and co-authors model high-velocity features in Type Ia supernova spectra with the TARDIS code. These features are extra absorption dips at higher velocity, seen in silicon and calcium lines of many events. Their frequency suggests a common formation path across most Type Ia supernovae.

The team models six well-observed supernovae, first fitting the photospheric components for each one. They then add Gaussian density boosts at high velocity and train neural networks to emulate their effect on the silicon line. A Markov chain Monte Carlo search finds the boosts that best match feature evolution. One density boost alone could not match silicon and calcium together. Neither delayed-detonation nor double-detonation models produced these features in their tests.
arxiv-2512-13891:
ChunJun Cao, Giuseppe Cotardo, and Brad Lackey introduce quantum anticodes, a new lens on quantum error correcting codes. Error correction protects quantum information from noise, and its local structure shapes how well a code works. Their symplectic framework treats a code as a symplectic space and studies its maximal special subspaces.

Anticodes are subspaces whose elements vanish on a chosen set of parts, forming a quantum analogue of a classical idea. The frame covers stabilizer and subsystem codes and extends distance notions in quantum codes. It yields new invariants for local algebraic and counting traits. Steps like puncturing and shortening follow, giving algebraic readings of the cleaning lemma, paired recovery, and weight enumerators.
arxiv-2512-14291:
Jiayan Cui and a large team present GLM TTS in a 2025 technical report on text to speech. The system aims for production use, with efficiency, control, and high fidelity speech from written text.

GLM TTS uses two stages: a text to token autoregressive model, then a token to waveform diffusion model. Trained on only 100k hours of speech, it reaches state of the art scores on several open benchmarks. Quality gains come from a speech tokenizer with pitch constraints and a GRPO based training frame that rewards clear pronunciation, speaker similarity, and expressive prosody. LoRA based voice customization and a hybrid phoneme plus text input give users precise control at low cost.
arxiv-2512-14391:
Huayang Li and co-authors introduce RePo, a method that changes how large language models assign positions to tokens. Standard models give each token a fixed place in line, which forces the attention layers to work out the structure of the input on their own. That leaves less attention for the content that matters most.

RePo instead learns positions with a trainable module, so placement reflects how tokens relate to each other. Tested by continued pre-training on OLMo-2 models, it improved results on noisy inputs, structured data, and long contexts. Analysis showed more attention reaching distant but relevant text.
arxiv-2512-14591:
Inverse mean curvature flow expands a surface outward at a speed set by the reciprocal of its curvature, and the weakest version of the flow can start from a single point. Existence is proved here for such a point-started flow, under stated conditions on curvature and isoperimetric shape, together with an optimal bound on its growth.

Part of the proof gives new decay estimates for the Green kernel of the p-Laplacian, and the authors note these estimates close a gap in the literature. Green kernels are basic building blocks for solving equations on manifolds. The results serve geometers who use flow methods to prove facts about the shape of spaces.
arxiv-2512-14691:
Zefan Cai and a large team ask whether video foundation models truly understand the world they imitate. These models now synthesize striking, coherent video, but serving as world simulators requires them to internalize the physical, logical, and spatial constraints that govern reality.

Their framework, MMGR, brings multi-modal generative reasoning to bear on that question, probing whether generated video respects the rules it appears to depict. Testing those constraints is a step toward simulators that can be trusted for planning and training. The work matters for anyone hoping video models will move from making clips to modeling worlds that behave consistently.
arxiv-2512-14791:
Ricardo Hueso and colleagues argue for a 30 meter class telescope in the Northern Hemisphere to watch the giant planets. The coming Extremely Large Telescope in the south will transform study of the outer planets and their moons. But its view of northern targets, and of sudden events there, will be limited at key times.

Uranus favors northern skies until 2055, and Neptune will favor them from 2027 for the next 90 years. Jupiter and Saturn swing between hemispheres on cycles of 10 and 30 years. Storms, impacts, and other surprise events on these worlds cannot wait for a better season. A northern giant with its own tools would keep such rare chances within reach.
arxiv-2512-14991:
Hanqing Jin and two coauthors teach an algorithm to control systems that drift randomly, using reinforcement learning. Their setting is diffusion processes with endless continuous states, bounded actions, and rewards that can grow polynomially. Such settings arise in finance, economics, and operations work, but their scale defeats fixed grids.

Their model based algorithm partitions the joint state and action space adaptively. Inside each cell it estimates drift, volatility, and reward, and it refines the grid whenever bias outruns statistical confidence. That balance of exploration and approximation yields regret bounds tied to horizon, dimension, reward growth, and a new zooming dimension made for unbounded diffusions. The bounds include older bounded results as a special case. Numerical tests, including multi asset portfolio choice, back the theory.
arxiv-2512-15491:
Omar Namnakani and co authors study paired gaze based input methods for phones in a 2025 paper. Looking at a target can select it, but each gaze technique has trade offs: dwell time is slow, pursuit needs moving targets, and gestures can be tiring. Combining two methods might keep the strengths of each.

In a user study with 24 people, sitting and walking, the team paired three methods for navigation and selection tasks. Using gestures to move and either dwell or pursuit to select cut task time and raised completion rates over single methods. Pursuit could hurt partners by adding visual clutter, while gestures for navigation lowered accidental selections.
arxiv-2512-15591:
Igor Dolinka and Robert Gray study right units of special inverse monoids in a 2025 math paper. A special inverse monoid is given by generators and relations of a special form, and its right units form a submonoid of practical interest. Gray and Ruskuc had shown this submonoid need not split as a free product in the expected way.

The authors prove such a split is possible only when the group of units is finitely presented. Along the way they characterize when an arbitrary subgroup is finitely generated or presented, using coset geometry and a boundary width condition. A second part realizes every finitely generated submonoid of a right cancellative presented monoid inside the right units of such a monoid.
arxiv-2512-15991:
Baerbel S Koribalski and a large team of astronomers report a striking galaxy discovery in their 2025 arXiv paper. Using the ASKAP radio telescope in Australia, they studied ESO 130-G012, a small spiral galaxy seen edge-on about 16.9 megaparsecs away. Radio images at 944 MHz came from the Evolutionary Map of the Universe survey.

The images reveal a huge hourglass-shaped outflow of gas rising at least 30 kiloparsecs above and below the galaxy's star-forming disk. That is at least three times the disk's own width, and odd for a galaxy with such a modest rate of star birth. The authors argue the galaxy's weak gravity lets the gas climb so high before falling back.
arxiv-2512-16491:
Theresa Eimer leads a large author team in codifying research practice in an arXiv report made public in 2025. Meta-algorithmic research covers algorithm selection, configuration, and scheduling. It runs huge experiments with many design choices. Each choice is a possible source of error. Those errors threaten the validity of the findings.

The report gathers best practices from across the COSEAL research network. Its subfields had been evolving their standards separately until now. The guidance walks the whole experimental cycle. It starts with framing research questions and picking a design. It goes on to running experiments, then analyzing and presenting results fairly. The result is a shared guideline for newcomers and practitioners alike. By unifying scattered advice, the authors hope to cut wasted computation. They also aim to make results in the field easier to trust and reproduce.
arxiv-2512-16591:
Marco Galoppo and three co-authors model our cosmic neighborhood in their 2025 paper on arXiv. Nearby structure, within redshift 0.1, bends the light and motion used to measure the universe's expansion rate, the Hubble constant. Ignoring that local lumpiness could bias the famous Hubble tension debate.

Their model stitches together inhomogeneous Lambda-Szekeres patches, exact lumpy solutions of Einstein's equations with a cosmological constant, and calibrates them against Cosmicflows-4 reconstructions of local velocities and density. From it they compute the lumpy expansion field and re-analyze low-redshift supernovae from the Pantheon plus catalogue. Correcting for local structure shifts the best-fit Hubble constant by about 0.5 kilometers per second per megaparsec, and in the direction that increases the tension. Local geography, it turns out, cannot explain the discrepancy away.
arxiv-2512-16891:
Haichao Zhang and coauthors present LinkedOut, a way to use video large language models for video recommendation without their usual costs. Such models hold broad world knowledge, but they decode slowly, take one video at a time, and lose fine visual detail when forced into words.

LinkedOut pulls knowledge-aware tokens straight from raw frames, guided by promptable queries and side inputs. A cross-layer mixture-of-experts fusion picks the right depth of features for each case. The design supports watch histories of many videos and fast sequential inference. On standard benchmarks it set new best scores, the first such method to work from raw frames with no hand-made labels, with clear gains from layer variety.
arxiv-2512-17191:
Sophie E. Deam and a large team build a near-Earth object model calibrated on Earth impactors, the meteoroids that actually hit us. The model covers bodies from 10 grams to 150 kilograms, about 1 centimeter to half a meter, far below the 10-meter floor of past dynamical models.

From 1,202 sporadic meteoroids caught by the Global Fireball Observatory, they debias the population and trace its path from the main belt. Best fits give a collisional half-life falling from 3 million years at 0.6 kilograms to 1 million years below that size. The inner main belt still dominates supply of the 1 to 10 meter pool, via the nu-6 and 3:1 resonances with Jupiter.
arxiv-2512-17291:
Anandu Kalleri Madhu and four co-authors find a leaner way to pose the traveling salesman problem to a quantum computer. The classic puzzle asks for the shortest route that visits each city once. Quantum machines are short on qubits, the basic units of quantum memory, so saving qubits matters more than raw speed here.

Their encoding tracks the roads between cities rather than the cities themselves, and a second trick shrinks the search space further. They test routes for four, five, and six cities on both simulators and real hardware. The best route for four cities came out of an IQM quantum machine. Against the standard node-based encoding, their method used fewer resources and ran more cleanly on small cases.
arxiv-2512-17491:
Louis Faul, Xavier Richard, Marie Bétrisey, and Christian Mazza study chemical reaction networks, the math models biologists use to describe how molecules interact inside cells. They focus on noncompetitive networks, whose resting states do not depend on reaction speeds and which can even act like simple neural networks. Their 2025 paper asks how such a network responds when outside signals disturb it.

The team describes each disturbance as a sandpile style process: add a molecule to a resting state, then let reactions settle the system into a new resting state. They show these networks are a special case of Abelian networks, a known framework from the study of self organized criticality. That link proves only some resting states keep recurring, matched exactly to a key algebraic object called the critical group.
arxiv-2512-17591:
Michał Czakon and Rene Poncelet check a shortcut that particle theorists used to finish landmark LHC calculations. Predicting three-jet and three-photon events at top precision needs two-loop math so heavy that teams approximated the color flow of quarks and gluons, keeping only the leading color terms. Full amplitudes without that shortcut have now arrived.

Feeding the full results in, the pair measure what the shortcut missed. For most published numbers, the missed subleading-color effects stay under 2 percent. The ratio of three-jet to two-jet rates is the outlier, shifting by up to 5 percent. Both standard cleanup schemes agree on the verdict. Since other theory uncertainties loom larger, past results stand, with one ratio now on firmer ground.
arxiv-2512-17791:
José E. Figueroa-López and Ruoting Gong study American put options in the last moments before they expire. A holder may sell early, and the price level that makes early sale wise is called the critical price. Their models let the stock jump suddenly, not just drift, with a steady random walk mixed in.

They cover two jump settings past work had skipped, one with wild downward jumps and one with endless small jumps. In both, the gap between the critical price and its final value shrinks like the square root of the time left, with exact constants given. They also expand the option price itself to second order near the boundary.
arxiv-2512-17891:
Kristoffer Wickstrøm and five coauthors want image models that can explain their own calls without extra training. Modern vision transformers are strong but opaque, and past explainable designs needed costly retraining and special setups. Their method, Keypoint Counting Classifiers, turns a trained model into one that shows its work.

The trick uses a skill these models already have: matching key points between two images. A class call then rests on counted matches that a person can see drawn on the picture itself. Tests against recent rival methods show clearer contact between people and the model. The work moves toward image tools that users can check at a glance.
arxiv-2512-17991:
Lucas L. Brugger, Cristhiano Duarte, and Bruno F. Rizzuti retell Schrödinger's cat, the famous puzzle of a cat that seems both alive and dead until someone looks. Their retelling treats quantum theory as an upgraded form of probability, built on each observer's beliefs. The cat scene becomes a case of remote measurement.

Two agents, Alice and Bob, share one quantum state from far apart. Each measures a local part, and the paper tracks how each one's beliefs should update. The shift in view does not solve the old puzzle by fiat, but it reframes it in terms of information and belief. The authors aim the piece at young scientists meeting the puzzle for the first time.
arxiv-2512-18391:
Leon Mans, Daniel Stremmer, and Malgorzata Worek compute a key process for the Large Hadron Collider: top-quark pairs that decay into a lepton and jets. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, gives the complete next-to-leading-order corrections. It keeps the finite width of the top quarks and the W and Z bosons, rather than treating them as stable particles.

The calculation includes doubly, singly, and non-resonant parts and their interference, across all starting particle combinations. The setting is the LHC Run III energy of 13.6 TeV. Special care goes to handling photons and jets so the results stay physically meaningful. The authors report total and detailed cross sections. They also measure how much smaller effects, like electroweak Sudakov logarithms, actually matter.
arxiv-2512-18491:
Mohammadreza Saghafi, Lamine Mili, and Karlton Wirsing study the noise that comes out of a real quantum computer. They ran a single-qubit circuit again and again on IBM superconducting machines and recorded the stream of outcomes as counts of zeros. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, treats that stream as a time series and probes its structure.

Using the wavelet leader method and multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis, they find strong multifractal behavior. The fluctuations are not pure randomness; they show layered scaling patterns across many time scales. That structure suggests filters tuned to those scaling features could strip noise more effectively. The work helps physicists understand how quantum devices behave under repeated measurement and points toward better noise reduction for near-term machines.
arxiv-2512-18691:
V. V. Flambaum and H. B. Tran Tan revisit a long-standing puzzle about charged spin-1 particles in this 2025 theory paper. Unlike electrons, vector bosons bound to a point-like nucleus have wave functions that fall to the center, and embedding the system in an electroweak-style theory does not cure the problem. The pair instead solve the Coulomb problem for a nucleus of finite radius and then shrink that radius toward zero, which lets them keep a key Upsilon term earlier spectrum calculations dropped.

Strange effects follow. The Upsilon term supports a tower of states inside the nucleus whose count diverges as the radius shrinks, triggering vacuum breakdown that screens the charge. Ordinary states persist but leak into the nucleus, and a negative particle's charge density flips sign near the center.
arxiv-2512-18791:
Yichuan Zhang, Chengxin Li, and Yujie Gu watermark speech made by text-to-speech diffusion models. Synthetic voices now sound real enough that owners need proof of origin and courts need tracing. Existing audio watermarks are usually built for one model and audibly degrade the speech. Their scheme, Smark, posted to arXiv in December 2025, aims to work across all such models.

Smark embeds the mark during the reverse diffusion process every TTS model shares, placing it with a discrete wavelet transform into the audio's stable low-frequency regions. That placement survives the generation process and resists removal. In simulated real-world attack tests, Smark leads on both fronts that matter: the speech still sounds clean, and the watermark reads back accurately. A universal, gentle watermark makes provenance practical for commercial speech systems.
arxiv-2512-19591:
Sana Begum Murtuja Shaikh and Priyanka Singh ask how living in a galaxy cluster reshapes the galaxy mass census. Clusters are the universe's most extreme neighborhoods, ideal for isolating what environment does to galaxy growth. Their data join the Kilo Degree Survey's nine-band photometry with an infrared survey, some three point seven million galaxies in all.

One hundred five clusters from the eROSITA eFEDS catalog overlap the patch, at redshifts where the universe was roughly half its present age. Mass functions are measured in radial shells out to five times the cluster's characteristic radius. The cluster signal stands clear out to twice that radius, then fades into the field.
arxiv-2512-19691:
Junze Ye and five colleagues, including physicians and machine-learning researchers, audit a benchmark that other AI systems are graded against. MedCalc-Bench tests whether models can compute clinical scores, but many of its reference labels were themselves drafted with language-model help. The team built a physician-in-the-loop pipeline to recheck those labels at scale and keep the benchmark honest going forward.

Their findings are sobering: at least 27 percent of test labels look erroneous or impossible to compute. On a physician-validated subset, recomputed labels matched expert truth far more often than the originals. Grading frontier models against the old labels understates their accuracy by a wide margin, and a training experiment shows models raised on cleaned labels perform better. Benchmarks, they argue, need active stewardship, not one-time release.
arxiv-2512-19991:
John Cartmell, Mihaela Cardei, and Ionut Cardei feed machine learning models through a Bloom filter first. Each data sample is hashed into a compact, fixed-length bit array, shrinking memory while scrambling the original feature values. The encoding needs no keyed hashing, though an optional key controls the mapping and would be required to reproduce a given representation exactly.

Six datasets spanning text messages, electrocardiograms, census and health records, and handwritten images put the idea through its paces, with four classifier families trained on the encodings. Performance stayed comparable to models trained on raw data or standard dimensionality-reduction outputs across several datasets, while memory savings were consistent. The authors pitch Bloom filter encodings as a general-purpose preprocessing step that preserves similarity structure and buys a measure of obfuscation.
arxiv-2512-20191:
Anar Dosi develops a homological approach for noncommutative complex analytic geometry. The setting is Fréchet algebras, a class within topological algebra used in analysis. He describes the shape theory of such an algebra through a Čech category built over it, a bookkeeping device borrowed from shape theory.

Within that approach, Dosi solves a function calculus problem: how to apply holomorphic functions to operators in a controlled way. The answer is expressed through a spectrum of that kind attached to a module. He applies the theory to the quantum plane of a shrinking operator, connecting the spectrum to the Putinar spectrum and, for Banach modules, to the Taylor spectrum. The paper is aimed at experts in operator algebras.
arxiv-2512-20391:
Georg Schildbach proposes collision avoidance for robot swarms that never talk at all. Most joint schemes lean on wireless links, yet real links suffer latency, packet loss, and even jamming or spoofing attacks. His Contingency Model-based Control replaces messages with shared rules agreed offline, much like traffic laws.

Each robot follows a contingency trajectory, and planes that cut the gap between neighbours in half act as hard avoidance constraints.
