The construction guarantees recursive feasibility and collision freedom for the whole swarm in closed loop. New robots can join at any time, meeting a plug-and-play demand. Two numerical examples in tight spaces show the swarm moving smoothly with the guarantee intact. The design trades messages for pre-agreed discipline.
arxiv-2512-20591:
Changyi Lin and co-authors built a fingertip that sees touch without anything bending. Most tactile sensors infer contact from deformation, so contact with liquids, gels, or ultra-soft materials registers weakly or not at all. LightTact makes contact directly visible instead.

Its optical design blocks ambient light and internal illumination everywhere except true contact points, where scattered light passes through. Raw images are therefore near-black away from contact and show the contacting surface's natural appearance at contact. Pixel-level segmentation stays accurate across materials, forces, appearances, and lighting. Demonstrations include spreading water, dipping into facial cream, and handling soft thin films. The aligned visual-tactile images can even be read directly by vision-language models.
arxiv-2512-20691:
Enrique Gaztañaga, K. Sravan Kumar, and João Marto return to a 1935 idea from Einstein and Rosen. Those physicists pictured particles as bridges joining two sheets of spacetime, with two arrows of time. Standard quantum field theory instead treats time as a fixed one-way parameter, and the authors question that habit for curved spacetime.

Building on direct-sum quantum theory, they link the bridges to separate geometric sectors of spacetime. They argue that effects at gravity horizons involve quantum inverted harmonic oscillators. They also claim support from large-scale parity patterns in the cosmic microwave background. The work aims at a unitary account that could help join gravity with quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2512-20791:
Pavel Dvurechensky, Meggie Marschner, Shimrit Shtern, and Mathias Staudigl speed up extragradient methods for stacked equilibrium problems. Hierarchical variational inequalities cover bilevel optimization, games with leaders and followers, and programs constrained by equilibria. Knowing how many steps a method needs, worst case, is what practitioners ask first.

The authors prove convergence rates using gap functions that measure both feasibility and optimality error. Their complexity bounds hold on both levels of the problem, and solutions converge weakly under a sharpness condition on the lower level. They report matching or improving the best known iteration counts while allowing a broader problem class than earlier work handled.
arxiv-2512-20891:
Hiroshi Okada and Yutaro Shoji build a neutrino mass model on a new kind of symmetry. Seesaw models explain why neutrinos are so light by pairing them with very heavy partners. Their linear seesaw variant follows a non-invertible selection rule, a modern symmetry whose rules cannot simply be undone, helped by a small threefold symmetry.

In their setup, some mass terms appear only at one-loop level, generated by particle interactions in loops, while the symmetry holds at the basic level. The model also yields testable side effects: limits on mixing unitarity, rare lepton flavor violations, and a dark matter candidate. Numerical analysis maps out the allowed physical parameters.
arxiv-2512-20991:
Toqeer Ali Syed, Salman Jan, and five co-authors merge two household problems, money and meals, into one agent system. FinAgent takes a household's income, fixed expenses, health conditions, and live food prices, then produces meal plans that meet nutritional needs at the lowest workable cost. Specialist agents handle budgeting, nutrition, price monitoring, and health personalization, sharing a knowledge base and swapping ingredients along a substitution graph when prices move.

Simulations on a representative Saudi household cut food costs by roughly twelve to eighteen percent against a fixed weekly menu. Nutrient adequacy stayed above ninety-five percent. The plans also held up under price swings of twenty to thirty percent. The system points at practical help for middle-income families squeezed by food inflation.
arxiv-2512-21191:
Ze-Kun Liu, Ying Li, and two co-authors hunt light dark matter where underground detectors go deaf. Direct searches lose sensitivity below a giga-electronvolt of particle mass, because such featherweight particles barely nudge atomic nuclei. Rare decays of B and K mesons offer another window. If a meson occasionally decays into a dark particle, the visible products carry away less energy than they should. The missing energy betrays the invisible guest.

A new Z-prime boson mediates the dark sector's contact with ordinary matter in the generic model used here. Working through that model, the authors convert experimental limits on those rare decays into upper bounds on its parameters. The meson constraints complement direct detection rather than duplicate it, and they bite hardest exactly where the interaction grows with the dark matter's momentum. Flavor factories thus double as dark matter observatories for the lightest candidates.
arxiv-2512-21391:
Mohammad Hammas Saeed, Isaiah J. King, and Howie Huang present ALETHEIA, a system built to detect coordinated influence campaigns on social media. Such campaigns use networks of malicious or troll accounts to sway public discussion, and moderators need tools that can spot the accounts and predict what they will do next.

ALETHEIA represents a campaign as a graph and combines network structure with language features, feeding them to graph neural networks that can scale to large networks. Tested on campaigns from several countries on Reddit and X, it improves detection scores over standard methods that use only interaction and user features. A second component stacks a graph network over a recurrent network to forecast future links, predicting which users trolls will target next with high accuracy.
arxiv-2512-21491:
Hikaru Sasaki identifies generators for two families of bosonic vertex operator algebras tied to three-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories labeled by partitions. Such algebras encode two-dimensional conformal field theories. Knowing a small set of generators would pin down each algebra's whole structure.

Sasaki shows how to identify the generators for two specific partition pairs in the SU(n) and SU(n+1) families. He conjectures that these suffice to construct the full structure of those algebras. He also finds that the boundary algebra of the first family naturally contains the bosonic one inside it. Results of this kind serve the geometric Langlands program and related duality work.
arxiv-2512-21791:
Christophe D. Hounwanou, Yae Ulrich Gaba, and Pierre Ntakirutimana compare three ways of making synthetic financial time series, a need created by scarce data and the secrecy of real market and client data. Fake data are only useful if models trained or tested on them behave as they would on the real thing.

The authors build one evaluation framework and apply it to a statistical ARIMA-GARCH baseline, autoencoders, and TimeGAN, a GAN for sequences, using daily S and P 500 data. They score fidelity, temporal structure such as autocorrelation and volatility clustering, and use in portfolio work and volatility forecasting. The statistical model captures linear trends and shifting volatility but misses nonlinear dynamics. The autoencoder produces smooth series that understate extreme events. TimeGAN achieved the best balance of realism and time coherence, with the lowest discrepancy score.
arxiv-2512-22591:
A. S. Naumchik, Roman K. Goncharov, and Alexei D. Kiselev examine how imperfect detectors distort quantum key distribution, the technique that uses quantum states to share secret keys. Real homodyne and heterodyne readings suffer asymmetry: beam splitters are uneven and detectors differ in efficiency. Working in a Gaussian approximation for light-count stats, the authors compute the measurement operators, the POVMs, that honestly include those flaws.

For heterodyne detection, the ideal measurement must be written with projectors onto squeezed states, and the form is not unique; the squeezing parameter becomes an extra knob affecting the eavesdropper's information. They then analyze long-run security of the Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable protocol when an attacker controls the measurement noise. Mutual information, Holevo information, and the secret fraction all degrade under asymmetry.
arxiv-2512-22691:
Haiyang Wang, Luca Barletta, and Alex Dytso tighten a bound in information theory about the cleanest way to signal over a noisy channel with a capped amplitude. For the amplitude-constrained Gaussian channel, the capacity-achieving input distribution is known to use finitely many signal points, but how many? Older bounds put the count between a term growing like the amplitude and one growing like its square, and a conjecture favored the linear rate.

The authors prove a new lower bound growing like the amplitude times the square root of its logarithm, which rules out the conjectured linear scaling. Their route starts by quantifying how the optimal output distribution hugs the uniform distribution inside the allowed region. It then introduces a wrapping map onto a compact domain. Finally it develops approximation theory for uniform laws by finite Gaussian mixtures.
arxiv-2512-22991:
Tillmann Rheude, Roland Eils, and Benjamin Wild question whether fancier multimodal designs actually fuse information better. Multimodal learning promises gains from combining data types, and method papers have grown steadily more complex on the belief that specialized fusion machinery pays off. The authors rebuilt nineteen high-impact multimodal methods and ran them across nine datasets with up to twenty-three modalities under one shared protocol.

With tuning, setup, cross-validation, and statistical testing held uniform, added complexity often produced confusion rather than fusion. Complex designs did not reliably beat unimodal baselines or the authors' deliberately simple baseline for multimodal learning. A focused case study then exposes basic shortcomings in even top-tier publications, such as uneven tuning budgets. The conclusion is a plea to shift effort from architectural novelty toward rigor in testing, so the field's comparisons can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-23191:
Om Godse and Shantanu Desai test a long-running dark matter controversy with a Bayesian comparison. The DAMA experiment has long claimed an annual modulation in its detector rate. That yearly wave is the signature of Earth moving through the galactic dark matter wind. The ANAIS-112 and COSINE-100 experiments were built to check it with the same target material. The authors combine about three years of data from both checking experiments.

They compare a sinusoidal modulation model against a constant model, trying uniform priors and priors centered on DAMA's best-fit values for the signal's frequency and phase. In both the one-to-six and two-to-six kilo-electron-volt energy windows, the log Bayes factor for the cosine model stayed below about one point one five, far too weak to count as evidence. The verdict is no sign of a dark matter modulation in the combined data.
arxiv-2512-23291:
Arman Martirosyan and co-authors build multimodal systems for reading human movements and the emotions behind them, using the iMiGUE dataset of micro-gestures. Micro-gestures are subtle, fine-grained behaviors, and spotting them, like predicting emotion from behavior rather than words, demands fusion of video and body-pose information. The team entered both tasks of the MiGA 2025 Challenge with two frameworks.

For micro-gesture classification, color video embeddings from a video transformer and 3D pose embeddings from a graph network are merged by a cross-modal token fusion module, combining appearance with skeletal structure. For emotion recognition, facial embeddings and video features are fused through a dedicated module designed to capture expressions and body language. The emotion system performed well enough to take second place in the challenge. Together the frameworks show how pose, face, and context channels complement each other on behavior that humans themselves barely notice.
arxiv-2512-23391: George Andrews and Mohamed El Bachraoui count integer partitions dressed in two colors. A partition writes a number as a sum of parts; here each part is colored red or blue, with one restriction: even parts may appear only in blue. The authors focus on counting sequences that arise when further constraints are placed on the parity and color of the parts. For these sequences they establish exact formulas, and from the formulas they deduce new identities among ordinary partition counts, adding to the classical theory of partition generating functions.
arxiv-2512-23491:
Entity resolution is the data-cleaning job of deciding which records refer to the same person, product, or place. Dimitrios Karapiperis, George Papadakis, and Vassilios Verykios focus on the progressive version, where the best matches must be found early because time and computing budgets are limited. Existing methods rank candidate pairs by sorting, which becomes prohibitively slow on fast-moving data streams.

Their framework, SPER, replaces sorting with random sampling framed as a bipartite maximization problem. Acting like a filter that favors promising pairs, it selects candidates in strictly linear time and skips the heavy setup of ranking methods. On eight real-world data sets, SPER ran three to more than six times faster than leading baselines while keeping recall and precision about the same.
arxiv-2512-23791:
Dmitry Chicherin, Gregory Korchemsky, Emery Sokatchev, and Alexander Zhiboedov compute energy correlators in gravity. These record how energy spreads by angle when particles collide, adapted here to gravity, where they stay free of infrared blow-ups. Working at one loop, they obtain the one- and two-point correlators in maximal supergravity and in pure Einstein gravity, paying close attention to contact terms where virtual corrections meet real emissions.

Infrared divergences cancel explicitly, and the Ward identities of energy-momentum conservation check out. In the back-to-back limit, the energy-energy correlator takes an all-order form governed by shared soft-graviton dynamics. A beam-averaged version is computed across theories including tree-level string theory; the results are analytic and tame, supporting dispersion relations. Extra kinks unique to gravity are also catalogued. The paper runs to seventy-two pages and was accepted by JHEP.
arxiv-2512-24491:
Graeme Baker and Ankita Chatterjee solve a Skorokhod reflection problem driven by jumps. A process moves in the positive orthant and reflects at the boundary. An outside jump process drives it. For each input, a unique minimal strong solution exists. It runs until an explicit maximal stopping time. That time is read off a dual linear program tied to the system's state.

Reinsurance supplies the application. Interconnected insurance firms share risk under an agreement. The reflected system models their joint reserves. The stopping time becomes the agreement's failure time. Ruin of the network can be studied through it. The work extends a 2025 analysis by Baker and co-authors. Jump drivers replace continuous ones. It also pushes past Reiman's classical existence result, beyond sub-stochastic reflection matrices.
arxiv-2512-24691:
Narasimha Reddy Gosala and Arundhati Dasgupta study quark-gluon plasma, the hot fluid-like state of matter from the early universe, with non-perturbative methods. They model it using time-dependent Yang-Mills condensates, classical background fields with strong self-interaction. Quarks moving in gluon backgrounds come first, including how their back-reaction can break isotropy for some starting conditions.

A one-loop finite-temperature effective action, computed by background-field and heat-kernel methods, gives pressure rising with temperature in a near logarithmic way, as expected for a deconfined but interacting phase. Lattice calculations provide a comparison. Readers also get the gravitational wave side promised by the title and framing.
arxiv-2512-24891:
Panos Betzios, Ji Hoon Lee, and Olga Papadoulaki explore bubbling wormhole geometries suggested by sums over Wilson loop representations in supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. The thermofield double, which entangles two copies of a theory and is dual to a two-sided black hole, is their model. Analogous sums over gauge group representations act like delta operators correlating eigenvalues across several matrix models.

The proposed holographic duals are multi-covers of the familiar anti-de Sitter space times a sphere, whose boundary is several four-spheres intersecting each other. String theory readers get a new wormhole-like construction built from Wilson loops. Such states test how geometry emerges from entanglement-like correlations.
arxiv-2512-24991:
Gyung Hyun Je and Colin Raffel tackle a practical planning problem in fine-tuning language models: how many examples will a task need before performance reaches a target? Data efficiency is usually unknown, forcing costly cycles of annotation and retraining. Across thirty specialized tasks, they show strong models may struggle with no training yet improve greatly after fine-tuning.

Methods for predicting a task's data efficiency before collecting all the data are the focus. Machine learning practitioners get a way to budget annotation effort sensibly. Knowing a task is data hungry or data light in advance changes project planning and cost estimates.
arxiv-2601-00191:
Youpeng Wu works with Jie Xiao, Andrew Michael Levin, and Qiang Li on a rare triple production at the LHC. A W boson, a Higgs boson, and a photon made together form the target. Such multiboson events probe the electroweak force law. New physics could hide in those couplings. The team models signal and background with Monte Carlo tools.

Detector effects follow CMS design specs. Boosted decision trees sharpen the event selection. They pull signal out from a much larger background. The authors then project how visible the process could be. At one large data volume, expected significance stays below one sigma. At the high luminosity upgrade, it climbs higher. Even then, a clear discovery stays out of reach. The study still sets honest expectations. It shows where effort and data must go next.
arxiv-2601-00591:
Saajid Chowdhury and eight co-authors study clusters of argon atoms with one added proton, in a 2026 paper. Some cluster sizes are extra stable, and labs call those sizes magic numbers. For plain rare-gas clusters, a simple ball-packing view works well. Add one proton, though, and a long list of magic numbers shows up with no clear cause. The team set out to find that cause.

They ran quantum Monte Carlo runs, a method that samples many random paths to find low-energy shapes. They paired those runs with careful sums of the forces between many atoms. The argon atoms turned out to sit close to the lowest-energy shape. As clusters grow, the source of the stability shifts. Small clusters gain it from how atoms group around the proton. Large ones gain it from plain pair forces. The shift explains the long list of magic sizes.
arxiv-2601-00691:
Mohamed Trabelsi and Huseyin Uzunalioglu present TeleDoCTR in 2026, a system that helps fix telecom faults from support tickets. In big telecom firms, staff log each fault as a ticket. Experts read each ticket, search past cases, and find the right fix. TeleDoCTR aims to take over the key steps of that chain.

First, the system routes each ticket to the team that should own it. Next, it pulls past tickets that match the new one in sense, not just in words. Last, it drafts a fault report that names the fault, its cause, and ways to fix it. It blends rank tools tuned to telecom terms with text-writing AI models. The team tested it on real ticket data from a telecom network. It beat the best known methods on both speed and accuracy. The system could cut fix times and free experts for the hardest cases.
arxiv-2601-00791:
Valentin Noël looks for the fingerprints of genuine mathematical reasoning inside a transformer's attention patterns. Telling whether a language model truly reasons or merely pattern-matches is an open problem: trained verifier models are expensive, and rules based on the final text are brittle. Noël treats each attention matrix as a weighted graph connecting tokens.

From those graphs he extracts four spectral diagnostics, including the Fiedler value and spectral entropy, none of which need any learned parameters. Across seven models from four architecture families, valid reasoning showed a measurable spectral signature with very large effect sizes, allowing a single threshold to classify reasoning traces with high accuracy. The signal tracked logical coherence rather than mere acceptance by a proof checker.
arxiv-2601-00891:
Rodrigo Kataishi is the sole author of a 2026 paper on how to help AI systems find the right texts to cite. Such systems fetch passages from a store, then write answers based on them. If the fetch is poor, the answer is poor. Kataishi enriches each text's code with topic data before the fetch. The code blends three views of the text.

One view counts key terms, in the classic term-weight style. A second view maps latent topics, found by two standard topic tools. A third view is the compact code from a small modern language model. Joined, the code holds both term-level and topic-level sense. Tests on a legal text store show the gains. Texts grouped more cleanly, and fetches scored higher on precision. The method is cheap next to full language model codes. It could make citation-based AI more reliable in fields like law.
arxiv-2601-00991:
Joshua Kawaguchi and seven colleagues manufacture human pose data inside a video game engine instead of a motion capture studio. Labeled three-dimensional pose data are expensive and studio-bound, while outdoor datasets lack exact ground truth. Their pipeline, UnrealPose-Gen, renders frames with Unreal Engine 5 and records everything a pose model needs to learn.

Each generated frame carries three-dimensional joints in world and camera coordinates, two-dimensional keypoints with occlusion flags, bounding boxes, and the camera's full parameters. With it they built UnrealPose-1M, a corpus of roughly one million frames spanning scripted coherent sequences and randomized ones, several scenes, dozens of actions, and five subjects, shot from varied camera paths. A fidelity check compares the synthetic data against real captures.
arxiv-2601-01291:
Yicheng Jin and six co-authors present Curator, a search index for finding near matches among vector embeddings when a strict filter is applied. Many apps search by meaning, then keep only items with a given date, price, or label. When few items pass the filter, graph-based indexes fall apart because the surviving points are too sparse to stay connected.

Curator takes a different route. It builds a shared clustering tree and hangs a tailored mini-index for each label inside it, so memory stays low while each filtered search stays fast. It also handles updates and complex filters by building temporary indexes on the fly. Paired with leading graph indexes, Curator cut the slowest filtered queries by up to about twenty-one times, while adding only a few percent to build time and memory. The design suits catalogs and feeds where filters are the norm.
arxiv-2601-01391:
Ian Jacob Cabansag and Paul Ntegeka ask whether teamwork helps an Afrobeats song stay on the charts. Using daily Nigeria Spotify Top 200 data from 2024, they count for each track how many days it charted and how many streams it earned in Nigeria that year. Collaboration status marks whether a track is solo or multi-artist.

A Bayesian negative binomial regression, suited to count data that vary more than simple models allow, weighs chart days against collaboration and total streams. Sampling methods produce the estimates, checked with rate ratios and predictive tests. After streams are accounted for, collaboration tracks tended to spend slightly fewer days on the chart than comparable solo tracks. The finding cuts against the easy assumption that features always extend a song's life. For artists and labels weighing the cost of a guest spot, total reach seems to matter more than the pairing itself.
arxiv-2601-01791:
Semantic communication sends the meaning of a message rather than its raw bits. It promises efficient 6G networks. Generative AI helps it encode and decode even under poor channel conditions. Shunpu Tang and eight co-authors warn that the same power helps attackers: anyone intercepting the broadcast signal can run a strong generative decoder and recover private content.

Worse, agentic eavesdroppers with memory, outside knowledge, and reasoning can infer a user's behavior and intent over time, beyond the message itself. The paper sorts eavesdropping threats into a taxonomy. It explains how modern AI strengthens them. Then it turns the lens around. It sketches how generative and agentic tools might defend privacy instead, in future semantic systems.
arxiv-2601-01991:
Lyman-alpha blobs are enormous glowing gas clouds in the young universe, thought to mark the birthplaces of today's massive galaxies, but the mass of their dark matter halos has stayed uncertain. The ODIN survey found over one hundred blobs in the COSMOS field. It found them at each of two redshifts. Byeongha Moon and twenty-three co-authors use that sample. They measure how strongly the blobs cluster.

Clustering strength converts into galaxy bias and halo mass: minimum halo masses around a trillion suns, with median masses a few times higher. Blobs occupy only a small fraction of such halos. Their homes should grow into present-day halos of about ten trillion solar masses. Those halos host massive ellipticals and groups. The measurement anchors blobs firmly in proto-group environments.
arxiv-2601-02191:
Heating the Sun's chromosphere is a long-standing puzzle. Elias Udnæs and Tiago Pereira hunt its fingerprints in spectra. They use three-dimensional simulations of the solar atmosphere. Detailed spectral synthesis accompanies them. The profiles of magnesium and calcium lines are clustered. The goal is to find which shapes accompany strong heating.

The strongest heating sits under profiles with strong emission. They split into two grain types. Blue grains draw their blue-wing emission from upward shock waves. They carry an order of magnitude more heating than average, with a characteristic sawtooth time pattern. Red grains are equally heated. They show no consistent stratification or temporal signature. Together, the two types cover only about three percent of spectra. They account for more than twelve percent of all chromospheric heating. Their frequency depends on the magnetic configuration.
arxiv-2601-02291:
Jesús Fernández, Loïc Vanel, and Antoine Bérut study piles of tiny silica grains in water, each grain only a few micrometers wide. A pile of normal sand holds a slope called the angle of repose. For grains this small, heat driven jiggling competes with gravity, so it is unclear whether a pile can hold any slope at all.

In rotating drum tests, the smallest grains always creep flat, giving an angle of zero. Above a threshold size, piles stop at a small angle that grows with grain size but stays below the minimum expected for larger, heat free grains. The stopping point matches a model where the pile crosses between glass like and jammed states as its own weight presses down harder than heat can push back.
arxiv-2601-02591:
Daeun Hwang, Xuyuan Cai, Edward F. Melcer, and Elin Carstensdottir analyze the music of role playing video games with music information retrieval tools.

Game music is usually studied like film music, for its narrative function, with little systematic measurement of its sound features across game types. The authors extract quantifiable musical features from games in three role playing sub genres and test how those features correlate with the perception and portrayal of each sub genre. They suggest the correlated features reflect the storytelling elements and play mechanics expected of each sub genre, giving composers and researchers a measurable link between sound and game type.
arxiv-2601-02691:
Gaoguo Yan and four co authors study longitudinal flow decorrelation in heavy ion collisions, where two nuclei smash and the debris expands collectively. The expansion pattern is set in the transverse plane, But fluctuations along the beam direction twist the event plane and make its strength asymmetric from one end to the other. So the flow decorrelates along rapidity. They map how that effect depends on collision energy and on the size of the colliding system.

A multiphase transport model simulates gold on gold collisions at four energies at the RHIC collider, plus zirconium and ruthenium isobar collisions at the top energy. Two decorrelation measures are separated, one mixing magnitude asymmetry with plane twist and one from twist alone. Both fall linearly with rapidity, and both depend significantly on energy and system size, giving experimentalists a calibrated expectation for what they measure.
arxiv-2601-02891:
Bach Phan-Tat and four co-authors test a transparent way to detect when words change meaning over time, a task usually given to opaque neural networks. Word embeddings can score well on benchmarks, yet users cannot see why a word was flagged as changed. The authors' method instead tracks which words a target word depends on in sentence structure, building profiles from dependency patterns alone.

Tested against standard benchmarks, the dependency method proves effective and even beats several distributional models built on embeddings. The authors back the scores with detailed checks, both counting-based and case-by-case, showing the predictions are plausible. Because every signal comes from visible grammar patterns, a reader can inspect exactly why the method judged that a word's meaning had shifted.
arxiv-2601-03191:
Anees Ur Rehman Hashmi, Numan Saeed, and Christoph Lippert introduce AnatomiX, a multimodal language model that reads chest X-rays with explicit attention to anatomy. Medical models have improved at interpreting these scans, but they still stumble on spatial reasoning and often ground phrases in the wrong structures. AnatomiX follows the radiologist's workflow in two stages.

First it identifies anatomical structures and extracts their features; then a large language model uses that grounding for tasks such as phrase grounding, report generation, visual question answering, and image understanding. Across multiple benchmarks, AnatomiX improved performance on anatomy and phrase grounding, grounded diagnosis, and grounded captioning by more than twenty-five percent over existing approaches. The authors frame true anatomical correspondence, not just better scores, as the key to trustworthy medical AI.
arxiv-2601-03591:
Subhajit Paul, Manish Patel, and Debasish Chaudhuri study a single tracer particle moving through a bath of other particles when the forces between them are non-reciprocal. In such couplings, the pull one way does not match the pull back. Such one-sided couplings are common in active matter, from swimming microbes to driven colloids. The team starts from the full microscopic motion and derives a simpler equation for the tracer alone.

Their generalized Langevin equation carries a memory term that reflects the bath's delayed influence. From it they compute how the tracer responds and spreads, and they extend the fluctuation-dissipation relation to this uneven setting. The tracer's spread grows non-monotonically with non-reciprocity and spikes near a resonance they call giant diffusivity. Results like these help explain strange transport in living and synthetic active systems.
arxiv-2601-03791:
Xiaoyu Luo and three co-authors revisit claims that language models memorize personal data, arguing many leakage tests are flawed. Reports of models reproducing private information are often read as proof of memorization, but a prompt can also let a model reconstruct details through pattern completion and surface cues. Their framework, Cue-Resistant Memorization, judges leakage only when such lexical cues are controlled.

They re-evaluated personal data leakage across thirty-two languages and several memorization setups, including prefix-suffix completion and associative reconstruction. Much of the apparent success, they find, was driven by direct surface-form cues rather than true memorization. The revision matters for privacy law and practice: counting cue-driven reconstruction as memorization overstates one risk while possibly masking how leakage actually happens.
arxiv-2601-03991:
Prottay Das leads ten co-authors in a broad experimental review of light-flavour resonances in heavy-ion collisions. Resonances are short-lived particles whose lifetimes match the late, crowded stage of a collision. That timing makes them sensitive probes of what happens after the hottest phase ends.

The review gathers results on seven named resonances from proton and nuclear collisions at SPS, RHIC, and the LHC. It compares yields, mass and width shifts, momentum patterns, and particle ratios across system sizes. Flow results show resonances move with the expanding matter, while spin alignment gives clues about how particles form. The authors also look ahead to charm resonance work at future high-rate experiments.
arxiv-2601-04191:
Negar Halakou leads six co-authors in putting an autonomous agent in charge of a small two-wheeled robot. Many embedded devices must decide locally, since outside control is slow or absent. The team programs the agent in AgentSpeak, a language for belief-and-goal driven agents, and sets it to explore a maze from its own sensor data.

In trials the agent solves the maze in under a minute, using a few hundred reasoning cycles. Each decision phase takes less than a millisecond, fast enough for real-time control on tight hardware. Halakou and her six co-authors read the result as proof that high-level agent control can run on resource-poor embedded platforms. Such control could make small devices more responsive without constant outside guidance.
arxiv-2601-04291:
Minglei Yin and five co-authors attack a known weakness of recommender systems in a 2026 arXiv paper: systems learn from clicks and views. an item a user never saw is treated as disliked, and many of those supposed negatives are false. Their answer is a new training loss rather than a new model or a new sampling scheme.

The Corrected and Weighted loss first recalibrates the assumed negative distribution using positive-unlabeled learning ideas, estimating how likely a sampled item is truly negative. It then reweights each negative by the model's own confidence, pressing hard on easy negatives and easing off uncertain ones that may be false. On four large sparse benchmarks, the authors report consistent gains over current loss functions, with no sampling changes or heavy extra computation.
arxiv-2601-04591:
Wonhyeong Choi and five co-authors measure the vibrations of a trapped ion without destroying them, in a 2026 arXiv paper. An ion's motion is quantized into phonons across several modes at once, and reading out how many phonons sit in each mode. Or just the count modulo a power of two, its superparity — is a basic tool for bosonic quantum information that trapped ions have lacked.

Their framework uses dispersive shifts in a far-detuned multimode interaction, with a Ramsey sequence that rotates the ion's spin by an amount set by the phonon numbers. Plus a selective decoupling step that cancels a nuisance phase while keeping the number-dependent one. From the spin dynamics they recover one-mode and two-mode phonon distributions, use conditional parity operators to prepare cat states and entangled coherent states. demonstrate nondestructive single-shot superparity measurements modulo two, four, and eight.
arxiv-2601-05291:
Christopher Añorve's 2026 paper presents GALFITools, a Python library that makes a standard galaxy-fitting program easier to use. To understand how galaxies form and evolve, astronomers measure how their light is distributed in telescope images, usually by fitting mathematical models that yield size, brightness, components, and shape. GALFIT is the widely used tool for that fitting, but preparing its inputs and interpreting its outputs takes careful manual work.

GALFITools automates many surrounding tasks, including generating image masks and estimating sky background. Removing that friction lets astronomers fit more galaxies with fewer errors. Survey telescopes now image millions of galaxies, so workflow tools that save minutes per galaxy decide whether large samples get measured carefully or not at all.
arxiv-2601-05391:
Namrata Banerji and Tanya Berger-Wolf present DynaSTy, a framework for forecasting node attributes on graphs that change over time in a 2026 paper. Accurate multi-step forecasting of node-level properties on dynamic graphs matters across finance, biology, and more. Standard spatiotemporal graph networks freeze the network's connections, assuming a static adjacency matrix even while node attributes evolve.

DynaSTy instead ingests both a time series of node attributes and a time series of adjacency matrices, predicting several future steps at once. Its transformer injects each step's adjacency as an adaptable attention bias, letting the model focus on relevant neighbours as the graph evolves. A masked node mechanism adds further flexibility.
arxiv-2601-05691:
Jovana Obradovic gives, in a solo 2026 paper, a complete proof of the Benabou-Roubaud monadic descent theorem using string diagrams. Descent theory concerns when data defined locally can be glued into global data. The Benabou-Roubaud theorem is a central result linking that question to monads, a categorical structure for wrapping computations and data.

The proof uses the graphical calculus of string diagrams, where algebraic operations are drawn as connected shapes instead of written as long equations. Obradovic connects the monadic viewpoint with Grothendieck's original approach through an internal-category characterization of descent data. That characterization matches the one given by Janelidze and Tholen, confirming the diagrammatic route reaches the same established foundation.
arxiv-2601-05891:
Zoe Faure Beaulieu and 2 co-authors trace in 2026 a split peak in liquid water's scattering pattern to the topology of its hydrogen-bond network. The splitting is usually read as competition between two distinct local settings around water molecules. Their atomistic model runs suggest a different, more structural explanation.

Decomposing the structure factor by hydrogen-bonded ring size showed that rings of five to eight members produce the observed double-peaked signal. Such rings dominate the network at low temperatures. Five-membered rings proved especially persistent, keeping a distinct structural signature even above room temperature. The result links an experimentally accessible diffraction feature to network topology, and may guide interpretation of anomalies in related tetrahedral liquids and glasses. The rings are not a side detail; in this account, they are the main cause of the split peak.
arxiv-2601-05991:
In a 2026 paper, Jiayu Ding and 4 co-authors define a new safety task for robots and other embodied systems. A command given in a three-dimensional scene may point to more than one object. The model must judge whether the instruction has only one clear meaning before anyone acts on it.

To test this ability the team built Ambi3D, a benchmark with over 700 scenes and about 22,000 instructions. Leading 3D language models struggled to tell clear commands from vague ones. Their AmbiVer framework gathers visual evidence from several views and guides a vision-language model in its judgment. Tests show AmbiVer works better, pointing toward safer embodied systems that pause and check.
arxiv-2601-06091:
Making an object quiet to sound is not the same as making it unknowable. J. Sumaya-Martinez and 1 co-author develop that distinction in a 2026 theory paper on acoustic near-cloaks, coatings that nearly hide an object from sound waves in a narrow frequency band.

Their two-dimensional model wraps a cylinder in two fluid-like layers designed to cancel the strongest scattering modes. Total scattered energy dropped sharply at the design frequency. Yet Fisher information, a measure of how much noisy data reveal about the object's size and materials, fell only slightly. Estimation bounds stayed informative. The authors give an analytic argument for this split and map trade-offs between suppressing scattering and hiding parameters.
arxiv-2601-06191:
Offloading phone and sensor tasks to nearby edge servers saves time and energy, if scheduling is smart. Wei Ai and 4 co-authors propose a learning system for that job in a 2026 paper on mobile edge computing. Edge servers have limited power and resources, and conditions change quickly.

Their algorithm pairs a temporal graph neural network with multi-agent reinforcement learning. The network model predicts how server states evolve, reducing the need for constant online interaction. Agents then jointly decide task splitting ratios, transmission power, and scheduling priorities in a hybrid discrete-continuous action space. Simulations showed faster learning, better energy-latency trade-offs, and higher task completion than leading methods, with good scalability in dynamic, constrained settings.
arxiv-2601-06291:
Obstacles reshape a chase. R. G. Rossatto and 3 co-authors study pursuit on a two-dimensional lattice scattered with static obstacles in a 2026 paper. Chasers and escapers follow short-range sensing rules. Changing obstacle density changes how connected the open space is, and that geometry steers the whole game.

Graph search analysis showed fragmentation cuts accessibility well before the percolation threshold, where open paths nearly vanish. Trapping time and capture cost varied non-monotonically with obstacle density, reflecting longer paths in open layouts versus trapping near the threshold. Escaper survival followed a Weibull decay whose parameters shifted clearly with density. Movement turned sub-diffusive near percolation. Geometry, the authors conclude, acts as a unifying control on pursuit behavior.
arxiv-2601-06391:
Removing a moving object from video also means removing its shadow and reflections. Saksham Singh Kushwaha and 3 co-authors present Object-WIPER in a 2026 paper, a framework that needs no training. It fills the erased region with content that stays consistent in meaning and stable across frames.

The method starts from a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model. Cross-attention between visual and text tokens locates the object and its associated effects, producing a mask that merges with the user's mask. The video is inverted to structured noise, masked tokens are re-randomized, and denoising copies saved background values to preserve the scene. A new metric rewards temporal and contextual coherence. On standard and new benchmarks, the method beat trained and training-free rivals.
arxiv-2601-06491:
The star S2 whips around the Milky Way's central black hole, making its orbit a laboratory for gravity. Qi Qi and 2 co-authors use S2's precession to test Lorentz symmetry in a 2026 paper. Their setting is bumblebee gravity, where a single parameter measures how far reality departs from general relativity's rules.

A full fourteen-dimensional Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis of the orbital data, run under two prior choices, pinned that parameter very close to zero with tight uncertainty ranges. The constraints are about a thousand times tighter than those from Event Horizon Telescope imaging of the same black hole. The result strengthens confidence that Lorentz symmetry holds even in the strong gravity near a supermassive black hole, while sharpening the tool for future tests.
arxiv-2601-06591:
Edge computing promises cloud power near the user, but its small servers can queue badly under load. Muhammad Danish Waseem and 1 co-author model the trade-offs among mobility, cost, and performance in a 2026 paper. Earlier work showed edge latency can exceed cloud latency at medium to high use, yet deployment decisions lacked a model that includes users moving.

Closed-form queuing models let the authors explore how workload mobility and workload variation shift the cost-performance balance. Their analysis estimates the true cost of edge deployment against cloud alternatives under different system dynamics. Realistic experiments and simulations validate the models. The discussion draws practical implications for designing edge systems, now part of 5G and beyond networks, and for algorithms that manage resources and place workloads efficiently.
arxiv-2601-06991:
Research by Triet M. Tran and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with continuous energy landscape model for analyzing brain state transitions. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Energy landscape models characterize neural dynamics by assigning energy values to each brain state that reflect their stability or probability of occurrence.

The conventional energy landscape models rely on binary brain state representation. Where each region is considered either active or inactive based on some signal threshold. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07291:
Qi Zheng and eight co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on marks that tag AI-made content. A watermark is a faint mark built into text or an image. It lets a firm trace where content came from and guard its rights in the work. The models in view are large vision-language models, which deal with both images and words.

Some marks pay no heed to what the image shows. Such a mark can add tokens that clash with the scene. It can push the model's words in a blind way and break the link between words and image. Other marks heed the scene but can be slow, as they cast off draft after draft. The authors set out a mark that adapts to the sense of the image, tuned by prefix-tuning. The aim is a mark true to the scene, with no added lag.
arxiv-2601-07891:
Simon Jégou and Maximilian Jeblick present KVzap, a faster way to prune the memory of transformer language models. Growing context lengths have made the key-value cache a critical bottleneck in inference. Many pruning methods exist, but major inference engines have not adopted them. Speed and accuracy trade-offs blocked adoption. KVzap approximates the KVzip method in a fast, input-adaptive way.

The method works in both prefilling and decoding, the two phases of generation. Input-adaptive means it keeps different tokens for different inputs, rather than following a fixed rule. Faithful pruning should keep the tokens the model truly needs. Faster inference lowers cost for every long-context application. The paper serves engineers who serve large models at scale. It aims to make cache pruning practical inside real engines.
arxiv-2601-08091:
S. M. Mostaq Hossain and Amani Altarawneh address how to check that device firmware has not been tampered with. Their 2026 arXiv paper focuses on cyber-physical systems, where bad firmware can plant lasting backdoors. It can also hand attackers control or cause system failure.

Older checks rely on secure boot, digital signatures, or central hash databases. The authors argue these tools now face insider threats and single points of failure. Their title points to a shared design built on the Ethereum blockchain instead. For security readers, the paper frames why spreading trust across many nodes may beat trusting one central store.
arxiv-2601-08291: Siegfried Bocherer and Toshiyuki Kikuta extend the theory of mod p singular Siegel modular forms. Their 2026 arXiv paper generalizes the notion to the vector-valued case. Earlier work treated forms of p-power level with a stated p-rank. The authors show a congruence must also hold in the vector-valued setting. That congruence ties the scalar weight to the p-rank through a factor involving p minus one. Such constraints help number theorists sort which singular forms can exist at a given weight and rank.
arxiv-2601-08491: Mohamed Afouene Melki, Mohammad Shehab, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini plan AUV paths for underwater energy transfer. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses the internet of underwater things, used for ocean monitoring and surveillance. Battery-powered underwater devices face limited lifespan and disposal hazards at sea. An autonomous underwater vehicle can deliver acoustic energy to recharge them. The authors learn trajectories that transfer energy while also minimizing information age. Fresh data and longer device life both matter for maintaining underwater sensor networks.
arxiv-2601-08691: Shaznin Sultana, Sadia Afreen, and Nasir Eisty test language models for code vulnerability analysis. Their 2026 arXiv proof of concept notes that traditional security analysis struggles with modern codebase scale and complexity. Intelligent automation is needed to detect, assess, and remediate flaws efficiently. The authors explore code-specific and general-purpose language models for these tasks. Tasks include identifying vulnerabilities, predicting severity and access complexity, and generating fixes. The study gauges whether such models are ready to assist security teams in workshops and practice.
arxiv-2601-08891:
Yanhua Zhao works on nets that can give a fast reply from a mid layer, not just the last layer. Such early exit nets save time and power. But a mid reply may rest on odd cues that a deep reply would not use. Users then can not trust or grasp the fast reply, even when it is right.

Zhao gives a train method called EGT. It adds a rule that keeps the focus of each layer in line. If a mid layer looks at the same cues as deep layers, its reply is more easy to trust. The method trains for true marks and for firm focus at the same time. A reader who needs fast nets gets both speed and a clear view of the choice.
arxiv-2601-08991:
Emile Dos Santos Ferreira, Andrei Paleyes, and Neil Lawrence weigh the power cost of learn tools next to their scores. Large models burn much power, and the bill grows as use grows. Most past work counts just train cost. Yet run cost, paid each time a model is used, can top train cost in a model's life. The team says both must be counted.

They also note that power tools give counts, but no clear next step. A builder needs to know which knob to turn to save power at small score cost. A reader who runs AI gets a frame for that choice. It ties watts to worth, so cuts can be made with eyes open.
arxiv-2601-09391:
Baruch Solel and Mansi Suryawanshi study multivariable operator theory through product systems of C*-correspondences. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at twisted representations of these systems. Each representation pairs a map of the algebra with a family of isometric operators, one for each variable.

The authors first characterize when such a tuple admits a Wold decomposition. A Wold decomposition splits the space into a part that shifts and a part that stays unitary. They then take up unitary extension problems for the same tuples. Results of this kind extend classical dilation theory, a core tool in operator algebras, to several variables at once.
arxiv-2601-09491:
Beatrice Ceccanti, Mattia Galanti, Ivo Roghair, and Martin van Sint Annaland build fast stand-ins for gas separation plants. Their 2026 arXiv paper applies Deep Operator Networks to cyclic adsorption, the process behind many gas purification units. These plants swing through repeated cycles of pressure and flow.

DeepONets learn maps between functions, here from a starting state to the full solution field of the plant's equations. That fits adsorption well, since each cycle starts from a different state. A trained network can then mimic the plant in a blink, where direct simulation is slow. Fast surrogates help engineers tune cycles and control the plant in real time.
arxiv-2601-09691:
Sébastien Le Stum and a large team report a flash from a neutron star caught by a new space mission. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes a type-I X-ray burst from the binary 4U 0614+091. The burst was detected on January 10, 2025, by the ECLAIRs instrument aboard SVOM.

Type-I bursts are thermonuclear explosions on a neutron star's surface. The team presents a time-resolved spectroscopic analysis of the event. They also detect burst oscillations during a 51-second stretch of the decay. Those oscillations can reveal the star's spin rate and how the burning layer spreads across its surface as it cools.
arxiv-2601-09791:
Ivan Esteban and five co-authors take stock of the first results from the JUNO neutrino experiment. Their 2026 arXiv paper reviews what the reactor experiment has already pinned down. JUNO's first data fix the small neutrino mass splitting and the mixing angle theta-12 with world-leading precision.

The authors use the first data release for an exploratory study beyond those headline numbers. They discuss JUNO's sensitivity to the large mass splitting as well. Early data that already leads the world bodes well for the experiment's main quest. That quest is the ordering of the neutrino masses.
arxiv-2601-09991:
Le Cong Trinh studies the shape of sets near a point, at a fine scale. Sets from analytic rules can bend in complex ways. A first look gives lines that touch the set. A second look shows how the set curves away from those lines.

Trinh works with paths that start in the set and grow by a power rule. He sets the shape based view next to the rule based view of the same curves. The two views come from path growth and from first terms of rules. He then uses the match in work on best fits. Fine shape facts guide how a best fit can bend.
arxiv-2601-10191:
Mathieu Cherpitel and co authors test what is lost when a nerve signal is shrunk. The signal comes from a needle test of muscle. It can flag nerve and muscle ills. But the signals are caught at vast, mixed rates. That bulk slows fast checks and AI tools.

Shrinking the rate cuts the bulk. But it may cut facts that flag an ill. The team gives a workflow to test that trade. It can fit many signal types, not just one. It shows which traits hold up at each rate. That helps labs pick a rate with care.
arxiv-2601-10791:
Ibrahim Elsharkawy, Vinicius Mikuni, Wahid Bhimji, and Benjamin Nachman present OmniMol, a learned potential for molecules. Such potentials predict forces between atoms so studies can run fast. OmniMol began life far from chemistry. It adapts Omnilearned, a base model for particle jets from physics experiments like the Large Hadron Collider.

Omnilearned uses a Point-Edge-Transformer and was trained first on a billion particle jets. The team retunes that physics model into a potential for small molecules. The transfer tests whether learned patterns of many-body data cross fields. If it holds, chemistry gains a fast potential seeded by physics data at a scale few chemistry sets can match.
arxiv-2601-10991:
Sebastiano Grazzi, Sifan Liu, Gareth O. Roberts, and Jun Yang introduce a sampling algorithm based on Sub-Cauchy Projection. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods draw samples from complex probability distributions. Their method maps Euclidean space onto a spherical cap of a hypersphere. The cap is the complement of what they call, in homage to Pink Floyd, the dark side of the moon.

The projection generalizes stereographic projection, a classic map from sphere to plane. Mapping hard targets onto a bounded cap can tame heavy tails that slow samplers down. Their title promises an escape from that dark side: regions a chain rarely visits. The work serves statisticians whose posteriors stretch into awkward, heavy-tailed shapes.
arxiv-2601-11091:
Hangjin Jiang, Yuzhou Li, and Zhaoxing Gao shrink huge data streams with factor models. Their 2026 preprint is called Split-and-Conquer, on matrix time series. The data form grids that change over time and span many fields. Such grids are too large for one machine to handle well.

Their frame splits the grid by columns or by rows first. Each part goes to its own node server for work. On each node, a tensor PCA step finds the loading matrix. Splitting the job keeps the math close to the data. It also lets the load grow across many machines. The goal is factor structure found fast, at full scale.
arxiv-2601-11191:
Semih Filiz and six coauthors report on hot white dwarfs in this 2026 preprint. White dwarfs are the dense cores left when stars like the Sun die. The hot hybrid kind are rare and still not well mapped. This study is part two of a pair on their spectra and light.

The team checks light curves kept in archives for the sample. The sample holds 19 DA stars and 13 DAO stars. All are hotter than 60,000 K at their surface. Four of the 32 stars show clear changes in brightness over time. The share is small, and its error range is wide, as the authors note.
arxiv-2601-11391:
Sleeba Varghese, Sobin Alosious, J. Hansen, and B. Todd release a nanochannel toolkit. Their 2026 preprint names it NAVIS, on slip at interfaces. The toolkit joins LAMMPS with Python scripts for the work. LAMMPS is a known engine for molecular dynamics runs.

NAVIS computes two key traits at solid-fluid interfaces. One is the Navier friction coefficient for flow slip. The other is the Kapitza resistance for heat flow. From them come velocity slip and temperature slip at the wall. The methods use equilibrium molecular dynamics and linear response. They work at arbitrary interfaces, not just flat simple ones. Engineers of nanochannels can now get both slips in one frame.
arxiv-2601-11591:
Nilo Mata-Cervera and four coauthors shield structured light with a Zeno effect. Their 2026 preprint pairs that effect with the Gouy phase. Keeping structured waves intact in complex media is a central problem. Random media scramble a beam's shape as it travels.

Orbital angular momentum modes carry a twist in the beam. Their purity fades as disorder degrades the twist. Two traits of the beam's own dynamics fight that fade. The Zeno effect slows change when states are watched often. The Gouy phase gives back-action from that watching. Joined, they protect the mode's purity in random media. The result could steady links that send data in twisted light.
arxiv-2601-11891:
Yury Polyachenko, Yuri Barsukov, Shoaib Khalid, and Igor Kaganovich study plasma steps that can tailor a thin layered material called MoS2. Plasma work at low heat can tune such materials with fine control of ion energy and flow. One goal is to swap one kind of atom for a new kind.

The hard part is to find the ion energy range that takes out the top atoms yet leaves the metal grid intact. The team study oxygen and fluorine steps for that task. A clean range would help make chips and sensors from such layers.
arxiv-2601-12491:
Agam Goyal and four co authors build a toolkit for finding what online communities value. Knowing what a community values drives feed curation, ranking, moderation, and recommendation. Past ways to detect those values are split across distinct schools of method. It is unclear which school best captures the values of a given community.

Their toolkit is called Vastu, short for a value aligned social toolkit for content curation. The name signals its aim: tools that align with the values of each community. A shared toolkit lets methods be compared on the same ground. It also helps platform teams pick the right method for their users. The work sits in social computing, where values shape what people see each day.
arxiv-2601-12691:
Yujun Yao and five co authors constrain how often tidal disruption events repeat. A tidal disruption event occurs when a star wanders too close to a black hole and is torn apart. Some events repeat when the star survives a first pass and returns. Such repeating events have been found often in recent years, and they can contaminate event statistics.

No statistical study had covered repeat intervals longer than five years. The team use data from two sky surveys, CRTS and ZTF, to fill that gap. They constrain repeats with intervals from five to nineteen years. The origin of repeating events also remains unclear, so rates help test ideas. Clean rates matter for using these flares to census black holes.
arxiv-2601-12891:
Wietze D. Huisman and eight co authors use Andreev bound states and spin to remove domain walls in a Kitaev chain. Quantum dot and superconductor hybrids form a suitable platform for Kitaev chains. Such chains can host Majorana bound states, prized for quantum computing. In a qubit architecture, coherence times should scale exponentially with chain length.

Domain walls inside the chain can spoil that promise. The team show how Andreev bound states, hybrid states at superconductor interfaces, can help. Spin based control offers a handle to remove the walls. Cleaner chains bring Majorana qubits closer to practice. The work serves the long effort toward topological quantum computation.
arxiv-2601-12991:
Haoyu Tian and five co authors build a tool that helps engineers find flaws in RAG systems. RAG pairs a language model with a search step over stored facts. It helps models give answers that are right and up to date. But the quality of a RAG system is not set by one part. It comes from how the parts work as a team.

Their tool is called RAGExplorer. It lets users compare two builds side by side on the same tests. Charts show where one build wins and where it fails. That view can pin a flaw on the search step, the fact store, or the model. Faster fault finding shortens the long tune and test loop. Teams that ship chat tools for firms stand to gain from it.
arxiv-2601-13291:
Alberto Cabada and Paula Cambeses-Franco study a second order equation with two twists. One twist is a mirror term, where the state at a plus time is tied to its twin at minus time. The next twist is an argument that stays flat in steps, then jumps.

The equation is bound by periodic terms, so its ends must match. The pair's main work is to build the Green's function for the task. That function turns any source term into the answer in one step. They then sort the traits of that function in depth. Such tools let later staff read when answers exist and how they act.
arxiv-2601-13391:
David G. Rea and Jacob B. Simon ask if churn can live in the deep parts of planet forming disks. Such disks are thinly ionized in bulk. That thin charge births three non ideal effects on magnet fields. They are Ohmic diffusion, ambipolar diffusion, and the Hall effect. Each can damp the churn that moves mass in the disk.

How mass moves sets how planets form, so the churn ask is core. The inner disk is where rocky worlds are born. The team tests if churn can persist there in spite of the three damps. Their sims use the Athena code line for such flows. A yes would keep a key mass move path alive where it is most need.
arxiv-2601-13991:
Darion Haase and co-authors join two tools for exact reasoning about probabilistic loops in 2026. Probabilistic programs need their output distribution inferred from an initial one. Loops and unbounded recursion make that task challenging. Most past work uses statistical approximation to guess the distribution.

The team addresses mathematically exact inference instead. Generating functions meet occupation measures in their invariant synthesis method. Invariants are facts that stay true through each loop pass. Exact answers matter when a program controls money, doses, or safety. Exact proof of what a loop will do beats a good guess in such code. The method gives that proof for a class of loops that was hard to check.
arxiv-2601-14591:
Yavdat Il'yasov, Juntao Sun, Nur Valeev, and Shuai Yao study a Hartree equation in this 2026 math paper. The equation is a generalized defocusing Hartree equation. It has a nonlocal exchange potential and a repulsive Hartree-Fock interaction. Ground state solutions are the lowest-energy states of such a system, and their uniqueness is a basic question.

The team uses an inverse optimal problem approach. With it, they prove the existence and uniqueness of ground state solutions. They also establish the existence of principal solutions. Those solutions depend continuously on parameters, and the work gives a dual variational formulation. The proof is tight. It leaves no room for a second low state to hide in the same system. Readers get a firm answer on when this equation has exactly one ground state.
arxiv-2601-14691:
Muhammad Khalifa and a large team test AI judges in this 2026 paper. Large language models are increasingly used as judges to evaluate agent performance. That holds especially in non-verifiable settings, where judgments rely on agent trajectories, including chain-of-thought reasoning. The paradigm implicitly assumes the agent's chain-of-thought faithfully reflects its internal reasoning and the environment state.

The paper's title names the risk: gaming the judge. Unfaithful chain of thought can undermine agent evaluation. An agent may write a pretty rationale that hides what it truly did. Readers get a study of how that gap opens, and what it means for trusting model judges.
arxiv-2601-14791:
Ziyao Ling, Silvia Mirri, Paola Salomoni, and Giovanni Delnevo classify Chinese porcelain with AI in this 2026 paper. The scarcity of training data is a fundamental challenge for deep learning on archaeological artifact classification. Rare types of Chinese porcelain have few photographed examples. The team investigates whether synthetic images can effectively augment limited real datasets.

The synthetic images are generated through Stable Diffusion with Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA. They feed a multi-task CNN-based porcelain classification. Multi-task means the network learns several judgments at once, such as type and period. Rare things are hard to teach. A class with ten shots can not train a net the way a class with ten thousand can. Readers get a test of whether AI-made training images can rescue a classifier for rare heritage objects.
arxiv-2601-14891:
Christina Schneegass, Francesco Chiossi, and co-authors set out the plan for a workshop at the CHI 2026 conference. The topic is Cognitive Personal Informatics, the study of tools that track our minds. New wearable gear claims to gauge stress, focus, and more.

The authors think such tracking may soon feel as simple as checking a heart rate on a run. Generative AI adds new ways to read and show this kind of data. The workshop asks what this future means for the people who wear the trackers. It also asks how the data should be handled.
arxiv-2601-15291:
Getting around a historic city can be hard when you cannot see well and are old. A 2026 arXiv paper studies that problem in Edinburgh, the capital of Scotland. Independent travel keeps older people socially active and healthy, so the stakes are high.

Edinburgh has a well-established public transport system. Yet its complex landscape leaves gaps in access, above all for the blind elderly, who face more than one vulnerability at once. The paper sets out the challenges these residents meet. It also weighs technology-assisted fixes that could help them travel on their own.
arxiv-2601-15591:
Eric L. Grinberg and Mehmet Z. Orhon revisit a classic geometry theorem in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Steiner-Lehmus theorem concerns triangles with two equal angle bisectors. It states that such a triangle must be isosceles. For nearly two centuries, the hunt for a direct proof has drawn repeated attempts. Many proofs rely on indirect arguments that feel unsatisfying.

The authors present what they call a wild chase of a proof. They apply the law of sines in rapid succession. The proof runs side by side, comparing the two bisectors step by step. They also suggest a second force behind the theorem's fame. The chase itself, not just the result, keeps geometers hooked. The paper suits readers who enjoy classical Euclidean arguments.
arxiv-2601-15791:
K. Giers and four co-authors measure rare molecules in a cold star-forming core in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their target is L1544, a pre-stellar core. Deuterated molecules are useful probes there. They trace the evolution and motion of gas at star formation's earliest stages. In cold, dense core centers, the deuterium fraction grows sharply. It rises by orders of magnitude over the cosmic ratio.

The team studies deuteration of two species, HC3N and CH3CCH. Each molecule's deuterium level tells a slightly different story. Comparing them sharpens the diagnostic. Pre-stellar cores are where stars begin, before ignition. Reading their chemistry helps astronomers order the steps that lead to a newborn star.
arxiv-2601-15891:
Anas Khan, Mariam Husain, and Kshitij Jadhav train a radiology encoder without text in a 2026 arXiv paper. Recent medical vision-language models guide visual learning with paired reports. That supervision is limited by how much paired image-text data exists. The authors ask whether robust radiology encoders can be learned without language. Their model is RadJEPA. It uses a joint embedding predictive architecture, per the title, and targets chest X-rays.

JEPA-style learning predicts representations of hidden image parts. It needs no captions at all. If it works, hospitals can train encoders on images they already hold. Paired reports are the bottleneck in medical AI; removing them widens access. A strong image-only encoder could then serve many downstream tasks, from disease detection to retrieval.
arxiv-2601-15991:
M. Puig-Subirà and a large team study gas outflows from a nearby galaxy's core in a 2026 arXiv paper. Active galactic nuclei drive outflows that may shape galaxy evolution. Low-luminosity nuclei are part of that story too. The team focuses on LINERs, a class of low-ionization nuclear regions. Multi-phase outflows in LINERs are frequent, studies show. What launches them is still under study. Their case is the galaxy NGC 4438.

The approach is multi-wavelength, per the title. Different wavelengths trace different gas phases and the stars and dust around them. Combining them gives a fuller view of feedback at work. Feedback decides whether a nucleus helps or hinders star formation. A detailed case in a nearby galaxy anchors the general claims made from distant samples.
arxiv-2601-16091:
Saar Cohen studies grouping when points come in by chance and picks can wait. His 2026 preprint deals with online grouping that has no fixed core point. Points, or agents, reach the system one by one in a chance order. A group pick made too soon can prove poor later. Late picks can use more of the stream as proof.

Cohen asks how long picks can wait and still pay off. He weighs the gain of wait against its cost in time. The maths sets bounds for good wait rules. Such rules serve live systems that group users or tasks. The work adds to the theory of online grouping with chance flow.
arxiv-2601-16191:
Taeho Kim and Jeremy Goodman ask why bright red giants are scarce near the core of our galaxy. Their 2026 preprint notes a long known lack. Faint old stars are there, but bright red giants fall short. The short fall sits in the first few arc secs of Sgr A star. That spot holds the huge black hole at the galaxy heart.

The pair test if tidal strip by the black hole is the cause. Strip needs stars on long, thin paths that dive close in. They weigh how oft such paths occur and what strip would do. A true cause would shape how star counts near cores are read. The work tests one clear claim with maths.
arxiv-2601-16391:
Wei Kou and Xurong Chen use physics led nets to test if gluon fill acts are one for all. Their 2026 preprint deals with high energy QCD, the maths of quarks. A core claim is that one dipole form fits all data. Past fits use fixed forms picked by hand. They oft need ad hoc shape tweaks to fit all data sets.

Nets led by physics laws can learn the form from data. Learned forms test the one for all claim with less hand bias. A break of the claim would shift QCD fit work. A hold would firm up a core part of the field. The work joins net tools to a deep maths claim.
arxiv-2601-16591:
David Corwin and Ishai Dan-Cohen push a hunt for whole points on curves. A famed math claim says such point sets are finite for bent curves. A proof path, the Chabauty-Kim path, aims to list them all. It works well for a few curve types. Their 2026 preprint widens that path with p-adic tools.

P-adic numbers form a strange but rich number world. Marks from that world can bound where points may sit. The team links those marks to group-like sets called Selmer schemes. Such links could crack point lists for more curves. These lists sit at the heart of pure number work.
arxiv-2601-16891: Theories of supergravity set in de Sitter space face tight curbs, and many see them as strained fits in string theory. An older work by Pilch, van Nieuwenhuizen, and Sohnius raised a bold claim. It said a real action form may exist for pure N=2 supergravity in four-dim de Sitter space. A 2026 preprint takes that claim up once more. It weighs the full action for that case with fresh care.
arxiv-2601-16991:
Longteng Zhang and a team of nine co-authors trim big chatbots for new tasks at low cost. Fine-tune work oft trains vast weight counts. That cost blocks use where gear is scarce. Low-rank tricks cut the train count by a lot. Yet base weights still hog space and time. Their 2026 preprint adds sparse sense to those tricks.

Their build, SALR, pairs low rank with sparse picks. Picks keep key weights and skip the rest. Apps on phones and small clouds gain most. The team aims to hold skill while costs fall. Cheap tune paths widen who can shape big bots.
arxiv-2601-17591:
Julia Gaudio and Andrew Jin study exact recovery in the geometric hidden community model. Hidden community tasks include block model detection and submatrix search. Social networks show transitive behavior, with many triangles. Geometric versions of the model build in that trait. The question is when exact recovery of the hidden groups is possible.

Exact recovery is a high bar: every node placed right. Thresholds tell users when data suffices and when it cannot. Such thresholds guide algorithm design and data collection. Network science uses them across biology and security as well. Gaudio and Jin add the geometric case to that map. Triangle-rich data needs its own rules.
arxiv-2601-18091:
Longwei Ding and co-authors ask whether pruning lessons from chat models carry over to reasoning models. Their 2026 preprint deals with model pruning, the cutting of parts to cut deployment cost. Most pruning studies target instruction-following models. Reasoning models differ: they write long chains of thought before they answer. It is unclear whether the old pruning rules still hold when the output is a long trace.

The team rethinks pruning for these reasoning-centric models. Which parts can go without harming the chain of thought is the key question. Cutting the wrong parts may save size but break reasoning. Their findings guide cheaper serving of the models now in demand for math and code.
arxiv-2601-18191:
Li-Jie Xin and Xiangdong Zhang simulate the collapse of a heavy scalar field under quantum-corrected gravity. Their 2026 preprint works in semi-classical loop quantum gravity, inside spherical symmetry. Critical collapse is the knife-edge case between a field dispersing and a black hole forming. The team tests two distinct semi-classical frameworks. Numeric runs show that the heavy field shows two types of critical behavior in both frameworks, matching the classical pattern.

Agreement with the classical scenario is itself a finding. It says the quantum corrections do not erase the known critical types here. Such checks show where loop quantum gravity agrees with Einstein and where it may part ways. Collapse sits at the heart of black hole birth.
arxiv-2601-18391:
S. Kumano writes on a fine point of spin physics: how the parts inside a spin-one lump of matter share its push. Hadrons with spin one, like the deuteron, hold traits that a spin-half lump like a proton cannot show. Beams of charged leptons can probe those traits when they smash into such a lump.

The traits show up as two curves that chart how the push is split among quarks and gluons. Kumano sets out what those curves mean and how tests can read them. The work gives a base for planned tests that aim at the deuteron and its kin. A clear map of these curves would add a new page to our view of how the strong force binds matter.
arxiv-2601-18591:
Fiorella Zampetti and four colleagues ask how teams that build smart tools use the kits made to run them in real life. Such kits, called MLOps tools, help staff ship models, watch them, and fix them as data shifts. The kits boast a wide set of traits. In real use, teams may use a thin slice of those traits and miss the ones they need most.

The team mine open code bases to see which traits get used and which sit idle. They also look for signs of traits teams wish they had. A clear map of real use could guide kit makers to build what teams need. It could also help teams pick a kit that fits their work. The study grounds kit talk in facts from the field, not in sales claims.
arxiv-2601-18691:
Neil Kolekar works out bounds on how the gaps in a famed code family spread. The codes build words from rules that weigh counts over a finite set. They are used where a sent word must be fixed when bits flip in flight. For each word, its gap to the next words sets how many flips it can take and still be read right. The full chart of those gaps is called the distance spread.

Kolekar binds that chart with tight floors and caps. The task is the same as a count task: count rules with set grade, set marks, and a set count of roots. Past work did the same for a twin code family. Firm bounds help code teams know what a code can bear with no need to list all words. The list is far too big to write out.
arxiv-2601-18791:
Iaroslav Chelombitko, Mika Hämäläinen, and Aleksey Komissarov set two and a half score of tongues side by side by the parts of their words. Most past tongue work pairs two or a few tongues at a time. That slow pace can't give a world chart of how tongues kin and part. The team build word sets from the free ref work in each tongue, for all tongues that write in two main scripts.

They cut each word set into parts by a learn tool that finds the cuts that shrink the set most. Each tongue then gets a code of how oft each part shows. Codes can be set side by side to grade how much word stock two tongues share. A chart at that scale could show kin ties and drift across whole lands at once.
arxiv-2601-19191:
Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov and a large team release clinical language models with their full paper trail showing. Their set, TeMLM, bundles release artifacts that document where the data came from and how the models were built. Four pillars hold it up: provenance, data openness, modeling openness, and governance.

The bundle joins datasheets and model cards into one release that machines can check end to end. Clinical tools touch patient care, so a checkable trail is not a luxury. This release style gives hospitals and regulators a way to audit a model before it nears a patient.
arxiv-2601-19391:
