Shi-fan Qi and Fan Li entangle a magnet's wave with a vibration across a distance. Long distance quantum entanglement is a core need for quantum information work. Their system is a hybrid: several separated magnon modes, waves in magnets, share one waveguide, and each touches its own phonon mode, a sound vibration.

The protocol breeds entanglement between the far apart magnon and phonon partners. Remote links between unlike carriers, spin waves and sound, suit hybrid quantum networks where each carrier does what it does best. The scheme adds a route to linking quantum devices that sit far apart.
arxiv-2601-19591:
Gianni Dal Maso and Davide Donati study a class of variational problems from the mechanics of materials. Free discontinuity problems allow a function to jump, modeling cracks or sharp interfaces. The functionals here have linear growth and live on functions of bounded deformation. The authors study what happens as a sequence of such functionals converges, in the sense called Gamma-convergence.

They prove a compactness result: from any such sequence, a converging subsequence can be extracted. They also outline the main properties of the limit functionals. Those properties lead to an integral representation of the limit. Such results tell engineers which effective model a fine-scale problem settles into. The work is part of the rigorous theory behind fracture and plasticity models.
arxiv-2601-19791:
Mingyue Xu, Gal Vardi, and Itay Safran study a curious training phenomenon called grokking. A model groks when it suddenly generalises long after it has memorised the training data. The effect was first seen in small neural networks on algorithmic tasks. It delayed understanding of when learning truly happens.

The authors prove grokking can occur in ridge regression, a classical linear method. They use over-parameterised models trained by gradient descent with weight decay. The proof shows three stages in sequence: early overfitting, a long plateau of poor generalisation, then the late onset of generalisation. Reducing grokking to a provable linear case strips away mystery. It gives the field a clean model for a puzzling effect.
arxiv-2601-19891:
Elizabeth Hillenkamp and four colleagues read the pre-explosion history of four exploding stars. Type IIn supernovae show narrow hydrogen lines that last a long time. The light comes from the blast wave crashing into dense material the star shed earlier. That circumstellar material is a record of the star's final centuries of mass loss.

Direct constraints on these progenitor stars are rare. The ongoing collision between ejecta and shed material gives a rare window instead. By studying four events, the team probes mass loss stretching back centuries before the explosion. The results test how massive stars die and how violently they shed their outer layers. Each event is a core-collapse seen through its own history.
arxiv-2601-20091:
Maciej W. Olszewski and colleagues improve the films behind high-performance quantum devices. Superconducting qubits made from tantalum thin films have produced the best microwave resonators and qubits so far. That makes tantalum attractive for quantum computing hardware. Until now, growing the right crystal phase directly demanded substrate temperatures above four hundred degrees.

The team uses krypton-sputtered tantalum films to reach scalable, high-performance devices. Avoiding extreme growth temperatures eases fabrication and widens the substrates that can be used. Materials advances set the ceiling for qubit quality. A more practical route to top-grade tantalum films could speed the whole field. The work targets the manufacturing side of quantum hardware. Heat is the block here. Hot growth shuts out cheap tools and thin films.
arxiv-2601-20491:
Xiaoqing Yue and four colleagues quantify how the choice of centrality measure affects studies of gold-gold collisions at moderate energy. Centrality says how head-on a collision was. It is a major source of systematic error in heavy-ion work, above all when probing the nuclear equation of state at high density.

The authors assess several determination methods and trace their effects on final-state observables that are sensitive to that equation. Knowing the size of this error bar is essential: claims about the stiffness of dense nuclear matter stand or fall on it.
arxiv-2601-20791:
Haonan Zhong and five co-authors tackle bias in AI video generation. Their 2026 paper presents FairT2V, a debiasing framework for text-to-video diffusion models. These models turn a written prompt into a short video. Their demographic biases, above all gender bias, remain largely unexplored. The team first analyzes where the bias comes from.

They show that it stems mainly from pretrained text encoders. Even neutral prompts pick up hidden gender associations inside the encoder. FairT2V then corrects that bias without any fine-tuning. The method is training-free, so it can wrap around existing models. The work gives video AI builders a way to cut bias at its source rather than patch outputs after the fact.
arxiv-2601-21191:
Xiulin Yang, Heidi Getz, and Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox ask what lets learners find grammar's hidden tree in a flat stream of words. Their 2026 paper studies statistical cues for language learning. Language arrives in a line, one word after another. Its structure is a hierarchy of nested phrases. The authors focus on the spread of function words. Words like the, of, and to are function words. They have long been argued to play a key role in learning.

Function words are frequent and tied to syntactic structure with care. They also align with phrase bounds. Those traits could cue a learner to where phrases start and end. The paper asks which statistical conditions support learning hierarchy from such cues. The answer bears on how children learn language so fast. It also informs how machines should be taught grammar.
arxiv-2601-21291:
Jie Tang, Pingping Xie, Jian Li, and Ping Tan work on filling in depth maps for scenes. A camera image plus a few depth readings must be turned into a full map of distances. Deep learning leads the field, but sparse and uneven depth inputs are hard for networks to use well.

The authors build a network based on belief propagation with Gaussian messages. The design spreads the few known depths across the image in a principled way. It aims to hold up even when readings are very sparse. Better depth maps support robots, self-driving cars, and tools that blend digital content with real rooms.
arxiv-2601-21391:
Minjae Cho and Huy T. Tran study how agents can learn when rewards are rare. An agent learns by trial and error, but sparse rewards give it almost no signal. Simple noise-based wandering is often too weak to stumble on success.

Inner rewards, built from the agent's own state, can guide the search. They can be mixed with the true reward or used to train helper policies. The authors propose a way to optimize policies with these inner signals. Better guidance for sparse tasks matters for robots and games where success is rare but vital to learn from.
arxiv-2601-21591:
Katie L. Y. Zhou, Anna T. Bui, and Stephen J. Cox study how a trapped fluid mixture sorts itself near walls. Some mixtures form an azeotrope, a blend that simple boiling cannot separate. Trapping such a blend in a tiny space may sort it in a way bulk methods cannot.

The authors use a density theory boosted by machine learning on a simple model mixture. They weigh the roles of the bulk fluid and the surfaces that confine it. Selective adsorption at walls could offer a new route to purify stubborn blends. That matters for chemical plants, where separation eats a huge share of energy.
arxiv-2601-21691:
B. Snow and A. Hillier study how mixing triggers cooling clumps in the Sun's outer atmosphere. Cool dense material is often seen inside the hot thin corona, as prominences, spicules, and coronal rain. Both the cool clumps and the hot surroundings sit at temperatures that look locally stable.

The puzzle is how the clumps form at all if each part is stable on its own. The authors show that mixing between the two can create instability where none existed locally. Mixed layers cool fast and condense into the observed rain. The mechanism links solar weather to a basic fluid process seen across astrophysics.
arxiv-2601-21791:
Valerie Tan, Luisa Jost, Jens Gerken, and Max Pascher review what is known about assistive technology for adults with ADHD. The condition involves inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, and it affects many adults, not only children. Adults face distinct problems at work and in higher education. Their 2026 paper gives early results from a scoping review.

A scoping review maps a whole field rather than testing one tool. The authors gather studies on technologies meant to help adults with ADHD in daily working life. Early mapping of this kind shows where tools already exist, where evidence is thin. And what designers should build next for workplaces that want to include these adults better.
arxiv-2601-21891:
Ivo Schulthess surveys an experiment built to probe quantum electrodynamics where fields are extremely strong. In such fields, theory predicts the vacuum itself can produce electron and positron pairs, an effect no lab has yet mapped in detail. The LUXE experiment at DESY in Hamburg is designed to enter this regime.

LUXE collides a high-intensity laser with the energetic electron beam of the European XFEL. This 2026 preprint looks from LUXE toward future colliders, asking what the experiment can teach about strong-field quantum effects and physics beyond them. Measuring pair production from empty space would test quantum theory in a regime where its strangest predictions have never been directly checked.
arxiv-2601-22091:
Juan Naranjo and co-authors use a quantum machine to design quantum tools. Many new tools rest on spins set in solids. These spins serve in sensors, in light sources, and in the bits of quantum machines. To design them well, teams must first work out how the spins act. That task is hard even for strong classic machines.

The team builds a way to run those sums on a quantum machine. It uses a broad spin law that folds in the main pulls on the spins. These pulls come from the spins' own split, from fields, and from near atoms. Good sums cut the slow loop of build, test, and build once more. That loop is how spin tools are made now.
arxiv-2601-22591:
Rajat Kumar Mishra and Arnab Saha study the kernels of maps between arithmetic jet spaces. Jet spaces encode how a scheme bends to high order, a key tool in modern number theory. Their 2026 preprint works with formal group schemes and the Frobenius map between the jets.

They show the map is induced by a natural ring map between shifted Witt vectors. Witt vectors are a classic device for lifting number systems. A clean source for the map firms up the theory's base. The work is deep pure math. It serves scholars of arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2601-22691:
Leonid Dorochko and Michał Wrona study where a famed split in problem hardness holds for infinite structures. Constraint satisfaction asks if a set of rules can all be met. Their 2026 preprint notes that the finite case was settled: each problem is easy or NP-complete, with no middle.

The Bodirsky-Pinsker conjecture claims the same split for a class of infinite structures. The team probe the border between what first-order logic can state and a wider logic. The work is deep theory of computation. Each border case trims the conjecture's unknowns. The split, if true, is a grand pattern.
arxiv-2601-22791:
Sabinakhon Akbarova, Felix Dobslaw, and Robert Feldt test whether language models can explain boundary tests in a way testers trust. Boundary testing probes inputs at their edges, where faults cluster. Their 2026 preprint notes that testers often struggle to say why a given edge case matters.

Model-written rationales could fill that gap, if they are sound. The team judge the value of such explanations in real quality work. Good reasons turn a bare test into a checked claim. The work serves software teams that must defend their testing. It weighs words against worth.
arxiv-2601-22891:
Jacques Cloete and three co-authors teach agents to follow task rules written in a formal logic. The logic, linear temporal logic, states step-by-step duties over time, like doing one thing before another. Agents must handle new tasks built from symbols they have not seen in training.

Their system, PlatoLTL, aims to generalize across those symbols rather than memorize them. An agent that reads rules flexibly could take new instructions without fresh training each time. That skill matters for robots and software agents facing changing jobs. Generalizing across symbols is the crux: the agent has to grasp the rule structure, not memorize which symbol stood where before.
arxiv-2602-00191: Yadang Alexis Rouzoumka and coauthors introduce GEPC, a training free probe for out of distribution detection in diffusion models. Diffusion scores often inherit near symmetries such as flips, rotations, and circular shifts from training data and convolutional nets. Most detectors use score size or local geometry and ignore those symmetries. GEPC measures, for a finite group, the consistency with which the learned score transforms, catching symmetry breaking even when score size stays flat. It needs only score checks, gives readable breaking maps, and shows gains on image benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-00291: Matilda Pitt and Robert J. B. Goudie propose a Bayesian Prevalence Incidence Cure model for survival estimation from electronic health records. Prevalence Incidence models use a two component mixture for that missing data, but they bias results when some people never reach the endpoint. The new PIC model adds a cure component, forming a three component mixture that estimates prevalence, time to incidence, and cure proportion. Covariates can affect each component, and Bayesian inference keeps the model interpretable for real world use.
arxiv-2602-00391: Alberto Mario Ceballos-Arroyo and team develop robust automatic brain vessel segmentation in 3D CTA scans using dynamic 4D-CTA data. They annotate brain vasculature from dynamic 4D-CTA head scans, using multiple time points to subtract bone and soft tissue and enhance arteries and veins. That reduces manual annotation effort for brain vessels.
arxiv-2602-00491: Zhaokun Yan and colleagues structure public health reasoning as a machine learning problem grounded in evidence, expert views, and safety limits. They introduce GlobalHealthAtlas, a large data set of 280,210 instances in 17 languages across 15 public health domains. A language-model-assisted pipeline with search, dropping repeats, evidence checks, and label checks builds and checks the data at scale. They also distil a field-matched evaluator from strong judgements of varied language models, scoring outputs for insight, term norms, common ground, completeness, reasoning, and accuracy.
arxiv-2602-00691: C. Alispach and colleagues assess gamma-ray detection with Cherenkov telescopes boosted by a ground array, using simulations. They place Single-Mirror Small-Size telescopes, SST-1M, inside a high-altitude water-Cherenkov detector array from the planned Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory. For this hybrid setup, flux reach above 10 TeV improves by about 60% for monocular observation and 30% for stereoscopic observation. The gain comes from better telling gamma rays from hadrons with extra water-array data.
arxiv-2602-00791: Shahryar Zehtabi and colleagues unify two strands of decentralised federated learning: gradient tracking against data variety, and coping with varied client resource access. Their Sporadic Gradient Tracking is the first method mixing both over general directed graphs, with client-own gradient work rates and varied, uneven message rates. Analysis under relaxed assumptions on gradient variance and client gradient variety gives consensus and optimal proofs despite on-off taking part. On image data sets, Sporadic Gradient Tracking beats well-known gradient tracking others.
arxiv-2602-00891: Ivy Xiaoya and colleagues develop the full theory of the quantum birthmark, a lasting, universal memory of initial states in quantum dynamics. Even in systems with fully chaotic, random spectra, the effect boosts long-time return probability of any moving state over overlap with a typical ergodic state. The universal contribution depends only on global symmetry class and accessible Hilbert-space size, not on small-scale dynamics. Quantum change thus keeps an unavoidable, symmetry-controlled mark of its origin, defying classical ergodicity and thermalization.
arxiv-2602-00991: Guang-Wei Mi and co-authors ask how Hawking radiation changes steering in a three-way quantum setup placed in Schwarzschild spacetime. They sort every steering type and every case set by how many modes a distant watcher can reach. When all three modes can be reached, radiation breaks steering, and the peak gap between one-way and two-way steering marks the line between those states. When only one mode can be reached, the black hole effect lifts steering a great deal.
arxiv-2602-01191: Lorenzo Baldi and co-authors map stubborn polynomials, non-negative on a shape yet with no odd power summing squares. Past work stayed with global cases on the projective plane, but the team fully sorts smooth curves. A polynomial on a smooth fully real curve is stubborn just when all its roots are real. That yields curves with no low-degree stubborn cases, yet stubborn cases must crop up at high degree on positive-genus curves. For degree-6 plane forms, stubbornness matches a real delta mark of at least 9.
arxiv-2602-01291: Bowen Yang and co-authors launch AMBER, a Lean 4 test that forces models to build answers before proving them. Past math tests lean on checking stated claims, skipping crafting concrete values or runnable plans, which applied math prizes most. Their frame compels agents to define plain answers first, then prove them right, across convex study, tuning, number algebra, and high-dimensional chance. Tests show current models strain on build jobs, with broad thought models beating narrow proof specialists, blamed on proof-tuned models losing grip on orders.
arxiv-2602-01491: Sahan Sanjaya and Prabhat Mishra introduce a sleep-based side-channel attack on ECDSA nonces. ECDSA rests on nonce secrecy, and partial leakage can expose the long-held private key through lattice cryptanalysis. Unlike standard power attacks, theirs exploits spikes from sleep-triggered context switches. Those fluctuations track nonce-dependent scalar multiplication steps, allowing recovery despite masked constant-time implementations. Tests on RustCrypto, BearSSL, GoCrypto, ARM, and RISC-V recover 20 nonce bits from sleep power envelopes. Sleep power spikes are a practical cross-platform threat, urging a cryptographic design rethink.
arxiv-2602-02091: Andrej Dudenhefner provides a novel proof for higher-order beta-matching undecidability, whether a first lambda-term can be beta-equivalent to a second term, shown undecidable by Loader. The proof encodes string rewriting as beta-matching. The approach has advantages: the proof is simpler to verify; string rewriting undecidability is already certified, yielding a certified Halting Problem reduction. The approach also identifies a uniform construction for beta-matching and lambda-definability. The proof is mechanized in the Rocq Prover.
arxiv-2602-02791:
Yuzhen Zhao and 2 co-authors classify which diffusion process generated an observed trajectory by first learning each class's drift, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. Each class is defined by a distinct drift function, the steady pull inside the random motion, and trajectories are sampled at discrete times.

The authors first derive the multidimensional Bayes rule for the problem. Their plug-in classifier fits each drift with neural networks, then applies that rule. Convergence rates for the excess misclassification risk separate the parts played by drift estimation, time discretization, and dimension. Exploiting diffusion structure helps: the drift is learned from every observed increment, sharpening guarantees over classifiers fed raw paths. Tests beat earlier methods in one dimension, stay effective in higher dimensions when drifts have compositional structure, and beat end-to-end trajectory classifiers.
arxiv-2602-02891:
Pruning large language models without any training is the goal of Prajna G. Malettira and 4 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Pruning removes layers, heads, or channels to make models cheaper to run. Judging each part alone misses how parts interact across the whole model, while training-aware search is expensive.

Their framework, TraceNAS, searches depth and width together. A zero-shot score checks how closely a pruned model's loss landscape matches the original. Discovery took hours on a single graphics processor, far less than training-aware methods. Tests on the Llama and Qwen model families followed. TraceNAS stayed competitive with training-aware baselines on commonsense and reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-02991:
Language models can plan during training yet seem short-sighted when generating, and Haijiang Yan and 2 co-authors offer a Bayesian explanation in a 2026 paper. Their account centers on context. Subtle differences between natural language and the language the model internalized mean self-generated context gradually shifts planning behavior during inference, creating an appearance of weak planning.

Two controlled experiments test the account. In a random-generation task, planning looked constrained under human prompts but strengthened as self-generated context accumulated. In a Gaussian-sampling task, conditioning on self-generated sequences reduced initial bias. Together, theory and evidence characterize how models plan ahead at inference time. The first step a model takes can be false, the authors show, because of the context it has built.
arxiv-2602-03091: Jingbang Guo's solo 2026 paper studies the dual algebras of discrete Hopf algebroids. Algebroids are algebraic structures that generalize groups and groupoids. They carry both a multiplication and a comultiplication. The paper's central result reframes comodules over such an algebroid as ordinary discrete modules over its dual algebra. That gives module-based tools for studying them.
arxiv-2602-03491:
Tables in images trip up vision-language models because layout and content are tangled together. Yingjie Zhu and 6 co-authors separate the two in a 2026 paper. They ask how to teach table reasoning with little annotation and no external tools. Their first framework, DiSCo, separates the table's structure from its meaning during multimodal alignment.

On top of DiSCo they build Table-GLS, which reasons from global structure down to local evidence in a guided exploration. The model examines the table's skeleton before filling in the flesh of cell contents. Across diverse benchmarks the approach strengthens table understanding, and it generalizes to table structures never seen in training. The result is a cheaper path to reliable table reading.
arxiv-2602-04091:
Systems approaching a period-doubling bifurcation relax ever more slowly. Edson D. Leonel and 2 co-authors give a phenomenological account of that critical slowing down in a 2026 paper. Starting from a Taylor expansion near the fixed point, they derive a reduced description valid at and near the bifurcation.

Three universal exponents govern behavior exactly at criticality: short-time response, long-time decay, and the crossover between them. A fourth exponent, for relaxation time, appears nearby. The theory, established for one-dimensional maps, extends to two-dimensional ones through center manifold projection. Numerical tests on the Hénon and Ikeda maps matched predictions closely.
arxiv-2602-04291:
The expert a router picks most is not always the expert that matters. Sudipto Ghosh and 3 co-authors introduce INFORM, an interpretability analysis for multi-expert language model systems, in a 2026 paper. Orchestrators that sequence model experts are widely used, yet their policies stay opaque.

INFORM separates interaction structure, execution order, and functional attribution. Testing orchestrators on math, code, and knowledge benchmarks with consortia of models, the authors found routing dominance poorly predicts functional necessity. Gradient sensitivity tells a different importance story than routing mass does. Designers optimizing the wrong importance measure may prune the experts their system actually needs.
arxiv-2602-04391:
Throwing away a teacher's mistakes wastes half the lesson. Jie Deng and 6 co-authors propose TrajFusion, which fuses wrong and right reasoning paths into single training samples, in a 2026 paper. Standard rejection sampling fine-tunes language models only on correct trajectories, treating supervision as a binary filter.

Fused trajectories interleave selected incorrect attempts, reflection prompts, and the correct path, explicitly modeling trial and error. Their length adapts to how frequent and diverse teacher errors are, shrinking to ordinary rejection sampling when errors teach nothing. No architecture or objective changes are needed. Challenging problems, where errors abound, gain the richest supervision.
arxiv-2602-04591:
Brahim Lemkalli and 5 co-authors build a mechanical material that lets waves pass one way but not back, in a 2026 paper on nonreciprocal kink waves. Their design needs no magnets or spinning parts, which earlier approaches often required.

Each unit is a prestrained hinged-beam circulator that snaps between buckled states. That snap creates an angular momentum bias, effectively breaking time reversal symmetry. Linked into a hexagonal array, the units form a chiral network. Soliton-like kink waves travel along edges and interfaces in one direction, surviving sharp bends. A Sine-Gordon type equation describes the motion. The work connects bifurcation dynamics, a theory of sudden state changes, with protected mechanical transport.
arxiv-2602-04891:
Matthew J Simpson and 2 co-authors wrote this 2026 tutorial on fitting mathematical models to real data. Scientists often write their model as differential equations, then need to find the parameter values that make the equations match measurements. The usual tools solve the equations again and again, which can be slow and costly.

The tutorial teaches a different method called generalized profiling. It judges a fit by two things at once: how well the curve matches the data, and how well it obeys the equation. Readers work through a set of hands-on exercises with ordinary differential equation models. Open notebooks on GitHub let anyone repeat every calculation. The authors aim to make a powerful but rarely used method easier to learn.
arxiv-2602-05091:
A debris removal planner that excels in training conditions may stumble when fuel runs short or time runs out. Agni Bandyopadhyay and Günther Waxenegger-Wilfing compare three planners for multi-debris rendezvous in this 2026 paper, presented at a space robotics conference in Sendai. All three must respect strict limits on fuel and mission duration in low Earth orbit.

The contenders are a learning-based policy trained under fixed conditions, the same policy trained with randomized conditions, and a classic Monte Carlo tree search. Across 300 simulated cases with refueling and realistic transfer dynamics, the fixed-condition learner won when conditions matched its training but degraded sharply when they shifted. The randomized learner adapted better for a modest cost at nominal settings. Tree search handled changes best of all, thanks to online replanning, but took far longer to compute. The authors suggest hybrids.
arxiv-2602-05191:
Long documents make attention expensive, because every new token looks back at a growing cache. Wentao Ni and 9 co-authors present Double-P in this 2026 machine learning paper, a sparse attention scheme that keeps only the tokens carrying most of the attention mass. Fixed-size top-k budgets cannot adapt to heads and layers whose attention spreads very differently.

Double-P works in two stages. A coarse pass estimates the important mass at cluster level, using size-weighted cluster centers, and a second pass spends token-level computation only where the estimate says it is needed. That hierarchy jointly trims selection overhead and the sparse attention computation itself. Across long-context benchmarks, accuracy stayed within a hair of full attention while attention overhead fell by up to about 1.8 times and end-to-end decoding ran up to about 1.3 times faster than leading fixed-budget sparse methods.
arxiv-2602-05391:
Dataset distillation compresses a training set into a tiny synthetic one that teaches almost as well. Qianxin Xia and 8 co-authors revisit the method when a pretrained self-supervised model supplies the prior, in this 2026 paper accepted at NeurIPS 2026. The standard approach, linear gradient matching, is heavy: every step loads thousands of real images and applies repeated differentiable augmentations to the synthetic ones.

The authors' theoretical re-derivation shows that gradient is really a local relative distribution, a flow from each class center away from the others, which explains the method's instability and cost. Their Statistical Flow Matching aligns global statistical flows instead, loading raw statistics once and augmenting once. The result matched or beat the state of the art with ten times less GPU memory and four times faster distillation, and extra augmentations, cheap for this method, bought further gains.
arxiv-2602-05791:
Each humanoid robot model usually needs its own trained controller, an expensive habit as designs multiply. Yufei Xue and 8 co-authors study cross embodiment control: can one policy run many humanoid bodies after a single training run? Their framework, XHugWBC, trains a generalist whole body controller across a broad spread of simulated morphologies.

Three ingredients carry the design: physics consistent randomization of body shapes, observation and action spaces aligned semantically across robots, and policy architectures that model morphological and dynamic properties. The policy absorbs motion priors from many randomized bodies, building a structural bias toward new ones. Experiments cover twelve simulated humanoids and seven real robots. The resulting controller transferred to unseen robots with no extra training, and stayed robust across the range. The authors present this as a step toward universal humanoid control.
arxiv-2602-06091:
Gravity might be able to link two separate masses in a quantum way, with no other force involved. Hollis Williams reworks the math behind that idea using twistor theory, a framework that describes physics without assuming spacetime distance at all. The usual treatment leans on Newton's law and a fixed gap between the masses.

Williams shows the linking phase between the masses stays well defined even with no spacetime geometry in place. The familiar distance-based form appears only after a special structure is added, which picks out one spacetime picture. The result separates the truly quantum part of these gravity tests from the geometry that usually frames them.
arxiv-2602-06291:
Grading research-level math solutions normally takes scarce expert time, since no answer key exists. Guijin Son and 7 co-authors propose judging a solution by its consequences. If a solution's method is sound, using it as an example should help solve nearby related problems that can be checked.

Their evaluator scores each candidate by that downstream usefulness, with no oracle needed. They tested it on fresh research-level problems, each with one expert solution and nine machine-made ones. The method ranked solutions better than reward models and language model judges. It also kept a wider gap between correct and wrong solutions, even on problems the underlying solver usually failed.
arxiv-2602-06391:
Before an AI agent can click or type, it must find the right screen element, and Zhongyin Zhao and 9 co-authors set out to master that grounding skill from the ground up. Many rivals start from vision models that already locate things well. This team starts from a base model with almost no grounding skill and builds the whole pipeline themselves.

Their model reached top scores on four public grounding benchmarks. Three factors get the credit. Careful data work unified open data sets and added augmentation, filtering, and difficulty grading. Training kept tuning the vision encoder for sharper perception. And resolution handling was maintained through training. The result shows grounding can be built, not just borrowed.
arxiv-2602-06491:
Random differential equations with coefficients that grow faster than linearly defeat standard fixed-step solvers. Xueqi Wen and 3 co-authors develop an adaptive Euler-Maruyama scheme for such superlinear stochastic diffusion systems. The step size shrinks or grows with the size of the drift and diffusion terms.

A truncated scheme stands by as a backstop whenever the adaptive step would fall below a floor, preventing collapse to uselessly tiny steps. Combining stochastic analysis with stopping time arguments, the authors prove strong convergence at the optimal half-order rate. Tests on stiff, non-stiff, and stochastic Lorenz systems showed better accuracy and speed than fixed-step and other adaptive rivals.
arxiv-2602-06691:
Shounak Ghosh, Rikpratik Sengupta, and Kazuharu Bamba construct a gravastar, a proposed black hole alternative with no central singularity. It sits inside a braneworld theory that adds a timelike extra dimension and negative brane tension. In that setting, they solve the modified Einstein equations across the object's three regions without the usual thin-shell shortcut. The core is modeled as a Bose-Einstein condensate and the shell as ultra-dense stiff matter.

Corrections from the higher-dimensional bulk make the shell's pressure uneven by direction, which helps hold the object stable, and the effective mass comes out suppressed or even negative. The authors check mass, energy, entropy, and shell thickness, and confirm the junctions between regions are consistent. They present the result as the first fully analytic, finite-thickness gravastar of this kind in this braneworld.
arxiv-2602-06791:
Jake McAllister Dorman, Edward Gillman, Dominic C. Rose, Jamie F. Mair, and Juan P. Garrahan study rare events in large language models: behaviors that are far from typical yet highly consequential when they surface. Because model use is now enormous, events never seen during development are likely to appear prominently once deployed. The paper offers an end-to-end framework for finding, estimating, and characterizing them.

The implementation spans theory, efficient generation strategies, probability estimation, and error analysis, illustrated with concrete examples. It is designed to work across models and contexts, not just one system. The authors argue that systematic rare-event analysis should become a routine part of evaluating deployed models, alongside standard benchmarks that mostly measure average behavior.
arxiv-2602-06991:
Seongbo Ha and five co-authors build a real-time SLAM system that maps a scene in both shape and language. The system rebuilds a dense field of language-aligned features from RGB-D input while tracking and mapping at low latency, bridging 3D seeing and language-based thinking. A top-K rendering pipeline renders high-size feature maps fast without warping their meaning.

To handle the mismatch between meaning and shape data and to curb memory use, a multi-criteria map manager prunes extra or inconsistent Gaussians while keeping scene wholeness. A hybrid tuner then refines shape and meaning jointly at different rates matched to each field's character. The system beats shape-only rivals on shape closeness, matches offline methods on meaning closeness, and runs at 15 frames per second.
arxiv-2602-07091:
Luca Cibinel and five co-authors offer a knowledge graph for transition metal complexes. Those compounds serve uses from catalysis to medicinal chemistry, and machine learning plus computational methods could aid their study a great deal. Yet such work needs accessible data sets that gather a wide range of information. Their data set, tmQM-RDF, collects rich, detailed descriptions of about 50,000 complexes, in Resource Description Framework form.

Descriptions cover both qualitative and quantitative facets. They record each complex's makeup in terms of its ligands, as well as its full molecular graph. An example shows the power of the representation: information in tmQM-RDF can drive complex manipulation tasks, reaching promising scores even with relatively simple probabilistic models. The data set thus gives computational chemistry a structured base for transition metal work.
arxiv-2602-07191:
Quantum computers in the cloud are scarce: users wait minutes to days for jobs that run in seconds. Many qubits sit idle because no system can share one machine between programs.  John Zhuoyang Ye and three co-authors present HALO, the first operating system design for fine-grained sharing of quantum hardware.

HALO places shared helper qubits where routing costs stay low and cross-talk between users stays minimal, letting several programs use one processor at once.  The design tackles the central bottleneck of quantum cloud computing: demand far outstrips supply.  Cloud operators and systems teams get a concrete architecture for squeezing far more work from each quantum processor.
arxiv-2602-07391:
Security testing for AI agents still leans on manual red-teaming or static benchmarks that cannot model an adaptive, multi-turn attacker.  Kunal Pai and two co-authors present NAAMSE, an evolutionary method that turns agent security testing into a feedback-driven tuning problem.

A single autonomous agent orchestrates genetic prompt mutation, hierarchical corpus exploration. Asymmetric action scoring, using model responses as a fitness signal to compound effective attacks while preserving benign-use correctness, so blanket refusal cannot count as security.  Across state-of-the-art models, evolutionary mutation amplifies vulnerabilities one-shot methods miss.  Security evaluators get an adaptive adversary that keeps pace with adaptive agents.
arxiv-2602-07791:
In hydrogen-bonded organic solids, protons are light enough that their quantum nature may reshape how the sample absorbs light. Sampreeti Bhattacharya and three co-authors combine first-principles Green's function theory with a method that treats protons quantum mechanically, studying excitons, the bound electron-hole pairs behind light absorption, in eumelanin.

They ask how much of the proton quantum effect comes from changes in structure alone, and find the effects also create direction-dependent, anisotropic behavior for excitons at the molecular level. The work clarifies an underexplored corner of organic optoelectronics, where hydrogen bonds were proposed to help excitons spread. Materials scientists modeling organic semiconductors get a more complete quantum picture.
arxiv-2602-07891:
Geometric foundation models promise strong 3D reconstruction, but they starve for diverse large-scale 3D annotations. Zihui Gao and seven co-authors turn to abundant internet video of static scenes, proposing SAGE, a framework that adapts geometric models from raw video without ground-truth geometry.

A hierarchical mining pipeline selects informative training trajectories, anchors global structure with sparse structure-from-motion point clouds, and enforces multi-view consistency through differentiable 3D Gaussian rendering. Replaying a small share of supervised data prevents forgetting. Applied to two different backbones, SAGE cuts Chamfer distance on unseen benchmarks. The work shows how the web's video flood can feed 3D learning despite noise and missing labels.
arxiv-2602-07991:
Neutrino oscillation parameters can be measured with solar neutrinos and reactor neutrinos, but the two setups carry information differently. Neetu Raj Singh Chundawat and Yu-Feng Li use quantum Fisher information to compare how precisely the solar parameters, the mass-squared difference and mixing angle, can be estimated in each case.

Reactor neutrinos evolve coherently in vacuum, and flavor readings saturate the information bound for both parameters over certain energy ranges, explaining those tests' high fine. Solar neutrinos, by contrast, arrive as incoherent mixtures, so the phase-based addition to information is absent. The analysis clarifies why reactor tests pin down these parameters so well and what solar readings fundamentally cannot add.
arxiv-2602-08091:
Smoothed particle flow copies fluids with bits, but results hinge on how well gradients are figured. S. Rosswog weighs modern SPH variants, focusing on nearly cleanly exact gradients, standard kernel gradients, and matching kernels that satisfy fit links exactly.

Most forms use shock loss with slope-limited imaging set off by shocks and noise, and one recent variant swaps loss for a Riemann solver. Shock tests prove unmoved to gradient accuracy, but wobble problems depend on it crucially: matching kernels perform best, closely followed by the simpler nearly exact gradients. Numeric fluid dynamicists gain a careful head-to-head guide for choosing forms where instabilities, not shocks, dominate.
arxiv-2602-08191:
Cloud autoscalers usually chase workload alone, ignoring energy and carbon costs that now constrain networks. Alisson O. Chaves and nine co-authors present NeuroScaler, an AI-native orchestrator that makes energy and carbon first-class concerns for cloud and edge services.

The system gathers multi-tier telemetry from power distribution units through bare-metal servers to Kubernetes-managed containers, linking load, performance, and power with machine-learning pipelines. A model-predictive control policy then optimizes energy while hitting service-level targets. In a live testbed running production servers and real services, NeuroScaler cut energy use by 34.68 percent against the standard Horizontal Pod Autoscaler while holding target latency. Green-cloud engineers gain a working, measured alternative to workload-only scaling.
arxiv-2602-08491:
Food segmentation models trained on still images score well on benchmarks, yet they stumble on video, where identities must hold steady over time. Keonvin Park and two co-authors study that gap for apples, training only on image data and testing on video with instance tracking. Their arXiv paper shows that strong per-frame scores hide temporal failure.

Lighting shifts, reflections, and texture ambiguity cause masks to flicker and identities to split, corrupting apple counts badly. Standard image metrics overstate real video performance because they miss those errors. The authors test remedies that need no full video labels, including temporal regularization and self-supervised consistency objectives. Readers get a diagnosis that points at image-centric training, not model size, as the root cause.
arxiv-2602-08691:
Equations with memory, where the present depends on the whole past through an integral, arise in fluids and diffusion alike. Bruno de Andrade and Marcos Gabriel de Santana study an abstract equation with memory terms in interpolation scales. Their arXiv paper proves that regular mild solutions exist locally, are unique, can be continued, and face a blow-up alternative.

The theory is then applied to Navier-Stokes equations with hereditary viscosity, using fractional power spaces of the Stokes operator. Reaction-diffusion problems with memory are also explored, with super-linear and gradient-type nonlinear terms. Readers get a rigorous base for evolution equations with memory, plus concrete uses in fluid and diffusion models.
arxiv-2602-08891:
The protocols that keep IPv6 networks running, like Neighbor Discovery and Router Advertisements, also open doors for spoofing and flooding attacks. Walid Aljoby and three co-authors propose a zero-trust edge design that unifies four defenses, against inside and outside spoofing and flooding, in a single programmable data-plane pipeline. Its key rule is to check identity before rate: fake packets are dropped early so flood statistics count only credible senders.

A concrete P4 design uses hop-limit bands, address-port bindings, and sketch-based counting, tested across fifteen attack scenarios. A software prototype and a SmartNIC implementation both run the same pipeline. The authors also discuss limits and next steps for the architecture.
arxiv-2602-09091:
The ancestors of today's galaxy clusters should have driven early star formation and reionization, and Chamilla Terp and nine co-authors hunt them with JWST. Using rest-frame optical grism spectroscopy of the Abell 2744 lensing field, they run a physically motivated Friends-of-Friends search for overdensities at redshift 5.5 to 7, finding six systems, five of them robust, each in a halo above a hundred billion solar masses.

Members of these dense environments are typically less massive yet equally metal-rich as field galaxies, with younger stars shown by bluer slopes and weaker Balmer breaks. Two of six overdensities show excess neutral-hydrogen absorption versus the field average. The census links dense environments, young enriched galaxies, and the gas that reionization had to clear.
arxiv-2602-09191:
Satellite-terrestrial networks promise coverage beyond terrestrial reach, but dynamic spectrum sharing must cope with varied terrain, moving users and satellites, and long space-to-ground delays. Hung Nguyen-Kha and six co-authors propose a digital-twin-aided framework that plans resources over time windows, joining long-term and short-term decisions to cut congestion. A virtual replica of the network predicts conditions for planning, while real-time data refines the result.

Two optimization problems formalize the plan-and-refine split, solved with compressed-sensing and successive convex approximation methods. Simulations on real traffic data over a 3D map of London show the approach beating benchmarks on congestion, with demonstrated adaptability and practical feasibility. The work offers a concrete path to managing tomorrow's integrated networks.
arxiv-2602-09291:
Ban Q. Tran and four co-authors study slot-in plans for trainable-slot quantum physics-taught neural nets applied to curved multi-species reaction-spread systems. Their wider build backs both old-style and fully quantum slot-ins, allowing a set side-by-side: a feedforward-net feature-map form against a tuned-quantum-circuit form, with ansatz, loss, and tuning held fixed.

Hardware-thrifty varied circuits and species-specific readout tools near coupled multi-field motion while a physics-taught loss holds up ruling equations, edge rules, and start rules. Cutting out the slot-in setup shows its pull on slope shape, setting scale, and quantum resource needs. Number tests on one- and two-dimensional reaction-spread equations show the setup's conduct across slot-in picks.
arxiv-2602-09391:
Hennadii Yerzhakov and Alexander Balatsky ask whether light can rewrite a superconductor's symmetry from within. They build a generalized time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau model for a pure s-wave centrosymmetric superconductor, then show microwave radiation inducing p-wave and d-wave components alongside the original order. The trick lies in gradient terms that couple the s-wave order to other symmetry-allowed components.

Singlet-to-singlet gradient terms are quadratic in spatial derivatives. Where spin-orbit coupling is present, linear terms linking singlet and triplet orders are also allowed. Through minimal substitution, these terms let the vector potential couple distinct order parameters, generating the new components. Shaping a superconducting state locally with a microwave beam, the authors suggest, adds a facet to the idea of quantum printing.
arxiv-2602-09591:
Reinforcement learning sharpens language-model reasoning but also stretches chain-of-thought outputs, raising compute costs. Daisuke Nohara and two co-authors train policies with several length-control methods across multiple base models in a controlled setup in their 2026 paper, asking how accuracy actually varies with output length. The relationship proves less simple than longer-is-better.

Across mathematical reasoning and code generation alike, accuracy rises then falls with length, peaking at an intermediate value. Mode accuracy, however, keeps improving with length even where sample accuracy plateaus or declines. The authors read this split as dispersion around an increasingly correct center: longer outputs spread wider even as their typical answer improves. Length control, they argue, must reckon with that dispersion, not just average length.
arxiv-2602-09691:
Knowledge boiling shrinks a larger teacher system into a smaller student, and in machine rendering it is often judged by render quality and run speed. Joseph Attieh and four co-authors argue that this counting ignores the green costs of making and serving the boiled system. Their 2026 case study tests typical boiling methods on both bespoke render models and large language models. Quality is weighed against compute cost with a life-cycle check spanning the full model life cycle.

The key finding is that the serving volume needed to repay boiling is serving-tied and can shift by several orders of scale under batching. Boiling is not alone greener: whether it pays off green-wise depends on how much the boiled system is truly served. Usable guidance follows for picking, building, and testing boiling methods under quality and compute-induced limits.
arxiv-2602-10191:
Stellar collisions in dense clusters forge exotic objects, from blue stragglers to seeds of supermassive black holes, but simulating them on the fly is costly. A 2026 paper led by Elena González Prieto, with nine co-authors, builds a grid of nearly twenty-eight thousand smoothed-particle hydrodynamics calculations of main-sequence star collisions across masses, ages, velocities, and impact parameters. Machine learning models trained on that grid predict merger, disruption, or flyby outcomes plus final remnant masses.

Nearest neighbors, support vector machines, and neural nets are compared, reaching balanced classification accuracy over ninety-eight percent and regression errors well under one percent. The trained models are released in the collAIder package, enabling rapid collision predictions inside N-body models of dense cluster dynamics.
arxiv-2602-10291:
Toric domains in four-dimensional space raise a shape question. Which product Lagrangian tori can a Hamiltonian map send into the domain? A 2026 paper by Richard Hind and Ely Kerman computes the Hamiltonian shape invariant for a broad class of toric domains, in Hind and Zhang's sense. New crossing findings on product Lagrangian tori in symplectic polydisks drive the argument.

For Hamiltonian maps sending certain product tori back into the polydisk, crossings are shown between images and a one-parameter set of product tori holding the original torus. For polydisks with area ratios below two, the result strengthens to crossings with the original torus itself. A soft side note builds a packing showing this rigidity vanishes when the family is swapped for a natural packing by Lagrangian tori.
arxiv-2602-10391:
Multiple zeta values have rich symmetry structure, and their cyclotomic and Hurwitz generalizations raise harder questions about which symmetries survive added variables and parameters. A 2026 paper by Ce Xu studies symmetries of these values with several variables and parameters, using contour integration and the residue theorem. Its main contribution is a set of symmetry formulas worked out directly from residue calculations, without algebraic regularization. The author then deduces matching symmetry results for cyclotomic multiple zeta values and for t-values of the same family.

The results extend recent symmetry work by Charlton and Hoffman, with fully explicit, regularization-free formulas where the series converge. They also prove the symmetry conjecture for these values with several variables and a single parameter. Examples and corollaries round out the paper, which closes with an open problem about other variants of multiple zeta values.
arxiv-2602-10791:
L. Albino and six co-authors map the internal structure of two light mesons in a 2026 paper. Using a lately new algebra model for the quark propagator and Bethe-Salpeter size of pseudoscalar mesons, they construct wavefunctions for the eta and eta-prime mesons. Projections onto a flavor basis yield light-front wavefunctions for combinations of strange and light quark states.

From an overlap model, the authors compute valence-quark broad parton spreads, which the model ties entirely to valence-quark spread amplitudes. Those spreads then yield spread functions and light-and-charge form factors through straightforward derivation. The paper offers a multidimensional portrait of two mesons whose mixing has long challenged simple quark models.
arxiv-2602-11091:
Safety, values, and culture rarely pull in the same direction. Usman Naseem and five co-authors ask whether one language model can satisfy all three at once. Most tests check each dimension alone, which hides the trade-offs between them.

Their answer is MisAlign-Profile, a single benchmark built on a data set spanning more than one hundred normative domains. Each prompt carries domain labels and a semantic type, with paired aligned and misaligned replies. Tests of general, tuned, and open-weight models reveal clear cross-dimension trade-offs. The work gives researchers a way to measure clashes that single-focus tests miss.
arxiv-2602-11491:
Generative Flow Networks can over-explore vast spaces, sampling low-reward regions too often. Xuan Yu and four co-authors propose CMAB-GFN, which joins a combinatorial multi-armed bandit frame to flow network policies. The bandit prunes low-quality actions, yielding compact high-scoring subspaces for exploration.

Restricting exploration to those subspaces speeds discovery of high-value candidates, while exploring other subspaces preserves diversity. Tests on multiple tasks show higher-reward candidates than current approaches. The work addresses a core tension in flow networks: exploration must be broad enough to find good regions, yet focused enough to avoid wasting samples on poor ones.
arxiv-2602-11691:
A platform that posts prices in a two-sided market learns only from accept or reject replies, yet must still maximize trade gains or profit. Yiding Feng and three co-authors map what regret is achievable across three mechanism classes: single-price, two-price, and segmented-price. For profit, a two-price design achieves regret that grows slowly with trader count and time horizon.

For trade gains the picture is sharper. Constant regret is possible in one-to-one trade, but even a one-seller, two-buyer market forces slowly growing regret under single prices. In many-to-many markets, two-price mechanisms suffer linear regret because bad pairings block near-optimal trade. Segmented prices, which group traders and price each group separately, restore slowly growing regret and draw a clear line between learnable and unlearnable pricing regimes.
arxiv-2602-11791:
Listing every binary word of a given length, in the style of Gray codes, usually costs extra time or memory that grows with length. Antoine Amarilli and five co-authors give the first two algorithms that enumerate all binary words while keeping both delay between outputs and auxiliary space constant, independent of length. Constant time per word and constant memory beyond the bits storing the current word are achieved in two new models: tape machines and deque machines.

More restricted models, queue machines and stack machines, cannot do the same with constant auxiliary space even with unlimited delay. A tape machine stores the word on one working tape that never grows, editing it to reach every word without duplicates. A deque machine stores the word on a double-ended queue with constant internal state. The main challenge in the deque model is detecting correctly when enumeration has finished.
arxiv-2602-12191:
Mapping class groups describe the symmetries of surfaces, and one question asks how connected they look far out at infinity. Michael Mihalik works alone here, closing the last open cases for closed surfaces. Groups for surfaces with edges or punctures were already understood, except for closed surfaces of genus 3 and 4.

He proves a broad result that any finitely presented group meeting his conditions is simply connected at infinity, and that result covers all closed surfaces of genus 3 or more. Since these groups are duality groups, a standard theorem then lifts the answer to higher connectivity tied to group dimension. Combined with earlier work, the paper gives a complete list for all mapping class groups.
arxiv-2602-12691:
Robot arms guided by vision and language models learn from messy real-world logs that mix old policies, live trials, demos, and human corrections. Judging a robot by the average quality of that mixed past can mislead training, since it does not reflect what the current policy would do. Rushuai Yang and thirteen co-authors propose ALOE, a method that scores each action chunk under the current policy instead, using chunked value learning and a cautious way of combining estimates.

That design gives steadier credit to the action chunks that matter most when rewards are rare, and it feeds into a policy update weighted by those scores. The team tested ALOE on four hands-on jobs: packing a phone, folding laundry, sorting several objects, and assembling a phone. On every task it beat other post-training methods for vision-language-action models.
arxiv-2602-13091:
Anomaly detection in images and video is usually framed as one-class classification: train only on normal examples. That assumption leaves methods vulnerable to label noise in training data. Declan McIntosh and Alexandra Branzan Albu present Bootstrap Aggregation Anomaly Filtering, which transforms any one-class anomaly detector into a fully unsupervised method. The trick exploits two traits of anomalies: they are rare and heterogeneous.

Several separately trained instances of supervised one-class classifiers sift the training set for anomalies, using modified bootstrap aggregation. No change to the underlying detector is needed; only the data bags used for training change. The method achieves state-of-the-art fully unsupervised results on MVTec AD, ViSA, and MVTec LOCO AD, including unsupervised logical anomaly detectors for images, a first for the field. Improvements to one-class classifiers transfer directly to the unsupervised domain.
arxiv-2602-13191:
Video language models must fit long videos into limited context windows, and keyframe sampling misses both broad events and fine details. Sayan Deb Sarkar and six co-authors exploit video codec primitives, motion vectors and residuals, which natively encode redundancy and sparsity without full-image encoding for most frames. Lightweight transformer encoders aggregate those primitives and align them with image encoder embeddings through pretraining that speeds end-to-end fine-tuning convergence.

Their system, CoPE-VideoLM, cuts time-to-first-token by as much as 86% and token usage by as much as 93% versus standard video language models. Varying keyframe and codec primitive densities maintains or exceeds performance on 14 diverse video understanding benchmarks, spanning spatial scene understanding, long-form understanding, temporal and motion reasoning, and general question answering. Codec primitives thus offer an efficient, information-preserving alternative to sparse keyframes.
arxiv-2602-13391:
Short gamma-ray bursts were firmly tied to neutron star mergers by GW170817. Whether mergers alone can explain every observed burst remains open, since gravitational-wave detections are still few. This study tests 64 binary neutron star population models against 16 years of Fermi-GBM burst data. It uses Monte Carlo methods and three jet geometries: a structured jet tuned to GW170817, a universal top-hat jet, and a varied top-hat jet.

Models with low local merger rates predict too few visible bursts to match the Fermi population, and they survive only with wide jets at odds with narrow cores seen in afterglows. Models near 100 mergers per cubic gigaparsec per year reproduce the population well, given plausible jet fractions and geometries. Alessio Ludovico De Santis leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13491:
LMC X-4 is a high-mass X-ray binary whose superorbital period ranks among the most stable known for Roche-lobe overflow systems. This paper analyzes 33 years of monitoring from five observatories, CGRO BATSE, RXTE ASM, Swift BAT, MAXI GSC, and Fermi GBM. Measured phases show a smooth long-term trend with systematic fluctuations on top, and quartic and sinusoidal fits beat cubic fits, with the sinusoidal model giving an 8,900-day modulation.

That timescale is too long to blame on a tertiary companion's orbit, and the fluctuations look like stochastic, glitch-like events over several hundred days. Total period variation over 33 years is just 0.55 percent, confirming exceptional stability. A soft-hard X-ray phase offset of 0.044 cycles in 2014 to 2024 fits an evolving disk model with a higher-harmonic term. Yi Chou is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13591:
Language-model agents thrive in virtual settings but rarely touch the physical world beyond direct control interfaces. AgentRob bridges online community forums, language-model agents, and physical robots through the Model Context Protocol. Agents join forums, read posts, extract natural-language commands, dispatch robot actions, and report results back to the community. Three layers organize the system. A forum layer supports persistent multi-agent interaction. An agent layer polls for mention-targeted commands, and a robot layer with vision-language controllers and Unitree Go2 and G1 hardware translates commands into robot primitives.

Multiple agents with distinct identities and bodies can coexist in one forum. That establishes that forum-mediated multi-agent robot orchestration is feasible. Wenrui Liu leads the work with fifteen co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13791:
Predicting transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations is key for grasping gene regulation and ranking large-scale perturbation experiments. Yet existing methods rely on static, possibly partial knowledge graphs or prompt language models for similar-function genes, retrieving links shaped by symmetric co-occurrence in text rather than directed control logic. MechPert encourages language-model agents to generate control guesses instead of relying solely on functional likeness. Multiple agents separately propose candidate controls with confidence scores, combined through a shared vote filtering false links into weighted groups for downstream prediction.

On Perturb-seq benchmarks across four human cell lines, MechPert improves Pearson correlation by up to 10.5 percent over similarity-based rivals in low-data settings with 50 observed perturbations. For experimental design, MechPert-selected anchor genes beat standard network center rules by up to 46 percent in well-studied cell lines. Marc Boubnovski Martell leads the work with eight co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14191:
Hamid Reza Hashempour and three co-authors design a 2026 arXiv safe radio system with drones and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces. A hovering drone carries a reconfigurable intelligent surface to serve many users, but dodgy energy-harvesting ears may spy, and channel facts are flawed. Drone place, power control, and sheet phases are tightly tied.

The goal is to maximize worst-case secret energy yield under flawed channel facts and discrete phase shifts. The problem is highly non-convex, so the authors build two matching approaches, starting with block coordinate descent plus step-wise convex guesswork for a secret energy yield form. The design weighs secrecy, energy use, and real hardware limits in one joint tune.
arxiv-2602-14291:
H. M. Shadman Tabib and 26 co-authors present a 2026 arXiv community resource for Bangla speech technology. Bengali remains under-resourced for long-form speech, despite its wide use. Bengali-Loop offers two benchmarks for realistic multi-speaker, long-duration content such as drama and natok.

The speech-recognition corpus holds 191 recordings, 158.6 hours, and 792,000 words from 11 YouTube channels, built by subtitle extraction with human-checked transcripts. The diarization corpus holds 24 recordings, 22 hours, and 5,744 manually labeled speaker turns. Baselines are 34.07% word error rate for Tugstugi and 40.08% diarization error for pyannote.audio, with standard protocols for reproducible evaluation.
arxiv-2602-14391:
Ali Salimi and three co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv federated learning framework for heterogeneous IoT devices. Device heterogeneity is a key challenge, since IoT networks mix devices with very different compute power, memory, and network conditions. ASA, or Adaptive Smart Agent, clusters devices adaptively by real-time resource profiles and tailors models to each cluster's capability.

An intelligent agent layer examines CPU power, memory, and network environment to sort devices into high-performance, mid-tier, and low-capability levels. Each level receives a model tuned to its power, keeping all devices engaged. On MNIST and CIFAR-10 benchmarks, ASA cut communication burden by 43 to 50%, improved resource utilization by 43%, and reached 98.89% accuracy on MNIST and 85.30% on CIFAR-10.
arxiv-2602-14591:
Evgenii Kniazev, writing alone, presents a 2026 arXiv automated method for classifying source code changes. The method clusters metric vectors computed for each code change, then an expert maps resulting clusters to predefined change classes. Automating the distribution step substantially cuts time needed for code-change review, while expert mapping keeps classes meaningful.

Clustering uses k-means with cosine similarity between metric vectors. Eleven source code metrics cover lines of code, cyclomatic complexity, file counts, interface changes, and structural changes. Validation on five software systems, including open-source projects Subversion and NHibernate, showed classification purity 0.75 plus or minus 0.05 and entropy 0.37 plus or minus 0.06 at a 0.05 significance level, demonstrating practical review support.
arxiv-2602-14691:
Goal recognition datasets carry a hidden bias from the planners that made them. Mustafa F. Abdelwahed, with co-authors, proposes multi-plan dataset generation to remove that bias. Old sets rely on heuristic forward search, which narrows the plans a recognizer ever sees.

Top-k planning yields several distinct plans for the same goal hypothesis. A new Version Coverage Score measures how well a recognizer holds up across those versions. Tests show the leading recognizer degrades sharply when observations grow sparse. The method gives fairer benchmarks for agents that must guess goals in realistic settings.
arxiv-2602-14891:
Alex Fullerton resets STIS first-order, medium-resolution response from sky runs and CALSPEC v11 star models for white dwarfs G191-B2B, GD 71, and GD 153. One more setup is reset by matching sky runs of second star BD +75 325 to a low-res STIS sky curve set on the same v11 models.

Steps for working out responses and checking PHOTTAB files ere they went live in CRDS on May 1, 2025, are laid out, with plots in a long annex. Snags, doubts, and tips close the note. Hubble star-light work thus gains a firmer brightness scale.
arxiv-2602-15091:
Khalesi and Salehi study mixture-of-experts models through the lens of communication theory. Such models split prediction across specialized expert sub-networks chosen by a gating step. This letter treats the gate as a stochastic channel working under a finite information rate, asking what limited gating bandwidth costs in learning.

Within an information-theoretic learning framework, the authors specialize a mutual-information generalization bound and develop a rate-distortion account of finite-rate gating. The analysis yields capacity-aware limits for communication-constrained expert systems. Numerical tests on synthetic multi-expert models confirm the predicted trade-offs among gating rate, expressivity, and generalization, tying how much the gate can say to how well the system learns.
arxiv-2602-15191:
Genovese and Piana derive the approximate message passing equations from belief propagation for the l2 minimization problem. The problem seeks the vector of smallest norm subject to a linear constraint, where the matrix is random with separate sub-Gaussian mean-zero entries. It can be viewed as the zero-temperature version of a statistical mechanics problem, with a suitable Gibbs measure on the solution space.

That measure has its own message-passing rules. The authors prove, in the easiest case, that the means from message-passing iteration in the limit satisfy the message passing equations. The result ties a usable stepwise algorithm to its physics roots, grounding AMP in message passing for this problem.
arxiv-2602-15491:
Sadok and colleagues fix a weak spot in neural audio codecs, the tools that squeeze speech and sound into compact codes. Most such codecs pack loudness and shape into one shared code space, so a mere change in input volume can shift the codes a lot. That waste shows up as repeat codes and as worse sound for each bit spent.

Their Equalizer method splits the signal first, on a short-term basis, into a gain part and a normalised shape part. Only the shape goes through the codec, while the gain is coded on its own with simple scalar steps and sent apart. Tests on speech with four well-known codecs show a large gain in sound per bit, plus a much simpler quantiser. The trick is easy to add to any neural codec.
arxiv-2602-15591:
Zyberaj and colleagues turn plain-language vehicle requirements into runnable tests. Testing software-defined vehicles is hard because requirements arrive as prose, specs mix text, tables, and diagrams, and test assets scatter across many tools. Their Req2Road pipeline uses large language and vision-language models to pull signals and behaviour logic from specs, then builds Gherkin scenarios and converts them into runnable scripts.

Retrieval-augmented generation preselects candidate Vehicle Signal Specification signals before mapping, and the VSS standard keeps signal references portable across subsystems and test benches. The team tests the pipeline on a child presence detection system, in simulation and on a real vehicle. Thirty-two of 36 requirements become executable scenarios, though human review and targeted fixes remain needed. The paper is a feasibility and architecture demonstration, not a claim of full automation.
arxiv-2602-15691:
Pastva and colleagues link the dynamics of biomolecular networks to cell types that experiments can measure, a central challenge in systems biology. They define a phenotype as a partial steady state committed to a given outcome while otherwise minimally constrained. For Boolean models, they define dynamical phenotypes as complete trap spaces that pin down chosen nodes tied to biomarkers, while leaving external inputs free.

Such phenotypes can be found fast without listing all attractors. Across four published models, including a 70-node model of T cell growth, the method recovers known cell types and activation states and points to outside conditions that sustain them. A further method picks informative nodes from canalization of Boolean functions, revealing cell state detail that adds to hand-defined types and that two attractor-based checks confirm.
arxiv-2602-15991:
Oliveira and colleagues rescue power law inflation by adding memory to cosmic expansion. In four dimensions the simple model predicts the right tilt for cosmic microwave background fluctuations, yet its gravitational wave signal runs too large for current bounds. A fractional scalar field changes the Friedmann and Klein Gordon dynamics with non local corrections.

Introducing a fractional order different from one suppresses the tensor signal while leaving the tilt almost untouched, with an explicit mapping between the order and the model parameters. Near values favoured by data, the model lands on a tilt near point nine six five and a tensor ratio below four hundredths. The potential comes out exponential on its own, and the fractional solutions act as stable attractors, giving future polarization surveys a clear target.
arxiv-2602-16091:
Amirali Rayegan and Tim Menzies ask if causal thought can make software analytics more steady. Decision trees are prized because they can be read and explained, and they serve defect prediction and tuning well. Yet most trees split on correlation, which links two things but cannot show that one causes the other. Past work finds both such trees and causal discovery tools shaky: correlation mixes up link and cause, while causal tools lean on short cuts that shift when inputs shift a bit.

The study tests split rules that use causal ideas, with conditional entropy and confounder filtering, to see if they add steadiness at no cost to predictive power. It draws on more than one hundred twenty multi-objective tasks from the MOOT set, using a preregistered bootstrap-ensemble protocol to gauge variance. Human expert judgments are also compared, to learn whose calls hold up best.
arxiv-2602-16191:
Eigenvalue problems for Fredholm integral operators with Green kernels are the subject of work by Shashank Shukla and coauthors. Their analysis targets rates of convergence for eigenvalue and spectral subspace approximations of a compact linear integral operator. Orthogonal and interpolatory projections at an odd number of collocation points project onto piecewise even-degree polynomials. Those points need not be Gauss points. That setup yields superconvergence of eigenfunctions under iteration.

Modified versions achieve faster rates than classical projection methods. The rate gain is verified by numerical examples. For readers in numerical analysis, the paper gives precise rates for a class of operators that arise widely in such equations. A careful choice of points and degree can squeeze extra accuracy from each round without changing the basic method.
arxiv-2602-16291:
Bo Yang presents a calculus of inheritance built from three primitives: mixin, definition, and reference. Just as lambda-calculus uses abstraction, application, and variable as the foundation of functional programming, it uses its three parts as the base of declarative coding. Joining modules, classes, objects, methods, fields, and locals under a single mixin idea, it models it simply as set union. Mixing is therefore commutative, idempotent, and associative.

That structure eliminates the multiple-inheritance ordering problem. Meaning is first-order and denotational, evaluated by tabling even for cyclic cases. It is distilled from MIXINv2, a practical build in which the same code acts as varied function colors and ordinary sums yield relational semantics of logic. Yang claims it is strictly more expressive.
arxiv-2602-16491: Marco Radeschi, Lorenzo Scoffone, and Michael Wiemeler classify Riemannian foliations of closed manifolds homotopy equivalent to CROSSes. The paper sorts these foliations into types for this class. Readers get an account of which ones can occur on such spaces. The result covers closed manifolds only, and it treats them in that setting.
arxiv-2602-16591:
Erik Boström, Anna-Karin Tornberg, and Ludvig af Klinteberg improve fast Ewald summation, a workhorse for Coulomb interactions in molecular dynamics. The method splits interactions into short-range and long-range parts. The long-range part is sped up with the fast Fourier transform. Accuracy and cost hinge on the mollifier in the kernel split and on the window function used for spreading and interpolation.

The authors use the first prolate spheroidal wave function for both roles, since it concentrates well in real and Fourier space at once. They give a full method account with rigorous error estimates and closed-form error approximations that set parameters to match a chosen tolerance. Tests show fewer Fourier modes and smaller windows than Gaussian or B-spline rivals at the same accuracy.
arxiv-2602-17091:
Kan Watanabe led a four-author team on a reviewer-side problem created by AI coding agents. Tools like GitHub Copilot and Cursor let developers spin out code, tests, and pull requests from plain-language prompts, but each pull request now carries more code for a human to review. A notable share of that AI-written code gets deleted in review, yet reviewers must still read it first.

The paper builds a prediction model that flags functions likely to be cut during pull request review. Functions deleted for different reasons showed distinct traits, and the model scored well on ranking doomed functions, reaching a strong discrimination score. The authors argue such predictions could help reviewers spend their attention on code that will survive, rather than wading through code headed for deletion.
arxiv-2602-17291:
Dongyi Yang led a four-author team proposing a lattice of levitated ferromagnets as a sharper probe of ultralight dark matter. A single levitated ferromagnet already senses weak magnetic-like signals with rare sensitivity. Replacing it with a lattice raises total polarized spin while preserving each magnet's intrinsic dynamic response, combining their signals in step.

Magnetic dipole-dipole interactions within the lattice are suppressed on the fly by a high-frequency magnetic field. That leaves the system effectively noninteracting, at the cost of a modest signal reduction from distinct renormalization of linear and quadratic spin responses. Collective readout scales well with magnet count, and projected reach beats single-ferromagnet setups, including for axion-photon couplings, where the lattice itself boosts the signal beyond current constraints over a broad mass range.
arxiv-2602-17391:
Rakesh Ranjan led a five-author team securing RIS-assisted MIMO links under a true-to-life hardware model. A multi-antenna sender sends secret notes to a target while an eavesdropper listens, and tunable surface units carry built-in circuit resistance, a practical non-ideal effect prior work often neglects. The goal is raising the secrecy rate under perfect channel state knowledge.

The team solves the problem with a low-cost joint setup based on an adaptive gradient method, tuning transmit coding and phase shifts. Since the exact problem is costly, a simpler variant raises channel power gap instead of the exact rate. Tests show that shortcut nears the true optimum at far lower cost, and the tuned step size scheme lifts secrecy rate and cuts time over fixed step size methods. Using a true-to-life surface model proves key for links, above all as values shift.
arxiv-2602-17691:
Craig Atkinson presents HELIX, a shape-based frame for bit-cut language models caught between dull and derailed outputs. Low heat settings give looping, mode-collapsed text, while high heat causes path drift and nonsense.
