HELIX tethers hidden-state paths to a pre-set truth manifold, splitting output entropy from hallucination.

A Unified Truth Score blends token-level meaning entropy with Mahalanobis distance from the manifold. When drift looms, graded steering vectors nudge signals toward sound regions while touching only a tiny share of tokens. On a four-bit model, scores hold up well even at high heat, and steering sparse focus layers alone corrects drift. High-heat outputs also reveal a creative store of far less doubled ideas.
arxiv-2602-17991:
Seokho Jeong and Minhyuk Kim improve maximum independent set preparation on Rydberg atom hardware, where adiabatic quantum computation offers a natural route to combinatorial optimization. The trouble is that the spectral gap shrinks as system size and connectivity grow, leaking population out of the ground state during finite-time evolution. Their fix, called Adjusted Detuning for Ground-Energy Leakage Blockade, reshapes the laser detuning profile to suppress that leakage.

The method adds no extra Hamiltonian terms and needs no iterative optimization loops. On a quasi-one-dimensional chain of ten atoms, the method beat the standard schedule by a wide margin. A schedule tuned on smaller cases transferred to larger two-dimensional triangular lattices of twenty-five and thirty-seven atoms. With a small heuristic offset, it stayed effective for harder cases, pointing to a scalable, hardware-friendly route for quantum optimization on neutral-atom platforms.
arxiv-2602-18091:
Filippo Faedi and team explain transport effects in chiral fluids, where the mobility tensor carries mirror-flipped off-line parts. Such fluids show interaction-boosted spreading and backward motion, effects absent in usual systems. Although seen in theory and noted in models, their tiny-scale origin had stayed unclear.

Using a motion-based off-balance approach, the authors analyze the steady-state drift of a tracer driven through a chiral fluid. Under strong twist, the tracer leaves a flipped density wake, with regions of particle pileups and gaps flipped versus the achiral case. That shape flip of the wake gives a unified cause behind both faster spreading and backward motion. The effects prove robust to changes in the interaction, showing their broad reach from odd movement.
arxiv-2602-18191:
Rounak Mukherjee and one co-author ask where neutron stars end and black holes begin. Their 2026 paper notes the boundary is open, a gap born of ignorance about matter squeezed past nuclear density inside neutron star cores. The team attacks the question with a physics-informed learning model guided by sky observations.

Trained on a broad, neutral set of matter equations, the Transformer model reads two shape traits of the mass-radius curve, called front and back bending. It first predicts peak mass and radius from those bends, then works backward to the sound-speed profile inside. The model says heavy neutron stars arise when sound speed peaks at low density, with strong back bending and an early switch to quark matter. It puts the peak mass near two and a half Suns, with smallest radius near eleven and a half kilometers at one point four solar masses.
arxiv-2602-18391:
Eric W. Fischer analyzes a key transformation in quantum electrodynamics coupled cluster theory. His 2026 paper studies the coherent-state transformation through its commutator with the polaritonic cluster operator, which does not vanish. A Hartree-Fock reference state set by that transformation yields a Lagrangian from coherent-state forms of the polaritonic Hamiltonian, cluster, and deexcitation operators.

The approach differs from earlier coupled cluster theory in its photon state basis, using photon-added coherent states, not shifted number states. The transformation renormalizes correlation energy and ground state, tied to the mean-field dipole value, breaking origin invariance for charged systems. Single-photon excitation shifts only the ground state, not correlation energy. At large cavity frequencies the renormalized ansatz nears the original form, while at low frequencies correlation energy diverges for molecules with nonzero dipole moment. That blow-up is discussed with multi-photon excited states and the cavity-Born-Oppenheimer frame.
arxiv-2602-18891:
How does AI change the daily work of research itself? Yuan An, writing alone in 2026, reports a pilot study in which a human researcher coordinated several LLM agents. The agents extracted data, built a corpus, generated artefacts, and evaluated them. Multiple-choice questions from SAT Maths served as the testbed.

Over a thousand questions were collected. Agents pulled questions from PDFs, turned open textbooks into structured forms, aligned questions with textbook content, and generated new questions at set difficulty and cognitive levels. A twenty-four-criterion framework judged quality. Average quality was high. Yet generated questions never matched expert-vetted baselines on all criteria. Gaps centred on skill depth, cognitive engagement, difficulty tuning, and metadata alignment. The researcher's job shifted from authoring to specification, orchestration, verification, and governance.
arxiv-2602-19191:
Electromagnetic waves in empty space follow a classic set of laws, and Xiaorong Zou looks for a neat formula that solves them outright. The paper treats a uniform material with no electric current, starting from smooth, repeating wave patterns as its initial state. Its answer has a simple analytic shape, so the starting pattern plainly fixes the wave that follows.

That clean shape makes the result useful in two ways. It can serve as a tool for building waves with chosen features, and it points toward answers for messier cases. Zou extends the work to a special case where current comes from a separate generator, and plans a follow-up for materials where current is present in general.
arxiv-2602-19391:
Skeletal polyhedra are discrete structures built from polygons as faces, two faces meeting at each edge, with a circular vertex figure at every vertex. Egon Schulte and Tomas Skacel lay out the blueprint for the snub construction, a method that twists a polyhedron into a new, snubbed form. The paper shows the construction works for regular and chiral skeletal polyhedra alike, in ordinary space.

The resulting snub polyhedra are vertex-transitive with strong local symmetry, meaning every vertex sits in the same kind of local pattern. Their combinatorial, topological, and geometric traits are described and shown through striking examples. The authors also examine when the construction yields uniform polyhedra and discuss how complete their list of generated structures is.
arxiv-2602-19591:
Small and medium enterprises make up 99.9 percent of United States businesses and generate 44 percent of economic activity, yet spotting high-potential ones remains an open challenge. Yijiashun Qi and two co-authors introduce SME-HGT, a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer predicting which SBIR Phase I awardees advance to Phase II funding using only public data. The graph holds 32,268 company nodes, 124 topic nodes for research, and 13 government agency nodes.

About 99,000 edges spanning three semantic relation types connect the graph. At a screening depth of 100 firms, SME-HGT hits 89.6 percent precision, beating random selection by 2.14 times, with a temporal protocol preventing information leakage. SME-HGT reaches an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.621 on a temporally split test set, beating an MLP baseline and R-GCN over five random seeds.
arxiv-2602-19691:
Neural networks usually gain power by growing deeper, but depth is not the only route to better learning. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yuhao Liu and three co-authors studies networks of fixed depth whose activation functions are smooth, and asks what such networks can learn about smooth functions.

The authors prove that widening alone lets these shallow networks reach the best possible rates for both approximation and estimation, up to small logarithmic factors. By contrast, networks with non-smooth activations such as ReLU stay limited by their depth: finer smoothness demands more layers. The work thus points to activation smoothness as a second lever, beside depth, for reaching optimal learning rates.
arxiv-2602-19791:
In unusual superconductors, the pairing symmetry shapes the whole superconducting phase, yet pinning it down from data is hard. A 2026 arXiv paper by Adam Hložný and three co-authors introduces a machine-learning strategy that reads pairing symmetry from quasiparticle interference images.

The approach combines theory-based calculation, tight-binding models, and symmetry-based sorting of the pairing function, all within a single-impurity setup. Tested on a single layer of niobium diselenide, a material open to experiment, the method solves the inverse problem from interference data with high accuracy for most pairing channels. The result suggests interference data carry rich, learnable clues about gap structure. That opens a practical path to precise pairing identification in quantum materials.
arxiv-2602-20091:
Retrieval-augmented generation feeds language models external documents. Retrieved sets mix useful and irrelevant material, and how that mix changes the model's inner workings is poorly understood. A 2026 arXiv paper by Samuel Yeh and Sharon Li studies retrieval-augmented generation through latent states rather than outputs alone.

The authors methodically analyze how different kinds of retrieved documents shift the hidden states of language models and how those inner shifts relate to downstream output behaviour. They worked across four question-answering datasets and three language models, under controlled single-document and multi-document settings. They trace how context fit and layer-by-layer processing shape internal states. The results explain aspects of model outputs in terms of representation shifts and offer guidance for retrieval-based generation system design.
arxiv-2602-20191:
Flexible use needs one language model to run at various bit levels as latency and memory budgets change. Current any-precision methods have flaws. Some rely on hardware-wasteful vector quantization. Others add scaling factors when switching bit-widths. Post-training quantization tuned for one fixed low precision holds up poorly when bit levels change at runtime. A 2026 arXiv paper by Dongwei Wang and ten co-authors traces that failure to outlier migration: the spread of sensitive tokens shifts across precisions.

Prompted by that observation, the paper proposes MoBiQuant, an any-precision mixture-of-bits quantization framework. It adjusts weight precision based on token needs, for changing budgets. Needy tokens receive more bits, robust tokens fewer. One model can thus serve many precision budgets without fresh tuning. Readers gain a token-aware route to any-precision inference that confronts outlier drift head-on rather than treating all tokens alike.
arxiv-2602-20291:
Valentin Bonas and three co-authors build a system that reads chart images, judges design, and suggests fixes. Charts shape scientific and journalistic communication, yet errors in them can mislead readers. Rule-based checkers flag violations but miss context and offer no redesign help. Asking a general language model gives inconsistent advice. This 2026 paper combines chart de-rendering, automated analysis, and iterative improvement into one feedback loop.

The system rebuilds a chart structure from its image, spots design flaws with vision-language reasoning, and proposes research-backed changes. Users apply chosen improvements and re-render the figure, learning design principles as they go. Tested on a thousand charts from the Chart2Code benchmark, it produced more than ten thousand recommendations in ten coherent groups, from axis formatting to color accessibility and legend consistency. The results point toward authoring tools that give structured, principle-based design feedback.
arxiv-2602-20391:
Bence G. Márkus and seven co-authors test whether aqueous chlorine dioxide radicals can briefly spin-label plastics for tracking. Plastic waste threatens nature, wildlife, and human health, and tracing, counting, and naming waste types matters for cutting, reuse, and cleanup. The team adds chlorine dioxide radicals to PET plastic and detects them with electron spin resonance spectroscopy. Its unpaired electron is highly tuned to its local setting through its coupling values.

Heat tests show they sit still when cold, giving clear anisotropic and hyperfine spectra fit by a model spin Hamiltonian. Even above the melting point of water, some motion stays blocked by the polymer matrix. A room-temperature time series then yields the spread rate of it in the polymer. The method can thus name plastic species by their local setting, giving a new tool for tracking plastic waste.
arxiv-2602-20491:
A spinning black hole can shed spin energy to waves through superradiance, and Supakorn Katewongveerachart and David Senjaya study it in equations for the spinning dyonic Kerr-Sen black hole. Working from the separable Klein-Gordon formula for a massive neutral scalar field in the low-rate, slow-spin regime, they use far-field matching to compute the bounce factor. No exact global bounce answer exists for this four-charge shape, so the matching setup enables a careful analytic treatment of near and far regions.

The authors derive the rule in full and show energy harvest happens only for co-spinning modes. Both charges suppress boost against the Kerr limit, while lighter co-spinning scalar fields broaden the window and raise the yield of spin energy harvest. Full work leads to a closed-form boost formula.
arxiv-2602-20691:
Tilt between a core's spin and the magnetic field may let one protostar drive several outflow parts. Shingo Hirano and two co-authors test that idea with magnetohydrodynamic simulations of cores, tracking protostar, disk, and outflows. The initial angle between core spin and field varies from zero to ninety degrees.

All models launch a classic disk wind along the disk normal. With large tilt, a spiral flow also forms along the disk plane. In a sample sixty-degree-tilt model, outflow shifts from disk-wind-led to spiral-flow-led. The spiral flow grows more massive than the disk wind, and both parts coexist. Across models, peak mass and size ratios of spiral to disk wind, plus lifetimes, rise past sixty degrees of tilt. The paper proposes that second tilted outflows in some systems are spiral flows, while the main bipolar outflow is the disk wind of that system.
arxiv-2602-21091:
Prediction markets thin out for long-horizon events because traders dislike locking up capital. Caleb Maresca tests whether interest-bearing positions fix that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper, using agent-based simulations with language-model traders. The design crosses two horizons, four days against two years, with interest present or absent.

Long horizons do degrade accuracy, but the observed pricing bias of under one percentage point is far smaller than theory and prior evidence suggested. Paying interest removes about eighty-three percent of the horizon effect on accuracy and more than triples participation, from seventeen percent to sixty-two percent of wealth. The author concludes the long-horizon problem may be overstated, and interest works mainly by drawing traders in.
arxiv-2602-21291:
Accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs could forge heavy elements, but only magnetized models deliver the right ejecta. Tetyana Pitik, David Radice, Daniel Kasen, Fabio Magistrelli, Patrick Chi-Kit Cheong, and Sebastiano Bernuzzi present the first end-to-end calculation in this 2026 arXiv paper. It runs from a magnetized, rapidly rotating collapse through neutrino-magnetohydrodynamics, radiation hydrodynamics with nuclear networks, and Monte Carlo radiative transfer.

Unlike unmagnetized models predicting proton-rich nickel-dominated ejecta, strong fields expel about a fifth of a solar mass of neutron-rich material quickly, enabling strong rapid-neutron-capture nucleosynthesis beyond the third peak. The lanthanide-rich kilonova shines mainly in the near infrared. Synthetic light curves match observations of a notable burst-kilonova event without tuning, for polar viewing angles.
arxiv-2602-22291:
AI safety usually studies how to push hostile examples back onto safe ground, but Sarthak Munshi and six co-authors argue for mapping the unsafe regions themselves. They introduce a framework for charting the Manifold of Failure in large language models, reframing flaw search as a quality-diversity problem. A search algorithm illuminates the continuous shape of failure regions, called behavioral attraction basins.

An Alignment Deviation metric steers the search toward behavior farthest from intended alignment. Across three models, the method reaches nearly two-thirds behavioral coverage and uncovers hundreds of distinct flaw niches, revealing sharply different shape signatures per model. Safety teams gain a map of where models break, not just a list of broken prompts.
arxiv-2602-22491:
Eleven-dimensional supergravity may admit a formulation invariant under E11, in which propagating fields appear through an infinite tower of higher duals. Guillaume Bossard and two co-authors show how to derive the propagating equations of those higher dual fields within E11 exceptional field theory at the linearized level. Starting from the pseudo-Lagrangian, they build parent actions for all higher-gradient dual fields tied to the three-form, the six-form, and the dual graviton.

The resulting equations force the Stückelberg fields to be pure curls, ensuring the higher duals carry the same physical degrees of freedom as the original supergravity fields. Extra Stückelberg fields, not predicted by the tensor hierarchy algebra, turn out to serve as sources for the Labastida tensors of the higher duals. The work puts the E11 dual-field program on firmer footing.
arxiv-2602-22591:
Haodong Chen and four co-authors ask where relevance lives inside a ranking language model. Zero-shot document re-ranking has moved from pointwise to listwise and setwise scoring, but generative scoring brings latency and shaky consistency. In-context re-ranking reads internal attention signals instead, skipping text generation, yet past work lumped all layers together.

The team compares generation, likelihood, and internal attention across ranking setups under one protocol. Relevance signals form a bell curve across transformer layers, which motivates Selective-ICR, a method that cuts latency by thirty to fifty percent with no loss of quality. On the reasoning-heavy BRIGHT benchmark, a zero-shot 8-billion-parameter model matched 14-billion reinforcement-learned re-rankers, while a 600-million-parameter model beat leading generation-based systems.
arxiv-2602-23191:
Xinyuan Chen and four co-authors present Uni-Animator, a diffusion-transformer framework that unifies sketch colorization for still images and video. Existing tools handle one task or the other. They suffer from sloppy color transfer with one or several references, loss of fine physical detail, and flicker or motion artifacts when movement is large.

Three fixes address the three faults. Visual reference enhancement via instance patch embedding aligns and fuses reference colors precisely. Physical detail reinforcement keeps high-frequency textures intact. Sketch-based dynamic RoPE encoding models motion-aware space-time links to hold temporal coherence. In tests the unified system matches task-specific rivals on both image and video colorization, offering cross-domain skill with high detail fidelity and steady motion.
arxiv-2602-23291:
Tommy Tang and two co-authors study when treatment effects can be identified despite unmeasured confounders that vary across space. Causal claims from observational data need identifiability, yet no general framework has covered this spatial setting. The paper works with a linear model under varied parametric assumptions about the covariance between the unmeasured confounder and the exposure.

The authors establish identifiability for many commonly used spatial models, for both discrete and continuous data, under mild conditions on observation locations and on the exposure-confounder link. They also flag models and scenarios where identifiability fails, warning that inference there needs caution. The map of where causal effects can and cannot be pinned down gives applied researchers firmer ground for spatial observational studies.
arxiv-2602-23391:
Nazanin Mohammadi Sepahvand and five co-authors propose REPO, a detox method that erases toxic codes instead of merely muting toxic outputs. Large language models trained on web data can produce toxic outputs, and prior shields based on DPO, NPO, and similar methods reduce harmful endings but not well. They fall to hostile prompting and are easily undone by fine-tuning-based re-learning attacks. Linear probing shows why: harmful paths remain present in model codes, so the edits are shallow.

REPO recasts detox as a token-level preference problem with a novel goal and liking data, forcing codes of toxic endings to converge toward their benign twins. Inner analysis shows the fine approach induces deep, local edits to toxin-holding neurons while keeping model utility. Tests report state-of-the-art toughness, stopping re-learning attacks and tuned GCG jailbreaks where older code- and output-based methods fail.
arxiv-2602-23591:
Tatsuo Nishitani completes earlier work on the Cauchy problem for non-effectively hyperbolic operators. For differential operators with non-effectively hyperbolic double traits, the paper studies the link between the Gevrey well-posedness threshold for strong well-posedness and the associated Hamilton map and flow.

Prior work showed the following. If the Hamilton map has a Jordan block of size 4 on the double trait manifold of codimension 3, the Cauchy problem is well-posed for all lower-order terms. The Gevrey class is 1 < s < 3. That result is optimal. The same holds when no bicharacteristics are tangent to that manifold, again optimally. The present paper removes the restriction on the manifold's codimension, thereby completing the result.
arxiv-2602-23691:
Wencheng Lu and 11 co-authors show superconductivity (SC) in the ternary perovskite hydride SrPdH3-x, made at low pressure and guided by theory-first math. Neutron patterns reveal the near-exact mix SrPdD two point nine, with ninety-six percent deuterium site share.

Readings of transport and magnet response set onset SC shifts at two point one kelvin for the H compound and two point two kelvin for the D compound. That inverse isotope effect is blamed mostly on quantum zero-point motion. Strong match between theory and lab work on heat standing and SC traits backs theory-guided SC finding. The work sets SC in this hydride family, growing the small set of lab-made ternary hydride SCs and showing the weight of quantum nuclear motion for right theory of low-pressure hydride SCs.
arxiv-2602-23991:
The ATLAS and CMS collaborations combine their searches for Higgs boson pair production from Large Hadron Collider Run 2 proton-proton data. The 2026 paper pools datasets from both experiments at the collider's second-run energy, giving the most sensitive joint look yet at a process that probes the Higgs self-interaction.

The combined upper limit on the total pair-production signal strength sits modestly above the Standard Model prediction, with the measured strength consistent with that prediction within large uncertainties. Observed significance remains low, near one standard deviation, close to the expected value for a Standard Model signal. Constraints are also set on the Higgs trilinear self-coupling and on the coupling of two Higgs bosons to two vector bosons. These constraints narrow the allowed ranges for both and tighten the test of the Higgs sector.
arxiv-2602-24091:
Noemi Luna Carmeno and two co-authors systematically review how the literature assesses artificial intelligence's impacts on environmental sustainability and human well-being. The 2026 paper screens thousands of records down to over a thousand studies, mapping a field that treats AI as transformative yet understands its consequences poorly.

Environmental studies concentrate narrowly on energy and carbon emissions. Most environmental studies portray AI's impacts as positive, a pattern driven by application-level studies, while well-being studies split nearly evenly between positive and negative. That split hides dimension-level differences: income and health impacts lean positive, while inequality, social cohesion, and employment lean negative. In short, the field sees the trees, not the forest. A wider lens would catch the missing effects. That wider view is the paper's plea.
arxiv-2602-24191:
Kush Grover and five co-authors study resilient strategies for stochastic systems, asking how much disturbance it takes to break a winning strategy. The 2026 paper formalizes resilience for agents that must stay robust when intended actions fail, for instance when an actuator malfunctions and the agent's chosen action cannot be executed.

The authors introduce resilience in the setting and lay out a set of problems. They cover Markov decision processes with reachability and safety objectives. To handle the stochastic setting they offer several ways to aggregate disturbance amounts, including expectation and worst case. They use measures to reason about disturbance sequences. The framework gives a language for asking not just whether a strategy wins, but how much disruption it can absorb before it fails.
arxiv-2603-00191: He and colleagues present LoDA, a task-driven decomposition for LoRA-based continual learning that builds general and truly task-specific subspaces. It solves two energy-based objectives to decouple directions for knowledge sharing and isolation, fixing LoRA down-projections on two subspaces while learning robust up-projections via gradient-aligned optimisation. After each task, a closed-form recalibration of the general update approximates a feature-level joint optimum along the task-shared direction. Experiments show LoDA beats existing continual learning methods.
arxiv-2603-00291: Manso studies how China's anticorruption campaign, launched when Xi Jinping took office in late 2012, changed land sales. Before the campaign, land sales suffered from corruption, especially around choosing between auction and listing, a two-stage method more open to corruption and linked to lower prices. Using a marginal structural model with fixed effects, she finds indictments in a prefecture significantly cut listing sales, more so when indictments run in consecutive months. Indictments also raise mean and median sale prices. The results suggest the campaign deterred corrupt allocation and curbed listings.
arxiv-2603-00391: Lyu and Lyu study a Hankel determinant for a perturbed Laguerre weight with pole singularities, widening the range and adding a stronger zero at the origin. Ladder operators for the orthogonal polynomials plus three compatibility rules express recurrence coefficients through four helper values that repeat step by step. Two helpers also obey coupled differential rules that collapse to a Painlevé III prime formula in a limit. Under double scaling the team extracts the unitary ensemble density and extends the study to a cubic pole case.
arxiv-2603-00491: Xiu and three colleagues make matrix classifiers tougher against noise by swapping surrogate losses for a Heaviside loss in a low rank support matrix machine. The low rank constraint captures global structure in matrix inputs, which vectorising would scramble. Theory pins down Karush-Kuhn-Tucker points with sufficient and necessary conditions, and a proximal alternating scheme solves every subproblem in closed form. Benchmark tests show the new model beats leading methods on accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2603-00691: Liu and eleven colleagues assess driving safety in older adults through everyday trips, replacing clinic snapshots that miss real road behaviour. Their AURA system combines richer in vehicle sensing, multi scale behaviour modelling, and context aware analysis to extract performance signs from routine driving. Fine grained actions are grouped into longer patterns for a fuller picture of functional ability. The work targets independence, service access, and social participation that driving supports in car dependent regions.
arxiv-2603-00791: Ruangkriengsin, Turk, and Stone analyse self diffusiophoresis of a spherical Janus particle near a planar impermeable wall, focusing on orientation and propulsion. The particle carries a small inert region inside a catalytically active cap, and near wall flow and transport resist numerical study under confinement and steep solute gradients. An asymptotic lubrication analysis for narrow gaps, with the inert region matching the lubrication region, covers axisymmetric and slightly tilted poses. Cap size decides whether a tilted particle rotates back to axisymmetric or keeps reorienting, fixing its near contact stability.
arxiv-2603-00991: Odersky and four colleagues put AI agents in a programming-language safety harness to stop leaks, side effects, and prompt-injection manipulation. Instead of calling tools directly, agents express intentions as code in capability-safe Scala 3. The type system tracks which effects each part of code may use. Local purity rules can force sub-computations to be side-effect-free, and experiments show agents generate safe code with no significant task loss while the type system blocks unsafe behavior.
arxiv-2603-01091: Blanco-Romero and four colleagues reframe harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks as economics: adversaries archive encrypted traffic today to break it with future quantum computers. With a testbed spanning TLS, QUIC, and SSH, they show keeping intercepted traffic costs almost nothing, so defense turns on decryption cost. Encrypted Client Hello forces bulk collection, while aggressive rekeying and larger key exchanges multiply quantum work, making the latter the stronger lever since storage inflation burdens defenders too.
arxiv-2603-01291: Kaneko, Niwa, and Baldwin propose JailNewsBench, the first benchmark for evaluating language model robustness against jailbreak-induced fake news generation across languages and regions. It covers 34 regions and 22 languages, with 8 evaluation sub-metrics scored by an LLM judge and 5 jailbreak attacks, with approximately 300,000 instances. Testing 9 language models, they find the maximum attack success rate reached 86.3 percent and the maximum harmfulness score was three and a half out of 5.
arxiv-2603-01491:
Kyu Beom Han, Jaeyoon Kim, Woo Jae Kim, and colleagues work on pulling shape, material, and light apart from photos in this 2026 study. Known as inverse rendering, that task gets hard when light bounces between surfaces in complex ways. Past tools trained on a few views often lack good cues for light seen from new angles.

Their method, RadioGS, adds a physics-based loss that checks each surface patch against a rendered match. The check gives feedback from unseen views and helps the model learn bounce light well. Built on flat Gaussian patches with fast ray tracing, it also adapts to new lighting in minutes at low cost. On standard test sets, RadioGS beat prior Gaussian-based tools while staying fast.
arxiv-2603-01691:
Domen Vres, Tjasa Arcon, Timotej Petric, and colleagues build a strong language model for Slovene, a less-resourced language. Their 2026 work notes that open models train mostly on English, so smaller languages and cultures get weaker service. The team sets out the steps needed to adapt a model well.

Their model, GaMS3-12B, starts from an open base and learns in stages with mixed-language data. Continued training uses Slovene plus English and three close South Slavic languages. Two rounds of fine-tuning on instruction data follow, drawn from English and Slovene examples. Tests cover Slovene benchmarks, translation from English, and a head-to-head arena. The model beats its base at its size and rivals a much larger commercial model in the arena.
arxiv-2603-01891:
C F Maximilian Nagy, Onur Celik, Emiliyan Gospodinov, and colleagues make action chunking work in live reinforcement learning. Their 2026 work groups actions into chunks, which helps exploration and value estimates on long tasks. The catch is that a critic must now judge whole action strings, which strains learning and data needs.

Past chunking methods were built for offline data, and they lag in purely online settings. Their algorithm, SEAR, is an off-policy online method designed for chunks from the start. A receding horizon scheme blends the perks of small and large chunk sizes as it acts. Tests on hard simulated manipulation tasks show SEAR beating top online rivals. It trains stably with chunk sizes up to twenty steps, a range where naive chunked baselines lose ground fast.
arxiv-2603-01991:
The ATLAS Collaboration searches for massive long-lived particles in proton collision data from the Large Hadron Collider. Their 2026 report uses data gathered from 2022 to 2024 at record collision energy. Long-lived particles would decay away from the collision point, leaving displaced vertices inside the detector.

Events must hold at least one displaced vertex with many tracks and at least one displaced muon. The muon need not attach to that vertex, which widens the net for exotic decays. Two signal regions split events by how far the vertex sits from the interaction point. Backgrounds come from fully data-driven estimates, not from simulation alone. No significant excess over background appears in the data, so upper limits are set on several supersymmetry benchmark models.
arxiv-2603-02091:
Anmol Kabra, Yilun Yin, Albert Gong, and colleagues test a cheap training idea in this 2026 paper. Language models get better at hard reasoning when trained with rewards on checked tasks. Good checked tasks are scarce, costly, or scored by slow, flawed judges. The team asks if fake, rule-made tasks can teach real skill instead.

Their fake tasks use made-up facts, so no real knowledge can leak in. Still, models trained on them scored far better on real multi-step questions. Gains held across hard and easy questions alike. The authors argue the fake tasks teach models to combine facts step by step. If so, cheap fake data could scale reasoning training widely.
arxiv-2603-02391:
Dongming Mei, Kunming Dong, Narayan Budhathoki, and colleagues model charge gain inside germanium detectors in this 2026 paper. Cold germanium crystals detect faint signals for physics experiments. Gain inside the crystal can boost charge and lower the threshold for detection. Safe use needs a forecast of the field strength where runaway gain starts.

Their framework bridges a simple upper bound with a fuller model of impact ionization. The fuller model adds how scattering changes with energy, plus rare fast carriers. Closed-form formulas give design-ready estimates at two standard cold temperatures. A workflow maps measured mobility and gain curves to bias targets, with error bands. Realistic transport lowers the critical field versus the simple bound. The gap between the two cold operating points also grows.
arxiv-2603-02591:
Rafi Hassan Chowdhury, Naimul Haque, and Kaniz Fatiha test image augmentation for Bengali handwriting recognition in this 2026 paper. Bengali is a resource-limited language with small labeled data sets. Small data invites overfitting, where models memorize rather than generalize. Augmentation artificially expands training images to fight that risk.

Five techniques were tested, alone and in combination, on a lightweight vision transformer. Methods included contrast enhancement, random rotation, random affine warps, and color jitter. Two Bengali character data sets anchored the evaluation. A pairing of random affine warps with color jitter won on both data sets. Its accuracy beat every other combination and the no-augmentation baseline. The analysis guides data-scarce language projects choosing augmentation recipes.
arxiv-2603-02891:
Peter Horvath, Ilia Shumailov, Lukasz Chmielewski, and colleagues steal neural network secrets by listening to the chip itself. Their 2026 attack, Kraken, targets the Tensor Core units that do most heavy math on modern graphics processors. Earlier side-channel work only reached the older general-purpose cores.

By estimating energy use near the chip, the team extracts model parameters with correlation power analysis tuned to the hardware layout. They also explore leakage from large language models at a distance. The chip's electromagnetic radiation carried readable signals even a meter away, through glass. The results warn that physical emissions, not just software flaws, can expose costly trained models.
arxiv-2603-03291:
Daniel Fein and four colleagues examine the reward models that steer language models toward human preferences. Such models can be gamed: a policy learns to please the scorer rather than do what people actually want. The 2026 study measures bias carefully in five high-quality reward models, including the best currently available.

Known problems persist: longer answers, flattering answers, and overconfident answers still score too well. The team also finds new biases, favoring one model's personal style and favoring answers by their order. Their fix, called mechanistic reward shaping, adjusts the model after training using its own internal signals. It cuts the simpler biases with very little labeled data, keeps overall quality, and carries over to cases outside the tuning set.
arxiv-2603-03891:
Jana Kopfova and Michael Ruderman study a differential equation with hysteresis that sits behind a feedforward control scheme. The equation couples a first-order system to the Krasnoselskii-Pokrovskii operator, a standard model of hysteresis that ignores rate. Such inversion-free control was put forward to cancel hysteresis in driven systems without inverting the model, which matters because it limits precision in devices from piezoelectric actuators to shape memory alloys.

The authors prove existence and uniqueness of solutions, bounded ends under bounded inputs, and global stability, and they also study periodic solutions and how stable they are. The case study is the measured, non-smooth and non-monotone hysteresis of a magnetic shape memory alloy actuator. The analysis is laid out as a series of theorems illustrated by numeric cases, giving the control scheme a firm mathematical footing.
arxiv-2603-03991: Dey and others present SAFE, a two-stage method for weakly supervised patch annotation in diabetic retinopathy screening. Early lesions are subtle and often missed for lack of annotation, while expert labeling is slow and incomplete. SAFE first learns structured discriminative embeddings from expert-labeled patches with a dual-arm network, then extrapolates labels to unannotated regions from spatial and meaning proximity.
arxiv-2603-04091: Warmers and colleagues propose CLIP-guided multi-task regression for plant phenotyping. Learning robust predictors from multi-view plant images is hard because of viewpoint redundancy and appearance shifts. Their level-aware framework jointly predicts plant age and leaf count with one model on CLIP embeddings. It merges rotational views into angle-invariant encodings and conditions features on light text priors encoding viewpoint level. On the GroMo25 benchmark it roughly halves mean age error and cuts leaf-count error substantially versus the baseline, while replacing the dual-model setup.
arxiv-2603-04891: Johan Linåker and the rest of the team study how European public-sector bodies build capacity to adopt, build. collaborate on open source software through support units called Open Source Programme Offices. From interviews with 18 representatives across 16 cases, plus two follow-up focus groups, they distill six distinct archetypes describing each office's structure, responsibilities, and contributions. The archetypes arrive with policy recommendations to help organizations design their own offices, framed as strategic instruments for digital sovereignty, economic growth, and better public services.
arxiv-2603-05191: Zhi-Chao Zhao and team reassess the scalar-induced gravity wave reading of pulsar timing array signals and its primordial black hole overproduction problem. Stretching the method to third-order gravity waves boosts the waves' spectral amplitude, easing the tension. Mixing cosmic microwave background and baryon acoustic swing data, they constrain the energy-density fraction of cosmological gravity waves, then add pulsar timing data for the waves' amplitude and peak rate. The favored region partly relieves the overproduction problem, and the reading survives adding a supermassive black hole binary background.
arxiv-2603-05291: Clemence Grislain and team offer ORCHID, self-training raising hierarchical diffusion policies online. Policies split handling between planner and controller, but coordination needs subgoal spreads. ORCHID filters policy samples by setting feedback, keeping joint successes, distilling them into both modules by supervised learning. Bidirectional co-change follows: the planner grounds subgoals in controller capabilities, while the controller specializes in planner paths. Supervised distillation avoids online hierarchical gradient-based reinforcement learning wobble. On CALVIN, a lightweight ORCHID model outperforms offline methods, including a twice-larger Vision-Language-Action model.
arxiv-2603-05591: Chen and colleagues introduce Thinking with Spatial Code, converting RGB video into explicit 3D representations coherent over time for physical-world question answering. Their spatial encoder parses videos into structured spatial code carrying 3D oriented bounding boxes plus semantic labels, letting language models reason over spatial variables. The encoder unifies 6D object parsing and tracking with geometric prediction, and language models are fine-tuned with reinforcement learning under a spatial rubric reward. On VSI-Bench, the model beats proprietary vision-language models, setting a new best.
arxiv-2603-05691: Wu and colleagues show weak-to-strong generalization improves scaling laws in random feature ridge regression. A strong student trained on imperfect teacher labels can outperform that teacher. Their main contribution derives a deterministic equivalent for the student's excess test error under teacher labels. Through it, they identify regimes where the student's scaling law improves on the teacher's, in bias-dominated and variance-dominated settings. Remarkably, the student may reach minimax optimal rates regardless of the teacher's scaling law, even when teacher error does not decay with sample size.
arxiv-2603-06091: Buonocore, Nason, Rottoli, Torrielli ask whether other legal re-summing rules for thrust in e-plus-minus wipeout can shift forecasts a lot. Fixed-order QCD forecasts near the two-jet limit use re-summing, yet matching rules differ through sub-leading terms. The authors compare paired-space re-summing against direct-space re-summing in the thrust value. At the double-log level, flipping the Laplace change yields meeting terms. From leading-log score the Landau pole makes the spread long-run, and setup biases exceed quoted doubts.
arxiv-2603-06391: Avrachenkov, Gregoris, and Litvak frame the Red Light Green Light algorithm as an optimization problem that computes steady distributions of large Markov chains. This view shows how the algorithm behaves step by step and proves exponential convergence for one class of chains. It gives useful scheduling plans that speed it up in practice for large chains.
arxiv-2603-06591: Peng and team trace how the position-zero attention sink in causal large language models arises from internal computation, finding a two-block subnet they term the P0-Sink Circuit. The circuit arises purely from causal focus patterns, with no semantic content required. From-scratch pre-training tests validate two parameter-free methods speeding sink formation, with earlier growth helping pre-training and downstream performance. Both methods beat the Transformer baseline and achieve Gated-Focus-comparable scores across wide settings.
arxiv-2603-07091: Vo and colleagues test how deep small language models reason about software architecture. They benchmark ten models under 7 billion parameters on generating Architectural Decision Records, scoring technical compliance and semantic diversity. Models above 3 billion parameters show robust zero-shot skill, while smaller models gain most from fine-tuning on one score. The results map where small models already cope and where they still fall short.
arxiv-2603-07491: Lee studies which regularity properties survive when one C-star algebra maps into another by a tracially sequentially-split order-zero homomorphism. Under suitable assumptions on either algebra, tracial m-comparison, tracial m-almost divisibility and tracial nuclear dimension below m all pass from the target algebra back to the source. The paper thus extends permanence results for dimension-type properties of simple unital C-star algebras.
arxiv-2603-07691: Xiao, Wang and Chen propose RoboPCA, pose-first affordance learning for robot handling from human demonstrations. Existing methods locate contact regions but leave poses to separate guessing, causing failures when regions and poses disagree. RoboPCA predicts contact regions and poses together, matched to the task, from instructions. A Human2Afford pipeline rebuilds 3D scene information and infers skill labels from demos, and the system beats baselines across images, simulation and real robots.
arxiv-2603-07891: Shen and colleagues tackle multi-agent path finding, where many agents need routes that never collide. Existing guidance paths steer LaCAM*, the leading anytime solver, but they rely on costly Frank-Wolfe optimization run before search and stay fixed once set. The authors instead build a light traffic map on the fly while LaCAM* searches, steering it away from crowded spots as conditions change. Tests on two MAPF variants show better routes than the best guidance-path methods.
arxiv-2603-08191: Sornette and colleagues show a non-normal route to chaos that breaks the usual story. Chaos is usually tied to local growth, with Jacobian eigenvalues set to exceed unity on the attractor. In dimensions above 1, that view fails: for non-normal cases, pointwise readings can suggest contraction throughout, while skewed eigenvectors still allow brief amplification. The authors build four low-dimensional maps showing this effect: partition-reinjected, phase-prescribed, feedback-driven, and affine-reinjected forms.
arxiv-2603-08391: Frey and colleagues ask if transformers think harder, know more, or do both. Chain-of-thought prompting lets models reason by stating steps in words. Looped transformers refine representations, saving parameters but losing storage, since layers get their own weights. Models use adaptive per-layer looping, where each block learns when to stop, plus memory banks. Looping helps math reasoning most, memory banks restore commonsense performance, and they beat a FLOPs-matched baseline with triple layers on benchmarks. Early layers loop little and use memory, while later do more.
arxiv-2603-09091: Jingxu Bai and colleagues review recent work on ultralong-range Rydberg molecules, bound states built from one or more Rydberg atoms. Such molecules are huge in size, hold rich rovibrational level patterns, carry fixed electric dipole moments, and react strongly to outside fields. The review sorts them into three kinds by how they bind: ground-Rydberg, Rydberg-Rydberg, and ion-Rydberg pairs. It covers how they form, their energy curves, lab sightings, and spectra, then looks at what may come next.
arxiv-2603-09291: Fuzhen Jiang and colleagues propose DenoiseSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that rebuilds 3D scenes from noisy multi-view images. Most pipelines expect clean inputs and fall apart when real noise and artifacts appear. They build a noisy-clean benchmark on RE10K with four noise types at controlled strengths. It trains end-to-end with clean 2D renderings alone as the training signal and no 3D ground truth, and beats both a vanilla baseline and a strong two-stage rival.
arxiv-2603-09491: Pedro Conceição computes the homotopy type of a moment-angle complex built over the face poset for injective word complexes. Topology increasingly informs the study of directed graphs, from pure combinatorics to connectome data. The answer is fixed by the h-vector of these complexes, a tight link between the two fields. Conceição also builds a related fibration of polyhedral products over ordered simplicial complexes.
arxiv-2603-10491: Fazilah Nothlawala and co-authors show entanglement among three parties by way of topology, using spin-skyrmion states. The shape of one photon is steered from afar through the spin of its partner. They add a new tool, a topological Bloch sphere, which holds both the entanglement and the topology of the state. With it they made the first quantum multiskyrmions, several small skyrmions in one structure, like their magnetic kin. Moving across the sphere showed motion driven by entanglement, a path toward sensing and multilevel encoding.
arxiv-2603-10691: Venelin P Pavlov and co-authors ask whether local observables alone can witness the breaking of ergodicity in quantum many-body systems. Most ergodicity measures use global quantities like level statistics, so a subsystem-level probe would be valuable. They take two random matrix theory predictions as the ergodic benchmark: how quantum Fisher information evolves, and a fluctuation-dissipation relation. Both are tested across three routes to non-ergodic behavior: integrability, many-body localization, and quantum many-body scars. The predicted behavior can flag the transition from local measurements alone.
arxiv-2603-10991: Stefan Böhringer proposes ForwardFlow, a frequentist answer to simulation-only inference. It replaces the Bayesian normalizing-flow machinery with a single summary network. Trained on simulated datasets, the network learns a summary statistic and maps it to the parameter. This solves the inverse problem. Collapsing layers shrink each dataset to its summary. Tests show finite-sample exactness and that the method stays robust with flawed data. They also show it can learn algorithms on its own. An EM algorithm for genetic data is learned without being programmed in.
arxiv-2603-11191: Zhuoli Ding, Ruben Verresen, and Zoe Yan create exact quantum many-body scars, rare nonthermal states that keep reviving inside an otherwise chaotic system, using kinetic frustration as the engine. Destructive interference among quantum paths builds the scars, and the simple construction fits known platforms from cold-atom simulators to Rydberg tweezer arrays, with lifetimes tunable by knobs that can be reached. A second scar in a Fermi-Hubbard model arises from fermionic exchange statistics. A heuristic based on eigenstate energy distributions helps guess and improve scar lifetimes.
arxiv-2603-11391: Nicholas Pulsone, Roee Shraga, and Gregory Goren match records across e-commerce domains. Labels for the target domain are scarce, but labeled data from other domains sits available. Fine-tuned language models lead entity matching yet hunger for expensive labels. Their BEACON framework spends a limited labeling budget wisely. Embeddings of candidate record pairs guide which out-of-domain examples to select. This happens under thin in-domain supervision, in a distribution-aware design. It beats state-of-the-art methods across budgets on domain-partitioned benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-11491: Booth and Vraciu link a three-variable algebra question to a two-variable one. The question is when monomial almost complete intersections in three variables hold the weak Lefschetz property. Their path runs through explicit formulas for one colon ideal's generators. With those generators, they build a matrix whose determinant controls failure of the property for level algebras. The determinant is a single polynomial, and its vanishing decides the outcome. In the level case, they also settle a few new cases of a standing conjecture.
arxiv-2603-11591: Pal studies the relaxed Newton method, a one-parameter family that widens the Newton root-finding scheme. Seen as rational maps on the Riemann sphere, these maps show rich global dynamics. Pal first sorts which rational maps can arise this way, using multipliers at their fixed points. For several explicit polynomial classes, the method converges for every parameter value. That luck does not hold in general: for any fixed parameter, some generic cubic breaks it. Pal also pins down when the Julia set is a straight line.
arxiv-2603-11791: Najar studies how neutral and charged particles orbit Kerr, Reissner-Nordström, and Kerr-Newman black holes, using the effective potential with relativistic fixes. He works out the circular orbits and the innermost stable circular orbits, a purely relativistic effect, both on paper and in plots. Charges sharpen the circular orbit radius, he finds. A larger product of particle and hole charge pushes the ISCO radius outward. He also derives the effective potential for the most general spacetime that the no-hair conjecture allows.
arxiv-2603-11891: Tran and co-authors test a cheaper way to predict inverted singlet-triplet gaps, where Hund's rule flips. Such inverted molecules could let OLEDs hit full internal quantum efficiency without heat. Standard predictors of these negative gaps cost too much to run widely. The team benchmarks their one-body perturbation methods, OBMP2 and O2BMP2, on 30 inverted-gap molecules. With the right spin-opposite scaling, O2BMP2 matches the accuracy of ADC(3) and EOM-CCSD. Its cost can fall to fourth-power scaling, suiting wide screening of new materials.
arxiv-2603-11991: Aarab builds BTZSC, a benchmark for zero-shot text classification that needs no task-specific labels. It covers 22 public datasets across sentiment, topic, intent, and emotion tasks. Four model families face off in the tests: embedding models, rerankers, instruction-tuned LLMs, and NLI cross-encoders. Modern rerankers take the top scores, while strong embedding models close much of the gap with the best speed trade-off. NLI cross-encoders level off as they grow, and the full test code is public.
arxiv-2603-12091: Gu, Ignatov, and Timofte search for neural network designs with LLMs in a tight feedback loop. The loop runs on one consumer GPU, with no fine-tuning of the language models. A sliding memory keeps the last five improvement tries, each stored as a problem, a fix, and an outcome. Failed runs count as first-class learning signals here, not waste. One model writes PyTorch code while a second handles diagnostic reasoning. Three frozen models improved sharply on CIFAR tests over long searches.
arxiv-2603-12191: Dadas and co-authors give Polish a long-context encoder model that reads up to 8192 tokens. Decoder-only models dominate recent NLP, yet encoders stay cheap and lean for classification-style tasks. Classic encoders read only short windows, which blocks long documents. Training first adapts positional embeddings, then continues pre-training over all parameters. Smaller compressed variants come from knowledge distillation for tight budgets. Across 25 tasks the model posts the best average among Polish and multilingual rivals, with clear wins on long texts.
arxiv-2603-12391: Asaduzzaman and co-authors simulate the Abelian Higgs model with a hybrid analog-digital protocol on qutrit hardware. Gauge theory studies on near-term machines need resource-light routes. Their pulse-based plan uses the three-level truncation of transmon hardware as a spin-1 map of the model. A gate-based Trotter version of the same two-site model runs for direct comparison. Both track real-time dynamics of field observables akin to electric field operators. Floquet drives, tuned interactions, and decoupling pulses shape the analog-digital runs.
arxiv-2603-13191: Haonan Huang presents QMatSuite, a platform that helps AI agents turn past experiments into lasting expertise. Agents can run many simulations, yet each run alone teaches them little. The platform logs findings with full provenance for later retrieval. Before new work, agents pull prior knowledge back in. Reflection sessions fix wrong findings and merge observations into cross-compound patterns. On a six-step quantum workflow, deviation from literature fell from 47% to 3%, and a new material hit 1%.
arxiv-2603-13391: Yuhong Dai and co-authors introduce WebVR, a benchmark for webpage recreation from videos. Prior web-generation tests use text prompts or still screenshots as input. Videos carry richer signals, like interaction flow, transition timing, and motion continuity. WebVR holds 175 webpages built by a controlled synthesis pipeline, not web crawling. A fine-grained visual rubric, aligned with human judgment, scores the recreated pages on many dimensions. Tests on 19 models showed large gaps in fine style and motion quality.
arxiv-2603-13791: Mukhopadhyay builds DeceptGuard, a system for spotting lies and scheming in large language model agents. It compares three kinds of monitors. One sees only actions and outputs, one also reads the agent's chain of thought, and one also reads hidden model states. Tests use synthetic deceptive and honest agent runs across twelve types of deception. The author reports that monitors with inner signals beat black-box ones, and a mixed ensemble scores 0.934 on held-out tests.
arxiv-2603-13891: Törnberg tests whether large language models bake racial stereotypes into text annotation. The study covers 19 models and over 4 million judgments in two experiments. Names linked to Black people draw more aggressive and gossipy ratings from most models. Asian names draw higher intelligence ratings but lower confidence ratings. The same sentence in African American Vernacular English is judged less professional and more toxic than in standard English. One exception appears in hiring scores, where fine-tuning seems to overcorrect.
arxiv-2603-13991: Wu and Smalyukh simulate nematic liquid crystals with radial basis functions under the Landau-de Gennes model. Grid-based codes struggle with complex shapes, while mesh-free radial basis methods adapt with ease. The authors stress gains in geometric flexibility and compute cost over cubic grids. Tests on liquid crystal and colloid systems recover the key topological and energetic features of equilibrium states. An adaptive node refinement step sharpens the fine structure of singular defects.
arxiv-2603-14091: Antunes and co-authors test FPGA acceleration of neural networks for four space mission tasks on an AMD ZCU104 board. Spacecraft sensors now gather more data than onboard storage and downlinks can handle. Two tool flows are compared: Vitis AI on the built-in DPU and custom Vitis HLS designs. Vitis AI runs up to about 34 times faster than the embedded ARM CPU, and custom designs reach about five-fold gains with wider operator support. Power per inference drops in all four cases.
arxiv-2603-14191: Dectot-Le Monnier de Gouville, Hamdaqa, and Chouchen mine the open YARA rule ecosystem at scale. YARA rules flag malware, yet shared rules vary in quality with little hard data. The study pulls 8.4 million rules from 1,853 GitHub repositories. Static checks score rule quality, and live tests run rules against thousands of malware and clean samples. Ten authors drive 80 percent of rule adoption, and most repositories sit idle for years. Live tests find real noise: false alarms and low recall.
arxiv-2603-14391: Witte and co-authors image alumina laser melt pools in 4D at 25 kilohertz with a new X-ray method. Spinning samples for tomography caps the frame rate, so fast melt and keyhole changes blur out. Their rotation-XMPI setup grabs three angled projections per time step, which frees speed from rotation rate. A self-supervised learning model rebuilds the 4D volume from those views. At the MAX IV source, the method resolves melt-pool shape and keyhole motion at 250 times the prior rate.
arxiv-2603-14491: Zou surveys the fast growth of private credit markets. Assets grew from 158 billion dollars in 2010 to nearly 2 trillion by mid-2024. The survey sorts theory and evidence around four questions. It asks why growth ran so fast and how direct lenders differ from banks. It also asks what returns investors earn and whether the sector risks the wider system. A single framework links monitoring, soft information and contract gaps. Fees eat most fund returns, the evidence suggests.
arxiv-2603-14591: Tranheden and co-authors replace the output head of language models with a lean retrieval design. Growing vocabularies make the dense head a heavy cost. It can hold up to 60% of model parameters and half of inference compute. FlashHead needs no training and treats head scoring as retrieval. Balanced clusters pack the vocabulary into hardware-friendly tensors. Multiprobe scoring checks thousands of clusters at once. A sampling step and selective quantization complete the design, with speedups shown on Llama, Gemma and Qwen models.
arxiv-2603-14691: Marchesi unifies branching transport network theory under one variational principle. Branching shapes in vessels follow a diameter scaling exponent. Wave impedance matching favors an exponent near two. Viscous-metabolic savings favor the cubic Murray value of three. Real arterial trees sit near 2.70, between both pulls. Wall thickness scaling breaks the cubic law and bounds the static optimum near 2.9. A game against the environment then sets a unique saddle point. Porcine coronary data give 2.72, close to the observed mean, Marchesi reports.
arxiv-2603-15191: Ebel and co-authors show that electron speed can tune how light and excitons mix, with no change to the sample. Most setups tune this mixing by reshaping a cavity or the host material. Here, transition radiation in a thin suspended film forms a resonance set by the passing electrons. That resonance mixes with excitons in a layered crystal. Film thickness and electron speed set the gap between the two. Changing the beam energy then sweeps the coupling smoothly. The setup gives a nanoscale test bed for exciton-light studies.
arxiv-2603-15291: Tian sorts out the long-run behavior of weighted residual dynamics tied to a rank-one projection. After a few steps, the process settles onto a fixed active subspace and follows a nonlinear rule there. He fully classifies the case where that space has dimension two. Either a cross direction stays fixed for good, or the coupled part collapses in full. This pins down the limit in that case. He also marks where higher dimensions gain more freedom.
arxiv-2603-15691: Wang argues that vibe coding needs contracts to stay trustworthy. In vibe coding, developers steer AI assistants with plain language prompts. The speed is real, but hidden logic errors slip in often. His VibeContract idea splits intent into explicit task sequences. Each task gets a contract for inputs, outputs, and limits. Developers check the contracts, and links tie tasks to code. Contracts then drive testing, runtime checks, and debugging. An example project shows the workflow in action.
arxiv-2603-15791: Ouyed powers superluminous supernovae with a late energy burst from a quark transition. Hydrogen-poor superluminous events need a strong, lasting energy source. His model lets the neutron star core turn to quark matter weeks later. The shift amplifies the magnetic field and forms a hybrid star. Stored spin energy then pours back into the expanding debris. Two power epochs split by the microphysics delay result. Light and spectra match events like iPTF13ajg and SN2010gx. Double peaks may probe quark matter traits directly.
arxiv-2603-15891: Domingues and Luzum rescale particle spectra to expose shared flow shapes. Heavy-ion spectra carry global scales from count and mean momentum. Stripping those scales leaves a bare shape per event. The shape stays near universal across centrality, system, and energy. Hydrodynamic simulations copy the scaling event by event. The team trains Gaussian-process emulators on the JETSCAPE hybrid model. Bayesian fits then read medium traits from shape alone. Shape data clash with spots favored by older summed measures. Transverse-mass spectra show a twin scaling.
arxiv-2603-15991: Dastgheib and Pourmahdian compare gaze and hand pointing for XR interfaces. Hand input tires users, while gaze input selects what it merely touches. Their web platform runs a multidirectional tapping task. Gaze declutter and hand target widening serve as adaptive aids. Sixty-nine people crossed modality, mode, and pressure factors. Hands beat gaze on speed, errors, and workload scores. Gaze errors were nearly all slips, at 99.2 percent. Hand errors were mostly misses, at 95.7 percent. Only the gaze aid ran clean in this dataset.
arxiv-2603-16091: Huang and Deng repair wrong QA answers by hunting counterevidence at run time. Many factual errors come from commitment, not missing access. Their CounterRefine layer treats the first answer as a testable guess. Answer-shaped queries fetch evidence for and against the draft. A guarded step then keeps or revises the answer. Revisions pass only through strict deterministic validation checks. SimpleQA gains reach 5.8 correct-rate points over one-pass RAG. Only 5.6 percent of outputs change in the full trace. Helpful flips outnumber harmful ones by 180 to 8.
arxiv-2603-16191: The ATLAS Collaboration searches for pairs of top squarks in proton-proton collision data. The events studied have two leptons of opposite charge, b-jets, and large missing momentum. The data combine the full Run 2 set at 13 TeV with early Run 3 data at 13.6 TeV. Machine learning classifiers help split signal from background. No excess over the Standard Model was seen. The team sets limits up to 1060 GeV for top squarks.
arxiv-2603-16391: Melis and Soler weigh ambipolar heating in the energy balance of solar prominences. Prominence threads hold cold, dense plasma in the hot corona. Magnetic dips suspend the plasma against gravity. Since the plasma is partly ionized, ambipolar diffusion can add heat. Their one-dimensional models enforce balance of forces and energy. Each model forms a cold thread, a thin transition zone, and a hot outer region. Thread lengths match observations for realistic settings.
arxiv-2603-16491: Puthenpurakal studies annihilators of local cohomology modules over invariant rings. The rings are fixed points of a group acting on a polynomial ring. The field is finite, with q elements. Dickson polynomials supply key elements inside these rings. His theorem places the first Dickson polynomials inside a radical ideal. The count depends on the module's data and the ring dimension. Several applications follow from the result. One gives a simpler proof of the Landweber-Stong conjecture.
arxiv-2603-16791: Saha and co-authors use automated refactoring to help novice programmers understand code. Their tool, CDDRefactorER, rewrites code under limits drawn from Cognitive-Driven Development. The limits curb control-flow complexity while keeping behavior and structure close to the original. On the MBPP and APPS benchmarks, across two language models, the tool cut refactoring failures by 54 to 71 percent. It also lowered the odds that refactoring raised complexity scores. In a study with novices, function identification rose 31.3 percent and structural readability rose 22.0 percent.
arxiv-2603-16991: Bennett and co-authors simulate the birth of the intracluster medium in a galaxy cluster. Mature clusters hold hot, enriched gas, while high redshift haloes are fed by cold filamentary inflows. Their zoom in simulation follows a cluster progenitor to redshift 2.7, with extra resolution in the halo gas. Between redshifts 4.4 and 2.7, a merger and AGN feedback reshape the gas from the inside out. Cold absorbers are destroyed, and inner gas heats into the X-ray regime. A Lyman-alpha halo stays detectable and turns more spherical.
arxiv-2603-17091: Carvalho and Pessil link quantization of measures with the metric mean dimension of dynamical systems. This quantity gauges complexity when entropy is not finite. They define a mean quantization dimension for invariant measures. They prove a variational principle: the metric mean dimension of a system equals the maximum such value over all of them. This also allows limits and suprema to be swapped in the Lindenstrauss-Tsukamoto results. The Katok and Shapira entropies share this trait, and a best case always exists.
arxiv-2603-17191: Kearney and co-authors present TAP-GPT, a tabular language model framework for few shot Alzheimer's disease prediction. Alzheimer's diagnosis uses tabular biomarker data that are often small and incomplete, where deep models struggle. Their system adapts TableGPT2 with tabular prompts and fine tuning for classification. They test it on four ADNI derived datasets, covering fluid biomarkers and MRI and PET imaging. TAP-GPT beat its backbone models and classical baselines in the few shot setting. It stayed stable under missing data without imputation.
arxiv-2603-17291: Bartl and Mendelson prove a sharp bound on the structure of marginals of Gaussian ensembles in high dimensions. They study random maps built from independent standard Gaussian vectors. For any set of directions on the sphere, they show the sorted entries of the mapped vector stay close to the matching Gaussian quantiles. The gap scales with the set's Gaussian width plus a log factor, over root N. The bound is sharp up to a log factor. The same pattern holds for many other random vectors.
arxiv-2603-17791: Mueller sizes up gluon occupancies in the saturation regime of nuclear matter. He asks how full gluon states get at momenta below the saturation scale. Without Sudakov effects, occupancies could grow without bound, he finds. Sudakov corrections cap them at a set power of one over the coupling. Running and fixed coupling runs give the same cap. Coherent and inelastic gluon distributions also match inside the saturated zone.
arxiv-2603-18891: Luo and co-authors present PromptHub for visual in-context learning with many prompts. Vision models learn tasks by copying pixel demonstrations. Fusing several prompts helps, but patch-wise fusion wastes context cues. PromptHub fuses with locality awareness, using spatial priors to gather richer context. Concentration, alignment, and prediction goals guide training together. Data augmentation strengthens the supervision signal further. Tests on three core vision tasks show PromptHub ahead of prior fusion methods. Gains hold across out-of-distribution sets and varied retrieval setups, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-19091: Jiang and co-authors argue that spectral graph networks for node labeling are neither spectral nor better. Such networks claim to filter graph signals in a frequency-like domain. The team names two flaws in that claim. Graph bases lack key traits of a true Fourier basis. High-degree polynomials can fit any response exactly, which voids the usual story. They prove that pass behavior in a common model stems from message passing, not spectral steps. Two directed models owe their scores to slips that turn them into message passers.
arxiv-2603-19491: Wilson studies congruences for partitions whose odd parts may come in k colours. Even parts are limited to at most one colour in this family. Work by Hirschorn and Sellers showed rich congruence patterns for these partitions. Wilson focuses on congruences that grow into infinite families modulo 3. The paper closes with open questions meant to guide further work on these partitions.
arxiv-2603-19591: Huang and co-authors present FuXi-ONS, a machine learning system that forecasts the global ocean as an ensemble. It gives short forecasts on a one degree grid for up to a year ahead. It tracks sea surface heat and height, plus heat, salt, and currents below the surface. The system learns how to perturb its runs. A module that reads the air above the sea keeps long runs stable. It beats single run baselines and runs far faster than standard systems.
arxiv-2603-19691: Barman and Mahatab derive an asymptotic formula for regular partitions counted with a shift. A partition is t-regular when no part is divisible by t. They count partitions that avoid divisibility by t plus one. Hagis found a formula for fixed t in 1971 with the circle method. Using the saddle point method, the authors extend it to wider ranges of t. Their version carries explicit error bounds. An application estimates zeros in the character table of the symmetric group.
arxiv-2603-19791: Fawaz and co-authors build text personas that mimic how real users make privacy choices. Such simulation helps align autonomous agents with user intent. It also makes large privacy studies cheaper to run. Older approaches feed language models raw histories or demographic traits. They trade off accuracy, readability, token cost, and coverage. The Narriva approach grounds each persona in past privacy decisions. It compresses those records into short summaries shaped by privacy theory. Across five datasets, accuracy reached up to 87 percent. Prompt token use fell by 80 to 95 percent.
arxiv-2603-19891: Azizi, Sarac, and Sundu predict masses for fully heavy pentaquarks, exotic states made only of charm and bottom quarks. They study states with three charm and two bottom quarks, and the reverse mix. Their tool is the QCD sum rule method, tried with three kinds of interpolating currents. For the three-charm states they predict masses near 14,277 to 14,479 MeV. For the three-bottom states the range is near 17,203 to 17,459 MeV. They also report coupling constants for each state.
arxiv-2603-20291: Paul and co-authors build a math framework for timing jitter in vehicle-to-vehicle links. Jitter arises as interference and vehicle spacing change over time. They define a limit-state marker that tracks system health through warning, failure, and recovery stages. They also define how much jitter the link can withstand and how load erodes it. Adaptive power control and link diversity pull the marker back within safe bounds. Their scheme cut average risk exposure about threefold versus fixed allocation.
arxiv-2603-20591: Ampudia and co-authors study how well a future collider could pin down the Higgs self coupling. Their concept pairs an X-ray free electron laser with a Compton photon collider. They use the channel where two Higgs bosons decay to bottom quarks. The run energy is 380 GeV in the photon system. An ensemble of boosted decision trees sorts signal from background. A genetic algorithm merges the outputs. They project a precision of 7 to 12 percent.
arxiv-2603-20791: Nguyen and co-authors learn Markov boundaries with neural autoregressive flows. A Markov boundary is the smallest variable set that predicts a target best. Past learning methods lean on nonparametric estimates and heuristic search. Their framework scores candidate sets with conditional entropy from information theory. A masked autoregressive network captures complex dependencies in the data. A greedy search then runs in polynomial time with analytic support. Starting graph search from learned boundaries also speeds causal discovery. Tests on real and synthetic data beat prior methods.
arxiv-2603-20891: Adrian and co-authors present a framework that learns data assimilation pieces end to end. Data assimilation estimates a system's state from partial, noisy observations. Good results depend on costly tuning and an accurate dynamics model. Their method learns the state, the dynamics, and filter settings at once, using a theory based loss. They test it on systems from aerospace, weather science, and biology. They also show known methods can be learned or tuned inside the framework, and give practical setup guidance.
arxiv-2603-20991: Basu and co-authors measure how compression errors move through transformer layers. Compressing weights makes large language models cheaper to run, but each layer adds error. They define a ratio, rho, of output error to input error at each layer. Below one, a layer absorbs error; above one, it grows. On six transformers, later rho values predict how much representations drift. This explains why early layer compression hurts more. They also rank layers for removal with two forward passes, beating a known method at lower perplexity.
arxiv-2603-21091: Borkar extends stochastic approximation theory to settings that are both non-Markovian and non-ergodic. Stochastic approximation studies iterative updates driven by random noise. His earlier work covered non-Markovian driving processes. Here the driving process also fails to be ergodic, so long run averages need not settle. He builds an analytic framework for this harder case. He then applies it to transformer based learning. The framework speaks to the attention mechanism and to continual learning, both of which depend on the full past in principle.
arxiv-2603-21191: Islamov and co-authors study batch size in stochastic conditional gradient methods. They work under a Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz condition and focus on momentum based methods such as Scion. Their analysis ties stepsize, batch size, and noise together. Larger batches first improve accuracy, then the gains saturate. The theory predicts the best stepsize and matches large scale training practice. They propose a schedule that grows batch size during training while keeping convergence guarantees. NanoGPT tests fit the predictions.
arxiv-2603-21291: Binder and co-authors propose closed-form conditional diffusion models for data assimilation. Diffusion models learn a score function from data and generate samples by reversing a noise process. Instead of training a neural network for the score, they use its analytic form. Kernel density estimation models the joint distribution of states and measurements. The method works in black-box settings, with no explicit model of the system or its sensors. On Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 problems, it beats ensemble Kalman and particle filters at small to moderate ensemble sizes.
arxiv-2603-21991: Pérez-Corral and co-authors add a learnable sharpness knob to GELU, easing the path from smooth networks to ReLU ones. Many deployment and compression tools expect ReLU-style piecewise linear models. Their lambda-GELU scales the input inside the Gaussian curve, and a larger lambda makes the gate act more like ReLU. Learning lambda proved unstable with naive updates, so they add a constrained form and an optimizer-aware rule. Across MLPs, CNNs, and Transformers, layerwise hardness profiles emerged. A hardening step then swaps in ReLUs.
arxiv-2603-22291: Sharma and co-authors grade language model answers to sexual and reproductive health questions in Nepali. People ask such questions in private chats to avoid judgment. Most grading schemes check accuracy alone. The team builds LEAF, a framework that scores accuracy, language, usability, and safety. Experts then grade answers to 14,000 real queries from over 9,000 users. Only about 35 percent of answers count as proper under LEAF. The rest show gaps in accuracy, fit, or safety. ChatGPT versions differ more in usability and safety than in accuracy.
