Faint distant populations in the bulge, halo, and satellites still carry recoverable chemistry, but standard pipelines grow imprecise or skip them. Training on low- and high-quality spectral twins of the same stars, the Vision Transformer rebuilds clean flux and predicts parameters with calibrated uncertainty. Label scatter fell for faint visits, with residual scatter of about 0.06 dex in surface gravity, and age precision improved for APOKASC giants.
arxiv-2604-26791: Roux and nine colleagues report chip-to-chip sharing of path-encoded entanglement over 80 kilometres between integrated silicon chips. Photon pairs from natural four-wave mixing in spiral waveguides travel a dual-core, steady fiber link. After sharing, Bell match reaches nearly 86 percent. With BBM92 on the same source, key rate reaches about two bits per second in the ideal regime. This marks silicon chips as viable for entanglement-based quantum key distribution.
arxiv-2604-26891: Kumar introduces a mod-n covering method for stable systolic inequalities, bounds on the shortest essential surfaces in a manifold. Prescribing a cohomology class mod n forces a cup product or index to stay nonzero, and a short integral lift yields the bound. The method sharpens the stable two-systolic bound for S2 x S2 to 2, holding for oriented four-manifolds with second Betti number 2. With a cowaist inequality it gives the sharp bound for odd complex projective spaces and an order m log m bound for sphere products.
arxiv-2604-27091: The CMS team reports the first top quark pair cross section in lead-lead collisions at over 5 TeV per nucleon pair, from 2023 data. The cross section is 3.42 microbarns in dilepton states, fitted with a multivariate discriminator over lepton kinematics and bottom-quark jet counts. The result matches perturbative QCD at next-to-next-to-leading order with nuclear parton distributions. Drell-Yan output and the top-pair to Drell-Yan ratio match predictions. All three cover central and semicentral collisions, probing top production versus impact parameter for the first time.
arxiv-2604-27191: Alrawkan and three colleagues introduce a neural-network approach to picking variables in linear regression. The task is choosing which predictors to keep in a model. Older routes add or drop variables step by step. Others penalize weak coefficients, as in LASSO and Elastic Net. Here a neural net learns which variables matter from ordinary least squares estimates. A simulation study checks how accurate it is across sample sizes and variances.
arxiv-2604-27291: MacMahon gives a shape-based test on certain closed subsets of the Riemann sphere. It implies that their hyperbolic convex hulls in 3-space have infinite volume. As a result, he describes sets in the Riemann sphere whose hulls have infinite volume. That answers a question of Danny Calegari. He further gives a geometric account of planar self-similar sets whose hyperbolic convex hulls have infinite volume. Sphere geometry thus links directly to hull size in three dimensions.
arxiv-2604-27391: Nesterov proves a big monodromy theorem for cyclic coverings of the projective line with Fp coefficients. The result generalizes earlier work by Achter and Pries, which covered only coverings of degree two and three. Instead of stretching their methods, he borrows the argument behind the matching integral-cohomology theorem. He plans to apply the theorem in later work to build infinitely many Galois extensions of the rationals. Those extensions carry PSL and PSU groups, with q free to be any prime power, however large.
arxiv-2604-27791: Don van den Bergh and three colleagues present singular distribution mixtures for Bayesian variable selection, holding rival models in one space. The formulation reproduces the spike-and-slab reading and shares the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance odds of reversible jump Monte Carlo. On a ten-predictor benchmark, both methods recover inclusion odds matching enumeration, while mixtures achieve comparable sample size per second. They show the approach in a sleep-and-memory regression and in factor selection for a partial credit model.
arxiv-2604-27891: Dennis and four colleagues ask whether packing a full procedure into the system prompt can beat outside agent orchestration on set tasks. They run 200 chats per setup across travel booking, Zoom support, and insurance claims, judged on five quality checks. The in-context route fails far less: travel fails hit 24 percent under orchestration versus 11.5 percent in context, Zoom 9 percent versus under 1 percent, and insurance 17 percent versus 5 percent. The authors argue that newer models no longer need an outside orchestrator for chats that follow a set procedure.
arxiv-2605-00091:
Achilleas Lazarides studies how kinetic constraints slow the dynamics of quantum many-body systems, in a modified version of the quantum East model. Local constraints like the East model's can produce sluggish motion or complete many-body localization. His modification borrows from random matrix theory: the connections between states in Fock space are randomized, making the model nonlocal in real space, while the organization into neighboring magnetization sectors is preserved.

Even with locality removed, he finds a transition between two distinct phases, one delocalized and one localized. What matters is the structure of the graph in Fock space, the abstract space of configurations. Geometric locality of spin flips is not the essential ingredient. Where the system lives matters less than how its states are wired together.
arxiv-2605-00191:
Murilo Coelho and 5 co-authors ask what makes a good leader in software work, as described by the people who do the job. They gathered 116 articles written by practitioners on the Dev.to community site. Each article was screened and coded for the leadership habits it praised or warned against.

The coding yielded 103 distinct practices, grouped into five areas covering people, process, growth, communication, and strategy. Praised habits center on people skills, delegation, and management craft. Micromanagement and poor communication top the warned-against list. The authors arrange all the practices into a single map. They conclude that software leadership rests more on managing people well than on technical skill alone.
arxiv-2605-00391:
Nayyer Raza and 7 co-authors train a neural network to spot, within moments, whether a gravitational-wave candidate involves the lower mass gap. That gap, between the heaviest neutron stars and the lightest black holes, is poorly mapped by telescope observations. Wave detections suggest it is not empty, and knowing quickly whether a merger sits there guides telescopes hunting for a visible counterpart.

Their model outputs two probabilities at once: that a component lies in the gap, and that the merger involves a neutron star. It infers much of what it needs from the source's chirp mass, calling high-mass mergers correctly. Low-mass systems trip it up, since telling them apart needs the mass ratio as well. Tested on real candidates from the latest observing run, its average errors stayed in the single digits, and the authors sketch how to sharpen it further.
arxiv-2605-00591:
Jiayu Li and 4 co-authors make prompt tuning of vision-language models robust to wrong labels in the training data. Models like CLIP already generalize well before any tuning, and their starting point is nearly optimal. Mislabeled examples, though, produce outsized gradient updates that can overwhelm that good start. The authors argue adaptation should be inherently conservative, especially against extreme updates from noisy samples.

Their method applies a double softmax normalization during tuning, with no hyperparameters to set. The double normalization creates a self-adaptive saturation zone: gradients from high-error, likely mislabeled samples are squashed, while informative updates pass through. In effect, gradient vanishing, usually a training nuisance, becomes a principled noise filter. Theory and experiments support the mechanism, and across noisy benchmarks the simple drop-in design beat more complex rivals built around handcrafted settings.
arxiv-2605-00891:
Hao Wang and six co-authors introduce X2SAM, a unified model that brings language-guided segmentation to both images and videos. Multimodal language models understand images at a broad level, but pixel-level perception lags. Foundation segmenters make high-quality masks yet cannot interpret complex conversational instructions, and earlier language segmenters usually handled only images or only videos, with limited prompt types.

X2SAM couples a language model with a Mask Memory module that stores guided vision features for consistent masks over time. One formulation supports generic, open-vocabulary, referring, reasoning, interactive, and grounded tasks for both media. A new video benchmark tests segmentation from interactive visual prompts. Joint training keeps strong segmentation while preserving general chat ability.
arxiv-2605-00991:
Shikhar Mittal, Prakhar Bansal, Harry Bevins, and Saurabh Singh use SARAS3 radio data to test Coulomb-like interacting dark matter through the cosmic dawn 21-cm signal. That signal can probe interactions between dark matter and ordinary gas. Earlier analyses focused mainly on gas cooling. The authors model the interaction self-consistently, including both extra cooling and suppression of structure formation, which delays early star formation and weakens early radiation backgrounds.

A joint Bayesian fit of a global signal model and a flexible foreground model finds signal parameters weakly constrained after foregrounds are accounted for. The non-detection still disfavors deep absorption features in the observed band. Comparing interacting and standard cold dark matter gives no statistically significant preference for the interacting case, though a meaningful upper bound on signal amplitude results.
arxiv-2605-01191:
Wenhao Li and eight co-authors introduce Sentinel-VLA, a vision-language-action model for robot manipulation with active status monitoring and error recovery. Such models bring broad world knowledge and generalization to embodied tasks, but they still struggle with limited reasoning, lack of status checks, and difficulty self-correcting during execution. A guard module watches real-time run status continuously.

Dynamic thinking or fix-up planning is triggered only when needed, such as at initial planning or after an error is detected, which keeps computation down. All training data across many tasks is generated and annotated automatically. A self-evolving continual learning method identifies capability boundaries and collects expansion data. An orthogonal adapter limits forgetting. Real-world tests show a large success gain over a leading baseline.
arxiv-2605-01391:
Alejandro Aparcedo and seven co-authors introduce VISTA, a benchmark for testing how well vision-language models follow who does what in video. Older tests lean on single-action clips, closed lists of traits, and narrow types of things, so they miss messy real scenes with many actors.

VISTA breaks each clip into entities, their actions, and the relations between them, which allows checks along spatial, temporal, and relational lines. It merges several data sets into one interaction-based scheme and holds about 12,000 curated video-question pairs of varied scene types and difficulty. The team runs 11 leading models through it and maps where each one fails. The fine breakdown shows biases and weak spots that a single score would hide, giving builders a clearer guide for design and training.
arxiv-2605-01791:
Ruiheng Geng and eight co-authors tune a ceramic that turns small temperature swings into electric charge, hunting the sweet spot between two kinds of phase change. Sharp first-order changes give a big pyroelectric kick but wear poorly; smooth second-order changes reverse cleanly but pay less. Which serves low-grade heat harvesting better was unsettled.

By sliding strontium into barium titanate, the team walk the material across that boundary and find the mechanism flips in a narrow band of compositions. One blend there hits peak lattice compatibility: leakage current drops by over a hundredfold while the polarization response stays strong. A multilayer device built from it delivers steady current near hot-water temperatures. It gives a solid energy per cycle at a few percent efficiency. It also survives ten thousand full cycles with no bias field or recharging. Transitional blends, they argue, balance yield and durability best.
arxiv-2605-01991:
Vishnu Teja Kunde, Jean-Francois Chamberland, Krishna Narayanan, and Jamison Ebert study sending text in real time by using a language model to predict the next symbol and then code it. Good prediction allows compression near the theoretical limit. When text arrives at a fixed pace and coded bits leave at a fixed rate, a queue forms and delay depends on code length and coder speed.

They compare Shannon, Huffman, arithmetic, rANS, and gzip coding under that setup. Their analysis splits delay from the coder itself from delay due to limited hardware, which will shrink over time. Huffman coding emerges as the practical choice for channels with extra capacity, balancing compression and delay well.
arxiv-2605-02591:
Wentao Zhang and three co-authors propose a new activation function for neural networks, built from Bernstein polynomials. Activation functions shape how networks learn. Piecewise linear ones are fast but have a kink at zero that can unsettle training, while smooth ones often rely on costly math operations. The authors aim to keep speed and gain smoothness at once.

Their function, called BerLU, uses a polynomial patch to create a smooth quadratic bridge in an otherwise linear shape. Theory shows the result is continuously differentiable and cannot stretch inputs, which supports stable gradients and guards against explosion. Tests across vision transformer and convolutional networks are reported in the paper. The broader claim is that constructive approximation, an old branch of math, is a practical design tool for network parts.
arxiv-2605-02691:
Yegor Bugayenko, Maxim Trunnikov, and Vladimir Zakharov present a compile-time optimizer for Java stream pipelines. The Stream API makes data code concise, but pipelines create many short-lived intermediate objects, which costs speed. Functional languages fix this with stream fusion, which merges steps at compile time so intermediates never form.

An earlier Java tool unrolled streams into plain loops, but it was sensitive to how lambda expressions use outside objects, and it restricted streams held in variables. The new optimizer takes a different route: it merges consecutive map and filter steps into a single mapMulti call, a feature available since Java 16. On nine benchmarks it was faster in two cases and comparable in most others. The team also applied it to Apache Kafka's bytecode.
arxiv-2605-02791:
Alessandro Scagliotti and Thomas M. Surowiec give a full mathematical treatment of risk-averse control for ensembles of systems under random inputs. In ensemble control, one fixed control must be chosen before the randomness plays out, and it must serve the whole family at once. Uses range from quantum control to training neural differential equations. The standard approach averages the goal over the randomness, which performs well on average but ignores bad outliers.

Working with systems whose dynamics are affine in the control, the authors secure the continuity needed to prove optimal solutions exist. The core result characterizes the map from control to state: its continuity between weak and strong senses, its smoothness, and the same traits for its derivative. That regularity then supports first-order conditions for risk-averse optima.
arxiv-2605-03091:
Shubham Harkare, Arvind Yogesh Suresh Babu, and Yash Kulkarni try to stop sentiment models from leaning on domain-only clues when they move to new text sources. Transformer models score well at home but drop sharply abroad, likely because they trust tokens tied to one domain.

Their Attribution-Guided Masking method spots highly attributed suspect tokens during fine-tuning and penalizes reliance on them, with an optional contrastive term and no target labels needed. In strict zero-shot tests across four domains, it stayed competitive with five strong baselines on the hardest transfer and showed which tokens drove the gap.
arxiv-2605-03491:
Adithya Mohan, Xujun Xie, Venkatesh Thirugnana Sambandham, and Torsten Schön evaluate self-driving policies under attack. They use real intersection data instead of pure simulation. Virtual testing misses structural and oversight effects in real recordings. Those effects shape how robust a policy really is.

Within a controlled data contract, they compare three approaches. The approaches are plain behavior cloning, transformer-based cloning with object tokens, and adversarial imitation learning. Nominal errors were similarly tiny. Yet robustness profiles split sharply by architecture and state design. Gradient attacks at inference pushed final position errors up to about eight meters. The work gives teams a clear way to test such systems before they go on the road.
arxiv-2605-03591:
Surya Jayakumar and Indrakshi Dey build a detector for faults and attacks in industrial Internet of Things networks, where wireless links are harsh and labeled examples of anomalies are scarce. Their method, Graph WPT+HOS, needs no labeled anomalies. It fuses three views of the same network data into one feature set.

A graph Fourier transform catches spatial inconsistency, a wavelet packet transform tracks brief time-frequency changes, and higher-order statistics reveal non-Gaussian shapes. Scores come from a Mahalanobis distance, converted to alarms by a one-sided CUSUM rule. Against six baselines under Rayleigh fading and domain shifts, the detector earned the best ROC and precision-recall scores and faster detection.
arxiv-2605-03791:
Antoine Ablondi formulates and solves an affine invariant version of the Minkowski problem. The classical problem asks: given a finite measure on the unit sphere, find a compact convex set whose area measure is exactly that measure. Earlier work solved an analogue for convex sets in Minkowski space invariant under certain affine deformations, which also settled the problem in some flat Lorentzian spacetimes.

Ablondi considers convex domains of oriented affine space invariant under affine transformation groups built from discrete subgroups dividing a convex cone. He proves these domains satisfy a local Steiner formula, which lets him define natural area measures and the affine invariant Minkowski problem. He then solves it by a variational method using convexity of a covolume functional, and interprets the results in affine spacetimes.
arxiv-2605-04191:
Amir Rafe and Subasish Das tackle a problem in survey research: public views on artificial intelligence are ranked answers, and different groups of people link those answers in different ways. A single diagram of links, shared by everyone, can hide that split.

Their method first lets the data suggest how many groups may exist, then fits a separate sparse link diagram for each group. On a 2024 Pew survey of nearly five thousand adults, a five-group model cut held-out prediction error by about a quarter compared with one shared diagram for all respondents.
arxiv-2605-04491:
Priya Kaushik and three co-authors independently evaluate the chat moderation system on Roblox, a gaming platform used daily by hundreds of millions, many of them children. Abusive users can use real-time chat to make first contact with potential victims, so the automated filters carry real safety weight.

The team collected about two million chat messages from four games across age groups, following ethical and legal norms and the platform's terms. Combining a hand-labelled sample with large-scale analysis, they study which unsafe messages slip through the filters and how policy-breaking users evade them. Their findings give an outside check on a system that had not been independently tested.
arxiv-2605-04591:
Ö. H. Yıldız, H. Bakış, and B. Özkardeş present a full photometric and spectroscopic study of EM Boo, a triple star system whose low-mass components orbit without touching. The light of three stars blends into one spectrum, making the faintest member especially hard to characterise.

For the first time, the authors separate the third star's spectrum from the combined light using a disentangling code, then generate synthetic spectra to read off each star's atmospheric properties. The third star's hydrogen line depth points to a temperature near seven thousand kelvin. Combining radial velocity and light curves, and comparing with stellar evolution models, they derive the system's physical parameters and evolutionary state.
arxiv-2605-04791:
Pietro Bonazzi and six co-authors release an open benchmark for recognising hand gestures from a smartwatch, filling a surprising gap given how widely smartwatches are worn. The data set synchronises motion sensing with a physiological signal, photoplethysmography, from a commercial watch.

It holds more than ten hours of recordings from fifty participants performing fifty-nine labelled gesture sequences, with a subject-independent evaluation protocol so models are tested on people they never saw in training. The authors add two new methods, a mixture-of-experts model and a low-rank adaptation for watch foundation models. Notably, the physiological signal alone added a substantial boost to recognition accuracy for fine gestures.
arxiv-2605-05091:
Hanbo Xie and three co-authors test whether asking people to think aloud improves the automated discovery of cognitive models from their choices. Models built from behaviour alone are often under-determined, meaning several different mechanisms fit the same actions. Spoken reasoning traces add a process-level constraint that pure choice data lack.

Applied to risky decision making, models discovered with think-aloud traces predicted held-out behaviour significantly better. For most participants the discovered models also changed structural class, shifting from explicit comparison toward integrated utility designs. The authors conclude that language data do not just improve fit, they reveal mechanisms that behaviour alone cannot recover.
arxiv-2605-05691:
The Hubble tension is usually stated as two numbers at odds: the expansion rate drawn from the early cosmos versus the one measured nearby. Seokcheon Lee argues that squeezing all of it into that single number hides where the gap lives. Different probes constrain different things: matter densities, ruler-scaled distances, calibrated brightness distances.

Lee recasts the comparison using the expansion history with its scale divided out, the rate's redshift shape relative to its present value. The scale mismatch remains, but the shape gap splits cleanly from it. The recasting shows which parts of the tension are about scale setting and which about cosmic history.
arxiv-2605-05791:
Haussmann and two colleagues close a gap between reinforcement-learning practice and theory. Deep off-policy methods control complex robots, yet theory has stayed confined to tabular or linearizable settings. The authors trace the gap to three isolated schools of work. Measure-based foundations ignore learning errors, error-propagation analysis lacks finite-sample estimation bounds, and generalization bounds cover only simplified topologies. Their unified framework treats fitted Q-iteration on general measurable spaces, a broad setting.

Linking measure-based probability with Bellman-operator contraction yields a finite-sample performance bound for adaptive data. Sequential Rademacher complexity is shown to control how well Bellman regression generalizes when the data collected depend on the policy in use. The analysis extends to the first cumulative online regret guarantee that holds path by path for fitted Q-iteration in continuous spaces. That lays foundations for formal study of deep reinforcement-learning algorithms.
arxiv-2605-06091:
Alexander Falk, Laurenz Nagler, Andreas Habring, and Thomas Pock improve Langevin sampling with a preconditioner that changes over time and position. Sampling from a peaked distribution faces two hurdles: reaching far apart modes, and exploring each mode's local shape well. Standard preconditioners use fixed side information and trade one hurdle against the other, the authors argue.

Their method, TIPreL, adapts its preconditioner as the sampler moves, aiming to handle both hurdles in one framework. They prove convergence in continuous time and for a tamed discrete version, under weaker conditions than prior work allowed. Experiments on a hard two dimensional example and a Bayesian logistic regression task back the theory. The method beat competing preconditioning schemes in those tests.
arxiv-2605-06191:
Shivali Dalmia, Ananya Mantravadi, and Prasanna Desikan evaluate language models at extracting clinical actions from hospital discharge notes. After discharge, patients must complete concrete follow up tasks, and missing one can harm safety during the move home. The notes bury those tasks in narrative prose, so extraction must be both fine grained and explicit to be useful.

A two stage prompting framework first breaks each note down, then pulls out actionable tasks in stages. Modern language models matched or beat supervised models at spotting whether a span is actionable, with no task specific training. Supervised baselines kept an edge on fine grained category labels, though. Error analysis shows many failures come from annotation conventions, and the authors call for data sets that record why a span counts as actionable.
arxiv-2605-06291:
Weiliang Yao and six co-authors reveal a winding feature in the magnon spectrum of chromium tri-iodide, a layered ferromagnet. This van der Waals material keeps its magnetism down to a single layer and hosts topological magnons, spin waves with nontrivial structure. It serves as an ideal test bed for how reduced dimension, magnetic order, and spin excitations interact in two dimensions.

Using inelastic neutron scattering on improved samples, the team uncovered the magnon winding around the K point of the hexagonal zone. That winding is a key signature of Dirac magnons, confirming the topological character of the excitations. At higher temperatures the magnon energy followed a square law renormalization, consistent with magnons interacting with each other. The results supply missing detail on this material's spin excitation spectrum.
arxiv-2605-06391:
Haruto Nakashima, Siddhartha Ganguly, and Kenji Kashima study unbalanced optimal transport for a class of constrained discrete-time linear systems. Transport methods usually compare measures with equal total mass. Their version handles unequal mass by balancing transport cost against closeness to reference measures, then adds system dynamics and constraints.

Working with Gaussian references, the authors show both the transport problem and its dynamical extension admit globally optimal convex formulations, similar to covariance steering. A test case shows the approach. The result gives control researchers a clean convex route for moving distributions under real system limits.
arxiv-2605-06591:
Richard Hildebrandt and nine co-authors introduce BRICKS, a compositional neural model for simulating how radiation interacts with matter. Such simulation matters in particle physics, nuclear and space engineering, and medical physics, but mechanistic simulators are slow and not differentiable. BRICKS instead learns a next-particle prediction kernel from local interaction data.

A hybrid transformer built on Riemannian flow matching generates variable-sized sets of outgoing particles and side effects for one incoming particle hitting a material volume. Kernels compose to simulate large, unseen material layouts with no retraining. The model runs much faster on GPUs, stays stable over multi-step rollouts, and ships with a new twenty-million-event dataset.
arxiv-2605-06691:
Z. F. Zheng, R. K. Lin, and J. M. Zhang revisit a classic question: why the one-dimensional Ising model never magnetizes spontaneously at any finite temperature. They approach it through the Landau free energy, first computing the model's density of states by a technique going back to Ising himself. The density's monotonic shape already hints that no spontaneous magnetization should appear.

Solving the model exactly in the thermodynamic limit with a maximum-term approximation, they show the Landau free energy grows with the magnitude of magnetization and curves upward at zero. Its second derivative there is positive yet non-analytic in temperature. Together these results prove the absence of spontaneous magnetization rigorously from the free energy side.
arxiv-2605-06791:
Matthew Stepney, Manda Banerji, Franz E. Bauer, Roberto J. Assef, and Guodong Li expand the census of heavily reddened quasars at cosmic noon. These luminous, dust-obscured quasars are thought to mark a brief phase of intense black hole growth and feedback, but small samples limited earlier statistics. The team assembles photometry for the brightest candidates and selects active nuclei with very red near-infrared colors.

Spectrophotometry from the SPHEREx mission confirms seventy-seven new reddened quasars between redshifts one and a half and nearly four. That more than doubles the known population, and it includes the first seven beyond redshift three. Most show an ultraviolet excess from scattered light. Compared with unobscured quasars they lack hot dust, supporting a blow-out phase where feedback clears the center.
arxiv-2605-06891:
Aditya Parikh, Stella Frank, Sneha Das, and Aasa Feragen tackle label bias in medical image segmentation, where annotation quality varies by group in a systematic way across demographic groups. Such bias skews model scores and audits, yet spotting it normally needs clean reference labels that rarely exist. Their adapted confident learning framework checks given labels against the model's own confident predictions to flag likely label errors right in training data.

The framework counts how many suspected errors there are and which way they lean, where standard overlap scores fail. Label bias also leaves a trace in the encoder's feature space, which they use for mitigation with a cleaner reference group they identify. Tests span fake to real data sets with varying bias.
arxiv-2605-06991:
Simon J. Jones, Dominic Liao-McPherson, and Marco M. Nicotra present a new method for constrained optimal control of linear systems over continuous time. Instead of discretizing first, they work directly in function space. The optimality conditions are packed into a nonsmooth equation, turning control into a root-finding problem.

A semi-smooth Newton method then solves that problem, and each update comes from solving a modified Riccati equation with reweighted costs. Simulations show the method works well and converges faster than linearly, up to the accuracy of the equation solver used. The approach offers a direct route for control problems with constraints.
arxiv-2605-07291:
Shilpa Chandra and nine co-authors evaluate voice anonymization with a metric that looks past classifier decisions. Standard checks use speaker verification error rates, which depend on a chosen classifier and threshold and can mislead about privacy risk. Similarity rank disclosure instead works on the feature representations themselves, with no threshold involved.

Applied to speaker, pitch, and phone embeddings from a recent VoicePrivacy Challenge, the metric exposed leaks and system-specific weaknesses that error rates missed. It also supports both average and worst-case disclosure analysis. The authors present it as a flexible, interpretable tool for judging how well anonymized voices truly protect speakers.
arxiv-2605-07391:
Qi Zhang and three co-authors speed up sparse matrix-vector multiplication, the workhorse of solver loops, on graphics chips. Real-world graph tables have uneven gaps that make the work hard to balance. MERBIT targets repeated use on such tables, with PageRank as its motivating workload.

At the global level it splits work evenly over nonzeros and row edges using merge-path ideas. Locally, each segment is coded in a compact bit-field tag, for better load balance and memory access patterns. On fifty large irregular datasets, MERBIT beat library and academic rivals, including NVIDIA's cuSPARSE, in both single and double precision.
arxiv-2605-08191:
Maria Stoica, Abdelrahman Hekal, and Alessio Lomuscio harden out-of-distribution detection against attack. Detectors that flag inputs unlike the training data are a safety staple, yet strong detectors can be fooled by adversarial perturbations tuned to their scores.

Their detector, ROSS, starts from median smoothing of a baseline score, which balances clean and attacked accuracy. The key extra step reuses the noisy samples drawn for smoothing: out-of-distribution inputs wobble more under perturbation than familiar ones, and that instability becomes a second signal. The result is symmetric robustness, holding up against attacks that push scores down as well as attacks that push them up.
arxiv-2605-08291:
Hyunmog Kim argues that graph neural networks succeed in chip design only under one condition. Their computation must match the algebra of the task. Design problems are all graph-shaped. Yet timing, placement, routing, and power analysis each run on unlike math. One generic message-passing scheme fits them unevenly.

Kim walks task by task. Static timing follows max-plus recurrences on a directed acyclic graph. Placement answers to hypergraph wirelength and density penalties. Congestion is a supply-demand field on a grid. Switching activity is a chance-based recurrence. Voltage drop is a linear system. The review maps which network designs align with each structure.
arxiv-2605-08391:
Nikunj Gupta, James Zachary Hare, Jesse Milzman, Rajgopal Kannan, and coauthors coordinate teams of reinforcement learning agents that each see only part of the world. Jointly good actions need knowledge scattered across teammates, yet every agent must commit without seeing the others' observations or plans. Earlier designs ignored the bottleneck, squeezed it into one mixing number, or added learned chatter channels.

SACHI treats coordination as structured information integration. Graph transformer convolutions over a coordination graph enrich each agent's state with receiver-sensitive signals from teammates before it acts. The method is evaluated on five cooperative tasks spanning spatial and other domains, testing whether richer pre-decision integration beats scalar mixing.
arxiv-2605-08491:
Marina Palaisti extends a way of measuring how nonconvex a function is at a point to functions that are smooth but not twice differentiable. An earlier index by Davydov and coauthors used the distance from the Hessian to the cone of positive semidefinite matrices, which needs a classical second derivative.

For functions with Lipschitz gradients, Palaisti replaces the Hessian with the Clarke generalized Hessian, the closed convex hull of limiting Hessians nearby. The same spectral measure then returns an interval whose ends are the least and greatest visible nonconvexity at the point. The index reduces to the original on smooth functions, vanishes on convex ones, and is unchanged by orthogonal coordinate changes.
arxiv-2605-08691:
Davood Dar, Dhyey Ray, and Neepa Maitra probe a strange late wobble in molecule dipoles. The wobble shows up long after a pulse of hard light ends. It shows up in a much used time based density method. The method uses a shortcut for how states swap. The team argues the wobble is an artifact. On its own, that way of stepping in time pumps up small, pure swings.

A newer form of the same theory shows no such growth. Edge rules for the grid play the key role, just as the claim says. Tests on nitrogen, with a range of swap rules, back the verdict. Chemists who compute gain a warning. Odd late acts may be a flaw of the scheme, not the molecule.
arxiv-2605-08891:
Thomas Dooms and three coauthors stretch a key tool for reading model guts from flat traits to curved sheets. Sparse autoencoders split model acts into traits folks can grasp. But key ideas can live on curved sheets of more than one size. Flat word lists fit such sheets poorly. Their bilinear form uses square latent terms. Those terms join cleanly in weight space. They allow shape checks that do not rest on one input.

Tests show curved shapes are in fact common. The new latents catch them and cut rebuild error in language models. Unlike priors still find the same input span. A live viewer shows sheet finds on a live model. The tool gives curved traits that stay in reach of math.
arxiv-2605-08991: Jacek Szybowski, Konrad Kułakowski, and Jiri Mazurek set the terms for sound use of the Heuristic Rating Estimation plan. The plan ranks picks from pair by pair checks, tied to base picks with known weights. It comes in sum and growth forms. Both forms can face full or part pair sets. The team states the terms for sound use in all four mixes. Worked cases show the sum form's clash grades are the best they can be. Choice work gains firmer ground for trust in the plan's ranks.
arxiv-2605-09191:
Hiroki Matsubara, Ryunosuke Takizawa, and twenty-six other co-authors tackle a hidden quantity in laser-driven fusion: how much energy the fast protons carry while still inside a solid target. That spread of energies drives nuclear reactions and heat deposit, yet normal detectors only see ions that escape. Strong electric and magnetic fields in the plasma also disturb their readings. Their 2026 paper uses reactions inside the target itself as a probe.

By measuring the amounts of two products made by proton hits on boron, the team rebuilds the energy spread of protons inside the solid. A side analysis also gives the total count of a key boron-proton fusion reaction, with uncertainty carried through. The method opens a direct window on proton behavior that drives these fusion tests.
arxiv-2605-09291:
Wan and three colleagues present dFlowGRPO, a single reinforcement learning framework for discrete flow models covering many probability paths and non-masked sources. Discrete flow models are flexible models for discrete data, and diffusion large language models count as a special case with a specific mixture path and masked source. The team derives the full trajectory probability for discrete flow models and formulates denoising as a Markov decision process, letting dFlowGRPO use conditional transition rates plus the posterior model in reinforcement learning.

Applied to FUDOKI, a new multimodal discrete flow model, dFlowGRPO is tested on image generation and understanding tasks. Results show dFlowGRPO outperforms existing GRPO-type methods for diffusion large language models on text-to-image generation, matches continuous flow models trained with FlowGRPO, and shows strong understanding. The work extends reinforcement learning beyond diffusion language models to general discrete flow models, a space GRPO work left open.
arxiv-2605-09391:
Mahadik and a colleague ask whether linear probes work better in persona coordinates, seeking checks for harmful behaviour that hold up when data shifts. Text-only checks fall short because models sometimes deceive on purpose and sandbag, changing behaviour during tests, while white-box probes reading model internals still fail when data shifts.

Following the Assistant Axis and Persona Selection Model, the team builds persona axes for lying and praise from contrastive persona prompts. The first main components from unsupervised PCA of persona vectors cleanly split harmful and harmless personas. Across 10 test sets, persona-based directions transfer in a real way, and probes trained on persona-PC projections work better than probes trained on raw activations. A single axis spanning many harmful and harmless behaviours lifts results across behaviours and sets, so persona vectors offer a useful starting bias for stronger behaviour probes.
arxiv-2605-09491:
Hashimoto and two colleagues explore CaMPL, the Categorical Message Passing Language, a functional-style concurrent programming language with semantics in category theory, namely linear actegories. Its core feature is message passing over typed channels linking concurrent processes. CaMPL supports controlled non-determinism through races that let processes adapt on the fly while running. Higher-order processes send other processes as messages, plus custom channel datatypes called protocols and coprotocols for infinite channel types or session types.

The type system comes out of a Curry-Howard-Lambek-like correspondence in concurrent code, set out by Cockett and Pastro in their work on the logic of message passing. It ensures a formal CaMPL program, one without general recursion, never deadlocks or livelocks. The article explores the type system, custom channel types, and controlled non-determinism through code examples after briefly sketching the math behind it.
arxiv-2605-09591:
Liang and four colleagues ask whether promptable segmentation models truly grasp the concepts they are asked to find. Models like Segment Anything 3 turn text prompts into masks, moving past fixed categories toward concept guided localization. Existing tests mostly score mask accuracy or object presence. They leave open whether a model grounds the queried concept or merely follows eye catching but misleading visual cues.

Their CAFE benchmark holds the target region and true mask fixed while changing surface looks, context, or material to plant false cues. It offers 2,146 paired samples across three trap types: superficial mimicry, context conflict, and ontological conflict. Models often draw accurate masks even for misleading prompts. Strong mask skill, the authors conclude, does not prove faithful concept grounding, and CAFE gives a controlled way to tell the difference.
arxiv-2605-09691:
Singh and Patel recast drug dynamics across body compartments as open quantum systems, simulating population drug movement with quantum circuits. Classic modeling uses ordinary differential equations for drug movement and effect. The authors instead encode four compartments in twelve qubits. The compartments are central, peripheral, effect site, and response. They evolve through PennyLane circuits where transfers appear as quantum jumps. Applied to Phase 1 clinical data, the quantum enhanced method fits far better than the classic baseline.

Parameter estimates match classic values exactly, proving quantum accuracy while improving error modeling. Tuning runs 42 percent faster in one stage, though API overhead raises total runtime by 53 percent across 242 million circuit runs. Dose guidance suggests 20 mg daily or 15 mg weekly for standard populations aiming at 90 percent marker suppression, with quantum methods showing greater response to population variety.
arxiv-2605-09791:
Kucharczuk and Skibski take up a gap in network science: most centrality scores rank single nodes, yet real choices usually pick a whole team of nodes that must work together. Their paper studies group vitality indices, scores that judge a group by how much the network suffers when the group is removed. It covers the full class of such scores, not just one example.

For every vitality index, the pair proves there is exactly one sensible group version, built from a group form of the Shapley value, a fair-share rule from game theory. They also give a set of axioms, basic rules that pin down the whole class, plus two indices that meet extra normalisation conditions. The paper closes by mapping which of these group scores can be computed with reasonable effort, including Group Attachment Centrality.
arxiv-2605-09891:
Kosikova and three colleagues fuse two partial views of city traffic into one network-wide picture. Floating-car traces cover many streets but skew by corridor and hour. Traffic cameras are precise but watch only scattered points. Their hybrid framework joins both sources to estimate and briefly forecast traffic volumes across a whole road network.

The model pairs a graph neural network, which learns how traffic states evolve over the network, with the Cell Transmission Model, which enforces flow conservation, capacity limits and spillback. An Ensemble Square-Root Kalman filter then calibrates predictions against camera readings. A flow-weighted transition matrix spreads those corrections to unobserved streets. Tested in Manhattan with probe traces and municipal cameras, it beat trajectory-only estimates.
arxiv-2605-09991:
Zhang and four colleagues revisit mode connectivity. That is the surprising fact that two separately trained networks can often be joined by a low-loss path. They ask what the optimiser has to do with it. Prior work largely ignored the optimiser's role. Through optimiser-induced implicit regularisation, they ask how connectivity behaves among solutions allowed by one given optimiser.

For two-layer ReLU networks, solutions from a single optimiser form a connected set once the network is wide enough. That holds for AdamW, Muon or others in the Lion family, and earlier work did not imply it. At large width, regions from two optimisers may be disjoint or may overlap, depending on regularisation. In a small-width example, AdamW and Muon land in disconnected zero-loss parts split by a provable loss barrier, and GPT-2 runs show same-optimiser paths preserving each model's spectrum.
arxiv-2605-10291:
Hyunso Kim, Hyo Kang, and Jaeyong Song ask whether generative AI changes who starts a business, and who succeeds at it. Their 2026 paper studies more than 160,000 product launches on Product Hunt, a platform where founders present new digital products to the public, around the release of ChatGPT-3.5.

Entry rose sharply after that release, driven disproportionately by solo founders. The shift was strongest in categories that had favored teams. Yet much of the growth was low-commitment, experimental entry, and it did not carry into the highest-quality outcomes. Team ventures grew stronger at the top of the platform rankings. Generative AI, the authors conclude, lowers the bar for solo entry while reinforcing team advantages at the top.
arxiv-2605-10391:
HTX and Mistral AI present Phoenix-VL 1.5 Medium, a 123-billion-parameter multimodal and multilingual base model tuned to Singapore and its region. Built as a sovereign AI asset, it tests whether a frontier model can be deeply localized with no loss of broad smarts or alignment. This 2026 technical report details its training and tests.

Continued pretraining from Mistral Medium 3.1 used a localized 1-trillion-token multimodal corpus, then a 250-billion-token long-context extension. Post-training added a human-annotated Singapore multimodal dataset plus curated text on Singapore culture, knowledge, and law, totaling 22 billion tokens, with 5 billion tokens of alignment via Online Direct Preference Optimization. The model hit top results for its size on Singapore multimodal, legal, and government-policy tests while staying globally competitive on general multimodal, multilingual, and STEM tests.
arxiv-2605-10491:
Alexandre Reber and three colleagues establish existence and uniqueness of cyclically monotone zero-couplings for infinite measures. M0 covers Borel measures on punctured Euclidean space, finite away from the origin but possibly infinite in total. Their 2026 paper avoids moment assumptions and allows infinite transport cost.

The authors introduce the notion of a zero-coupling. They establish CM zero-couplings for pairs of measures in M0. Under a Hausdorff-dimension condition on the first measure and when one measure has infinite mass, they prove uniqueness. That gives a Brenier-McCann analogue here. They identify when the zero-coupling is proper: the second measure equals the push-forward of the first measure by a CM transport map. For regularly varying measures, a CM coupling admits a tail limit equal to the unique proper zero-coupling of the exponent measures.
arxiv-2605-10591:
L.A. Calderón and I. Ojeda study nonconstant rational solutions of Abel equations. The equations take the form x-prime equals A3 of t times x to the n3, A2 times x to the n2, and A1 times x to the n1. Exponents satisfy 1 less than n1 less than n2 less than n3. Their 2026 paper proves every such solution has the form x equals 1 over p of t.

The authors use the Newton-Puiseux polygon at infinity to bound the degrees of p. Under a nondegeneracy hypothesis, edge polynomials yield bounds for the number S of rational solutions. Over the complex numbers, S is at most n2 minus 1 plus 2 times n3 minus 1. Over the real numbers, S is at most 12, with sharper parity-dependent estimates. Rational solutions matter because they admit a geometric interpretation via invariant algebraic curves.
arxiv-2605-10791:
Shengxiang Gao and colleagues give PathISE, a plan for learning useful path hints for knowledge graph question answering. Training good find models tends to need top-notch middle hints such as question-tied paths or subgraphs, which cost much time and funds to get.

PathISE brings in a light transformer-based guess tool that rates how much a link path tells, to build fake path-level hints from answer-level tags alone. These hints are boiled down into a language-model path maker, whose made paths are tied to the knowledge graph to give tight proof for step-by-step answer thought. Wide tests on three sets show PathISE hitting top or best question answering scores, with reuse hints that lift old models. It needs no dear language-model-tuned hints.
arxiv-2605-10991:
Linhai Zhang and Yulan He study test-time personalization, scaling inference compute for personalized language models instead of rebuilding the model. Sampling many candidates from a personalized policy and picking the best with a personalized reward model should raise utility, but standard reward models fail to deliver the gain.

Theory shows oracle selection grows expected utility logarithmically with candidate count, setting a ceiling for test-time scaling. A unified scaling law decomposes any reward model's best-of-N curve into four measurable quantities, exposing two failure modes: user-level collapse and query-level reward hacking. A probabilistic reward model whose learned variance counters both failures restores consistent scaling across models and tasks. Personalization teams get both a diagnosis and a fix for test-time scaling.
arxiv-2605-11091:
Shubhankit Singh, Hassan Shaikh, Kuldeep Raghuwanshi, and Keshav Bulia present ASD-Bench, a four-axis benchmark of AI models for autism spectrum disorder screening. Existing screening tools suffer single-architecture tests, narrow-axis scoring, and near-exclusive adult focus, hiding age-specific patterns critical for early intervention.

Across children, teens, and adults, the benchmark scores classical models, neural networks, deep tabular transformers, and TabPFN v2. It tests prediction, calibration, interpretability, and attack robustness, using a curated set of 4,068 AQ-10 records. Adults prove easiest, with many models reaching perfect scores, while teens cap lower, and key features shift across cohorts as social masking develops. The Heuristic Aggregate Penalty, penalizing missed cases heavily, adds deployment realism. Clinical AI teams get age-aware evaluation for screening tools.
arxiv-2605-11191:
Aidan Gleich, Eric Laber, and Alexander Volfovsky develop adaptive policy learning under unknown network interference. Adaptive testing with interference faces two problems: learning how interference spreads, and using those dynamics to allocate treatments for maximum revenue.

Their Thompson sampling algorithm jointly learns the interference network and optimizes treatment allocations via a Gibbs sampler. It hands back an optimized treatment policy together with an estimate of that network, supporting causal analyses of direct, indirect, and total effects. For additive spillover models, total reward grows linearly with the treatment vector, scaled by latent-score coefficients. The team proves a Bayesian regret bound for exact posterior sampling. Empirically the Gibbs-based sampler matches this rate and stays sublinear even when the additive spillover assumption breaks. Test designers get policy learning that does not assume the network is known.
arxiv-2605-11291: Nguyen and three colleagues characterize optimal representations in contrastive learning when classes are imbalanced. With balanced classes, optimal representations collapse to class means forming an equiangular tight frame. For imbalanced classes across a large family of losses, they prove same-class samples still collapse to class means, with an angular symmetry set by class proportions and solvable by convex optimization. Under extreme imbalance they prove minority collapse, where all minority samples merge into one vector past a threshold.
arxiv-2605-11591: Xian and four others propose logit-attention divergence calibration against position bias in multi-image search. Multimodal large language models perform strongly in multi-image search yet suffer position bias, with predictions driven by input order over meaning. The authors find output logits heavily biased while internal attention maps stay aligned with visual evidence. Their training-free method uses attention signals for instance fix at run time, needing only a small tuning set. On MS-COCO-based benchmarks it greatly lifts order steadiness and beats rivals by over 40 percent.
arxiv-2605-11891: Zhaojiacheng Zhou and five colleagues build Proteus, a self-evolving red team for agent skill ecosystems. Because an attacker can rewrite a skill using audit and runtime feedback, single-shot audits understate risk. Proteus searches a five-axis attack space through an audit-sandbox-oracle pipeline, then expands successful attacks along new paths and objectives. Across eight test cells it reached 40 to 90 percent attack success within five rounds, and the strongest public auditor still admitted up to 41.3 percent of joint-success attacks.
arxiv-2605-12191: Pranshu Gaba and Shibashis Guha solve two guarantee problems for window payoffs in MDPs. Sure-almost-sure asks whether every outcome reaches at least alpha, and almost surely beta. Sure-limit-sure asks the same with probability at least one minus epsilon for each epsilon. Window mean-payoff requires that, from every point, the average payoff tops a threshold in a window. In the fixed variant, with window length in unary, both sit in P; in the bounded variant, both sit in NP intersect coNP. The authors bound strategy memory.
arxiv-2605-12291: Roy, Mitra and Singh look for a shortcut to test whether a relativistic fluid theory respects causality. They exploit a quirk of boosted frames, where higher-order wave terms fade at near-light speeds. Stability at zero wave number can then reveal the causal region, even for waves of nonzero momentum. They test the idea on conformal Müller-Israel-Stewart theory and recover the required causality conditions while staying inside the theory's low-energy range.
arxiv-2605-12491: Song and five colleagues ask whether vision transformers really need every image patch to talk directly to every other patch. Their VECA model routes global information only through a small set of learned cores, while all dense patches stay intact and update across layers. That change cuts attention cost from quadratic to linear in patch count for a fixed core budget. Unlike earlier latent-token designs, it avoids squeezing the spatial representation itself. The result supports both global recognition and dense prediction without direct patch-to-patch links.
arxiv-2605-12791: Danhoni, Mullins and Noronha frame out-of-balance jet momentum broadening within QCD effective kinetic theory through a moment series of the medium distribution function. They compute the leading near-balance part to the spatial jet broadening tensor within the 14-moment model. It is set by the medium shear-stress tensor. That result maps QCD effective kinetic theory to per-event thick fluid models, turning local shear-stress fields into uneven fixes to jet broadening in heavy-ion crashes.
arxiv-2605-12991: Kumarappan and Mujoo test the claim that multi-agent sycophancy comes from RLHF alignment. Across four model families, untrained base models flip under peer pressure just as much, averaging even higher yield than instruct versions. Activation patching traces the corruption to a slim band of middle layers in which attention supplies the decisive push. A single correctly arguing dissenter cuts yield by 54 to 73 points, while the best prompt defence fails outside its design surface.
arxiv-2605-13091: Eicher describes how finite-dimensional Schubert cells in the affine flag variety of SL2 split into orbits. The split runs under a chain of subgroups of codimension one to four of the Iwahori group. The short note gives the orbit decomposition for every such cell, working through the subgroup chain one codimension at a time.
arxiv-2605-13691: Yan-Ming Chen and Dan-Bo Zhang study quantum information scrambling via local random probes. They track scrambling flow with mean open info under local random probes. They derive an exact formula under Haar-random probes as a function of local reduced density matrix purity. Using the old shadow plan with single-qubit random Pauli probes, they extract mean open info across wide parts. Tests across many-body cases show mean open info reveals distinct scrambling ways.
arxiv-2605-13891: Benner, Mehrmann, Prajapati and Sharma pin down stability radii for a class of energy-losing Hamiltonian setups ruled by differential-algebraic equations. Such setups mix change laws with fixed constraints. The paper states just when they stay robustly stable. It then gives exact tests and bounds for the point where that stability fails under tweaks that keep the setup's form.
arxiv-2605-14191: Li and four co-authors offer CoReDiT, a structured token pruning framework for diffusion transformers. They generate striking images and video but cost heavily, capping scale and on-device use. CoReDiT scores local redundancy in the latent token lattice with a linear-time spatial coherence score, skipping extra tokens in self-attention. Skipped attention outputs are rebuilt by pooling spatially neighboring retained tokens, preserving a dense representation. A progressive, block-adaptive schedule ramps pruning up, giving bigger budgets to blocks and denoising steps at higher overlap.
arxiv-2605-14291: Zhao and four co-authors propose MMGuard, proactive multimodal data protection against unauthorized fine-tuning of large vision-language models. Unauthorized scraping and training on multimodal web data pose IP and privacy risks to owners. MMGuard makes unlearnable samples by injecting imperceptible noise exploiting LVLM learning. The perturbation creates a shortcut by cutting training loss, causing overfitting to noise and degraded inference. A cross-modal binding disruption shifts LVLM attention to enforce a spurious noise-target link.
arxiv-2605-14591: Cebere, Even, Bleistein and Bellet introduce Zero-Run privacy auditing, which audits a trained model after the fact with no retraining and no control over data inclusion. Two fixed sets are used: known training members and known non-members. Since membership is no longer randomised, score gaps may reflect distribution shift rather than leakage. Drawing on causal inference, the authors formalise this confounding and propose two corrections, one global and conservative, one sharper and instance-dependent.
arxiv-2605-14791: Xu and Borrett discuss two agentic systems that push AI beyond helpers toward autonomous discovery in cosmology. CMBEvolve targets tasks with clear numeric goals. It uses language-model-guided code evolution and tree search. CosmoEvolve targets open-ended workflows via a virtual multi-agent research laboratory. Tests apply CMBEvolve for out-of-distribution detection on weak-lensing maps. CosmoEvolve is applied to autonomous ACT DR6 data analysis. There it finds non-trivial pair and scale patterns and produces analysis-grade outputs.
arxiv-2605-14891: Hadji and team present hierarchical image tokenization for multi-scale super resolution, building on Visual Auto-Regressive work. VAR models split image tokenization into additive scales via residual codes, fitting well with super resolution. Prior works generate only at a fixed scale and rely on large models or large tagged sets. It represents images at varied scales while sharing tokens. A Direct Choice term, using only low-high pairs, pushes the model to prefer high-resolution output. A model reaches top results without outside data.
arxiv-2605-14991: Francesco Pastori and ten colleagues train a deep learning model to predict, from pre-treatment CT scans, which ovarian cancer patients will respond to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Early non-responders could skip ineffective therapy and reach surgery sooner. The model encodes scan slices, aggregates them into a volumetric embedding with attention, and trains with classification plus contrastive losses. On 280 patients it reached an ROC-AUC of 0.73 and an F1 score of 0.70 on the test cohort.
arxiv-2605-15491: Vincent-Daniel Yun, Junhyuk Jo, Sai Praneeth Karimireddy, and Sunwoo Lee fix the harm from pruning whole layers of large language models. Cut layers leave the next live layer with inputs unlike those it trained on. The team works out a closed-form linear map from a small tuning set. It rebuilds the gap left by cut layers. Past no-train fixes stay inside tight map families. Theirs hits the free best of the alignment goal. Tests show gains in accuracy and perplexity on varied backbones and prune plans.
arxiv-2605-15591: Pengfei Li, Lijing Xing, Dongdong Wang, Dumitru Mihalache, David Laroze, and Boris A. Malomed report parametrically driven pure-quartic solitons, self-trapped waves governed by fourth-order dispersion rather than the usual second-order kind. They establish still solitons in the full system with loss and gain, and moving solitons when losses vanish, mapping stability regions across parameter space. They also explore how unstable states evolve and show that collisions between traveling stable solitons are elastic.
arxiv-2605-15891: Junjie Shan studies the dual Minkowski problem under group symmetry. The problem asks which measures can arise as surface-like data of a convex body. For groups with no nonzero fixed points, he gives complete existence conditions. These turn on how the measure concentrates on group-invariant subspaces, up to a critical endpoint. At that endpoint the problem becomes the logarithmic Minkowski problem. The origin-symmetric case falls out as a special case.
arxiv-2605-16191: Brenner, Dorfman, and Platt test whether AI coding systems can generate novel scientific hypotheses, using photovoltaic structures as a test case. A coding agent plus LLM tree search first reproduced known 3D photovoltaic results, then found nominally better designs that exploited reward hacking, such as levitating disconnected tiers. After the agent patched the physics engine with constraints, the search found genuinely improved designs with different collector areas and zenith tracking. The workflow shows coding agents plus tree search can drive discovery for problems with a score function.
arxiv-2605-16491: Winterhalder and 19 others show how rotational broadening complicates finding reflection signals in spectra of exoplanet daysides. Finding bounced day-side light is hard, and the faint signal has yet to be seen. They present a reflection spectra metric for how good systems are for reflection studies, picking KELT-9. A planted-signal test on their CARMENES time series shows response to rotational line broadening. The search found nothing, and the test reveals the need to account for rotational broadening in spinning stars with large spin-orbit tilts.
arxiv-2605-16591: Wang, Wang, Bakalova and Hahn ask how few-shot examples combine inside a language model to form its function vector, the direction that steers task behavior. They show an n-shot vector is well matched by adding example-level pieces. Yet context reweights those pieces toward clearer, more informative examples. A causal split finds Query-Key routing drives most of the gain, especially when examples are ambiguous, while Value effects vary more.
arxiv-2605-16691: Machihara, Miyazaki and Ozawa give one integral route to the conservation laws of nonlinear Schrödinger equations with power-type terms. Using the Duhamel form and Strichartz bounds, they avoid smoothing and added steps. That identity then yields charge, energy, and momentum conservation, plus the pseudo-conformal law and virial laws. The route unifies proofs first made by Ozawa and later done by others.
arxiv-2605-16791: Gowda and colleagues strengthen parallel algorithms for envy-free-up-to-one-good allocation. For two agents, depth falls from logarithmic-squared to logarithmic in goods, and work from m log m to linear. They extend this to any constant number of agents with NC algorithms, plus randomized near m-over-n depth algorithms. Their methods bypass the CC-hardness of simulating Round Robin, and prove that simulation CC-complete. They give envy-free-up-to-k allocations for k near root m in randomized NC.
arxiv-2605-16991: Netík and Martinková estimate multiple-choice item difficulty before any answers exist, tuning a transformer on wording instead of hand-made features. They target reading items, whose difficulty rests on inference across passage, question, options, while the base model sees one undifferentiated sequence trained on difficulty. Two extensions beat that base model at the smallest size: a component-wise variant encoding parts apart and a multi-task variant adding a question-answer task. The multi-task variant wins on every metric, and component-wise encoding wins on rank ordering.
arxiv-2605-17091: Jiang and Sun build a forecasting method that guesses the local rule driving a system, rather than its next state directly. Their system squeezes short space-time snippets into rule summaries, then anchors those summaries to a small set of sample rules. Tests on a fluid equation, weather data, and a simplified atmosphere model show steadier results when data are scarce or dynamics shift. The gains trace to the anchored samples, not to sheer model size.
arxiv-2605-17191: Lin and Yu study stability for minimizing Yamabe metrics on compact manifolds that have a boundary, in Escobar's sense. They show that a function nearly minimizing the Yamabe energy yields a conformal metric quantitatively close to a true minimizer in its class. The gap between the two is controlled by a suitable power of the energy deficit, giving a precise stability estimate.
arxiv-2605-17491: Di Yu and colleagues break the noise-agility trade-off in integrated lasers with a design that pairs ultralow phase noise with ultrafast tuning. Strong synthetic feedback in a Pockels-tunable, resonator-enhanced Bragg reflector suppresses noise without an ultrahigh-Q resonator, relaxing the photon-lifetime limit on tuning speed. Their hybrid laser shows a 29-hertz short-term linewidth with a loaded Q of only 0.62 million, plus sub-exahertz-per-second tuning and low chirp nonlinearity. Demonstrations cover LiDAR ranging and fiber acoustic sensing.
arxiv-2605-17691: M. Mikail Demir and M. Abdullah Canbaz benchmark language models on precedent treatment classification. To address shortcomings of standard accuracy, the paper introduces a robust evaluation framework. The authors benchmark language models on a new dataset of 239 legal citations and propose an Average Severity Error metric for error impact. Gemini 2.5 Flash leads a high-level task at about 79 percent, while GPT-5-mini tops a fine-grained schema at about 68 percent. The work establishes a baseline, provides a new dataset, and introduces a metric for this legal reasoning task.
arxiv-2605-18091: Daniel Julian Nader studies passage of shifted Fock states through an upside-down oscillator barrier, with and without a Kerr effect. Semiclassical methods match overall passage but miss short-time flats that appear when regions of Wigner-function dips cross the barrier. With Kerr effect, echoes from Kerr boundaries push waves into forbidden regions, an effect methods cannot reach. These wave effects leave peak passage the same, bounded by the first positive energy fraction already stored in the Fock states' phase-space structure.
arxiv-2605-18291: Fionnuala Curran asks in a 2026 paper how much intrinsic randomness an extremal measurement can yield beyond the projective kind, a question left open for general cases. She characterizes the randomness from any unbiased extremal rank-one case on any state, solving it fully in dimension two. Four-outcome qubit cases of this type are tomographic, and she proves the maximum amount can be generated wherever a SIC measurement exists.
arxiv-2605-18791: Chengrui Xiang and five colleagues build SpecX, a large benchmark for spectroscopy across model types. Older spectral benchmarks stay small, poorly matched across types, or narrow in scope. SpecX gathers about one point seven million molecules across six spectral types. It supports tasks such as finding molecules and reading spectra, and tests show specialist models lead on signals while language models lead on high-level reasoning.
arxiv-2605-18891: Yanhang Li, Zhichao Fan and Zexin Zhuang audit claims that unlearned models remember forgotten content in their traces. When the answer looks clean but the trace leaks erased material, the gap is read as proof of hidden weight memory. Their tests use a distilled model with memorized fictional authors. Swapping the trace for a neutral prefill on identical weights can make the gap vanish, shrink or reverse. Such a gap thus neither proves nor rules out weight memory, and the authors recommend a template-swap check beside the standard audit.
arxiv-2605-18991: Mihai Christodorescu and thirteen colleagues argue that agent security is a systems problem, not a model problem. The language model driving an agent should be treated as an untrusted component, with security invariants enforced at the system level. Efforts to harden the model alone, the dominant view, cannot suffice. Drawing on decades of systems security research, the authors set out core design principles with predictable guarantees. They test the principles against eleven real-world attacks on agents and name the research challenges blocking implementation.
arxiv-2605-19091: Daniel Monroe and four colleagues unify three chess-modelling goals, playing strength, human move prediction, and interpretability, in one architecture called Chessformer. It treats board squares as tokens, adds a geometric attention bias adapted to board geometry, and predicts moves with a source-destination policy head. A human-move model built on it matches human moves 57.1 percent of the time with under a quarter of earlier parameters. Integrated into Leela Chess Zero, it adds over 100 Elo and has beaten Stockfish in tournaments. Its square-based design supports interpretability.
arxiv-2605-19291: Shubo Li, Yuefeng Han, and Xiufan Yu introduce factor-augmented stochastic gradient descent for high-dimensional learning. Standard two-stage methods first learn representations offline and store full data, which scales poorly. Their method instead works purely on streaming data, weaving latent factor structure directly into the optimization steps. They also supply the first theory that folds factor-estimation error into stochastic gradient analysis, proving moment convergence under shrinking step sizes and mini-batch updates. The result gives a firmer footing for reliable large-scale learning.
arxiv-2605-19791: Shuai and Zhang unite early inflation with late cosmic acceleration in a single non-singular model, replacing the Big Bang singularity with a quantum bounce. Loop quantum cosmology drives a superinflation phase that sets up slow-roll inflation, while a coupling to mass-varying neutrinos freezes the scalar field once neutrinos slow down, triggering dark energy. Tracing the background from bounce to today, they fit supernova, DESI baryon acoustic oscillation and microwave background data. The unified framework matches current precision observations closely.
arxiv-2605-20191: Marco Bombieri, Simone Paolo Ponzetto and Marco Rospocher study how language models depict disabled people in simulated social media posts. They compare model-made posts from disabled viewpoints with posts written by real disabled people, on tone, sentiment, words and themes. Models often paint disabled lives in overly rosy terms that miss lived reality. Posts with and without disabled people also show a slant: career and fun topics attach mostly to others, feeding exclusion.
arxiv-2605-20391: Chhabra treats large behavior populations as geometric energy landscapes whose warping can be read before major shifts. Applied to the Tor anonymity network over 67 daily windows, the method finds a stable nine-dimensional load-bearing subspace, validated at 16.8 sigma above the noise floor. Its main gates show no false alarms on 24 stable windows. Forensic work on a confirmed February 2026 infrastructure event rejects relay departure, naming connectivity loss without topology change as the failure mode.
arxiv-2605-20591: Sunday Ogundoyin, Muhammad Ikram, and Rahat Masood audit web-deployed medical language models for hallucination and abuse. They assess 6,233 custom medical GPTs, sampling 1,500 in depth, plus ten open-source models. Between 25 and 30 percent of the custom models show low factual accuracy, and 33.6 to 54.3 percent breach operational thresholds. Over half of action-enabled models miss adequate privacy disclosures, exposing systemic gaps in safeguards.
arxiv-2605-20691: Dong-Dong Hou and Egon Schulte show that string C-groups of two-power order project onto a common string C-group. String C-groups are exactly the symmetry groups of abstract regular polytopes, shapes defined by combinatorial rules. A special polytope C_d, found by Conder, has the fewest flags among high-rank regular polytopes with two-power symmetry. Its symmetry group is a quotient of every such string C-group of the same rank, making C_d the unique minimal polytope under covering.
arxiv-2605-20791: Dan Zhu and three colleagues report the first mass determination of electroweak vortex rings in the Standard Model. They establish precise values of 18.01 and 26.80 TeV for solutions with different winding numbers. Repulsive interactions shape the internal geometry, while complex current patterns yield a neutral analogue of Ampere's circuital law. The findings set energy scales for future collider searches in the years ahead and suggest a self-stabilizing pinch mechanism.
arxiv-2605-21291: Guillermo Baltà and colleagues examine how hadronic resonances affect B decays to K mesons and tau pairs. For light leptons, resonances can be dodged with mass cuts. For tau modes, missing energy makes the mass spectrum hard to rebuild, and hadronic sites cannot split regions as cleanly as Belle II. So the authors include resonances, notably psi-two-S, in predictions at several kinematic points for LHCb, CMS, and Belle II.
arxiv-2605-21491: Srujan P Mule and co-authors teach language models to forecast research success through comparative idea evaluation. Evaluating hundreds of AI-generated ideas without exhaustive experiments is a bottleneck. They ask whether models can forecast empirical success before experiments run. Given a goal and two candidate ideas, predict which performs better on benchmarks. On eleven thousand four hundred eighty-eight idea pairs, fine-tuning lifts accuracy to seventy-seven point one percent, beating GPT-5 at sixty-one point one percent.
arxiv-2605-21791: Kevin Hernández proves completeness of the Klein-Gordon oscillator eigenfunctions in one and three spatial dimensions. The proofs give the closure rules from standard facts of Hermite and generalized Laguerre polynomials, plus spherical harmonics in three dimensions. Because the Klein-Gordon field is scalar, the proof runs strictly simpler than the Dirac oscillator case: no cancellation between unlike parts is required. The result covers both the line and ordinary three-dimensional space.
arxiv-2605-21991: Gustavo Yepes and Daniel de Andres review machine learning for galaxy clusters, spanning theory and estimates of cluster properties from observed tracers. They discuss masses from Sunyaev-Zel'dovich, X-ray, optical, and motion data, showing how AI methods capture nonlinear traits, projection effects, and complex morphology. Simulations play a central role in training, with baryonic modeling and uncertainty quantification, with intracluster light among those treated. The chapter closes with limits and prospects, urging flexible simulations paired with AI to exploit next-generation surveys for precision cosmology.
arxiv-2605-22091: Vivienne Bihe Chi and co-authors survey film characters with language-model agents to measure gender values encoded in mainstream film. From 160 United States films from 1990 to 2019, they build 734 agents for characters from script dialogue and scene descriptions, condensing personas through expert reflections and simulating survey responses. Against historical survey data, the agents exaggerate gender gaps and show greater volatility across decades than real survey populations. Narrative sharpens gender contrasts rather than homogenizing them, breaking cultivation theory's mainstreaming claim and suggesting AI trained on such films takes on this style.
arxiv-2605-22191: Shuche Wang and co-authors ask whether optimistic gradient predictions can improve bandit convex optimization regret in a prediction-adaptive way. Under single-point feedback, an unavoidable square-root-T regret lower bound persists even when cumulative prediction error is small, since gradient estimation variance hides prediction benefits. To overcome this, they propose Two-Point Variance-Reduced Optimistic Gradient Descent for two-point feedback. The method aims to turn accurate predictions into better regret bounds. The paper thus separates what single-point feedback cannot exploit from two-point gains.
arxiv-2605-22391: Radzikowski and Chen present Epicure, three sibling ingredient embeddings trained from scratch on a multilingual recipe corpus. The team pools 4.14 million recipes from 11 sources, then normalises raw ingredient strings to 1,790 canonical entries. Two graphs seed three Metapath2Vec variants that share architecture and settings. Cooc walks co-occurrence links only, Chem walks typed compound paths only, and Core blends both. The three models thus sit at distinct points on a chemistry-versus-recipe-context spectrum.
arxiv-2605-22491: Guidec and Mahéo investigate relay-based synchronisation of conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) in opportunistic networks. In such networks, information spreads only through fleeting pairwise radio contacts between mobile peers. CRDT replicas update locally yet converge through background synchronisation. Whether replicas converge, and how fast, depends on radio contact patterns. Mobile relays are proposed as a boost, with new protocols and metrics for convergence.
