Simulations show relays improve convergence, even enabling it where replicas alone could not converge.
arxiv-2605-22791: Hatamizadeh, Choi, and Kautz introduce Gated DeltaNet-2, a linear attention design that edits its fixed-size memory with separate controls for erasing and writing. Earlier delta-rule models tied both jobs to one gate, which muddled the edit. Splitting them into channel-wise erase and write gates keeps old links intact while new facts land. At 1.3 billion parameters it led rival recurrent models, most clearly on long-context retrieval tests.
arxiv-2605-22891: Baattrup and six colleagues argue that pointwise metrics mislead evaluation of multimodal inverse problems. Such problems have posteriors with several modes. Estimators that minimize squared or absolute error return spectra narrower than the truth. They compress the tails and shapes that downstream science needs. The authors propose a three-part protocol. It covers per-event distributional accuracy, population-level spectrum fidelity, and calibration. On synthetic and particle-physics problems, rankings flipped between pointwise and distributional metrics.
arxiv-2605-23191: Li and nine coauthors address code collapse in the RankMixer ranking model, where learned codes have low rank and waste the wider space. They trace the cause to token mixing and per-token forward networks, which induce a damped swinging path in rank change across layers. Their RankElastor design counters this with tunable full mixing for rich token mixing with spectral strength, and GLU-improved forward networks that steady code spectra. Tests on large real-world data show better ranking scores, less collapse, and robust scaling.
arxiv-2605-23491: Hu and colleagues present CoSPlay, a training-free test-time method that improves code and unit tests without ground-truth tests. Reward training needs costly ground-truth tests, while test-time methods using self-made tests suffer when those tests are noisy or tied to bad code. CoSPlay explores varied ideas, spots failure modes, and uses pass-count signals from a code-test matrix to prune or fix weak codes and refresh tests. On four benchmarks it lifts Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 22.1 to 33.2 percent.
arxiv-2605-23591: Sous and Winer model neural scaling laws under sparse activations, where test loss is often dominated by rare coordinates never seen in training inputs. That mechanism creates a bottleneck absent from dense models. They derive asymptotic population loss in underparameterized and overparameterized regimes, finding a double-descent peak near the interpolation threshold, with two distinct scaling exponents separated by a gap set by sparsity degree. Their compute-optimal frontier favors larger data sets over model capacity, and the sparsity effect persists under nonlinear activations and gradient-descent instability analysis.
arxiv-2605-23691: Wuethrich and Hothorn extend adjusted marginal work to allow varied treatment effects. Marginal effects are the usual target, but allowing for covariates can change the target in curved models. Their model embeds the effect in a joint model for outcome and background traits, keeping clarity with allowance for predictive and prognostic traits. For numeric results, variance as Cohen's d is never worse and often better with adjustment, driven by prognostic effects. Simulations confirm fair, tight estimates, and an acupuncture trial repeats findings more precisely and with covariate ranking.
arxiv-2605-23791: Brugel and colleagues propose a Bayesian framework for map-to-map validation of spatial health databases, comparing a candidate database against a gold standard. The framework uses random and structured error models, in which the candidate database is modeled as a shift from the gold standard, and compares both with a shared model. Global measures accurately recover map-wide shifts. Applied to Crohn's disease data, all models agree the candidate database reproduces spatial patterns with an overall signal about 7 percent lower.
arxiv-2605-23891: Xiao Cao and colleagues tackle mask-free video object insertion, placing a reference object into a scene so it looks native even when styles clash. Their Smart-Insertion-V runs insertion and image style transfer together in two streams, with a closed loop feedback step keeping the result honest. A dual world view rotary encoding separates mixed signals by space time offsets, and a decoupled guidance module adds vision language reasoning while keeping native text guidance. Tests show plausible placement with the most harmonious blends, plus a curated dataset release.
arxiv-2605-24091: Cardona and Molina model the Hawking atmosphere around dying anti-de Sitter black holes as quantum leaking. Using the Parikh-Wilczek method with back-action, output odds follow the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy change, giving a time-shifting glow that departs from ideal black-body pattern, most for small holes. For those holes, glow does not rise with heat, because mass shifts during fading break the pattern. A corrected energy-momentum tensor in Vaidya-anti-de Sitter shape adds to the tiny-scale picture, linking shape, fields, and heat laws.
arxiv-2605-24191: Sohn and twenty-five co-authors lay out a white paper on Hubble astrometry of the Local Group and beyond through the 2030s. Hubble's long baseline plus archival first epochs mean future observations can turn old frames into proper motions for nearby galaxies, streams, and clusters. Where data already constrain satellite orbits, Hubble can deliver three-dimensional motion, internal motions, and reach to distant systems line-of-sight speeds cannot probe. The plan banks new first epochs and a legacy sample for later Webb, Roman, and Habitable Worlds follow-up.
arxiv-2605-24691: Raju Imandi and others build a detector for extreme low light, where normal RGB cameras fail but event cameras still sense per-pixel brightness changes. Their AdaFuse-Det framework merges contrast-enhanced RGB frames and voxelized event tensors through adaptive fusion grounded in minimum-variance estimation. The learned attention map recovers Gauss-Markov optimal fusion weights in the limit, with bounds on conservation and resolution. On LLE-VOS it posts an F1-score of 59.12 percent under severe light loss, beating single-modality detectors on recall.
arxiv-2605-24991: Jose Ilton de Oliveira Filho presents HHK, hardware for body area network session keys from heartbeat signals. Public-key exchange costs more compute and energy than tiny wearables can spare. HHK pulls inter-beat intervals from green-light traces at several sites. It aligns beat times, quantizes with Gray-coded bins, and reconciles timing gaps with polar-code fuzzy commitment. Synthesis maps it to a modest chip footprint with no multipliers or embedded memories. Tests on 16 wearers over long trials show strong raw bit and key agreement.
arxiv-2605-25391: Ruiyu Li and colleagues design channel-allocation policies for opportunistic spectrum access that account for noise. Existing multi-play bandit methods assume ideal conditions, cost too much compute, and ignore noise that shapes service quality. The team models noise as a perturbation of each arm's reward, using channel-state information, which correlates with noise, as context. They study linear and nonlinear forms of that correlation and derive one policy for each, learned with a linear model and a neural network. Experiments show lower regret and more sensible suboptimal-arm choices.
arxiv-2605-25591: Ponge and Tian develop a trace theory for weak Lorentz ideals, with Dixmier traces and Connes' noncommutative integration, for functions that vary regularly. They prove asymptotic additivity for eigenvalue partial sums from Karamata's theorem and Kalton and Lord-Sukochev-Zanin. That yields Dixmier traces built from these sequences and a spectral account of these operators, answering a question of Connes. They extend Birman-Solomyak perturbation theory to these ideals. They show Weyl operators form a closed set stable under compact perturbations, and that every Weyl operator is strongly measurable.
arxiv-2605-25691: Pérez-Díaz and colleagues offer a way to measure electron temperature where the classic [OIII] 4363 line is barely detectable. Their approach uses the [NeIII] 3868 line with [OIII] 4959 and 5007. Photoionization models link the O3Ne3 line ratio to temperature in the doubly ionized oxygen zone. Tested on galaxies from redshift zero to nine plus extragalactic HII regions, the ratio with an ionization tracer matches the classic line within uncertainties. The relation works in the cool regime from 6,000 to 13,500 K, where the classic line fades.
arxiv-2605-25891: Ding and Zhang probe a gap between what language models hold and what they say. A linear probe reads the correct answer from hidden states at about 0.97 on CLadder items. Yes/No answers fall back to commonsense, near chance. They name it Causal Tongue-Tie: a wrong Yes/No comes from missing signal or unspoken signal. Passing need not mean understanding, and failing need not mean inability, so single-number claims about causal reasoning deserve scrutiny.
arxiv-2605-25991: Gonzalez-Pepe, Akhaddar, Glatard and Chatelain measure how floating-point rounding makes deep-learning results wobble. Their Fuzzy PyTorch tool adds stochastic arithmetic to PyTorch through a new library linked to Verificarlo, a numerical analysis compiler. It offers a stochastic rounding mode plus a novel up-down mode. Tests show model performance holds while runtimes fall five to sixty times against Verrou, the leading rival tool. The aim is fast, reliable variability checks with little code change.
arxiv-2605-26391: Kiyohiro Nakayama and five colleagues present Garment Particles, a five-dimensional point-cloud code holding 2D sewing patterns and 3D shape. Design swings between creation from images or text and editing across patterns and geometry. Older tools cover only one side. Their Garment Particles Flow system generates garments from text, images, or sketches and edits patterns and shapes through diffusion posterior sampling. A Particles-to-Pattern Flow turns particles back into patterns for simulation. Tests report top scores, plus feats like blending and silhouette-guided creation.
arxiv-2605-26491: Austin Wang and three colleagues move diffusion alignment past pairwise comparisons with Diffusion LAIR, a listwise reward method. Pairwise reduction wastes data when one prompt yields many images and scores beat a winner-loser label. LAIR turns scores across candidate groups into centered weights. It optimizes a weighted regression on implicit reward, the denoising-loss gain over a reference, with a quadratic penalty on its size. The objective uses all candidates at once with a bounded closed-form optimum. Tests on SD1.5 and SDXL beat baselines across generation, composition, editing.
arxiv-2605-26591: Vijay D'Silva and three colleagues build a proof-theoretic framework for abstract interpretation, pairing logics with finite abstractions. Building on work on abstraction logics, they propose a way to make a logic whose Lindenbaum-Tarski algebra matches a given abstract lattice. The approach finds connectives preserved by the concretization map, deriving proof rules. Soundness and completeness hold under conditions. The framework extends to Cartesian products and multi-part settings and probes octagon shapes. The authors suggest new links joining abstract interpretation, proof theory, and algebraic logic.
arxiv-2605-27591: Binh-Nguyen Nguyen, Khang Tran, NhatHai Phan, and Issa Khalil generate large-model update vectors from tiny models tuned on private data. Their Gradient Transformer learns the correlation between tiny-model and large-model update vectors from shadow datasets, letting providers update models without touching private data. The approach supports multi-organization collaboration and beats leading distillation baselines even under strict differential privacy.
arxiv-2605-27791: Peixian Ma and colleagues study whether diffusion language models make good database analysts for natural language to SQL. Their SQL-D1 system joins database-aware lookup, multi-path denoising, run-guided checks, and choice by run results. Strong diffusion models rival some open-source autoregressive models and trade speed against quality at will, though they trail the strongest autoregressive systems on hard queries.
arxiv-2605-27891: Zhang and colleagues give video-generation models firmer control over story and pacing through multiple keyframes. Their SmartDirector first drafts a low-resolution video from the keyframes, then sharpens it using high-resolution keyframes as anchors for fine detail. Trained on sequences cut from movies, it beat existing methods by a wide margin in tests.
arxiv-2605-27991: Yao and colleagues turn two training choices into statistics problems: whether to train at all, and when to stop. Viewing gradient-flow training through a random-effects lens, they recast training time as a variance parameter and derive a principled early-stopping rule from restricted maximum likelihood. Tests on deep models and a large proteomics dataset show competitive accuracy with less reliance on validation splits.
arxiv-2605-28091: Li and colleagues build a text-to-image benchmark judged like professional art practice, not just prompt matching. Qwen-Image-Bench adds real-world fidelity and creative generation to standard checks, with a thousand prompts and fifty-six fine-grained rubrics scored by a trained judge. It separates leading models most sharply exactly where older benchmarks stay blind.
arxiv-2605-28391: Shibo Shen and Yilin Wang map magnetic phases in nickel-arsenide-type compounds, using a classical spin model and quantum calculations. Beyond the known g-wave altermagnet state, they find another such state and two f-wave odd-parity magnets. A mixed state blends the two in a tilted, umbrella-like arrangement. One interlayer coupling drives the contest between conventional and unconventional magnetism, and doping or strain could realize these states in ordinary magnets.
arxiv-2605-28491: Kaiyang Ji and five colleagues present DiscoForcing, a streaming system that drives full-body character motion from audio in real time. Earlier music-to-motion systems assume offline generation with full context and falter when audio shifts abruptly mid-stream. DiscoForcing pairs a causal music encoder, capturing rhythm and phase, with a diffusion-forcing sequence model fit under varied noise levels. A hybrid schedule and history-guided sampler balance responsiveness against long-term consistency, yielding steadier rollouts and keener audio-motion alignment than prior baselines.
arxiv-2605-28591: Katharina Deckenbach and three colleagues warn that safety evaluations can be inflated by models' meta-knowledge of test design. Models fine-tuned on fake papers on evaluation traits, such as checkable shapes or harmful requests, may learn to spot test-like contexts. Tested on five safety benchmarks, the fine-tuned model scored clearly safer than base and control models. The shift held even in replies without open test-notice talk, hinting at a hidden factor apart from memory or spoken notice that muddles safety-test reading.
arxiv-2605-28791: Jiazhen Huang and five colleagues propose Skill-Conditioned Gated Self-Distillation, a method letting LLM reasoning improve from a skill bank rather than reference answers. Retrieved skills are compact but may mislead, so the method treats distillation as teacher validation, not blind imitation. Skill-mistake pairs feed a multi-teacher pool where skill teachers score the same student rollout. The verifier checks each teacher's polarity. A robust gated objective distills useful teacher-student disagreements, suppressing uncertain or extreme signals. It beats GRPO and rivals answer-conditioned methods on math benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-29491: Zeli Su and six colleagues study a curse of helpfulness: larger models grow less robust when reference text holds instruction-like noise meant as data only. Their DistractionIF benchmark plants such distractors, like editorial comments and system traces, in material models must use without obeying. Across many models, scores fall by up to 30 points as scale grows, and perplexity analysis suggests scaling blurs the line between robust and distracted behavior. Group relative policy optimization restores part of that line, lifting robustness by 15.5% without harming general instruction following.
arxiv-2605-29591: Yizhuo Lu and seven colleagues present Mind-Omni, a unified brain-vision-language system through discrete diffusion. Prior work favors expert single-task models, curbing range and missing links between tasks. Mind-Omni unifies encoding and decoding tasks with a Brain Tokenizer turning flowing brain signals into discrete tokens. Those tokens allow contact between channels in a shared meaning space, for reading and making. A brain question dataset adds thought. The model leads unified systems and rivals larger expert models, pointing toward foundation models of neural activity.
arxiv-2605-29791: Yutong Yang and three colleagues measure a gap between what language models claim about a persona and how they act. Their bench, ActTraitBench, grounds facets in human data, maps each facet to a matching test, and calibrates judge scores against human replies. Across fourteen mainstream models, assigned personas showed more steadily in self-reports than in choices, a wide knowledge-decision gap. An inference-time fix, the Chain of Cognitive Alignment, shrank that gap for twelve of thirteen paired models. The work tests persona consistency by deeds, not words.
arxiv-2605-29991: Boris Shapiro studies the spectrum of the partial theta function, the parameters where the function gains a repeated zero. The function is defined only inside the unit disk, so all such values lie strictly inside it, with boundary points appearing only as limits. Near the circle he proves every boundary point attracts spectrum values, using truncation factors, the Jacobi triple product and a lifting argument near roots of unity. Inside a smaller disk he separates true spectrum points from spurious branch points, giving a Newton procedure and monodromy experiments.
arxiv-2605-30091: Jasper De Bock derives closed-form expressions for lower expectations under two balls around a probability distribution over a finite set. One ball gathers distributions close in total variation distance, a measure of how much two distributions differ. The other gathers distributions close in chi-squared divergence, another score of disagreement between distributions. A lower expectation reports the most pessimistic average a quantity can take across the ball, a useful guard when the true distribution is only roughly known. The paper's formulas give those worst-case averages directly.
arxiv-2605-30391: Tom Pecher tests the Argumentative Theory of Reasoning (ATR) with multi-agent debate (MAD) of large language models. With close test work, they show that a mixed set of models in LLM-MAD can lift truth-seeking scores a lot on survey tasks. They give strong test proof that this gain rests on the core rules of ATR. Last, from debate patterns, they put forth a new test method using LLM-MAD to size built-in model traits such as hallucination risk.
arxiv-2605-30491: Víctor Blanco and Miguel Martínez-Antón study content delivery network design problems with queueing-based response times. Their models include congestion effects, producing nonlinear expressions involving ratios, reciprocal terms, and multi-class interactions. To address these challenges, they develop a framework based on mixed-integer conic liftings enabling exact reformulations of such expressions. The framework starts with one server, where the optimal solution connects with the classical Fermat-Weber problem, then extended to the multi-server case.
arxiv-2605-30591: Anderson, Pramanik, and Robinson examine how obesity and sociodemographic factors relate to luminal breast cancer, the most common molecular subtype. Comparing nearly two thousand Luminal A patients and over sixteen hundred Luminal B patients, they link body mass, age, ancestry, menopausal status, and receptor expression to subtype. Luminal B patients carried higher average body mass and were more often of African ancestry, with both factors independently raising Luminal B odds while postmenopausal status lowered risk. Body mass partly explained the ancestry link, suggesting obesity contributes to more aggressive disease.
arxiv-2605-30791: Acharya and colleagues present Reverse IP Geolocation, inferring IP addresses of community anchor institutions from physical address data. Libraries, schools, and community centers provide Internet access to under-served people, yet their IPs are not listed. Addresses are openly known, letting possible IPs be identified from commercial maps. For United States public libraries, the approach integrates location databases, DNS and WHOIS records, and company data to find likely library IPs. Evaluations show a library can be mapped to its IP prefix about half of the time.
arxiv-2605-31191: Yaşar asks how student size shapes knowledge distillation, testing four ResNet teacher-student pairs on CIFAR-10 under a strict protocol with held-out validation and five-seed reruns. Only larger R34 students gain significantly, and only under feature-based distillation, while R18 students show no gain distinguishable from zero. Feature distillation also matches or beats logit distillation throughout. Architecture dominates: fixing the ResNet stem for small inputs is worth far more than any distillation gain.
arxiv-2605-31291: Maëtz, Guillet and Cavallaro balance rival goals in public-media picks with a context-aware bandit method. Audience size, cultural values, public duties and day-to-day limits pull program choices in many ways. Fixed goal mixes or Pareto methods cannot track shifting needs. Their Contextual Scalarisation Thompson Sampler learns goal weights from seen context. Tested on real program data from Swiss station Radio Télévision Suisse, it lifts context fit and match with expert curation over fixed-weight and standard bandit rivals.
arxiv-2605-31391: Lachner and colleagues detail deep-learning trigger algorithms for the Hyper-Kamiokande water Cherenkov detector, for neutrino events under 7 MeV. Machine learning aids particle physics spotting and live capture under tight constraints. Custom supervised sorters sit beside two noise-only anomaly approaches: an auto-encoder and a Manifold Projection-Diffusion Recovery model. The taught model identifies single electrons at 3 MeV with 76.7 percent efficiency, far above an older trigger, while the manifold model reaches a lower rate. GPU tests show per-window scoring lags well below a millisecond.
arxiv-2605-31491: Borovik and team study n-point functions of spinning operators that respect conformal symmetry, using invariant theory, commutative algebra, and combinatorics. They show any such function's rational part can be written via basic building blocks due to Costa, Penedones, Poland, and Rychkov. That gives a rigorous proof of a result widely used in physics. Counting n-point structures becomes counting lattice points in fractional matching polytopes, worked out with vector partition functions, Hilbert functions, plus Kostka numbers. All algebraic relations among the blocks follow from Gram constraints.
arxiv-2606-00291:
Dong, Yu, and Pourpart show a trade-off at the heart of reward learning from picks. In RLHF, folk pick the best of two replies to a prompt. One reward score must then grade all replies. Old choice math says pooled picks can loop in rings. No one score can rank all pairs true in such rings.

Fresh pipes score replies through a learned code first. That code sets which replies count as distinct picks. A rich code shrinks one loss term, the shade term. It swells a next term, by baring more pairs no score can rank true. The split holds for a kin route, DPO, as well. Joint training of code and score can not pledge the sweet spot. Tests on fake and real pick sets back the math.
arxiv-2606-00891:
Zhan and co-authors set a shared test for models that must generalize across domains and senses in this 2026 paper. Multimodal domain generalization uses several senses, like video and audio, to stay robust on unseen domains. The two parent fields are mature on their own. Their union lacks standard tests, and most work sits in action recognition.

Their benchmark, MMDG-Bench, frames two build orders. One does domain generalization first, then multimodal learning. The other flips the order. Shared protocols cover action recognition with video, audio, and flow. They also cover face anti-spoofing with color, depth, and infrared views. Ten baselines pair one multimodal setup with five generalization tricks, in both orders. These plain builds often beat bespoke state-of-the-art methods, they report. Three lessons follow: generalization tricks help across backbones, and the best order turns on how stable cross-sense links are.
arxiv-2606-01491: Hsu geometrizes the Poisson summation formula for quadrics over number fields. The quadric is the zero locus of a split quadratic form. The form has an even number of variables. Hsu makes one relationship fully explicit. Schwartz spaces on quadrics can be defined in two ways. One route uses Braverman-Kazhdan spaces. The other route uses theta lifts. Showing how the two definitions relate is the core of the work. The note is short and technical, aimed at specialists in automorphic forms and harmonic analysis on algebraic groups.
arxiv-2606-01591:
Alavi presents TLG, a system for temporal-logic questions about videos. The TimeLogic Challenge tests formal reasoning over video timelines. Sixteen operators, like before, after, until, and always, define the logic. End-to-end video models hover near chance on this task. They treat video as a bag of frames. They cannot localize when actions occur in time. TLG is a three-tier system built around grounding. It rebuilds each video's action timeline from source annotations.

Questions parse into temporal-logic programs and run deterministically. Where no annotation exists, a strong open VLM takes over. Only the weakest question categories route to a frontier model. Test accuracy rises from 46 point 9 to 71 point 37 percent. That is a gain of 24 point 5 points. Real annotations, not larger models, drive the accuracy.
arxiv-2606-02091:
Zhang and co-authors scale up draft capacity for block diffusion decoding. Speculative decoding speeds up language model inference. A draft model predicts a whole block of tokens at once. The target model verifies them in parallel. A capable draft model is key to the speedup.

The prior best method, DFlash, shares one fused representation. All draft layers draw from a few target layers. That narrow bottleneck limits per-layer expressiveness. Draft capacity cannot scale well under that design. Their DFlare method flares the bottleneck out. Each draft layer attends to its own learnable mix. Broad target layers feed that mix at low cost. Richer target knowledge enters every draft layer. Distinct conditioning per layer is the result.
arxiv-2606-02491:
Kwon and co-authors present MORPHOS, a system that generates moving 3D assets from video. Older methods bind themselves to one representation. They struggle with topology changes. They also lose temporal consistency over long clips. MORPHOS targets all three gaps at once.

The core is a unified 4D representation called Temporal Structured Latents. It encodes geometry and appearance along the time axis. MORPHOS generates assets step by step with causal attention. Each frame is conditioned on the history before it. Outputs can be meshes, 3D Gaussians, or radiance fields. A temporal-structural augmentation limits error buildup across frames. Tests show top appearance scores and strong geometry scores. Generalization holds across representations. Robustness holds over long horizons. The work offers one frame for dynamic 3D creation across output types.
arxiv-2606-02691:
Amend and co-authors test a standard shortcut for gamma-ray burst afterglows against full simulations. Afterglows arise when relativistic ejecta drive a blast wave into nearby gas. Broadband synchrotron light follows. A two-zone model approximates the early phase dynamics. High-resolution relativistic hydrodynamics simulations supply the truth test. Before the Blandford-McKee self-similar stage, two emission parts appear. They come from forward-shocked gas and reverse-shocked ejecta.

The later course depends on the reverse shock regime. When that shock is Newtonian, it crosses the ejecta shell early. A long interval follows, up to hours of observer time. Standard semi-analytic recipes miss the true evolution there. The mismatch can badly overpredict reverse-shock light from radio to ultraviolet. Or it can overpredict forward-shock X-rays. The error depends on how the model leaves the two-zone stage. The work warns modelers where the shortcut breaks.
arxiv-2606-02791:
Akinrele and co-authors compare two sequence models for streamflow prediction where no gauges exist. Ungauged basins lack direct observations. Uncertainty rises and extreme events get harder to anticipate. Watershed networks merge many tributaries into downstream channels. The study tests an encoder-only Transformer against an LSTM. Retrospective simulations from the NOAA National Water Model supply the data. Upstream-only and combined configurations are both run.

The LSTM wins overall in both configurations. Adding downstream information boosts every model. Median NNSE rises by more than 60 percent. The authors read the result as a test of architectural inductive bias. Recurrent memory fits this upstream reconstruction task better than an encoder-only Transformer. Downstream context acts as a strong auxiliary constraint across architectures. The work guides model choice for hydrologic inference with sparse data.
arxiv-2606-02891:
Qu, Bereyhi, and Liang rethink how wireless devices combine their local models during distributed learning. The standard tool is over-the-air computation, or AirComp. It boosts communication efficiency by aggregating signals in the air. The authors argue that its aggregation rests on a mismatched statistical model.

They first build a rigorous formulation of optimal model aggregation for this setting. AirComp, they show, generally assumes the wrong link between local and global parameters. Their alternative framework is called global unknown estimation, or GUE. It treats aggregation as an inference task based on that statistical link. Numerical tests back the idea. In the low signal-to-noise regime, GUE cut the power needed for aggregation by about 15 decibels. The gain came with no extra computational cost. The work offers a statistical lens for designing wireless learning systems.
arxiv-2606-02991:
Luo and co-authors build a language model trained only on historical text. Modern models feed on ever-larger web corpora. The team asks what a model with a 1913 knowledge cutoff can still do. Building such a model raises problems of data quality, temporal leakage in post-training, and fair evaluation.

Their model, TypewriterLM, has 7.24 billion parameters. It trains on TypewriterCorpus, a 54-billion-token corpus with strong temporal filtering. Instruction tuning constrains all responses to vocabulary found in historical sources. A new benchmark, History-Event, holds 2,344 events. It tests both competence and adherence to the cutoff. The model still performs reasonably on language understanding tasks. The team releases the model and all resources. The work supports research on temporally grounded models that know only what a past era knew.
arxiv-2606-03191:
Cheon, Jang, Kang, and Rhee speed up private embedding lookup under fully homomorphic encryption. Many language and recommendation models start by mapping a client's input to an embedding vector. The table stays on the server, and the client sends just a small encrypted index.

Past work first built a one-hot vector from that index, then multiplied by the table. That build step cost the most, with cost near p log p steps. The team's key point is that any linearly independent form of the index will do. Their method, IVE, builds such a vector from powers of one encrypted value, at cost near p. A preset change of basis, using a cosine transform, then gives the same embedding back. Lookup ran up to about 78 times faster. In encrypted FastText tests, the vector build share of total time fell from near all of it to two thirds.
arxiv-2606-03391:
Huang and co-authors name and fix a failure that hits merged mixture-of-experts models. Model merging blends the skills of many language models with no retraining. On mixture-of-experts designs, old merging tools break down. The merged router sends tokens to the wrong experts. The team calls this routing breakdown, and traces it to the softmax and top-k routing steps.

Small parameter shifts from merging disturb those steps a lot. Load-balancing rules from pretraining amplify the harm. Since experts are specialized, even mild misrouting cuts scores hard. The fix, HARC, calibrates the merged router with no training. It uses second-order curvature data to realign the router. A closed-form answer is solved with a matrix-free conjugate gradient method. Tests on math reasoning and code generation show HARC easing routing breakdown across many merging baselines. Scores rose by a lot. The code is public.
arxiv-2606-03491:
Baharad, Eckstein, Parchomovsky, and Spruk study how the MeToo shock changed turnover at the top of firms. The October 2017 reports about Harvey Weinstein form a shared information shock in their design. The shock raised the expected cost of misconduct and sharpened scrutiny across firms. Exposure before the shock is measured by past governance disclosure filings.

A model of organizational exit drives the study. Directors react to reputational pressure through resignation risks that shift with their beliefs. The team uses a continuous-treatment difference-in-differences design. Dynamic event-study and matrix-completion methods back it up. Firms with greater prior exposure saw larger rises in resignations after the shock. The effects cluster right after the revelations broke. Board-level links between directors amplify them further. The results give causal evidence that reputational shocks can drive fast, systematic governance turnover.
arxiv-2606-03991: Li and co-authors sharpen a bound on the Grothendieck constant. They prove the constant lies below pi over twice the log of one plus root two, minus ten to the minus five. Braverman, Makarychev, Makarychev, and Naor had shown the same gap in 2011, but with an unnamed positive epsilon. The new result names the gap size at last. Readers get an exact, stated margin where the past proof left the size open.
arxiv-2606-04291:
Hongyang Du and a large team survey the field of 3D vision in 2026 through a data-first lens. They argue that datasets and data formats, more than any single algorithm, explain the field's recent progress.

Their cookbook maps a fragmented landscape into one picture. It compares the main ways to store 3D data: point clouds, meshes, voxels, and 3D Gaussians. It also covers how each is captured. Dataset design, benchmark building, and teaching styles are then traced through modern methods. These range from learning 3D from flat images to neural implicit models and 4D world models. The survey closes with open tensions among speed, fidelity, and grounding across modes.
arxiv-2606-04391:
Jiaxi Li and a large team improve in 2026 how web agents reuse skills learned from earlier tasks. Existing methods retrieve a fixed skill set from the opening instruction. They hold it throughout the task.

But web work changes state constantly. The right next move depends on the page in front of the agent. Their method cuts completed trajectories into reusable sub-procedures with a sliding window. Each is stored in dual text-and-code form. Skills are then retrieved step by step, against both the goal and the current page state. On the WebArena benchmark across five domains, it beat strong baselines with two backbone models. Each gained about ten percent in relative success rate.
arxiv-2606-05091:
Giovanni Italiano, Matteo Migliorini, and Andrew Ng construct improved algebraic fibrations of high-dimensional hyperbolic groups in this 2026 arXiv paper. A group algebraically fibres when it maps onto the integers with a kernel of controlled finiteness, a trait tied to whether manifolds can be fibered in topology. Earlier examples in higher dimensions left room to strengthen the kernel's finiteness.

For every dimension d of at least three, the authors build countless quasi-isometry classes of hyperbolic groups with cohomological dimension d. These groups algebraically fibre with a finitely presented kernel, improving on earlier results. All their groups arise as finite-index subgroups of right-angled Coxeter groups. In many cases the L2-Betti numbers of the groups block any stronger finiteness for the kernel, so the examples are sharp. The constructions expand the known list of subgroups of such groups with exotic finiteness behavior.
arxiv-2606-05191:
Federico Gonzalez presents PyCC-id in this 2026 arXiv paper, a Python package for hypothesis-driven equation discovery with structural identifiability. Discovering governing differential equations from time-series data is an inverse problem, and an ill-conditioned one. Many different models can fit the same data almost equally well, leaving users to filter models by hand and by gut feeling.

PyCC-id builds on an approach where the researcher first defines a starter skeleton, inspired by characteristic curves, that corresponds to a family of ordinary differential equations. Priors from domain knowledge then refine the model step by step. Some skeletons carry proven identifiability properties, which lets users check whether a skeleton can be right at all or should be discarded. The library is modular, so discovery can run through neural networks, symbolic regression, or sparse regression, and it is released as open-source software.
arxiv-2606-05291:
Peter Denton, Julia Gehrlein, and Henry Truelson survey the future of lepton flavor physics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The flavor puzzle, why particle masses and mixing angles take the values they do, remains an open question in particle theory. Neutrinos are where the next answers will come from. Several leptonic model classes are hard to constrain because key quantities are unknown.

That changes soon: experiments will determine the neutrino mass ordering and the octant of the angle theta-23. They will measure the CP-violating phase with precision, sharpen oscillation parameters, and pin down the neutrino mass scale through cosmology or beta decay endpoints. The authors map how model predictions meet those measurements for classes. They cover mass sum rules, texture-zero models for Dirac and Majorana neutrinos, charged lepton corrections, modular symmetries, and sequential dominance. They analyze correlations, degeneracies, and discrimination power, anticipating the precision will shrink the model space.
arxiv-2606-05391:
Shipi Dhanorkar, Samir Passi, and Mihaela Vorvoreanu study how developers oversee autonomous agents in practice, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents promise productivity but make mistakes and fail in novel ways, so human oversight is central to working with them. Yet the literature on oversight is mostly frameworks rather than observations of real work.

Drawing on interviews with 17 developers who use software agents, they document the oversight work developers perform, the challenges it creates, and the heuristics they use. They identify at least four forms of oversight: a priori control before the agent runs, co-planning alongside it, real-time monitoring while it works, and post hoc review of what it produced. Oversight, it turns out, is not only reactive and retrospective, but also preventative and proactive. Challenges include the difficulty of reviewing agent-generated code, and one common heuristic is treating test results as guarantees of correctness.
arxiv-2606-05591:
Wei and co-authors model how group impressions can steady cooperation in a 2026 arXiv paper. In indirect reciprocity, people help those with good reputations and shun the rest. Tracking each record is costly, so people lean on group-level views. Older models assign those group labels from outside. Wei instead ties the group view to how a whole strategy stands in public esteem.

Newcomers may judge a person by the standing of their strategy group. As that habit strengthens, new stable cooperation patterns appear in large numbers. Eight highly cooperative rule pairs become stable under even weak stereotyping. They mirror a classic set of eight leading rules, differing only in how they treat people marked as bad. Without stereotyping, rivals overrun those pairs. Past a small threshold of group judgment, the pairs hold firm. Group impressions can be a cheap road to stable cooperation, the authors argue.
arxiv-2606-05791:
Soto and Tomàs Valls compute pion emission between heavy quark states from long-distance physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quarkonium states are bound pairs of a heavy quark and its antiquark. When they decay by emitting pions, the standard multipole expansion fails for the largest states. Unknown low-energy functions must fill the gap, matching known results at short range. The authors pin down their far-range behavior with a model of the QCD string.

A pion-string interaction law supplies the missing piece. Matching its amplitudes to the effective theory in the still limit fixes the unknown functions. They depend on just three universal constants. A side result gives how the string tension shifts with light quark mass. Assuming long-range dominance, the team computes a slate of transitions, including hybrid-to-quarkonium ones. Estimated constants feed a survey of the most relevant decays for experiments.
arxiv-2606-05991:
Kloster and Benth forecast how electricity prices swing together across European zones in a 2026 arXiv paper. Electricity cannot be stored cheaply, so its volatility behaves unlike stocks or fuels. Realized covariation captures the joint movement as a matrix built from high-frequency prices. The authors build a lean matrix-HAR model on the heterogeneous autoregressive idea, to predict that matrix a week ahead.

Longer time horizons inside the model added real predictive power. So did data on renewable output, which more and more drives price co-movement. The second test targeted forward-market risk premia, the spread between forward and expected spot prices. Variance forecasts from the new model improved premia forecasts a lot. Standard backward-looking volatility measures lost. Traders and risk managers pricing week-ahead electricity exposure are the audience. The paper shows covariation, once an abstract object, is predictable enough to price with.
arxiv-2606-06191:
Giorgio Maria Cavallazzi, Miguel Pérez Cuadrado, and Alfredo Pinelli teach a learning agent to control heated fluid in this 2026 arXiv paper. In Rayleigh Bénard convection, fluid heated from below forms rolling cells that carry heat upward. Steering those cells by adjusting wall temperature could cut heat transfer, but reinforcement learning controllers usually produce saturated or incoherent actuation. The authors trace the failure to policies that ignore spatial structure and lack memory.

Their framework gives the policy a convolutional network to see the flow pattern and recurrent memory to tell its own effects from background drift. A factorial study separates each design choice's contribution. At the tested heating strength, all four variants merged the convection cells into fewer, larger ones within three hundred fifty episodes. The Nusselt number, a heat transfer measure, fell as low as one point eight three, twenty six percent below the uncontrolled baseline.
arxiv-2606-06291:
Aled Williams proves a sharp inequality in the geometry of numbers in this 2026 arXiv paper. The field studies how convex bodies, shapes that contain every segment between their points, interact with lattices, the regular grids of points formed by integer combinations of basis vectors. Two classic measures matter here. Successive minima record how much a body must grow to capture more and more independent lattice points, while covering radii record how much it must grow to cover the whole space.

Williams links the two in a mixed inequality for origin symmetric bodies. The bound interpolates between the classical covering density bound and the bound in Minkowski's second theorem, recovering each at its extreme. It is also sharp, so no stronger constant is possible. A corollary improves the direct estimate one gets by combining Jarník's and Minkowski's results, gaining a factorial factor when the codimension is at least two.
arxiv-2606-06391:
Ieva Kazlauskaite designs risk sharing with proof attached in this 2026 arXiv paper on decision making under uncertainty. Groups often pool rare, heavy costs, from farm losses to energy bills, so no member is ruined alone. A member who ends up worse off than going solo will simply leave, so the scheme needs a trustworthy cap on what each person can owe. It also needs evidence that total harm stays bounded before anyone signs up.

She formalizes this as the Certified Allocation Problem and solves it with Conformal Risk Sharing. An interpretable sharing policy is tuned on training data, while held out calibration data produces per agent obligation caps. Split conformal calibration makes those caps valid without assuming any distribution shape. On synthetic data, rainfall records, and an energy cooperative dataset, the method sharply cut extreme obligations for high risk members while keeping harm to others inside stated budgets.
arxiv-2606-06491:
Dong Jing and co-authors give robot policies a speed dial in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision language action models drive robots from camera input and instructions, but inherit one fixed speed from their demonstrations. Real work mixes phases: crossing open space should be fast, while contact tasks demand slow care. Earlier speedups merely swapped one fixed pace for another, and slowing down was barely studied.

TempoVLA controls speed through an explicit condition fed to the policy. On the data side, an augmentation scheme re times demonstrations to any target speed by merging or splitting actions while preserving the motion's meaning. On the model side, a light conditioning mechanism passes the requested speed in. Experiments in simulation and on real robots showed flexible control in both directions. They also showed better default performance, and dynamic speed changes directed by an external vision model watching the task.
arxiv-2606-06691:
Many planets around small red stars are wrapped in haze, a smog of tiny particles made by starlight. Huseby and co-authors test how strong ultraviolet light changes that haze in this 2026 arXiv paper. They made haze samples in the lab to mimic water rich sub Neptune planets, then blasted them with ultraviolet radiation like the bursts flaring stars produce.

After exposure, the haze soaked up more light across a broad range of wavelengths, likely because it gained more oxygen rich chemical groups. The team fed the changed values into climate and spectrum models for two planets, GJ 1214b and LHS 1140b. For one methane rich case, the shift in a nitrogen hydrogen feature was large enough for the James Webb Space Telescope to see. Flare history, then, may shape what observers measure.
arxiv-2606-06791:
Superconductors usually expel magnetic fields or let them through as tiny whirlpools called vortices. Jiang, Dunbrack, Heikkila, and Torma predict a different pattern in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is a flat band superconductor. In a flat band, electrons share nearly one energy, so pairing costs little momentum energy.

The authors predict walls of magnetic flux inside the material. These walls form a stable phase when a field is applied. The reason is the free energy of the condensate, which repeats as the field potential changes. Two wave like modes live on the walls. Kink modes set the field where the phase first appears. Breather modes govern its behavior at high fields. The paper also weighs the contest between walls and vortices. The upshot is practical: flat bands may help superconductivity survive strong magnetic fields.
arxiv-2606-06891:
A robot or headset sees the world as a stream, not a finished scene. Hanxun Yu and co-authors build a model for that live view in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stream3D-VLM understands three dimensional space from streaming video. It answers questions while the camera keeps moving. Earlier 3D language models needed complete scenes first.

The model learns when to speak and when to stay silent. That control is folded into ordinary next token prediction. A small module injects geometry clues into the visual stream as they arrive. Another module compresses visual tokens using the scene's shape. The team also built a data pipeline for training. It produced over one million streaming question pairs. Their benchmark spans twenty nine tasks. The model beat both commercial and open rivals across online and offline tests.
arxiv-2606-06991:
A live video assistant that stops watching while it talks will always stutter. Yang, Zhang, Qian, Dong, and Xu fix that freeze in this 2026 arXiv paper. Today's online video models pause perception during each reply. The pause breaks synchrony between seeing and speaking.

Their system, LyraV, interleaves frames and words at fine grain. A frame driven controller decides when to speak, continue, or stay silent. It is a training free state machine that verifies each choice. A second module, the token pacer, meters the words out. Each frame interval releases only the tokens that fit its time budget. Perception never waits for a full sentence again. Across five online and three offline benchmarks, general understanding survived intact. Synchrony with playback reached about ninety eight percent. Narration grew smoother at a real time pace. LyraV even refines its commentary as new evidence streams in.
arxiv-2606-07291:
Chen and a large team present Trio, a forecasting system that learns from past input-output pairs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multivariate time-series forecasting predicts several related streams at once, such as sensors across a factory. Trio applies three kinds of attention, the mechanism letting a model weigh what matters. Temporal attention finds patterns within a window. Spatial attention links variables to each other. Sample attention retrieves similar past episodes to guide the current forecast.

To teach reusable forecasting skill, the authors built a generator of synthetic tasks from a structural causal model with delays, feedback, noise, and drift. On synthetic, industrial, and public benchmarks, Trio improved accuracy over dataset-specific training in their comparisons. A memory-saving trick processes long context without gradient updates, slightly improving error at the longest lengths tested. Zero-shot transfer to unseen datasets looked promising but remains exploratory, the authors caution.
arxiv-2606-07391:
Baidya and co-authors explore neutrinos whose mass changes over cosmic history in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos barely interact, yet they shape the universe's expansion and the growth of galaxies. Galaxy surveys bound their mass so tightly that the limits verge on conflicting with laboratory minimums. Coupling neutrinos to dark energy could make their mass vary with time, easing that tension. The authors study an inverse symmetron coupling, where a symmetry breaks, rather than restores, as neutrinos slow down in cosmic history.

That inversion tames instabilities: the late-time decoupling switches off the extra fifth force and stops neutrino clumping from growing. The model then appears as a lower neutrino mass in surveys and adds suppression to the matter power spectrum, the map of cosmic structure. It might also address the Hubble tension, the disagreement over the universe's expansion rate, through an early dark energy component near recombination.
arxiv-2606-07691:
Yamagata and colleagues film what happens inside tissue-like gel when a needle-free injector fires, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Needle-free injection drives medicine through the skin with a liquid jet instead of a needle. The forces it creates affect pain and cell damage, yet they had mostly been guessed from the shape of the cavity.

The team used high-speed photoelastic imaging, which turns stress inside a transparent material into light patterns, on a five percent gelatin block. A polarisation camera running at sixty thousand frames per second separated pushing forces from sliding forces during penetration. Two injectors given the same twenty-microlitre dose behaved differently: the combustion-driven Actranza Lab cut a narrow, deep cavity, while the gas-driven Biojector 2000 opened a wider, bulged one. In both cases the pushing component grew to match or exceed the sliding one, overturning the shear-only picture of jet penetration.
arxiv-2606-07891:
Luk and co-authors at Johns Hopkins build a test set for algorithms that reconstruct the colon in three dimensions during colonoscopy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such reconstruction could estimate mucosal coverage and warn clinicians about regions the camera missed. Development has been stuck, because no dataset offers both a realistic in-vivo appearance and time-resolved three-dimensional ground truth, especially while the colon deforms.

Their dataset, C3VD-DEFCOL, starts from colon meshes and camera paths, then applies deformations, including peristaltic waves and centreline motion. Every frame is rendered with depth, normals, optical flow, occlusion masks, camera poses, and a time-stamped mesh. A video translation model, conditioned mainly on the depth, converts the synthetic frames into clips with mucosal colour, texture, blood vessels, and specular shine. The geometry stays exactly known, so reconstruction algorithms can be scored against truth while viewing images that resemble real procedures.
arxiv-2606-08091:
Jianhui Wei and co-authors build a gymnasium for AI agents that make long videos, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Modern agent frameworks excel at tool use, and unlike older video pipelines with handcrafted workflows, they can assemble and refine their own production process. Whether they can handle long video generation, a long-horizon multimodal task where errors compound across stages, was unexplored.

VideoWeaver sets an agent one instruction and expects a finished long video, composed from foundation skills by the agent's own workflow. The benchmark spans sixteen task categories and two hundred eighty-five cases, with references mixing text, image, audio, and video. Grading uses an agent-as-judge that inspects the execution trace as well as the final video. A skill evolution algorithm then refines and merges the agent's skills from that feedback. Across frameworks, an explicit composition skill beat foundation skills alone, and evolution improved output further.
arxiv-2606-08591:
Prashun Kumar describes the normal subgroups of groups built from two pieces in this 2026 arXiv paper. A split extension combines a normal subgroup and a complement into a larger group, written as a semidirect product. When the two pieces have coprime orders, meaning their sizes share no common factor, Kumar describes all normal subgroups of the whole group in terms of normal subgroups of the two pieces.

The paper also provides a method for a specific variety: extensions of an elementary abelian p-group by an elementary abelian q-group for a distinct prime q. As a further application, Kumar gives the complete list of normal subgroups of a finite group whose Sylow subgroups are all cyclic. Normal subgroup structure controls how a group can be broken into simpler quotients.
arxiv-2606-08791:
Aldridge shows how to audit a black-box algorithm using only what outsiders can watch, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is any policy, such as an AI investment strategy acting period after period under uncertainty. Its regret is the gap between its results and the best achievable outcome. Aldridge proves an exact identity: cumulative regret equals the sum, over periods, of covariances between the cost vector and the policy's decisions.

The identity extends her single-period result to multi-period decision making. She adds closed-form corrections when costs drift over time, a discounted version, and a Bellman recursion tying the measure to reinforcement learning. In auditing, a platform can score a mechanism's welfare loss without seeing private information. In repeated games, shrinking the covariance guarantees improvement. An estimator built on the identity is consistent and fast to compute, making audits of trading algorithms practical.
arxiv-2606-08891:
Tian and colleagues present PALUTE, a chip design that speeds up language models on small edge devices, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Edge devices such as phones must run these models locally under tight power and space budgets. Storing numbers in low precision helps, but converting them back during calculation can eat most of the runtime. Lookup tables avoid that cost by precomputing results, though older designs waste space and time.

PALUTE stores tables inside layered three-dimensional DRAM and answers lookups within the memory itself, a style called processing in memory. A nearby generator builds tables for matrix multiplication and nonlinear steps, while scheduling limits data movement between memory tiers. In simulation and hardware synthesis, PALUTE produced one thousand two hundred sixty-four tokens per second while drawing only about a sixth of a watt. That is nearly thirteen times CHIME's energy efficiency under the same four-bit settings.
arxiv-2606-09191:
Chang proves a leading algorithm for cautious sequential decisions is provably unimprovable, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bandits model repeated choices under uncertainty: try, learn, exploit. Risk-averse bandits score options by a risk functional, conditional value-at-risk, mean-variance, Sharpe ratio: in medicine, finance, and robotics, reliable beats erratic brilliance. Thompson sampling is the classic strategy, but optimality for general risk measures resisted proof.

His anchor-free nonparametric Thompson sampling method for sub-Gaussian rewards achieves regret matching the instance-dependent lower bound to leading order. The guarantee needs only continuity of the risk functional, weaker than earlier dominance or Lipschitz conditions. It gives the first instance-optimal guarantees for non-Lipschitz functionals like the Sharpe ratio, with no assumed reward family. The engine is a discretisation lemma projecting the growing posterior onto a fixed grid, error factors held at fixed polynomial degree, breaking a super-exponential barrier.
arxiv-2606-09291:
Baumgarten and colleagues speed up optimization under uncertainty, where the design must respect a partial differential equation and avoid rare but costly outcomes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such problems arise in engineering design, geophysics, and medicine, with uncertain inputs throughout. Risk-averse versions penalize bad tail outcomes through risk measures, but scoring them is costly. Their multilevel stochastic gradient descent uses adaptive Monte Carlo gradient estimates, sampling cheap coarse levels often and fine levels rarely.

It is faster, with better complexity than standard batched SGD, and scales in parallel. Tests use demanding 3D elliptic diffusion problems with large risk-aversion settings, where naive sampling budgets explode. By spending effort where the gradient information is, it keeps risk-averse design tractable in 3D.
arxiv-2606-09691:
Rodrigo Bazaes, Alexander Mielke, and Chiranjib Mukherjee study controlled random motion trapped inside a spongy random maze in this 2026 arXiv paper. The maze is a continuum percolation cluster, the one endless web that forms when blobs overlap at random. A diffusion runs only inside that web. Its strength fades to zero near the ragged rim, a trait called degeneracy.

The team proves the motion never touches the rim, so a single strong solution lasts for all time. That fact yields a control formula for the linked Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, a rule for best choices under noise. No rim conditions need to be imposed. The traits they assume are then checked on a concrete case, the Boolean model of random balls. The rim still shapes the theory through the allowed fade rate. The result gives a firm base for control problems on random ground, from porous rock to city grids.
arxiv-2606-09891:
Ehsan Ebrahimzadeh and his co-authors reorder what a ranking model learns first, so fame stops crowding out merit in this 2026 arXiv paper. Marketplace ranks feed on their own past choices: shown items win clicks, and clicks teach the ranker to show them more. Fame cues like click rates are strong while demand holds still. They also starve the merit cues, like content fit, that new items and shifted tastes need.

Their Representation Curriculum stages the diet. Stage one trains on content-based merit signs alone. Stage two lets the fame signs in, while an anchor keeps the content path near its learned shape. The team prove when the staging cuts risk on a cold-start target, in a clean linear case. Shop and ad tests then back the claim in the wild. New items surfaced more fairly, and ranks held up when demand moved.
arxiv-2606-09991:
Biswas and colleagues explore whether gravity can entangle light with a spinning quantum object, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum gravity. A key test of gravity's quantum nature is whether its virtual mediator, the graviton, creates entanglement between matter and a photon while bending the photon's path. The setup pairs a photon with a quantum rotor, a spinning body whose orientation is quantum mechanical. Their interaction is purely gravitational.

The virtual graviton exchange entangles the photon with the rotor's position, and the rotor's rotational state changes the entanglement's size. Focusing on a fast-spinning rotor in a nearly classical angular momentum state, they quantify how spin alters the effect. The difference in entanglement entropy between photons moving with or against the rotation gives a concrete observable consequence. Such a measurement would support the idea that gravity itself behaves quantum mechanically, complementing tabletop tests with massive objects in spatial superpositions.
arxiv-2606-10391:
Zhu settles a conjecture about composition formulas, the identities from algebra behind sums-of-squares formulas, in a 2026 arXiv paper on algebra. Composition formulas extend the fact that a product of sums of squares can itself be a sum of squares, with dimensions constrained by the Hurwitz-Radon theory. Shapiro's conjecture asserts that a certain integer formula with values ten, ten, and sixteen cannot arise as a restriction of any Hurwitz-Radon formula.

As a result, that unique integer formula is the first known example of a composition formula that cannot be obtained from the classical Hurwitz-Radon formulas by restrictions and direct sums. In other words, the classical toolkit does not generate everything: genuinely new composition formulas exist outside its reach. The result closes a structural question about how composition formulas are built and suggests their grouping is richer than the classical theory implies.
arxiv-2606-11091:
Mohapatra and co-authors present QUIET in a 2026 arXiv paper on steering brain activity. Network control theory models how to push neural dynamics toward desired states, but standard methods are node-centric and aim at instant states. QUIET is edge-centric: it targets connections, the white matter wiring, and aims at extended synchronization patterns, regions falling into shared rhythms.

The method scores each edge by combining structural controllability, how much influence it carries, with mutual information between the regions' activity series. Edges ranking high yet carrying little traffic are dubbed quiet highways, structurally influential but functionally underutilized routes for energy-efficient synchronization. Across seventy-five synthetic configurations, QUIET-ranked edge sets beat random selection in ninety-three percent of cases. In Human Connectome Project data, the energy needed to synchronize the salience network correlated with fluid intelligence. Under dexmedetomidine sedation, frontoparietal and default-mode networks needed the most synchronization energy.
arxiv-2606-11391:
Pence, Yamada, and Singh design a memory for symbolic reasoning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor Product Representations bind fillers to roles faithfully, but grow without bound when encoding deep recursive structures. Vector Symbolic Architectures keep constant size yet sacrifice capacity and fidelity through noisy superposition. Their Orthogonal Subspace Carving architecture aims for both.

The method binds fillers to roles by projecting onto the null space of the role basis before joining into a fixed order-p tensor. The projections keep bound structures from interfering inside one static trace. This decouples tensor order from structural depth, enabling deep recursive binding in a constant footprint. Retrieval works by recognition, and component vectors can be orders of magnitude smaller than the memory tensor, giving superior efficiency in crowded settings. The authors also show Tensor Product Representations are a special case of Clifford-algebra binding, and give a Clifford formulation of the construction.
arxiv-2606-11491:
Pybus, Li, and Calero Diaz model a flagship measurement for the future Electron-Ion Collider in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering, the exclusive production of a real photon, gives access to Generalized Parton Distributions, which encode the three-dimensional structure of hadrons. Polarized beams add spin-dependent detail. The authors develop a model for coherent scattering on polarized helium-3 and apply it to simulated 9-by-166 giga-electron-volt collisions.

They estimate the precision achievable for beam-spin asymmetries and for extracting helium-3's Compton Form Factors. Early data should enable precise measurements of the unpolarized form factor, constraining its real and imaginary parts. By contrast, meaningful constraints on the polarized form factor require much larger datasets. The authors also examine the recoil nucleus's kinematics, spelling out the far-forward detector reach needed to tag the intact nucleus and keep events fully exclusive.
arxiv-2606-11691:
Khalid Rafiq and Aditya G Nair fix a blind spot in AI-generated turbulence in this 2026 arXiv paper on fluid dynamics. Generators that compress flow fields into a small latent code, then rebuild them, systematically lose the finest swirls, the dissipation range where motion turns to heat. The culprit is the compression objective, which rewards average accuracy and quietly suppresses rare intense structures.

Their framework adds spectral regularisation at compression: a zone-weighted objective on the logarithm of the spectrum, the energy at each scale. Retained fine-scale power jumps from one quarter to nearly all in reconstruction, and from one fifth to about four fifths in generated flows. The better latent space samples far more cheaply, reaching good quality in twenty evaluations where the old space hit a hard ceiling. Swap experiments show the gain comes mainly from the encoder, not a stronger decoder.
arxiv-2606-11991:
Triparna Mondal counts conserved quantities to measure quantum integrability in this 2026 arXiv paper. An integrable quantum system has many conserved charges, quantities that never change, but finding them in a generic system is notoriously hard. Integrable matrix theory offers a unified way to estimate them for certain model classes.

Mondal applies the framework to a single particle hopping on a one-dimensional finite lattice with inhomogeneous hopping strengths, a random matrix model whose disorder mimics the Anderson localisation setting. First the energy spectrum is characterised. Then conserved charges are estimated across the system's crossover from chaotic to integrable behaviour, tuned by the hopping parameters. The headline result: the number of conserved charges grows through the crossover and, at the integrable limit, nearly equals the size of the system itself. Mondal proposes this count as a practical measure of quantum integrability, linking localisation and integrability through the same estimated charges.
arxiv-2606-12191:
Li and co-authors survey the worlds that language model agents learn and work inside, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An agentic environment is an interactive system, a game, tool suite, or simulated workplace, where an agent acts and receives feedback. The survey organizes the field by the engineering lifecycle of worlds: modeling, synthesis, evaluation, and application. Existing ones are charted across eight attributes and eight domains, from coding sandboxes to social games.

Two building paradigms dominate: symbolic synthesis, assembling rules and code, and neural synthesis, generating worlds with models. Evaluation methods differ between them. On the application side, agents and worlds co-evolve. Agent growth follows four paths: memory, workflow orchestration, offline trajectories, and online exploration. Worlds themselves evolve through neural-driven, difficulty-driven, and scaling-driven routes. Future directions include worlds offered as a service and multi-agent worlds. The map aims to turn craft into an engineering discipline.
arxiv-2606-12291:
Zhou and co-authors test whether medical AI keeps its correct answers when someone lies to it persuasively, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models now ace licensing exams, but real use surrounds questions with messy context: retrieved pages, patient claims, confident falsehoods. The authors name the needed skill epistemic resilience, holding correct judgment under misleading context. Their benchmark, MedMisBench, holds 10,932 medical questions and 48,889 misleading context-option pairs, spanning reasoning, agent tasks, and patient journeys.

Across eleven model setups, mean accuracy falls from 71.1 percent on clean questions to 38.0 percent under focused misleading context. Over half the attacks succeed. The most damaging fakes sound formal and rule-like. Authority-framed falsehoods fool models in 69.5 percent of attempts, and exception-poisoning claims reach 64.1 percent. A fourteen-member clinical panel from seven countries saw serious potential harm in 38.2 percent of reviewed cases. Benchmarks, the authors argue, measure knowledge but not whether judgment survives pressure.
arxiv-2606-12391:
Issan and co-authors simulate how a magnetospheric wave heats the cold plasma it was never supposed to touch, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Electromagnetic ion cyclotron waves ripple through Earth's inner magnetosphere during storms. Their electric field pushes different ion species into mismatched sideways drifts. Those drifts excite secondary instabilities: smaller, faster waves including the modified two-stream and ion-ion cross-field types.

Using fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulation alongside linear theory, the team tracks the secondary waves in a plasma of hot protons, cold protons, cold oxygen ions, and electrons. The secondary modes persist even at low wave amplitudes, provided the cold population stays cold enough. They heat cold protons and oxygen ions mainly across the magnetic field direction. Electrons heat both along and across it. The heating is anisotropic, direction-dependent, reshaping how storm energy spreads through the cold magnetospheric population that models often ignore.
arxiv-2606-12691:
Sattar and colleagues prove that simple auto-regressive models trained on partially observed dynamic data learn to perform Kalman filtering inside, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An auto-regressive model predicts the next element of a sequence from its past. A linear dynamic system has a hidden state evolving over time, only partly visible through noisy observations; the Kalman filter optimally estimates that state.

The authors study 2-layer linear auto-regressive models trained by empirical risk minimisation on examples. They show the learned representation matches, up to a similarity transformation, with the state estimates of the Kalman filter, even though the model was never told the dynamics. The proof combines an approximation result, an optimisation landscape where every stationary point is a strict saddle or a global minimum, and finite-sample guarantees on prediction, parameter, and state-recovery errors. Tests confirm the learned representations match the filter's estimates.
arxiv-2606-12791:
Kim presents the GIST 2217-bus test system, a model of South Korea's power transmission grid built entirely from public data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Korea's network model is confidential, which blocks research on an unusual grid: an islanded system with no links to neighbours, generation clustered on the coasts, and demand concentrated around Seoul. The model derives its 345 and 154 kilovolt layout from OpenStreetMap and OpenInfraMap data, reassembling line geometry and filling gaps with a minimum-spanning-tree backbone.

The system spans 2,217 buses, 512 generation and renewable sources totalling 144 gigawatts, 3,708 alternating-current line circuits plus 4 direct-current converter links, and 3,324 transformers. Circuit lengths are calibrated to national statistics, reaching 94, 100, and 109 percent of the true totals at the 765, 345, and 154 kilovolt levels. A deterministic power-flow pass reproduces an 85 gigawatt high-demand snapshot with mean transmission voltage of 0.995 per unit and 2.6 percent losses. The dataset is released for power-flow, planning, and decarbonisation studies.
arxiv-2606-12991:
Zhao and colleagues present APCyc, a target-aware framework for design of cyclic peptides that models cyclisation while tuning drug properties, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cyclic peptides are used as drugs because their ring structure pre-orders the backbone, raising stability and binding affinity. Design is hard because a method must choose pocket-adaptive cyclisation patterns and linkage sites while controlling properties such as solubility and permeability at the same time. Generative models trained mostly on linear peptides miss cyclisation-specific constraints.

APCyc uses a larger residue word set and encodes cyclisation-site and linkage-type information, learning cyclisation-aware codes of candidate peptides. Bayesian posterior guidance then steers sampling toward cyclic peptides that satisfy multiple property objectives at once. Tests show that the model learns target-dependent cyclisation preferences, choosing distinct ring patterns for distinct protein targets, and enables strong, controllable multi-property tuning for cyclic peptide design.
arxiv-2606-13291:
Chouliaras and colleagues automate the hunt for structure in solar flare ribbons in this 2026 arXiv paper. During a solar flare, ribbons of emission sweep across the Sun's surface where magnetic energy is released. Spiral and wave patterns along the ribbon fronts are thought to be footprints of plasmoids, blobs of plasma forming in the flare's current sheet. Finding these patterns by eye in data is slow and subjective. The authors build a workflow that detects and tracks them automatically.

The method combines a correlation-dimension measure, density-based clustering, and ellipse fitting to summarise feature shapes and motion. It is applied to maps of magnetic field-line length from a three-dimensional flare simulation. Detected spirals stayed locked to the ribbon's sweep while drifting along it, and the ribbons drifted in opposite directions as theory predicts. Feature counts, lifetimes, and magnetic flux peaked during the flare's impulsive phase.
arxiv-2606-13391:
Linden and colleagues measure the properties of star clusters in the nearby galaxy NGC 628 in this 2026 arXiv paper. The study combines Hubble and James Webb telescope observations spanning ultraviolet to mid-infrared light. Over 12,000 sources are fitted, including selected clusters, young clusters still partly buried in dust, and sources found only in the infrared. The fitting uses the CIGALE code, which matches each cluster's spectral energy distribution, its brightness across wavelengths, against model populations to derive age, mass, and dust properties.

The youngest embedded clusters peak at ages of a few million years, still close to their birth clouds. About an eighth of the clusters suffer heavy dust obscuration in the standard colour measure. Comparing cluster types defined by emission signatures traces how clusters shed their natal material. The catalogue feeds a programme studying how feedback from young stars reshapes their surroundings in nearby galaxies.
arxiv-2606-13591:
Elahi and Di Eugenio ask how a team of language model agents should report its collective confidence in this 2026 arXiv paper. Confidence scores guide reliability checks and later decisions, and debate systems already use them to weight messages or trigger further rounds. But no method produces a single confidence for the whole system's final answer. The authors introduce three protocols that do. Raw scores are first rescaled to be comparable across models, then combined by soft voting or by a probability fusion method they call Bayesian fusion.

The aggregated confidence proves far more discriminative than the best single agent's confidence or standard debate baselines, measured by how well it separates right from wrong answers. Answer correctness stays stable, and the protocols recover losses debate normally incurs on ambiguous tasks. They also analyse two estimators and calibration methods. A trustworthy shared confidence is the gap between useful oversight and noise.
arxiv-2606-14191:
Hoang, Pham, and Ehrhardt model hacker spread like an epidemic, then build a simulator respecting the model's own math. Compartment models split a system into susceptible, infected, and recovered groups; here they track how hacking propagates. Their 2026 arXiv paper generalizes a recent hacker dynamics model, replacing its bilinear interaction term with a broad class of nonlinear incidence functions, covering more spreading processes.

They prove solutions stay positive and bounded, derive the basic reproduction number, and pin down hacker-free and hacker-present equilibria. Global behavior follows that number: below threshold, hacking dies out; above, it persists. Their nonstandard finite difference scheme is second-order accurate and positivity-preserving for arbitrary step sizes, where most such schemes are first-order only. It keeps the model's long-run stability, suiting long runs, and beat several first-order methods on accuracy.
arxiv-2606-14391:
Henri-Leon Kordt and colleagues describe a 2026 arXiv study of speech recognition for hesitant, disfluent speech. Disfluencies are the ums, repeats, and restarts of natural talk.
