Fourteen researchers from three continental regions split the topic into eleven issues. Pairs of experts drafted best-practice notes on each, from stating a chance to showing change over time. Some rules are blunt: always name the group a rate refers to, keep one format through a document, and avoid one-in-x phrasing, which readers judge poorly. Visual formats, plain labels, and honest treatment of doubt all get sections. The primer ends with guiding principles aid builders can apply directly.
europmc-pmc4053991:
Lin Li and a large team catalogue the long noncoding RNAs of maize, in Genome Biology in 2014. These transcripts, longer than two hundred letters and making no protein, were well mapped in animals but barely in this major crop.

Pooling public databases and thirty sequencing data sets, the team found over twenty thousand candidate noncoding RNAs. Most appear to be raw material for small RNAs. A stricter set of about seventeen hundred high-confidence entries remained. These run short, carry few exons, and over half switch on in just one or a few of the tissues tested, a pattern backed by their epigenetic marks. In crosses followed through more than a hundred inbred lines, expression of these RNAs was steered more by distant genetic factors than by nearby ones.
europmc-pmc4075091:
Mónika Lippai and Péter Lőw reviewed how cells pick and choose what to destroy through autophagy, the process that wraps cargo in membranes for breakdown. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International in 2014. Autophagy was once seen as indiscriminate, but it can in fact be selective.

Two cell systems, the proteasome and autophagy, were long viewed as separate, yet they share targets and regulators. Adaptor proteins such as p62 bind tagged cargo on one side and the autophagy machinery on the other. That lets cells single out damaged mitochondria, invading germs, and certain proteins for engulfment. Two ubiquitin-like protein systems are needed to build the wrapping membrane. The review explains how tagging gives autophagy its selectivity.
europmc-pmc4138991:
Adam McCluskey, Phillip J. Robinson, and a large team built improved versions of dynasore, a research drug that blocks dynamin, a protein needed for cells to swallow material. Their study appeared in Traffic in 2013. Dynasore itself proved weak in practice because it binds the detergents used in screening assays.

Bound to detergent, dynasore's potency collapsed, spoiling its value as a tool. The team synthesised a focused family of relatives, the Dyngo compounds, by moving or adding hydroxyl groups. Five showed better potency, less detergent binding, and lower cell toxicity. The best was many times stronger than dynasore against dynamin in its helical form, while sparing its ring form. Two compounds blocked dynamin-dependent uptake in cells.
europmc-pmc4218791:
Wilhelm Klümper and Matin Qaim pooled farm studies on genetically modified crops in PLoS ONE in 2014. GM soybean, maize, and cotton spread fast among farmers, yet public argument over their effects never settled. The pair gathered the scattered farm-level evidence into one statistical summary.

Across 147 original studies from field trials and farm surveys worldwide, adoption cut chemical pesticide use by 37 percent on average. It also raised yields by 22 percent and lifted farmer profits by 68 percent. Insect-resistant crops gained more than herbicide-tolerant ones, and farmers in developing countries gained more than those in developed ones. Some studies lacked the detail needed for full checks, the authors note, but the overall pattern of benefit was robust.
europmc-pmc4253991:
Stephan C. Bischoff, Jerry M. Wells, and seven co-authors reviewed the gut barrier as a treatment target in BMC Gastroenterology in 2014. The intestinal wall must do two opposite jobs: block germs and toxins, yet let water and nutrients through. Its leakiness, called intestinal permeability, is set by a layered barrier of mucus, cells, and tight seals between them.

Diet and gut microbes tune the barrier daily, while poor blood flow, infections, toxins, some drugs, and overdosed nutrients can pry it open. A leaky barrier is tied to bowel diseases, liver disease, and wider metabolic trouble. The review also grades the tests used to measure permeability, noting each probes a different part of the wall and results are hard to compare. Fixing the barrier, the authors argue, is an underused route to prevention and therapy.
europmc-pmc4279791:
Lars Skjærven, Xin-Qiu Yao, Guido Scarabelli, and Barry J Grant describe a major update to Bio3D, a software package for studying how proteins move. Their paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2014. A protein's job depends on its motion, yet tools for comparing structures, simulations, and family history were mostly separate.

The update links these views in one R package. New features run motion analysis across many related proteins at once. They measure how movements in one part of a protein couple to another. They also place those results next to sequence and structure change over evolution. The package is aimed at researchers who want dynamics and evolution in a single work flow.
europmc-pmc4299491:
Traver Hart, Kevin R Brown, Fabrice Sircoulomb, Robert Rottapel, and Jason Moffat built reference lists of genes that human cells can and cannot live without. Their paper appeared in Molecular Systems Biology in 2014. Genome wide screens knock down or knock out genes one by one to find which ones a cell needs, but stray effects and unmeasured error rates clouded the results.

From many screens the team derived gold standard sets of essential and nonessential genes. These sets let labs score how accurate a screen is and compare RNA interference with the newer CRISPR method on firm ground. Genes needed only by cancer cells stand out as drug targets, so cleaner screens sharpen that search as well.
europmc-pmc4301191:
Anoop S V Shah and eleven co-authors showed that a sharper blood test, read with sex specific cutoffs, finds many missed heart attacks in women. Their study appeared in The BMJ in 2015. Troponin, a protein released by damaged heart muscle, is the standard test, but the usual single threshold was set in a way that favors men.

Over eleven hundred patients with suspected heart attack syndrome were judged with a high sensitivity troponin test using lower cutoffs for women. Diagnoses of heart attack in women doubled, while men's rates barely moved. The findings imply that current practice under diagnoses women, and that sex specific thresholds can close much of the gap.
europmc-pmc4333291:
Guangyou Duan, Dirk Walther, and Predrag Radivojac studied where chemically modified proteins sit inside protein interaction networks. Their paper appeared in PLoS Computational Biology in 2015. After a protein is built, cells tag it with chemical groups that change what it binds; these post-translational modifications are known to tune interactions one by one.

Across twelve modification types and nine species, modified proteins held more interactions and more central network positions than unmodified ones. Phosphorylated proteins were the most consistently central, while sugar tagged proteins sat toward the edges. In the human network the same pattern held. The results suggest modifications are placed at control points of the cell's wiring, a hint for finding disease genes.
europmc-pmc4452191:
Tamás Rőszer, writing alone in Mediators of Inflammation in 2015, examined the M2 macrophage and the markers used to identify it. M2 macrophages are immune cells linked to healing, tissue balance, metabolism, and hormone signaling, and they vary a lot in form and behavior. Researchers usually name them by a set of surface and internal markers, including receptors, enzymes, growth factors, and immune signals.

Many of those markers have jobs that are still unexplored, so Rőszer asks whether the marker set truly picks out one cell kind or hides several subgroups. The review updates the signals from tissue and from the hormone system that push macrophages into the M2 state, and considers the deep evolutionary roots of these healing functions. It urges care in labeling cells before assigning them roles in disease.
europmc-pmc4510691:
Benjamin S. Halpern leads a ten-author team mapping how human pressure on the ocean changed, in a 2015 Nature Communications paper. Fishing, climate shifts, and waste from land and sea all press on marine life at once. Managers need to know where the total load is rising fastest and which pressures drive the change.

The team remapped combined impact scores across the world ocean over five years. Nearly 66% of the ocean, and 77% of national waters, showed rising impact, driven mostly by climate pressures. Five percent of the ocean was both heavily hit and getting worse. Ten percent had very low impact that was falling. The maps point managers to where action matters most and stress climate action.
europmc-pmc4515091:
Henning Sirringhaus wrote a solo anniversary review of organic field-effect transistors for Advanced Materials, covering 25 years of work in the field. These transistors switch current using carbon-based semiconductors instead of silicon. Early versions were far too slow for real products, but steady materials gains changed that picture.

Performance has improved by three to four orders of magnitude, and some organic devices now clearly beat the amorphous silicon standard. Sirringhaus surveys small-molecule and polymer materials with strong charge speeds, then explains the physics of how charge moves through such loose, disordered solids. The target use is flexible screens, where bendable backplanes must drive each pixel. The review closes by judging how much more performance the physics may allow.
europmc-pmc4557491:
Mayowa O. Owolabi leads a twelve-author review of stroke's toll in Africa, in the Cardiovascular Journal of Africa in 2015. Data on stroke across the continent were scattered and thin. The team searched the literature from 1960 to June 2014 and added Global Burden of Disease model figures to project where the burden heads.

Community studies found yearly stroke rates as high as 316 per 100,000 people after age adjustment, and prevalence up to 981 per 100,000. Model estimates showed significant rises in age-adjusted incidence, death, and disability between 1990 and 2010. Compared with rich countries, African stroke strikes younger, kills more often, and differs in type mix, for reasons still unexplained. The authors warn the load will grow without action.
europmc-pmc4575991:
A. Jemat, M. J. Ghazali, M. Razali, and Y. Otsuka review surface treatments for titanium dental implants, in BioMed Research International in 2015. A dental implant succeeds when jaw bone grows tight against it, a bond called osseointegration. The metal's surface decides much of that bond, and makers treat it by adding coatings or etching material away.

Drawing on 18 years of published work, the review compares methods head-to-head. Surface roughness emerged as a key driver of bone contact, cell growth, and resistance to twisting out, even though titanium's strength was never in doubt. Acid-etched surfaces and applied coatings performed best overall. Marrying good roughness with titanium's mechanical strength, the authors conclude, is the recipe for lasting implants.
europmc-pmc4589691:
Zhi-Ping Liu, Canglin Wu, Hongyu Miao, and Hulin Wu build a database of gene control networks, in Database in 2015. Genes are switched by transcription factors and tuned after the fact by microRNAs, and those relationships were scattered across dozens of databases and papers. RegNetwork pulls them into one searchable map for human and mouse.

The team integrated documented interactions among transcription factors, microRNAs, and target genes from 25 source databases. They also predicted further links from the DNA binding-site patterns of transcription factors, and folded those in, labeled by origin. The result is a genome-wide network spanning both transcriptional and post-transcriptional control, offered free for biomedical researchers building models of regulation.
europmc-pmc4589791:
Aritro Nath, Irene Li, Lewis R. Roberts, and Christina Chan link fat uptake to liver cancer spread, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Liver cancer is the second-leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and what drives its progression is poorly understood. The team's clue was CD36, a surface protein that imports free fatty acids, found at high levels in advancing tumors.

Treating human liver cancer cells with fatty acids deepened their epithelial-mesenchymal transition, the shift that lets tumor cells move and invade. Blocking CD36 chemically softened that shift. The fatty acids switched on the Wnt and TGF-β pathways, plausible triggers of the transition program. Patient weight did not explain the effect, pointing at the uptake machinery itself as a drug target.
europmc-pmc4597191:
Santiago Zelenay and colleagues' 2015 study centres on how tumours use cyclooxygenase enzymes, known as COX, to escape immune attack. Their test system was mouse melanoma carrying a Braf mutation, grown in mice with working immune systems. The work appeared in Cell and also covered breast and colorectal cancer cells.

Tumours needed to make prostaglandin E2, a COX product, to keep growing. Removing COX or its partner enzymes left tumours open to immune control and shifted them toward anti-cancer inflammation. The same COX pattern appeared in human skin melanoma samples. Combining COX blockers with anti-PD-1 treatment cleared tumours in mice, which points to COX drugs as possible partners for immune therapy.
europmc-pmc4654491:
Working with colleagues, Minghui Li published a 2015 study identifying the male sex-determining gene in Nile tilapia, a major farmed fish. Sex control matters in fish farming, and tilapia sex follows an X and Y chromosome system. A duplicated copy of the anti-Müllerian hormone gene sits on the Y chromosome. The work appeared in PLOS Genetics.

The duplicate, called amhy, differs from the X copy by one amino acid change, and it is active in male gonads from five days after hatching. Knocking it out with CRISPR turned genetic males into females, while adding it to genetic females made them male. Knocking out its receptor also fully reversed sex. The results name amhy as the essential trigger of male development in this species.
europmc-pmc4657091:
A team led by Ru Liu published a 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of high uric acid and gout prevalence in mainland China. Raised uric acid, called hyperuricemia, feeds gout and tracks with diabetes, blood pressure, and kidney disease. The team searched five databases for studies from 2000 to 2014. The work appeared in BioMed Research International.

Thirty-six articles provided forty-four studies. Pooled prevalence came to 13.3 percent for hyperuricemia and 1.1 percent for gout. A statistical check for publication bias did not overturn the estimates. Region, city versus countryside, coastal versus inland setting, wealth level, and sex all related to prevalence. The authors offer the figures as a base for local public health planning in China.
europmc-pmc4665391:
Nicolas Servant and colleagues presented a 2015 software pipeline called HiC-Pro for processing Hi-C data. Hi-C experiments map which DNA regions touch each other across the genome, revealing its three-dimensional folding. Raw output needs mapping, filtering, and correction before use. The paper appeared in Genome Biology.

HiC-Pro takes raw reads through quality control to normalised contact maps, within and between chromosomes. It includes a fast version of the iterative correction method and a compact data format. Where genotype data exist, it can build separate contact maps for each parental copy of the genome. Tests on several datasets showed large jobs finishing in reasonable time. Code and documentation are freely available.
europmc-pmc4682791:
Alberto Mazzoni, Henrik Lindén, Hermann Cuntz, and four colleagues tackled a measurement problem in PLoS Computational Biology in 2015. Simple point-neuron network models are widely used to study brain circuits, but real experiments often record the local field potential, a summed electrical signal from many cells. Point neurons have no shape, so they cannot produce that signal directly. The team searched for the best stand-in signal from model output.

They fed the model network's input currents into a detailed three-dimensional network of shaped neurons and recorded its true field signal. A fixed weighted mix of the simple model's synaptic currents matched that signal closely, across recording sites and cell shapes. The result is a simple formula that lets modelers compare their networks with real recordings. That makes model tests against lab data far more direct.
europmc-pmc4821891:
Daan R. Speth and four co-authors read the genomes inside a full-scale wastewater reactor in Nature Communications in 2016. The reactor cleans ammonium from sewage with a shortcut process run by microbial granules, and its sludge seeds plants worldwide. Yet most of its microbial citizens had unknown jobs.

From the mixed DNA the team rebuilt 23 near-complete genomes covering most of the community. The granules hold two worlds: an outer aerobic zone of nitrifiers and feeders on waste organics, and an inner oxygen-free zone. There, many kinds could partly run denitrification, forming a nitrite loop that boosts efficiency. Nineteen genomes had no close known relative, and six belonged to groups never grown in a lab, one the most complete of its kind yet.
europmc-pmc4880591:
José Muñoz-Dorado and co-authors reviewed myxobacteria in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2016: social bacteria that move, hunt, and survive as a group. The best studied kind, Myxococcus xanthus, glides over surfaces in swarms. Cells travel alone on slime trails or in packs, pulling themselves with tiny grapples called pili that extend and retract at each cell end.

When a swarm meets prey, the group floods it with shared enzymes and feeds together. Starved swarms build fruiting bodies: most cells die to feed the rest, some become tough spores, and some stay as rods. Spores survive hard times and sprout fast when food returns. Signal systems that keep the group acting as one get close review.
europmc-pmc4880791:
Italo Trizano-Hermosilla and Jesús M. Alvarado compared questionnaire reliability measures by computer simulation in Frontiers in Psychology in 2016. Cronbach's alpha is the most used check of whether test items hang together, yet its limits are well known and rivals such as omega and glb exist. Real tests break alpha's assumptions: items differ in quality and answers skew to one side.

Across simulated tests, omega beat alpha in every condition the pair tried. With skewed items, omega and the glb measure both served best. Alpha clings to use by habit, the study suggests, while better tools sit ready. Applied researchers gain a clear rule: report omega, above all when items skew.
europmc-pmc4920991:
Geoff Wong and five co-authors present reporting standards for realist evaluations. Their paper appeared in BMC Medicine in 2016, as part of the RAMESES II project. Realist evaluation asks how and why a program works, for whom, and in what settings. Use of the method was growing in health services research, but no shared rules told authors what a good report must include.

The team built the standards with an online Delphi panel of experts. They recruited 35 panel members from 27 organisations across six countries and nine fields. Over three rounds the panel agreed on 20 items that reports should cover. Response rates stayed high in each round. The authors hope the list brings more consistent, rigorous reporting. They also expect the standards to change as the method itself develops.
europmc-pmc4937091:
Ewa Niedzielska and six co-authors review oxidative stress in diseases that destroy brain and nerve cells. Their review appeared in Molecular Neurobiology in 2016. Oxidative stress is an overload of reactive oxygen molecules that damage cell parts. The review covers amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. In each, patients and lab models show higher markers of oxidative damage and weaker antioxidant defenses in brain and body tissues.

The authors gather trial and animal evidence on how the imbalance builds. They then survey drugs that try to restore balance, from antioxidants to agents that raise the cell's own defenses. Results so far are mixed, and studies often disagree on which markers matter most. Still, they argue the imbalance itself is a steady feature of these diseases. That steadiness keeps redox, the balance of oxidation and defense, on the list of treatment targets.
europmc-pmc4963991:
Shijin Xia and seven co-authors update the state of inflamm-aging research. Their review appeared in the Journal of Immunology Research in 2016. Inflamm-aging names the chronic, low grade inflammation that builds with age. The term was coined in 2000, and the field has grown fast since. The state is tied to Alzheimer's disease, atherosclerosis, heart disease, type II diabetes, and cancer. The authors review the concept, its pathological features, and the mechanisms proposed to drive it.

They then survey interventions and treatment strategies aimed at the process. Progress in the past decade, they note, is real but incomplete. The paths from background inflammation to specific diseases remain unclear in detail. The authors argue that pinning those paths down is the field's main task. Only then, they say, can prevention and therapy move from broad anti-inflammatory hopes to targeted care for age linked disease.
europmc-pmc4974791:
Wael Nassar and nine co-authors test stem cell vesicles as a treatment for chronic kidney disease. Their trial report appeared in Biomaterials Research in 2016. Extracellular vesicles are tiny packets shed by cells that carry signals to other cells. Vesicles from umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells might calm kidney inflammation without the risks of live cell therapy. Forty patients with stage III or IV kidney disease joined; twenty received two vesicle doses and twenty a placebo.

The treated group improved on kidney function measures, including filtration rate, creatinine, urea, and urine albumin. Their blood also showed a calmer immune profile, with more anti-inflammatory signals and fewer inflammatory ones. The control group showed no such gains. Benefits lasted months rather than years. The authors call the approach safe in this small trial and worth larger testing.
europmc-pmc4980791:
Steve Horvath leads a large team comparing epigenetic aging rates across racial and ethnic groups. Their study appeared in Genome Biology in 2016. The epigenetic clock estimates age from chemical marks on DNA. It might explain puzzles such as women's lower death rates despite more illness, and longer Hispanic life expectancy despite higher metabolic risk. The team measured clock rates in blood, saliva, and brain samples from seven groups.

Two rates were tracked: an intrinsic rate set by the marks alone, and an extrinsic rate that also reflects immune cell mix. In blood, Hispanics and Tsimane Amerindians aged slower on the intrinsic scale but faster on the extrinsic one than Caucasians. African-Americans showed lower extrinsic rates. Extrinsic rates also tied weakly to inflammatory risk factors for heart disease. The authors present group differences in aging pace as real and worth deeper study.
europmc-pmc5048391:
Graham Fairfoul and a large co-author group test spinal fluid for Parkinson's-type diseases in the Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology in 2016. Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies are driven by clumping of the protein alpha-synuclein, yet early diagnosis is unreliable. Their test, called RT-QuIC, exploits the clumping itself: a trace of abnormal protein in spinal fluid seeds runaway clumping of fresh protein in a tube, which a dye then reveals.

The test caught ninety-two percent of dementia with Lewy bodies cases and ninety-five percent of Parkinson's cases, while every Alzheimer and control sample stayed negative. Diseases driven by the rival tau protein also tested negative, which sharpens the test's aim. Three people with a sleep disorder that often precedes these diseases already tested positive, hinting the test could flag disease before symptoms. Larger follow-up studies are the stated next step.
europmc-pmc5068791:
Alessandro Cassini and a large group of co-authors weigh the burden of hospital infections in Europe in PLoS Medicine in 2016. Infections caught during care harm patients and mark poor quality, but their total health cost had never been set beside other diseases in one measure. The team took a European survey of hospital infections from 2011 and 2012 and turned prevalence into yearly cases and disability-adjusted life years for six common infection types.

They estimate 2,609,911 new cases a year across the European Union and European Economic Area. Together the six infections cost about 501 healthy years per 100,000 people each year. Hospital pneumonia and bloodstream infections carry over sixty percent of that burden, ahead of urinary, surgical site, gut, and newborn infections. The model is built openly, so others can repeat it and can test how much burden a prevention program would save. The authors call for stronger prevention and control.
europmc-pmc514491:
Matt Kaeberlein, Kathryn T. Kirkland, Stanley Fields, and Brian K. Kennedy reported a yeast aging study in PLoS Biology in 2004. Eating less slows aging in many species. In yeast, the effect was blamed on switching on a protein called Sir2. That protein limits toxic DNA circles that build up in old mother cells.

The team found a second route. Cutting calories helped even yeast lacking Sir2, and combining calorie restriction with either extra Sir2 or removal of a circle-promoting gene produced the longest-lived yeast reported at the time. Cells lacking both Sir2 and that gene gained more from calorie restriction than cells with Sir2 present. The evidence says the diet and the protein work in parallel pathways, a pattern the authors suggest may hold in higher animals too.
europmc-pmc5198891:
Rosalind E. Howes and six co-authors survey the global epidemiology of Plasmodium vivax. This parasite is the most widespread human malaria, putting 2.5 billion people at risk. It has long stood in the shadow of Plasmodium falciparum, toward which most control programs were aimed. Vivax plays by different rules. Its blood-stage numbers stay low, its transmissible forms appear before illness does, and dormant liver stages wake later to cause relapses.

Those traits shape where vivax thrives and how it spreads. Many infections cause no symptoms, yet the parasite is not benign: severe and even fatal illness occurs. Resistance to chloroquine is spreading, and primaquine, the drug against relapse, is hard to deploy well. The authors argue that elimination plans built for falciparum will stall unless they account for what makes vivax different.
europmc-pmc5210591:
Cath Tyner and a large team at the University of California, Santa Cruz gave the 2017 update of the UCSC Genome Browser database in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017. Running since 2001, the browser shows sequence alignments and annotation tracks laid over reference genomes, and it is free and open source. Its databases back a wider tool suite for queries, downloads, and alignment work.

The year's changes include redesigned home and gateway pages and a multi-region display that can show only exons, only genes, or custom regions. New browsers cover the brown kiwi, the crab-eating macaque, and the Malayan flying lemur, with updated assemblies for eight more species. Support grew for newer data types such as CRAM files, RNA sequencing expression, and long-range contacts between DNA regions. A new mirror site opened in Japan.
europmc-pmc5293491:
Ming Wu, Aljoscha Nern, W. Ryan Williamson, Mai M. Morimoto, Michael B. Reiser, Gwyneth M. Card, and Gerald M. Rubin mapped visual projection neurons in the fruit fly in eLife in 2016. These neurons carry processed visual signals from the optic lobe to higher brain centers. The team focused on lobula columnar cells, projecting to distinct brain structures called optic glomeruli.

They described 22 different cell types. Switching individual types on with light in freely moving flies triggered specific behaviors, and for two types the response closely mimicked the natural escape from a looming object. Live brain imaging showed those same two types respond to looming stimuli, while another ignored loom and tracked small moving objects instead. Lighting up cells on one side of the brain only could steer flies toward or away, depending on type. Each type thus reports a particular visual feature tied to its own behavioral program.
europmc-pmc5299391:
M. Cacciottolo and colleagues linked particulate air pollution, APOE genes, and brain aging in Translational Psychiatry in 2017. The team combined a US-wide cohort of older women from the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study with experiments in transgenic mice carrying human APOE variants.

Women living where fine particles exceeded EPA standards faced 81 percent higher risk of global cognitive decline. They faced 92 percent higher risk of dementia, with the harm strongest in carriers of two APOE epsilon-4 copies. In mice, 225 hours of urban nanosized particles over 15 weeks raised brain beta-amyloid, the Alzheimer's protein, and increased its toxic oligomer forms, again worse with epsilon-4. The particles also shrank connections in the hippocampus's CA1 region and cut a key glutamate receptor subunit, effects seen even in normal mice, and pushed cultured cells toward amyloid production. Dirty air, the authors conclude, speeds pathological brain aging.
europmc-pmc5370391:
Peter Simmonds and co-authors gave the official profile of a virus family in the Journal of General Virology in 2017. The profile sums up the world taxonomy body's report on the Flaviviridae. These are small viruses wrapped in a fat coat, with a single strand of RNA as their genome. Most infect mammals and birds, and many are picky about their host.

One genus, Hepacivirus, holds hepatitis C, a grave human liver pathogen. The largest genus, Flavivirus, rides mostly on insects and ticks, and holds yellow fever and dengue, both major threats to people and stock. The profile lays out the build of the virus ball, with its core protein and coat proteins, and the size of the genome for each genus. It walks through how the viruses copy themselves and sort into their kinds. The short form gives labs one shared map of the family.
europmc-pmc5395891:
Arnold Y. L. Wong, Jaro Karppinen, and Dino Samartzis review low back pain in older adults in a 2017 paper in Scoliosis and Spinal Disorders. Back pain is a top cause of disability past age sixty. Most cases are vague and pass, but older people are prone to certain clear causes and to pain that stays. No past review had pulled together what makes care for this group distinct.

Older adults more often have pain from bone crush breaks, tumors, spinal infection, or a narrowed spinal canal. Worn spines, other illnesses, low activity, changed pain handling in the brain, and dementia all shape care. So do genes, sex, and ethnic background. The authors call for cheaper, more personal care plans and list study needs.
europmc-pmc5408091:
Ernesto Panadero reviews self-regulated learning in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Psychology. Self-regulated learning covers how students steer their own study: the thoughts, checks, habits, drives, and feelings that shape learning. It has become a core topic in the study of how people learn. Panadero takes six leading models of the process and pulls each apart in the same way, covering its history, its parts, its proof, and the tools built on it.

He then sets the six side by side on points such as their phases, how they treat thought and drive, and how much runs on habit. Past pooled studies show the models do not help all students alike; gains differ by age and school level. He closes with four paths for future work and advice for teachers who train students to study with more control.
europmc-pmc5437291:
Yan and co-authors present BLISS, a method to map DNA double-strand breaks across the whole genome. Their methods article appeared in Nature Communications. Breaks in both DNA strands are grave lesions. They arise in normal cell life and from damage. Gene editing tools also cut DNA, sometimes at wrong sites. Older mapping methods lacked sensitivity or ease. Some needed large samples. Others missed breaks repaired by certain paths.

BLISS labels breaks directly where they sit. It works on fixed cells or tissue slices on a slide. Tagged breaks are copied by linear amplification. That keeps input needs low. Unique molecular tags let the team count breaks, not just find them. Samples can be pooled for scale. The authors profiled breaks in cancer cells, stem cells, and liver tissue. They also ranked two editing enzymes. Cpf1 proved more specific than Cas9 in their tests.
europmc-pmc5458491:
Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres describe a pipeline workflow added to the RELION cryo-EM program. Their article appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section D. Cryo-EM structure work is expanding fast. New users flood into the field. RELION analyzes single particles by empirical Bayesian methods. Key parameters come from the data themselves. That design lowers the expertise barrier. Until now the program lacked an explicit workflow.

The pipeline treats processing as a graph. Data objects form the nodes. Jobs form the connecting edges. RELION 2.0 defines 14 node types. It implements 18 job types. Each job consumes nodes and produces nodes. Chaining them builds a full procedure. A new graphical interface hosts the system. Users start by importing micrographs or movies. Standardized procedures become easy to share. Processing can run on the fly during acquisition. De novo 3D reference building stays external, they note.
europmc-pmc5496491:
Suarez-Carmona and co-authors present a review in Molecular Oncology on two partners in cancer spread. One is chronic inflammation inside tumors. The other is EMT, a program that loosens cancer cells from their neighbors. Cells that run this program invade more and resist death. Each process feeds the other, they argue.

Inflammatory signals can switch EMT on in tumor cells. Those changed cells then pour out more inflammatory factors. Immune cells such as macrophages join the loop as well. The review ties this axis to metastasis in several cancers. Breaking the loop is a candidate aim for new drugs.
europmc-pmc5543591:
Vijayan and co-authors present a review in the Journal of Intensive Care. Their subject is procalcitonin, a protein linked to calcitonin. Levels of it rise fast during bacterial infection. The authors ask how well it can flag sepsis, a whole-body response that can damage organs.

Older markers, such as C-reactive protein and white cell counts, are not specific for sepsis. The review argues procalcitonin has stronger value for diagnosis and outlook. Its levels can also guide antibiotic use and track response to treatment. Still, it cannot by itself split bacterial from viral cases. Readers get a balanced case for one test, plus its limits.
europmc-pmc5573791:
Yan and co-authors report a metagenome study of hypertension. They compared stool samples from 60 patients with primary hypertension and 60 matched healthy controls. Whole-metagenome shotgun sequencing read the gut microbes in depth. Gut microbes are thought to play a part in heart and vessel disease.

Patients showed a marked gut imbalance. Diversity inside each sample was lower, and the mix of species had shifted. Harmful or opportunistic bacteria were more common in patients. Helpful short-chain fatty acid makers were richer in controls. Nearly 54,000 microbial genes differed between the groups. A marker set split patients from controls with fair accuracy. Readers get a detailed portrait of how the gut changes with high blood pressure.
europmc-pmc5605691:
Miriyev, Stack, and Lipson present a new soft actuator material in Nature Communications. Soft robots need muscles that run on their own power. Rival options demand kilovolts, external pumps, or give tiny movement. Their composite needs none of those.

The material is silicone rubber filled with tiny ethanol bubbles. An electric current heats the mix. The ethanol boils, and the bubbles swell hugely. Strain reached up to 900 percent. Stress reached 1.3 megapascals, at a density under that of water. The stuff costs about three cents per gram to make. It can be molded, cut, or printed into shape. The team shows it driving soft robotic devices. Readers see a cheap path to untethered soft robots.
europmc-pmc5691891:
Palazon and co-authors study how killer T cells adapt inside tumours. Their research article appeared in Cancer Cell. Tumours often lack oxygen. T cells use hypoxia response factors there. The team deleted key factors in mouse CD8 T cells. They tracked tumour growth and blood vessels.

One factor, HIF-1 alpha, proved essential. Its loss weakened the killer state. Tumours got fewer infiltrating T cells. Tumour cell killing dropped too. Vessel patterns changed as well. Deleting VEGF-A had a mixed effect. Tumours grew faster, yet vessels also shifted. Human breast cancer data matched the pattern. The authors say this axis shapes tumour immunity. It matters for immunotherapy design.
europmc-pmc5704491:
Lin and co-authors study how loose protein segments shape droplet formation in cells. Their work concerns liquid-liquid phase separation, which builds cell structures without membranes. One such class is RNA granules, which handle RNA tasks. Many granule proteins mix folded parts with disordered regions of simple sequence.

The team built test proteins by joining a disordered segment from FUS to a folded partner system. The wild-type segment cut the threshold for droplet formation eightfold. Changing its tyrosine sites weakened that effect. The count of changes mattered, not their place. Removing all such sites or adding phosphate groups raised the threshold again. The results show how cells might tune granule traits.
europmc-pmc5710991:
Cutland and co-authors present a case definition and guidelines for low birth weight in studies of vaccines given in pregnancy. The work comes from the Brighton Collaboration Low Birth Weight Working Group. It supports the safety data work of maternal immunization programs.

Low birth weight means a first weight below 2,500 grams. The paper sets out how to collect, check, and report such cases in a shared way. It also gives the wider facts behind the term. More than 20 million such births occur each year, most in low and middle income lands. These infants face a far higher risk of death and later health harm. A shared definition helps vaccine studies compare results across sites and spot real safety signals.
europmc-pmc5725991:
Zell and co-authors give a short taxonomy profile of the Picornaviridae virus family. The text sums up a report from the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses. This family holds small RNA viruses with no outer envelope. It spans more than 30 genera and more than 75 species.

The profile covers virus shape, genome layout, and how these viruses copy themselves. Most infect mammals and birds, though some occur in reptiles, amphibians, and fish. Well known members cause polio, colds, and foot-and-mouth disease. Spread is mainly by stool and mouth routes or through the airways. The authors also point readers to the full ICTV report and data sources.
europmc-pmc5736591:
Gordon and co-authors build the full gene set, or pan-genome, of a model grass. They assembled the genomes of 54 lines of Brachypodium distachyon from scratch. A single line holds only part of the species' genes. The shared set tells a fuller story of variation.

The pan-genome holds nearly twice the genes of any one line, they report. Genes found in all lines serve core, vital tasks. Genes found in some lines serve defense and growth, and change faster. Those spare genes sit near jumping DNA pieces. The work shows spare genes shape traits across the species.
europmc-pmc5742691:
Cheng and co-authors study how stem cell exosomes protect disc cells in the spine. The soft center of each disc loses cells as discs wear down. Mesenchymal stem cells can slow that loss, for unclear reasons. The team tested tiny packets, called exosomes, that these stem cells release.

The packets entered disc cells and held back their death, they report. The packets carry miR-21, a small RNA scarce in dying disc cells. MiR-21 blocks PTEN and switches on a survival path in the cells. Injecting the packets into rat discs eased cell death and disc wear.
europmc-pmc5743791:
Nagaya and co-authors review fluorescence-guided surgery for cancer. Surgeons still rely mostly on white light and touch to find tumors. Glowing probes can mark tumor tissue during the operation itself. Clearer margins could mean fuller removal and less harm to healthy tissue.

The review covers probes now in use and many new ones in growth. Some probes glow at all times, while others switch on near tumor targets. Antibody based probes get close attention. The authors weigh how these tools might cut leftover tumor and second operations. Safety gains from sparing normal tissue are also covered.
europmc-pmc5814791:
Conrad and co-authors chart heart failure trends in the United Kingdom. Planners need current counts to fund care and research. The team mined linked health records for 4 million people. Records ran from 2002 to 2014.

Age-adjusted incidence fell 7 percent over the period. Yet new cases rose 12 percent as the population grew and aged. Total people living with heart failure rose 23 percent. Patients arrived older and with more other illnesses. Poor areas saw 61 percent higher incidence than rich ones. Their patients also fell ill years sooner. Readers get the numbers behind a growing care burden.
europmc-pmc5817791:
Du and Lovly explain how receptor tyrosine kinases switch on in cancer. These receptors pass growth cues into cells. Humans carry 58 of them. When their signals jam on, cells grow, move, and spread.

Genomic studies keep finding altered kinase genes in tumors. Four routes drive the faulty firing. Mutations can lock a receptor in its on state. Extra gene copies can flood the cell with receptors. Chromosome swaps can fuse receptors to new partners. Some tumors also bathe themselves in their own growth cues. Each route points to a matching drug choice. Readers get the logic behind targeted cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc5834591:
Brendel and co-authors argue that short-chain PFAS chemicals need tighter European control. Their analysis appeared in Environmental Sciences Europe. Industry swapped to these short-chain compounds as long-chain cousins faced bans. The replacements were assumed to build up less in bodies.

The authors show a different danger profile. Short-chain PFASs move fast through soil and water. Their breakdown products barely degrade at all. Drinking water picks them up, and treatment plants cannot strip them out. Exposure thus becomes permanent and hard to reverse. The paper urges listing them as substances of very high concern under REACH, then restricting them.
europmc-pmc5850791:
Barratt and co-authors assemble the evidence base for global guidance on male infertility diagnosis. Their analysis appeared in Human Reproduction Update. The World Health Organization sought recommendations it could offer worldwide. The group worked through eight prioritized clinical questions.

The questions span how common male infertility is and who needs full evaluation. They test the worth of standard semen measures. They weigh lifestyle factors, antioxidant supplements, and genetic screening. Cancer history and varicocele repair get their own scrutiny. Each answer grades the supporting evidence honestly. Gaps flagged along the way map the research still needed.
europmc-pmc5877591:
Lee reviews the balance between Th17 and Treg cells in autoimmunity. The article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Both cell types grow from the same naive CD4 T cell stock. Both need a TGF-beta signal to start developing. Yet their mature roles stand opposed to each other. Th17 cells drive inflammation and autoimmune attack. Treg cells calm immune responses and keep tolerance.

Recent work has found many factors that tip this balance. Signals come from T cell receptors and costimulatory receptors. Cytokines, metabolic pathways, and gut microbes also weigh in. Lee sums up these advances and their disease links. Grasping the balance could sharpen ideas about tolerance.
europmc-pmc5880391:
Benichou and co-authors review heart rate variability in type 2 diabetes. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS ONE. Heart rate variability is the standard gauge of heart nerve damage. The team pooled 25 case-control studies with 2,932 patients. Measures came from 24-hour Holter recordings. Patients numbered 1,356, and healthy controls 1,576. Every main variability measure ran lower in diabetes patients.

Both branches of the autonomic system showed reduced activity. Blood sugar levels tracked with several of the measures. Time since diagnosis also played a part. The authors link the pattern to cardiac autonomic neuropathy. That condition carries a high risk of heart death. The findings support routine checks of heart nerve function.
europmc-pmc5893591:
Oliver and co-authors track marine heatwaves over the past century. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Marine heatwaves are long spells of unusually warm ocean water. Recent events drew wide public and science interest. No global century-scale assessment existed before this study. The team combined satellite records with in situ measurements. Gridded monthly datasets filled the early decades.

From 1925 to 2016, heatwave frequency rose by 34 percent. Average duration rose by 17 percent over that span. Annual heatwave days thus climbed by 54 percent. Rising mean ocean temperatures explain most of the trend. Further warming should bring still more heatwave days. Such events harm ecosystems and coastal economies alike.
europmc-pmc5908791:
Liau and co-authors explain how SOCS1 blocks JAK and STAT signalling. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. SOCS proteins damp cytokine signals as feedback control. SOCS1 is the strongest member of that family. It can tag signals for removal, like its relatives. It can also block JAK enzymes directly.

Their structures show why the direct block works so well. A small region of SOCS1 fits the JAK substrate groove. That fit blocks later phosphorylation steps. SOCS1 poorly recruits the Cullin5 tagging partner, they found. It also acts apart from the interferon receptor itself. Readers get a precise model of this immune brake.
europmc-pmc5946491:
Baxter and co-authors review the effects of integrated care in the UK and abroad. Their systematic review appeared in BMC Health Services Research. Health systems worldwide are testing better joined-up models of care. The authors searched major databases for work from 2006 to March 2017. Grey literature from the UK was included too. They kept studies that measured real effects on service delivery.

In all, 167 studies were eligible for the review. The team found evidence of better perceived quality of care. Patient satisfaction and access to care also improved, they report. Evidence on costs and system-wide effects stayed inconsistent or limited. UK and international results differed little overall.
europmc-pmc6080491:
De Jager and co-authors present a multi-omic atlas of the aging human frontal cortex. Their data paper appeared in Scientific Data. Samples come from two long-running aging studies. Together they follow over 3,322 older adults. Each person gave yearly thinking tests during life. Brains received structured exams after death.

The first data wave spans six assay types. Genome sequencing, methylation, and RNA profiles lead the set. Sample sizes run from about 640 to 2,090 per assay. More protein and metabolism data are on the way. Many donors died without dementia. That makes the set useful for healthy brain aging too. Readers get a shared resource for Alzheimer's research.
europmc-pmc6084991:
Chen and co-authors estimate the global burden of overweight and obesity in pregnancy. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. The team drew on data from 184 countries. Trends ran from 2005 through 2014. A panel model tested drivers like food supply and city growth.

In 2014, about 38.9 million pregnant women carried excess weight. Of those, 14.6 million counted as obese. Middle-income countries showed the sharpest rises. India held the largest count, at 4.3 million. In the United States, about one million obese pregnant women were estimated. Food energy supply and urbanization pushed counts up. Readers get a global call for healthier food environments.
europmc-pmc6090091:
Bubb and co-authors review the cingulum bundle, a ring-shaped tract in the brain. Their review appeared in Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews. The bundle arcs over the corpus callosum. It runs from frontal areas down into the temporal lobe. Fibers join and leave it all along its length.

The review details each connection segment by segment. Damage studies in rats, monkeys, and humans follow. Imaging shows cingulum faults across many psychiatric conditions. Functions shift along the tract's length. The authors contrast its damage effects with fornix damage. Memory and emotion both run through this tract. Readers get an integrated map of a complex limbic pathway.
europmc-pmc6102891:
Lu and co-authors review oxidative stress in female reproduction. Their review appeared in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology. Reactive oxygen species act as a double-edged sword. At normal levels they carry signals cells need. In excess they damage tissue and fertility.

Balance between oxidants and antioxidants guards the system. The review traces stress through each reproductive stage. It covers egg growth, hormone cycles, and fetal development. Diseases in view include polycystic ovary syndrome and endometriosis. Preeclampsia also features. Four signaling pathways link stress to these disorders. Readers get a compact guide to a fast-growing research area.
europmc-pmc6127991:
Zhang and co-authors wrote a review in Respiratory Research asking whether macrophages help or harm in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This lung disease scars the lungs steadily and has no known cause. Over the past decade, macrophages have emerged as key players in how it develops.

The review explains how macrophages shift between two broad states. The M1 state helps heal wounds after injury to the air sacs. The M2 state calms inflammation and ends the healing response. In this disease, healing goes wrong after repeated injury. The authors sum up what drives these shifts and how the interplay with fibroblasts feeds scar tissue. That knowledge may point to new therapies.
europmc-pmc6157091:
Vaughan and co-authors report in Eurosurveillance on two cases of monkeypox imported to the United Kingdom in September 2018. One case was diagnosed on 7 September in Cornwall, the other on 11 September in Blackpool. The two were not connected to each other. Both patients had recently traveled from Nigeria, where monkeypox circulates.

Monkeypox is a rare viral disease found mainly in Central and West Africa. These were the first cases diagnosed outside Africa since 2003. The report describes how each case was found and confirmed. It also details the public health response, including tracing and grading contacts. The account is a record of how an imported rare disease is handled.
europmc-pmc6190891:
Mortaz and co-authors wrote an update in Frontiers in Immunology on neutrophil function in severe inflammation. Neutrophils are front-line defenders against microbes in the innate immune system. They come in varied forms and can flex their function. That flexibility helps regulate immunity.

The same cells can turn harmful. When overactive or poorly controlled, they damage tissue in severe inflammation and after trauma. They also modulate the wider immune system after serious injury. The review surveys neutrophil subpopulations and what each does during and after infection. Mechanisms by which neutrophils steer other immune cells are discussed. The update weighs defense against collateral damage in the sickest patients.
europmc-pmc6248091:
Fitzmaurice and co-authors report world cancer burden for twenty-nine cancer groups. Their analysis appeared in JAMA Oncology. It draws on the Global Burden of Disease Study for 195 countries. Measures cover new cases, deaths, and years of healthy life lost. Both early death and years lived with illness are counted. The years covered run from 1990 to 2016.

Such numbers show where cancer control lags and where it gains. The authors note that few countries have met past pledges to cut early deaths from long term diseases. Cancer is not one disease, so each group needs its own plan. Fair control needs steady funding and methods that fit local needs. The full tables let health leaders compare their country with others. Trends over time reveal which cancers are rising fastest.
europmc-pmc6249991:
Bhaskaran and co-authors linked body mass index to death rates in a huge UK cohort. Their study appeared in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology. Records covered about 3.6 million adults in primary care. Death records were matched to weight records over many years. The team studied overall deaths and deaths by cause. Never smokers were analysed apart to cut bias from smoking.

Weight showed a J shaped link with overall death risk. Risk was lowest near a body mass index of 25. Below that point, higher weight went with lower risk. Above it, each five point rise raised risk by about a fifth. Most causes of death followed the same broad pattern. Transport accidents were the main exception. The scale of the study gives firm ground for weight guidance.
europmc-pmc6306491:
Fu and Jiang review how dendritic cells shape CD8 T cell immunity in tumors. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Dendritic cells present tumor material to T cells. This cross-priming can spark attacks on the cancer. The tumor setting often twists that process. It can turn priming toward tolerance instead.

The authors focus on one dendritic cell subset. These CD103+ type 1 cells drive cross-priming best. They show how tumors suppress these cells. They also weigh ways to restore their function. Future directions include memory T cell responses. Better dendritic cell support could strengthen cancer immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc6369191:
Haney and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Chemistry that reassesses host defense peptides. These small peptides were long studied only as antimicrobial peptides. Research now shows they also fight biofilms, steer immune responses, and calm inflammation.

The authors argue the field chased direct bacterial killing too narrowly. Killing power drops sharply under body-like conditions, and no peptide antibiotic has yet won approval. They propose viewing each function as its own activity landscape within chemical space. Different sequences can then be tuned for different jobs. The review closes with emerging roles and ways to unlock the peptides' therapeutic promise.
europmc-pmc6376691:
Turan and co-authors present a discussion article in BMC Medicine on intersectional stigma and health. The concept covers people who carry several stigmatized identities at once, such as race, gender, class, and illness. Most past research studied each stigma alone, which misses how they combine.

The authors survey the existing literature and find clear health effects from layered stigma. They point out gaps in how researchers measure and analyze these joint effects. Worked examples show promising qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods. They call for better instruments and for interventions that build on shared identity and social support. Such tools would help providers design fairer health programs.
europmc-pmc6403191:
Foster and co-authors review clusterin in Alzheimer's disease, in Frontiers in Neuroscience. Clusterin is a protein that helps fold other proteins outside cells. Gene studies tie it to Alzheimer's risk, but its role stays disputed.

The protein also moves lipids and shapes immune responses. Under stress it can appear inside cells, for reasons still unclear. The review weighs claims about where cell clusterin comes from. It also borrows lessons from cancer and other diseases where clusterin acts. Pinning down its job could clarify one of the disease's genetic risks.
europmc-pmc6429491:
Yanai and Yoshida review the protective effects of adiponectin, a hormone released by fat tissue whose blood levels fall in obesity. That drop has been linked to the artery disease and metabolic problems that accompany weight gain. The pair gather evidence on how adiponectin acts and what raises its levels.

Adiponectin calms inflammation and oxidative stress, which improves insulin resistance, cuts liver glucose output, and helps muscle burn glucose and fat. It also protects insulin-producing beta cells, raises HDL, and lowers triglycerides through several named enzymes and transporters. Weight loss, exercise, and certain diabetes, lipid, and blood-pressure drugs all push levels up, suggesting practical routes to benefit.
europmc-pmc6439691:
Dorsheimer and co-authors examine clonal hematopoiesis, the age-linked expansion of blood cell clones carrying mutations, in 200 patients with chronic ischemic heart failure. Such clones, especially in the genes DNMT3A and TET2, were already tied to coronary disease and inflammation. Their meaning for patients who already have heart failure was untested.

CHIP proved common in the cohort, and carriers matched non-carriers on standard clinical measures apart from age. During follow-up, 37 percent of carriers died against 24 percent of non-carriers, and DNMT3A or TET2 mutations in particular predicted more deaths and repeat hospitalizations. The authors present clonal hematopoiesis as a new, potentially targetable risk factor in heart failure.
europmc-pmc6471991:
Muhammad and co-authors report experiments on hesperetin, a citrus flavonoid, against lipopolysaccharide-driven brain inflammation in mice and cultured cells. This article has since been retracted, and it is presented here as a retracted record; its findings should not be relied on. As published, the study claimed the compound calmed microglial activation and lowered TNF-α and interleukin-1β through the TLR4 and NF-κB pathway.

The paper further claimed protection of memory in water maze testing, with treated mice finding the platform faster and crossing its old position more often on the probe day. Antioxidant defenses and synaptic proteins were also reported restored. Readers should treat every result as withdrawn.
europmc-pmc6486691:
Liang and co-authors find that a circular RNA spun from the β-catenin gene is not merely regulatory but is itself translated into protein. Circβ-catenin runs high in liver cancer tissue, and silencing it curbs malignant behavior in culture and in animals while lowering β-catenin protein without touching its messenger RNA.

The circle produces a novel 370-amino-acid isoform of β-catenin, starting at the usual start codon and ending at a stop created by circularization, translated with help from an internal ribosome entry sequence. The isoform shields full-length β-catenin from GSK3β-driven destruction, switching the Wnt pathway on. A supposedly non-coding RNA thus manufactures an oncoprotein fragment.
europmc-pmc6486891:
McGrattan and co-authors review whether what people eat can cool the brain inflammation that drives cognitive ageing and Alzheimer's disease. Fifty million people live with dementia worldwide, a figure projected to triple by 2050, and diet ranks among the few levers ordinary people control. Microglia in the ageing brain smolder, pushing out interleukin-1β and interleukin-6.

Mediterranean and DASH eating patterns, rich in omega-3 fats, antioxidants, and polyphenols, associate with protected cognition, and cohort work ties higher dietary inflammatory index scores to worse overall function and verbal memory. Routes run both direct and indirect, through the gut microbiome and systemic circulation. Human intervention trials with brain imaging are the missing evidence, the review states plainly.
europmc-pmc6517691:
de la Cuesta-Zuluaga and co-authors study age and sex patterns in gut microbe diversity. Their study appeared in mSystems. It pools adult cohorts from four regions. Those regions are the United States, the United Kingdom, Colombia and China. Higher gut diversity has been linked to better health.

In the U.S., U.K. and Colombian cohorts, diversity rose with age in young adults. The rise levelled off at about age 40. Young women had higher diversity than young men. That sex gap did not hold in middle age. Machine learning tests confirmed the pattern. In the Chinese cohort, links with age and sex were minimal. The authors offer the results as a frame for later work.
europmc-pmc6687891:
Kircher and co-authors mutate twenty disease-linked regulatory elements base by base. Their study appears in Nature Communications. Most disease variants fall in noncoding DNA. Their effects remain hard to predict. The team combined mutagenesis with reporter assays. Every base position was altered in turn. Over 30,000 substitutions and deletions were measured. Promoters and enhancers of known disease genes featured. Targets included TERT, LDLR, and HBB.

Effects varied sharply between elements. Binding site density differed widely across them. Conservation scores predicted function unevenly. Other scores fared no better. The dataset now benchmarks scoring tools. Doctors can check observed mutations against it. Judging harm from a variant gains firmer ground.
europmc-pmc6836491:
Luo and co-authors review anti-cancer compounds from Chinese herbal medicine, in the journal Chinese Medicine. Many classic herbs yield molecules that kill cancer cells in the lab. Their effects include halting growth, triggering cell death, and blocking spread. Some also help standard chemotherapy work better. The authors gather the key advances reported since 2011.

Compounds covered include curcumin, berberine, artemisinin, emodin, and triptolide, among many others. For each, the review sets out the cancers tested and the pathways involved. Some compounds reverse drug resistance or calm the immune side of tumours. The authors aim to show where this traditional source might feed modern drug design.
europmc-pmc6863391:
Neumann and co-authors report a study in Cell Stem Cell on repairing the brain's wiring insulation. In multiple sclerosis, the fatty myelin sheath around nerve fibres is lost. Progenitor cells should rebuild it, but with age they stop answering the signals to mature. That failure locks in decline. The team asked whether the ageing itself could be undone.

Aged progenitor cells from rodents showed worn metabolism and DNA damage, signs of cell ageing. Fasting reversed those signs. So did metformin, a common diabetes drug. Treated old cells regained their ability to form myelin-making cells. The work suggests an approved drug might restore repair capacity in chronic demyelinating disease.
europmc-pmc6870991:
Arkin and co-authors describe KBase in Nature Biotechnology. KBase is the United States Department of Energy's systems biology knowledgebase. Genomics now produces data on thousands of organisms and their communities, in many forms at once. Making sense of it needs shared tools and shared data models. KBase was built to supply both.

The platform wraps analysis tools as apps that all work on one data representation. That design lets results feed each other and warns users when data they built on changes. At the time of writing it offered over 160 apps, covering genome assembly, annotation, and comparison. The authors present it as infrastructure for predicting biological function from genes to ecosystems.
europmc-pmc6872491:
Priestley and co-authors report a pan-cancer genome study in Nature. Cancer that has spread, metastatic cancer, causes most cancer deaths and responds poorly to treatment. Its genome may differ from the original tumour's. The team sequenced whole genomes of metastatic solid tumours across many cancer types, the largest such study to their knowledge.

They gathered 2,520 pairs of tumour and normal tissue, surveying more than 70 million somatic variants. Whole-genome duplication appeared in 56 percent of the tumours. Mutation patterns largely mirrored those of the matching primary cancer types. Rare in-frame insertions clustered in known cancer genes at telling hotspots. The authors offer the dataset as a base for personalised treatment of late-stage disease.
europmc-pmc6891691:
Lourenço and co-authors review natural antioxidants for the food industry, in the journal Molecules. Antioxidants keep foods from spoiling as fats and pigments react with oxygen. Synthetic versions are effective but face consumer suspicion over possible ill effects. Plants offer alternatives. Herbs, spices, seeds, fruits, and vegetables all carry antioxidant compounds, often in parts the food chain throws away.

The review covers the main plant sources and how the compounds are extracted and stabilised. It then surveys uses: as preservatives inside foods, and in active packaging films that protect from the outside. Berry and ginseng extracts already show such effects in trials the authors cite. Cost and dose control remain the practical hurdles.
europmc-pmc7077191:
Xu and co-authors systematically compare the two SARS coronaviruses in the journal Viruses. SARS-CoV caused the 2003 SARS outbreak, and its relative SARS-CoV-2 emerged from patients with unexplained pneumonia linked to a Wuhan seafood market, causing COVID-19. Both jumped from animals to humans, and both alarmed the world. A side-by-side account was needed while the second crisis was still young.

The comparison works through incubation, origins, diagnosis and treatment methods, genome and protein sequences, and the mechanisms by which each virus causes disease. Similarities include droplet and close-contact spread between people; differences in epidemiology and clinical features are drawn out in parallel sections. The authors wrote partly as a reference for responders deciding which SARS lessons carry over and which mislead. Their work captures an early, structured attempt to understand a new pathogen by holding it against its closest known relative.
europmc-pmc7080791:
Ranallo-Benavidez, Jaron, and Schatz present genome profiling tools in Nature Communications. Before building a genome, researchers profile it from raw sequencing reads: counting short word frequencies, called k-mers, estimates genome size, heterozygosity, and repetitiveness. Most profiling methods assume normal diploid genomes. Polyploid species, with more than two chromosome sets, break those rules.

GenomeScope 2.0 applies combinatorial theory to model how k-mer frequencies spread in heterozygous and polyploid genomes, and infers the main traits fast across thousands of simulated and several real datasets. Its companion, Smudgeplot, reads pairs of heterozygous k-mers to show and estimate ploidy and genome structure. The team validated the approach on the variable-ploidy nematode genus Meloidogyne and on the extreme case of the octoploid strawberry, Fragaria x ananassa. Both tools are public on GitHub. The work extends reference-free genome checks to the many species whose doubled genomes once defied them.
europmc-pmc7198091:
Soraci and co-authors validate the Italian version of the Fear of COVID-19 Scale. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction. Italy was among the countries hit hardest by the pandemic. Fear and anxiety rose widely there. A standard scale lets researchers measure that fear consistently.

The sample held 250 Italian participants. They completed the fear scale plus anxiety, depression, and phobia measures. Statistical tests checked the scale's structure and reliability. The Italian version formed one stable dimension, as designed. Its scores lined up sensibly with the other measures. The authors judge the tool sound for research and screening. It gives Italian studies a shared yardstick for pandemic fear.
europmc-pmc7245191:
Yoshimoto reviews the proteins of SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19. The article appeared in The Protein Journal. Cases and deaths were growing at an exponential rate when it was written. Understanding the virus's parts is a first step toward drugs and vaccines. The review walks through each protein the virus makes.

Structural proteins build the virus particle itself. Nonstructural proteins run the copying of its genome. One of them, NSP16, helps disguise viral RNA from the cell's alarms. It caps the RNA in a way that mimics the cell's own messages. Comparisons with the earlier SARS virus run through the review. Sequence alignments show where the two viruses match and differ. Readers get a parts list for the pandemic virus, protein by protein.
europmc-pmc7301291:
Laster Pirtle, writing solo, argues that racial capitalism is a fundamental cause of COVID-19's unequal toll in the United States. The article appeared in Health Education and Behavior. Black deaths were heavily overrepresented, with Detroit, Michigan used as a case study. The author applies a theory that names a social condition a fundamental cause when it shapes many diseases through many routes.

Racism and capitalism together, the argument runs, build conditions that raise risk for poor people and people of color: other diseases that interact with COVID-19, housing segregation, homelessness, and medical bias. They also ration flexible resources such as medical knowledge and freedom that could soften the blow. Because such causes repeat across pandemics, the author insists interventions must address social inequality itself to achieve health equity.
europmc-pmc7312091:
Ng and co-authors argue that a healthy pregnancy rests on how well the womb lining gets ready, in a step called decidualization. Their review notes that in humans this prep starts late in each monthly cycle, before any embryo is there. The lining shifts its hormones, chemistry, and immune stance to greet a blastocyst.

When the prep falls short, the placenta forms badly. The fallout can be miscarriage, preeclampsia, early birth, slow fetal growth, or diabetes in pregnancy. Past tries to stop these ills have mostly failed. The team blames a wrong aim: care has chased the seed, not the soil. On their view, the quality of that early prep is the main driver of pregnancy health, so care should start before conception.
europmc-pmc7336091:
Moore and co-authors survey Canadian families in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity on children's movement during COVID-19. Lockdowns closed schools and sports, raising fears about activity, screen time, and sleep. Parents of children aged 5 to 17 answered an online national survey, with 1,472 taking part.

Only 4.8 percent of children and 0.6 percent of youth met the combined movement guidelines during restrictions. Activity and outdoor time fell, while sitting and screen time rose and sleep lengthened. Parental encouragement, parents being active themselves, and owning a family dog all linked to healthier habits. Some families also took up new hobbies. The findings can guide efforts to protect child health in future crises.
europmc-pmc7352291:
Iddir and co-authors review diet, immunity, and inflammation during the COVID-19 crisis in Nutrients. With much of the world confined at home, they ask how food can best support the immune system. An optimal immune response, they note, rests on adequate diet, starting with enough protein for antibody production.

Low levels of nutrients such as vitamin A or zinc are tied to higher infection risk, and poor nutrition often travels with inflammation and oxidative stress. Vitamin C, vitamin E, and plant compounds like carotenoids push the other way. Vitamin D gets special attention for its contact with the virus's entry route into cells. Readers get a nutrient-by-nutrient guide to eating for immune defense.
europmc-pmc7383091:
Hikmet and co-authors map where the COVID-19 virus's doorway protein sits in the human body, in Molecular Systems Biology. ACE2 is the surface receptor the virus uses to enter cells, so its locations hint at which organs are vulnerable. The team stained tissues for the ACE2 protein across more than 150 cell types.

Strong expression appeared in gut lining cells, kidney tubules, gallbladder, heart muscle cells, placental cells, and parts of the eye and blood vessels. In the airways, expression was surprisingly limited, seen in few cells in only some people. The pattern helps explain gut and kidney involvement in the disease. The authors offer the atlas as a resource for entry studies and treatment design.
europmc-pmc7404091:
Capelletti and co-authors overview ferroptosis in liver diseases in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by iron and by the buildup of damaged fats in cell membranes. It looks and behaves differently from other death patterns.

The fingerprints are precise: loss of the repair enzyme GPX4, redox-active iron present, and oxidation of particular membrane fats. Pathways from amino acid handling to the p53 and Nrf2 systems tune how vulnerable a cell is. The review first lays out the mechanisms and the chemicals that start or stop the process, then walks through liver diseases, acute and chronic, where ferroptosis contributes. Triggering or blocking it could treat disease, depending on the organ's problem.
europmc-pmc7424491:
Tanase and co-authors review how type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, and fatty liver disease feed each other. In nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, fat builds up in the liver without heavy drinking. Each of the three conditions raises the risk of the others.

The authors trace the shared roots in body chemistry and immune activity. Fatty liver can range from mild fat buildup to inflammation, scarring, and liver cancer. The review covers screening and noninvasive tests that find the disease early. It weighs how current diabetes drugs affect liver fat. New drug targets get a look as well. The piece gives a broad view of three linked diseases that now affect many adults worldwide.
europmc-pmc7504791:
Fhu and Ali review fatty acid synthase as a rising target in cancer care. Lipid making has drawn fresh focus in tumor research. Tumors need fat building blocks to grow and can burn fat for energy.

The enzyme, called FASN, sits at the center of lipid control. It helps tumors with fat-making traits grow and survive. It can rewire tumor cells for flexible energy use under stress. It also shapes organelle work, sugar use, and amino acid handling. New blockers of FASN are in early clinical trials now. The review gathers proof that this enzyme matters across many cancers. It makes the case for FASN as a drug target worth the trials under way.
europmc-pmc7507691:
Ghelli Luserna di Rorà and co-authors review the WEE1 kinase family in cell division, cancer, and therapy. Blocking the DNA damage response has drawn strong interest in cancer care. WEE1 kinases guard the cell cycle and spot DNA damage.

WEE1 and its kin PKMYT1 act as tumor suppressors in healthy cells. In cancer cells they can act more like growth aids. The review gathers data on their changes in blood and solid tumors. It covers how 36 chemo and radiotherapy agents interact with the checkpoints these kinases run in preclinical work. Trials of WEE1 and PKMYT1 blockers, alone and in pairs with other drugs, get a full survey. The authors weigh where these blockers fit in cancer care next.
europmc-pmc7509391:
Hippisley-Cox and co-authors test if blood pressure drugs change the risk of severe COVID-19. The drugs are ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Doubt about their safety in the pandemic ran wide.

The cohort drew on 1205 general practices in England with 8.28 million participants aged 20-99 years in the data set. Of them, 19,486 people had COVID-19 disease and 1286 received intensive care in the study. Both drug classes linked with a reduced risk of COVID-19 disease after full adjustment. Neither linked with a higher risk of intensive care. Effects differed by ethnic group in the results. The authors say the drugs look safe on this point. Ethnic gaps in effect deserve more study, they add.
europmc-pmc7550191:
Watson and co-authors determine the structure of the bacterial ribosome at fine detail. They used cryo-electron microscopy on the Escherichia coli 70S ribosome. The global resolution reached 2.0 Å.

The maps show clear positions for protein and RNA residues. Chemical interactions and modifications are visible in detail. The team found unusual backbone changes in ribosomal proteins. One type may be conserved across all life domains. Water structure around the small subunit is extensive. Contacts with tRNAs, mRNA and an antibiotic are shown. The models support deeper study of translation. They also aid tools for future cryo-EM work.
europmc-pmc7559591:
Knoll and co-authors present an R package for testing cancer incidence projection methods. Forecasts guide prevention, screening and health policy work. Long registry data are not available in many countries.

The package is called incAnalysis. It supports Bayesian models fitted with INLA tools. The team tested models of varied complexity in depth. Long-term data came from three cancer registries for benchmarking. Coverage stayed above 90% for Bayesian age-period-cohort models. Simple intercept-only models fell below 20% coverage. Bias grew and precision fell for longer forecasts. Complex models gave the lowest precision overall. The package lets researchers compare approaches in one place.
europmc-pmc7561091:
Siegel and co-authors analyze prostate cancer cases and survival in the United States by stage and group. Their data span the years 2001 to 2017 for cases across the whole country. Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death among men there.

Registries recorded 3.1 million new cases from 2003 to 2017 in the data set. Localized cases made up seventy-seven percent of that total number of new cases. Regional, distant and unknown stages made up the rest of the recorded cases. Distant-stage cases rose in share from 2010 to 2017 over the study period. Ten-year survival for localized cancer was one hundred percent in the data. Five-year survival for distant cancer rose from twenty-eight point seven percent to thirty-two point three percent. The report details survival gaps by race, ethnicity and age group for health planning use.
europmc-pmc7593591:
Gruber-Vodicka and co-authors present phyloFlash, a tool for small-subunit rRNA profiling from metagenomes. The SSU rRNA gene is the standard marker across life. It is often missing from metagenome-assembled genomes.
