The software gives fast taxonomic classification from that gene. It also assembles sorted SSU rRNA reads on target. Results link back to assembled genomes through graph parsing. The design covers bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes alike. A cleaned reference database anchors the workflow. Tools for comparing many samples are included. Recovered genes can join standard metagenomics pipelines with ease. The suite helps tie microbe identity to older literature and probes.
europmc-pmc7596191:
Huan, Kong, Mou and Yi review antimicrobial peptides across many fields of use. These small peptides occur widely in nature. They form part of innate immunity in many organisms.

Peptides can inhibit bacteria, fungi, parasites and viruses. Rising antibiotic resistance has renewed interest in them. Uses span medicine, food and animal farming. Agriculture and aquaculture uses are also covered. The review sets out peptide classes and how they act. Design methods for new peptides are explained. Factors in the environment that alter activity are covered. Anti-coronavirus peptides get special attention in the review. Open problems for the field are listed at the end.
europmc-pmc7641391:
Kellam and Barclay review antibody responses after SARS-CoV-2 infection and the risk of reinfection. Timing and strength of humoral immunity were not yet known. That knowledge shapes pandemic planning and vaccine dosing.

As of April 17 in that year, 2,114,269 people had been infected. Deaths stood at 145,144 worldwide at that date. The review first covers SARS and MERS antibody patterns. Severe cases of those diseases gave lasting antibodies. Mild cases often showed weak or fast-fading responses. Early SARS-CoV-2 serology studies are then summed up. Work in primates on reinfection is also covered. Pressing research needs close the review. Seasonal cold coronaviruses offer a further comparison for immunity length.
europmc-pmc7727191:
Xu and co-authors review CD44, a surface protein tied to tumor growth and spread. CD44 comes in a standard form and many variant forms. It marks cancer stem cells in many tumors. It also drives the shape shift that lets cancer cells move and invade.

CD44 feeds into many signal paths that steer growth, spread, and drug resistance. High levels often mean a poor outlook for patients. Trials have tested antibodies against CD44 for safety and effect. The authors set out its structure, its controls, and its roles step by step. They frame CD44 as a drug target worth the effort to hit well.
europmc-pmc7734391:
Kruk and co-authors call for a revolution in health system quality. It lands in the era of the Sustainable Development Goals. Past frames judged care by structure, process, and outcomes. The authors argue that high quality must now be defined around the user and across the whole system.

They set out an updated frame for what a high-quality system is and does. Poor quality, they argue, is now a larger barrier to health than lack of access alone in many places. Trying harder inside weak systems will not fix this. The report urges deep redesign, with care that is safe, effective, timely, fair, and centered on people.
europmc-pmc7820391:
The GBD 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators break down the causes of world vision loss in 2020. Many causes can be prevented or treated. An aging world population raises demand for eye care. The team compared causes across three decades.

Estimates cover 1990 to 2020. The authors rank each cause by its share of blindness. They do the same for milder vision impairment. A key aim was counting avoidable blindness. That figure tests progress toward the VISION 2020 goals. World Health Assembly targets provide another yardstick. The findings show where treatment backlogs sit. They point to cataract and uncorrected focus error as huge, fixable loads.
europmc-pmc7855591:
Chen and co-authors map where the SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor ACE2 sits in human and mouse brains. The virus uses ACE2 to enter host cells. It can affect the brain, among many organs. Where ACE2 lies in the brain was still murky. The team mined public brain gene datasets.

ACE2 ran high in the choroid plexus. The thalamus's paraventricular nuclei also stood out. Many neuron types carried the gene. Some support cells and vessel cells did too. The hippocampus showed few positive cells, and the prefrontal cortex none. Mouse brains matched the broad pattern. The smell bulb ran high in mice, though. The map hints at routes for brain symptoms in COVID-19.
europmc-pmc7857391:
Cantuti-Castelvetri and co-authors identify neuropilin-1 as a helper for SARS-CoV-2 cell entry. Both this virus and the earlier SARS virus use ACE2 as receptor. Their tissue patterns differ, though. That gap hinted at extra host factors.

Neuropilin-1 sits on cell surfaces in key tissues. The team shows it eases the virus into cells. Infection rates rise where it is present. Blocking it lowers entry in lab tests. The factor may explain spread into certain organs. It also marks a fresh point for drug design. Entry blockers could target this helper alongside ACE2.
europmc-pmc7864991:
Chaibun and co-authors build a rapid electrochemical test for SARS-CoV-2. Standard PCR testing is slow and needs costly machines. Their sensor uses rolling circle copying to grow the signal. Probes carry labels that report on contact.

The one-step test reads the virus's N and S genes. It can spot as little as 1 copy per microliter. Results come in under 2 hours. The team checked it on 106 patient samples. Of these, 41 held SARS-CoV-2 and 9 held other lung viruses. Every result matched the PCR verdict. Signal strength tracked PCR values closely. The authors pitch it for on-site, real-time use.
europmc-pmc7945491:
Burger presents an address on the standing of the medical profession and the divine origin of medicine. Burger led the Netherland Medical Association three times. Each term brought a presidential address on the doctor's place and task. This paper translates the last of the three, given at Middelburg in 1925. Passages of purely local interest have been cut.

Recovery from grave illness feels like a gift from heaven, he begins. Poets and philosophers have praised health as the greatest earthly blessing. The art that restores it was held to be divine in pagan times and in Christianity alike. Apollo, the healing god, passed the art to his son Aesculapius. The address traces that belief through scripture and history. It asks what such reverence means for how doctors should see their calling.
europmc-pmc7946091:
Skavlem presents a study of the scientific life of Thomas Bartholin. The paper was read before a Wisconsin medical history seminar. The name Bartholin was bound up with the early growth of science at the University of Copenhagen. Caspar Bartholin fostered that growth first. Under Thomas Bartholin, professor of anatomy, it reached its height. Copenhagen could fairly be called the school of the Bartholins in his day.

He drew disciples from Denmark and abroad to work around him. Teaching in Latin let him reach students of every tongue. He pressed on them a love of scientific truth and a standard of high-grade research. His followers carried the school's anatomy across Europe. Names such as Lyser, Seger, and Stensen figure in that spread. Skavlem traces how one professor built a lasting scientific house.
europmc-pmc7960691:
GBD 2019 Hearing Loss Collaborators present a global study of hearing loss and its burden from 1990 to 2019. Hearing loss limits access to speech. That can harm learning, development, and social life. The study updates world estimates of how many people live with it. It also measures the years lived with disability that it causes, and forecasts the picture to 2050.

An estimated 1.57 billion people had hearing loss in 2019. That is one in five people worldwide. Most of them, 62.1%, were older than 50 years. The largest count of moderate-to-complete loss sat in the Western Pacific region. As populations age, the total will grow. The authors name proven helps: child screening, hearing aids, and care for ear infections. The burden falls hardest where health care is weakest, they note.
europmc-pmc8024391:
Sterner and Sterner review the limits of CAR-T cell therapy and the strategies meant to beat them. CAR-T cells are patient T cells re-engineered to hunt cancer. The approach produced striking results in some B cell leukemias and lymphomas. Anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy won FDA approval in 2017. Yet many barriers still cap its reach.

The pair list severe, life-threatening toxicities among the chief problems. Antigen escape lets tumors dodge the engineered cells. Trafficking into solid tumors is poor, and infiltration weaker still. The tumor microenvironment further blunts the cells. The review then covers fresh engineering ideas. These aim to raise anti-tumor power while cutting toxicity. Training a workforce for this complex therapy also gets attention.
europmc-pmc8026591:
Ye and co-authors build a pyroptosis-based gene signature to predict survival in ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer carries a very poor prognosis, and good predictors are scarce. Pyroptosis is an inflammatory form of programmed cell death. The team first compared tumor and normal ovarian tissue. They found 31 pyroptosis regulators with differing expression, enough to split cases into two subtypes.

Using the TCGA cohort, the authors weighed each gene against patient survival. A LASSO Cox model distilled the list into a 7-gene signature. Patients in the low-risk group survived far longer than the high-risk group. The score also sorted a separate GEO cohort correctly. It stayed an independent predictor beside clinical traits. Immune activity looked weaker in the high-risk group, tying the signature to tumor immunity.
europmc-pmc8140091:
Grubman and co-authors separate plaque-eating microglia from their neighbors and read their gene programs. Microglia guard the brain, but their variety in Alzheimer's disease is murky. The team sorted mouse microglia by a dye that marks amyloid plaques. Cells carrying plaque material formed one pool, clean cells another. Gene reads split the pools along distinct paths. Aging and disease bent those paths differently.

Plaque-carrying microglia misexpressed genes tied to late-onset Alzheimer's risk. The same program appeared in a subset of human microglia. Those human cells came from brains of people with the disease. Plaque-free cells instead looked prematurely aged by signature. They held more swallowed synaptic material inside them. Yet they actively ate fewer synaptosomes in live tests. A regulator, HIF1α, emerged as a dial for that eating. The split clarifies which microglia do what. Alzheimer's therapy may need to address them separately.
europmc-pmc8204491:
Guzior and Quinn examine how gut microbes transform human bile acids. The liver makes primary bile acids for digestion and signalling. Microbes in the gut then remake them into many new forms.

Four classic changes have been known since the early 1960s. They strip amino acids and edit the cholesterol core in set ways. New work adds fresh transformations to that list. These secondary bile acids shape the microbiome itself. Their shifts have been linked to cirrhosis, bowel inflammation, and cancer. The review maps a quiet chemistry with wide effects.
europmc-pmc8220791:
Zhao and co-authors compare measures for counting RNA sequencing output. Picking the wrong measure can distort comparisons between samples. TPM, FPKM, and normalised counts all stay in wide use.

The team used replicate samples from 20 patient-derived xenograft models. The set held 61 tumours across 15 cancer types. They judged how reproducible each measure proved across replicates. Downstream gene expression calls formed part of the test. No consensus measure existed before this check. Their results help analysts pick a measure with evidence. Inter-sample comparison was the heart of the test they ran.
europmc-pmc8260991:
Proal and VanElzakker overview biological factors that may drive long COVID symptoms. A share of patients keep wide-ranging symptoms for many months. Their illness is called long COVID, or post-acute sequelae of COVID-19.

The authors argue that drivers likely differ between patients. Several factors may act at once in one person. They review how RNA viruses beyond SARS-CoV-2 cause lasting harm. Candidate routes include viral persistence and immune misfiring. The paper gathers the evidence for each route. It frames tests that could split long COVID into clearer types. No single factor is asked to explain every case.
europmc-pmc8344591:
O'Toole and co-authors present pangolin, a tool that assigns SARS-CoV-2 genomes to lineages. Genome sharing during the pandemic reached an unmatched scale. Data grew by orders of magnitude, outrunning older methods.

Pangolin gives a sequence its most likely lineage. It follows the Pango dynamic naming scheme. Genomics teams worldwide built it as an open effort. Assignments update as the lineage tree grows. The tool became a shared language for variant tracking. Outbreak reports could name strains the same way everywhere. That consistency underpins the variant news the public follows. The scheme stays dynamic as new lineages appear.
europmc-pmc8571891:
Zhu and co-authors review the oncogene KRAS in colorectal cancer prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment. Colorectal cancer varies widely at cell and molecular levels. KRAS is one of its most common mutated genes. Faults in it lock the protein on, which drives growth signals without pause.

About 40 percent of cases carry KRAS mutations, per the authors. Patients with them face a poor outlook. Testing for KRAS faults is routine before treating spread disease. KRAS was long called undruggable, a view now cracked. New inhibitors aim at the G12C form of the fault. The review weighs those drugs and the precise care this patient group needs.
europmc-pmc8632791:
Colin and co-authors review the many jobs of flagellar movement and chemotaxis in bacteria. Swimming bacteria follow gradients of food and other signals. The basic machinery is well known from model species. Less clear is what this behavior does for the cells and their groups in real settings.

The review argues that finding food and good niches is a core job. Movement also speeds up how bacteria settle new places. It shapes group acts such as swarming and biofilm growth. Trade-offs between growth and movement run through these roles. The same system can serve distinct ends under distinct conditions. Readers get a broad view of a classic model system.
europmc-pmc8634691:
Aristovnik and co-authors describe a global survey dataset on how the first COVID-19 wave hit higher education students. Lockdowns reshaped study, social life, and well-being. The online survey ran from May 5 to June 15 in 2020. It was offered in seven languages.

The final dataset holds 31,212 responses from 133 countries. Students reported on study life, home study tools and skills, social life, and feelings. They also gave background and life circumstance details. The dataset is shared for other researchers to use. It lets teams compare student experience across countries and groups. Few surveys of the pandemic's first wave match its scale.
europmc-pmc8639891:
Yu, Zhang, and Guo review conductive materials used as dressings for wound healing and skin repair. These dressings carry electric signals that can help tissue mend. The review covers the agents that make them conductive, from polymers to inorganic nanomaterials. It also covers the many forms the dressings take.

The authors set out three routes by which these materials aid healing. Uses tested in living models get a full look. The review then turns to open problems. Moving these dressings into clinics will take more work on safety and design. Readers get a broad map of a fast-growing corner of wound care.
europmc-pmc8759291:
Pan and co-authors identify a circular RNA, circNEIL3, that drives glioma growth and suppresses immune attack. Gliomas are the most common malignant brain tumors and carry a poor outlook. Circular RNAs are stable, ring-shaped RNAs found in many tumors. Sequencing of tumor and normal tissue flagged this one as raised in glioma.

Levels rose with tumor severity. Tests in cells and animals confirmed that it fuels tumor growth. It protects a known cancer protein from breakdown. Tumor cells also pack it into exosomes and send it to macrophages. Those macrophages then take on an immune-suppressing state. The authors name it a marker and drug target.
europmc-pmc8775991:
Fahed and co-authors update the science and care of metabolic syndrome for 2021. The syndrome clusters insulin resistance, harmful blood fats, belly obesity, and high blood pressure. Its roots mix genetic and acquired factors under chronic low-grade inflammation. Left untreated, it raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease sharply.

Heart disease is the top cause of death and illness worldwide. That scale makes the syndrome a major public target. The review opens with the history and spread of the condition. It then covers tissue changes and body mechanisms in current detail. Newest steps in care and prevention close the account.
europmc-pmc8833991:
Hajam and co-authors review oxidative stress and its role in disease and aging. Cells make reactive oxygen and nitrogen species during normal work. Antioxidants, both enzymatic and not, normally keep them in check. When production outruns defense, oxidative stress builds. Tissues then take damage over time. Aging itself is linked to this slow buildup.

The review explains how reactive species drive harmful signaling. It covers their part in brain diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. Chronic kidney disease gets its own section. So do heart disease, lung disease, and cancer. DNA damage from these species is treated in depth. The authors close by seeking natural remedies. They want prevention and treatment grounded in this chemistry.
europmc-pmc9226391:
Zhang and co-authors review CAR-T cell therapy in blood cancers, its chances and its hurdles. The therapy has achieved striking success in relapsed or refractory B cell cancers. CD19 and BCMA are the most common targets so far. Many new targets are now being explored.

Serious side effects can threaten life, including cytokine release syndrome and brain-related toxicity. Infections, low blood counts, and clotting problems also occur. Many patients relapse because the antigen is lost, the cells fade, or the tumor environment suppresses them. The review covers targets, toxicities, and resistance in turn. Practical advice for care teams is included. Readers get a balanced view of a breakthrough therapy still being refined.
europmc-pmc9387091:
Cousins and co-authors argue that PFAS pollution has already crossed a planetary boundary. They tracked four long-lived perfluoroalkyl acids in rain, soil, and surface water worldwide. Levels were compared with recent health and environmental guideline values. These chemicals barely break down and ride the water cycle endlessly.

Rainwater levels of PFOA and PFOS often far exceeded US drinking water advisory values. The four-acid sum often broke Danish drinking water limits too. Rain also pushed global soils past proposed Dutch guideline values. Sea spray keeps the acids cycling between ocean and air. The authors say this spread is poorly reversible. They call for rapid cuts in PFAS use and emissions. Waiting, they argue, only deepens a lifelong exposure problem.
europmc-pmc9623991:
Han and co-authors summarize the machinery of exosome biogenesis and its use as a cancer drug target. Exosomes are key couriers between cells in health and disease. Their making runs through four main steps in sequence. Cargo sorting comes first, then vesicle body formation. Transport and fusion with the cell surface close the chain.

Each step can run by more than one mechanism. ESCRT dependent and independent routes both appear. Ceramide and tetraspanin paths add further variety. Mixed routes explain why exosome groups are so uneven. Cancer cells hijack the system for their own gain. They tweak gene output, protein marks, and signals to reshape output. The review sorts those tricks by step and player. Drug plans that strike exosome making are then weighed. Such plans may slow spread and drug resistance, they argue.
europmc-pmc9812791:
McNamara and co-authors show that microglia govern myelin growth and integrity in the adult brain. Myelin wraps axons so signals travel fast and true. What keeps that wrapping healthy was unclear before. Brain macrophages were suspects with no clear assignment.

The team found resident microglia are key for adult myelin health. The result held in both mice and human tissue. Microglia were not needed to build myelin in youth. They were needed to tune its growth afterward. Without them, myelin grew too thick and then broke down. Thinking performance suffered along with the myelin loss. A shifted fat metabolism state appeared in myelin making cells. The TGF-beta signaling axis controlled that state change. The authors flag microglia as drug targets for myelin diseases. Aging and nerve wasting diseases top the candidate list.
europmc-pmc9865891:
Krylova and Feng review how exosomes form, leave cells, and enter other cells. Exosomes are membrane vesicles about 40–200 nm wide that cells release into their surroundings. They carry proteins, lipids, and several forms of RNA and DNA. Interest has grown in their use as disease markers and drug targets.

The review traces cargo sorting from early endosomes through later trafficking steps. It covers release into body fluids and uptake by target cells. Exosomes support cell balance, waste removal, and long-range signaling. Disease can disrupt or hijack this system. The authors update molecular detail from recent work to aid future exosome experiments.
europmc-pmc9890491:
Cambier and co-authors examine two chemokines, CXCL8 and CXCL12, and their roles in health and disease. Chemokines guide the movement and activation of white blood cells. CXCL8 is the strongest human signal that draws neutrophils to infection and injury. CXCL12 holds leukocytes in bone marrow and supports blood cell formation.

The review details how each chemokine binds receptors such as CXCR1, CXCR2, and CXCR4. It covers dimer formation, gene control, and chemical changes that tune activity. CXCL8 drives inflammation and cancer-linked processes, making it a drug target in trials. CXCL12 shapes embryo growth, blood formation, and new vessel growth. Together they show how opposed signals balance cell movement.
europmc-pmc9942591:
Yariv and co-authors describe an updated ConSurf server for reading evolutionary data in macromolecules. ConSurf estimates how fast each site in a protein, RNA, or DNA changed over evolution. Slow-changing sites often mark catalytic or binding roles. The server gives a quick route to those signals.

Since the last report in 2016, the interface became easier to use. Homolog search now runs through hidden Markov model tools inside the pipeline. Redundant sequences are removed to form a clean, representative set. Rates can be mapped onto molecular structures for clear reading. AlphaFold models for nearly all UniProt proteins raise its value. The update helps researchers spot functional regions with less effort.
famous-affinities-of-history-the-romance:
The third volume of Lyndon Orr's Famous Affinities of History opens on the Texas frontier. The Wives of General Houston begin with the chalked letters G. T. T., gone to Texas. Sam Houston, numbered with the quality by birth, anchors the tale. Orr uses the joke to enter a world of bankruptcy, warrants, and reinvention.

Lola Montez and King Ludwig of Bavaria follow, a dancer unseating a king. Gambetta and Léonie Léon join French politics to devotion. Lady Blessington and Count d'Orsay glitter in exile. Byron and the Countess Guiccioli, Madame de Staël, and Karl Marx widen the canvas. Lassalle's fatal love for Helene von Dönniges and the actress Rachel close the volume. Orr's affinities here are revolutionaries and exiles, loved as hard as they fought.
french-constitution-1791:
France adopted its first written constitution in September 1791, the work of the National Constituent Assembly. The Revolution had begun in hope two years before, and the Assembly tried to settle it into ordered liberty. The result was a constitutional monarchy: a king kept on his throne, ruling beside an elected Legislative Assembly.

The charter divides power, promises equality before the law, and guards property and speech, while limiting the vote to men who paid set taxes. The king accepted it under pressure after his failed flight to Varennes. War and radical anger swept the settlement away within a year, and the monarchy fell in 1792. The constitution remains the charter of the Revolution's hopeful phase, liberty under law before the Terror. It also records what the men of 1789 thought a free state should be.
frus-1861-d191:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Cassius Clay on 6 May 1861. Clay was the new American minister to Russia, bound for St. Petersburg. The letter is document 191 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay was a Kentucky emancipationist with a fighter's fame. Russia, under a young czar who had just freed the serfs, watched America with rare warmth. Seward's May letter sent Clay to the one great court that leaned toward the Union. Clay's fame as a duelist and emancipationist made him a marked man at any court. A marked man at court drew eyes, which Clay turned to the Union's gain.
frus-1861-d291:
Word from Mr. Harvey reached Washington on 28 July 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 291 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d91:
On 22 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in his firm autumn tone. The letter is document 91 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late October letters from Seward carry the feel of a man who has found his wartime stride. The orders are brief, the tone is firm, the goals are clear. This note to London shows the Secretary in full command of his far flung front. The orders assume Adams's full grasp, a trust the Secretary rarely gave so freely. Full command in the chief bred full effort in the man who served him.
frus-1862-d191:
Document 191 is the second Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams dated 18 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams served as American minister in London, the post his father and grandfather had also held in earlier years.

Paired letters on one date often mean one carried the Secretary's orders while the other passed papers or news. The Adams legation answered in kind, and the printed file grows thick. For readers tracing how the Union kept Britain at arm's length in late 1862, the paired dispatches of November are core evidence. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d291:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 23 June 1862 in a letter printed as Document 291 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote two days before the Seven Days battles began, in the last quiet of the Richmond campaign. French observers expected the capital's fall to settle the war's foreign side. His report belongs to that expectant week, and its value lies partly in its timing. It preserves what Paris believed just before events proved it wrong. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d391:
Document 391 is the second Seward dispatch to Simon Cameron dated 6 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to St. Petersburg together.

Same-day pairs on the Russian route mattered because sailings were rare; a missed mail could cost a month. Clerks therefore batched the post's business carefully. This second letter completes the September brief for St. Petersburg, and the pair together shows Washington briefing its Russian envoy on the invasion crisis as it began. Letters to Russia favored broad lines of policy over fast-changing battle news. The czar's government had freed its own serfs in 1861 and watched America's struggle closely.
frus-1862-d491:
On 2 April 1862 James Shepherd Pike sent this report from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 491 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Pike wrote days before the battle of Shiloh, in a lull when European opinion was weighing the war's cost against its likely end. The Dutch, careful neutrals with worldwide trade, wanted the fighting stopped but would not move first. His report measured that mood for Washington. Ministers' letters in this season also carried the small change of diplomacy: visits, dinners, and remarks that hinted at policy. Pike's blunt style makes his contributions to the volume unusually readable.
frus-1862-d591:
Dated 2 June 1862, this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Thomas Corwin was printed after the order of 7 June in the volume's Mexican file. It is Document 591 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The two June instructions, read together by date, show Seward handling the Mexican question in successive layers as reports from Corwin arrived. France's advance in Mexico posed the Union a problem it could not solve by force that year. So it solved it by record. The record held clear protests, kept promises of sympathy, and a paper trail for the future. Corwin's post was where that trail was laid. The letter is a working part of the longest-range policy in the whole volume.
frus-1862-d691: On 3 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. De Long. The letter is document 691 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering the run of dispatches De Long had sent that winter. The evidence names both men and the date, but it does not state De Long's post or the letter's topic.
frus-1862-d91:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 5 July 1862. It stands as Document 91 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d191:
Writing from London on 7 May 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 191 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d291:
Washington's orders to London on 17 September 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 291 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d391:
In Washington on 16 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 391 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d491:
The date 5 May 1863 heads a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d591:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 18 July 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d691:
Edwin M. Stanton, the Secretary of War, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 October 1863. The note is document 691 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. Unlike most letters in this run, it comes from inside the Lincoln cabinet itself.

War and foreign affairs often met. Army and navy acts at sea or on the border could stir trouble with Britain at any time. Stanton's note brought the War Department's facts or views to the man who had to answer for them abroad. The reader sees the home side of diplomacy here. Before Seward spoke to foreign envoys, he needed word from his own team.
frus-1863p1-d91:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 25 February 1863, the second day in a row he wrote to London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 91 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Day-after-day letters from the secretary often chased a point that would not wait for the next steamer. For London, the points were steady ones: fair dealing from Britain, and a stop to warships for the South. This letter keeps that press on. It is a mid-run sheet, plain in form, whose weight comes from the chain of orders it belongs to.
frus-1891:
Chile dominates the 1891 volume almost alone. Its two blocks dwarf every other country file. Civil war in Chile drives the correspondence. China follows at a great distance. Its Peking letters report a decree on the audience question. Denby calls the Emperor's action voluntary and spontaneous. Italy, usually brief, takes a sharp special file.

It prints the killing of Italian prisoners in New Orleans. The attack of March 14, 1891 fills the section. Rome demands answers for its dead subjects. The file mixes consular reports with public anger. Brazil, Central America, and Austria fill standard places. The volume's shape is lopsided by crisis. A South American war and a lynching crowd out routine. Diplomacy here reacts to violence twice over.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d191:
Acting Secretary of State Edward Stettinius wrote to Wallace Murray, the State Department's adviser on political relations, on 5 November 1943. The short secret note passes on items from that day's meeting with President Roosevelt, some for Murray's information and some needing action.

Roosevelt admits he does not grasp the Middle East oil problem and asks for a two-page brief on it at once. He floats a trusteeship for the region shared by Russia, Britain, and America. He also wants a four-power commission for French West Africa, and he sounds annoyed with de Gaulle. A final item, on Turkey, is marked secret and passed on only in conversation, so its content stays off the page.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d291:
John Martin, Prime Minister Churchill's private secretary, sent a short secret covering note to Harry Hopkins at Cairo on 23 November 1943, enclosing a British telegram from Jedda dated 15 November. Churchill, writing as Colonel Warden, had asked Martin to show Hopkins the telegram and have it returned.

The enclosure reports King Ibn Saud's complaint from Mecca. An American representative in Jedda had put seven pointed questions to him about Saudi arms requests to Britain: what was asked, what was promised, and what had arrived. The king answered that fifty light reconnaissance cars were promised and none had come. The British minister calls the questions unfortunate, since they suggest distrust between the allies, and urges a quick joint agreement on arms for Saudi Arabia.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d391:
Three unrelated reports for the President at Tehran were gathered into a secret telegram Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt from Washington on 29 November 1943. It is a typical Hull digest, moving from China to Portugal in a few lines.

Chungking reports news from a Chinese source who had lately seen Japanese and puppet officials at Nanking. Japan keeps making unsuccessful peace offers to Chiang's government. Former foreign minister Matsuoka left Japan on 7 October. His errand was to try to arrange peace between Germany and the Soviet Union. A consul at Kweilin reports Changteh in flames and Changsha expected to fall with only token defense. Finally, Salazar's speech of 26 November stressed British and American assurances of Portuguese sovereignty over the Azores, and Portuguese press accounts set that American part in italics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d491:
Madame Chiang Kai-shek wrote to President Roosevelt on December 5, 1943. She had stood beside her husband, Generalissimo Chiang, at the first Cairo Conference in November, serving as his voice in English, and China had won public pledges in the Cairo Declaration. The State Department printed her letter in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Few figures moved between the Chinese and American leadership as Madame Chiang did; she had addressed the United States Congress earlier in 1943. A letter from her to Roosevelt carried the weight of the China theater and of her own standing in Washington. It shows the personal diplomacy that held the Chinese alliance together.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d91: Roosevelt replied to Ambassador Winant in London on November 2, 1943, the same day Winant's dispatch in this series was written. The answer is Document 91 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. President-to-ambassador letters in wartime often carried guidance too sensitive for wider files. The record names the parties and the date only. The reply rests in the Foreign Relations volume with the other papers of that full day.
frus-1944-quebec-d191:
Mackenzie King's notes, reprinted by the editors, preserve his conversation with Roosevelt just before dinner at Quebec. King raised Canada's part in the Pacific war. Canada was prepared to fight Japan, he said, but in the northern or central regions. Roosevelt answered that a token representation should suffice, and that nothing might be needed for some time.

The president hinted Canadian men might be useful driving the Japanese from northern China toward the war's end. He also said Canada should have a token force to march into Berlin. On Russia, King asked directly what part Stalin would play against Japan. Roosevelt repeated what had been said earlier and added that Stalin had given his word himself.
frus-1944-quebec-d291:
An editors' note bridges Quebec and the Hyde Park meetings of September 17 to 19, 1944. Roosevelt reached home on the morning of September 17. Churchill arrived a day later with his wife, daughter Mary, and a party including Leathers, Ismay, and Moran, leaving on the night of September 19 for the Queen Mary and England. Guests included the Duke of Windsor at lunch and Morgenthau at dinner.

Because Churchill was a guest in Roosevelt's home, their conversations were informal and unminuted, as was the president's custom. Leahy's account lists the substance. There were political questions on Italy, Yugoslavia, and Russia. There was signature of the Octagon report, and drafting of a statement on Italy. Finally came a discussion of atomic energy, military and industrial, which produced an initialed aide-mémoire.
frus-1944-quebec-d91:
Treasury staff prepared a briefing book dated September 9, 1944. Briefing books gather facts and positions for busy leaders. The State Department printed this one in the Quebec 1944 volume. It appeared three days before the conference opened.

A briefing book aims to give one reader everything needed. Treasury officials packed figures and arguments into a single volume. Money questions awaited the leaders at Quebec that month. They included aid to Britain and Germany's economic future. For readers, the book shows how departments arm their chiefs. Pages of staff work stood behind each short summit discussion.
frus-1945-50-intel-d191:
The memorandum of 28 March 1947 is the work of the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 191, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d291:
On 17 June 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 13th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. Readers meet it as document 291 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time.

A memorandum of conversation is the note a participant or aide wrote after a talk, setting down who was there and what was said. For a reader, the gain is scene and voice, rare goods in a file of stiff forms. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d391:
A letter dated 29 July 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 391 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

A formal letter was a step above a memo: it put a request or a stance on record under the writer's signature. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d91:
Minutes of the eighth meeting of the Advisory Committee on Intelligence are dated 3 December 1946. The committee advised the State Department on its intelligence work. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A committee still meeting in December 1946 shows the State Department's intelligence function settling into a lasting, smaller form. The eighth meeting's minutes record routine where the autumn of 1945 had recorded upheaval. Readers can measure the change across the volume: from frantic memos about survival to numbered meetings about business. That settling is itself a result worth noting, the sound of a new order becoming normal inside an old department.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d191:
Hold everything on Italy, Stettinius cabled from Caserta on 30 January 1945. His top secret message to Acting Secretary Grew, sent from Allied Force Headquarters in Italy, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It concerns a joint statement he had not yet seen.

The Combined Civil Affairs Committee has prepared a proposed joint statement on Italy. Stettinius hopes Grew will hold up any action on it. He has not seen the text, but the feeling at headquarters is that issuing it in its present form would be most unfortunate. He asks Grew to cable the full text and its status. The message runs through a channel marked for the acting secretary's eyes alone at the far end.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d291:
The American chiefs met at Malta on 30 January 1945 and set their house in order first. These Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, open the staff conference that preceded the leaders' talks at Yalta. General Marshall leads the recorded business.

First comes the agenda paper for the combined talks, C. C. S. 765/8, which the chiefs agree to recommend for approval. Marshall points out its additions, among them the combined bomber offensive and planning dates for the end of both wars. Next, an overall review of cargo shipping wins approval of the Joint Staff Planners' recommendations. The third item turns to the fighting itself: strategy in northwest Europe, placed on the table for examination and discussion with the British.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d391:
General John Deane, head of the American Military Mission in Moscow, wrote the questions for the first staff meeting with the Soviets. His memorandum of February 7, 1945, lists what to ask. Had Soviet plans for operations in the Far East changed since October? Would the Soviets need a Pacific supply route once war with Japan began?

More questions follow. Would Moscow agree to American air forces operating from the Komsomolsk-Nikolaevsk area? Each question carried a negotiation inside it. Deane, who dealt with the Soviet staff daily, framed the asks that the chiefs carried into the secret February 8 meeting.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d491: Justice Byrnes would beat the communiqué home, and Stephen Early planned for it in this telegram to Jonathan Daniels of February 10, 1945. Byrnes should reach Washington early the next week, and the press would surely want a conference with him. Early and Byrnes had talked, and Byrnes understood the position. Early suggested Daniels and Walter Brown arrange it if the press wished. One condition held firm: the final communiqué must appear before Byrnes said anything. The wire shows the administration scripting a key homecoming.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d91:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson put his views on the peace machinery in writing on 23 January 1945. His memorandum to the Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It lists the points he had tried to make at their meeting the day before.

Stimson recalls that the Moscow Conference of 1943 had in view two bodies. One was a general body open to all peace-loving states, large and small. The other was a stopgap body of the four large powers, to guard security while order was restored. The powers that won the war, he argues, must keep the world safe until a lasting system stands. Their stopgap body should be formal, and hard at work.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d191:
Stalin agreed to take up the Trieste question at the summit in a message to President Truman dated July 6, 1945. The short note, printed in translation, is document 191 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Truman's message of June 25 about Trieste, Istria, and Yugoslavia.

The matter has a number of questions demanding their mutual consideration, Stalin writes. He is prepared to discuss them at their meeting in Germany. The message reached Truman at sea, relayed by the White House Map Room on July 7, and Stalin sent Churchill a similar note the same day. Behind the calm wording stood a live dispute: Yugoslav forces held Trieste, the Western Allies had just forced a partial pullback, and the city's future was unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d291:
Acting Secretary Grew gave London the tentative American answer on the satellite treaties in a telegram dated June 23, 1945. The message to Ambassador Winant is document 291 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It responds to the British proposal to move straight to peace treaties with Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria.

Washington fully agrees peace should come as soon as possible, Grew writes. But treaty talks, with their hard territorial questions, cannot finish quickly, and meanwhile the United States will not drop its demands for real participation in the control commissions. Nor is it convinced that peace with the present governments, above all in Romania and Bulgaria, would best serve democratic principles, even if it sped the Soviet troops' withdrawal. The plan: keep peace as the goal, demand a real voice now, and press the Yalta principles on governments and elections.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d391:
Destruction of the German battle fleet is urged in a Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum to President Truman dated July 10, 1945. American policy, the chiefs recommend, should be that all German naval vessels be destroyed, sunk on the high seas or scrapped. Only a limited number would be kept for experiments and tests, plus auxiliaries still of use.

If the European Advisory Commission nations could not agree, Washington should still press for the destruction of all capital ships and submarines: battleships, pocket battleships, and cruisers named among them. Smaller craft would be divided. The memo, signed by General Marshall, shows the military mind set on ending German sea power outright.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d491:
General Anders and his Polish troops in Italy are the concern of Kirk's cable from Caserta of June 28, 1945. Broad, a British officer, had shown Kirk a Foreign Office telegram just received. It instructed Broad, if the supreme commander saw no objection, to proceed to the Polish general headquarters in Italy. There he was to explain to General Anders, in as favorable a manner as possible, why Poles abroad should welcome the formation of the new Polish government.

Broad was authorized to give Anders the story of the Moscow negotiations, much as Washington's circulars had outlined it. He was also to point out the obvious advantages accruing to Poland from the constitution of the new government. The cable shows London managing its Polish soldiers' reaction to the Warsaw settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d591:
Top secret minutes record a meeting of the Committee of Three in Washington on June 26, 1945. They form document 591 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Present were Stimson of War, Forrestal of the Navy, and Grew, the acting head of State.

The three took up a proposed warning to Japan. Stimson read a draft memo he had written for the President, and the group weighed its effect at home and abroad. All agreed the tone was about right. Even if Japan did not yield, they felt, a clear warning could do no harm. It might firm U.S. resolve for an all-out fight if Japan held out. A joint subcommittee was tasked to draft the warning itself, with named men from each of the three departments.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d691:
Ambassador Wilson reported Turkey's minister's reply to Washington's cautious line on June 26, 1945. His urgent wire from Ankara is document 691 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Wilson had conveyed the final paragraph of the Department's June 23 instruction that morning.

The acting foreign minister thanked the U.S. for its interest and promised to keep Wilson fully informed. Turkey, he said, could hardly be expected to respect a Soviet view claiming Turkish land and bases. He pressed Wilson for Washington's reaction to Britain's proposed approach to Moscow. Told the U.S. view, he said he understood it, but hoped for more at the summit. At the Big Three meeting, he urged, the U.S. should back equal sovereignty and independence for all states. He added that Soviet units were leaving Poland and Hungary for Bulgaria, movements that looked like threats.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d91:
Major General Crawford reported General Parks's findings from Berlin to General Deane on June 23, 1945. The urgent telegram from SHAEF headquarters in Frankfurt is document 91 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Parks had flown in the day before to inspect the ground the Soviets had picked for the conference.

The report is encouraging. The Crown Prince's palace at Potsdam suits the joint sessions well, and the Babelsberg housing area on the Griebnitz lake has been cleared of Germans and is being renovated. The American compound holds about 70 houses and some 500 people, with overflow space needed at Zehlendorf in Berlin. Parks was warmly received by General Kruglov. Crawford lists three permissions still needed, covering extra ground, free use of the supply highway, and a bigger working party.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1091:
American staff drafted this fuller version of the Italy policy paper at Babelsberg on July 20, 1945. It repeats the aims of the earlier draft: Italian independence, recovery, and free choice of government in time. A peace treaty, drafted fast by the new Council of Foreign Ministers, would end Italy's odd double status.

Three steps would meanwhile honor Italy's help in beating Germany. The powers would announce an early treaty, promise such economic aid as is practical, and back early Italian elections. The Allied Commission would hand duties to Rome faster. Outdated surrender clauses would be suspended, while Italy still pledges to meet Allied military needs and keep only the forces the Allies allow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1191:
A second memorandum from the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date 19 July 1945. The flow of staff papers shows the chiefs feeding views to the team through the whole summit. Each note took up the questions from the armed forces' standpoint.

By the third day, the talks were moving from speeches to trades. The chiefs' staff kept pace, putting the services' needs and warnings in writing. This paper continues the series from the opening days. Read in a row, the memoranda form a military diary of the summit, kept by the men who would have to enforce its terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1291:
On 19 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Someone had to think each question through on paper first; papers like this one are that thinking. The chiefs' staff supplied it in a steady flow through the talks.

A staff note from the third day belongs to the phase when stands were still soft. Facts and warnings could still move the envoys' minds. This memorandum carries the services' view at that open moment. It survives in the official record as part of the chiefs' near-daily counsel to the men who bargained for the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1391:
Mikołajczyk's diary continues with an entry dated 29 July 1945. He was then in the middle of the Potsdam weeks, watching the settlement of Poland take shape around him. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A diary kept day by day catches what later memoirs smooth away: rumor, waiting, and hope rising or falling on small news. This entry belongs to the summit's final stretch, when the leaders were drafting their closing texts. For readers, the value is closeness. The great questions of 1945 appear here at the scale of one man's day. Borders, armies, and governments fill a page written down before he knew how the story ended.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-91:
Minutes kept by a note-taker named Page record a Potsdam meeting on July 24, 1945. Several staff members took turns writing the American record of the conference sessions. Their sets of minutes were later printed side by side in the second Potsdam volume. Where wording mattered, having more than one set helped editors check the sense of a remark.

Page's record gives the meeting in direct, workmanlike form. Readers see points made, answers given, and the order in which topics came up. Such notes were never meant for print at the time. That is part of their worth: they show the talks as staff heard them, not as press offices later framed them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d791:
R. Borden Reams, information officer in the Secretary's office, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn on July 27, 1945. Document 791 concerns the conference's public face. An information officer handled the press side of a summit. Reams wrote inside the American team as the talks neared their close. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

Press work at Potsdam walked a fine line. The talks were secret; the world's papers were hungry. Readers see an officer managing that gap from inside. The document adds a rare strand to the volume: not what was decided, but how word of it would be handled. It shows secrecy as a task, not just a rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d891:
American members of the Economic Subcommittee reported to the Secretary of State on August 1, 1945. Their report covers the fight over Article 19 of the Economic Principles. That clause set the order for paying Germany's import and reparation bills.

All three sides in fact agreed on two sentences. Reparations must leave Germans enough to live on, and paying for approved imports ranks as a first charge on exports. The Americans still insisted on an added note about gear covered by the Reparations Agreement. The British agreed, but the Soviets refused. With that, the whole subject failed to reach agreement.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d991:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the American minister in Switzerland on July 24, 1945. The same text went to the missions in Sweden, Portugal, and Turkey. Each envoy must formally notify his host government of a claim by the powers occupying Germany. They claim title to, or control of, all German-owned or German-run assets.

Host governments are asked to take no step that clashes with that control. Britain has agreed to the warning for neutral states, and France has signaled its missions will join. The Russians have been told their consent is assumed. Envoys should also urge their fellow occupying-power colleagues to deliver the same notice.
gao-gaoreports-b-296391:
Photo Science protested the terms of a Navy call for survey work in GAO decision B-296391, dated July 25, 2005. The work mapped wild habitats and old sites. It used GPS tools and map data systems. Sites lay in four western states. The firm said the work was design work under the Brooks Act.

GAO denied the protest. The agency had room to find this was not survey work of that kind. The tasks were to find, gauge, and study sites. They were not the land survey work the Act guards. The Brooks Act pick rules thus did not bind this buy. The call could go on as a normal contest.
gao-gaoreports-b-297291:
Computer Cite protested an Air Force award for phone support work in GAO decision B-297291, dated December 23, 2005. The winner was D. S. Information Systems. The site was Hickam Air Force Base in Hawaii. Work was also due at other state sites there. The buy was an 8(a) set-aside. The firm hit marks and claimed a clash of roles.

GAO denied the protest. Marks for the bids were backed by the record. They were sound on the facts shown. The clash claim did not undo that base. Marks that rest on a full record will stand. Broad claims with no flaw in the notes will fail. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297691:
Israel Aircraft Industries protested a Navy award for ship sensor systems in GAO decision B-297691, dated March 13, 2006. The winner was FLIR Systems. The user was the Coast Guard. The goods were infrared visual sensor systems for cutters and craft. The firm's tech bid was cut as not fit. It hit marks for the bids.

GAO denied the protest. The record showed many spots where the firm's bid missed key call terms. Those misses were real and backed by the record. A bid with many key misses can be cut as not fit. The firm did not show those finds were wrong. The award thus stood on the bid gaps.
gao-gaoreports-b-299291:
MCS Portable Restroom Service protested an Air Force buying path for portable chemical toilet services. The sites were the Air Force Academy and Farish Memorial Park in Colorado. The firm is owned by a service-disabled veteran. GAO ruled in B-299291 on March 28, 2007.

The agency chose a plain small business set-aside. The firm urged a set-aside for veteran-owned firms like its own. GAO held that the agency skipped a required step. It had to probe first if the work fit that class of set-aside. The rules grant that class a fair first look. The agency also could have made a sole-source award on set facts. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-311391:
Eomax Corporation lost its protest; the GAO decision is B-311391, dated June 23, 2008. The Army sought search cams for aid crews in small towns. The cams sit on poles to peer in tight, smoky spots. The award went to Maxa Beam Searchlights, Inc. Eomax bid a high price for its cam kit. Its cams switch sense modes with no ease.

GAO denied the protest. The file backs each flaw found in the Eomax kit. Size, pledge terms, and mode shifts all drew fair marks. Price piled on the flaws. A kit with those flaws at a high price is not best value.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-191:
Federal Research, GAO-05-191 of February 25, 2005, asks if two agencies kept a clean line when they teamed with an industry group on health studies. A National Institutes of Health unit and an Environmental Protection Agency office each worked with the American Chemistry Council. The work probes how chemicals harm health. NIH took a gift from the group to help pay for its share.

Such ties could sway study results that touch the chemical trade. GAO checks the legal base for each deal. It checks how each agency weighed and curbed clash-of-interest risk. It checks NIH gift rules too. Both agencies need sharper clash reviews, the title finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-291:
Unemployment Insurance, GAO-05-291 of March 17, 2005, asks how jobless aid touches a worker's life over time. The plan, made in 1935, is run by the Labor Department with the states. It pays part of lost wages for a spell. It props up the whole economy in slumps too. In fiscal year 2004, about 8.8 million workers drew $41.3 billion in aid.

GAO asks how many folks ever draw aid in their early work years. It asks how many draw it more than once. It asks if use shifts with time, trade, or job type. Long-span youth survey data lets it trace one group across years of work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-491:
Pension data filed on Form 5500, and why it reaches users so slowly, is the subject of GAO-05-491, a report dated June 3, 2005. The form is the chief source of facts on private pension and benefit plans. The Labor Department can take about 3 years to release some usable data from it. GAO examined what the form holds, why release lags, and what the form still lacks.

Three agencies use the filings chiefly to check compliance with pension and tax law. The lag has several causes. Filers may take up to 285 days after the plan year to submit the form. About 98 percent of filings arrive on paper, taking far longer to process, with twice the errors. Labor also holds the research file until every filing for a year is done. That can add up to 2 years. GAO found the form still misses key facts despite years of fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-391:
Each year GAO grades a set of major weapon programs in one volume. The report numbered GAO-06-391, issued March 31, 2006, assesses selected major weapon programs. Defense planned investment in new weapons had nearly doubled in five years. It rose from about $700 billion in 2001 to nearly $1.4 trillion in 2006. Most of the 52 programs covered are major defense buys.

GAO gives Congress and defense leaders an independent check on each program. It flags risk when a program's path to knowledge departs from best practice. Cost growth, delays, and shortfalls have long marked this area. Readers get program-by-program checks and higher-level lessons. The volume is updated each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-491:
Collecting child support costs money, and Washington pays most of the bill. GAO's July 6, 2006 report, GAO-06-491, reviews child support enforcement costs. Congress set federal standards for the program in 1975. State agencies run it, and a federal office oversees it. The federal government repays states 66 percent of their administration costs. Services include collecting payments from noncustodial parents and passing them to families.

GAO tracked net federal spending on administration from fiscal year 2000 to 2004. It found which cost types drove the totals. It studied steps states took to manage costs. More focus on labor costs and cost audits could cut federal spending, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-91:
Risk-based protection of ports and other key sites is weighed in GAO report GAO-06-91, dated December 15, 2005. Congress and the President had called for homeland security work to rest on risk management. That means sizing up threats in order, then acting on them.

GAO followed three parts of the Department of Homeland Security. The Coast Guard guards the nation's ports. One office gives port security grants. A third builds ways to judge risk across all key sites. GAO tracked how far each had come with risk methods. It also set out the blocks each still faced in going further.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1091:
Indoor dust cleanup after the World Trade Center fell is revisited in GAO report GAO-07-1091, dated September 5, 2007. The September 11, 2001 attacks and tower collapse spread debris dust over Lower Manhattan. The Environmental Protection Agency ran a test and clean program from 2002 to 2003.

In 2003 the agency's inspector general urged fixes, and drew lessons for future disasters. A 2004 expert panel helped shape a second, voluntary program, set out in 2006. GAO gauged how far the agency took in that advice. It checked limits on the panel, the fullness of public facts, and how the agency priced the work. Concerns raised need action, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-591:
Beach water testing in the Great Lakes gets a mixed grade in GAO-07-591, a GAO report released May 1, 2007. Germs in water and sand can sicken swimmers. The BEACH Act told the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to set pathogen limits for states. It also funds state testing and public warning programs. GAO checked how the act was carried out around the lakes.

EPA had done much of the work, but two core tasks lag years behind: the pathogen studies and the new water quality rules built on them. States must still use slow, dated tests, so closure calls come late. The grant formula also assumed a full $30 million yearly fund that never arrived. EPA had not reworked the split for leaner years. GAO urged a firm timeline for the science and a fairer grant split, so warnings reach swimmers in time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-691:
NASA's push to join its business systems into one is reviewed in GAO-07-691, issued July 20, 2007. The effort is called the Integrated Enterprise Management Program. It began in April 2000. GAO has flagged NASA's contract tracking as high risk since 1990, in part for weak systems. The report checks steps NASA took since September 2005 to run the program with care. It also asks whether NASA planned for the needs of the whole agency.

NASA had sharpened how it tracks needs, tests software, and weighs risks. It set clear marks for when a project phase could start and end. Weak spots in setting needs and in schedules still slowed the work. They forced a squeeze on tests of the core finance upgrade. NASA also lacked one shared plan for how the agency should work. GAO made five recommendations to close the gaps. NASA agreed with all five.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-791:
Reviews of old federal rules are surveyed in GAO-07-791, a report GAO issued on July 16, 2007. Congress and presidents order agencies to recheck rules on the books. Reviews can keep, change, or scrap a rule. GAO studied nine agencies that issue most federal rules. It counted their reviews from 2001 through 2006. It checked how they plan and report the work. It also asked what helps or hinders the reviews' use.

The nine agencies reported over 1,300 completed reviews. A full tally is impossible, since loose reviews often go undocumented. Most reviews test whether a rule works as planned. Others aim to cut burdens or recheck cost and gain estimates. Methods and reporting vary a lot by agency. That spread hurts openness about what reviews find. GAO saw room to make reviews more effective and more visible. Clearer records would let Congress and the public judge the results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-91:
Restated financial statements at federal agencies are studied in GAO-07-91, dated October 5, 2006. At least 7 of 24 major agencies restated fiscal 2004 figures in 2005. GAO examined restatements at nine agencies in depth. Nine of the 11 restating agencies had first won clean audit opinions. Users need to know why figures changed and what shifted. GAO judged the agencies' explanations for clarity and speed. It also judged the auditors' reports on the restatements.

None of the nine explained the changes well, GAO found. Two did not even label their statements as restated. Footnotes lacked detail on causes and effects. Six agencies boasted of clean opinion streaks without noting the restatements. That silence misleads statement users, GAO said. Audit reports shared the same gaps. GAO made 11 recommendations to the budget office. They aim at clearer restatement guidance for managers and auditors. The office said it would take the advice under advisement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-291:
Yellowstone bison and a disease pact are reviewed in GAO report GAO-08-291, dated March 7, 2008. Some bison carry brucellosis, a disease that can abort cattle pregnancies. Montana ranchers fear spread if bison roam out of the park. In 2000, three federal and two state agencies agreed on a joint management plan. The deal has stayed contentious ever since.

GAO measured progress under the plan's steps. It judged the plan's soundness and how well the agencies carry it out. Ranchers, park staff, and state officials all gave views. The title gives the thrust: both the pact and the management behind it need improvement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-691:
Oil and gas from federal lands sold for more than $75 billion in fiscal year 2007. Firms paid about $9 billion in royalties. GAO-08-691, dated September 3, 2008, asks whether the public gets a fair share and whether the royalty system can bend with prices.

The U.S. take in the deep water Gulf of Mexico ranked 93rd lowest of 104 systems in a June 2007 study. Royalty rates do not shift on their own when prices jump, and old leases cannot be reworked. Past one-off fixes may have cost billions in lost revenue. GAO backs a full review by an outside panel.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-891:
Passport demand exploded in 2007 when new travel document rules took hold. Waits hit 10 to 12 weeks in summer, more than double the norm. GAO-08-891, dated July 25, 2008, asks how the State Department got caught short and what it did to catch up.

The department guessed demand too low and warned its payment agent too late. Tracking of single applications was poor, and stated wait times were wrong, which drove many people to apply twice. Four task forces and rapid hiring lifted output. More rule changes loom in June 2009. GAO urges one long-term plan and tracking from the day an application lands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-91:
Weapons technology needs protection against tampering if it is stolen or captured. GAO-08-91, issued in January 2008, follows up on the Defense Department's anti-tamper policy, set in 1999 to shield critical technology in U.S. weapon systems. A 2004 GAO report found program managers struggling to apply the policy. This report checks what DOD has done since and what still blocks managers.

DOD raised awareness through a Web site, an online training module, and research on generic techniques. What it never issued, GAO found, is departmentwide direction, so each service improvises. A Navy database meant to map critical technology across DOD sits incomplete: the Missile Defense Agency's data is too classified for it, and the Air Force has not fully joined. GAO recommends departmentwide direction and better tools.
garland-main-travelled-roads-1891:
Hamlin Garland's Main-Travelled Roads made his name when it appeared in 1891. Harper's later lists group it with Prairie Folks, Rose of Dutcher's Coolly, and The Eagle's Heart. A note from Garland dated March 1, 1922, fronts this printing.

The tales show farm life in the Middle West with no trace of romance. Mortgaged farms, brutal winters, worn-out women, and the slow crush of debt fill the pages. Under the Lion's Paw stands out as the most cutting farm story in American writing. Readers who hoped for cheerful pioneer tales got a shock, and a new realism in fiction was born.
gissing-new-grub-street-1891:
George Gissing published New Grub Street in 1891, his definitive novel of the writing life in London. Hack writers starve while mediocrities prosper, in the bitterest portrait of literary trade written. Gissing, who had starved, knew every rung of the ladder they climb and fall in London.

Edwin Reardon, a novelist of talent, cannot write the three-volume potboilers the market demands and sinks toward death in poverty. Jasper Milvain, his friend, treats literature as a trade, charms editors and widows, and rises by knowing the business of books. Amy, Reardon's wife, leaves him for failure and in time weds the rising Milvain, in Gissing's coldest turn of the screw. The title names the old Grub Street of hired pens, reborn in the magazine age. The book remains the set text for every writer who has feared the market's verdict.
golden-days-for-boys-and-girls-vol-xii-j:
Golden Days was a weekly paper for boys and girls, published at Philadelphia by James Elverson. This number, volume twelve, number six, is dated January 3, 1891. Its pages mix serial tales, short stories, and puzzles with a thick fringe of advertisements. A Morse telegraph outfit for three dollars leads the offers, and a cake of Sapolio scouring soap gets a motto: birth is much, but breeding more.

The ads are half the fun now: beard elixir, magic lantern views, bicycles on easy payments, and asthma cures by mail. Between them ran the stories that kept young subscribers waiting for the next week. Such papers were the cheap libraries of their day. This single issue is a time capsule of what American children read, wanted, and were sold in 1891.
golden-days-for-boys-and-girls-vol-xiii-:
Volume thirteen of Golden Days, the Philadelphia weekly for the young, opens with this number, dated November 28, 1891. James Elverson published the paper, which lived on serial stories told week by week. The front pages here are given to advertisements, as was the custom. One offers crayon portraits free for thirty days, to spread the maker's name. Another repeats the Sapolio motto: serve yourself, and your friends will think more of you.

Inside, tales of adventure and home life ran beside jokes, puzzles, and letters from readers. The paper aimed to be wholesome as well as thrilling, a safe weekly guest in the family home. Surviving numbers are now valued less for any one tale than for the whole picture they give. It covers the reading, the goods, and the dreams offered to American boys and girls in the 1890s.
grillandi-tractatus-de-sortilegiis-latin:
Paolo Grillandi, an Italian judge who served the papal court, wrote his treatise on sorcery in the earlier sixteenth century. It circulated here in the Frankfurt Tractatus duo of 1591, a standard gathering of witchcraft law. Grillandi writes from the bench, and his Latin sets out inquisitorial demonology at its most systematic.

He defines sorcery, divides its kinds, and lays down how courts should prove it. Confession, witnesses, and signs each get their rules. The treatise taught judges across Italy and beyond how to run a witch trial. Law for the witch courts is here written by a judge who knew them from inside. Its system is the point, and the terror, of the book.
guaita-essais-sciences-maudites-2-1891:
Stanislas de Guaita reads the Fall through Kabbalah in Le serpent de la Genese, first part, from 1891. The work forms the first part of the second series of his Essais de sciences maudites. De Guaita led the French occult revival with aristocratic learning and total conviction in magic as a hidden science of the soul.

The serpent of Genesis becomes, in his hands, a key to cosmic law. Hebrew letters, myths, and rites are weighed page by page here. He writes for initiates, dense with symbol and reference throughout. The book shows Paris occultism at its most erudite in the eighteen nineties, a world of salons, orders, and secret doctrine.
guaita-serpent-de-la-genese-1891:
Stanislas de Guaita published Le Serpent de la Genèse in 1891, the first part of a planned large work on evil and the occult. De Guaita was a French poet and Martinist who helped revive occult study in Paris. He read the Bible's serpent as a key to a hidden tradition.

Through Genesis and later lore, de Guaita traced the serpent as a symbol of secret knowledge, temptation, and hidden powers. He drew on Kabbalah, old grimoires, and tales of sorcery and poison. The work is dense, learned, and openly on the side of the occult against a purely material age. It shows French occultism at its most literary and ambitious.
guaita-temple-de-satan-1891:
De Guaita launches his Essais de sciences maudites with Le Temple de Satan, in French from 1891. The volume defends esoteric Christianity against two foes at once.
