Material science on one side and black magic on the other both draw his elegant, scornful fire in this cornerstone of the French occult revival.

He presents magic as a sacred science with strict moral law. Satan's temple, in his telling, is error built into a system. Parisian occultists took the book as a manifesto of their cause. It stands at the head of his life's work, the portal through which readers enter his grand design of essays.
hardy-tess-1891:
Thomas Hardy published Tess of the d'Urbervilles in 1891, a novel about a poor country girl in Wessex. Tess Durbeyfield learns her family claims kinship with an old noble line. Sent to claim kin, she meets Alec d'Urberville, who ruins her. She later finds love with Angel Clare, a parson's son learning farming.

Tess tells Angel her past on their wedding night, and he cannot forgive her. Hard work, desertion, and want follow before a final, fatal reunion. Hardy subtitled the book the story of a pure woman. Its attack on double standards shocked Victorian readers. It remains his most loved and argued-over novel.
hartland-science-fairy-tales-1891:
Edwin Sidney Hartland, an English man of law and lore, wrote this study of fairy tales in 1891. It was one of the first books to treat the tales as a theme for strict study. Hartland held that tales keep the marks of the old ways of the folk.

He traces one tale type, the swan maid, through land after land and age after age. The Melusine tale, the fairy bride who is part snake, stands at the heart of his case. The book shows how one tale can map the spread of lore round the world.
herbart-textbook-psychology-1891:
Johann Friedrich Herbart wrote his Lehrbuch zur Psychologie, Textbook of Psychology, in 1816, and Margaret K Smith translated it in 1891. Herbart, who held Kant's old chair, treated psychology as a science of the soul's mechanics. Ideas, in his picture, press, check, and lift each other like forces in a crowded field.

From that mechanics Herbart builds his accounts of perception, memory, feeling, and desire. The textbook is spare and ordered, meant to ground his famous pedagogy in the mind's real workings. His Science of Education grows straight from this root, as the evidence of the two books shows. Smith's English carried the system to American students of the mind.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol10-1891:
The tenth and last volume of the Guiding Symptoms closed the set in 1891, eleven years after Hering's death. A project begun from one man's proving notebooks had grown into the largest symptom record of its school. Volume X completes the alphabetical run of remedies.

Its pages follow the house style: symptoms by region, ranks marked, characteristic signs lifted clear. With the set whole, a prescriber could trace almost any proved sign to its remedy. Later abridgments drew heavily on these volumes, yet the full ten still reward anyone who wants Hering in his own fullness.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's second volume appears here in a separately produced transcription of the Milman edition, distinct from the other volume two in this library. It opens with chapter sixteen in eight parts, Gibbon's long inquiry into how Rome's government treated the Christians from Nero to Constantine. Chapter seventeen then describes the foundation of Constantinople, its palace, finances, and military system.

Chapter eighteen takes up Constantine's character and his sons, and the middle chapters fight over Athanasius and the Alexandrian church, councils at Rome and Sardica included. The narrative moves toward Julian and the Goths. Two transcriptions of one volume let readers compare texts, and this one's contents are laid out chapter by chapter in full.
how-to-read-heads-or-practical-lessons-o:
James Coates wrote these practical lessons on reading heads, issued in 1891. The price was one shilling. Coates lectured on mental science and hygiene at Glasgow. He edited a phrenological annual as well. Professor L N Fowler supplies a preface to the little book.

A moral and intellectual type is read first: Professor Drummond's head. Applied phrenology then sorts heads by temper and power. Sturdy, buoyant men are told to school their mental and moral powers, Coates writes. Self-denial and temperance guard the weaker-stamina readers. The lessons aim at usefulness prolonged, not mere fortune-telling. It is phrenology as self-help, in a cheap and handy form.
husserl-philosophie-der-arithmetik-1891:
Husserl's Philosophy of Arithmetic, published in German in 1891, was his first book. He had trained as a mathematician in Vienna and Berlin, then turned to philosophy under Franz Brentano. The young scholar asked a deceptively plain question: how does the mind grasp number?

The book studies counting, collecting, and the signs we use for numbers, trying to ground arithmetic in acts of the mind. Its method leans on psychology, the very approach Husserl would attack nine years later in the Logical Investigations. A sharp review by Gottlob Frege helped push him toward that change. The debut already shows his care for exact description, straining against the limits of his teachers' psychology. It is the starting point of the long road to phenomenology.
ibsen-hedda-gabler-archer-1891:
Henrik Ibsen wrote Hedda Gabler in Norwegian, and William Archer made this English version in 1891. Archer, the critic who brought Ibsen to England, knew the playwright's aims at first hand. Hedda is often called his most dangerous heroine, a caged mind with pistols and pride.

Hedda, wed to the dull scholar Tesman, is bored, pregnant, and trapped in respectability. Her old flame Lövborg returns with a great book and a wild past of drink. Hedda burns his manuscript, lends him a pistol, and is trapped by Judge Brack's knowledge. She shoots herself rather than live under scandal and another man's power over her life. The play's cold grip and Hedda's mystery keep stages busy to this day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdallah-ibn-sa: Abdallah ibn Saura is counted by Moslem traditionists among the opponents of Mohammed in Medina. He was rabbi of the Banu Tha'laba ibn Fityaun, and one of the most learned rabbis of the city. His fellow Jews put him forward in debates on faith with Mohammed. He is said to have called on Mohammed to take up Judaism. Asked about a Torah law on adultery, he owned Mohammed a prophet, then took the words back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-ben-nat: Abigdor ben Nathan of Avignon was a French Talmudist who flourished in the thirteenth century and into the start of the fourteenth. He is known here as a teacher. His pupil was Abraham ben Nathan, the author of "Ha-Manhig." In that work the master is named twice, the entry notes. One date helps fix his life in time. In 1304, the year when "Ha-Manhig" was written, Abigdor was still living. No work of his own is named in this short notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abudiente-691:
Abudiente is the name of a Marano family of Lisbon. Gideon Abudiente, late in the sixteenth century, is the first bearer the entry can name. Early in the next century his son and other kin moved to Amsterdam. There they came back to the synagogue in the open. Some went on to Hamburg, and others to London. In England the kin dropped the second name and called themselves Gideon.

Short lives of six men of the family fill the rest of the entry. Abraham was a Dutch scholar and mystic who died after 1666. Moses Gideon was a poet and Hebrew grammarian. He was born at Lisbon, moved to Amsterdam about 1624, and died at Hamburg on February 24, 1688. His Hebrew grammar came out in part at Hamburg in 1633. Judah put out a Hebrew-Spanish word list for the young in 1675. Solomon left poems in script at Oxford.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-age-old-891:
Many Bible terms mark the last years of life. The most common, zaḳen, links to the word for beard. Gray hair stands as the clear sign of age. Other terms mean full of years or rich in years. One Mishnah passage sets sixty as one stage of age and seventy as a greater one. A psalm sets the span of life at seventy years, or eighty for the strong.

The sages knew the ills of age in full. Ecclesiastes sings a dirge on failing powers. A Mishnah likens teaching the old to writing on a scraped scroll. Lore says Abraham was the first man shown as aged. The close sets true age in the mind, not in years. A clean life, one voice says, is ripe old age in itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcan-michel-10:
Michel Alcan was a French engineer, politician, and author. He was born at Donnelay, in Meurthe-et-Moselle, in 1801. He died at Paris in 1877. As a young mechanic he won a silver medal from the Society of the Friends of Labor. He took part in the Paris revolutions of 1830 and 1848. In 1848 the voters sent him to the National Assembly, where he sat with the party called the Mountain.

He later trained as an engineer at the Ecole Centrale. In 1845 he became professor of spinning and weaving at the Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers. He held that chair until his death. In 1859 he joined the Jewish Consistory of Paris. In 1867 he rose to the Central Consistory, in the place of Salomon Munk. His books treat the textile trades, from raw stuff to woven cloth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfasi-isaac-be:
Isaac ben Jacob Alfasi was a leading Talmudist born in 1013 near Fez in North Africa. He died at Lucena in Spain in 1103. He studied in Kairwan under Rabbis Hananeel and Nissim. In 1088, charges by two informers forced him to flee to Spain. He later served as rabbi and judge at Lucena.

His fame rests on the Halakot, a code drawn from the Babylonian Talmud. The entry explains how he weighed both Talmuds in his rulings. It also covers his work as a teacher. His students included Joseph ibn Migash. A set of 320 responsa also survives under his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almond-1291:
Almond names both a tree and its fruit in the Bible. The Hebrew name comes from a root that means to waken or watch. Jeremiah plays on that root in a vision. The tree wakes first from the sleep of winter. In about January its bare boughs burst into bloom. The blooms fade from pink at the base to white at the tips.

The tree is a native of western Asia. Its fruit was prized as a fine food. Jacob sent almonds as a gift in Genesis. Aaron's rod bore almonds in the book of Numbers. In old age verse the blossom stands for gray hair. Most readers take that verse in Ecclesiastes that way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-american-jewish:
American Jewish Publication Society was set up to spread Jewish books. Isaac Leeser founded it at Philadelphia in 1845. It was the first group of its kind in the United States. A sister group rose at Richmond that same year. Its books came out under one shared title. That title was Jewish Miscellany.

Fourteen works are listed in the entry. Tales, lives, and books of faith fill the set. Grace Aguilar wrote more than one of them. In 1851 fire took the Hart Building in Philadelphia. The plates and books of the group were stored there. The group ceased to exist after that loss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ancona-1491:
Ancona is an old city on Italy's Adriatic coast, capital of a province of the same name. Syracusan refugees are said to have founded it. It was among the first Italian cities to shelter Jews, though their records begin only in the Middle Ages.

Jews there lived at first in peace, with schools, synagogues, and a cemetery. Later rulers forced them into a ghetto and made them wear badges. Under papal rule, popes granted trade rights and bank permits that drew more settlers, including exiles from Spain and Naples. The entry follows that mixed record of welcome and restriction across the centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antiochus-vi-15:
Antiochus VI was king of Syria, son of Alexander Balas, and he died in 142 B.C. Like the boy king before him, he reigned mostly in name. Diodotus Tryphon, his father's old general, proclaimed him king as a minor in 146 B.C. and held the real power.

The Jews first backed his rival, Demetrius II, then switched to Antiochus as Demetrius proved shifty and false. The young king confirmed Jonathan the Hasmonean in all his grants and made Simon commander to the Egyptian border. The brothers repaid him with wins over Demetrius. But Tryphon grew alarmed at Jewish strength, the entry says, and began to plot against them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-armory-1791:
Only three times does the word armory appear in the Authorized Version, and each use is traced here. In Jeremiah chapter 50 it is a figure of speech: the Lord opens his armory and brings out the weapons of his anger. In the Song of Songs chapter 4, a tower of David is said to be built for an armory, with a thousand bucklers hung on its walls.

The third use, in Nehemiah chapter 3, is a place in Jerusalem. Ezer son of Jeshua repaired the city wall opposite the entrance to the armory at the turning of the wall. From these passages the entry concludes that buildings were set aside to store arms, as Solomon kept five hundred golden shields in the house of the forest of Lebanon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asche-tobiah-be:
Tobiah ben Ezekiel Asche, also called Tobiah Schlochow after his town, was a German Talmudist. He served as rabbi of Zempelburg at the start of the nineteenth century. His book Et Barzel, Iron Pen, explains points of halakic law, the legal side of Jewish teaching. Tobiah did not live to print it.

His son Gershon, rabbi of Prenzlau, published the work at Berlin in 1832. Gershon added writings of his own to his father's book. He appended Nikrat ha-Zur, Cleft in the Rock, also on legal themes. He also added the funeral speech he had delivered at his father's grave. The entry is short, and the son's care for the father's work is its warmest fact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-atomism-from-gr:
Atomism is the theory that matter is built of atoms, parts too small to split. Greek schools split on the point. The Eleatics held that matter can be divided without end. Democritus, Leucippus, and Epicurus held the reverse. Divide a thing again and again, they said, and a point comes where it cannot be cut. That unsplittable unit is the atom.

Later, Muslim thinkers called the Motekallamin took up the theory. They reshaped it to serve a doctrine of creation from nothing. Their atoms are made by God and remade at his pleasure. Jewish thinkers, the entry says, opposed the theory across the board. Saadia argued that atoms with no size could never build bodies with size. Maimonides gave a whole chapter of his "Guide of the Perplexed" to fighting the Kalam version of the doctrine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ayyas-judah-219:
Judah Ayyas was a commentator and a strict judge of cases. He was born in North Africa about 1690. He died at Jerusalem on Sept. 11, 1760. He studied the Talmud at Algiers under Solomon Ẓeror. From 1728 to 1756 he served as dayyan of Algiers, much sought for rulings on ritual points. In 1756 he left for Jerusalem by way of Leghorn.

Ayyas was a strict Talmudist with no taste for questions outside the Law. His books, all printed at Leghorn, run to seven. They include a commentary on Maimonides' code and a volume of legal answers on the four Ṭurim. The answers shed light on Jewish life in North Africa in his day. From one of them it appears that cases of bigamy were not rare among Eastern Jews of the eighteenth century. The Algiers community rules are appended to that volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacau-2291:
Bacau is the capital of a district of the same name in Moldavia, in Rumania. Of its 15,000 people, about half were Jews when the entry was written. The wider district held 150,000 souls, of whom 15,667 were Jews by the census of 1899. The community ranks among the oldest in Moldavia. Its cemetery stones reach back to the start of the eighteenth century.

The town's old wooden synagogue burned in 1853. A new one rose the same year, beside twenty prayer houses. The community was run by a small elected committee. Its funds came chiefly from the gabella, a tax on meat and poultry paid by Jews in place of state dues. The entry lists the town's rabbis and its gifts: houses left for firewood for the poor, a shelter for travelers, and 500 ducats left by Phineas Edelstein for a hospital.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakst-isaac-mos: Isaac Moses Bakst was a lecturer at the Jewish Rabbinical College of Jitomir. He died there on June 18, 1882. The entry is short and gives a few plain facts. He was father of Nicolai Bakst. He wrote "Sefer ha-Ḥinnuḥ," printed at Jitomir in 1868, a Hebrew method for beginners made to fit Jewish schools in Russia. For many years he also owned a Hebrew printing office in Jitomir. A note adds that one bibliography spells his name "Baxt."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-of-r-jo: Baraita of R. Jose is, in one use, simply another name for a known work. The hosted entry is a single sentence of substance. It says some of the old scholars gave this name to the Seder 'Olam Rabbah. It then notes that a different Baraita bears the same name as well. For that second one it sends the reader to Brüll's "Jahrbücher," volume five, page 99. No contents, date, or author for either work are stated in this brief note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-b-zebi-h: Baruch b. Ẓebi Hirsch was a casuist who lived in Poland at the end of the eighteenth century and the beginning of the nineteenth. His "Shema'tata de-Rab" (Teachings of the Master) holds elucidative discussions of halakic questions that Samuel Edels had raised but left unsolved. The work had four parts. Only one part was published, under the title "Sheṭara Berurin," at Wilna in 1819. The entry names no town for him and gives no dates beyond the centuries stated.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beaucaire-prove:
Beaucaire is a city in the department of Gard, France, where a Jewish community arose early in the twelfth century. Its members lived among Christians with equal rights at first. The count of Toulouse guarded them and gave them public posts.

Attacks came in 1195, and later kings penned the Jews into a set quarter and seized their goods. Heavy taxes and canceled debts fill the later record. No Jews came back after the expulsion of 1394. A final section names scholars born or living there. In 1340 the king wiped out debts owed to Jews, then let them collect such debts again in 1368.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-wolf-b: Benjamin Wolf ben Daniel was rabbi in Chomsk, in the government of Grodno, in Russia. He published Naḥlat Binyamin, or Benjamin's Inheritance. That work holds festival sermons and a homiletic commentary on the Passover Haggadah. It came out at Cracow in 1642. The entry gives no dates for his birth or death and no other works, so the record stands as a name, a post, a book, and a printing date.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-leo-3091: Leo Berlin, a Russian lawyer and son of Moses Berlin, was born at Vitebsk on Nov. 22, 1854. He schooled at St. Petersburg and read law at Bern, in Switzerland, taking his degree in 1878. A doctorate in criminal law from Moscow followed in 1881. His marriage met a bar at first, since his bride was a Catholic and the state barred her union with a Jew. Help from the poet Turgenef at last won the needed leave. He later headed a St. Petersburg law firm while living in Brussels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bet-ha-midrash-:
Bet ha-midrash means "house of study." It was the high school of Jewish learning. Students gathered there to hear exposition of the Law. The entry contrasts it with the bet ha-sefer. That primary school taught Scripture to children under thirteen. Tradition claimed 480 synagogues in old Jerusalem. Each one held both kinds of school.

The entry traces the institution from Temple times onward. It describes pupils seated at their teachers' feet. It gives rules for conduct inside the house. Sleeping there was forbidden, with a Babylonian exception. The bet ha-midrash ranked above the synagogue in honor. A synagogue could become one, but not the reverse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-julienne-: Julienne Bloch was a French educator and writer. She died on November 12, 1868. Her father Simon founded "L'Univers Israélite." She was the eldest of his four daughters. At sixteen she earned a license to teach. Teaching her young coreligionists became her life. She directed a Lyons girls' institution for two years. Later she taught at her sister's Passy school. Her "Lettres Parisiennes" ran from 1854 to 1861. Her father's paper carried them. A panegyrist praised their true French wit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bona-sforza-349:
Bona Sforza was a Polish queen born in 1493. She died in 1557. As second wife of King Sigismund I, she was noted for beauty and energy, but hated in Poland for intrigue and greed.

Bona sold high offices, and her courtiers took bribes. Her favorite Peter Kmita took money from Jewish and Christian merchants alike. Each side paid for his promise to guard its interests. In Sigismund's last years she held power equal to his, and often ruled alone. Many papers granting privileges to Jews bear her name. Later rulers of Poland confirmed those Jewish privileges after her time. The papers that grant them in her name are still extant, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boslanski-yom-t:
Yom-Tob Lipman ha-Kohen Boslanski, called R. Lipele Mirer, was a Russian rabbi born in 1824. He died in Mir on Dec. 26, 1892. For the last eighteen years of his life he headed the community in Mir.

Boslanski ranked among the greatest rabbinical authorities in Russia. He went to St. Petersburg several times as a spokesman for the Jews. He was an early lover of Zion and backed farm work in the fallow year in Palestine. In 1889 he tried to form a society to buy land for a new colony there. His responsa, Malbushe Yom-Tob, came out at Wilna in 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bresnitz-heinri: Heinrich Bresnitz was an Austrian author and journalist born at Czernowitz in 1844. In 1867 he founded a periodical in Vienna called Der Osten. In 1869 he started a political journal, Der Patriot. From 1879 to 1886 he owned and chiefly edited the Morgen-Post. He wrote political pamphlets on the constitutional party and on the Ausgleich. In 1893 Bresnitz went to Bulgaria, the entry ends. It gives no later facts, no death date, and no account of his work in that land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cahan-abraham-3:
Abraham Cahan was a Russian American novelist and labor leader born July 7, 1860, in the government of Wilna. His Orthodox family moved to Wilna in 1866, where he trained for the rabbinate. Secret study of Russian led him instead to a teachers' institute, finished in 1881. Police attention for his part in the revolutionary movement drove him to flee. He reached New York in June 1882.

In New York Cahan became the pioneer socialist leader among Jewish working men. He gave the first socialist speeches in Yiddish in the United States and edited early Yiddish socialist papers. He also wrote for English newspapers. His fiction pictured immigrant ghetto life, and his novel Yekl, from 1896, drew praise in America and England. Howells compared his work to Stephen Crane's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantor-georg-39:
Georg Cantor was a German mathematician born at St. Petersburg on March 3, 1845. He came to Germany at age eleven for school. After Zurich he studied at Berlin until 1867 and took his doctorate there. In 1869 he began teaching at Halle, rising to professor ten years later. He stayed at Halle for his career.

Cantor created the theory of sets, or multiplicities, on his own. His 1883 book on its foundations won him world fame at one stroke. From it came his account of the continuum and his theory of transfinite numbers. The entry also credits his strict theory of irrational numbers, built beside the work of Weierstrass and Dedekind. It calls his ideas hard yet fruitful for all later analysis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carvallo-jules-:
Jules Carvallo, a French engineer born at Talence, Gironde, in 1820, took top honors at the Ecole Polytechnique and the Ecole des Ponts et Chaussées. He built rail lines in southern France, including the Bouzanne viaduct. In Spain he directed canal work on the Ebro and set up irrigation in its delta.

Carvallo later ran railroad works in Italy and a rail line from Pampeluna to Saragossa, then led a Spanish water company. His papers treat embankments, cheap and stable public works, and chain bridge movement. Amid that work he helped found the Alliance Israélite Universelle. He served for many years on its executive committee.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chelub-4291: Chelub is a Hebrew word meaning a cage, as in Jeremiah v. 27. It is also the name of two men. The first was a brother of Shuah and father of Mehir, of the tribe of Judah, as I Chronicles iv. 11 states. The second was the father of Ezri, David's chief gardener, as I Chronicles xxvii. 26 states, with a date of 1014 B.C. given there. The Septuagint forms of the name are noted for both uses. The hosted entry is only a few lines long and adds nothing further.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-levi-ali-:
Levi Ali Cohen, a Dutch physician and medical author, was born on Oct. 6, 1817, at Meppel and died on Nov. 22, 1889, at Groningen. He took his medical degree at Groningen in 1840 and practiced there. In 1858 he headed the provincial statistics bureau. From 1865 he led the state health board for several provinces.

He helped reshape the medical laws of the Netherlands. King William III sent him as delegate to the Brussels hygiene congress in 1876. For fifty years he served Groningen's congregational committee. He edited medical journals from 1844 to 1877 and wrote on diabetes, medical history, and public health. One early work, from 1843, read the book of Job as natural history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-confession-of-s:
Confession of Sin is set by Scripture as a road to atonement. Leviticus v. 5 orders the guilty man to confess the thing he did. Aaron confessed Israel's sins over the scapegoat. Numbers v requires confession from any man or woman who sins against another.

Its effect is remission, the entry argues from David's case. Nathan answered his confession with word that the Lord had put the sin away. Forms of confession take up most of the piece: private prayers of the Talmud, the alphabetical confessions traced to geonim of the eighth century, and set texts for the Day of Atonement. Confession also marks bathing before that day, a bridegroom's wedding, and a sick person's last days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-isaac-da-:
Isaac da Costa was a Dutch poet, born at Amsterdam on Jan. 14, 1798. He died there on April 28, 1860. His father Daniel was a leading merchant, kin to Uriel Acosta. His mother was a near relative of the economist David Ricardo. The poet Bilderdijk guided his studies and became a close friend. Isaac took law and philosophy degrees at Leyden in 1818 and 1821.

Soon after his marriage he was baptized, under Bilderdijk's sway. He was still honored as Bilderdijk's heir among Dutch poets. He wrote fifty-three poems and much on theology. His Israel en de Volken surveys Jewish history to the nineteenth century. Yet he kept love and respect for his former coreligionists, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cuba-4791:
Cuba is the largest island of the West Indian groups, in the Atlantic Ocean. Jewish ties to it start with Columbus in 1492, when several Jews sailed with him. On Nov. 2, 1492, Columbus sent Luis de Torres inland to learn the island. One scholar holds that Torres settled in Cuba and died there. Baptized Jewish women sent to the Indies were among its early settlers.

The Inquisition in Cuba fills the middle of the article. In 1613 Francisco Gomez de Leon of Havana confessed he was a Jew and died for his faith. His fortune of 149,000 pesos was seized. More arrests and extortions follow, dated 1627 and 1636. Later notes tell of a Jewish interpreter with Admiral Vernon in 1741 and of Jacob Franks feeding the British navy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-danon-meir-benj: Meïr Benjamin Menahem Danon was a rabbinical writer and chief rabbi of Sarajevo in Bosnia. He lived in the first half of the nineteenth century. His one named work is Be'er ba-Sadeh, A Well in the Field. It is a supercommentary, a comment on a comment. Its base texts are Rashi's notes on the Pentateuch and the notes of Elijah Mizraḥi on Rashi. The book was published at Jerusalem in 1846. The entry gives no dates for his birth or death. One brief source is cited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidsohn-rober: Robert Davidsohn, younger brother of the journalist Georg Davidsohn, was born at Danzig on April 26, 1853. He joined his brother's paper, the "Berliner Börsen-Courier," writing satirical reviews of actors, actresses, and singers. Beaten in a feud with the singer Lilli Lehman, he left Berlin for Italy to gather historical material. There he built a strong reputation as a historian. His books include a study of King Philip II Augustus of France and Ingeborg in 1888, and a history of Florence in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-domicil-12691:
Domicil is a person's true, fixed, permanent home, the place he means to return to when away. Under Jewish law, settling somewhere with intent to stay makes that place one's domicil at once. The status holds for civil and religious purposes alike. Intent may be stated openly or shown by acts.

Twelve months of free residence, or buying a house, bound a man to local taxes. Shorter stays triggered staged duties to charity funds. Thirty days meant the free kitchen, three months general charity, and nine months burial funds. The Rabbis split residents into men of the town and mere inhabitants. Placing food for two meals could even fix a Sabbath domicil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dosa-b-tebet-52: Dosa, son of Tebet, was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. In his name the haggadist Huna passed down a saying on man's two worst instincts. God, it says, planted in His world the urge to idolatry and the urge to illicit love. The first has long been rooted out in Israel, but the second still stands. Whoever resists that second urge, God counts as having resisted both. The entry adds that Tebet, a month name used as a surname, occurs nowhere else.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-earnest-money-5:
Earnest-money is a part payment by a buyer that binds a bargain. In the old law, full payment gave title to property. Part payment did the same. Even a perutah, the smallest Palestinian coin, paid on account could seal a sale.

Later rabbis limited that rule to land. Movable goods passed only by taking hold of them. Still, backing out after earnest was paid counted as bad faith. A set curse fell on the party who broke his word. For land, earnest-money made the sale at once, unless local custom asked for a deed. The unpaid rest then stood as a loan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eisenstein-juli:
Julius Eisenstein, born Judah David, was a Russian-American writer. He was born at Meseritz, in Russian Poland, on Nov. 21, 1855. In 1872 he emigrated to the United States. He settled in New York, where he still lived in 1903.

Eisenstein first rendered the United States Constitution into Hebrew and Yiddish. That version appeared at New York in 1891. His Classified Psalter of 1899 gives the Hebrew text with a fresh translation. He also tried a reworked Shulhan Aruk with commentary. In print he fought over the Kolel Amerika fund for Palestine's poor. He wrote a history of Russian Jewish emigration to America in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elias-ney-5591: Ney Elias was a British consul and explorer in Asia. He died in London on May 31, 1897. As a young man he found his way to China. In 1871 he set out to cross all of Asia by land. He crossed the Gobi desert by a path no one had mapped. He passed through lands torn by revolt on the way. Later he served the Indian government on missions in the hills. In 1885 he crossed the whole Pamir range. In 1891 he became consul-general at Meshed in Persia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elkanah-5691: Elkanah was the father of the prophet Samuel. He lived at Ramah, in the district of Zuph. His line is traced back to that same Zuph. The entry works through tangles in his family record. One word in Samuel seems to make him an Ephraimite. The family lists in Chronicles make him a Levite of Kohath. Both can hold, the entry shows by a like case. A Levite could be named for the tribe he lived among. His great-grandson was Heman, the temple singer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emin-pasha-edua:
Emin Pasha was born Eduard Schnitzer, a German explorer. He was born at Oppeln in Silesia on March 28, 1840. He was killed in the Kongo Free State in Oct. 1892. His parents moved to Neisse when he was two years old. He was baptized there as a Protestant in 1846. He studied medicine at three schools and passed his exam in 1864. He left for England, Italy, and then Turkey that same year.

In Turkey he served as a health officer at Antivari. He then served as doctor to a Turkish pasha of rank. After a short trip home he sailed for Egypt in time. He reached Khartum on Dec. 3, 1875. There he joined Gordon Pasha in the far south. He took the name Emin and won Gordon's trust fast. Gordon made him governor of the Equatorial Province. Hard posts of state fell to him in that role.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephor-lit-super: An ephor was a state officer in Sparta of old. Other Greek lands used men of the same title. The Jews took up the word for posts of their own. Ephori served in the Temple at Jerusalem in one text. A like post shows up at Babylon in another. In the Byzantine age an ephor watched prices and weights. He sat in the frame of the Jewish town body. The entry notes more Greek titles for Jewish posts. A rabbi could be called a teacher in Greek dress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ethnarch-chieft:
Ethnarch was a title in the Greco-Roman world for the head of a community who was not a fully independent ruler. The entry traces the title through Jewish history. Simeon the Maccabee bore it beside the high priesthood. Josephus also calls him ethnarch, though one scholar cited here doubts that. The title needs care, since sources use it loosely.

Rome gave the title formally to Hyrcanus II, though Pompey refused him a crown. A coin may call Herod the Great ethnarch, but his son Archelaus clearly held the lesser title after being judged unfit for king. The head of Alexandria's Jews also bore it, and Origen used it for the patriarch of Palestine. Aretas of Damascus had an ethnarch too, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falk-eduard-599:
Eduard Falk was a German publicist who died in Paris on July 7, 1863. Meant first for trade, he turned to study and graduated from Berlin University in 1858. He entered state service as an assessor and wrote at the same time for the Magdeburger Zeitung. Pamphlets on the day's questions made his name.

His 1859 pamphlet backed Austria against Napoleon III, and the Duke of Coburg backed its larger edition. Other works defend Prussia's task in Germany, answer a French attack, and explain England's constitution, a book soon translated into English. At Paris, planning a work on political law since the French Revolution, he was run over by an omnibus and killed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-france-formerly:
France, once called Gaul, forms the westernmost part of Central Europe. Its Jewish history here runs from Roman times to the modern age. Jewish settlement came by trade and chance travel, the entry argues, not by the banishment of Jewish princes. No written proof of Jews there dates earlier than the fourth century. In 425 a decree barred Jews and pagans from practising law and holding public office in Gaul.

Church councils then took up the Jewish question, beginning with Vannes in 465. Jews are traced in Marseilles, Arles, Narbonne, Clermont, Orleans, Paris, and Bordeaux. Later parts treat badges, bans on usury, and Christian servants under French kings. A Paris dispute of 1273 and royal ordinances of the 1280s are covered in detail. The long entry ends with the modern community. Its assembly revised the prayer-book and dropped some prayers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-gabriel: Gabriel Fränkel was a court Jew of the margraves of Ansbach about 1700. The entry is very short and gives no dates for his birth or death. It says he was very influential at court. It also says he was highly esteemed by the Jews of the margravate. He kept his leading position until his death. In reward for his faithful services, all the privileges granted to him were continued to his heirs. That was done by a special charter in 1730. One short source line closes the notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedrichsfeld-:
David ben Zebi Hirsch Friedrichsfeld was a German and Hebrew author born about 1755 in Berlin. He died on February 19, 1810, in Amsterdam. In the Prussian capital he took in the learning and ideas of the Hebrew writers of his day. In 1781 he went to Amsterdam. There he became one of the leaders in the fight for Jewish freedom. For that cause he wrote two works in 1795 and 1797, on the civil rights of the Jews.

He also wrote for the chief Hebrew journal of the age. A book of 1808 defends a friend's work and treats how the Sephardim say Hebrew. His last book, of 1809, is a life of Hartwig Wessely. Some of his works are still in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gama-vasco-da-6: Vasco da Gama, the Portuguese finder of the sea road to India, drew strong help from Abraham Zacuto, star scholar to King Manuel. Zacuto work aided the voyage, as such help had aided Columbus. As fleet chief Gama sailed from Lisbon on July 8, 1497. He had first met Zacuto and taken leave of him before the whole crew. The entry points readers to the fuller tale under Gaspard da Gama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-giscala-6691:
Giscala was a city of Galilee, not far from Tyre, and the home town of the patriot John of Giscala. After pagan neighbors from Gadara, Gabara, and Tyre captured and burned it, John defeated the attackers, rebuilt the city, and walled it in 66 C.E. The entry weighs Josephus's claims about the city and finds some of them hard to credit.

The city held out longest of all Galilean towns against Rome. Titus attacked with 1,000 horsemen in 67 C.E.; John asked a Sabbath truce and slipped away at night, and the walls were then razed. The entry also notes Giscala's fine oil and raw silk, and a tradition that Paul's parents lived there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gomez-manuel-67: Manuel Gomez was a physician born about 1580. His parents were Portuguese, and he was born at Antwerp. He studied medicine at Evora. He then settled as a doctor at Amsterdam. His book "De Pestilentiæ Curatione" appeared at Antwerp in 1603. A third edition came in 1643. He is said to be among the first to call milk useless against confirmed phthisis. Amato Lusitano esteemed him highly. Gomez was also a poet. His verses on the spider, the ant, and the bee joined his metrical commentary on a Hippocrates saying, printed in 1643.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grossmann-ignac: Ignacz Grossmann was a Hungarian physicist. He was born in Gönez-Ruszka, Abauj county, on Feb. 16, 1823. He died in Budapest on May 21, 1866. Prague University taught him mathematics and teaching method. He taught at Györ-Sziget from 1847 to 1851. In 1854 he became principal of the Pest Jewish community's girls' school. In 1857 a commercial school called him as professor. In 1862 he turned railroad engineer. The entry credits him as the true inventor of the mercurial air pump. He also found a new way to build gasometers in 1854.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habillo-simon-b: Simon ben Judah ben David Ḥabillo was rabbi at Hebron in the middle of the seventeenth century. He was a contemporary of Moses Zacuto, who approved his works. He wrote two books. "Ḥebel ben Yehudah" comments on the Passover Haggadah and came out at Mantua in 1694. "Ḥeleḳ Yehudah" comments on the book of Ruth and was printed with the text at Venice in 1695. A prayer by Ḥabillo, shaped like Psalm cxix, stands before the Ruth work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halevy-halfan-e:
Élie Halévy, born at Fürth in 1760, was a French Hebrew poet and author who died at Paris on Nov. 5, 1826. He was father of Fromenthal and Léon Halévy. He went to Paris young and became a cantor. His Talmud learning and gift for verse won him the regard of French scholars, above all the Orientalist Sylvestre de Sacy.

His first poem, "Ha-Shalom," hailed the treaty of Amiens and was sung in Paris's synagogue in Hebrew and French on Nov. 8, 1801. In 1808 he wrote a prayer for the anniversary of Wagram. In 1817 he helped found the weekly "L'Israélite Français," which folded within two years. His "Limmude Dat u-Musar" of 1820 is a school-book of religion drawn from the Bible, with French rendering and the rulings of Napoleon's sanhedrin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hartog-marion-7:
Marion Hartog, born at Portsea on Oct. 22, 1821, was an English writer. Educated at home, she and her sister Celia wrote poems and stories as girls. Their book "Early Efforts" came out in 1838. Marion then taught in London and published tales of Jewish history for young readers.

In 1845 she married Alphonse Hartog and opened a school for young children, which she ran until 1884. She founded the "Jewish Sabbath Journal" in 1855, though it soon folded for lack of money. Her tales drew on Bible history and on later Jewish life in England. The entry closes with her children, several of whom won fame in study, science, painting, and music.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-b-samuel:
Hayyim ben Samuel ben David of Toledo was a Spanish rabbi and author. He lived at the end of the thirteenth century and into the fourteenth. He studied under Solomon ben Adret. His book "Zeror ha-Hayyim" sets out the laws for Sabbath and festival services, but it stayed in manuscript.

A second work, "Zeror ha-Kesef," sums up rabbinic law in five parts. It draws on the Geonim and on great teachers of Spain and France. Joseph Caro and Moses di Trani both cite it. Hayyim also wrote new readings on the Talmud. A namesake book in verse, on deep mystical topics, is also credited to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilbuth-ferdin: Ferdinand Heilbuth, born at Hamburg in 1826, was a French painter. He became a French citizen ten years before his death. His work is marked by lively color and strong expression in faces. He showed at the yearly salons from 1853 on. Named works include scenes with Rubens and with Titian's son, views of the Thames and the Seine, and a pawnshop scene now in the Luxembourg. He excelled as a portrait painter. France made him a knight of the Legion of Honor in 1861 and an officer in 1881. He died on Nov. 19, 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heresy-and-here:
Heresy and heretics are treated here through Greek and rabbinic terms. The Greek word first meant a division or party. Josephus used it for Sadducees, Pharisees, and Essenes. Rabbinic speech used minim and several other labels for heretics and deniers.

Maimonides is summarized at length. His lists name those said to have no share in the world to come. They include deniers of God, prophecy, resurrection, and the Torah's divine origin. The entry then turns to legal status. Jewish courts did not try heresy cases, it says. Yet rules barred a heretic's offerings, testimony, and ritual writing, and treated his slaughtered animals as forbidden food.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hilberg-isidor-:
Isidor Hilberg, born May 28, 1852, at Byelaya Tzerkov in Ukraine, was an Austrian philologist. His family moved to Vienna in 1856, where he was educated. He studied classical languages at Vienna and took his doctorate in 1874. He spent half a year in Italy in 1875.

Hilberg became a lecturer at Vienna in 1877, then taught at Prague from 1879. In 1882 he became professor at Czernowitz. He served as its rector in 1898. His books edited a Greek romance and set out laws of Greek verse form and syllable weight. A later work treated word order in Ovid's pentameter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-samson-r:
Samson Raphael Hirsch, born at Hamburg on June 20, 1808, was a German rabbi who chose that calling over trade. He studied Talmud at Mannheim under Jacob Ettlinger from 1823 to 1829. At Bonn he studied beside his later foe, Abraham Geiger.

Hirsch led districts at Oldenburg and Emden before Moravia in 1846. His Nineteen Letters of 1836, printed under a pen name, gave Orthodox Judaism a fresh, strong voice in fine German. From it the entry dates Neo-Orthodoxy. In 1851 he took an Orthodox group at Frankfort and built it to about 500 families. His works include a Pentateuch comment and a Psalms translation. He died at Frankfort on Dec. 31, 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hobah-hiding-pl: Hobah, glossed as hiding place, was a place north of Damascus. Abraham reached it while chasing Chedorlaomer's beaten army, in Genesis. One scholar identifies it with a modern place 60 miles north of Damascus. Damascus Jews instead name a village not far from their city, the entry reports. Rashi, following an older source, reads Hobah as a stand-in for Dan. He links the name to sin, for a golden calf later stood at Dan. A Jerusalem Targum gives yet another rendering of the name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horwitz-bernard: Bernard Horwitz was a chess player and chess writer born in 1809 in Mecklenburg. He died in London in 1885. A pupil of Mendheim in Berlin, he ranked among the Pleiades, seven leaders of a new chess school there between 1830 and 1840. He settled in England about 1845 and played in most tournaments until 1862. With Kling he published Chess Studies in 1851, a book on end games. They also issued a chess journal in four volumes. His last book appeared in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-iddo-791: Iddo was a seer, or prophet, whose words were aimed against Jeroboam. Chronicles quotes him as a source for the lives of Solomon, Rehoboam, and Abijah. His work bore the title Midrash of the Prophet Iddo. Josephus and Jerome take him for the prophet who denounced Jeroboam's altar and was then killed by a lion, as told in Kings. Jerome also makes him the Oded of Chronicles. The entry gives no dates or place for Iddo himself beyond those royal reigns and writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-de-leon-8: Isaac de Leon was one of the last rabbis of Castile, a native of Leon who lived at Toledo. He was a pupil of Isaac Campanton and, like Moses de Leon, a cabalist and a believer in miracles. Joseph Caro and others honored him with the title "the great teacher." He was over seventy when he died, some years before the Jews were expelled from Spain, and many pupils mourned him. A work once ascribed to him, the entry notes, was proved by Azulai to belong to a later writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-ben-samu:
Israel ben Samuel Ashkenazi of Shklov was a Talmudic casuist born at Shklov about 1770 who died at Tiberias on May 13, 1839. He belonged to the Shklov circle drawn to Wilna by Elijah, the Gaon. Among the last to arrive, he studied under the Gaon for less than a year, yet won his trust. The Gaon chose him to prepare his commentary on two parts of the Shulhan Aruk for print; it appeared at Shklov in 1803.

Israel later moved to Palestine and headed the German and Polish congregations of Safed, then of Jerusalem. He also traveled Europe as an emissary, gathering alms for the Holy Land's poor. His chief work, "Pe'at ha-Shulhan," printed at Safed in 1836, fills a gap in Caro's code: the farm laws that bind only in the Holy Land. Into it he worked the Gaon's notes on Zera'im and a commentary of his own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacques-pasha-j: Jacques Nissim Pasha, a Turkish army surgeon, was born at Salonica in 1850 and graduated from the school of medicine at Constantinople in 1874. As a captain he served at the Haidar Pasha hospital and joined a detachment to Bosnia and Herzegovina. He later directed the Central Hospital of Salonica and inspected health services for its vilayet. He died at Salonica on Aug. 25, 1903, from gangrene caught while dressing a wounded soldier's wound. He held Turkish orders and led the local Biḳḳur Ḥolim society.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeremiah-8591:
Jeremiah, known by that single name, was a Palestinian scholar of the fourth century. Born in Babylonia, he showed little promise as a boy there. He moved to Caesarea in Palestine and grew fast as a student. His chief teacher was his countryman Ze'era, who loved him like a son, and Abbahu also taught and prized him.

His hunger for exact knowledge made him over-subtle. His objections often raised laughter in the school, and at last his fellows put him out of the academy. Later, when a hard point of law stumped the masters, his humble written answer solved it, and the school took him back. From then on he stood as its head.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-ben-joezer:
Jose ben Joezer of Zeredah was a rabbi of the early Maccabean period from a priestly family. With Jose ben Johanan he opened the age of the zugot, the pairs who led the Sanhedrin. He may have studied under Antigonus of Soko. Jose stood firmly against Greek influence and ruled that lands outside Palestine were unclean.

His dispute with his colleague over laying hands on festival sacrifices was the first legal dispute named in the Talmud. Yet he was also known for three lenient rulings and for deep piety. Tradition says he was among sixty pious men put to death by the Syrian general Bacchides. A midrash tells of his calm words to Alcimus on the way to his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-isaa:
Joseph ben Isaac Bekor Shor of Orleans was a French tosafist, Bible commentator, and poet of the second half of the twelfth century. He studied under Jacob Tam, Joseph Caro, and Samuel ben Meir. He stayed on warm terms with Jacob Tam and traded learned letters with him. Gross showed that the tosafist Joseph ben Isaac of Orleans and Bekor Shor were one man.

Beyond tosafot on most of the Talmud, he wrote a sharp commentary on the Bible. He held even closer than Rashi to the plain sense of the text. He saw double tellings of the same story in Scripture and gave natural reasons for wonders. His note on Lot's wife reads her delay, not a sudden change, as her ruin. His Pentateuch commentary survives in manuscript, with parts printed. He also wrote penitential poems.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-junior-right-ge:
Junior right is the custom by which a father's goods pass to his youngest son. It stands against primogeniture, the right of the eldest. One guess holds that the custom grew up in herding days. The eldest son moved on with his share of the flocks, while the youngest stayed to take the father's place.

Among Jews in historic times the eldest took the lead, yet the old tales point the other way. Jacob, Rachel, Benjamin, Ephraim, Moses, David, and Solomon all look like youngest sons with the birthright. Jacobs, cited here, thought later law's clash with those tales shaped many Genesis stories. The entry notes that his view won no wide support.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kann-edouard-91: Edouard Kann, a French musician born at Paris on Feb. 28, 1857, studied under Massenet and Duvernoy before bringing out his own stage works. In 1895 he produced "Ruth," an oratorio, at Lyons, and operas followed: "Gaitanne," in two acts, in 1898, and "Maritorne," a one-act comic opera. The entry also names three shorter pieces among his later output, "Le Baptême du Printemps," "La Syrinx," and "Le Lion Amoureux."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kley-wilhelm-93: Wilhelm Kley was a German economist and educator. He was born at Steinbach on June 25, 1869. He taught for several years at various schools. He then studied political economy, pedagogics, and philosophy at four universities. After taking his doctor's degree he taught at the school for builders at Cassel. Since 1901 he has directed the technical and commercial school of Harburg. His books treat occupational diseases and workers' insurance. He also wrote on consumption in the light of statistics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kowner-abraham-:
Abraham Uri Kowner, a Russian Hebrew critic born at Wilna about 1837, won fame by attacking many Hebrew Maskilim in print. His essays ran in Ha-Karmel and Ha-Meliẓ before he turned on those papers' editors. A bank defalcation then brought him banishment to Tomsk in Siberia. There he embraced Christianity and became a government official.

Two small books hold his case. The first, dated 1865, argues that Hebrew must fit modern needs or yield to Judæo-German for teaching. It praises a few named writers and faults the rest as harming the language. The second, dated 1868, answers his critics and hits hardest at the editor of Ha-Meliẓ.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamech-vigorous:
Lamech names two men in Genesis, and the entry treats both. The first, a descendant of Cain, had two wives, Adah and Zillah, and sons who began tent life, music, and metal work. His speech to his wives in Genesis iv is read by modern scholars as praise of his son's forged weapons. A legend says the blind Lamech killed Cain by mistake, then killed his own son by a clap of grief.

The second Lamech, a descendant of Seth, fathered Noah at age 182 and lived 777 years. The entry notes that the Cain and Seth lists share names such as Lamech and Enoch. Scholars cited take the two lists as two forms of one older list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lazarus-nahida-: Nahida Ruth Lazarus, a German authoress born at Berlin on Feb. 3, 1849, came from a Christian family. Her first husband was Dr. Max Remy; she still signs her work Nahida Remy. Widowed, she embraced Judaism and in 1895 married Professor Moritz Lazarus. Essays and novels on history, art, and theater fill Berlin journals. Her dramas begin in 1870. Later books treat the Jewish woman in 1892 and prayer in Bible and Talmud the same year. An autobiography came in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-letteris-meir-h:
Meir Halevi Letteris, called Max, was an Austrian scholar and poet. He was born on Sept. 13, 1800, at Zolkiev and died at Vienna on May 19, 1871. His family of printers came first from Amsterdam. At twelve he sent a Hebrew poem to Nachman Krochmal, who urged him toward German, French, and Latin letters.

Letteris studied at Lemberg, then worked as a Hebrew corrector in Berlin, Presburg, and Prague. He took his Ph.D. at Prague in 1844 and settled in Vienna in 1848. His fame rests on his Hebrew poems of 1860 and his Hebrew version of "Faust," called "Ben Abuya," in 1865. His song "Yonah Homiyyah" became widely loved, and he shaped modern Hebrew poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-joseph-hia: Joseph Hiam Levy, an English economist, was born in 1838. He studied at the City of London School and the City of London College. He entered the British Civil Service and joined the Board of Education in 1862. He rose to examiner of school accounts and retired in 1902. Levy was a leading member of the National Liberal Club. He founded its Economic Circle and edited its "Transactions." He also edited "The Individualist" and "Personal Rights." He lectured on economics at two London colleges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lincoln-9991:
Lincoln, the county town of Lincolnshire, England, was once the second town of the realm. For that reason many Jews lived there before the expulsion. They settled on Steep Hill, between the old Roman colony and the new castle and cathedral. The first mention of them comes in 1159, in a pipe-roll entry of £40.

Aaron of Lincoln ran his vast lending work from this town, and his house still stands. At the attacks that opened Richard I's reign, Lincoln's Jews fled to the castle and lived. St. Hugh, the bishop, may have curbed the mob, the entry suggests. In the 1194 tax list Lincoln ranks second to London in payment, and first in the number of Jewish names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lolli-david-100: David Lolli was an Italian physician born at Göritz in 1825, and he died at Triest in 1884. He studied medicine at Padua and Vienna. When war for Italian freedom broke out, he left his studies to join volunteers at Padua and Venice. He caught cholera in the besieged city and recovered. He later practiced at Triest and kept working for Italian unity at great personal risk. He wrote on magnetism, cholera, and love, much of it left unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marburg-10391:
Marburg is treated in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as two towns, one German and one Austrian. The Hessian Marburg first names Jews in a document of 1317. They already had a community, a synagogue, and their own quarter. By 1452 the synagogue was demolished and the cemetery in Christian hands, so expulsion had come.

The article follows a slow return. Landgrave Philipp let Jews stay provisionally in 1532, and two settled in 1536. Numbers stayed tiny for centuries, six families in 1744 and eight in 1776. Freedom of residence swelled the community to about three hundred by 1902. A handsome synagogue rose in 1897, with schools and a pupils' home beside it. The Austrian Marburg, second city of Styria, held about a hundred Jews. There they had settled in the late thirteenth century as respected merchants. They owned houses, fields, mills, and vineyards in a ghetto with synagogue and bath-house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattithiah-b-jo:
Mattithiah ben Joseph, called the Provençal, served as chief rabbi of Paris and of all France from 1360 to 1385. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was the son of Joseph ben Johanan of Treves, rabbi of Marseilles, and a pupil of teachers in Provence and Gerona. In 1360 King Charles V appointed him over the Paris community and the newly organized communities of France. He also exempted him from wearing the Jewish badge.

The entry credits him with founding a rabbinical school at Paris. The school drew many pupils, and eight of them went on to lead communities of their own. The entry also works through his probable identity with two other names in the records. Those names are Mattithiah Treves and Mattithiah the Frank. It weighs the honorific “touchstone” that Isaac ben Sheshet applied to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meisels-dob-ber:
Dob Berush Meisels, a Polish rabbi who sat in parliaments, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik. Born about 1800, he married into a wealthy family, worked as a banker at Cracow, and in 1832 became its rabbi, though part of the community followed a rival. In 1848 Catholic votes sent him to the Austrian Reichsrath at Kremsier, where, teased for sitting with the left, he answered, "Jews have no right!" He died at Warsaw on March 17, 1870.

From 1856 he was rabbi of Warsaw, and in the crisis of 1861 he threw his weight behind Poland, marching with clergy to honor the insurrection's first victims. The Russians arrested and expelled him, then let him return in 1862. The entry credits his loyalty with shielding Warsaw's Jews from massacres that some Polish leaders had planned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merab-10691: Merab, the elder of Saul's two daughters, receives a three-line notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn. Saul formally offered her hand to David on one condition, that he distinguish himself in the war against the Philistines. David did so, but Saul broke his promise and gave Merab instead to Adriel the Meholathite. The entry cites the fourteenth and eighteenth chapters of First Samuel and records nothing else of her: a marriage promised, earned, and withheld, preserved in a handful of verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizmor-shir-le-:
Mizmor Shir le-Yom ha-Shabbat — a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day — is the superscription of Psalm 92, and Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen trace its musical life in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The psalm opens the Sabbath at evening service, returns in the morning's verses of praise, and is read again after the Torah at afternoon service.

Musically, the article admits, the northern rite has no fixed tradition for it, so cantors and choirmasters filled the gap with settings of their own. One stands out: Schubert composed verses one to eight for baritone, solo quartet, and chorus, printed in Sulzer's Schir Zion and performed at the London Symphony Concerts. In practice the congregation reads the psalm and the cantor takes the closing verses in elaborate chant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mohammed-10291:
Mohammed, founder of Islam, receives one of the Jewish Encyclopedia's major articles. Its authors are Richard Gottheil, Mary W. Montgomery, and Hubert Grimme, and it was published in 1906. It begins with a birth at Mecca between 569 and 571. He was a posthumous child, motherless at six. He passed from his grandfather's guardianship to his uncle Abu Ṭalib's. By Meccan custom he was nursed among desert Bedouins.

The writers handle the legends coolly. One legend gives the boy supposed epileptic symptoms. Another tells of the Syrian caravan journey once used to explain his knowledge of Judaism and Christianity. No such journey was needed, since Mecca itself held both faiths within reach. At twenty-five he traveled for the wealthy widow Ḥadijah. She offered him her hand on his return. The long article follows the career to his death at Medina in 632.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-b-hill:
Mordecai ben Hillel was a German halakist of the thirteenth century. He came from one of Germany's most prominent families of scholars. Solomon Schechter and Louis Ginzberg write about him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died as a martyr at Nuremberg on August 1, 1298. His wife Selda and their five children perished with him. Little else of his family life is known.

His lineage ran back through his grandfather Hillel. It reached Eliezer ben Joel ha-Levi and Eliezer ben Nathan. A bitter residence suit at Goslar was decided in his favor. It likely drove him to settle at Nuremberg. His master was Meïr of Rothenburg. In Meïr's presence the young Mordecai already pronounced independent decisions. He quotes Meïr's tosafot, responsa, and oral teachings throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-isaac-of-:
Moses Isaac of Kelmy, known as the Kelmer maggid, was a Russian traveling preacher born at Slonim in 1828. Louis Ginzberg and Peter Wiernik wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He preached his first sermon at fifteen and studied on after his marriage. Israel Lipkin saw his gift and urged him to make preaching his life's work.

For nearly fifty years Moses Isaac traveled from town to town, and his arrival was an event in each community. His sermons joined religion to practical ethics, and he boldly denounced unrighteous men, which brought him persecution and even attacks. He founded societies for religion and charity wherever he preached. His sermon collection, Tokahat Hayyim, appeared at Wilna in 1897, two years before his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-book-of-1:
The Book of Nahum is a Minor Prophetic book built around the fall of Nineveh. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia study of it. Its three chapters announce the downfall of the Assyrian empire to a downtrodden Judah. The first describes a theophany of judgment and promises refuge to those who trust in God.

The second chapter shows Nineveh stormed, its river gates open, its palace in flames. The third calls it a city of blood and sets fallen Thebes as its warning. The article dates the book between Thebes' fall in 664 and Assyria's end, favoring about 608. Modern finds at Nineveh, it says, confirm the prophet's picture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-navarro-11391:
Navarro names a Portuguese family close to two kings. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Moses Navarro was body-physician to Pedro I. He was also chief rabbi for nearly thirty years. He died at Lisbon about 1370.

Moses used royal favor to help fellow Jews. His son Judah farmed the royal taxes for huge sums. A later Moses served John I as doctor and chief rabbi. In 1391 he brought the king a pope's bull. It banned forced baptism, robbery, and killing of Jews. The king then made that shield a law in 1392. Spanish Jews fleeing terror found shelter under it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olmo-jacob-dani:
Jacob Daniel ben Abraham Olmo was an Italian rabbi and poet. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Ferrara about the year 1690. He died there on the first day of Pentecost, 1757. He read the Talmud first with his father.

Olmo later read with Isaac Lampronti, a famed teacher. He took his rabbi's diploma in the year 1715. He rose to head the rabbis' school at Ferrara. He also served as preacher to the flock there. Some of his rulings stand in books by other rabbis. His own first ruling came out at Venice in 1715. He wrote hymns for Italian prayer books as well. One long poem of his ran to 277 stanzas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ossifrage-11791: The ossifrage is an unclean bird named in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the lists in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Men know it as the lammergeier, a great vulture. Its name comes from its way with bones, its dear food. It drops bones from a great height on the rocks. The fall breaks them so it can feed on them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-papo-eliezer-be:
Eliezer ben Isaac Papo was a Bulgarian rabbi and author. Isidore Singer and N. T. London wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Sarajevo, in Bosnia, in his age. He died in the year 1824, by the entry's tale. He held the rabbi's post in Silistria till his death.

Eliezer led a life of strict faith at all times. He took but a small bit of food each day. He held back from each kind of joy in life. For this, men gave him the surname of the Saint. His chief book was Pele Yoez, a work on good traits. It sets its rules in the order of the letters. It came out at Constantinople in the year 1824. A second book of his held sermons in Torah order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peiser-raphael-:
Raphael ben Jacob Peiser was a rabbi of Peisern. He worked in the eighteenth century as a Talmud scholar. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His fame rests on two books of novellae.

His first book bears two titles, Or la-Yesharim and En Yaakov. It gives fresh readings of six Talmud treatises. It also comments on parts of the Passover Haggadah. Both parts came out together at Dyhernfurth in 1778. A second book, on two more treatises, followed in 1805. Novellae are new insights on old texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phenicia-12091:
Phenicia was a narrow strip on the Mediterranean's east coast. Joseph Jacobs and Louis H. Gray wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It ran some two hundred miles along the sea. The Lebanon range closed it off inland.

The Bible never names the land as such. It calls its people Sidonians instead. The Greek name may come from the word for purple. That dye, from the murex shell, made the whole coast rich. Tyre, Sidon, and Byblos led its city states. The land never formed one single kingdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-proselyte-from-:
Proselyte is the word for a convert to Judaism. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Greek translators used it for the Hebrew word ger. The first sense of ger is a matter of doubt, they say. Most now hold it meant a stranger living in Palestine.

Such a stranger put himself under the guard of the people. He lived among them as a kind of client. After the exile the word took a new sense. It came to mean a full convert to the faith. The article traces both senses through Bible and later law. It shows what rights and duties each sense carried.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabban-lit-our-:
Rabban, meaning our teacher, is a title of the highest rank. The Editorial Board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was given to patriarchs alone among the Jews. Those men led the Sanhedrin as its heads. The first man to bear the title was Gamaliel the Elder. All later patriarchs bore it after him in turn.

Frankel gives a ground for that first grant of the title. Gamaliel led the Sanhedrin with no second head beside him. So he stood as the sole master of the house. From that fact the title Rabban grew, in Frankel's view. The article weighs that view and lists the title's bearers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ratisbonne-alph:
Alphonse-Marie Ratisbonne was a French convert to Catholicism born on May 1, 1812. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Strasburg. He died at Jerusalem on May 6, 1884.

The article says he took a law degree, then visited Rome. There, on January 20, 1842, he gave up the Jewish faith. His conversion drew many pamphlets with opposing views. He entered the order of Notre Dame de Sion. He had first trained with the Society of Jesus. Ratisbonne founded a monastery at Jerusalem. He wrote a work on the litanies of the Virgin. The entry is brief but marks dates and places clearly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rodelheim-12791:
Rödelheim is a Prussian town near Frankfort on the Main. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A Jewish community likely existed there by the mid thirteenth century. Town archives fix Jewish legal status in 1290.

The article stresses the town's Jewish printing presses. Carl Reich ran a press in the mid eighteenth century. He printed works by Zamosc, Friedberg, and Levi. Wolf Heidenheim and Baruch Bashwitz later founded a famous press. Their Oriental and Occidental printing house issued major texts. Five Pentateuch editions appeared from 1818 to 1821. Festival books and the Haggadah followed. In 1905 the town held one hundred thirty Jews. Its institutions include hospitals for Jews and for all faiths.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosin-david-128:
David Rosin was a German theologian born at Rosenberg, Silesia, on May 27, 1823. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his doctorate in 1851 after study at Berlin and Halle.

Rosin headed a Berlin religious school opened under Michael Sachs in 1854. In 1866 he became professor at the Breslau rabbinical seminary, succeeding M. Joël. He taught preaching, Bible commentary, and Midrash there until his death. His writings include a study of the ethics of Maimonides. He also edited the poems of Abraham ibn Ezra in five parts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sagerin-lit-fem:
A sagerin, literally a female sayer, led other women in public prayer. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Francis L. Cohen wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The custom answered a real gap in women's worship.

Synagogue practice separated the sexes, even back in Temple days. Women could appoint a prayer leader from among themselves, by tradition. Yet boys got far more Hebrew teaching, so many women lacked the language. In eastern Europe women therefore gathered in small groups to pray. The most fluent reader read the supplications aloud, in the local vernacular.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-ammi: Samuel ben Ammi was a Palestinian amora of the beginning of the fourth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He is known through his controversies with other scholars of his age. He read one verse in Chronicles to mean that King Abijah left fallen Israelites exposed. Their faces would rot beyond knowing, so their widows could not remarry on proof. The reading stands in the Palestinian Talmud and in Genesis Rabbah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanhedrin-12291:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this long Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Sanhedrin. The word comes from the Greek synedrion, meaning an assembly. It named the highest court and ruling body at Jerusalem. The Roman governor Gabinius used the term in 57 B.C. He split Palestine into five districts, each headed by a sanhedrin. Bacher argues the word was current far earlier.

The article then tests a hard question. Talmudic sources describe a Great Sanhedrin in the hall of hewn stone. It ruled on the Temple, priests, and sacrifices. Josephus and the Gospels show a different body. Their Sanhedrin handled trials, verdicts, and politics. Büchler held that two separate bodies sat side by side in Jerusalem. The article lays out the evidence on both sides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sar-shalom-ben-:
Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sar Shalom ben Boaz. He was Gaon of Sura, head of its great academy. He held the gaonate for ten years. He died about 859 or 864. More than one hundred of his responsa survive. Many appear in the collection Sha'are Ẓedeḳ, printed at Salonica in 1792.

Sar Shalom's answers show a mild and tolerant temper. He forbade robbing a non-Jew outright. He warned people not to take on rules they could not keep. When a community's vow proved too hard, he let it break the vow. Community leaders in distant lands consulted him. He answered them as a friend, not a commander. He explained how Sura's customs differed from Pumbedita's. Then he left the choice to them. Yet he punished violence and usury with a firm hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-segovia-13391:
Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Segovia. The Spanish city stands in Old Castile, between Burgos, Toledo, and Avila. When Alfonso the Sixth took it, a sizable Jewish community already lived there. In 1294 that community paid 10,806 maravedis in taxes. Its Jews grew rich in trade, tanning, and cloth making.

Segovia's Jews suffered in the civil war between Pedro and Henry de Trastamara. Christians looted their goods and their loan notes. In 1410 a charge of desecrating the host fell on them. Bishop Juan de Tordesillas believed the story. The king's physician, Meïr Alguades, was arrested and two leading Jews executed. A poison charge followed, and many more Jews died or fled. In 1412 the great synagogue became a church. The Jews were driven from their old quarter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shalmaneser-ene:
Shalmaneser ruled Assyria from 727 to 722 B.C., after Tiglath-pileser III. Joseph Jacobs and J. F. McLaughlin wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Second Kings says he made Hoshea, king of Israel, his vassal. Hoshea then plotted with Egypt and withheld his tribute.

In answer, Shalmaneser invaded Israel and jailed Hoshea. He besieged Samaria for three years before taking the city. Israel's people were carried off to Assyria. No records of this king survive among Assyrian inscriptions. A Babylonian chronicle says he destroyed Samaria and died in his fifth year. The entry joins the Bible's account with that spare outside record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiskes-saul-b-:
Saul ben Judah Löb Shiskes was a Polish rabbinical scholar who died at Wilna in 1797. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He died at an advanced age in that city. His name rests chiefly on one scholarly book.

That book, Shebil ha-Yashar, comments on Alfasi's great code. Only its first part was ever published, at Wilna in 1839. Solomon, younger brother of Hayyim of Volozhin, helped with the work. Solomon annotated it and contributed to parts of it. Shiskes lost a son, Zebi, who died in 1771 at twenty-two. The brief entry preserves a scholar known through one partly printed book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-halaft:
Simeon ben Halafta was a teacher between the tannaitic and amoraic ages of rabbinic learning. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was a friend of Hiyya and often differed with him. Their disputes concerned homiletic readings of Scripture passages.

Simeon lived at En-Tina, near Sepphoris in Galilee. He visited the patriarch Judah the First at Sepphoris sometimes. He had been Judah's pupil in earlier years. Poverty pressed him so hard that Judah often relieved him. Age and weakness finally stopped his visits entirely. When Judah's son asked him for a blessing, he gave one. God grant you neither shame others nor be shamed, he said. The patriarch called that no empty phrase at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siwan-13791:
Siwan is the third month of the church year in the Jewish calendar. Cyrus Adler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It is the ninth month of the civil year. It has thirty days and matches June, roughly. The Feast of Weeks falls on its sixth and seventh days.

The third, fourth, and fifth days mark a special time. They recall the three days of preparation before Sinai. Weddings may be held on those days during Sefirah. The Talmud calls Siwan 6 the New Year of the Two Loaves. The entry also lists fast days kept in the month. Each fast recalls a sad event in Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-samuel-:
Samuel Solomon was an English quack born in 1780. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He flourished in Liverpool as an eccentric figure. He became known as the inventor of a patent cure. That cure was called the Balm of Gilead.

Sales of the balm made him a large fortune. In 1805 he moved to a grand house in Kensington road. His home, Gilead House, had fine gardens and shrubberies. It became one of the sights of the town for years. Streets named Gilead, Balm, and Solomon still mark his link there. He died in London in 1818, leaving two children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-starokonstantin:
Starokonstantinov was a city in the government of Volhynia, Russia. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews settled there soon after the city was founded. By 1648 it had a considerable Jewish community in place. That year Cossacks and Tatars killed most of its Jews.

Polish general Wishnevetzki had defended those Jews very bravely. In 1651 the hordes captured the city anew and burned it. In 1659 the inhabitants beat off a siege by Vygovski. In 1793 the city passed to Russia with the Ukraine. By 1905 Jews made up about sixty percent of 17,000 people. The city had two synagogues and five prayer-houses then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stuttgart-14091:
Stuttgart is the capital city of the kingdom of Württemberg. Isidore Singer and Theodor Kroner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Its first records date to the rule of Eberhard the Illustrious. Jews appear there by the Black Death years. In 1348 and 1349 local Jews died as martyrs in flames.

A ghetto and a Jewish school stood in that early period. Traces of Jews return in records from 1393. Under later counts, one Moses Jäcklin gained citizenship there. Letters of protection guarded him and his household. Others bought similar patents for set sums of florins. One settler at Cannstatt could lend money at capped interest. The long entry pieces together a sparse medieval record. It shows Jews living under bought and fragile rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tabori-robert-1:
Robert Tábóri was a Hungarian author born at Almas in 1855. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on November 10 of that year. He studied at Baja, Budapest, and Vienna. In 1874 he began work as a journalist in Vienna.
