Research on rhythm disorders has concentrated on atrial fibrillation, leaving the slow-heart side understudied. The authors used California health care databases covering nearly twenty-nine million adults over a decade and a half. They modeled which personal traits, illnesses, lifestyle factors, and air pollution exposures preceded a pacemaker for this block.

Nineteen factors raised risk, led by older age, male sex, and cardiovascular disease. More usefully, several were changeable: heavy drinking, tobacco use, cannabis use, and obesity each added risk. Black and Asian or Pacific Islander patients faced lower risk than White patients. Because a pacemaker treats the failure but does not prevent it, these modifiable predictors deserve prospective study as prevention targets, a near-empty field.
plos-pone-0356691:
Xue Hu and five colleagues search for shared immune signals between two very different diseases, diabetic kidney disease and Parkinson's disease, in this 2026 analysis. The two conditions affect unrelated organs yet are statistically linked and both involve abnormal innate immunity. The team re-analyzed several public gene-activity datasets from kidney and brain tissue, then checked cell-level data to locate the signals.

The honest headline is restraint: after strict statistical correction, the broad overlap between the diseases shrank to very little. Two immune genes kept pointing in the same direction in both diseases and sat in inflammation-heavy cells, but they did not pass the toughest significance tests. Computer experiments hinted at a candidate drug and at regulatory changes, again without firm significance. The authors present the overlap as a partial, testable lead rather than a proven shared pathway.
plos-pone-0356791:
Yanhong Jiang and colleagues surveyed 504 resident physicians in China's standardized training system about the psychological price of residency. Their 2026 multicenter study measured perceived stress, effort-reward imbalance, burnout, and depressive symptoms with validated scales, then modeled the chain linking them, using hospitals in the country's south.

The burden was heavy: more than eight in ten residents reported burnout, over a third high stress, and more than a quarter screened positive for probable depression. The statistical chain ran in sequence, stress feeding a sense of unfair effort, unfairness feeding burnout, and burnout feeding depression, on top of a direct stress-to-depression link. The authors argue hospitals must fix the effort-reward terms, not just offer resilience tips.
plos-pone-0356891:
Grace Kyule leads household surveys of tobacco use among adolescents in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Nigeria, and Kenya. Tobacco habits start young, and industry marketing is pushing into African markets, yet data covering teens both in and out of school were scarce. Trained teams interviewed more than eighteen thousand young people aged ten to seventeen at home in a recent year, using harmonized tools across the three countries.

About one in fifteen adolescents reported using tobacco in the past month. Rates differed sharply by country, with Congo highest by far and Nigeria and Kenya much lower. The surveys counted smoked and smokeless forms separately and modeled which traits predict use in each country. Kyule and colleagues say prevention must be built country by country, since one regional pattern does not fit all three.
plos-pone-0356991:
Ke-Lang Lou and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It formally describes a new plant species, Mazus zhewanensis, in the family Mazaceae. The plant comes from Eastern China, and the species name reflects its home region.

Describing a new species means recording how it differs from its relatives so other botanists can recognize it. Such papers add one more entry to the catalog of China's rich flora and give conservationists a named plant to track. Taxonomists and regional flora writers are the core readers, and the description becomes the reference point for all later work on this species.
plos-pone-0357091:
Higinio Fernández-Sánchez and colleagues analyzed survey data from 450 homeless young people in Houston, Texas. The participants were aged sixteen to twenty-five. The team measured how many had experienced sex trafficking. Their 2026 cross-sectional study was drawn from the baseline of a nurse-led HIV prevention trial. It screened for exploitation with a standard five-item tool. It compared rates across age, gender, race, sexuality, and foster care history.

Nearly one in four participants reported experiences matching sex trafficking. Young women were more than twice as likely as young men to report it after adjustment. The authors call for routine, trauma-informed screening wherever homeless youth seek services. They also want outreach designed to reach the young women most affected. Long-term studies of how trafficking begins, and how its harms unfold, are needed too.
plos-pone-0357291:
Shahid Mohammad Ganie, Pijush Kanti Dutta Pramanik, and Zhongming Zhao build computer models that estimate lung cancer risk in their 2026 paper. Instead of scans, the models use everyday health and habit details, such as lifestyle and clinical signs. The team combined five simpler learning methods into grouped models and tested them on plain, balanced, and enlarged versions of their data.

Grouped models beat single ones, and the stacked version, which layers strong models together, scored best overall. Two explanation tools then showed which factors pushed each person's risk up or down, keeping the system open to inspection. Clear reasoning like this matters if doctors are ever to trust such scores when choosing who needs early screening.
plos-pone-0357791:
Isabella DeStefano and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on feeding late preterm babies. They are born a few weeks early, make up most preterm births, yet were largely skipped by nutrition research. The team reviewed nearly nine hundred such infants at a New Jersey hospital, recording growth through the first year alongside guideline adherence and whether feeds were fortified with extra calories.

Smaller babies were far more likely to receive fortification, and fortified infants started smaller by every measure: weight, length, and head size, at birth and discharge. That gap is the point: fortification goes to infants already behind. The study tracks how trajectories evolved at six and twelve months. The work is framed as evidence for tailoring nutrition to birth weight rather than treating all late preterm infants alike, a group too often assumed to feed like full-term babies.
plos-pone-0358191: Ramar and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on scoring care habits for a disabling swelling disease. Filarial lymphedema, caused by a worm infection, swells limbs and needs daily home care. The team built a pilot scoring tool for how well patients follow management and prevention routines. A simple score can show clinics which patients need more support to stop the swelling from worsening.
plos-pone-0358491:
Benjamin Shaw, in a single author theory article in PLOS ONE in 2026, models a quiet chemical detail inside a rocket propellant ingredient. Hydroxylammonium nitrate, a salt used in propellants and studied for how it breaks down, dissolves into charged ions. Sometimes a positive and negative ion stick together as a contact pair, which can change how the mixture reacts and flows. Shaw's simplified theory predicts how many such pairs form.

He covers warm to hot conditions and dilute mixtures in water, methanol, and ethanol. In the two alcohols, the pair count is predicted to peak when just a small amount of the salt is present, rather than rising steadily. Water mixtures show no such peak. Knowing where pairs concentrate helps researchers interpret decomposition experiments and judge when this hidden species might steer a mixture's behavior.
plos-pone-0358591:
Wei Feng and four colleagues published a lab methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their topic was a cheap, fast way to pull DNA from the tissues of adult zebrafish, a small fish used in genetics labs around the world. The method relies on a resin called Chelex-100 instead of costly kits.

Feng's team laid out the steps and showed that the resin approach yields DNA fit for lab use. Speed and low cost matter most in labs with tight budgets or large numbers of fish to test. A simpler extraction step lowers the bar for student labs and for groups screening many fish in studies of genes, disease, and development.
plos-pone-0358791: Singh and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a germ that learns to resist a last-resort drug. Klebsiella pneumoniae can cause severe lung and blood infections. As the bacteria adapted step by step to colistin, the team tracked how their full protein set changed. Watching resistance evolve in the lab shows which protein shifts doctors should fear in real outbreaks.
plos-pone-0358891:
Najia Rahim, Sadia Shakeel, Maryum Nouman, Sadia Asim, Javeria Chaudhry, and Zulqarnain Hassan wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It reports the development and clinical validation of an HPLC method, a laboratory technique for measuring substances in liquid samples. The substance measured is paclitaxel, a chemotherapy drug, in blood plasma.

The samples come from patients with breast cancer, where knowing the exact drug level in blood can guide dosing. Validation means proving the method measures precisely and reliably in real clinical samples. Hospital laboratories and cancer pharmacology teams are the readers who need a trustworthy paclitaxel assay of this kind.
plos-pone-0359091: Ariyakajorn and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on turning a friendly bacterium into a tiny factory. The strain, Lactococcus KTH0-1S, was fitted to display an enzyme, beta-galactosidase, on its surface. Whole cells carrying the enzyme then made lactosucrose, a useful sugar, efficiently. Using whole cells as catalysts can cut costs in food making, since the enzyme needs no costly cleaning.
plos-pone-0359591:
Yezi Liu, Shengchen Zhang, and Hai Li published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies Olympic Villages, the housing built for athletes during the Games. The question is how these temporary event spaces become permanent urban communities after the closing ceremony.

The authors propose a physical-relational-legacy framework, joining the buildings themselves, the social ties formed, and what the event leaves behind. Many host cities struggle with underused Olympic districts, so a framework for conversion has wide use. Urban planners bidding for or inheriting mega-event sites are the readers for this guidance.
plos-pone-0359791:
Yuwen Chen and co-authors studied in 2026 what keeps soil clumps stable in the spruce forests of the Central Tianshan Mountains. The forests are made of a regional spruce, Picea schrenkiana variety tianschanica, growing on mountain slopes where soil loss is a standing risk. Soil aggregates, the crumbs that hold soil together, protect against erosion and store water and carbon.

The authors measure how stable those aggregates are across the forest and test which factors explain the differences, such as litter, roots, and soil chemistry. Mountain forests shelter the headwaters of rivers used far below, so the condition of their soil reaches beyond the trees. The findings inform how these forests should be managed as climate and grazing pressures change.
pmc-10655391:
Congke Zhao and eight colleagues published a lung disease study in two thousand twenty-three on a heat shock protein in pulmonary hypertension. In this disease, lung artery walls thicken until the heart strains. A helper protein, Hsp110, rises in patients, but its role in the artery lining cells was unknown.

The protein ran high in patient blood and in rat models of the disease. Under low oxygen it pushed lining cells to multiply and move abnormally, by locking onto a signalling partner called STAT3. Screening found a small compound that breaks that grip. The compound calmed the abnormal cell behaviour in dishes and eased vessel thickening in rats. The authors propose the protein pair as a drug target.
pmc-10688091:
Yu Zhang and six co-authors trace how a drop in salt wakes seagrass seeds, in a 2023 study. Eelgrass, the commonest seagrass of northern temperate seas, spreads by seeds that must germinate underwater. Salt level is the master switch, and restoration projects need to understand it.

Combining gene activity and protein measurements, the team watched germination ignite as salinity fell. Calcium and lipid signaling switched on first, relayed through a kinase cascade. Stored starch, fats, and proteins mobilized to fuel the sprout. The dormancy hormone's production and signaling were throttled down while the growth hormone's rose. Cell walls loosened and remodeled for emergence. The molecular timetable gives marine restoration a practical handle: manage the salt, and the seed's own machinery does the rest.
pmc-10695591:
Wei-An Chen and co-authors report a labor pain catheter that landed in the wrong space yet worked safely. Epidural analgesia is the standard for labor pain, but a catheter can slip into the subdural space by accident. Unnoticed, drug given there can cause dangerously high blocks. A 29-year-old first-time mother had the catheter placed at the standard lower-back site for her induced labor.

Within fifteen minutes of a test dose, her legs weakened, her arms numbed, and her blood pressure fell by a quarter. The team recognized the misplacement early and switched to tiny, carefully titrated doses through the same catheter. Pain stayed controlled below the target level for over twelve hours, with no pressure drops or nerve signs. Scans after delivery confirmed where the catheter lay. The authors stress early recognition and present images of how fluid spreads in the subdural space.
pmc-10701791:
Penélope Correia and co-authors report a single complex operation in a 2023 case paper. The patient, a woman of fifty-eight, had a large hernia beside a stoma, an opening in the belly that drains waste. Hernias of this type are hard to fix, and the best fix, closing the stoma, raises risk when paired with rebuilding the belly wall.

Before surgery, the team used two aids to prepare the belly: a toxin that relaxes the side muscles, and slow air filling to stretch the cavity. They then closed the stoma and rebuilt the wall in one operation. She left the hospital on day eight with no problems. Six months on, there was no sign of the hernia returning. The authors say careful patient choice stays the key to this combined plan.
pmc-10704791:
Dawit Hawaria and co-authors report the first find of an invasive malaria mosquito in southern Ethiopia. Their 2023 study concerns Anopheles stephensi, an urban malaria carrier spreading in East Africa. World health officials have urged stronger tracking and control where it invades or may invade.

The team surveyed Hawassa City for larvae and adult mosquitoes over several months. They checked breeding sites, reared larvae for identification, and set traps indoors and outdoors. The species turned up in a notable share of breeding sites and made up a large share of reared adults. Lab tests confirmed the identity beyond shape alone. Early warning matters because this mosquito thrives in cities, where malaria control has long focused on rural patterns.
pmc-10706491:
Martina Magnani, Anna Claret, Enric Gisbert, and Luis Guerrero feed trout on insect meal and ask diners what they think, in a 2023 study. Mealworm flour is courting fish farmers as a stand-in for fish meal. Trout were raised on diets with varying insect shares, then fillets went to sensory panels. The insect-fed fish tasted and felt no different from the controls.

Consumers were another matter. Asked about buying and paying for such fish, a measurable share balked at the idea of insect-fed trout. Knowledge and attitudes, not flavor, drove the hesitation. The authors say the science of the feed is ready before the public is, and the industry must mind that gap.
pmc-10707591:
Eun Jin Park leads a team on muscle mass and heart events after stents. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses CT scans at the low back. Low muscle mass is a non classic risk for heart disease.

Folks who got heart stents and had CT scans joined the study. Muscle index was read at the first low back bone. Folks were grouped in four bands by that index, split by sex. Death and major heart events were tracked for three years. Both rose a lot in the low muscle bands. The link held after checks for other traits.
pmc-10716091:
Angelo Armandi and co-authors study how steady a new spleen stiffness measure is, in a paper from 2023. The measure uses a sound-based scan at a higher rate than usual. It can flag high pressure in liver veins, a serious effect of advanced liver disease, but the best way to take it was unclear.

The team studied more than two hundred and fifty exams, each with up to twenty single scans. They compared the middle value of each short protocol with the middle of all twenty scans. Exams with more than twelve scans stayed close to the full value with high confidence. High stiffness values needed more care than low ones. Results also varied by cause of disease. The paper gives a practical rule for clinic use.
pmc-10725691:
Nyi Nyi Zayar and colleagues published a 2023 study of chronic disease risk around tuberculosis in Myanmar. Tuberculosis patients may also face diabetes and hypertension. Their household contacts share many exposures. The team screened patients, contacts, and the general public in Yangon. Risk behaviors were recorded too.

Hundreds joined each comparison group. Smoking, drinking, and poor diet were examined as middlemen. Patients and contacts differed from the public on several risks. Shared households may spread behaviors as well as bacteria. Integrated screening could catch two disease families at once. TB clinics offer a ready platform for that.
pmc-10727691:
Cuiling Zhang and co-authors survey oncology nurses in China on heart side effects of cancer care in this 2023 paper. Chemotherapy can damage the heart while curing cancer. Nurses watch patients daily and give the guidance that catches trouble early. Their cardio oncology knowledge was unmeasured in this setting.

The survey covered tertiary hospitals in Shanxi Province. A questionnaire built from current literature tested disease observation, health guidance, and treatment delivery skills. Group comparisons used standard statistical tests. Correlations linked knowledge scores with nurse traits like training and experience. Results aim to show managers where teaching is needed most. National nursing policy now demands holistic care, which raises the bar further.
pmc-10728791:
Jasper Faber leads a large team that builds a guide for eHealth tools. Their work from twenty twenty-three aids folks with low social standing. Such folks gain less from eHealth, which widens health gaps.

The guide is web based and meant for pro builders. Phase one drew on two past studies for its content. Phase two shaped its design with pro users in rounds. Pros face many snags when they build for this group. A full guide could ease those snags a lot. The team tells how the guide was built.
pmc-10735791:
Mroz and seven co-authors read in twenty twenty-three how past care of a parent with brain decline shapes folks for care roles yet to come. More adults now care more than once in a life. Talks with thirty-two mid-life past carers fed the study.

All told of gains in know-how that made them more ready. Some also kept or grew their faith in their own skill. Others lost faith and dread the next role or shun it. Aid should build both know-how and faith, they urge, fit to each carer's tale.
pmc-10735891: Kirsten Corazzini introduces a 2023 journal session presenting two award lectures in the field of aging. The Joseph T. Freeman Award lecture was given by Joe Verghese of the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, honored as a leading clinician in research and care. The second lecture, for excellence in rehabilitation of aging persons, was given by Brad Manor of the Marcus Institute for Aging Research, recognized for helping older people regain function.
pmc-10736391:
Toni Calasanti, Sadie Giles, and Jing Geng study how gender and sexuality shape the care spouses give partners with dementia, with a focus on emotion work, in a paper from 2023. Emotion work means managing your own feelings to steer someone else's mood, for example to calm them or win their cooperation.

The analysis rests on deep interviews with sixty-nine older caregivers, straight, gay, and lesbian. Straight husbands rarely did emotion work, though they did manage their own feelings. Straight wives did it heavily, softening their feelings to gain compliance or bring calm and happiness. Gay and lesbian spouses also did emotion work and mixed it with a task-focused style. The authors argue that same-sex couples' more equal sharing shapes their care.
pmc-10736591:
Heather Fuller, Andrea Huseth-Zosel, Emily Kinkade, Bryce Van Vleet, and Melisa Hajdar report a longitudinal study of older adults coping with the COVID-19 pandemic, published in two thousand twenty-three. Seventy-six Midwestern adults aged seventy to ninety-seven were interviewed in five waves between spring two thousand twenty and mid two thousand twenty-two. At each wave they rated their coping, quality of life, and stress. They also answered open-ended questions about daily life during the pandemic.

Ratings of coping and quality of life rose significantly between the first and final interviews. Thematic coding found four coping patterns: staying occupied, seeking social support, cultivating an adaptive mindset, and future planning. After vaccines arrived, the meaning of these themes shifted toward a new normal and appreciation of personal resilience.
pmc-10736791:
Elayna Seago and Benjamin Katz link diet to thinking in older adults in this two thousand twenty-three study. Intake of ultra-processed food is rising worldwide, and past work tied diet patterns to thinking outcomes without pinning down which skills are involved. The team drew on two Health and Retirement Study sources: the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol and a health care and nutrition study with a food questionnaire. Foods were classed as ultra-processed under the NOVA system.

Tests that held age, gender, and self-rated health fixed compared thinking across groups by ultra-processed intake. Processing speed stood out: it was the skill most closely tied to ultra-processed intake. Other measures and most recall measures showed no such tie. The authors give these findings as a sharper map of how ultra-processed diets track with thinking, and a path toward work on how the link works.
pmc-10738091:
Jung Kwak, Elizabeth Kvale, Sarah Mills, and Snehal Patel describe the joint design of a trial that adds community health workers to hospital palliative care, in a paper from 2023. People with dementia are hospitalized far more than their peers. Those from minoritized groups face more moves between care settings and less access to comfort care. The team aims to test support that eases those hard transitions.

The design grew from talks with patients, families, and frontline staff. A needs survey covered thirty-four patient and caregiver pairs. Interviews added views from palliative providers and social care experts. The planned trial pairs each patient with a health worker during the hospital stay. Designers focused on language and cultural gaps in care. Early checks cover whether families join, stay, and find the help fair.
pmc-10738491:
Laurie Ruggiero, Elizabeth Orsega-Smith, and Sophia Kayatta survey diabetes risk and daily habits in older adults at senior centers, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. One hundred fifty-nine adults with a mean age in the mid seventies answered an unsigned survey. Questions covered illness, risk marks, habits, thought, and social life.

Three quarters sat at high risk for pre-diabetes, and one third had been told they have it. One fifth had diabetes and near two thirds had high blood pressure. Most rated their health as good, got regular activity, and slept about seven hours. Very few of them smoked at all. Readers see senior centers as ripe sites for prevention programs shaped to member wishes.
pmc-10739091:
Richard Munoz and seven co-authors surveyed high-risk older veterans in south Florida about their health and care use, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. The veterans were flagged by the VA system as most likely to face hospital care or death. Only a share of those invited replied, and nearly all who did were men.

Trouble getting transport to care was linked to both emergency visits and hospital stays. How veterans rated their own health also linked to emergency use. The team sorted veterans into four groups, marked by low mood, lack of a caregiver, limits in daily function, or being homebound. The groups are meant to guide better-matched care and support.
pmc-10740991:
Lorinczy and three co-authors review antibiotic shortages in hospitals, in work from twenty twenty-three. Shortages force staff to swap drugs, delay care, or use less ideal options. The review sums up recent reports and checks them against the record in Hungary.

The team searched five databases for studies from twenty to twenty twenty-three that used set search terms. They then matched the drugs in shortage in the papers with the Hungarian health authority database. Two groups emerged: drugs short in both sources, and drugs short in only one. Comparing handling methods across countries may help hospitals plan fair, safe responses when key antibiotics run out.
pmc-10741891:
Gyeongah Park, Qian Ge, Zhen Jin, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It traces how a stroke in the front of the brain stirs up the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, and points to an acid-sensing channel as a key amplifier.

Post-stroke anxiety and depression are common and deadly, yet their wiring is unclear. The team triggered a small stroke in the prefrontal cortex of rats with a chemical injection. The pathway from that region to the amygdala grew stronger afterward. A channel that senses acidity, named ASIC1a, helped drive the boost in synaptic plasticity. Rats lacking the channel failed to show the extra strengthening. The authors say the channel could be a target for protecting mental health after stroke, and that the circuit link reframes where post-stroke disorders begin.
pmc-10743191:
Anja Kovanda and a team of co-authors published a 2023 evaluation of a new genetic test for a common inherited muscle disease. The disease, known as FSHD, weakens the face, shoulders, and arms. It is caused when a repeated DNA segment on chromosome 4 shrinks and switches on a harmful gene.

The standard test, Southern blotting, is slow and can be confused by a similar repeat on another chromosome. The team tried optical genome mapping, which images very long DNA strands to measure the repeat directly. In patients whose blot results were unclear, the new method found the shrinkage the blot had missed. In new cases tested both ways, results agreed fully. The method can also point to the rarer second form of the disease.
pmc-10743691:
Eduardo Izquierdo-García and colleagues tune glowing coumarin dyes that target cell powerhouses. Their chemistry study from twenty twenty-three explores deep-red and near-infrared emitters. Long-wavelength light penetrates tissue and avoids cell glow interference. Such dyes make better probes for live-cell imaging.

The COUPY dye family gathers mainly inside mitochondria. Changing the dye backbone shifted colour and stability. One electron-pulling group gave exceptional light stability. It also pushed emission further toward the infrared. Cell uptake and exact cell location changed with structure too. The study maps which tweaks give which imaging traits. Probe designers can now pick properties deliberately.
pmc-10745891:
Anallely Lopez-Yerena and co-authors test if eating tomato soffritto shapes blood vessels and platelets in adults with overweight and obesity. Their 2023 trial was randomised, with a cross-over plan. It studies a cooking base in wide use in the Mediterranean diet.

Forty people got one hundred grams of soffritto each day, or a control, for forty-two days. They then crossed to the other arm. Aggregation of platelets set off by collagen got better by a share that counts, with soffritto, when set next to control. Aggregation set off by a second agent also fell in the soffritto group. No effects that count showed for how the lining of blood vessels works. Nor did they show for body measures, for lipid profile, or for blood counts. Tomatoes hold many known traits for health. But soffritto on its own had been looked at in few cases before this trial.
pmc-10750391:
Charidy Suarez-Ramos and five co-authors test a fluid injection technique against dry needling for shoulder muscle pain. Their randomized trial was published in twenty twenty-three. The pain syndrome centers on tender trigger points in the upper trapezius.

Patients received either ultrasound-guided injection of anesthetic saline between muscle layers or plain dry needling of the trigger points. Both groups learned daily self-stretching. Pain and quality of life were tracked short and long term. The fluid method is thought to free gliding between muscle and its sheath and to quiet nerve branches. The trial measures whether the newer, wetter technique beats the needle alone.
pmc-10753391:
Yasoda Satpathy and seven co-authors check how well a big US cancer base catches cases by race and roots. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The base is a prime well for cancer work, but its hold on each group gainst the full state count was not known. More than five million folks with breast, colon, lung, or male gland cancer in two spans were set side by side.

Catch rates ran low most for Hispanic folks and for American Indian or Alaska Native folks in both spans. Gains came for all, yet the Hispanic gain lagged the white gain. Some cancer kinds did close the gap. The team urge work on where these folks seek care.
pmc-10763891:
Kohyoh Murata, Kosuke Kataoka, Ryuto Sanno, and five colleagues report two cricket genomes in this two thousand twenty-three paper. They sequenced the complete mitochondrial genomes of the band-legged ground cricket and a temperate form of the lawn ground cricket, both collected in Japan. The genomes ran about fifteen thousand and sixteen thousand base pairs respectively. Each contained the standard set of thirteen protein-coding genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and twenty-two transfer RNA genes.

Gene orientation matched other members of their superfamily, and gene order matched their family. In phylogenetic analysis, each Japanese cricket grouped with a counterpart collected in China. Comparing amino acid differences across the protein-coding genes suggested each pair actually comprises separate species. The authors offer the sequences as resources for phylogenetic and taxonomic work on the ground cricket family, where molecular data help untangle look-alike species.
pmc-10783991:
Khudheeja Ahmed, Juwayria Ahmed, and Mohammed Ahmed report a case where a very slow heartbeat cleared after heart artery opening, in a twenty twenty-three paper. Slow heartbeats are usually managed with watchful care and then a pacemaker. In this patient, the slow rhythm and its symptoms faded after angioplasty widened a narrowed heart artery. The team sets out the case to argue for a fuller workup before device surgery.

Their point is that blocked heart arteries can sit behind some slow rhythms. Treating the blockage may fix the rhythm and spare the patient an unneeded pacemaker. The authors call for case-by-case care plans rather than a fixed path for all slow-heartbeat patients.
pmc-10809391:
Lu Ren and co-authors link a sleep disorder to thinking problems in Parkinson's disease, in work published in 2023. In rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, people act out their dreams, and it affects 30 to 40 percent of Parkinson's patients. The team compared patients with and without the sleep disorder, plus healthy controls, using a brain-scanning method based on near-infrared light during a word fluency task.

The patients with the sleep disorder showed weaker activation across several frontal brain areas. The drops sat in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex on both sides and the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex. One activation measure in the right frontal area fell as the sleep disorder grew more severe. The authors conclude that the sleep disorder worsens executive function in Parkinson's disease through reduced frontal activity. The finding ties a visible sleep symptom to the brain basis of a common cognitive complaint.
pmc-10820991:
Adèle Mangelinck and eleven co-authors mapped how two kinds of T cells respond in a standard lab test, in twenty twenty-three. The test mixes immune cells from two donors and is widely used to judge immune drugs. The team tracked CD4 and CD8 T cells with flow tools, protein assays, and single-cell gene reads over time.

The two kinds shared classic signs of response, such as growth and raised output. But they differed in timing, strength, and the signals they released. Three new markers stood out in the reacting cells. Gene reads mapped cell talk at the contact point and pathways switched on downstream. The authors say the map can help judge drugs and point to new immune therapy ideas.
pmc-10831691:
Shaheera Fatima and co-authors present a review, published in 2023, of natural bubble shuttles that ferry drugs into the brain. The blood-brain barrier blocks most drugs; only a small share of new brain compounds cross it. Exosomes, tiny bubbles shed by cells, cross that wall by nature. They are kind to tissue, stable, and low in immune fuss, and they home to set targets.

The review sets out the flaws of man-made carriers first. It then maps how exosomes are loaded, aimed, and tested for brain care. Their traits cut stray effects on off-target tissue. Gaps in supply and standard methods still slow clinic use. Natural shuttles could open the brain to drugs that now fail at the gate.
pmc-10834691:
Farhad Pourfarzi, Aziz Kamran, Maryam Zare, and Jafar Mohammadshahi run, in a study whose journal version is dated 2023, a web-based lifestyle program for women in Ardabil, Iran, during the COVID-19 years. Diet and movement feed immune strength, and the team asked whether online coaching could improve both, and perhaps lower infection risk. Three hundred three women without prior infection were split between eight online sessions and a waiting list.

The coached group improved clearly on weight, body mass index, and the balance of energy, carbohydrate, protein, and fat in their diets. Activity rose over the study in both groups, walking included, so the program's edge there was partial. Antibody levels climbed in both arms as the pandemic rolled on. The authors conclude that web coaching can firm up nutrition and activity at distance, a useful template for reaching women where clinics cannot.
pmc-10871091:
Blaj, Cucu, Tamba, and Turliuc wrote a review in twenty twenty-three on a swelling pathway in brain aneurysms. An aneurysm is a weak bulge in a brain vessel that can burst. Blood flow stress and swelling are closely tied to how bulges form and grow. A master pathway, called NF-kB, drives much of that swelling. The review traces how signals in that pathway alter vessel wall cells. It covers muscle cells, lining cells, and the scaffold between them.

The authors list the pathway's triggers and gene targets most tied to bulges. They sum up current tactics to block the pathway in this setting. Such blockers could calm vessel wall swelling and slow bulge growth. The review adds a guide for future treatment research.
pmc-10911091:
Jinsheng Zhu and five colleagues study how TikTok use shapes self-perception among Chinese university students, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. Short video apps are gaining more note round the world. The team applied self-perception theory with talk-based methods. They looked at app use and how students grasp the self.

Identity, attitude change, how they felt, and civic acts stood out as the top aspects. Positive and negative parts together shaped how short video values were spread. Students craft a self on purpose through their app use. The findings feed mind research on Chinese university students. Short videos, the authors show, are not passive fun for this group. They reshape, in real time, how students see who they are.
pmc-11446391:
Zhe-Yi Kuang and seven co-authors review making PHA plastics that break down in nature, by feeding organic wastes to microbes, in a two thousand twenty-three biotechnology review. Polyhydroxyalkanoates can be made again and again from fresh feedstock and break down fully in nature, but high making cost keeps them from competing.

Waste feedstocks from factories, farms, city waste, and food processing could cut costs while easing pollution. The review covers engineered metabolic pathways for varied PHA types, treating wastes from other fields first, and downstream recovery. It then faces the blocks to factory-scale making and sketches possible ways out. The authors place waste-fed fermentation as the route toward PHAs truly matching oil-based plastics.
pmc-11532391:
Zena Jensvold and three co-authors study the cell's machinery for silencing jumping genes in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The HuSH complex mutes retrotransposons, DNA elements that copy themselves around the genome. The team found a second version of the complex, HuSH2, built around a sister protein. The two complexes settle at different places in the genome and do not overlap.

The first complex guards the LINE-1 family of jumping genes. The second instead mutes a set of gene regulators and immune response genes. Computer models of protein shapes guided tests of how the parts bind. The balance between the two complexes tunes how strongly LINE-1 is held down. The work refines our picture of genome defense.
pmc-11532491:
Lechner and co-authors build a cost model for making modern lithium-ion battery cells at gigawatt-hour scale. Cost models are key to judging if a cell design can compete in the market. Shape, chemistry, and factory process all shift the final price per unit of stored energy.

Their bottom-up method adds each cost layer from raw materials to finished cells. It outputs full cost, marginal cost, and levelized cost for varied production routes. Planners can then test how a new geometry or chemistry changes plant economics before building. The model supports smarter bets on battery factory design.
pmc-11539691:
Homa Baghaei Ravari and co-authors published this randomized trial in 2024. Men on methadone treatment for addiction often battle depression, anxiety, and craving, all of which raise relapse risk. The team tested cranial electrotherapy stimulation, a gentle electrical treatment applied to the head. Sixty patients at one Iranian center were split evenly into treatment and placebo groups. The treatment arm received forty-eight half-hour sessions.

Questionnaires measured mood and craving before and after. Between the groups, depression and anxiety showed no significant difference after treatment. Craving, however, ended clearly lower in the treated group, at about thirty-three points against forty-two. Within each group, several symptoms eased over time, including craving in the treated arm. The authors conclude the stimulation did not lift mood beyond placebo. Its real effect was on craving, the symptom most tied to returning to drug use.
pmc-11569191:
Uttam Pyakurel and five colleagues evaluate a compact cone-beam CT design meant to bring brain scanning to the patient's bedside. Flat-panel cone-beam systems are cheap and portable but scatter radiation badly over large volumes, blurring soft tissue. Their prototype adds a novel antiscatter collimator and a data correction method.

On anthropomorphic phantoms, the new system sharply improved soft tissue visibility, measurement accuracy, contrast, and resolution, reaching values comparable to standard hospital CT. Its contrast-to-noise performance came within about twelve to thirty-one percent of the reference scanner. The authors argue the approach could enable practical point-of-care head CT for early stroke diagnosis, hemorrhage detection, and surgical navigation.
pmc-11574791:
A team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four on medication errors by family caregivers at home. Informal caregivers give much of the medicine taken by patients cared for at home, often with little training. The authors set out to learn what drives their mistakes.

An online survey in Spain drew six hundred eighty-five caregivers, about half of them with more than twenty hours of training. Caregivers reported an average of over thirteen avoidable errors each per year. Errors ran higher among untrained caregivers, men, close relatives of the patient, those with outside jobs, and those using external aids.
pmc-11575491:
Emma England, Carrie Pratt, Mostafa Elshahed, and Noha Youssef present a 2024 study on oxygen tolerance in gut fungi. These fungi live in the stomachs of plant-eating animals and are strict anaerobes: oxygen should kill or stall them. Yet they seem to survive trips through air when they spread between hosts.

The team grew two fungal strains across a ladder of redox levels, set by adding a reducing chemical. Both grew well at negative values, as expected. One strain also grew once without the chemical, at a positive value far above gut conditions. Four more species passed the same test, while two failed. The result shows some gut fungi can actively grow, not just survive, in harsher chemical settings.
pmc-11577891:
Kenji Miki and co-authors show that a fuel pathway in brain tumors can be a drug target, in a study from 2024. Glioblastoma is a fast, deadly brain cancer that rewires how it feeds. Some tumors burn sugar fast, while others lean on their cell batteries. The team profiled thirty-eight tumor samples from two hospitals to sort the types.

In battery-leaning tumors, proteins of the battery chain ran high together. So did proteins that break down glutamine, an amino acid fuel. The two sets moved in step and against the sugar-burning set. Blocking the glutamine path slowed growth in cell lines rich in those proteins. Plain sugar-leaning lines were less affected. The authors say sorting tumors by fuel type could guide treatment. Battery-type tumors may yield to glutamine blockers.
pmc-11584591:
Ernani Tiaraju de Santa Helena and seven co-authors gauged sleep quality in adults in a city in southern Brazil, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The city was first settled by Germans. The team interviewed two thousand three hundred thirty-three people aged twenty to seventy-nine and scored their sleep with a standard index.

About thirty-three percent had poor sleep. The share was higher in women, at forty percent, and in older adults, at forty-four percent. Poor sleep tracked being female, smoking now or in the past, low mood, taking five or more drugs, and rating one's own health as fair or poor. A Germanic cultural tie, more schooling, and being at work each went with better sleep. The authors say poor sleep clusters with clear social, cultural, and health traits that care can target.
pmc-11585091:
Liyou Lian and three co-authors studied a simple blood ratio in pacemaker patients in a 2024 paper. The ratio compares hemoglobin, the oxygen carrier in blood, with the spread of red cell sizes. The team asked whether the ratio predicts major heart events after a pacemaker is implanted.

The study followed 595 patients in China for a median of two years. About sixteen percent had a major event, such as heart failure, a heart attack, a stroke, or death. Patients with a high ratio had a much lower risk than those with a low one. The link held up under several statistical checks, suggesting the cheap ratio may help flag risk.
pmc-11587791:
Hong-Da Zhang and co-authors study irregular heartbeats in intensive care patients in this 2024 paper. Atrial fibrillation is the most common rhythm disorder in these wards. The team split patients by whether the disorder was long-standing or appeared fresh during the illness. They drew on a large United States hospital database.

The study covered just over forty-eight thousand ICU patients. About a quarter developed fresh atrial fibrillation, and that group died most often over the next year. A third of them were gone within twelve months. Statistical models still showed higher risk after other factors were weighed. The results mark fresh rhythm trouble as a warning sign worth close watch.
pmc-11589691:
Peter Moran and co-authors read the full genomes of brown trout to find the gene basis of two life paths, in a paper from 2024. Some trout migrate to the sea, while others stay in their home river for life. Both paths persist side by side, and the gene balance behind them was unclear.

The team sequenced close to two hundred trout from five river pairs in Ireland. Each pair sat above and below a waterfall that blocks upward migration. Hundreds of genome regions differed between the sea-going and resident fish, spread across many genes. The genes touched energy balance, reproduction, salt handling, immunity, daily rhythms, and nerve function. Diversity patterns helped sort genes by the trait they shape: the urge to migrate, the migrant lifestyle, or its rewards.
pmc-11593791:
Talia Zamir and co-authors study how a support program serves mothers who face breast or ovarian cancer, in a 2024 paper. Patient navigation programs guide people through care and offer teaching and support. Many of the women served are raising children at the same time, yet little is known about how their children's ages shape their needs.

The team examined records for 1,758 women helped by a national cancer group. About seven in ten were mothers, most with adult children only, though nearly a third had only young children. Mothers of adult children reported worse day-to-day health than mothers of young children, yet both groups used the program in much the same way. For mothers of young children, better health linked to lower genetic risk and a stronger sense of control.
pmc-11594291:
Constanza Schapheer and co-authors catalogued the microbes living on and inside oriental cockroaches in a 2024 study. This species is one of the world's major pest cockroaches, sharing homes with people worldwide. Its bacteria can threaten health, yet some also serve the insect's own biology.

The team collected cockroaches in Santiago, Chile, and sequenced DNA from their outer shells and guts. They found diverse bacterial lineages, including helpful symbionts and species known to infect humans. They also inferred what these communities do for a living. A first detailed map of this pest's microbes informs both disease risk and new angles for controlling the insect itself.
pmc-11603691:
Pan Peng and Zhisheng Liu used a large United States health survey to ask whether inflammation carries part of the link between daily movement habits and chronic kidney disease. The survey covered over twenty-seven thousand adults from twenty to eighty, across eleven years. Activity and sitting time came from a standard activity form, and blood tests gave three inflammation scores.

Active people had lower kidney disease odds, and heavy sitters had higher odds. Two inflammation scores each carried a small share of both links, around two percent. The authors say easing inflammation is one small path by which moving more and sitting less may protect the kidneys.
pmc-11603991:

pmc-11606091:

pmc-11610091:

pmc-11610491:

pmc-11610591:

pmc-11613891:

pmc-11615191:

pmc-11621191:

pmc-11621591:

pmc-11622691:

pmc-11625891:

pmc-11628191:

pmc-11632091:
Miao Cheng, Chia-huei Tseng, Ken Fujiwara, Shoi Higashiyama, Abby Weng, and Yoshifumi Kitamura present a 2024 study building an Asian database of emotional body movement. pmc-11635891:

pmc-11637291:

pmc-11639091:

pmc-11640391:

pmc-11641191:

pmc-11641291:

pmc-11641991:

pmc-11642891:

pmc-11643491:

pmc-11643691:

pmc-11644791:

pmc-11647991:

pmc-11648091:

pmc-11651491:

pmc-11655891:

pmc-11656991:

pmc-11657891:

pmc-11662091:

pmc-11662191:

pmc-11663391:

pmc-11663791:

pmc-11664291:

pmc-11667691:
