pmc-11672591:
Ashlesha Kaushik and co-authors present a 2024 review of a deadly heart valve infection tied to drug-proof bacteria. The germ, a resistant form of staph, can grow in slimy mats called biofilms. Those mats shield the germ from drugs and from the immune system. Infections on fake valves and heart devices are the hardest to clear and often end in heart failure or stroke.

The review covers how the infection starts, how it shows, and how doctors confirm it. Set criteria now include modern scans that can spot mat-based infection. Care needs long courses of strong drugs, often in pairs, and surgery to remove infected parts is common. The authors stress that mat growth is the core reason these cases resist standard care.
pmc-11672691:
Praveenraj Elancheliyan and a team including Agnieszka Chacinska uncover two guardians of the protein import gate in human mitochondria. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The gate, TIM23, pulls proteins into the power plant's core or inner skin, and its human form was poorly mapped.

Humans carry two versions of one gate part. A protein family called prohibitins steadied both versions. A second protein, OCIAD1, joined the prohibitin complex to shield one version from a shredding enzyme. Its own level, in turn, answered to the gate's state. The pair forms a control axis that tunes each gate version differently. The work clarifies how cells keep their import machinery in balance.
pmc-11673991:
Blokhin and a large team study fat like molecules in the placenta of pregnant breast cancer patients after chemo in twenty twenty-four. Sphingolipids steer cell growth and death, so their balance guards the placenta. Gene activity for the pathway's enzymes was checked in seven patients and eight healthy peers. Fat levels were measured as well.

Many enzyme genes ran far hotter in the cancer group. Yet the fats they control held at healthy levels. The team reads this as a shield: the placenta spins up both build and break paths to hold balance. The guard may protect the newborn too. The claim is new and needs deeper study.
pmc-11674591:
Söğütlü, Altaş, Altıntaş, Altaş, Akova, and Özkars present a study from twenty twenty-four on air pollution and child asthma emergencies in Istanbul. Records cover eight years of pediatric asthma visits at one large hospital. Visit counts are modeled against daily pollutant levels. Nitrogen oxide rises track more visits in their models. A mixed pollutant factor also pushes visits upward. Sulfur dioxide oddly tracks fewer visits, against the pattern. The authors suspect hidden confounders behind that odd result.

Families should be told about environmental triggers, they urge. Asthma care plans can use pollution warnings. More study is needed to untangle the sulfur result. The work is ecological, reading city-level exposure.
pmc-11675091:
Cristina Padilla, Marzena Pępczyńska, Cristian Vizueta, and five colleagues reinforce edible films with plant nanocrystals in this two thousand twenty-four materials paper. Gelatin forms films for edible coatings and food packaging but needs support, shape memory effects included. How it interacts with cellulose nanocrystals is complex and poorly understood. The team added low nanocrystal doses, two, six, and ten percent by weight, to mammalian gelatin films at low moisture and studied structure and performance.

The nanocrystals blocked gelatin's triple helix formation, cutting one crystallinity measure from about twenty-two to twelve percent at the highest dose while slightly raising overall crystallinity. The water monolayer in the films fell. The composites stiffened and gained thermal stability with more nanocrystals. Shape memory suffered: recovery magnitude and speed both dropped despite clear molecular links between the parts. The study maps the trade-offs for packaging designers.
pmc-11676191:
Jianyun He, Lan Cheng, Xinxin Cheng, Yuting Wang, Xiaoxia Lin, and Shufang Xia study whether gut microbes carry part of the link between diet quality and cancer fatigue in breast cancer patients. Their cross-sectional study was published in twenty twenty-four. Fatigue is very common in this group and drags down outcomes.

Diet and fatigue were scored in three hundred and forty-two patients; a subset gave stool and blood samples. About forty-four in each hundred had fatigue. It tracked with low intake of protein, several vitamins, fiber, and minerals, and with a low healthy eating score. Fatigued patients had less varied gut microbes and an unhealthier mix, plus altered tryptophan chemistry. Mediation checks suggested microbes partly carry the diet effect.
pmc-11676291:
Xiangxiang Wang and seven co-authors map a family of ammonium carrier genes in quinoa. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Quinoa is a grain-like crop from the Andes with rich, well-balanced seed protein. Ammonium is a direct nitrogen source for plants, and carriers move it across cell walls. That flow shapes yield and seed quality.

They find a full family of carrier genes, with varied levels in root, stem, and seed at each growth stage. In a yeast strain that lacks its own carriers, most of the quinoa genes restore uptake. One sits in the cell membrane, as a carrier should. A network study names the gene switches that may rule nitrogen flow.
pmc-11676391:
Vieira and co-authors survey the fungi that cause anthracnose, the main disease of chayote in Brazil. The blame had long sat with one species, Colletotrichum orbiculare. No recent check of which species attack Brazilian chayote existed. The team gathered fungal samples from sick fruit and leaves across growing regions. A first gene screen covered 44 samples to gauge diversity. A smaller set of 22 got deeper gene reads.

The work describes two new species in the C. magnum group. That finding shows the disease has more than one cause in Brazil. Knowing the true culprits helps breeders and growers pick better controls. Misnamed fungi can send disease programs down the wrong path.
pmc-11677291:
Abrar Aljohani and Miki Nakazawa-Miklasevica published a breast cancer study in two thousand twenty-four on a gene called DSCC1. The gene helps copy DNA and hold sister copies together. Earlier network analysis flagged it as a leading gene in invasive breast cancer, but its link to outcomes was untested.

The team checked gene activity in two large patient cohorts and protein levels in one hundred Saudi patients. High DSCC1 activity marked more aggressive tumour features in the big datasets. The hospital samples let them tie protein levels to age, grade, size, and outcome. The authors present DSCC1 as a candidate warning marker for spread risk and treatment planning in early disease.
pmc-11677791:
Ailing Yang and co-authors test whether a fungus living quietly in a weed's leaves helps that weed invade, in a 2024 study. The weed, Ageratina adenophora, carries heavy loads of Colletotrichum fungi without symptoms. The team added three fungal strains to plants and watched growth, defense chemistry, and survival under attack and stress. Without threats, the fungi cost the plant: photosynthesis markers and biomass fell while defense markers rose.

Under attack, effects split by strain and enemy. Two strains blunted one pathogen yet worsened another; the third strain flipped the pattern. Under drought or poor soil, the fungi turned helpful, boosting stem length, chlorophyll, or dry weight. The authors conclude the leaf tenants are fair-weather friends: a burden in calm times, a shield in hard ones, and thus quiet allies of invasion.
pmc-11677891:
Ning Yuan and five colleagues add charred, iron-dusted material to pig manure compost and watch phosphorus change form, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Nano iron oxide was known to help compost mature. Its effects on phosphorus availability and bacterial communities were not.

Pig manure and straw composted under four treatments: plain control, two doses of biochar-supported nano iron oxide, and the higher dose plus calcium peroxide. The combined treatment ran hottest; one lower dose produced the most mature compost by carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. Phosphorus speciation and bacterial community structure were tracked through the process. Manure compost returns phosphorus to fields; keeping it in plant-available forms rather than lost ones decides its fertilizer worth.
pmc-11677991:
Ilze Irbe and co-authors test fungus-based building materials in a 2024 study. They made mycelium biocomposites from farm, wood, and paper waste streams. The team checked strength, heat flow, and fire behavior for use as insulation.

Composites with waste fibers and birch sanding dust showed the best bending strength. That strength rivaled common plastic foams and some commercial building materials. Hemp-based composites had the lowest heat flow, matching standard insulation. The materials also resisted fire better than many plastic foams, with lower heat and smoke release. The authors conclude these composites could serve as a green option for building insulation.
pmc-11678491:
Jiang Wan and co-authors catalog plant compounds from a rare Chinese shrub in this 2024 chemistry paper. The team studied twigs, leaves, and flower buds of Kolkwitzia amabilis. They isolated 39 compounds in total.

The haul included 11 iridoid glycosides, 20 triterpenoids, and 8 phenylpropanoids. Four compounds were new, including two built from paired iridoid units. Others carried an unusual alkaloid scaffold never seen in this plant family. Tests showed one new compound moderately blocked ACC1, an enzyme that builds fat, at 9.6 micromolar strength. Three others blocked ATP-citrate lyase, a related enzyme. Such blockers interest researchers studying fat metabolism and disease.
pmc-11679791:
Min Song and co-authors track industrial chemicals through the sea life of Laizhou Bay on China's Bohai Sea coast, in a 2024 paper. The chemicals, short-chain chlorinated paraffins, linger in the environment for years. The team measured them in bay water, in seabed sediment, and in 28 species of marine animals, then worked out how the chemicals build up as they move through the food web.

Levels in animals varied hugely, from about 70 to more than 47,000 nanograms per gram of fat. The mix of chemical forms in animals differed from the mix in water and sediment, showing that bodies select what they keep. The chemicals grew more concentrated at each step up the food chain, with magnification factors from about 2.2 to 3.0. How strongly they built up depended on how much they dislike water, a property tied to chain length and chlorine content.
pmc-11681591:
Marco Tomasino and a large team published a registry study in two thousand twenty-four on stress cardiomyopathy complicated by shock, comparing men and women. Takotsubo syndrome can crash the heart's pumping until blood pressure collapses. Sex differences in that severe form were unknown.

Of four hundred twelve shocked patients, about seventeen percent were men. Men were older, smoked far more, had weaker heart pumping, and needed breathing machines and hospital days more often. Infections also hit them harder. Yet death rates matched between sexes, in hospital and at five years, even after matching. About thirteen percent died in hospital and twenty-two percent by five years. The authors call the syndrome's shock equally lethal for both sexes.
pmc-11684391:
Li Li and co-authors shine ultraviolet B light on blue grained wheat to trace how pigment compounds and their genes respond over time, in work from twenty twenty-four. The blue layer gives this wheat special nutrition. Flavonoid levels under the light decide much of that value.

Chemical profiling found over eighteen hundred compounds, including three hundred forty flavonoids. Total flavonoids fell with exposure time, yet flavones and flavanols grew richer and more varied. Gene reads flagged over forty-two thousand shifted genes, with one hundred fifty-one in the flavonoid pathway. Key enzyme genes dipped early, then rose. One gene stood out in the joint network analysis as a hub of the response.
pmc-11684491:
Mohammed Alanssari and a team of co-authors report a hard case of immune destruction of red blood cells, in two thousand twenty-four. Their patient also had sickle cell disease, which already strains red cells. The immune attack caused severe anemia that kept returning despite many treatments.

Steroids, immune globulin, an antibody drug, and immune-suppressing drugs all failed to hold a response. A drug that blocks the cell's protein disposal units finally brought a favorable response. The authors add the case to growing evidence for that drug class in severe, stubborn cases of this kind. They note the precise causes of the immune attack remain largely unclear.
pmc-11685091:
Yibo He and four co-authors review how single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, methods that read gene activity cell by cell and in place, are reshaping research on Alzheimer's disease. Their review came out in 2024. The disease erodes memory and thinking, and its biology varies sharply between cell types.

Reading single cells has revealed distinct states of microglia and astrocytes, two brain cell types that drive inflammation and nerve cell damage. Some microglia groups are tied to the disease and to known risk genes. Spatial methods add location, showing how cells interact in tissue. The authors argue that combining these tools with other data is essential for finding new drug targets and markers, and for moving toward care tailored to the individual patient.
pmc-11689491:
Bronwyn Keefe presents a 2024 talk on micro-credentials, short skill badges, and their use in training the aging-services workforce. Many who care for older adults never got formal training for that work, while clients grow more diverse and complex. Boston University's aging center built online certificate courses with state and community agencies. The badges build career ladders in a field losing staff fast.

Trainees showed clear gains in core aging skills, knowledge, and confidence. About half took the courses for career growth or personal interest, and half because work required it. Skills-based hiring is rising as employers drop degree demands. Academic-community pairs, the talk argues, can retool the care workforce at scale. Examples from the field ground the case.
pmc-11690191:
Frank Oswald, a solo author, rethought the role of place in aging research in two thousand twenty-four. Environmental gerontology studies how older people relate to their surroundings, from home to neighborhood. After decades of work, Oswald argues the field needs fresh theory for fast-changing societies.

He sets out lasting issues, like how an aging person interacts with the home, and new ones, like technology use in a digital world. He reviews theories of person-environment relations, stressing ideas like transaction and co-construction. Western studies are over-represented in the proof he cites, he notes. The paper ends with a synthesis of how theory can meet both old and new challenges.
pmc-11690291:
Michelle Putnam and Susan Stark wrote a 2024 article on a basic question that two fields rarely discuss together. When is disability the thing to be explained? And when is it part of the explanation? How researchers place disability in their models shapes what they conclude about later life.

In aging research, disability is often treated as a personal trait that cuts independence. In disability research, it is more often a situational factor. Living with disability is harder in some settings, but it does not by itself remove independence. The two fields also differ on onset age and type of disability. The authors note a recent shift: a major health institute now counts disability as a social determinant of health. That opens a chance, they argue, for aging researchers to rethink how disability is defined and measured across the life course.
pmc-11690491:
Ellen Csikai and co-authors review how family members cope with caring for seriously ill older relatives, in this 2024 scoping review. Caregiving can run for years, and the end-of-life phase loads families hardest. The team screened hundreds of papers on community-dwelling caregivers and kept eight studies that met their rules. Samples ranged from eight to a few hundred people.

Across the studies, caregivers leaned on the same few strategies. Problem-solving handled the practical load, emotion-focused coping handled the feelings, and leaning on other people ran through both. Six studies were qualitative, giving the picture texture. The authors argue that knowing these patterns helps professionals spot struggling caregivers early. Support and resources can then be aimed where they protect the caregiver's own health.
pmc-11690991:
Deanne Tibbitts and seven co-authors published a study in 2024 on continuous passive monitoring of daily function and symptoms in older adults with prostate cancer. A common hormone therapy for this cancer, androgen deprivation therapy, raises the risk of physical and cognitive decline. When its side effects occur, and how broad they are, remains poorly understood.

The researchers equipped homes with infrared motion sensors, door sensors, a watch, a bed mat, a biometric scale, an electronic pillbox, and software tracking computer use. Weekly online surveys recorded symptoms, while clinic tests assessed physical and cognitive function. Seventeen of fifty-two men who were approached enrolled in the study. Most who declined felt the plan would be too demanding. Four in five of those who enrolled stayed for fourteen months. Sensor data arrived well for most devices, with watch-based sleep data the weakest. The team calls the approach feasible.
pmc-11691291:
Eric Vogelsang and Sara Moorman test whether doing more social activities, and doing them often, protects thinking in older adults, in work from twenty twenty-four. Social activity is often summed into one index score. Such sums can hide which activities actually matter.

Two national surveys of older Americans supplied tens of thousands of observations. By the sum score, each added activity and each step up in frequency tracked better cognition in both data sets. Split apart, the story narrowed: volunteering in one survey and club membership in the other were the lone activities tied to every cognition measure. The authors warn against reading health effects off raw activity counts.
pmc-11691891:
Molly Wylie and three co-authors report in twenty twenty-four on a rural aging network run by Lutheran Services in America. Many older adults in rural areas wish to stay in their homes. Yet care, rides, and other help can be hard to reach. The network links local groups in four states to close those gaps.

A three year review of the work found close to five hundred older adults had contact with the network. More than half were sent on to services they needed. People with tight incomes were sent on more often than those whose income met their needs. Talks with older adults and care partners showed gaps in rides, tech training, and language help. Users praised the network as a one stop source of help.
pmc-11691991:
Jiao Yu, Yi Wang, and Xi Chen study neighborhood disorder and brain health in older adults in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A messy, unsafe-feeling neighborhood may harm thinking in later life. Two paths were proposed: stress buildup in the body, and less physical activity.

The team used a national retirement study covering more than four thousand adults aged sixty-five and older without dementia. Higher perceived disorder predicted poorer thinking scores at a later wave. A small share of the effect ran through physical activity. The body stress measure, by contrast, showed no clear mediating role after personal factors were counted. The authors highlight behavior as the active pathway.
pmc-11692491: Quentin Price, Disa Basu, and Huaibin Cai wrote a short report in 2024 on two enzymes that produce a signaling molecule called 2-AG. The enzymes work in the dopamine-producing neurons that are lost in Parkinson's disease. Earlier work linked mutations in one enzyme to an early-onset form of the disease. That enzyme is the main producer of the signal there, but a related second enzyme is present too. The report sets out the next experiment: reducing both enzymes at once in mouse neurons to see whether movement symptoms appear.
pmc-11692991:
Faith Hopp used ChatGPT in 2024 as a research assistant to measure ageism in coverage of the United States presidential election. Ageism, a term coined by gerontologist Robert Butler in the nineteen sixties, means discrimination based on age, and it hung over President Biden's campaign. Hopp had the program collect mainstream media articles mentioning Biden and score how often ageist language appeared. And of what kind, in the month before and the month after his June debate with Donald Trump.

The ageist themes coded included claims that Biden was a bad leader, untrustworthy, mentally or physically unfit, and incompetent or irrelevant as a likely choice. Across the twenty-three articles sampled, ageist statements about Biden increased in the month after the debate weighed with the month before. The African American press carried fewer such statements in both periods, though paywalls limited how much of that coverage could be looked at.
pmc-11693891:
Abu Hossain Muhammad Ahsan and co-authors survey safety culture among college level students in Bangladesh, in work from twenty twenty-four. Safety beliefs, awareness, and attitudes shape how students act in labs, halls, and daily campus life. The survey reached more than sixteen hundred students at sixteen schools.

Students scored at moderate levels on all three safety scales. Women led on awareness and attitudes, while men led on beliefs and values. Students with disabilities or past accidents showed higher awareness and attitudes. Private school students scored lower than public school peers on two scales. Age, gender, and school type tied to every scale. The authors urge tailored programs that account for those gaps.
pmc-11699291:
Leila Claveau, Neil Hudson, Paul Jeffrey, and Francis Hassard used flow cytometry to track microbes in drinking water in two thousand twenty-four. Water plants need fast ways to see if bacteria are growing. The method sorts intact cells by how much nucleic acid they hold.

Cells with high nucleic acid reacted fast to nutrient changes, which makes them good signs of fresh growth. Cells with low nucleic acid fit stable water with slow food sources. Chlorine and nutrient inputs shifted the balance between the two groups. The authors say fingerprint patterns from the method, paired with cluster analysis, catch more change than the simple ratio alone.
pmc-11709391:
Diana Hobbs and nine co-authors compare tau deposit patterns across typical Alzheimer's disease and two atypical variants, one attacking vision and one attacking language. Their study came out in 2025. Tau scans were mapped against nine biological properties of the cortex.

Across all three groups, tau accumulated most where the cortex had expanded most over evolution, and vessel health tracked tau strongly. Beyond that shared pattern, the variants diverged: gene expression and myelin related to tau differently in each. The vision variant tied tau to cortical thickness in the opposite direction from the others. The authors say these fingerprints can explain why the same disease presents so differently, and may guide variant-specific research.
pmc-11711391:
JaeEun Koh, Juyoung Khwarg, Young Lag Cho, Kyung-Sang Yu, and Jae-Yong Chung compare two tablet forms of a new antibiotic in two thousand twenty-four. The drug, delpazolid, targets gram-positive bacteria that resist older drugs. The two forms differ only in their filler mix, so the body should handle them alike.

Twenty-four volunteers took each form once, in random order, with blood drawn for twelve hours after each dose. Peak levels and total exposure were close between forms. Total exposure met the standard band for same-drug proof, while the peak's range ran a bit wide. Safety checks ran alongside the blood work. The study supports swapping the filler mix in production.
pmc-11721291:
Sherif Khedr and a large team study, in twenty twenty-four, a DNA-sensing pathway in diabetic kidney disease, and how its role differs by sex and age. Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of chronic kidney pathology. The team used young and aged diabetic rats, plus human diabetic kidney tissue. The pathway, cGAS/STING, senses stray DNA and triggers inflammation. It was upregulated in diabetic rats versus healthy controls, and in human diabetic kidneys. Its activation pattern differed between males and females, and the gap grew with aging.

Gene sequencing of kidney cortex in both sexes and ages highlighted key molecules in the pathway. The authors propose cGAS/STING as an essential contributor to disease development. Tailored therapy may need to account for sex and age, they suggest.
pmc-11728391:
Andrea Duminuco and co-authors review emergencies in blood medicine and how to treat them, in work published in 2024. These crises progress fast and can kill, so recognition and early action decide outcomes. The review walks through the mechanism, signs, diagnosis, and management of each major emergency.

Conditions covered include high blood calcium from cancers, white cell overload in leukaemia, sickle cell crises, and tumour lysis syndrome after cancer cells break down. Transfusion reactions range from mild allergy to shock. A clotting-and-bleeding disorder tied to one leukaemia type gets special attention. Newer therapies add cytokine release syndrome to the list, a fierce immune reaction that teams must catch early. The article serves as a practical guide for front-line clinicians.
pmc-11967391:
Nayoung Kim looks back on a landmark Korean study of stomach bacteria, in a memoir-style paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Helicobacter pylori infection drives stomach disease, and policy needs prevalence data. In nineteen ninety-seven the Korean study group designed a nationwide survey of people without symptoms.

Blood samples came from 5,736 participants across Korea during nineteen ninety-eight. Their ages ran from one month to seventy-nine years. Antibody testing found infection in about seventeen percent of children and sixty-seven percent of adults. Questionnaires probed risk factors alongside. The retrospective describes how the multicenter effort was organized. Such baseline data anchored decades of Korean prevention policy for pylori-related disease.
pmc-12085791:
Malcolm Smith and a large team of co-authors summed twenty years of preclinical drug tests in child cancers. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, covers a national program set up in two thousand four. It tests targeted cancer drugs in mouse models of child tumors, hand in hand with drug firms. Child cancers have their own biology and few patients, so new drugs lag far behind adult care. Sub types split the small pool yet more.

The team draws the core lessons of those two decades: which models told true, where drugs won or failed, and how picks for trials should be made. Readers in child oncology get a field guide from the largest such test run.
pmc-12175291:
Tom Pennance and a team of co-authors built a fast gene test for a parasite in its snail hosts. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with Schistosoma mansoni, a worm that needs snails to spread. True counts of snail infection guide both field and lab work. Old checks by microscope miss young infections and take too long. Their test reads DNA from snail tissue in less than ninety minutes.

The test can catch parasite DNA half an hour after a snail meets the worm. Firm reads of how well the worm takes hold come four to seven days after contact. Set targets for two snail hosts act as built in controls. Readers who track this disease get a quick, sure tool to map spread through snails.
pmc-12400391:
Radha Chauhan and her five co-authors survey, in a 2025 review, how dentists manage the soft tissue around a tooth when fitting crowns and other fixed restorations. Control of the working site matters for patient comfort and safety. It also governs the dentist's access and view, on which everything else depends.

The review stresses that a fixed restoration succeeds or fails on the accuracy of its impression. The mold must capture the prepared finish line of the supporting tooth exactly. Gum retraction techniques push the tissue aside so the finished piece can sit precisely on that line, shrinking the gap between restoration and tooth. The authors frame careful tissue handling as serving treatment quality, prevention, and appearance at once, and they look ahead to where the field's methods are heading.
pmc-12662891:
Asmaa Mahmoud Elmesiry and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five randomized trial of vitamin C infusions in newborns with sepsis after surgery. The babies were full-term and on breathing machines. Antioxidant support might ease their lung and circulation strain.

Fifty babies received standard care with either vitamin C or a placebo drip. Breathing settings and oxygen needs were tracked over five days. The vitamin group needed lower breathing pressures and less oxygen by day three. Time on the ventilator was shorter, and fewer babies needed circulation-support drugs. The blinded design strengthens this small but striking result.
pmc-12663191:
Alberto Colletti and co-authors ask what is lost when sea fans vanish from the Mediterranean floor. Forests of the gorgonian Paramuricea clavata shelter rich communities, but heat and other pressures are thinning them. The team compared the small animals and algae living inside and outside these forests at several sites in the Gulf of Naples, Italy, scoring both species counts and what each species does.

Life inside the forests was richer in species and in roles. Colonial species that feed on passing food thrived there, while short-lived light feeders dominated outside. Forests also held more variety from spot to spot, a sign of more niches on offer. The authors say the findings show how one habitat-forming species can shape whole communities, with lessons for what wider losses would mean.
pmc-12672691:
El-Helw and four co-authors make new chemical compounds and test them against mosquito larvae. The target, Culex pipiens, spreads viruses, and many standard insecticides no longer work well against it. The team built pyrazole, pyridine, and pyrimidine compounds around a benzoquinoline core.

Three compounds killed larvae best, with half-lethal doses near 180 to 235 micrograms per milliliter in lab strains. The same compounds needed higher doses against a field strain, but resistance stayed low. One pyridone compound performed worst. The authors map which structural changes help or hurt activity. They suggest more tuning could yield compounds fit for mosquito control programs.
pmc-12677991:
Hammad and five co-authors report a rare fat lump with bone grown inside it in this twenty twenty-five case report. Fat lumps are most often soft and safe, but this type grows deep in muscle and can come back. Late finds can be hard to split from a harsh fat cancer on scans.

Inside, a man in his late forties came in with a soft lump low in one leg. The lump now and then made the leg tingle and feel numb to touch. Scans showed a bright fat mass with hard lime bits in its core. Surgeons cut the lump out at its edge, and his signs cleared in full. Lab checks named it a fat lump with stray bone formed inside.
pmc-12690991:
Jin Pan and seven co-authors show that the amino acid methionine helps goat muscle fat cells make more fat, the marbling that grades meat quality. Their study came out in 2025. That methionine influences fat storage was known; the route it takes inside the cell was not.

In cultured goat fat precursor cells, moderate methionine doses boosted both cell growth and fat formation, with the best effect at a middle dose and weaker effects at higher ones. Gene readouts showed methionine switched off several fat-related genes, including one transporter gene. Forcing that gene on blocked fat formation, and methionine undid the block; silencing the gene promoted fat formation further. The authors identify that gene as methionine's likely lever on marbling.
pmc-12693191:
Maria Elena Carazzolo and co-authors published this perspective article in 2025 on mantle cell lymphoma, an aggressive form of blood cancer. Its course is shaped heavily by changes in the TP53 gene, first spotted in this disease in 1996. Patients whose tumors carry such a change tend to resist standard drug-and-antibody treatment and live shorter lives, no matter how the change is detected.

Despite that record, routine testing for the gene change at diagnosis is still rare. The authors blame the lack of standard test protocols, the cost of gene sequencing, and the weak reliability of a cheaper stain-based stand-in test. They review newer multi-layer molecular methods for reading TP53 status. They also note trials of drug-free or targeted regimens built for these patients, with promising early results. Their plea is for cheap, standard testing so care can be matched to risk.
pmc-12693991:
Oliver Vickers and co-authors build a magnetic sensing system that tracks how the parts of an artificial hip move against each other. Their study appeared in 2025. A smart implant that reports its own motion could warn surgeons about dislocation risk and odd wear. The team embedded a three-axis magnetic sensor and a small magnet into standard replacement hip parts. A robot arm swung the joint through set routines while cameras recorded the true motion.

The sensor read the parts' relative angle to within four degrees and tracked the ball slipping from its socket, a subluxation event, to within two tenths of a millimeter. The authors call it proof that magnetic sensing can ride inside a hip implant and report joint behavior continuously after surgery.
pmc-12700891:
Mozhgan RaeesiNejad, Hamed Kaveh, and Hassan Feizi test treatments that keep bell peppers fresh in cold storage, in a study from 2025. Peppers spoil fast and suffer in the cold, which cuts their market life. Two regulator sprays can slow ripening and shield tissue. The team varied when each spray was applied: before harvest, after harvest, or both.

Two pepper types went into cold storage for twenty-eight days. A nitric oxide donor sprayed before harvest worked best for both. It kept vitamin C and antioxidants high and held weight loss down. Treated fruit also kept its membranes intact and showed less chilling harm. Picking the right timing mattered as much as the spray itself. The authors offer growers a clear, cultivar-aware plan for storage.
pmc-12701591:
Christoph-Martin Ufermann leads a nine-author team describing a new Brucella bacterium isolated from tree frogs, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Brucella species cause brucellosis, a grave zoonotic disease. Atypical strains that sit outside the classical group keep emerging over time. One was found not long ago in a White's tree frog.

The frogs in this study were first checked for a fungal disease. They had come in with skin abnormalities that drew the eye. Careful microbiology work named the isolate as a member of the non-core Brucella clade. It sits close to atypical strains from recent human cases in Australia. Tests in routine use often mix such bacteria up with their relatives. That makes it hard to keep watch on them. The results back the view that amphibians may be reservoirs for emerging Brucella pathogens.
pmc-12704891:
Candasamy Sadanandane and co-authors run a large field trial of a bio-larvicide against malaria mosquitoes in Chennai, India, in two thousand twenty-five. The target, Anopheles stephensi, breeds in city water tanks. Chemical sprays raise safety worries, while bio options are few.

Three forms of the product Natular were dosed into overhead tanks. A slow-release tablet cut larva and pupa counts by over ninety percent for eight to nine weeks in all seasons, at one tablet per two hundred liters. pmc-12835591:

pmc-12836991:

pmc-12865991:

pmc-12876191:

pmc-12957991:

pmc-12960591:

They note the pathways could offer new prevention targets for diabetic patients.
pmc-13087091:
Mohammad Saeidi led a team that wrote, in two thousand twenty-six, on air trapped in the skull after a spinal drug for surgery. The ill state is pneumocephalus. pmc-13100291:
Priyanka Tomar and Neethi Varadaraja Rao review how health workers should be trained for a warming world, in this scoping review from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13130391:

pmc-13133191:
Ghulam Mustafa Nandwani, Mubeshar Hassan, Devanand Lohana, and Prasad Bollina published a study in 2026 on foreskin checks after circumcision. Many hospitals send every removed foreskin to the lab as routine. The team asked if that routine finds real disease or changes care.

pmc-13134991:

pmc-13150691:

pmc-13213191:

pmc-13216291:

Men needed higher benzodiazepine doses than women only in the younger groups, and mortality showed no sex gap at any age. The authors describe the traditional sex gap in withdrawal as narrowing.
pmc-13217991:
Israa Ahmed Qutob and a large multinational team surveyed public knowledge and attitudes toward cancer clinical trials across the Middle East and North Africa in a 2026 paper. Trials are essential for developing new cancer treatments, yet enrollment in the region stays low. The survey set out to measure what people know and how they feel about taking part.

Between March and May 2024 the team collected 5,422 usable responses through an online and in-person questionnaire, with Egypt and Bahrain supplying the largest shares. About 63.5 percent of respondents knew the basic concept of a clinical trial, but only 9.1 percent showed a high level of knowledge. Attitudes leaned negative: 83.8 percent said they were reluctant to participate, even though 77.6 percent wanted more information about trials. Employment, chronic illness, and earlier research experience were linked to better knowledge, pointing to education as a lever for raising trial participation.
pmc-13218091:
Chien-Liang Liu and co-authors report a 2026 study that trains machine learning models to flag patients whose kidney function is headed for steep decline after acute kidney injury. Many survivors of a sudden kidney injury recover unevenly, and some slide toward dialysis without clear warning signs. A tool that spots the dangerous pattern early could trigger protective care in time.

The cohort covered 88,632 adults with repeated kidney tests after discharge, drawn from more than 665,000 readings taken between 2010 and 2017. Modeling separated patients into three trajectories, and the group whose filtration rate stayed low faced the strongest link to later kidney replacement therapy. A gradient boosting model using only ten variables identified membership in that risky group with an accuracy score of 0.974. The slope of kidney function in the first three months mattered most. The authors note the data came from one health system, so outside testing is needed.
pmc-13218191:
Youn Young Choi and a Korean team present the DOMINO trial in a 2026 protocol, comparing doxycycline with a macrolide for childhood Mycoplasma pneumonia. Mycoplasma is a leading cause of pneumonia in children, and macrolide-resistant strains surged in East Asia, causing treatment failures. Doxycycline works against resistant strains, but doctors avoid it in children over tooth-staining fears.

The open-label trial runs at fourteen hospitals in South Korea and randomizes 208 children aged three to seventeen with confirmed or suspected disease. One group receives doxycycline for seven to fourteen days, the other a five-day azithromycin course. A rescue rule lets azithromycin patients switch if they fail to improve within about three days. The main outcome is how quickly fever settles in the first seventy-two hours, with treatment failure, hospital stay, and side effects tracked. Tooth colour is checked at day twenty-eight, especially in children under eight.
pmc-13220591:
Fan Pu and colleagues design a family of cancer drug candidates aimed at CDK7 in a 2026 paper. CDK7 does double duty in cancer cells, switching on the cell cycle and enabling the transcription that growth depends on, which makes blocking it attractive. The team set out to build inhibitors by locking a molecule into a rigid four-ring shape, a strategy, conformational restriction.

Their azaindole and indole-fused pyrimidine tetracycles emerged from that design, and one compound, 7a, stood out. It inhibited CDK7 at a concentration of 1.9 nanomolar, edging out a benchmark candidate, and it killed colorectal cancer cells at a similar concentration while sparing related CDK enzymes. In mice carrying colorectal tumors, 7a produced dose-dependent tumor suppression without toxicity. The authors present the compound as both a tool for probing CDK7 biology and a lead structure whose behavior needs optimizing before drug development can proceed.
pmc-13221991:
Guanjun Zhao and co-authors pool evidence on a simple blood ratio as a survival marker in cervical cancer, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The ratio divides lymphocyte counts by monocyte counts before treatment. Four databases were searched through November 2025 for studies linking that ratio to survival.

Eighteen studies with 22 cohorts and 5,127 patients qualified. Low ratios tracked with clearly worse overall and progression-free survival in both simple and adjusted analyses. The link held in younger patients, in surgical cohorts, and at lower cutoff values. The authors present the ratio as a cheap risk-stratification tool, while asking for prospective work to fix a standard cutoff.
pmc-13222591:
Xu-Qi Yu and Fei Xiao respond to a letter critiquing their cesarean delivery study, in a 2026 reply on statistical interpretation. Their work compared phenylephrine dose needs in women tilted fifteen degrees left versus lying flat during cesarean birth. Critics argued that finding no significant difference does not prove the two positions equivalent.

The authors point to near-identical effective dose estimates and heavily overlapping confidence intervals, plus a relative potency close to one. They concede the small up-and-down design widens uncertainty and individual variation adds more. Still, they hold that the primary outcome is robust for that method, and that routine tilt solely to cut vasopressor need looks unnecessary on their evidence.
pmc-13227191:
Ching-Chieh Lin and Chih-Yang Hsu report, in a case study whose journal version is dated 2026, a kidney injury from a contrast dye that was swallowed, not injected. Contrast dyes can hurt kidneys when given into blood vessels, but harm from an oral dose is exceedingly rare. Their patient, checked after bowel surgery with swallowed Urografin, showed the classic pattern. Kidney markers rose within two days, peaked around day four, and settled back within two weeks.

The risk factors explained the case. They were diabetes, recent surgery that rebuilt part of the urinary tract through the bowel wall, and a blockage. The blockage kept the dye sitting in the gut, where more of it could leak into the body. Fluids alone restored full kidney function. The authors warn that in post-surgical or high-risk patients, even swallowed dye deserves kidney checks.
pmc-13227491:
Mustapha Balarabe Idris, Bhekie Mamba, and Fuku Xolile review supercapacitors built from porous carbons made out of waste. They focus on a known gap: lab tests with a three-part setup often report far higher charge storage than real two-part devices deliver. The review explains why the simpler setup can inflate results, through low material loading, narrow voltage ranges, fluid effects, and ignored internal losses.

The authors then weigh how pore size and layout shape real device behavior. Very high surface area alone often fails, because ions still need open paths and the carbon still needs to carry current well. Layered pore designs and added atoms get a careful reappraisal, with real gains set apart from overstated ones. The review closes with design rules for electrodes that hold up under real test conditions, plus notes on scale-up, repeatability, and environmental cost.
pmc-13229391:
Jacqueline K Kueper and a large team run a 2026 prospective study of COVID-19 rebound, the return of virus or symptoms after apparent recovery. Their outpatients chose for themselves whether to take the antiviral combination nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir. Participants tested themselves frequently with supervised rapid tests and reported symptoms for fifteen days. Of 669 analysed patients, about two thirds had taken the antiviral.

Rebound over fifteen days was clearly commoner in the treated group, for both viral detection and symptoms. Initial clearance came at similar speed in both groups, but among patients who cleared, later viral and symptom rebounds were each much likelier after treatment. The study quantifies a phenomenon previously known mainly from anecdotes, informing how patients should be counselled.
pmc-13229591:
Rui Wu and colleagues test in 2026 whether a graft that includes the outer bone layer works better than plain bone graft in hip shelf surgery. Their model used rabbits with hip socket dysplasia created by six weeks of leg casting. Animals then received no surgery, a shelf operation with bone graft, or the same operation with the layered graft.

After four and eight weeks, tissue from the layered graft group formed smooth, cartilage-like tissue, while the plain graft group formed none. Gene tests showed stronger cartilage markers in the layered group, and the new tissue also held up better under pressure tests. Coverage of the socket improved in both graft groups. The layered graft also slowed damage to the joint cartilage more clearly.
pmc-13231191:
Mercedes Perez-Heredia and colleagues pilot in 2026 video dental visits for adults in rural parts of Andalusia, Spain. Reaching a dentist is hard in remote areas, and health plans see digital visits as one way to close the gap. Staff trained with practice simulations first, and visits ran on the public health system secure platforms.

Most video visits finished the case in one call, and patients rated satisfaction near the top of the scale. Nearly four in five consultations were fully resolved without travel. Older patients struggled most with the technology, and many needed family help or had connection trouble. Human support for setup, not just the platform itself, decides whether remote dentistry serves older rural patients well.
pmc-13231991:
Shuai Fan and co-authors built a microneedle patch that both treats diabetic wounds and reports on their state. Diabetic wounds stall in a hostile environment of oxidative stress, low oxygen, and infection, and dressings cannot adapt as conditions change. The patch's needles carry a catalytic nanozyme that mimics two protective enzymes, clearing reactive oxygen, releasing oxygen, and fighting bacteria at once.

Its backing layer holds a sensor that visibly tracks peroxide levels in the wound in real time. In diabetic mice, including wounds infected with drug-resistant staph, the patch sped closure and grew new blood vessels and collagen. It also shifted immune cells from an inflammatory to a healing mode through a known protective pathway. The authors call it a step toward self-managing wound care.
pmc-13232591:
Helcio Felippe and colleagues build in 2026 an information-based yardstick for comparing group-style networks called hypergraphs. Real systems often link more than two members at once, as in group chats or team projects. Older comparison tools only handle pairwise links, so group structure slips past them.

Their framework turns any chosen notion of overlap into a fair, normalized score drawn from mutual information. Scores can zoom from broad resemblance down to fine detail within one link size or across sizes. Tests on synthetic networks checked that the scores behave sensibly, and real datasets revealed clear structural patterns. Principled comparison should help sort, cluster, and flag odd group networks in fields from biology to social science.
pmc-13232791:
Kalpana Jnawali and colleagues survey in 2026 what changed for menstruating women in Achham, Nepal after the government tore down seclusion huts. Custom forced women and new mothers into rough huts during periods, a practice called Chhaupadi that is now punishable by law. Interviews covered three hundred eighty-five girls and women across six wards of one rural municipality.

Nearly everyone said the huts in their area had been demolished, and most women now stay in a separate room at home instead. About one in ten still used huts in secret, which shows the custom bending rather than ending. Under half used sanitary pads, and many burned used pads or threw them into water sources. Safer rooms are a gain, while disposal and supplies lag behind.
pmc-13233191:
Conrad Weidt and colleagues published a 2026 transplant study on letermovir, a drug that prevents cytomegalovirus infection after stem cell transplantation. The virus normally provokes strong T-cell responses that help rebuild the wider immune system, so blocking it raised a question about delayed recovery. The team compared 276 virus-positive patients across two eras of care.

Ninety-nine patients received letermovir prevention, while 177 earlier patients were managed with pre-emptive treatment after viral detection. Clinically significant infections in the first hundred days dropped sharply with letermovir. By eighteen months, overall immune reconstitution rates were similar in both groups. Some cell types recovered on different schedules, including earlier natural killer cell peaks, yet the authors conclude long-term immune rebuilding stays intact.
pmc-13233391:
Ze-Ying Wang, Qin-Bao Zhang, and Xiao-Ming Zheng published a 2026 review of comprehensive treatment for acute ischemic stroke in China. Stroke of this type, caused by a blocked brain artery, is the leading cause of death and disability among Chinese residents. The review follows the whole care chain, from pre-hospital emergency response through clot-busting drugs and artery-opening procedures.

Drawing on national guidelines, real-world practice data, and quality control reports, the authors grade the strength of evidence behind each step. They cover acute complications, secondary prevention, and rehabilitation, then weigh the system's strengths against regional imbalance in care quality. The article closes with directions for raising treatment standards nationwide, aiming to give hospitals and policymakers a shared reference.
pmc-13233491:
Benjamin Bizer and colleagues published a 2026 study of an artificial intelligence assistant for dosing tacrolimus after kidney transplantation. The drug prevents rejection, but correct doses vary widely between patients and mistakes can harm the graft. The team built TacroDose AI on GPT-4, bound by their center's dosing protocol, and tested it on 300 simulated clinical scenarios.

The first version followed the protocol in about seventy-three percent of cases, with a worrying share of serious errors. After the prompt was tightened, a version called TacroAI 2.0 reached adherence above ninety percent and cut serious errors to one percent. Consistency between repeated answers also improved. The authors frame the design as a template for safe AI prescribing support, pending real-world validation.
pmc-13233891:
Jennifer A Rode and colleagues published a 2026 ethnographic study of telepresence robots in a hybrid university class. Remote students and professors joined through mobile robots that let them move and be seen in the room. The team followed the class over time, watching the small acts of coordination, called articulation work, that make remote participation feel courteous rather than awkward.

Drawing on Murray's idea of transformation, the authors argue that success means remote users feel fully part of the distant room, not like viewers of a video feed. Grounded theory analysis extends earlier work on courtesy to explain how users overcome the glitches that block that feeling. When transformation happens, they conclude, telepresence supports a deeper embodied presence than ordinary videoconferencing.
pmc-13234291:
Yisheng Chen and a large co-author group reviewed in 2026 how treatment for bleeding inside the brain has changed since the 1960s. Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage is a severe stroke type, often tied to high blood pressure in deep brain areas. The review covers early care, drug treatment, and the biology that drives damage after the bleed. Rehabilitation receives close attention alongside medicines.

Sections weigh exercise programs, stem cell approaches, and newer physical methods for recovery and brain repair. Drug options for later phases are assessed through trials from early to late stages. The authors highlight combined care that links the brain with the rest of the body. They also note limits around dosing, timing, and differences between patients that still block routine use.
pmc-13234491:
Sama Amirkhani-Ardeh and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how tech can ease loneliness and communication problems for older hospital patients. Long-stay and acute care wards often split patients from family through limited visiting, poor mobility, and mental decline. The team searched five sources for studies printed between 2015 and 2025. Thirty-five papers met their rules across in-depth, numeric, and mixed designs.

Curbed motion, memory problems, and hospital habits all deepened isolation in the covered studies. Tools ranged from video calls and tablets to body-worn sensors for keeping contact. Video and phone tools helped many patients, yet gains varied from person to person. With patients, caregivers, and staff in designing the tools improved usability in several reports. The authors call for easy to use, well-supported digital options and stronger study designs in future work.
pmc-13234591:
Joly Alexandre and colleagues studied in 2026 how bladder filling affects the position of the rectum's surrounding tissue during radiotherapy. Their prospective comparison concerned patients with locally advanced rectal cancer receiving radiation before surgery. The tissue layer around the rectum, called the mesorectum, forms the main treatment target. Its front part sits directly against the back wall of the bladder.

Movement of the front mesorectum decreased from its upper part toward its lower part. A full bladder routine proved less reproducible from session to session than an empty bladder routine. Emptying the bladder slightly raised doses to nearby organs while staying within international limits. The authors suggest uneven safety margins around the target can improve accuracy until adaptive radiotherapy becomes routine. Their findings help clinics choose a bladder protocol for pelvic treatment.
pmc-13234791:
Waralee Ruankham and nine colleagues screen a family of synthetic sulfonamide compounds for multitarget action against Parkinson's disease. Sixteen related molecules were tested in a toxin-based cell model of the disease, in computer docking, and through network pharmacology mapping.

Four compounds stood out, shielding neuron-like cells by boosting antioxidant defenses, blocking death signaling, and steadying mitochondria. They also engaged two key enzymes and mapped onto neurotransmitter targets. Those include dopamine transporters and monoamine enzymes. With no current therapy halting Parkinson's advance, the authors name these multitarget compounds for further work as preventive and control agents.
pmc-13237691:
Ahmed M. Ashour reviewed completed drug trials for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in women in 2026, working from the ClinicalTrials.gov registry. The condition is a lasting loss of sexual desire that causes distress, and few drugs are approved for it. Nine trials met his rules, most of them randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled in premenopausal women.

Two drugs dominated the trial record: flibanserin and bremelanotide, both acting on brain pathways. Trials measured desire and distress with standard surveys, though the choice of main outcomes and how fully results were reported varied. Safety reporting was inconsistent across the registry entries. Ashour finds real progress alongside lasting gaps, and he argues that shared outcome standards would make future trials comparable.
pmc-13237791:
Joaquin Santander and a large team give a fresh way to build tiny heat-to-charge makers on chip, with a rock-like film. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six.

Small lone kits need their own power, and waste heat is rich all round. Tiny heat makers turn that heat to charge. The team joins a high-grade heat rock with chip craft, for dense packs of the makers. Their test film is a doped form of a known oxide, laid on flat chip forms. The oxide maker's yield is read in the shown span. The aim is a green, spread source for low-drain kits.
pmc-13237891:
Li and colleagues nearly switch off methane production in the rumen by combining two known blockers at low dose. Cattle belch out methane, a potent greenhouse gas, as microbes ferment their feed. Red seaweed, Asparagopsis taxiformis, blocks that process strongly, but there is not enough seaweed to feed the world's herds at standard doses.

The team cut the seaweed dose down and paired it with a synthetic blocker, 3-NOP. Together, the pair still achieved near-complete shutdown of methane formation in their tests. Using far less seaweed per animal could make a proven climate tool practical at farm scale, if the effect holds in living herds.
pmc-13237991:
Gabriel Riegner and co-authors formalized two ways in 2026 to estimate brain activity timescales from resting-state fMRI scans, and to attach honest error bars to them. Timescales describe how long each brain region integrates signals, and they map onto the brain's functional hierarchy. Older methods assumed a strict exponential decay and reported no uncertainty, which blocked proper statistical testing.

One method fits an autoregressive model in the time domain, while the other fits the decay of correlation directly. Simulations showed the time-domain approach recovers values more accurately when the model is imperfect, and it stays fast on large scans. Applied to Human Connectome Project data, the maps matched known brain organization. Workable Python code accompanies the methods.
pmc-13239491:
Ludovica Cella and colleagues published a 2026 study teaching software to outline the prostate on ultrasound. High-frequency ultrasound gives sharp prostate images. Doctors use them to guide biopsies. Outlining the gland by hand is slow. A real-time artificial intelligence tool could help.

Videos from fourteen patients trained the model. Thousands of frames were annotated by experts. A richer image-augmentation strategy beat basic training. Overlap accuracy improved by a fifth. Speed tests checked live use during procedures. The seminal vesicles were outlined too. Reliable instant outlines could steady biopsy targeting. Staging of prostate cancer may also benefit.
pmc-13239691:
Taylor H Jacobs and co-authors review surgical care for necrotizing enterocolitis, a devastating bowel disease of premature babies, in a 2026 article. The condition sparks intense intestinal inflammation that can kill bowel tissue and spread infection through the body, and no cure exists beyond supportive care and, when needed, surgery.

The review explains how clinicians judge when medicine alone is failing and an operation becomes necessary. It compares the two main approaches, opening the abdomen to remove dead bowel versus placing a drain, and stresses saving as much intestine as possible. New additions around the time of surgery that might improve survival and long-term feeding are also discussed.
pmc-13240391:
Erdal Aglar and colleagues profile pistachio varieties grafted onto a hardy local rootstock in a 2026 orchard study. Eleven genotypes growing in the Hizan district of Bitlis, Türkiye, were compared for fruit size, yield, splitting, and nutritional content at harvest in 2023.

Differences between genotypes were wide, with kernel yield share ranging from about thirteen percent to nearly forty-seven percent. Protein content topped out in the smallest-fruited genotype, while another combined the best yield with strong quality. Potassium was the most abundant mineral throughout, and one genotype led on several minerals at once. A single fatty acid, oleic-type 9-octadecenoic acid, dominated the oils. Two genotypes stood out for growers.
pmc-13240891:
Malhotra and colleagues at Yale weighed practice patterns and Medicare payments between female and male diagnostic radiologists. The analysis used federal payment data from 2017 through 2021. It covered thirty-three thousand radiologists billing Medicare fee-for-service. Women made up about a quarter of that workforce.

Female radiologists grouped in academic posts, urban areas, and very large groups. Two thirds of breast imaging specialists were women. On average, women got eighty-six percent of the total payments men did, while billing fewer cases and patients. Yet their average payment per service ran higher overall, a gap that closed within subspecialties.
pmc-13242691:
Hema Malini and co-authors ran design workshops with diabetes patients to learn what a self-care app must do to be used for years, not weeks. Their qualitative study appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. Twenty-seven adults with type 2 diabetes joined two focus group workshops and talked through their daily management. The team analyzed the discussions thematically, looking at current habits, pain points, and wishes for digital help.

Three themes emerged: what patients know and do now, the challenges that wear them down, and what they expect from an app. Participants asked for simple, interactive support covering food, physical activity, and emotional strain, not just blood sugar logging. Many diabetes apps fail because they are built without this end-user voice, the authors argue. Co-designing with patients, including honest limits about who was in the room, gives the future app a better chance of fitting real routines.
pmc-13243991:
Cherney leads a large team reporting subgroup results from twenty twenty-six on a kidney drug pair. The trial tested vicadrostat, a drug that blocks aldosterone making, alone or with empagliflozin. All patients had chronic kidney disease and were on standard care.

Five hundred eighty-six adults took part for fourteen weeks. Doses varied, and some got a placebo instead. The main measure was albumin in urine, a sign of kidney harm, plus blood pressure and kidney function. This report splits results by diabetes status and by body weight. The split helps show if the drugs work the same across patient groups, or if effects differ.
pmc-13244391:
Yuan Ji and co-authors used a national health survey to ask how sleep apnea risk lines up with men's sex hormones. Their analysis appeared in Sexual Medicine in 2026. It covered 2,218 United States adult men from the 2015-2016 national examination survey, with apnea risk scored by a prediction index and hormones measured by precise laboratory methods. Models adjusted for demographics, clinical factors, and, crucially, body weight.

Men at higher apnea risk showed lower total testosterone and lower sex hormone-binding globulin. Free testosterone, the fraction tissues can actually use, was preserved, a pattern the binding protein helps explain. Body mass strongly moderated the relationships, tying the hormone picture to obesity as much as to breathing. The authors describe a profile of low total but intact free testosterone in men flagged for apnea. Clinicians, they suggest, should check the free fraction before diagnosing hormone deficiency in such men.
pmc-13244891:
Thomas Ichim and colleagues combined two anti-aging strategies in mice, arguing each frees the other. Their study appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2026. Worn-out senescent cells poison their neighborhood with secretions that block repair. Stem cell therapy alone cannot supply young replacement cells at will. Their regimen paired SenoVax, a vaccine that hunts senescent cells, with stem cells grown from pluripotent sources. Two mouse models, chemical liver injury and drug-driven whole-body aging, received either treatment or both.

The combination outperformed each therapy alone across the board. Liver failure measures improved, tissue sections looked healthier, and the molecular signature of fast aging reversed. Aging markers fell while repair signals, including Klotho and growth factors, climbed back. The authors read this as synergy: clearing senescent cells lets transplanted stem cells actually repair. They title the claim boldly, extending healthspan and lifespan. Human translation remains distant.
pmc-13247291:
Bakshi, Tyagi, and Jaglan surveyed chronic pain patients about everyday painkillers in this 2026 Journal of Patient Experience study. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs, are sold over the counter across India and widely used for months at a time, yet patients rarely report side effects. The team questioned two hundred one long-term users at a primary care clinic in Haridwar with a structured questionnaire on knowledge, attitudes, and experienced harms.

Nearly half knew little about the drugs' risks, two thirds held negative attitudes toward them, and over half did not follow their prescriptions. Two thirds reported actual adverse effects, and most wanted to stop the drugs or switch to alternatives. The authors call for patient education and a rethink of how freely these medicines are used.
pmc-13247591:
Haruhiko Yamazaki and co-authors study radioactive iodine uptake in rarer thyroid cancers in a 2026 cohort study. These cancers spring from follicular cells but are not the common papillary type. How eagerly each subtype soaks up iodine guides whether the treatment can work.

The study covers 114 patients treated from 2005 to 2025 at one center. Subtypes ranged from quiet follicular cancers to poorly differentiated ones. Iodine uptake ran high in spread sites, reaching most lung and bone deposits and all lymph node deposits checked. Uptake stayed strong whatever the subtype or the share of solid growth patterns. The results back offering iodine therapy widely in this family.
pmc-13247791:
Yue Wu and a large team chart white matter network changes in major depression in a 2026 imaging study. White matter wires brain regions together, and its wiring pattern can be mapped from scans. How that map shifts in depression, and which genes sit behind the shifts, was unclear.

Scans from 1,154 patients and 1,026 controls across many sites fed the analysis. Patient networks showed tighter clustering and faster overall routing than control networks. Disrupted nodes clustered in big tracts like the corpus callosum and cingulum. Gene maps tied the changes to myelin making, fat metabolism, and cell stress genes. The genes stayed active across many life stages.
pmc-13248791:
Zhang, Long, and Li linked tobacco smoke exposure to spine fractures in U.S. adults, in a 2026 analysis. They used national health survey data spanning two decades and measured smoke exposure through cotinine, a nicotine breakdown product in blood, rather than self-reports. More than thirty-one thousand adults were included after full adjustment for other factors.

Heavier exposure tracked with higher fracture prevalence in a steady, dose-like pattern. People whose blood levels marked them as active smokers faced about forty-one percent higher risk than unexposed adults. Subgroup checks gave consistent results. The authors present the finding as one more reason for strong tobacco control measures.
pmc-13248891:
Catak and a large team report the first child born without working CTLA-4 genes, in a 2026 Journal of Human Immunity paper. The child developed severe autoimmunity in infancy, with swollen lymph tissue and stunted growth, and detailed testing showed chaotic T and B cell behavior.

The faulty gene made an unstable protein that cells destroyed quickly, leaving only a trace of the brake in place. Treatment with abatacept, a drug that substitutes for CTLA-4, calmed the disease and restored control. The authors link leftover protein levels to illness severity across related disorders.
pmc-13249191: Congdon reports this news and perspectives piece in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2026. It examines the biological age scores that consumer wearables now hand their users. Those scores rest on proxy signals such as sleep, heart rate, and daily activity rather than direct measures of aging. The piece asks how accurate and useful such estimates are, and where marketing runs ahead of the science behind them.
pmc-13249591:
Ryunosuke Fukushi and seven co-authors review a small set of cases of high-grade spinal sarcoma. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. These rare tumours grow in the spine, where tight space often blocks a clean cut-out. Past work ties wide removal to better local control, but cases that cannot be cut have poor results.

They split the cases into those who had surgery with spine rebuild and those who did not. Tumour size at first was much the same in both groups. Spread was common in both. The surgery group kept the power to walk far more often. A survival gap showed but was not firm, given the small count. Surgery may guard life quality, they say.
pmc-13250191:
Chronis and co-authors test two questionnaires for spotting flares in psoriatic arthritis, periods when symptoms suddenly worsen. Their 2026 RMD Open study enrolled one hundred fifty adults with the disease. Each patient completed the FLARE Questionnaire and a shorter impact questionnaire, and answered one direct question about whether they felt in a flare.

The FLARE tool proved consistent and stable when repeated one week later in fifty-one patients. It agreed moderately well with patients' own flare judgments. Even so, the shorter impact questionnaire matched flare judgments about as well in accuracy tests. The authors conclude that the shorter tool alone may be enough for defining flares in practice and in research.
pmc-13250391:
Lenay and colleagues look for throat features that flag serious sleep apnea during a routine ear, nose, and throat exam. Their 2026 Laryngoscope Investigative Otolaryngology study enrolled one hundred ten snoring patients suspected of obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome. Each patient had a standardized airway exam, recorded scope viewing, and an overnight sleep recording.

Two examiners agreed strongly on most airway features when scoring the recordings. Age over forty-five, a narrowed space behind the soft palate, and an oversized epiglottis each independently predicted moderate or severe disease. Male sex and a standard airway score also tracked with severity in simpler checks. The authors say a careful anatomical exam during ordinary consultations can pick out patients who need full sleep testing.
pmc-13250491:
Yolanda Eraso and colleagues describe the 2026 ENABLE study, which built a symptom diary for breast cancer survivors. Some grow worried when pharmacies switch them between brands of the same drug, and no tool existed to help with those concerns.

The team used a person-based design method that mixes theory, past evidence, and patient input at every stage. Planning drew on an online forum with 277 users plus interviews with patients and pharmacists. Workshops and further interviews then shaped the diary itself, with a patient advisory group consulted throughout. Patients and pharmacists both saw community pharmacies as the right setting for brand discussions. Both groups backed a diary that helps women track symptoms and judge whether a brand change caused them.
pmc-13251191:
Katz and co-authors test whether brain perfusion scans can pick which wake-up stroke patients should get clot-busting drugs. Their 2026 African Journal of Emergency Medicine study reviews fifty-seven such patients at a Johannesburg hospital between 2022 and 2024. Wake-up strokes are hard to treat because nobody knows when the blockage began.

Twenty-two patients received thrombolysis after imaging, and their stroke severity scores fell by about two thirds by discharge. Patients not treated improved less, with scores down by under half over the same period. One treated patient bled in the brain without getting worse, and deaths in the treated group were unrelated to the drug. The authors conclude perfusion imaging can guide safe treatment selection in this setting.
pmc-13251491:
Carson Halliwell and co-authors ask whether growing frailty predicts new hip or knee osteoarthritis, using Canadian aging data reported in 2026.
