The team also tested whether the link runs stronger in women, as some earlier work suggested.

Both indexes told the same story: each added health deficit raised the chance of developing lower-limb osteoarthritis over the follow-up. The increase was about five percent per deficit point in both men and women. A formal test for a sex difference came out negative for both measures, even though women carried higher frailty scores at every visit. The authors conclude that easing frailty deserves attention as a way to cut future joint disease in either sex.
pmc-13251591:
Sriram Balasubramani and a team of co-authors report a blood test study for serious liver disease, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. The team used a method that measures many proteins at once in blood plasma. They drew on a large British health cohort, plus two smaller groups at higher risk.

Twenty proteins were linked to bad liver outcomes or stiff liver tissue in all groups. A score built from five of those proteins beat two older lab scores at predicting harm. It also held up for people with obesity or diabetes. The work points to a blood test that needs no biopsy or scan.
pmc-13252791:
Kecheng Su and co-authors extend a gold-rush-inspired search algorithm in this 2026 computing paper. Optimisation problems with several goals at once, such as drone routes that must be both short and safe, need methods that balance trade-offs rather than chase one score.

Their multi-objective version adds a reference-point selection scheme and an external archive to hold the best trade-off solutions found. Against seven rival algorithms on 18 standard test problems, it led on closeness to ideal answers, spread, and quality. The top four methods then planned drone paths weighing length against obstacle threat, where the new algorithm again performed strongly. The authors claim both theory and field value.
pmc-13253091:
Chaubey and a large team show how high blood sugar loads immune cells with iron and thereby feeds tuberculosis bacteria. Their 2026 iScience study addresses the dangerous pairing of diabetes and tuberculosis, whose mechanism was poorly understood. The tuberculosis bacterium craves iron, and immune cells normally starve it by withholding the metal.

Macrophages grown in high glucose, and cells from diabetic mice, held more iron and displayed more iron-import receptors. Bacteria inside those cells also carried more iron and thrived. Removing iron with a chelator drug sharply cut bacterial loads in the lungs and spleen of diabetic mice. The authors call the effect a glucose legacy and propose iron removal as an add-on treatment.
pmc-13253191:
Halle Petrie and colleagues mine five decades of FDA reports on anaphylaxis from two common chemotherapy drugs in a 2026 evaluation. Carboplatin and paclitaxel are mainstays for gynecological cancers, and both can trigger life-threatening allergic reactions that interrupt treatment. The team catalogued reports filed between 1970 and 2023.

Paclitaxel ranked third among all drugs in fatal anaphylaxis reports, and carboplatin ranked tenth. In total anaphylaxis reports the pair placed ninth and fourteenth respectively. The share of reactions proving fatal held steady at eight to ten percent over the past decade. Roughly seven in ten reactions occurred in women, reflecting the drugs' heavy use in cancers of the ovary and womb. Reports for both agents climbed significantly over time. The authors argue the numbers justify wider readiness with desensitization programs, which let allergic patients keep receiving the drug safely.
pmc-13253991:
Hakan Baltacı and Zihni Duman comment on a heart cyst case in a 2026 letter. They discuss a report of a 21-year-old man with a hydatid cyst, a parasite-caused fluid sac, in his heart's right ventricle. He was given albendazole, a parasite drug, while planned surgery waited, and the cyst burst during two months of follow-up, causing anaphylactic shock.

The writers argue early surgery should be the main treatment, since heart cysts can burst at any time from constant heart motion. Drug therapy should support surgery, not delay it, and close scan follow-up can help time the operation, they say.
pmc-13255691:
Maria Cristina Pirosa and a multinational team report a 2026 phase Ib trial, SAKK 66/18, combining two targeted drugs in relapsed or hard-to-treat B-cell lymphoma. Copanlisib blocks the PI3K pathway while venetoclax releases a brake on cell death, and laboratory work hinted the pair might cooperate. Patients in the trial had exhausted standard options.

In practice, side effects forced dose reductions, and the study stopped early. Even so, some patients' tumors shrank, including a few complete disappearances. Tumor profiling suggested that lymphomas leaning on particular signaling routes benefited most. The authors present the trial as both a caution and a lead: combining targeted drugs needs careful dosing, and choosing patients by tumor biology may matter more than the pairing itself.
pmc-13257191:
Mihailo Mladenović and colleagues compare herbal extracts that slow starch digestion in a 2026 laboratory study. Blocking alpha-amylase, an enzyme that breaks down starch, is one route toward gentler blood sugar control. Five plants and coffee were extracted with solvents safe for food use.

Ethanol extracts blocked the enzyme most strongly, led by sage at nearly eighty percent and blueberry leaf above half. Polyphenol totals did not track blocking strength, which warns against simple assumptions. Blueberry leaf held the most polyphenols, followed by roasted coffee. Ethanol extracts also acted against Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. Sage and blueberry leaf look most promising as functional food ingredients. Further work must confirm effects in people before any diabetes claim can be made.
pmc-13257491:
Azmat Chandio leads a 2026 comparison of steel reinforcing bars from six induction furnace producers. Bars were checked against the ASTM Grade-60 standard for chemistry, structure, hardness, and pulling strength. Hot seawater corrosion tests added a durability angle across a warm temperature range.

Most bars met minimum requirements, yet quality swung widely between makers. The best producer reached high yield and tensile strengths, while the weakest samples fell low on strength and one showed worryingly low stretch before breaking. Martensite rims in some bars explained part of the strength pattern. Impurity levels and case-core structure varied as well. Construction regulators gain evidence that furnace steel needs batch vigilance. Coastal builders should weigh the corrosion findings before trusting any single supplier's certificate alone.
pmc-13257791:
Souheir M. Alia leads a 2026 randomized trial of nutrition education for people living with HIV in Dubai. Sixty-three clinic patients were split between six individual teaching sessions built on a health belief framework and usual care with a brochure. Scores for what patients knew, felt, and did, plus intake of immune-linked nutrients, were tracked over five months.

Teaching clearly improved knowledge, attitude, and practice scores compared with the control group. Food intake gains mostly failed to follow, with vitamin E the only immune nutrient rising significantly. Diet records combined frequency questionnaires with two recall days for accuracy. Public health readers in the Middle East and North Africa get a first regional trial of its kind. Knowing and doing split apart here, so future programs need shopping, cooking, and access support beside classroom lessons.
pmc-13258691:
Paweł Kwaśnicki and co-authors ask what pretty glass costs a solar panel. Building-integrated photovoltaics often hide cells behind decorative ceramic printing on the cover glass. Their 2026 study prints nine colored coatings of varied density and measures what light and power survive.

Clear reference glass passed the most light, while printed samples let through roughly sixty to eighty percent in visible bands. The coatings mainly starved the cell of current, trimming power by about a fifth to a third. Voltage barely moved across samples. Chemistry checks confirmed the prints are glassy layers fused during firing, a workable trade between looks and output.
pmc-13259191:
Diana Popescu, Ștefan Cula, and Lidia Parpală measure how 3D printing settings change the electrical behavior of conductive plastic, including how it drifts after printing. Carbon-black-filled PLA filament can print parts with built-in electrical features cheaply, but its resistivity data are process-dependent and scattered. Three temperatures, two speeds, and three layer heights were crossed, with three specimens per configuration.

Resistivity at printing time ranged narrowly across settings, and crept upward over fifty hours of post-print observation. Factorial analysis named printing temperature the dominant influence on average resistivity both fresh and aged. The study's novelty is treating repeatability and drift as first-class properties, which anyone designing printed sensors or circuits must budget for.
pmc-13259391:
Baohui Zhang and coauthors lower the working temperature of an ethanol vapor sensor through crystal design in a 2026 study. A molybdenum oxide and MXene composite was grown in one hydrothermal step. The MXene sheets seeded growth that freed new crystal faces on the oxide.

The best composite worked at one hundred twenty degrees, far below typical oxide sensors. Response to a standard ethanol dose beat the plain oxide at that temperature. Response and recovery completed within tens of seconds in tests. Selectivity against other vapors and month long stability both held up. Breath and workplace safety devices gain a cooler, lower power sensor.
pmc-13260091:
Judd Kalkhoven builds a strict theoretical meaning for athletic injury from first rules. His paper from twenty twenty-six holds that the idea is badly set out today. In daily use, the meaning mixes pain and whether a player can play in as core marks. That mix brings blur, clashes, and science that will not stay steady.

Kalkhoven uses metaphysics and a formal method for making ideas exact. Old logic and the thought of Aristotle, with its fixed natures for things, ground the new meaning. A sound meaning should help science foretell, test, and repeat results. The meanings in use now hurt all those aims, he holds. The paper splits what injury is from how it shows up. Sports science gains a firmer base to track injury the same way each time.
pmc-13260391:
Nezahat Hamiden Karaca and colleagues studied in 2026 how parents' views of risky play relate to preschoolers' motor creativity in Türkiye. Risky play involves thrills, uncertainty, and mild physical risk, and parents largely decide how much of it children get. Their study gathered data on 367 children aged four to six in public preschools.

Children who took part in more risky play showed greater motor creativity, the knack for inventing new and flexible movements. Mastery motivation, the drive to persist at hard tasks, carried part of that link. The chain from play to motivation to creativity ran stronger in boys than in girls. The authors say parents act as gatekeepers whose choices can either cramp or support bold exploration. They encourage play settings that let children test limits safely.
pmc-13260691:
Songul Bayrak and Hasan Ozdemir present a 2026 food packaging study of agarose films enriched with ascorbic acid, better known as vitamin C, for fresh-cut apples. Cut apples brown quickly through an enzyme-driven reaction, shortening shelf life. The team made films from agarose, a seaweed-derived gel, with added ascorbic acid. They confirmed the acid was incorporated into the films. They then tracked film properties and antioxidant and antimicrobial activity. Apple browning was followed over twelve days of storage.

The strongest film, the fourth formulation, had lower moisture, solubility, and swelling than plain agarose film, and higher opacity. Its radical-scavenging activity scored 90.53 percent and 94.03 percent on two standard antioxidant tests. Inhibition zones reached 30.6 millimetres against E. coli and 30.0 against Staphylococcus aureus. Coated apples kept better color and showed lower browning enzyme activity, at 79.2 units against 131.3 in controls.
pmc-13260791:
Chukwuemeka Nwokocha and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of markers for myocardial injury, meaning damage to the heart muscle. Known markers include cardiac troponins and natriuretic peptides, while newer markers such as sST2 and galectin-3 add clues about outlook. The review pulls this landscape together and notes the confounders that cloud it. Modern sensitive tests also pick up chronic rises in kidney disease, aging, and heart failure, which blurs their meaning for acute injury.

To close the gap between marker science and bedside practice, the authors propose the C.A.L.I.B.R.A.T.E. framework. Its steps integrate clinical context, assay traits, likelihood, injury mechanism, marker profiles, rule-out and rule-in thresholds, add-on tests, time kinetics, and causes with other illnesses present. They argue the future lies in combined, algorithm-driven reading of pooled data, rather than reading any single marker alone.
pmc-13260991:
Matthieu Delaye and co-authors present a 2026 study finding cancer care plans that could also cut greenhouse gas emissions, drawn from the ESMO 2025 congress. Nearly three thousand abstracts were given at that major cancer meeting. The team reviewed all of them and picked studies hinting at meaningful downstream cuts in drug use, visit counts, treatment length, or care load. Emissions for each plan were worked out using a drug carbon-footprint database and standard emission factors.

Ten abstracts were chosen, spanning prevention of disease, treatment step-down, reduced dose or length of drug therapy, marker-guided treatment choice, and non-drug measures. Several plans showed no worse or better clinical outcomes while greatly lowering treatment-related emissions. Notably, none of the chosen studies had directly assessed green impact. The authors call for adding green endpoints, as standard, to clinical research to find such win-win options.
pmc-13261091:
Siming Wei and co-authors describe a 2026 microsurgical approach to rebuilding an ear damaged by burns. Burn scars behind the ear have poor elasticity and blood supply. Scar tightening also displaces and deforms the ear. Rebuilding its complex three-dimensional shape is a major challenge in reconstructive surgery.

The team presents a single-stage strategy for cases where local skin is unsuitable and the same-side scalp fascia is not viable. They carve a framework from the patient's own rib cartilage. Coverage comes from a free flap of temporoparietal fascia taken from the opposite side of the head and connected microsurgically. The authors propose this as a valuable option for complex post-burn ear deformity. The sample presents the technique and its rationale rather than a series of patient outcomes, so results for individual patients are not reported here.
pmc-13261291:
Mohd Aizuddin Mohd Zulastri and co-authors present a 2026 case linking sinus pauses to cognitive dysfunction. Sinus node dysfunction slows the heart's natural pacemaker. Repeated drops in blood flow to the brain can cause memory lapses even without fainting. The authors argue this cause should be kept in mind for older patients with unexplained, shifting cognitive decline.

Their patient was a 66-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation and heart-structure disease. After valve surgery in 2023 she developed worsening memory lapses and brief lapses of attention rather than fainting. This pattern fit tachy-brady syndrome, where fast and slow rhythms alternate. Her thinking improved after her pacemaker implant and tuned medication. The authors advise long rhythm tracking to find such treatable causes. They note a pacemaker may restore brain blood flow and reverse symptoms.
pmc-13261691:
Estella Martin and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on microplastics moving through a Florida food web. Bottlenose dolphins in Sarasota Bay swallow microplastics, and so do the fish they eat. The team asked whether the plastics in two prey fish match those inside the dolphins, a sign of transfer through feeding.

Earlier work found plastic in every dolphin checked and in most prey fish. New samples covered dolphin stomachs and droppings plus the guts and muscle of toadfish and pinfish. Particles appeared in about eighty-three percent of dolphin samples and over ninety-six percent of both fish. Fibers dominated, and chemical tests confirmed common plastics in all three species. Pinfish carried heavier loads per gram than toadfish.
pmc-13261891:
Pengyi Yang surveyed in 2026 how computation can guide the programming of cell fate for medicine and research. Rewriting a cell's identity serves disease modeling, drug discovery, and regenerative therapy, yet the search space of factor combinations explodes quickly. His synthesis gathers methods for naming cell types, inferring gene networks, and tracing developmental paths.

Such tools have been used to rank transcription factors and small molecules worth testing in the laboratory. Newer data from single-cell and spatial profiling, plus perturbation screens and deep learning, widen the predictive reach. Yang flags real hazards: models can drift when moved between settings, hide their reasoning, or fail to reproduce. He organizes the field as an iterative design-test-learn loop, where each laboratory round feeds the next prediction. The piece aims to make protocol design more systematic.
pmc-13261991:
Mehran Falaknaz and colleagues compare gene networks in a wheat ancestor that shrugs off drought with a cousin that wilts. Aegilops tauschii donated part of bread wheat's genome and still guards drought tricks breeders want. Their 2026 systems study contrasts tolerant and sensitive lines under water shortage.

The tolerant line's network formed tight, coordinated modules, firing hormone signals, water channels, and cell wall tools together. Its promoters bristled with drought-response switches ready for action. The sensitive line's web hung loose, with hubs turned down instead. Flavonoid defenses and energy pathways completed the tolerant package, pointing breeders to concrete gene targets.
pmc-13262591:
Yixuan Zhang and colleagues calibrate a muscle relaxant so surgeons can still hear nerves complain. During scoliosis correction, motor signals warn when the spinal cord is threatened, but relaxants can mute them. Their 2026 dose-finding study enrolls twenty-six adolescents under total intravenous anesthesia.

A staircase method nudged each next patient's mivacurium infusion up or down by the previous patient's response. The team hunted the doses where half, and nearly all, patients keep reproducible signals at a set stimulus. Nobody moved unexpectedly, breathed early, or suffered airway spasm. Blood pressure and heart rate stayed calm throughout the delicate operations.
pmc-13262691:
Chengyu Peng and co-authors test tiny packages released by stem cells as a treatment for dry eye injury in a 2026 journal article. Dry eye can leave the cornea's surface cells under hyperosmotic stress, stress from overly salty tears, which kills cells and slows healing. The packages came from stem cells taken from human umbilical cords.

In lab tests, the vesicles helped human corneal surface cells grow and repair under that stress. They lowered oxidative damage, chemical harm from unstable oxygen molecules, and kept the cells' energy centers working. They also reduced two inflammation signals and quieted a pathway that drives inflammation. The authors propose the vesicles as a possible new treatment route.
pmc-13263191:
Ilan S Schwartz, Bert Gerrits van den Ende, and Ferry Hagen sequence the genomes of seven fungal type strains in a 2026 journal article. Emergomyces fungi cause severe infections, mainly in people with weakened immunity, around the world. Using long-read sequencing, the team built fresh genome assemblies for the reference strain of each of the seven species and compared them with related fungi.

The average genome measured about 33 million bases, with G and C content varying by species. Comparing average nucleotide identity, a whole-genome similarity measure, showed values of 85 to 100 percent within the set. Similarity between the twelve species tested ran lower. The work also formally validates the species descriptions for two members, Emergomyces crescens and Emergomyces soli.
pmc-13263291:
John Iceland and Jaehoon Cho examine material hardship in a 2026 study of United States households, asking why rich households report far less hardship than poor ones. They look at four forms of hardship: trouble paying bills, food hardship, housing hardship, and problems with the neighborhood itself.

Using survey data from 2021, the pair compared poor households with affluent ones, defined by income at least five times the poverty line. The factors linked to hardship looked much the same in both groups. Income gaps explained most of the bill and food gap, while wealth gaps explained most of the housing gap. A disabled member in the home was tied to hardship at both income levels.
pmc-13263491:
Wei-Hsiang Tseng and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on preventing cytomegalovirus infection after stem cell transplantation. The virus often reactivates when immunity is suppressed. The preventive drug valganciclovir can itself lower blood counts, so the team compared a low daily dose with an ultra-low dose given every other day.

Among 66 patients, early virus reactivation was somewhat more common on the ultra-low dose, about twenty percent against about fourteen, but the gap was not statistically significant. Late reactivation was rare in both groups. The important difference was tolerance: nearly half of the low-dose group had to stop treatment over low blood counts, against about seventeen percent on ultra-low dosing. Survival was similar.
pmc-13263891:
Huiying Li and colleagues hunted in 2026 for genes that drive lung cancer spread, landing on a little-studied zinc finger protein called ZNF528. Single-cell sequencing of metastatic tumors showed the epithelial compartment swollen and this gene switched on within it. Their study moved from that signal into cell and animal experiments.

Silencing the gene slowed tumor cell growth, migration, and invasion, while forcing it on sped all three. The protein pushed cells through the shape-shifting transition that precedes spread, working partly through a known partner gene. In mice, extra ZNF528 produced bigger tumors and more lung deposits. Its linked genes clustered in growth and invasion pathways, including NF-κB and MAPK routes. High expression also tracked with poor patient outlook in clinical cohorts. The authors nominate it as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13264091:
Alyssa Naimi and colleagues review septic cardiomyopathy, a brief heart weakness during severe infection, in a 2026 article asking whether it is a distinct condition. Unlike long-term structural heart disease, this weakness appears quickly through swelling, metabolic stress and small-vessel problems, and it often reverses within days. Overlap with other acute heart syndromes makes naming and diagnosis unclear.

Doctors now rely on ultrasound imaging, strain measures and blood markers, plus the overall course of illness. Heart magnetic resonance imaging may add detail on swelling and scarring. Care stays basic and focuses on treating the sepsis itself. The review proposes a broad definition and weighs targeted heart drugs that remain in doubt for routine use.
pmc-13264191:
Joshua Jacob and colleagues test one session of two-handed task practice after stroke in a 2026 study. Eleven chronic stroke survivors and ten similar adults without stroke completed hundreds of trials of a natural everyday bimanual task. Movement time, errors and coordination were measured before and after, and magnetic stimulation probed how strongly each side of the brain drives the opposite hand muscles.

Both groups finished faster without making more errors. Only the control group improved coordination between the hands. Brain excitability rose on both sides in controls, yet stroke survivors showed gains only in the less affected hemisphere pathway. Connections between hemispheres did not change. Practice helps speed quickly, but coordination after stroke may need different or longer training.
pmc-13264391:
Megan A Cimino led a large team on a 2026 paper about Velella velella, a floating sea creature known as the by-the-wind sailor. Mass strandings on the US West Coast draw crowds but still puzzle scientists. The team asked why these creatures have turned up so often in recent years.

They built one data set from 10 sources, covering life stages from larvae to adults and years from about 1900 to 2025. Strandings and at-sea sightings since 2014 were unmatched in the record. Wind patterns in years with Velella favored drift toward the coast. No clear link showed with surface fronts or El Niño, but counts of a seabird, the phalarope, may serve as a proxy sign.
pmc-13264591:
Monique Malta Francese led a 2026 clinical study of an experimental toothpaste made with titanium tetrafluoride and chitosan, a natural polymer. Fluoride in toothpaste guards teeth, and how long it stays in the mouth after brushing matters. The team measured fluoride kept in saliva and in the film that grows on teeth.

Twenty people tried four pastes in turn, including the new mix, a standard fluoride paste, and a paste with no fluoride. One hour after brushing, the new paste raised fluoride in saliva and tooth film to levels like the standard brands. At twelve hours, levels in saliva had fallen back, but fluoride in the solid tooth film stayed high. The authors say the new paste could maintain fluoride stores in the mouth.
pmc-13264891:
Kristy Lynn Hawley and colleagues describe trauma care in Morocco after a visiting delegation in a 2026 report. At Morocco's invitation, the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma assessed trauma care capacity and suggested system improvements. The visit followed rapid development and the damaging 2023 earthquake. Road injuries remain the leading cause of injury death.

The delegation met officials in Rabat and visited hospitals in Fes and Marrakech in November 2024. Gaps included weak prehospital care, no national trauma registry, and uneven hospital resources. Rehabilitation, mental health care, and child trauma services were also limited. The authors argue Morocco can now build a fairer national trauma system.
pmc-13264991:
Na Li and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of nanoparticle forms of polymyxin B, a last-resort antibiotic for drug-resistant Gram-negative infections. The drug's use is curbed by kidney damage in up to half of patients, nerve harm, and spreading resistance. Wrapping the drug in tiny carriers may fix these limits, and the review maps the field from lab to clinic.

Carriers help in three ways: gathering drug at infection sites, releasing it slowly to blunt toxic peaks, and co-delivering partners that reverse resistance. The authors list the main blocks to clinical use: thin safety proof, weak targeting, immature large-scale production, and no standard quality control. Poor penetration of bacterial biofilms is another gap. They propose fixes in materials, smart targeting, standard production, and resistance monitoring.
pmc-13265191:
Wen Ma, Ke Liu, and Lei Wang combine many machine learning algorithms with simulated gene knockouts to find diagnostic genes in stomach cancer. Their 2026 study focuses on genes tied to ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death process shaping this cancer.

Intersecting several gene sets yielded fifty-three candidate genes enriched in ferroptosis and tumour pathways. Over one hundred algorithm combinations competed to build the best early-screening model. The winning five-gene model scored extremely high accuracy in training and in two independent validation groups. Single-cell data showed where the five genes act in tumours. Computer knockouts then probed the functional networks these diagnostic genes may control downstream.
pmc-13266191:
Long Yang and co-authors, in a 2026 photonics study, examine a terahertz metamaterial design that tilts rectangular holes to break vertical mirror symmetry. Tilting excites an out-of-plane bound state in the continuum, a mode that traps light-like waves with very low loss. The work addresses a gap, since most earlier sensors used in-plane symmetry breaking instead.

Raising the tilt angle strengthened field confinement at the resonance, while also letting more radiation leak out for coupling to free space. A gold coating raised the quality factor when tilt stayed below five degrees, without hurting detection sensitivity. Readers gain a concrete route toward sensitive terahertz sensors for refractive index and thickness measurement.
pmc-13266691:
Nis-Julian H Kneusels and colleagues test polymer coatings that stabilise silicon battery anodes, published in 2026. Silicon stores much lithium but swells hugely and reacts with electrolyte, shortening cell life. Flexible polyphosphazene coatings were cross-linked onto thin silicon films. Electrochemical cycling and structural tracking compared coatings.

A partly fluorinated coating performed best, passing five hundred cycles. Efficiency improved over uncoated and alternative coated electrodes. A new software package tracked lithiation voltages during cycling. Those traces revealed stress changes and interface build-up during ageing. Coating design emerges as a practical route to longer-lived silicon anodes.
pmc-13266891:
Takumi Kawase and colleagues report in 2026 on robotic repair of a leaking mitral valve in patients aged eighty and older, at a university hospital in Osaka. They reviewed 170 robotic repairs done between 2019 and 2024, comparing sixteen octogenarians with 101 patients aged sixty-five or younger. Older patients arrived with more blood pressure problems, rhythm disorders, and lung conditions.

Extra procedures, such as tricuspid repair and rhythm surgery, were more common in the older group. Even so, valve leakage fell to mild or less in every older patient, physical performance scores held steady, and all went home without major complications. Carefully selected octogenarians, the authors conclude, can do well with robotic repair.
pmc-13267791:
Ricardo Guerrero-Hernández and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of relict fir forests in western Mexico. The Jalisco fir survives in only six populations where two mountain ranges meet. These leftover forests face ongoing threats, yet little was known about what shapes their structure. The team sampled 38 plots across about 100 kilometers, naming and measuring every woody plant and recording sixteen local factors.

Sites held from three to 25 woody species. The fir made up from about a fifth to nearly all of the stand's trunk area, sharing space with oaks and pines at some sites. Tree size patterns suggested some stands were multi-aged while others showed disturbance. Height above sea level and slope best explained fir bulk, with yearly humidity also playing a role. The authors propose listing the species as Endangered.
pmc-13267891:
Eleanor Roy and colleagues present a 2026 case report on immunotherapy in a patient with both lung cancer and arthritis. Immune checkpoint drugs free the immune system to attack cancer, but they can flare autoimmune disease. Such patients are usually shut out of trials. Their patient was a 70-year-old woman with spread non-small cell lung cancer and active rheumatoid arthritis on immune-suppressing drugs.

She first received standard chemotherapy. When the cancer grew, a care team agreed to add the checkpoint drug pembrolizumab. Scans later showed a complete response, with no visible cancer. Her arthritis did not flare. She finished two years of the drug in March 2022 and stayed in remission through August 2025. The authors argue that careful patient choice can make this treatment safe.
pmc-13268191:
Yidong Wang presents a 2026 study on assigning trains across multi-station railway hubs. Big cities increasingly have several stations, and planners must decide which trains serve which station so lines and platforms are used well while passengers travel cheaply. Wang built a math model that seeks the lowest combined cost for trains and passengers, respecting limits on stops, line capacity, station tracks, and traveler demand.

A case study on a real-style multi-station hub tested the model against two other planning scenarios. The optimized plan cut total cost slightly against one and by a few percent against the other. It also spread use of lines and station tracks more evenly. Wang closes with practical recommendations for railway departments dividing work among hub stations.
pmc-13268991:
Xin-Yi Zhang and co-authors report in 2026 a likely new subspecies of the bacterium Rickettsia felis found in Asian tiger mosquitoes caught in Qingdao, eastern China. They collected 232 mosquitoes and compared five genes of the bacterium against known relatives. Individual genes matched different named strains at high similarity, painting a mixed portrait.

When the five genes were combined into one family tree, the strains grouped closest to Rickettsia felis, an emerging human pathogen carried by fleas, mosquitoes, and booklice. The authors propose a subspecies name honoring the Laoshan area. Whether this bacterium can make people or animals sick is still unknown, a gap they flag for future work given the mosquito's wide reach and biting habits around homes.
pmc-13269591:
Serena Munteanu and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 using zebrafish to model a human heart muscle disease tied to the DSP gene. In people, shortened versions of this gene weaken the left heart chamber without widening it. Whether exercise helps or harms carriers was unclear.

Fish carrying the matching defect showed weaker heart pumping, disorganized muscle fibers, and disturbed cell signaling at rest. Moderate exercise partly restored heart function and improved endurance without raising deaths. In human carriers, those who were physically active were diagnosed younger but had no worse disease or more rhythm events. The authors suggest exercise may modify this disease rather than drive it.
pmc-13270391:
Simone Maifredi and co-authors published a case series in 2026 on three patients with Sézary syndrome, an aggressive skin T-cell lymphoma, treated at one center. A stem cell transplant from a donor is the only potentially curative option. The antibody drug mogamulizumab was used first to control disease before transplant.

The drug rapidly cleared circulating cancer cells and brought significant clinical improvement in all three patients. All then received transplants with a thiotepa-based gentler preparation. Each patient achieved early, stable full donor cell takeover and complete remission. Graft-versus-host disease, where donor cells attack the body, occurred after transplant but was manageable with standard therapy. The authors support early use of the drug as a bridge.
pmc-13271091:
Meidan Nong is lead author of a 2026 journal article on DNA methylation, chemical marks on DNA that can change gene activity, and obesity in young Chinese men. The team first sequenced blood DNA from four men with obesity and three matched controls, then checked the findings in a larger group.

The follow-up work covered 35 patients with obesity and 34 healthy controls and found fifteen differing methylation sites, two regions, and three genes. One site in the LGI1 gene showed a negative link with body mass index: as the mark rose, weight scores fell. The authors suggest methylation may play a role in obesity, with the LGI1 mark as a possible early indicator.
pmc-13272091:
Saroj Chandra Lohani and coauthors test in 2026 whether fecal microbiota transplant can calm lingering inflammation in HIV infection treated with antiretroviral drugs. Even when the virus is suppressed, gut microbe balance stays disturbed and microbes leak across the gut wall, keeping the immune system activated. The study used mice carrying a human immune system and human-like gut microbes.

One group of infected mice received the transplant alongside standard drug therapy, while controls received drugs alone. Gene and microbe sequencing compared gut communities and intestinal gene activity between groups. Transplanted mice showed shifts toward a healthier microbial mix and lower immune activation markers.
pmc-13272291:
Xue Wang and coauthors review in 2026 smart hydrogels designed to regenerate the tissues that hold teeth in place. Periodontal disease destroys ligament, cementum, and jaw bone, and a scaffold that responds to local signals could guide orderly regrowth. Hydrogels suit the role because living cells tolerate them well.

Newer gels react to internal cues such as reactive oxygen and tissue enzymes, or to outside triggers like light, heat, and electric fields. Some carry probiotics that rebalance mouth microbes, while others embed metal frameworks that release ions to fight germs and build bone. The review maps fabrication routes and the signaling pathways each design exploits.
pmc-13272591:

pmc-13272891:

pmc-13273391:

pmc-13273591:

pmc-13273691:

pmc-13274591:

pmc-13274891:

pmc-13275591:

pmc-13275791:

pmc-13276091:

pmc-13276291:

pmc-13277191:

pmc-13277391:

pmc-13277491:

pmc-13278491:

pmc-13278791:

pmc-13279391:

pmc-13279591:

pmc-13280091:

pmc-13280391:

pmc-13280591:

pmc-13280691:

pmc-13280791:

pmc-13282791:

pmc-13282891:

pmc-13282991:

pmc-13283191:

pmc-13283391:

pmc-13283591:

pmc-13284191:

pmc-13284491:

pmc-13284591:

pmc-13284691:

pmc-13284891:

pmc-13285391:

pmc-13285691:

pmc-13285991:

pmc-13286791:

pmc-13286891:

pmc-13287091:
Seth Etuah and colleagues weigh oil palm growing against household food security in Ghana in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Cash crops promise income but eat land that once fed the family, and the debate over which force wins had gone unresolved locally. Surveys covered 416 farm households in the Ashanti and Central regions, 201 of them oil palm producers. Interviews and focus groups backed the numbers, and two statistical methods corrected for who chooses to grow palm.

Dietary diversity improved for palm growers in both regions, a clear gain. Food access, though, split by place: it improved in the Central Region while worsening in Ashanti. Land shifted under palm also shrank the ground left for food crops everywhere. The authors read the mixed verdict as a warning against one-size policy, since local conditions decide whether the cash crop feeds or starves the household.
pmc-13287291:
Shiying Qu and co-authors collected 96 healthy pea plants in 2026 from eight fields near Palencia in Spain. They grew out the bacteria and fungi living inside the roots, after nodules were removed. Each microbe was identified from marker gene reads, and community patterns were matched against soil and weather measures.

Bacteria varied more between fields than fungi did. A few bacterial genera turned up almost everywhere, while Fusarium led the fungi. Soil silt share tracked bacterial patterns strongly. Exchangeable magnesium tracked fungal patterns. Weather showed no clear link at that scale. The authors propose the catalogue as groundwork for testing single strains in the field.
pmc-13287591:
Yulin Zou and colleagues interviewed clinical experts in China in 2026 about why people with lupus often struggle to take their medicines as planned. Transcripts were coded into 38 themes, split between eighteen factors that help and twenty that hinder, across patient, illness, treatment, care, and money domains.

Every expert named relief of symptoms as a help. Complex dosing, harsh side effects, and high cost were the most shared barriers. Well-managed side effects and personal teaching were the leading helps. Care-side factors held most helps, while treatment-side factors held most barriers. The authors propose simpler regimens, steady follow-up, and supportive policy together.
pmc-13288491:
Hao Liu and colleagues offer a 2026 perspective on light-emitting materials that contain no heavy metals. Their focus is organic compounds that glow at room temperature through phosphorescence, and how far those materials have come toward matching metal-based emitters inside organic light-emitting diodes, or OLEDs.

Recent design work has lifted the electroluminescence of these organic materials close to that of older metal complexes, the authors note. They also discuss using the materials as sensitizers that feed energy to narrow-spectrum multi-resonance emitters, a pairing aimed at sharper, high-resolution displays. The outlook they sketch is meant to guide cheaper, metal-free OLED development.
pmc-13288691:
Surakshya Pokharel and colleagues describe a practical way to design an intervention bundle with the doctors who will use it, in a 2026 Canadian methods paper. Their target was over-ordering of laboratory tests in hospitals, and their material came from virtual audit and feedback sessions held in four Calgary hospitals during 2021.

Twelve sessions involved 83 family and internal medicine physicians, who named obstacles and ideas, mapped them along a patient journey, and ranked them with a matrix. Barriers were sorted with the Theoretical Domains Framework, and ideas were matched to behavior change techniques. The resulting bundle combined policy changes, order-system tweaks, education, and audit with feedback, tailored around stable patients.
pmc-13289091:
Krysta Andrews and colleagues present a 2026 review plan on parenting and autism. The review asks how parenting shapes child symptoms. Autistic children often face high emotional strain. Their behavior can also be hard to manage. Past studies give mixed answers.

The team will search five databases. Studies must cover children aged 6 to 17. All must have a clear autism diagnosis. Each must measure parenting in some way. Inner and outer symptoms are the main outcomes. Two reviewers will screen each study. Bias will be graded with two tools. Results will be pooled with a random model. Checks will probe why studies differ.
pmc-13289191:
Chayanit Kongsuk and colleagues study mental health checks in teens with lupus in 2026. Checks ran at set visits six to twelve months apart. It held 120 teens aged 12 to 18. Most were girls, at 90.5 percent. Surveys tapped low mood, worry, and sleep.

Of the group, 117 gave full paired data. Low mood scores fell at the second visit. Worry scores also fell a bit. Sleep quality scores improved too. Fatigue and pain scores stayed flat. Disease activity stayed low throughout. More teens hit remission at visit two. Mood gains did not track disease scores closely.
pmc-13289291:
Chang Ma headed a 2026 modeling study on whether promoting daily oral self-care pays off in China. Mouth diseases affect nearly half the world and cost a great deal, yet proof on prevention value in China was thin. The team built the China Oral Health Model for people aged 12 or older to test policy options.

The model tracks yearly moves between healthy teeth, cavities, gum disease, tooth loss, and no teeth, using national survey data from 2015 to 2017. Three habits were tested: brushing twice a day, flossing, and using mouthwash, each modeled as lowering disease starts and worsening. Costs came from market prices, and views covered urban and rural groups. Results frame lifetime tooth loss avoided against program cost for planners.
pmc-13290091:
A drug that blocks the mitotic motor protein KIF18A stopped the growth of chromosomally unstable osteosarcoma cells in a 2026 study by Qiang Yan and co-authors. Osteosarcoma survival has barely improved in decades, so the team looked for a weakness tied to the unstable chromosomes common in this bone cancer.

Working with whole-genome-doubled clones from the SJSA1 cell line plus the U2OS and MG63 lines, they removed KIF18A or applied the inhibitor AM-1882. Both approaches wrecked spindle assembly, triggered the spindle assembly checkpoint, and cut cell growth; in mice, AM-1882 also shrank tumors without the toxicity seen with standard chemotherapy. The results mark KIF18A as a promising target for this cancer.
pmc-13290191:
Elizabeth M Buie and co-authors track appendix removal rates across rich countries in a 2026 population study. Data came from regions of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development between 2000 and 2023. The team computed yearly change in operations per hundred thousand people. They also compared rates just before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Statistical tests hunted for turning points in each region's trend.

Pooled rates fell by about three quarters of a percent per year across the period. Twenty-four regions declined clearly, seven rose, and nine held steady. Thirty regions showed at least one turning point, and seventeen reversed direction after theirs. Pandemic years brought an extra drop of about six percent against the pre-pandemic baseline. The authors credit differences in access, imaging habits, and antibiotic-first care for the spread. They urge continued tracking to plan surgical services wisely.
pmc-13290391:
A growth factor speeds the sheet-like crawl of skin cells that closes wounds, Jonah Spencer and colleagues show in 2026. Their study asks how heparin-bound epidermal growth factor, HB-EGF, changes the forces behind collective migration in a wound-healing assay.

Using traction force microscopy on an epithelial monolayer, the team found that HB-EGF made cells move faster and in straighter, better coordinated paths, an effect that depended on phospholipase C signaling. Forces rose both at the sheet's edge and inside it. A theoretical model matched to the data suggested that extra propulsive force in both places explains the faster advance, and images of actin fibers and adhesion sites backed the model. The work ties a chemical signal to the physical push of healing.
pmc-13290791:
Some cleft risk genes may act by steering DNA methylation, A. L. Petrin and colleagues show in a genetic study from 2026. Most risk variants for nonsyndromic orofacial clefts sit in non-coding DNA, so the team tested whether they change methylation at regulatory sites, the so-called meQTL mechanism.

Screening ten cleft-linked variants in 409 cases and 456 controls against genome-wide methylation profiles flagged 23 candidate links, nine of which held up in 358 cleft-discordant sibling pairs. The strongest tied a variant near the MYC gene region to methylation at a developmental enhancer, with effects concentrated in saliva-derived tissue. Single methylation sites did not fully explain the genetic risk, though. Petrin and colleagues infer coordinated epigenetic changes across regions, with most effects peaking in childhood, as the likelier route from variant to cleft.
pmc-13290891:
Snubbing friends for a phone, phubbing, grows across early adolescence but along four distinct paths, Jun Zhao and Shoufeng Li report in a longitudinal study from 2026. They followed 1,488 middle school students in Jiangxi Province, China, over three waves about four months apart. The question: how does the habit develop, and does total phone time predict its course?

On average phubbing rose significantly, yet mixture modeling split students into low-and-rising, medium-and-stable, high-and-declining, and very-high-and-sharply-declining groups. Baseline phone time predicted where a student started. Heavier users began with more phubbing and were likelier to land in high-starting groups. But their phubbing then grew more slowly or fell. Zhao and Li call phone time a useful but limited marker, and argue prevention should be tailored to trajectory, not one-size-fits-all.
pmc-13291491:
One carrier both brings copper in and sends it out of mitochondria. Mohammad Zulkifli leads a 2026 study of the carrier SLC25A3. Copper is vital for the cell’s main breathing enzyme. How copper exits the inner matrix was a long gap.

A copper drug that dumps its load in the matrix gave the clue. Cells without the carrier lost copper and enzyme power. Feeding copper past the missing carrier did not rescue the enzyme. Copper instead piled up and triggered a toxic death. Tests in bacteria confirmed the carrier can export copper. It thus guards both enzyme building and cell safety.
pmc-13292391: A 2026 correction adds a missing statement to two 2025 Cochrane Evidence Synthesis and Methods articles about evidence searches. One proposed borrowing the case report format to describe messy search strategies, using humanitarian work as its example. The other set out a process model for finding trial studies for evidence reviews. Both appeared without a Conflicts of Interest statement, omitted by the publisher Wiley in error. The added statement declares the authors have no conflicts of interest, and the articles' content and conclusions stand unchanged. Only the correction notice is available here.
pmc-13292591:
Qiwen Huang, Fangyuan Yang, Siyu Wu, and Peirong Jiao clone a pigeon antiviral protein and test its strength, in a 2026 study. Interferon lambda guards epithelial surfaces against viruses, yet its pigeon version was uncharacterized. The team read the gene's coding stretch at 561 bases, making a 186-amino-acid protein. Its sequence matched the shearwater version most closely and the human one least. Bacteria then manufactured the protein for testing.

The lab-made protein fought two viruses in step with dose: vesicular stomatitis virus and H9N2 bird flu. Reporter tests showed it switching on antiviral defense genes through the expected signaling promoter. Messenger levels of three defense genes, Mx, OAS, and PKR, also climbed with dose in chicken cells. The authors suggest the protein could become a treatment for avian viral diseases. Poultry lack many targeted antivirals, so an innate immune drug candidate draws interest.
pmc-13292691:
Yusuf Adewale Adejola, with co-authors, tests a 2026 forecasting idea for free-range egg farms: can machine learning trained on other farms predict a flock's laying rate and spot slump days early? Production and weather records from four commercial farms covered 106 flocks and 35,346 flock-days. Three random forest models were built, one on the target farm alone, one on the other three farms, and one on everything.

Judged on the held-out farm, the home-grown model reached a median AUC of 0.86 with an error of 2.8 in laying-rate points. The foreign-farm model classified slightly better at 0.89 but regressed worse, with error near 4.98 in the results. Pooling all data flipped the pattern again, best regression, weakest classification. The authors conclude cross-farm prediction genuinely works, though more data does not automatically mean better forecasts.
pmc-13292991:
Chaobao Liu and co-authors untangle, in a 2026 mouse study, how oxytocin brain cells drive different defenses when mice face social attack. The same hormone system can push fighting back or running away, and the wiring behind that split was unclear.

Social defeat switched on oxytocin cells in a brain hub called the paraventricular nucleus. Two output paths behaved oppositely during attack: one toward a reward area quieted, while one toward the amygdala fired up. Separate input circuits steered fight-back versus escape and later social avoidance. Cutting the hormone receptor in each target area cut the matching defense, showing distinct circuits for each act.
pmc-13293391:
Yanni Huang and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, whether good childhood experiences lift well-being in university students through stronger resilience. Students in Yunnan Province, China, face study and job strain that can drag down life satisfaction.

A total of 1,104 students at four universities filled scales on positive childhood experiences, resilience, and well-being. Good early experiences linked to higher well-being both directly and partly through resilience, which carried part of the effect. Building resilience in school settings may thus help well-being take root. The authors warn that a single-region sample limits how far the findings stretch.
pmc-13293691:
Leo Kar Lok Lai and a team of co-authors shared their center's record of valve in ring work on the tricuspid valve. Their series, from twenty twenty-six, deals with balloon grown valves set inside old repair rings. Two paths in were used: through the neck vein and through the groin vein. The rings were of the incomplete kind. The series is small and from one center.

Success ran higher by the neck path than by the groin path. No access harm came with the neck path, while the groin path had one such case. Leaks round the valve were less oft by the neck path too. Ring type swayed leak rates as well. Readers who do valve work get a first head to head of paths.
pmc-13293891:
Thomas Krumpen and colleagues link Arctic warming to deep-sea change in a 2026 study of Fram Strait. As glaciers break apart faster, icebergs carry more rocks and debris that later drop to the seafloor, creating hard patches where animals can settle. Seafloor surveys, four decades of ship records, backtracking, and a transport model were combined.

Dropstone density and patchiness rose locally, and iceberg sightings jumped in the early 2000s. Most bergs traced to major outlet glaciers in northeast Greenland and the Russian High Arctic. A more mobile sea ice cover also carried bergs farther. The shift may remake habitats and raise hazards as Arctic shipping grows.
pmc-13293991:
David W. J. McQuarrie and Matthias Soller detail the gel shift assay for RNA-protein binding in a 2026 step-by-step protocol. When a protein grips RNA, the pair moves more slowly through a gel, revealing strength and binding style. Their example uses recombinant ELAV, a classic RNA-binding protein made in E. coli.

Guidance covers making and purifying radioactive RNA by in vitro transcription, preparing protein, and setting serial dilutions in a microtiter plate for clean binding curves. Native low-crosslinked gels separate free RNA from complexes at high resolution. Troubleshooting notes and figures aim to make the old but powerful method reproducible for new labs.
pmc-13294291:
Aleixandre Brian Duche-Pérez and colleagues argue in a 2026 perspective that patient-side barriers are the weak link in cancer pain care. Strong guidelines and drugs exist, yet pain stays poorly controlled. Fears about addiction and side effects, fatalistic beliefs, weak pain reporting, low adherence, and thin knowledge are often brushed aside as side issues rather than core drivers.

Barriers grow from personal beliefs meeting culture, emotion, poor communication, and system limits, the authors contend. Routine barrier screening, culturally aware talk, tailored teaching, supported self-care, and follow-up audits should become standard. Services should grade understanding and adherence, not pain scores alone.
pmc-13294491:
Magdalena Binder and a large team randomize coaching styles for app-based movement therapy in spine arthritis for a 2026 trial. Spondyloarthritis stiffens the back, and exercise helps, but app users quit often. Seventy-eight patients, mean age 51 years and 68% female, exercised 2–3 times weekly for 6 months with personal coaching, AI video coaching, or no coaching, with spine mobility and pain tracked.

Every group improved mobility clearly by 3 months, with index drops of 0.6 to 0.7 points in the reported ranges, and pain fell substantially in all arms. Coaching type did not separate outcomes in the early results shown. Structured digital exercise itself carries much of the benefit.
pmc-13294991:
Yupeng Shi and co-authors review how chemists design magnetic resonance probes that can picture amyloid-beta in the living brain, in a 2026 survey. Amyloid-beta clumps mark Alzheimer's disease, appearing as single strands, small clusters, fibers, and plaques with different toxicities. Seeing which forms are present, early and without radiation, could aid diagnosis and drug testing. A probe needs three parts working together: a hand that grips amyloid, a signal unit, and a way across the blood-brain barrier.

The review compares grip molecules from peptide mimics to antibody fragments, and signal units based on gadolinium, manganese, iron oxide particles, or fluorine. Binding changes how water protons relax or shifts exchange-based signals, turning grip into contrast. Performance in transgenic mouse models is weighed, with sensitivity, specificity, and safety flagged as open problems. Future probes may target the small toxic clusters or combine imaging with treatment.
pmc-13295091:
Matthijs Vynck and colleagues present tougher data-cleaning methods for metabolomics in a 2026 article. Long instrument runs drift and form batches, and a few wild quality samples can spoil standard corrections. Their three new methods down-weight or absorb such outliers instead of letting them bend results.

Two methods use flexible additive models that can also weight samples and judge how well control samples represent a run. All three sit inside a free software package with plots for checking performance and support for parallel computing. In simulated and real datasets, the robust methods restored signals better and cut drift, with one variant performing best overall.
pmc-13295491:
Barlina Konwar and Kwang-sun Kim review programmable gut care for type 2 diabetes in a 2026 article. Diabetes care usually treats the condition as a hormone problem alone, ignoring the gut microbes that help steer metabolism. Artificial intelligence and multi-layer biological data may close that communication gap.

Virtual patient models, called digital twins, can forecast how designed teams of helpful microbes will behave during treatment. Combined data layers feed those predictions and allow therapy to adjust in near real time. The authors present the gut as a system that can be engineered precisely, moving care away from one-size plans toward personal, adaptive control.
pmc-13295691:
Jianxing Li and colleagues sharpen a computer vision model for spotting cyanobacteria in a 2026 study. These blue-green organisms can poison water, yet naming them under the microscope is slow expert work. Busy backgrounds, mixed sizes, and uneven sample quality make automatic detection tricky.

An existing detection model was upgraded to pull features more efficiently, merge views across scales, and place finds more reliably. On a reorganised public set covering seven cyanobacteria types, the tuned model scored best on average detection across the groups. It also stayed small and fast enough for real use, supporting automated water checks and earlier pollution warnings.
pmc-13295791:
Luuk van Esveld and colleagues compare modern arthritis drugs by patient-felt outcomes in a 2026 review and network analysis. Head-to-head proof on pain, tiredness, activity limits, and mental health was missing across drug classes. Trials were gathered with machine learning help and pooled through network methods.

Ninety-nine studies entered the pool, though agreement between them varied from tight to very loose. Two drug classes trimmed activity limits slightly more than the standard class, while rituximab ranked best overall across felt outcomes. Earlier disease and worse starting scores predicted bigger felt gains. The results help doctors match drug choice to the symptoms patients care about most.
pmc-13295991:
Han Zhang and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol on Baduanjin, a gentle mind-body exercise, for fall risk in older adults with knee osteoarthritis. Such patients fall more often and get hurt worse, and the exercise helps balance, but how it works in the brain is unclear.

Seventy-two patients will be split between Baduanjin, brisk walking and health talks for twelve weeks. Fall-risk questionnaires lead the measures, with balance, walking, leg strength and brain scans alongside. Scans focus on the balance network in the brain. Follow-ups continue twelve weeks past training to see if gains hold.
pmc-13296091:
Raúl Cobo and co-authors examine, in 2026, the eyes and retinas of the common kestrel, a small falcon that hunts by sight. Kestrels carry two sharp-vision pits in each retina, and the team map their structure and the light-sensing cells inside them.

Both pits were packed with colour-vision cells and held few or no rod cells used for dim light. Cell makeup varied across the retina in ways matching a daylight hunter's needs. The authors say the detailed anatomy clarifies how raptors process visual information and supports comparisons with other birds of prey.
pmc-13296891:
Arijit Patra and co-authors lay out, in 2026, a standard build-and-run guide for a prism-based microscope that watches single molecules glow and trade energy. Such measurements reveal how biomolecules bend and move, but results hinge on exact alignment and calibration that guidance rarely covers fully.

Their framework spans the full optical layout for two-colour work, alignment checks, surface preparation, flow control and light-protection tricks for long sessions. Benchmarks for signal quality, fading and colour bleed set clear operating limits. A model DNA system demonstrates the pipeline, from recording through to motion analysis.
pmc-13297291:
Yi-Lin Guo and colleagues test an iris rhizome extract used in Chinese medicine against inflammation in a 2026 study. The plant, Chuan She Gan, traditionally treats inflammation-related disorders. Its alcohol extract was profiled chemically, then applied to immune cells provoked with a bacterial toxin.

Four characteristic plant compounds were identified in the extract. Treated macrophages made less nitric oxide and fewer inflammatory messengers, in step with the dose given. The effect ran through quieting the NF-kappaB pathway while a neighbouring pathway stayed largely untouched. In poisoned mice, one oral dose lowered several inflammatory markers in the blood. The work supplies a pharmacological basis for the traditional use.
pmc-13297791:
Thi Thu Ha Le and colleagues link picky eating to stunting among toddlers of ethnic minority families in mountainous northern Vietnam, in a 2026 study. Stunting, being too short for one's age, stays common in these communities. Three hundred forty-one children aged twelve to thirty-five months in two communes were measured, and caregivers described feeding habits.

Nearly two children in five were picky eaters, and one in four was stunted. Picky eating more than tripled the odds of stunting after other factors were counted, and snacking before main meals raised the odds as well. Zinc shortage was common in blood tests but lost its link once other factors entered. Feeding behaviour belongs on the programme agenda, the authors argue.
pmc-13298191:
Balagangadhar R. Totapally introduces a 2026 special issue on current challenges in paediatric critical care medicine. Ten papers from several countries reflect a field changed by better technology, organ support, and cancer therapy, with children whose care needs keep growing more complex. Persistent problems include sepsis, airway emergencies, trauma, and acute brain crises.

Other papers cover anaphylaxis spotting in Türkiye, drug poisoning in Romania, foreign body aspiration in Bulgaria, septic heart dysfunction, critically ill children with cancer in Saudi Arabia, and low platelet counts. Emerging priorities named include transport systems, advance care planning, and chronic complex conditions. Totapally frames timely spotting and joined-up systems as the recurring lessons.
pmc-13298391:
Feeding egg to allergic toddlers in tiny, growing doses freed nearly all of them from the allergy within six months, report Silvia Karina Carrión Sari and colleagues in a 2026 prospective study. Thirty-one children under two with IgE-mediated egg allergy received oral immunotherapy using pasteurized liquid egg white.

At six months, 93.5% could eat every form of egg, including raw, without reacting, compared with none of twelve historical controls on avoidance diets. Reactions during dose build-up were common at 77.4% but mild, and allergy blood markers and skin tests shifted toward tolerance. The authors back early treatment in specialist centers as an alternative to strict avoidance.
pmc-13299091:
Turmeric's active compound shielded heart cells from sugar damage in a dish, report ZeYue Xu and co-authors in a 2026 cell study. They grew primary heart muscle cells in high glucose, a stand-in for diabetic injury, and tested whether curcumin could limit the harm.

Curcumin raised cell survival and antioxidant enzyme activity, steadied mitochondrial voltage, cut reactive oxygen production, and reduced cell death. Protein measurements fit two protective pathways switching on: Nrf2, which commands antioxidant defenses, and PI3K/AKT survival signaling. The survival protein Bcl-2 rose while the death promoter Bax fell. The authors offer the mechanism as a foundation for studying curcumin in diabetic heart disease.
pmc-13300291:
L Panchetti and co-authors report long-term results, published in 2026, from the VOMALC-PeAF registry on first ablation for persistent atrial fibrillation. Vein isolation alone gives modest lasting success in this group. One plan adds ethanol infusion into the vein of Marshall plus lines across the atrium. The registry, drawn from many centers, matched 151 patients who got the added plan against 75 who got isolation alone.

After a median follow-up of twenty-two months, freedom from atrial arrhythmias off drugs reached 82 percent with the added plan, against 47 percent with isolation alone. A complete block across the mitral isthmus strongly pointed to success, while long-standing disease pointed to return of the rhythm problem. Repeat ablation was far less common after the added plan, at under five percent against about twenty-seven percent. Safety was much the same in both groups, with few major problems in either.
pmc-13300391:
A Schade and co-authors share very early experience, published in 2026, with a dual-energy ablation catheter for ventricular rhythm problems. The catheter switches between radiofrequency and pulsed field energy during point-by-point treatment, and lab work suggests combining both can deepen lesions. The series covered eleven patients having repeat ablation for extra beats or ventricular tachycardia, or with substrate buried inside the heart wall.

Safety rules shaped the work: nitroglycerine preceded energy near coronary vessels, and pulsed field delivery was avoided close to valves and the conduction system. In the ventricular tachycardia cases, complete success, meaning no rhythm could be triggered afterward, was reached in five of seven patients. One prolonged triggered rhythm during pulsed field delivery and one heart block in a septal case were noted. Six-month follow-up was still pending, and the authors call for larger cohorts.
pmc-13301391:
H Wang, Y Zhang, and D Benditt test a fibrosis threshold on heart scans as a warning sign for ablation failure in a 2026 cohort study. Sixty-six patients with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation had the back wall of the left atrium imaged by a PET and MR technique before vein isolation. They wore week long rhythm monitors across twelve months. The dividing line was whether scar covered more than a quarter of that wall.

Above the line, recurrence struck about fifty-seven percent of patients within a year, against only seven percent below it, and the gap held within the persistent subgroup too. Adjusted models kept heavy fibrosis an independent predictor, raising the odds seven to eleven fold. Adding the scan measure discriminated better than clinical factors alone. The authors propose the quarter wall cutoff as a triage tool: patients past it may need more than standard isolation.
pmc-13301891:
Two disabled enzymes that normally chew fungal walls became the bait in a fast fungus test, Wei Yuan and colleagues report in a 2026 assay study. Their sandwich ELISA targets beta-1,3- and beta-1,6-glucans, shared bricks of fungal cell walls, using catalytically dead glucanase mutants as capture tools. Pre-coated plates compress the whole workflow to about forty minutes.

The assay out-detected standard ITS-based PCR for two test yeasts under study conditions, and it flagged a wide sweep of yeasts and molds. In a first clinical check, all twenty-one dermatophyte-positive samples lit up, while twenty negative samples stayed dark. The authors offer the low-cost platform as a broad screening step before slower confirmatory testing.
pmc-13302091:
Nan Xu and co-authors pool evidence in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on blood flow restriction training after knee ligament reconstruction. The method pairs light exercise with a cuff that partly limits blood flow, aiming to rebuild thigh muscle without heavy loads that healing tissue cannot bear. Earlier trials disagreed on how much it helps.

Seventeen studies with 643 participants were found, and twelve fed the pooled analysis. Training added to normal rehabilitation improved thigh strength with moderate-certainty evidence, and functional recovery also improved, though that evidence was weaker and more varied. No clear benefit appeared for balance or pain, and no serious harms were reported. Pressures above eighty percent of full occlusion looked stronger, a point the authors call exploratory.
pmc-13303091:
Tara R. Hawkinson and co-authors identify, in a 2026 study, excessive sugar-tagging of proteins as a driver of Alzheimer's disease rather than a bystander. Such tags, called glycans, decorate proteins and guide their behaviour in the brain. The team combined chemical mapping of mouse and human tissue with isotope tracing of tag turnover.

Brains with Alzheimer's showed built-up glycosylation fuelled by faster tag production, a pattern shared across models and post-mortem samples. Dialling down tag-building enzymes improved cognition in diseased mice, while feeding the supplement glucosamine made it worse. Health records echoed the warning: patients taking glucosamine declined faster and survived less well. The authors propose glycan metabolism as a treatment target.
pmc-13303591:
Andrea Bloise heads a 2026 study of asbestos that occurs naturally in rocks near the Pollino Massif in Basilicata, southern Italy. Villages in the area have recorded 124 mesothelioma cases, raising concern about fibers that were never mined for sale.

Tremolite asbestos samples from local outcrops were examined with electron microscopes, X-ray methods, and heat tests. About half of each sample held long, very thin fibers of the size class viewed as most cancer-linked. Iron sat within the fiber structure, a feature tied to harm in the body. The detailed profiles give health officials a firmer base for judging local risk.
pmc-13303891:
Şamil Şahin and co-authors track, in a 2026 study, how the nose tip settles during the year after rhinoplasty done with a new pentagonal support graft. Tip rotation and projection drift as swelling fades and scars mature, unsettling patients and surgeons. Standardised photographs at surgery, six months, and twelve months captured the movement.

Both measures, the lip-to-nose angle for rotation and a standard ratio for projection, fell significantly over the year. Most of the change happened inside the first six months, with later shifts smaller and slower. Skin thickness made no difference to the late pattern in this series. The authors read the curve as normal healing behaviour of the graft design, pending head-to-head prospective comparisons.
pmc-13304791:
Sylvie Bambara, Marie Claire Isingizwe, and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, sewage monitoring for gut and lung pathogens across Africa, with Rwanda in focus. Clinic reporting misses many infections where labs are scarce, yet everyone connected to a sewer sheds evidence daily. Sewage tracking promises community-level early warning at modest cost.

Screening over twelve hundred records narrowed the pool to full-text studies with pathogen-specific sewage data. The synthesis finds sewage testing catches both sick and silent infections and can flag hotspots before clinics notice them. Uneven sampling, virus decay in warm effluent, and differing lab workflows remain the main obstacles. The authors urge investment in lab capacity and shared protocols so cities like Kigali can fold sewage signals into routine disease watch.
pmc-13306391:
Kacper Łoś reviewed rest brain wave tests as signs of schizophrenia in a 2026 review. Early care helps, and cheap brain wave tests could aid if clear signs split sick people from healthy ones.

Searches from 2008 on three data banks cut 467 hits to 19 studies with 1242 sick people in the final set. Work with smart AI tools and task tests was set aside to keep clinic ready checks in focus. The team weighs how firm the wave signs are for real world use in care. The team says firm wave signs could one day cut time to first care for sick people.
pmc-13306991:
Niall Leahy reported heart pain from a germ called Toxoplasma in a healthy young man in a 2026 case note. The germ can hit heart muscle and its sack at once, but this is rare and most seen when immune strength is low.

Chest pain came after a flu like ill spell, and blood tests showed heart harm with no weak pump in the reported checks. Germ tests fit a fresh first catch, while tests for germs of the virus kind stayed clear. Drugs for swelling eased pain fast, and a heart scan later showed past muscle swelling.
pmc-13307191:
Alberto Gómez-Moreno mapped tools and programmes for activity in older adults in a 2026 scoping review. Work followed standard scoping guidance across community, clinic and residential settings for studies from 2019 to 2026 on adults aged sixty and over.

Fifty-one studies entered, using twenty different activity instruments in reported counts, most of them validated. Samples and goals varied widely, with most work on people aged 65 or more in the United States and Canada.
