pmc-13327491:
Timothy L Jackson and a large trial team report extended follow-up from the STAR trial in a 2026 article. The trial tested one-off stereotactic radiotherapy against a sham procedure for wet age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of sight loss in older adults. It ran in 30 NHS hospitals across the United Kingdom.

In total 411 people aged at least 50 with long-standing, previously treated disease took part, with 274 given the real 16 Gray treatment and 137 given the sham. After two years of monthly study visits, care returned to local practice while masking stayed in place, and data were gathered again at years three and four. The later visits weighed injection counts, letter-chart vision, safety, and costs.
pmc-13327991:
Yan Yang, Jianhua Shi, and Xiaoying Gu study how family functioning shapes self-care in heart failure couples in a 2026 survey. They enrolled 212 patients with chronic heart failure and their spouses at a hospital in Nantong, measuring family cohesion, symptom perception, spousal caregiving, and patient self-care with standard scales. A partner-effects model separated each person's influence on self and spouse.

Patients scored their self-care at 155.73 on average on the index used, with symptom management the weakest part. Family function helped self-care directly and also through two routes, sharper symptom perception and stronger spousal care, with the spouse's family view carrying its own direct share of 40.0 percent in the partner analysis. Treating the couple, not the patient alone, is the lesson.
pmc-13329091:
Tomohiko Doigami and colleagues evaluated a novel cotton-like bone graft for jawbone defects after cyst removal. Their 2026 clinical study tested a composite of beta-tricalcium phosphate, poly-L-lactic acid, and polyglycolic acid, prized for handling, three-dimensional shapeability, and bone-forming ability, where no prior clinical outcomes had been reported. Twenty-eight patients, nineteen men and nine women, mean age 47.5 years, received the graft after cystectomy.

Among 28 cystic lesions, 27 were odontogenic cysts and one was a nasopalatine duct cyst. Both long- and short-axis defect lengths fell markedly by six months postoperatively, against preoperative and one-month values, while CT values rose significantly from one to six months. At six months, 39.3% of patients reached full bone continuity. No serious adverse events occurred. The authors conclude the material offers excellent handling and clinical safety as a novel graft for jawbone defects following cystectomy.
pmc-13329591:
Shahrukh Khan and co-authors review blood markers of protein use in farm animals in a 2026 article. Protein is costly and wasted nitrogen harms the environment, yet standard digestion checks via gut or dung samples are slow and hard to scale. Blood tests could give a quicker, repeatable window on digestion and nitrogen loss.

Markers covered include urea nitrogen in blood and milk, uric acid in birds, amino acid profiles after meals, and wider metabolic panels. The review spans cattle and single-stomach species. It warns that kidney function, energy balance, feeding stage, and sampling time can skew readings. A panel of markers, read together under shared standards, will serve precision feeding and breeding best, the authors argue.
pmc-13330791:
Sigit Adi Prasetyo and colleagues test a leaf extract against gut inflammation in rats in a 2026 study. Graptophyllum pictum, known locally as daun wungu, holds compounds that may calm swelling and guard the gut wall. Thirty Wistar rats were split into five groups of six, with colitis triggered by DSS in most groups.

Care ran for 10 days by mouth: standard drug, extract alone, or both together. All treated groups gained more weight than untreated colitis controls in the reported results. Stool form improved most with standard drug and with the pairing. Swelling markers fell and gut fatty acids recovered toward normal, best in the paired group. Tissue damage scores also dropped with care.
pmc-13331391:
Zachary A. Sorrentino and a large team give a technical guide and case series on clot removal for child stroke in a 2026 article. Child stroke with large vessel block is rare and device work is hard in small vessels. The team searched their centre database for patients over 28 days and under 18 years treated from 2012 to 2023.

Seven patients aged about 1 to 17 years entered the series in the reported counts. Causes spanned clotting disorders, heart problems, and procedure mishaps. Six of seven reached strong vessel reopening grades in those results. Most recovered well at last follow-up, over an average span near three years. A guide by age and leg artery size is offered.
pmc-13331991:
Fang Guo and co-authors engineered a light-controlled bone scaffold in 2026 work aimed at large bone defects that heal poorly when blood supply is weak. Plain PEEK plastic scaffolds can be printed to fit a defect and bear load, but the material is biologically inert and does little to invite new vessels or bone cells.

Their design coats porous PEEK with polydopamine carrying black phosphorus sheets and strontium ions. Gentle near-infrared warming to 40 to 42 °C releases the ions on a timed cascade. In cell tests the scaffold boosted vessel cell growth, movement, and tube formation, and pushed rat stem cells toward bone through the ERK1/2 pathway and raised HSP70. In rabbit thigh bone defects, light treatment sped early vessel growth and bone fill, supporting the scaffold for poorly supplied repair sites.
pmc-13333291:
Miriam Herrmann and a large team release a standardized laser scanning dataset of European forests in 2026. Ground-based scanners capture forest structure in fine 3D detail, but earlier public sets used mixed methods and covered little ground, blocking fair comparisons between sites.

The collection covers 121 plots of 50 by 50 m across five campaigns in Germany, Czechia, two Spanish regions, and Norway. All were scanned with the same RIEGL VZ-400i instrument and one shared processing workflow. Each plot ships with a cleaned point cloud at 1 cm resolution and tree-level measures such as trunk diameter, height, and leaf type. It also carries shapefiles for plot edges and scan and tree positions, a preview image, and notes on terrain, climate, and soil. The authors intend the set for comparing forest structure across ecosystems and benchmarking segmentation and inventory methods.
pmc-13333391:
Yi Zhong and colleagues report an early comeback of a fatty tumor in the throat of a young man, in a 2026 case report and literature review. Well-differentiated liposarcoma grows slowly and rarely spreads, but it loves to return where it started. The hypopharynx is an exceptionally rare site, above all in the young.

The 24-year-old had felt something in his throat for a month. Scope examination showed a lump under the lining of the left hypopharynx. MRI showed an enhancing mass with no neck node spread. It was removed through the mouth, and tissue study showed mature fat with atypical cells. Staining for MDM2, CDK4, CD34, and p16 plus a gene test proving MDM2 amplification sealed the diagnosis. Healing looked fine. Yet scope checks at 2, 2.5, and 4 months showed the tumor regrowing at the cut site. The authors stress molecular diagnosis and close surveillance after clean-looking removal.
pmc-13333591:
Chunyuan Xi and colleagues track household chaos through the COVID years in a 2026 family study, asking how families rode out the disruption and what the ride cost their teenagers. Household chaos, the noise, crowding, and routines of a home, surged during lockdowns, and parents and children did not always experience it alike.

Reports came from 506 adults and 93 youth, who recalled chaos before, during, and after the pandemic alongside youth health measures. Growth modelling separated three paths: a low-chaos thriving group at 35.2 percent, a moderate resilience group at 40.3 percent, and a high-chaos worsening group at 24.5 percent. Younger teenagers agreed with parents more than older ones did. Youth on the worsening path carried more behavior problems, distress and anxiety, worse sleep, and less positive affect than the other groups. The authors advise pandemic planning to measure each family member's experience rather than treating the household as one unit.
pmc-13333691:
Wei Wu and co-authors tested a three-scope surgical approach for gallbladder stones combined with common bile duct stones in a 2026 retrospective study. Their method joins laparoscopy, choledochoscopy, and duodenoscopy in one treatment plan.

The team checked 40 patients treated at Wuhan Central Hospital between June and December 2024. Thirty patients received the combined three-scope approach, while ten had endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography followed by gallbladder removal. The groups were weighed on operating time, blood loss, bile duct width, recovery milestones, hospital stay, and complications. In the combined group the average operation lasted 152 minutes with modest blood loss, and two patients got pancreatitis that settled with treatment. The study weighs a single joined-up procedure against the usual two-step route.
pmc-13334091:
Anam Ahmad and co-authors investigated alpha-klotho, a circulating protein tied to healthier aging, and its links with insulin resistance in a 2026 analysis of older adults. Whether body weight changes that relationship was a central question.

The secondary analysis used the Invecchiare in Chianti cohort, covering 825 community-dwelling adults aged 55 and older, with alpha-klotho and metabolic measures taken three years after enrollment. Among 370 overweight participants, each log unit of alpha-klotho was associated with higher HOMA-IR, a standard insulin resistance index, after adjustment. Links with fasting glucose appeared as well, while associations with insulin alone did not hold. The counterintuitive direction in overweight adults complicates the protein's healthy-aging story and invites closer study.
pmc-13334791:
P. Ndacyayisenga and colleagues study 2026 hand hygiene practice among health care providers at the University Teaching Hospital of Kigali. Hand hygiene is a critical, cost-effective way to prevent hospital infections, yet global rates among providers remain low at about thirty-nine percent. Few studies in Rwanda have examined providers' knowledge, views, and practice, and factors shaping rates remain underexplored.

The cross-sectional study involved 254 providers selected via stratified sampling. Data came from direct watching with the World Health Organization hand hygiene form plus a self-administered survey. Correlation and linear regression in SPSS version 25 identified factors shaping rates. Overall rates were about fifty-four percent, higher among doctors at about sixty percent than among nurses. The study gives Rwandan hospital leaders a local baseline for improvement.
pmc-13334891:
Mikaela A. Barbour and colleagues review 2026 tiny vessel stalling as a common small-vessel pathway to stroke risk and poor recovery. Tiny vessel stalling means brief interruption of blood flow within individual tiny vessels, a potential indicator of cerebral small-vessel failure that may contribute to stroke risk and recovery. Stroke still ranks among the top causes of death and disability around the world, yet many patients cannot get existing treatments, which points to a need for better prevention and earlier detection.

Stroke is usually seen as a large-vessel disorder, but small-vessel failure may strongly shape both the odds and the results of brain vessel injury. Because tiny vessels have extremely narrow lumens and low flow speeds, they are vulnerable to blockage by white cells, rigid or clumped red cells, platelet aggregates, or fibrin-rich tiny clots.
pmc-13335091:
S. Rettschlag and co-authors mapped the germs living in the Eustachian tube in 2026, weighing healthy ears with chronically blocked ones. The tube ventilates the middle ear, and chronic obstructive dysfunction can lead to chronic ear illness and cholesteatoma. Nobody had systematically studied which germs usually colonize it. At a German referral center, the team sampled thirteen patients and thirty-seven healthy controls during surgery, using a contamination-minimized suction method.

Lab culture grew over five hundred bacterial strains. Healthy controls carried more diverse groups, with notably more genera than patients. Sequencing-based microbiome study proved a living bacterial group in the tube itself. The results reframe the Eustachian tube as inhabited territory, not a sterile pipe. If disease includes a shrunken or altered group, future treatments might aim to restore it rather than simply sterilize the area.
pmc-13335391:
Qian Ni and seven co-authors track how heart rate paths over time link to death in very ill patients with both atrial fibrillation and heart failure. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. More than eight thousand ICU patients from two large data bases were in the pool. Rate marks came from the first thirty days of care.

Higher base rates tied to higher thirty-day death risk in step. Three rate paths were found, and a path that rose over time tied to near three-fold death risk. Wide swings that grew tied to like risk. Kidney work and vent use changed the links. The team says live rate watch may help sort short-term risk, with more checks due.
pmc-13336091:
Fang Zhao and co-authors present a luminescent thermometer in two thousand twenty-six based on rare ultraviolet light from divalent ytterbium ions. Optical thermometers read temperature without contact, and their precision rests on the chosen signal. Ytterbium's ultraviolet glow had seldom been used for this purpose.

The ions sit inside a borate crystal stable from about eighty to four hundred twenty kelvin. Under heat, the glow brightens and its spectrum shifts both ways, as heat spreads electrons among excited levels with distinct responses. Combining several signals by multiple linear regression multiplied the sensitivity. A lifetime-based signal reached a striking relative sensitivity near twenty-eight percent per kelvin. The authors offer the approach as a general recipe for extracting temperature from light.
pmc-13336391:
Jeseung Lee, Sophie Leanza, and Ruike Renee Zhao introduced springs made from rod origami in a 2026 engineering study. Springs anchor vibration control everywhere, but a normal spring's stiffness is fixed at manufacture, while machines face changing vibration environments.

Their RodOri springs are built from pre-stressed, naturally curved elastic rods. Tuning each rod's natural curvature and cross-section programs when it snaps through buckling and how stiff it feels afterward. Assembling springs of equal length but different snapping points creates a multistable metamaterial that reconfigures step by step as load rises. Each stable state carries its own resonance behavior, giving broad and fine control of dynamic response. Simulations and experiments support the design principle for adaptive mounts and isolators.
pmc-13336891:
Jie Yang and co-authors weave bamboo-like carbon fibers into a free-standing battery cathode in a 2026 study. Lithium-sulfur batteries store much energy, but sulfur products wander between electrodes and reactions crawl. Their film grows ultralong nitrogen-doped carbon fibers from melamine over an aluminum catalyst, then loads sulfur and coats it with polyaniline.

The binder-free film gives orderly channels that trap wandering sulfur species, cushion swelling, and carry charge fast. The polymer coat grips those species chemically and evens out lithium return. After 500 cycles at 1.0 A per gram, capacity loss averaged just 0.047% per cycle in cycling tests. Self-supporting cathodes could lift energy-dense battery designs.
pmc-13336991:
Frederic Rudlof and colleagues measure how mixed tiny particles sort themselves inside spray-dried clusters in a 2026 study. Layered supraparticles serve photonics, medicines, and printed manufacturing, but how strongly layers form under set recipes was unclear. Microscope imaging quantified sorting across particle size ratios and mix shares.

Against intuition, bigger size gaps did not always layer more. At low small-particle shares, size ratios near 3–5 layered best, shifting lower as the small share rose in the mapped trends. Simulations matched the pattern: small particles slip through gaps between large ones when scarce, while a drift effect dominates when plentiful. The map helps design clusters with planned inner architecture.
pmc-13337391:
Zichao You, Li Jiang, Ying-rui Liu, and Ming Ming Yang sort diabetic macular edema into five treatable patterns in a 2026 review. This swelling of the central retina is a leading cause of vision loss in diabetes. Standard anti-VEGF injections help many patients, yet a large share respond poorly because the disease mixes several mechanisms.

Multimodal imaging, especially OCT and its angiography variant, reveals markers of activity such as retinal fluid and bright foci. Other markers forecast vision, including inner layer disorganization, light-sensor damage, and poor blood flow. Grouping markers yields leakage-dominant, inflammatory, and tractional types, plus focal-treatment and poor-prognosis types. The authors propose matching therapy to type and adjusting as markers change.
pmc-13337591:
Michał Wójcicki and co-authors review how bacterial viruses can restore failing antibiotics in a 2026 article. Resistance is outpacing new drug discovery, leaving old antibiotics to save. Bacteriophages kill bacteria directly, but their deeper value may be evolutionary: bacteria that adapt to dodge phages often pay for the changes.

Dodge moves such as capsule loss, surface changes, or altered efflux pumps can leave bacteria weaker, less able to form biofilms, or newly sensitive to antibiotics. Case reports and experiments show phage-antibiotic pairs suppressing growth better than either alone and re-sensitizing resistant pathogens. Adding CRISPR tools could strip resistance genes precisely. The review maps these trade-offs as a strategy to extend the working life of existing drugs.
pmc-13340691:
An inflammatory tumor in a teenager's pelvis is presented by Nazila Heidari's team in a 2026 case report. The 14-year-old Iranian boy had three weeks of fever, abdominal pain, nausea, constipation, and weight loss, plus pelvic pain, with a firm mass felt low in the abdomen.

Imaging showed a lobulated mass between bladder and rectum with dead tissue inside and slight fluid. Surgeons removed a 10 × 8 cm mass stuck to the omentum, losing only about 20 mL of blood. Tissue study confirmed inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor. He stayed well with no return at six months, though long watch is advised since these tumors can recur.
pmc-13341491:
A hormone-like protein guiding the heart through pregnancy is studied by Albert Blasco-Roset and colleagues, in their 2026 paper. Meteorin-like, or Metrnl, rises in late pregnancy, largely from the placenta, while the heart grows and later shrinks back after weaning.

In normal mice, pregnancy growth deepened during lactation and reversed fully afterward, with fat burning rising in gestation then easing. Mice lacking Metrnl instead developed exaggerated, stretched heart growth, piled lipid into the muscle, and recovered slowly after weaning. The protein thus seems to keep reproductive heart remodeling flexible and reversible in mice and, by circulation patterns, possibly in humans.
pmc-13342191:
Gum disease worsens blood sugar through the gut in diabetic mice, in a 2026 study by Qianjia Pan and colleagues. Forty mice were split into healthy, periodontitis, diabetes, and combined groups of ten, with gum disease induced by silk ligatures and diabetes confirmed by glucose testing.

In diabetic mice, adding periodontitis significantly raised fasting glucose and glucose tolerance area, alongside inflammatory shifts and lower HDL cholesterol. Healthy mice with gum disease showed raised C-reactive protein without glucose change. Fecal 16S sequencing mapped how gut communities shifted across groups, supporting a mouth-gut axis in metabolic disease.
pmc-13342891:
Kyungmi Jang and Philip S Zeitler review prediabetes in children and teens in 2026, a topic made harder by puberty itself. Rising youth obesity brings more abnormal blood sugar, yet the natural drop in insulin sensitivity during puberty often fades afterward, so many young people return to normal sugar levels on their own.

The review covers definitions, risk factors, screening advice, and care options, and questions adult cutoffs applied to youth. Broad screening is not advised; testing targets higher-risk groups, and weight gain best predicts advance to type 2 diabetes. Lifestyle change stays the main response, since drugs have not yet proven useful in youth, and child-specific definitions remain an open need.
pmc-13343091:
Michel Bobbia and co-authors present a 2026 air quality dataset from Rouen, France, built to serve a smart mobility project run by the city region. Fixed stations alone leave spatial gaps, so mobile sensors riding on buses were added to map nitrogen dioxide and particle pollution street by street.

Ten bus-mounted sensors logged readings every 10 seconds, joined by 18 traffic-light sensors, six fixed stations, and two extra units near a reference station. Data ran from January to November 2025 and include bus speed, GPS position, and weather measures such as humidity and temperature. The set supports calibration research and data fusion work for cleaner city transport planning.
pmc-13345591:
Daniel S. Green and co-authors test heart CT scanning during emergency stroke care in a 2026 Sydney study. Standard ultrasound of the heart finds few stroke-causing clots, so the center added ECG-gated cardiac CT to its hyperacute imaging run for 117 patients between 2022 and 2024.

Among 69 patients confirmed with ischemic stroke, the scan found a heart clot in 18, a yield of 26 percent. Clot carriers more often had past hypertension, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation, and blocked brain arteries. In the 49 patients who got both tests, CT found clots in 29 percent while ultrasound caught just 2 percent. Clot presence also tracked with worse recovery at three months.
pmc-13345791:
Xiaojuan Lin and colleagues reported in 2026 a striking long response to olaparib maintenance in a 92-year-old woman with advanced uterine serous cancer carrying a BRCA2 mutation. Treatment choices at that age are often narrowed by other illnesses and frailty, raising the risk that effective therapy is withheld.

After surgery that could not remove all disease and single-drug carboplatin, she received the PARP inhibitor olaparib, which targets cancers with faulty DNA repair. Her partial response lasted forty months and the drug was well tolerated. The case suggests that molecular profiling should not be skipped on age grounds alone, since it can open a gentler, lasting option for very elderly patients.
pmc-13346691:
Chinaecherem P Okafor and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the causes and patterns of cancer disparities worldwide. Unequal cancer outcomes weigh most heavily on underserved groups, yet the scale, drivers, and best responses differ by cancer type and population, and no single explanation covers them all.

Drawing on government data and peer-reviewed research, the review examines how social, economic, geographic, and health system factors combine to create distinct disparity patterns. It also weighs what kinds of research and policy responses are most likely to narrow gaps, arguing for rigorous, multi-disciplinary frameworks rather than one-off programmes. The synthesis serves readers who need a coherent map before designing interventions that actually reach those left behind.
pmc-13347391:
Christian Tentellino and colleagues pair two readouts to catch drug harm to nerve cells earlier, in a methods study published in 2026. Electrical spikes from rat nerve cells on a microelectrode array were tracked alongside Raman light spectra. Which report cell chemistry, before and after dosing with gabazine, a compound known to trigger seizure-like firing.

Linking the two streams by cross-correlation surfaced changes that either stream alone could miss, since electrical tests can overlook shifts across the many ion channels in a cell. The authors propose the paired watch as a sharper screen for hidden neurotoxic effects during drug discovery, before candidates move toward patients.
pmc-13347791:
Natalie Alaniz and Khameeka N. Kitt examine a signalling helper called Asef in aggressive breast cancer cells, in a cell study from 2026. Extra Asef was added to MDA-MB-231 cells, with and without growth factor dosing. Placement of Asef, its partner Rac1, the growth receptor, and cell fibres was tracked over 24 hours.

Extra Asef cut stress fibre formation while raising both cell movement and growth in the reported assays, placing Asef inside the receptor-to-Rac1 chain that steers cell behaviour. Growth factor dosing pulled Rac1 to meet Asef at the cell edge, while fibre layout stayed otherwise near normal, sharpening the picture of how these cells spread.
pmc-13351691:
Ashley Mathew, Zhaosheng Jin, and Ehab Al Bizri review the shifting role of sugammadex in infants in 2026. The drug wraps around muscle relaxants such as rocuronium and reverses their effect, and it is approved for adults and children aged 2 years and older. Use in younger infants rests mostly on case reports and small studies.

Their comment centres on a phase IV trial by Mensah-Osman and co-authors in children from birth to under 2 years. Infant bodies handle drugs in immature ways, and young nerve-muscle junctions react unevenly to relaxants. Trial data on drug levels, safety, and effect could put infant use on firmer ground.
pmc-13353191:
Victoria Julia Christine Holzer and colleagues study cold stress effects on a membrane-shaping protein in Synechocystis in 2026. Low temperature stiffens the thylakoid membranes that host photosynthesis in this cyanobacterium. The team tracked the CurT protein, which helps curve those membranes, under cold conditions.

Cold stress lowered CurT build-up while reshaping membrane structure and cutting photosynthetic output. A shared bottleneck under cold masked differences tied to CurT alone. The authors model CurT reduction as a protective move that hardens membranes when flow and bending are challenged by cold. Results widen knowledge of how photosynthetic microbes adjust to cold and may inform crop cold hardiness work.
pmc-13353891:
Dongyan Chen leads a 2026 measurement study quantifying fake signals in electrochemical strain microscopy of battery materials. The method probes nanoscale ion motion, but surface height features can inflate readings and mimic real ion activity. Inactive single-crystal silicon with carved trenches served as a clean reference that mimics grain boundary shapes.

Resonance analysis showed amplitude gains can arise purely from contact stiffness shifts caused by feedback loop delay, with no ions moving at all. Repeated silicon samples confirmed the effect, and tests on a graphite anode and a Na2Zn2TeO6 solid electrolyte showed the artifact persists in real battery materials. Calibration against silicon gives users a way to size and discount the crosstalk.
pmc-13354391:
Abdihakim Ali Nour and Sakarie Mustafe Hidig argued in a 2026 letter that emergency departments should start rule-directed heart medicines earlier. Many people with acute heart disease first reach care in the emergency department, yet starting proven long-term drugs is often left to inpatient teams or later outpatient visits. That delay can break continuity between acute care and ongoing care.

The letter notes that sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 blockers and other evidence-based care have shown consistent benefit in heart failure and related problems. Beginning them during the emergency visit could close a gap in the care pathway. Doctors gain a concise case for treating the urgent department as a starting point for long-term care, not only a site of stabilisation.
pmc-13354991:
Sonia Rahimi and co-authors reviewed studies in 2025 on procrastination in medical students, meaning the willing delay of a task despite known harm. Medical school is high stress, and putting work off is common among its students. The team searched three databases and kept 26 papers that met their rules.

Studies looked at delay in school work and in bedtime, and linked delay to lower grades, weaker self-control skills, and lower self-esteem. Delay also linked to more stress, anxiety, and phone overuse. The authors urge programs that help students spot their delay habits and feelings early, with clear goals and support to break the pattern.
pmc-13356891:
Prest and colleagues piloted Encompass in 2026, a group program for caregivers of young children with complex neurodisability, meaning lasting conditions that affect movement, learning, and daily care. The program was first built with parents in low- and middle-income countries to lift caregiver well-being, health knowledge, and confidence. The team adapted it for two deprived urban areas in the United Kingdom and tested both delivery and evaluation methods against preset traffic-light criteria.

Eight caregivers took part. Delivery quality and follow-up form completion met the top green standard, while recruitment and attendance landed at amber, signaling small fixes before a larger trial. Caregivers and facilitators praised the shared facilitation model, the hands-on approach, and peer support, and flexible options such as joining online aided access. Cost tracking proved workable. The authors judge the program ready for a larger evaluation with sharper recruitment.
pmc-13357091:
Jing Chen and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how well machine learning detects lymph node spread in esophageal cancer before surgery. Early spread is hard to spot in standard pre-surgery checks, and reported model accuracy varies widely. They searched four databases for studies before May 2026 and pooled 49 original studies, twenty of them using image-based features called radiomics.

Models reached a summary accuracy index of about 0.79 in validation data. Models mixing radiomics with clinical features did best, at about 0.82. The authors favor that combined approach for cost and accuracy, while urging caution over mixed study quality and more testing in diverse data.
pmc-13357591:
Guanzhong Zhao, Kaihui Liu, and a large team build a very keen microphone from a thin carbon sheet. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, uses reduced graphene oxide, a form of carbon one atom thick in layers. The sheet hangs free over a wide frame. It is eight centimeters wide but far less than a micron thick.

The sheet bends a lot under tiny pressure, which makes it catch faint sound. Its signal stands well above noise at speech tones. Across a broad tone range, it beat a standard small microphone at picking out speech from nine meters away. The team says the build method can make such large thin sheets in a stable way.
pmc-13358591:
Mulyati Sri Rahayu and co-authors study fitness in office workers in a 2026 paper. Staff who sit all day often gain weight and lose lung power, which drags down aerobic fitness. The team asked how much body mass index and vital lung capacity, the most air a person can blow out, predict top oxygen use.

They tested 75 male university staff with a step test, lung blowing tests, and basic body measures. Joining these simple measures can show which quiet risk signs track low fitness best. The findings support cheap workplace health checks that catch falling fitness early, before it turns into heart or lung disease.
pmc-13358991:
Riccardo Guglielmo and co-authors follow depressed patients on a newer treatment in a 2026 study. Esketamine, a nasal spray related to ketamine, is offered when standard drugs fail. Trials proved it can lift symptoms, but how patients actually function over months in daily care was less clear. The team tracked 60 patients at several centers for six months.

Symptom scores and disability scores improved at every check. By month six, about 78 percent had responded and 47 percent were in remission, while a third reached full functional remission. The gap between feeling better and functioning fully is the study's sober point: recovery takes longer than symptom relief.
pmc-13359991:
Ki Choon Sim and co-authors review gentler ways to assess bladder cancer in a 2026 paper. Bladder cancer returns often and demands close tracking, but the standard tools, a scope in the bladder and surgical sampling, are invasive and can understate the stage. The review covers urine and blood markers alongside imaging measures that need no cutting.

Special MRI scans, scored by a system called VI-RADS, stand out for judging how deep a tumor grows and sorting risk. The authors also weigh how scans may forecast treatment response and recurrence. Joining these markers into one decision path could spare patients some procedures while keeping care precise.
pmc-13360891:
Dipika Jain examined who gets left out of health insurance in India in a 2026 study. The work looks for patterns of exclusion based on age, gender, and past illness. Jain studied the field at many levels, from the national health scheme to 14 state policies. Policies from four government and five private companies, for both single buyers and groups, were also reviewed, along with past research.

The findings show that policies miss the distinct health needs of groups like women, children, and older adults. Rules and gaps in coverage leave these groups less protected than others. In a country pushing for care for all, such blind spots matter a great deal. The study gives reformers a map of where policy design shuts people out.
pmc-13361891:
Shaowen Zhong, Quan Sun, and Lili Yu reviewed bone-based treatments for diabetic foot ulcers in two thousand twenty-six. One approach, periosteal distraction, slowly stretches the membrane around bone and is used as a last resort when ulcers will not heal. How it compares with rival methods was unclear.

Dozens of comparative studies were sorted into three groups by treatment type. Formal pooling was not possible for one group. Pure distraction matched a rival bone transport method on blood flow, pain, and harms, while combined regimens improved short-term blood flow measures. Overall support stayed weak. Foot specialists get a sober verdict: promise, but no firm proof yet.
pmc-13362391:
Jon Stephen Yarbrough and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on gum disease and a drug that blocks the CD38 protein. CD38 breaks down NAD+, a molecule cells need for energy and repair, and old immune cells carry more of it. The team gave young and old mice with gum disease the blocker 78c or a dummy shot for four weeks.

Mice on 78c had higher NAD+ levels in the liver and spleen, and old mice had more in the jaw as well. Both young and old treated mice lost less jaw bone than untreated mice. The results back CD38 blocking as a path worth testing for gum disease care.
pmc-13362491:
James Tsimiklis and Theodore Athanasiadis compare two ways to give a steroid shot for stubborn chronic cough in a 2026 clinic study. The shot targets a nerve in the voice box area that drives cough sensitivity. Their new method uses a thin camera through the nose to guide the needle, treat both sides, and confirm placement, while the older method relies on surface landmarks alone.

Of 142 patients, about 84 percent in the guided group said their cough improved, versus about 48 percent in the landmark group. Cough and voice scores also improved more with guidance, and side effects stayed rare in both groups. The authors back the guided method for cough that resists standard care.
pmc-13363991:
Yangyang Sun and colleagues present a 2026 study on a nanofiber mat that cools surfaces in full sun without using power. Spun from polylactic acid laced with tiny calcium carbonate grains in humid air, the fibers came out porous, with countless inner interfaces that scatter sunlight. The team compared the mat with plainer spun versions for sun reflection and ran outdoor cooling trials.

The loaded porous mat bounced back over nine tenths of sunlight, far more than plain versions, and sat about ten degrees cooler than its surroundings at the trial peak. Buried in soil, it broke down visibly within eighty days. The authors offer the recipe as an easy path to green cooling covers for buildings, vehicles, and outdoor gear.
pmc-13364291:
Hammad Hussain and co-workers review work up to 2026 on how plants use marks on histone proteins to cope with salty soil. Salt harms crops across wide farm areas. These marks can switch stress genes on or off, and teams of plant proteins add, remove, or read them.

The review links key marks to salt response gene sets and to plant stress memory that can last across years of growth. It also weighs new tools, from single cell maps to gene edits that place marks by design. The aim is crops that yield well on salty land.
pmc-13364791:
Liu-Xia Yuan and co-workers study in 2026 a tiny RNA bit that runs high in liver cancer and may drive its growth. The bit, found by a gene chip scan, sat high in tumor flesh, cell lines, and blood. High ranks track with poor life odds and may aid early spotting.

Cell tests show the bit speeds growth, move, and spread, and cuts cell death. Its knock down flips each trait. The bit seems to mute a guard gene that slows spread paths. The team casts the bit as a mark and aim for liver cancer care.
pmc-13365291:
Melanie Fisher and colleagues published a 2026 study of benign nerve tumors grown in engineered gels. These ear-nerve tumors stiffen as they grow. Stiffness and sticky surroundings send different signals. Normal dishes cannot separate those signals. The team built two adjustable gel systems.

One gel confined cells without stickiness. The other mimicked fibrous tumor tissue. Stiffer confinement slowed spreading in the plain gel. Stress signals inside cells rose under pressure. Releasing the stress reversed those signals. A growth pathway drug was also tested. Separating force from chemistry clarifies tumor behavior. It may reveal which signal drugs should target.
pmc-13366091:
Mohammad El-Dakdouki and co-workers build in 2026 a magnetic image probe that homes to a cell mark named CD44, found on many tumor cells. They coat iron grains with a tuned form of a joint sugar gel that grips the mark more tight than the plain gel. Breast tumor cells in tests take up the tuned grains well.

Cell pull of the grains runs through the gel's own lock path. The grains do no harm at top test dose. In a magnetic image scan, cells with tuned grains shine more than twice as bright as plain gel cells. The probe could light up mark rich tumors.
pmc-13368891:
Judith de Ruijter-van Dalem and six co-authors track how long pain, calm, and mind drugs begun in hospital run on past it. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, reads a Dutch center's past years.

Many patients get such drugs in care for a short need. The risk is that use rolls on past the stay, with no fresh look. The team took grown patients who got a new such script at leave or at a clinic visit, and whose use ran on. They were tracked for a year, by the center's own files and by drugstore logs. The aim is the true span of such use.
pmc-13369191:
Grant Hill and colleagues design two-way pathways that pull lithium out of layered oxide electrodes. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses cobalt oxide as the model host. Electric intercalation can extract lithium selectively from brines. Few electrode materials have been explored for this job.

Lithium and sodium ions compete inside the layered host. A two-phase balance between sodium-rich and lithium-rich forms governs selectivity. Deep intercalation, leaving few empty slots, favours lithium. The race between ion exchange and insertion decides the path taken. That race can be tuned quantitatively by conditions. Paired extraction and recovery steps become designable. Battery recycling and brine mining both need such selectivity.
pmc-13372191:
Jean Martinien Engoue and co-authors describe jaw bone care in an 82-year-old woman in a 2026 case report. She had taken a bone drug for weak bones for 15 years. After a tooth was pulled, dead jaw bone showed and would not heal, a known risk of such drugs.

Care began with germ drugs and a mouth rinse. The surgeon then broke the dead bone into small bits and took it out bit by bit, a gentler path than one big cut. Checks at two years and past were clean. The team thinks the soft touch may cut harm and lower the chance of the sore coming back.
pmc-13374291:
Uğur Tekeoğlu and colleagues test whether speaking and listening skills predict internet gaming disorder in middle school students in Turkey in a 2026 study. Weak verbal communication may push young people toward digital games as an easier social outlet. The team surveyed 495 middle school students in spring 2025 with scales for gaming disorder, gaming thoughts, listening styles, and speaking confidence.

Gaming disorder fell as speaking self-efficacy rose. Relational and analytical listening also fell as gaming disorder rose, while transactional listening rose with it. Hierarchical regression and moderation analyses, with false discovery control, tested which skills predict disorder most strongly. The findings point to communication training as a possible prevention lever for gaming problems in early adolescence.
pmc-13375191:
Azam Amzajerdi and five co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether a guided tour of a newborn intensive care unit can ease stress in new parents. Babies born preterm often land in such units, and the experience can weigh hard on their parents. The trial ran at a hospital in Tehran from 2020 to 2021, with 130 parents of preterm infants.

Parents were split into three groups. Two groups received a thirty-minute orientation tour of the unit, and one of those also received orange aromatherapy. The third group got standard care. A day after the visit, both tour groups showed lower stress and depressed mood scores than the control group. Scores tied to the baby's appearance and to the change in the parent role also fell. An hour after the visit, no gap had shown yet. The authors back a tour at the first visit, with or without aromatherapy.
pmc-13375391:
Vaibhav Jaiswal and co-authors summed up robot surgery in emergencies in a 2026 review. Belly work in a crash or a grave belly ill is hard on the body. Robot rigs give 3D views and wrist-like tools that beat stiff scope tools, but their use in rush care is in doubt.

The search spanned five data banks to March 2026 and used firm steps. Work was split in two sets: rush belly ills and crash wounds. Scores held swaps to open cuts, skill wins, time, ward stay, harms, and cost. The sum maps where robots may fit in rush care and where open hands stay king.
pmc-13375891:
Alexandra F. Muratore and co-authors filmed brain work at food choice in a 2026 study. Folk with a grave eat ill pick low-fat, low-sugar food to the point of self-starve. How the brain weighs such picks was the ask. Women with the ill and healthy peers did food and non-food choice tasks in a scanner.

Both groups weighed proof in much the same way as they chose. Brain acts split at food choice, though. Healthy peers lit a memory zone, while the ill group lit that zone plus a control zone. The split may show why food picks feel like hard work in this ill.
pmc-13377091:
Corey Richier and colleagues test whether brain age prediction reveals accelerated ageing in generalised anxiety disorder in a 2026 study. Higher predicted brain age gaps have been linked to several psychiatric disorders, and anxiety is tied to ageing markers. A convolutional neural network trained on 3,511 controls was tested on 1,595 people with generalised anxiety and 4,552 healthy controls from the ENIGMA-Anxiety working group.

Four MRI input types per person fed an ensemble model, and predicted age minus actual age gave the brain age gap. Model performance was consistent across groups, allowing a fair comparison of gaps and their variability between anxious and healthy brains. The study tests whether anxiety leaves a measurable ageing signature in brain structure that could guide early intervention.
pmc-13377991:
Brown Beckley, Vincent Amarh, Adesola Olalekan, and Innocent Afeke trace drug resistance in a staph lineage in Ghana in a 2026 study. Staphylococcus aureus is a major infection threat, and one lineage, ST152, has become dominant there while carrying a potent toxin gene. The team asked how methicillin resistance arose inside that lineage.

They analyzed close to three hundred public genomes of the germ from Ghana, from people and animals. ST152 made up more than a quarter of them. Family trees showed resistance arose many times on its own, as the resistance cassette was picked up again and again. Even so, one resistant branch now dominates. That branch carries extra resistance genes, a plasmid type, and a glue protein gene that may aid spread. Drug-sensitive strains sat inside resistant clusters, showing how fluid the trait is.
pmc-13380191:
Hiroyuki Okawa reports a young man whose severe high blood pressure and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome overlapped, in a 2026 case report. The 22-year-old arrived with severe hypertension, lung bleeding, and acute kidney injury, plus low platelets and blood-breaking anemia. Both conditions cause small-vessel clotting damage, and their overlap is rarely untangled.

Doctors started blood pressure control, round-the-clock blood filtering, steroids, and plasma exchange for suspected immune disease. Clear immune tests, preserved ADAMTS13 activity, and clear stool cultures led them to stop plasma exchange and taper steroids. Blood counts improved briefly, but kidney failure persisted and lung bleeding returned with a marked drop in complement, pointing to complement-driven disease.
pmc-13380291:
Jocia Fenomanana and colleagues report a 2026 study of inherited haemoglobin variants in Madagascar, where data have been scarce. These inherited blood conditions include sickle cell disease and thalassaemias. The team reviewed test results from a university hospital for patients sent for analysis between 2014 and 2019.

In total 553 patients were tested with a gel method that separates haemoglobin types. Only about a quarter had a normal result. The most common finding was the sickle cell trait, followed by sickle cell disease itself. Combinations with thalassaemia also appeared, while thalassaemia alone was rare. The study also discusses limits of the test method for a low-resource setting.
pmc-13381991:
Tahir Turk and colleagues describe a 2026 study co-designing water, sanitation, and hygiene messages with communities in Kiribati, a Pacific island nation. South Tarawa faces open defecation habits, crowding, poor facilities, and safety worries around sanitation. Campaign messages work better when local people help shape them.

The team interviewed 12 key informants and ran eight focus groups. In total 73 community members took part across seven villages. Message ideas and branding were developed inside those groups, and people rated their impact with a simple smiley-face scale. Analysis produced four main themes and many subthemes. The process offers a model for behaviour-change campaigns in other Pacific island settings.
pmc-13382691:
Md Akhtarul Islam and colleagues wrote a 2026 reply to a comment on their model of adsorption kinetics, the study of how substances stick to surfaces from liquids. Their interface reaction model aimed to give rate constants for sticking and release that do not depend on operating settings. A comment questioned hidden assumptions and whether the equations were dimensionally consistent.

In reply, the authors accept the simplification made in building the model. They then work through the dimension of every term to show the equations are consistent. The model treats the boundary between two phases as sharp, with exchange happening by reaction at that boundary. The exchange aims to prevent future confusion on this point.
pmc-13382791:
Ellen Werner and a large Dutch team estimate how many patients must take bezafibrate to prevent one liver transplant or death in 2026 work. The drug is used off-label in primary biliary cholangitis, a liver disease, when standard care leaves key blood levels high. The team paired Dutch cohort survival data with effect sizes from a Japanese study.

By their math, treating 15 patients for five years, or 7 for ten years, would prevent one transplant or death. Patients with the highest liver enzyme levels needed the fewest treated to gain the same benefit. The clear numbers may help doctors and patients weigh second-line therapy choices together.
pmc-13383391:
Kasperi Mikkonen's team tested whether a usability scale for psychological interventions holds up in Finnish primary care, in a 2026 psychometric study. The Intervention Usability Scale, adapted from the System Usability Scale, is meant to capture how usable therapists find an intervention, but its structure and reliability were unclear. The team gave the Finnish version to professionals trained in guided self-help or face-to-face cognitive behavioral therapy.

Exploratory analysis favored a three-factor structure, contradicting earlier one- or two-factor accounts. Confirmatory analysis fit moderately in the self-help group after handling correlated residuals and cross-loadings, and measurement invariance held across demographic groups. The structure did not replicate in the face-to-face group, warning against assuming the scale travels across intervention formats.
pmc-13385691:
Khani and colleagues screen blood pressure medicines in silico as blockers of the PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint in cancer, in 2026 computational drug discovery research. Antibody checkpoint drugs work well but penetrate tissue poorly, cost heavily, and provoke side effects, while no molecule has proven itself for this target. The team docked 20 dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers into the checkpoint complex with software, using the inhibitor CA-170 as a reference. They ranked compounds by binding fit and interaction pattern.

Three blockers, pranidipine, isradipine, and efonidipine, showed the most favorable profiles against the checkpoint interface. Molecular dynamics simulations, which watch the complex move over time, confirmed the interactions held, especially for pranidipine. Khani stresses the work is computational: a repurposing hypothesis that cheap heart drugs might double as checkpoint inhibitors, needing laboratory and animal testing. The attraction is speed and cost, since the candidates' safety profiles are documented from decades of use.
pmc-13389491:
Kenneth P Hough's team found that tiny bubbles from airway control cells rewire helper T cells in asthma by carrying energy units. Small outside-cell bubbles run cell talk, but whether they carry energy units to feed asthma airway swelling was unknown.

Bubbles from asthma donors hit T cell sensors and moved energy units, driving antigen-matched firing toward Th17 and Th2 profiles through oxidant-linked NF-kB signals that blocking could blunt. A fission switch, DRP-1, loaded energy units into the bubbles, and nose transfer worsened allergic airway swelling in mice, showing a new asthma workings.
pmc-13390091:
Karen Supply, Simon Corthals, and Araceli Diez-Fraile report, in 2026, early outcomes for the All-on-4 full-arch implant method in difficult jaw shapes. The method fixes a full set of teeth on four implants loaded the same day, offering an alternative to removable dentures.

In this retrospective series covering patients treated from November 2023 to February 2025, computer-guided dynamic navigation was reserved for unfavourable arches, while freehand placement was used elsewhere. Each arch received four implants holding a screw-retained temporary bridge. The authors report clinical and X-ray outcomes and whether the selective strategy proved workable. Implant dentists gain real-world evidence for matching navigation effort to anatomical difficulty rather than using it for every case.
pmc-13390291:
Jiaqi Xu's team studied TRIM15, a tag-adding ligase protein, in ovarian cancer, where its role had been unclear despite links to other cancers. Tumour and normal tissue checks plus cell tests tested whether TRIM15 drives growth and spread by tagging the protein paxillin for tagging.

Ovarian tumours ran TRIM15 high, and switching off it slowed cancer cell growth and spread, while mass scans found paxillin among its binding partners. The work positions TRIM15-driven paxillin tagging as a workings of ovarian cancer advance and a lead treatment target. Blocking this route may slow spread in future work.
pmc-13392391:
Siqi Yang's team engineered Escherichia coli for homotypic L-valine fermentation, growing anaerobically on glucose and ammonia with L-valine as the sole product, a feat no known microbe had achieved. They reinforced the valine pathway, blocked mixed-acid fermentation and alanine synthesis to create an NADH driving force, then evolved the strain to remove growth bottlenecks.

The evolved producer converted glucose in a 320-cubic-metre reactor to 83.6 grams per litre of L-valine within sixty hours, at 0.55 grams per gram of glucose, eighty-five percent of theoretical maximum. Amplified pathway, extra electron sinks, and global regulatory reprogramming drove a tenfold gain in anaerobic growth and making rate.
pmc-13392991:
Ülfet Akgün, Arzu Hatipoğlu, and Tarik Eren created a family of acrylate plastics carrying bromine atoms, built as a flexible starting point for later chemical tailoring. Bromine both slows flame spread and offers a handle that chemists can swap for other groups. The team converted a common ring compound into a brominated building block using acrylic acid and a brominating agent, then linked the blocks into chains with a standard initiator.

Two follow-up reactions showed the platform's range: a cage-shaped amine was attached to some bromine sites, giving charged segments, and azide groups replaced other sites, opening the door to click chemistry assembly. Both swaps stopped at partial conversion, which the authors treat as a feature for tuning properties. They point to flame-retardant materials, ion-exchange membranes, and antimicrobial coatings as plausible destinations.
pmc-13393291:
Raha Hassanpour Faramoushjani and Sanam Ansari reviewed a decade of work applying deep learning to evolutionary genomics. They sorted a scattered literature that is often treated as one field despite sharp inner contrasts. Fifty studies from 2016 to 2025 passed set screening. The reviewers argue the applications fall into three partly overlapping domains, each with its own logic.

Population genetics leans on simulation-based inference. Phylogenetics uses neural networks to speed tree building, or to mimic it, under set conditions. Representation learning trains DNA and protein language models whose features transfer to other tasks. Across all three, ease with complex data is the shared strength. Recurring weaknesses include hard-to-read models, sensitivity to training guesses, uneven scoring habits, and heavy computing demands. The authors offer their domain map as a scaffold for future method building.
pmc-13393691:
Hye-Yeon Hwang and colleagues present OpenCRISPR-1, an AI-designed gene editor, in a 2026 study. Standard CRISPR-Cas9 tools can edit DNA at chosen sites, but high-accuracy variants often lose power or restrict guide design, limiting clinical use.

The team compared OpenCRISPR-1 with Cas9 across 28 sites in human cells, plus stem cells and fibroblasts, checking both on-target editing and off-target changes with deep sequencing. Virus-like particles delivered the editors, and prime-editing versions were also built and tested. The paper offers a promising editor that keeps Cas9-level power with tighter accuracy.
pmc-13394391:
Kamal and colleagues study, in 2026, what happens when lithium is deposited onto borophene, a one-atom-thick sheet of boron grown on an iridium crystal. Decorating two-dimensional materials with alkali metals is a way to tune their electronic behavior, since lithium donates electrons. Using electron microscopy, X-ray spectroscopy, and computer models, the team tracked where the lithium sits and how it changes the sheet.

Lithium stayed on the surface rather than slipping underneath the borophene, a route called intercalation, unfavorable here. Adsorbed lithium distorted the borophene lattice, especially after the sample was annealed, and its strong bonds to boron and iridium upset the layer's charge balance. At a coverage of 1.5 monolayers, the lithium binding energy fell to 55.79 electron volts and its spectral peak widened by 30 percent against the low-coverage case. After heating, boron spread across the surface, a caution for future functionalization attempts.
pmc-13394791:
Cancer Science retracts, in a 2026 notice, a 2008 study on the guard protein p53 and a hepatitis B virus protein. The study came from J.-H. Wang and co-authors and claimed that the virus protein wakes p53 by adding phosphate tags. A third party raised doubts, and the journal looked into the figures. The editors found repeated image copying across several blot panels in three figures.

The study team could not supply the old raw data, given the years that had passed. Two authors dispute the claim of copying, and the rest did not reply. The editor, the Japanese Cancer Association, and the publisher agreed to retract. They judge the results and claims unreliable.
pmc-13395391:
M. Breitfeld and co-authors shrink, in 2026, drug pairing tests for E. coli onto a single microscope slide. Checkerboard tests vary two drug doses in a grid to spot pairs that help each other. Their platform packs more than twenty thousand tiny droplets per slide. A full grid is ready in under twenty-five minutes.

The team confirmed growth across droplet sizes and set base drug doses. A known helpful pair, amoxicillin with clavulanate, beat a resistant strain as expected. Other pairs ranged toward mild conflict. Fat profiles of the germs shifted near the dose edge, hinting at stress. The authors see a fast screen for drug pairs in many cell types.
pmc-13395891:
Thomas Agerbo Gaist and colleagues tally, in 2026, fifteen years of autoimmune encephalitis in Denmark. The illness, an immune attack on the brain, has grown better known as antibody tests spread. National test centre data from 2009 to 2023 gave 198 patients with proven antibodies. Records were reviewed to confirm cases and track care.

The NMDAR antibody led the list, ahead of LGI1 and others. Fresh cases rose about ten percent a year, reaching a few per million people yearly. Rates ran highest near the national test centre, which hints that local skill finds more cases. Second-line immune care grew for the lead type, while steroid-sparing care fell. Care paths shifted with growing know-how.
pmc-13395991:
Dandan Wang and co-authors examined whether a blood fat called lipoprotein(a) leaves stroke survivors more prone to thinking problems a year later, in a 2026 analysis. The work sits inside the Third China National Stroke Registry and uses patients who had an ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood flow to the brain.

Blood levels of lipoprotein(a) and of C-reactive protein, a general marker of inflammation, were taken at the start. Thinking was scored a year on with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and a score of 22 or less counted as impairment. The team used several statistical methods to test whether inflammation carries, or changes, any link between the fat and later thinking.
pmc-13396191:
Mariam M. Farouk and co-authors turned Egyptian bentonite clay into a sponge for hexavalent chromium, a toxic metal that taints factory wastewater. Their 2026 study coats the clay with benzalkonium chloride, a common disinfectant ingredient, which flips parts of the surface to a positive charge that grabs the negatively charged metal.

Lab checks confirmed the coating changed the clay's structure and surface area. Batch tests then varied the coating load, acidity, contact time, clay dose, starting metal level, temperature, and shaking speed to find the best removal recipe. The work offers a low-cost use for a plentiful local clay in cleaning industrial water.
pmc-13396491:
Yo Han Song and co-authors made a steroid-free lotion for eczema-prone skin out of a plant compound sealed inside tiny fat bubbles. Their 2026 study targets atopic dermatitis, the itchy, relapsing skin disease usually managed with steroid creams whose side effects limit long use.

The active compound, tryptanthrin, barely dissolves in water, so little of it crosses the skin when used plain. Loading it into liposomes, small spheres of fat, improved its stability, the lotion's moisturizing feel, and how steadily the drug released. Tests then moved to human skin cells in the lab, the first step in judging whether the formula calms inflamed skin safely.
pmc-13396991:
Rohit Thalla and co-authors review a fiery form of cell death as a driver of myelodysplastic syndromes, blood disorders where the marrow makes too few healthy cells and may tip into leukemia. Their 2026 review centers on PANoptosis, a combined death program that merges three classic routes: pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis.

One giant protein complex, the PANoptosome, runs all three at once, and marrow stem cells in these syndromes die too readily, leaving blood counts low amid inflammation. The problem sharpens in patients whose tumors carry splicing gene mutations. Sorting how this joint death switch is triggered could point to drugs that spare the marrow's failing stem cells.
pmc-13397091:
Shonosuke Tajima and co-authors describe a 71-year-old woman whose breast cancer seeded a rare, deadly reaction in the lungs, diagnosed while she was alive by threading a catheter into the heart. Their 2026 case report concerns pulmonary tumor thrombotic microangiopathy, where tumor cells and clotting choke the lung's small arteries.

She came in breathless on effort with a cough, low blood oxygen, and scans showing hazy, nodular lungs but no large clot. Ultrasound showed a strained, enlarged right heart. The catheter study confirmed severe pulmonary hypertension, with mean pressure of 46 millimeters of mercury. Because this condition is usually found only at autopsy, a living diagnosis matters.
pmc-13397391:
Leyla Ay and co-authors test whether simple blood inflammation indices predict outcomes in cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Their 2026 retrospective study follows 580 patients treated at the Medical University of Vienna, tracking ratios built from neutrophils, lymphocytes, platelets, and inflammatory proteins at treatment start and over three months.

Higher baseline neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, C-reactive-protein-to-albumin ratio, and systemic immune-inflammation index each predicted shorter overall survival, while a higher lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio predicted longer survival. Several indices also predicted progression-free survival. No baseline index predicted blood clots, but a doubling of the platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio within three months signalled higher clot risk. The authors conclude these cheap indices carry prognostic information, and that their early changes may flag patients heading toward thromboembolism.
pmc-13397691:
John A Holland and others review full elder workup for late-stage chronic kidney disease in a 2026 system-wide review. Older adults with stages 4 to 5 kidney disease often live with frailty, multi-illness, thinking problems, and function decline, yet kidney services do not usually gauge these elder conditions.

Using PRISMA 2020 guidance, the team hunted MEDLINE, Embase, and trial lists up to November 2025 for studies of adults aged 60 and older getting multi-area geriatric workup. Results covered clinic results, choice-making, and rollout. The review shows whether geriatric workup sharpens fitted kidney care choices in kidney clinics.
pmc-13397791:
Lai Jiahan and colleagues mapped human papillomavirus types and cervical lesion severity among women referred for colposcopy in western China. Their 2026 study draws on 2,934 patients seen at the People's Hospital of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region between January 2018 and June 2025. Colposcopy referral populations in this multiethnic region had been poorly described, limiting precise triage after screening.

High-grade lesions made up 44.2 percent of biopsy results, and HPV16 accounted for 46.0 percent of positive detections, rising to 70.4 percent in cancer specimens. HPV52 and HPV58 formed a smaller second cluster. Combining HPV16 and HPV18 results with cytology scores improved detection of the most severe lesions, and high-grade disease peaked near ages 35 and 51. The findings help clinicians in Xinjiang target follow-up and screening by virus type and age.
pmc-13399391:
Xin Zhao and colleagues followed 45 patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease who took finerenone for a year, in a 2026 real-world study from a single center. Finerenone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor. Because excess aldosterone activity is tied to insulin resistance, the team suspected the drug might ease that resistance as well as protect the kidneys. They tracked two insulin resistance measures at the start, six months, and twelve months.

The patients averaged 52 years old, most were men, and their diabetes control was poor at entry, with a mean HbA1c of 9.2 percent. Over the year, median HOMA-IR fell from 34.40 at baseline to 19.44 at month twelve, a change the Friedman test put at P of 0.038 as reported. No patient stopped treatment because of high potassium, a common worry with this drug class. The authors read the results as a manageable safety profile alongside metabolic improvement.
pmc-13399591:
Tauram Javed and colleagues recount the anesthetic management of a 29-year-old woman with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A whose pheochromocytoma returned in the opposite adrenal gland, in a 2026 case report. She had her right adrenal removed, then her thyroid and parathyroids, in 2022. Routine follow-up in 2024 found her symptom-free but with plasma normetanephrine above 760 picograms per milliliter and a left adrenal nodule on imaging.

Before surgery she was prepared with the alpha blocker doxazosin and the beta blocker metoprolol. The open left adrenalectomy proceeded under general anesthesia with invasive blood pressure monitoring and infusions ready to counter the hormone surges such tumors release when handled. Once the tumor came out, her noradrenaline support was stopped quickly because her pressures held steady on their own. She recovered without incident. The authors stress meticulous preparation, vigilant monitoring, and a multidisciplinary team for recurrent pheochromocytoma in this syndrome.
pmc-13400191:
Shan Zhang and colleagues trace a skin-protective chemical to a familiar bacterium: indolelactic acid, made by Cutibacterium acnes, the skin's most abundant microbe, in a 2026 study of eczema. Metabolomics found the acid depleted both in affected skin and in cultures of patient-derived strains.

In mouse models of barrier damage, smearing the compound on skin activated the aryl hydrocarbon receptor in skin cells. It raised the tight junction proteins that seal the skin and suppressed interleukin-33, an alarm signal. Barrier integrity recovered and the rash eased. The authors frame the compound as a key part of barrier repair, and as a candidate therapy that restores a function healthy skin microbes normally supply.
pmc-13400391:
Robert G Yoder and colleagues review, in 2026, kneecap instability in children with Down syndrome. The kneecap can slip partly or fully out of place, and about one in five people with Down syndrome develop the problem. Repeated slips can injure cartilage and raise the risk of early joint wear.

Children without symptoms are treated without surgery, the authors explain. For those with painful, repeated instability, surgery has shifted toward soft tissue methods that spare growing bone. Reported repeat rates after surgery range widely, from none to one in five. The review stresses that solid outcome studies in this group are still missing and should guide future care choices.
pmc-13400991:
Temesgen Bedassa Gudeta and Sandiswa Figlan survey, in 2026, Cercospora leaf spot disease across mungbean farms in Ethiopia. Mungbean is a major cash pulse in the lowlands, valued for protein and soil improvement. The fungal leaf spot, however, severely limits production, and its national distribution was poorly mapped.

Inspectors visited 496 farms in 33 districts across five regions during the 2024 and 2025 seasons. The disease appeared in every district, with field prevalence rising from about eighty-five percent to over ninety-one percent between years. The worst incidence and severity clustered in certain districts and linked to high elevation, heavy weeds, minimal tillage and late weeding. The authors urge targeted, research-based management in the hardest-hit districts.
pmc-13401291:
The WHO ACTION Trials Collaborators wrote a 2026 commentary on the ACTION-III trial's lower dose of antenatal corticosteroids. These drugs are given before preterm birth to mature the baby's lungs. The standard 24-milligram regimen dates back more than fifty years and was never formally dose-tested.

Evidence across species, backed by human drug-level studies, suggests lung maturation depends on sustained low steroid levels rather than high peaks. Modeling indicates that 2 milligrams of betamethasone phosphate, injected every 12 hours for four doses, keeps fetal levels in the target range found in experiments. That range is about 1 to 4 nanograms per millilitre, reached without the excessive peaks of standard dosing. The commentary lays out that reasoning amid worries about dose-related harm, especially in late preterm babies later born at term.
pmc-13401391:
Canmiao Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a boy who had both Sjögren-Larsson syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. Central precocious puberty, an unusually early start to puberty driven by the brain. The two conditions almost never appear jointly, so each documented case adds information.

The child came to hospital with enlarged testicles and pubic hair. Scaly skin and intellectual disability pointed toward Sjögren-Larsson syndrome, and gene sequencing confirmed two harmful variants in the ALDH3A2 gene. Slightly advanced bone age, ultrasound signs of pubertal development, and raised hormone levels established the early puberty diagnosis. He got triptorelin acetate injections for the puberty, while the syndrome itself was managed with skin moisturizing and rehabilitation. Follow-up showed delayed growth, underlining how hard combined care can be.
pmc-13401591:
John Tredinnick-Rowe and colleagues carried out a 2026 scoping review of dental care access and oral health improvement in Gypsy, Romany, and Traveller communities in Europe. These populations live with poor oral health and recognised unmet need, blocked by layered barriers to seeing a dentist.

The reviewers searched Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and a dentistry database, plus grey literature, for English-language studies on oral health improvement or care access in these communities. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts, and full texts independently, and the included work was analysed thematically and charted. From 436 initial results, only 18 publications qualified, a thinness the authors flag at the outset. The review maps what evidence exists on barriers and interventions, and where the literature simply has gaps.
pmc-13402591:
Deng and co-authors describe, in 2026, the RNA-copying enzyme of Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus. The tick-borne pathogen causes outbreaks with fatality rates above 30 percent across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East. The L-protein both transcribes and replicates the genome, making it a prime drug target. Using cryo-electron microscopy, they solved the core polymerase alone and bound to the genome's 5-prime promoter end.

The polymerase proved larger than relatives in bunyaviruses, with about 2,130 residues in the core, of which 1,505 were visible in the RNA-bound model. It also carried domain insertions unique to the nairovirus family. The promoter RNA sat in a hairpin held by a single base pair, and binding triggered the protein to close over it. pmc-13402691:
Eleonora Bianca and colleagues built a safety-oriented model to predict when a mountaineer's big toe reaches a dangerous cold threshold. Their 2026 study introduces Duration of Safe Exposure, the time until big toe skin temperature hits 15 degrees Celsius under given footwear, air temperature, and activity. Frostbite risk in extreme cold depends on those interacting factors, yet footwear testing lacked a unified safety metric.

Four chamber campaigns produced 96 time series across 10 protocols, and a long short-term memory network predicted toe temperature from mean skin temperature and operating conditions. Training penalized both trajectory error and threshold-crossing mistakes, matching the safety goal. The framework gives boot makers and expedition planners a testable exposure estimate, while chamber results still need mountain validation.
pmc-13402991:
Weston T Powell and co-authors write to the editor about how rhinovirus infection and the cytokine interleukin-13 rewrite DNA methylation in airway lining cells at genetic sites tied to asthma. Childhood asthma varies hugely between patients, and the airway epithelium, which fields viruses and pollution first, helps set that variety. Methylation marks laid down after exposures can lock in altered gene behavior long after the trigger passes.

The team uses organotypic bronchial epithelial cultures, grown to mimic real airway structure, to test whether virus plus interleukin-13 leave persistent marks at asthma loci. Their angle is balance: weak early interferon invites heavy viral growth, which then provokes the exaggerated response tied to flare-ups.
pmc-13403591:
Daniel J Valdivia and colleagues told in 2026 of a brain mass that looked like a tumor yet proved to be a tuberculosis abscess. The 43-year-old man had well-controlled HIV and a past bout of lung tuberculosis. Worsening one-sided headaches led to a scan showing a small ring-shaped mass near language cortex.

Surgeons removed the mass while he stayed awake so speech areas could be mapped. Tissue tests found TB germs and confirmed the abscess call. He recovered with no new nerve deficits and kept improving at follow-up. The case warns that infection can hide behind tumor-like scans.
pmc-13403891:
Chen Ai and colleagues designed sound-triggered particles in 2026 to reprogram support cells inside hard breast tumors. Those support cells weave a dense mat that blocks immune cells and keeps the tumor quiet. Killing them outright can backfire, so the team chose to retrain them instead.

Retrained cells began showing tumor pieces to helper immune cells, which thinned the mat and let fighters in. The partner drug killed tumor cells in an immune-stirring way. In mice, the pairing lit up both immune arms and curbed the quiet tumor state.
pmc-13404191:
Valentina Evdokimova led a 2026 rat study linking estrogen-driven breast tumors to ancient virus-like bits in our DNA waking up. Such bits, called retroelements, can stir immune alarms when they switch on. Rats prone to estrogen-fed breast tumors showed early duct growths with these bits active.

pmc-13404491:
Katherine E Harding leads a 2026 protocol for the WaitLESS trial, which tests a demand-management model in specialist clinics in Melbourne, Australia. Long waits for outpatient specialist care harm patients, and earlier work showed the STAT model can cut them. STAT stands for Specific Timely Assessment and Triage, a method that matches clinic capacity to real demand.

Eight specialties will adopt the model in a stepped wedge design, two at a time every three months. Each clinic first studies past demand, clears part of its backlog, and then protects slots for new patients. The trial tracks waiting times and list sizes alongside adoption, acceptability and cost. A six-month baseline period and at least six months of follow-up frame the rollout.
pmc-13404791:
Cihangir Kaymaz and colleagues sort patients with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension into types, in 2026 work on 297 people. The disease, high pressure in lung arteries without a clear cause, varies widely between patients. Grouping by shared traits may sharpen treatment choices.

Machine learning clustering used age, pressure measures and other illnesses at baseline. One group of 198 patients was younger, with a median age of 40, few other illnesses but severe circulation problems. The other 99 were older, mostly women, with high rates of obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure. Despite similar overall risk scores, the younger group showed worse heart coupling and higher vessel resistance, and received triple drug therapy more often.
pmc-13406591:
Xiaona Song and co-authors review VacA, a toxin of the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori, in a 2026 article.
