Certain gene variants, named s1 and m1, track with worse disease including stomach cancer.

New structural work using cryo-electron microscopy reveals how the toxin assembles and punches channels into cell membranes. Those details explain much of its damaging behaviour. The authors look ahead to subunit vaccines designed to neutralise the toxin's immune-damping effects. Better control of an infection carried by nearly forty percent of people worldwide is the prize.
pmc-13407891:
Jianping Jiang and a large team published a genomic survey in two thousand twenty-six on drug-resistant Klebsiella spreading outside hospitals. This bacterium was long seen as a hospital problem. Resistant strains are now turning up in community patients, with little known about their structure.

The team sequenced over two thousand resistant outpatient samples from forty-two states. Spread was driven mainly by one resistance gene riding on a family of mobile DNA rings. The gene had reached hundreds of bacterial lineages and travelled with stress and metal tolerance traits. Nearly half the samples formed clusters spanning several states. Most came from older women with urinary infections, where oral drugs increasingly fail. The authors map targets for a possible vaccine.
pmc-13408691:
Veronica Morea and colleagues compare in 2026 a rare family of proteins that combine two control tricks at once. One is control by an outside effector molecule. The other is negative cooperation between their own identical subunits. Negative cooperation means the first bound ligand makes the next binding harder, flipping the usual allosteric story. Few proteins do both, so the set on hand for matching is small.

Across unrelated examples, four features recurred. Every protein is built from identical subunits. Each subunit binds exactly one main ligand and one effector. Full saturation with effector is not needed for full effect. Binding also distorts the subunits unevenly, breaking their symmetry. The authors argue that regulation of this kind works at the level of the whole assembly, not just within one subunit. That point refines the classic textbook models of allostery.
pmc-13409091:
Michael Naughton and colleagues interrogate the records of one point two million British patients in 2026 to ask what questionable prescribing costs the health service. Potentially inappropriate prescribing means medicines whose risks likely outweigh their benefit for that patient. The cohort, drawn randomly from a national primary care database, covered adults aged forty-five to sixty-four followed from 2018.

Taking ten or more medicines multiplied the odds roughly sevenfold, and multimorbidity, female sex, and frequent consulting all raised the likelihood. Those exposed consulted their GP slightly more often the next year, though their mortality over the following years was no higher. The authors argue the burden is common enough in middle age, not just old age, to deserve systematic review programmes.
pmc-13410391:
Weixiang Tao and colleagues report in 2026 on a membrane that turns salty dye wastewater into electric power. Where salty and fresh water mix, the energy gap can be harvested as current. Dirty industrial streams hold that energy too, yet they are rarely tapped.

Their membrane pairs a molybdenum sulfide layer with a treated porous crystal layer, tuned so an inner electric field forms at the join. That field speeds selective ion flow across the sheet. Under a strong salt gradient the setup reached peak power near the top of its class. In mock wastewater with salt and a red dye, it made still more power while breaking the dye down at the same time.
pmc-13411191:
Danielle Bruno and colleagues checked whether Indiana's AHEC Scholars program steers health students toward rural practice. The 2026 study followed five student groups from 2018 to 2023, pairing classroom learning with hands-on work in rural and underserved towns. It then tracked both stated plans and actual jobs a year after graduation.

Students left the program far more willing to work in rural towns than when they entered, and that intent lined up with where many actually practiced. The paper offers state planners evidence that paid rural exposure during training can help fill lasting rural care gaps.
pmc-13411991:
Yan Liu and co-authors examine, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study from Shanghai Changhai Hospital, whether adding hemoperfusion to regular dialysis helps patients live longer. People on maintenance dialysis die at high rates, most often from cardiovascular disease. The study followed 640 patients with end-stage kidney disease treated between 2015 and 2023, of whom 221 also received hemoperfusion sessions.

Over follow-up, 348 patients died, about a third of them from cardiovascular causes. Models that treated hemoperfusion as a time-varying exposure linked the added therapy to a lower risk of death, with hazard ratios near 0.7. A matched comparison of 173 patients per group pointed the same way, supporting a survival benefit worth testing prospectively.
pmc-13412391:
Vroni Hischa, Frank Niklas, and Korbinian Moeller test in 2026 which early skills feed mathematics achievement across primary school. Number sense and working memory are both known predictors, yet their changing weights by grade were unclear. Number line estimation and working memory predicted maths skills at every grade level in their path model. Nonverbal reasoning added predictive power in first, third, and fourth grades. The pull of number line skill grew significantly stronger by third grade than in the first two years. The authors read the pattern as a fingerprint of formal maths teaching.
pmc-13412891:
Rendy Agustian and colleagues review in 2026 fifteen patients whose fluid around the heart was drained surgically at a referral centre in a tuberculosis-endemic region. Needle drainage relieves pericardial effusion quickly, yet fluid tests alone often miss the underlying cause when the disease sits outside the heart. Every patient arrived short of breath, and two thirds showed tamponade or its approach. Surgery succeeded technically in all fifteen cases recorded. Tissue most often showed non-specific chronic inflammation, though it pinned a firm diagnosis in three patients, including two tuberculosis forms and one metastatic cancer. Stay and outcome details round out the series.
pmc-13413091:
Nicholas K Pappa and colleagues set out in 2026 a surgical technique for repairing turf toe, the big-toe joint injury familiar in football and soccer. The injury strikes when the planted toe is forced into extreme bend, tearing the capsule and plantar plate beneath the joint; severe tears in athletes often need surgery. Their method works through a small camera port to inspect the joint and wash out pooled blood before rebuilding the tissue.

Reconstruction uses all-suture knotless anchors, which remove bulky knots that can irritate soft tissue, reinforced with a strip of suture tape across the repair. The authors argue the knot-free build lowers suture burden inside the small joint and may speed recovery. Indications such as gross instability and loose fragments are also reviewed.
pmc-13413491:
Maria João Moreno and colleagues review in 2026 how researchers measure the way small drug-like molecules attach to fatty cell membranes. Readers get a map of the main quantities used in the field, from partition measures to binding descriptions, tied to the assumptions behind them. Limitations receive direct treatment, including how model membranes differ from living ones. The authors aim the synthesis at scientists choosing methods for pharmacokinetic and biophysics questions.
pmc-13414591:
Laura Vitiello and co-authors study how obesity relates to immunity and survival in severe lung disease, reporting in 2026. Seventy patients with advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease were split by body mass index, below or above 30. Blood tests covered inflammation, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and T cell groups.

Patients with obesity showed more lymphocytes and higher CD4 and CD8 T cell counts, alongside lower inflammation scores. Oxidative stress and DNA damage markers matched between groups. A high level of Torque Teno virus in blood appeared more often in leaner patients. Five-year survival did not differ, suggesting body mass alone predicts little here.
pmc-13415491:
Timothy Arnaut and colleagues surveyed 550 American adults in 2026 about food noise, the intrusive food thoughts that disrupt daily life, before and after starting injectable semaglutide for weight control. Most respondents were women with obesity who had used the drug for at least four months, and they recalled their pre-drug thoughts on a five-item questionnaire.

Median food-noise scores fell from 13 to 6 out of 20, and agreement with food-noise statements dropped from roughly half to roughly one in six. The paper gives weight-care teams real-world numbers on a symptom patients describe often but trials rarely measure.
pmc-13415691:
Eugene Li and colleagues engineer plants that glow in proportion to the nitrate they can actually use, in 2026. Soil nitrate swings across place and time, and lab extracts give only snapshots that may not match what roots experience. Their sentinel plants turn nitrate sensing inside living tissue into a measurable light signal.

Sensors tracked nitrate in farm soils while the plants grew in them. The same platform characterized a small microbe team that converts air nitrogen into plant available nitrate. Reading nitrogen through the plant itself ties the measurement to uptake and physiology. Growers could one day watch field nitrogen status continuously rather than by sample runs.
pmc-13417091:
Hebat-Allah S Tohamy builds a bacteria sensing platform from farm waste in a 2026 study, turning pomegranate skin and sugarcane bagasse into carbon based materials. The system spots two common pathogens, Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, by the acid shifts their growth creates. Colour and fluorescence both change in response, giving two readouts at once.

Lab calculations backed the pH switching behaviour. The platform also killed bacteria in tests, hinting at food safety and clinic uses.
pmc-13417491:
Mamdouh Al-Harbi and co-authors study how fermentation length changes compounds made by two sponge linked bacteria from the Red Sea, in a 2026 report. Extract makeup shifted with time, from fatty alcohols and esters early to aromatic compounds later. The longer Enterobacter culture fought Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli more strongly. Film blocking activity varied by strain and timing. Tuning culture length, the authors conclude, is a simple lever for richer natural product yields.
pmc-13417991:
Jiang and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on adding fluorine to a charge-carrying plastic used in wet, salt-based settings. They made two versions of a polymer built for organic electrochemical transistors, devices that switch current in watery fluids. One version carried fluorine on part of its backbone and one did not, and compared both.

Its transistors switched on at a lower voltage, but passed less signal and moved charge more slowly, partly because the material formed fewer ordered crystals. pmc-13419191:
Titilola Gbaja-Biamila and colleagues describe a designathon, a team contest where young people in Nigeria help build HIV prevention services meant for youth. Young people here means ages 14 to 24 years, the group such services most need to reach. Crowd-based design pulls the users of a service into shaping it, which builds ownership and keeps services in use.

Past work links that kind of engagement to better uptake of preventive steps. The paper sets out the contest method in full so other programs can copy or adapt it for their own settings.
pmc-13419991:
Hao Li and colleagues pool studies on whether insulin resistance quietly weakens heart squeeze before any heart failure shows. Insulin resistance drives much cardiometabolic disease, and early muscle weakness can be caught by speckle-tracking ultrasound, a method that follows tiny heart wall movements. Their review covers observational studies in adults only.

Common resistance scores fed the analysis, from hormone-based formulas to fat-based index values. Subgroup work split people with and without type 2 diabetes to see if the link held in both. A firm pooled link would argue for heart checks in people whose sugar control is slipping, long before symptoms begin.
pmc-13420291:

The method joins a midline cut through the breastbone with a side-opening cut, forming a half-clamshell opening. This combined approach gives surgeons wide access to huge tumours that block standard views. The team reviewed care given between 2021 and 2024 at their hospital.

All three patients had the tumour removed together with a lung, a step called pneumonectomy. Two patients developed complications after surgery but recovered well with treatment. The third patient had a smooth recovery with no major problems. The authors present the combined incision as feasible and safe for very large chest tumours in selected patients. They note the series is tiny, so wider use needs more cases and longer follow-up.
pmc-13420591:
Sarah Smith writes a 2026 editorial on hard childhood events and troubled eating habits, and on how loosely the link between them is often drawn. Films and public talk can make disordered eating look like a sure result of early adversity, which flattens very different lives into one simple story.

Smith urges care in tying each kind of early event to each kind of eating behaviour, and in naming what sits between them. Readers get a plea for precise language, so risk is described fairly and no child is written off as bound for illness.
pmc-13421491:
Polten and colleagues report a 2026 study of a new lab model of cervical cancer that lacks the human papillomavirus link found in most cases. pmc-13422091:
Chen-Yi Tang and colleagues mapped a new bone-building pathway in 2026 centered on the receptor Gpr125 and its partner Gper1. pmc-13422291:

pmc-13423991:

pmc-13424091:
Khan and colleagues present in 2026 a quantum computing method for spotting intrusions in network traffic while using as few qubits, the basic units of quantum computers, as possible. Qubits are scarce on today's machines, which limits quantum security tools.

Thresholds are set so the false alarm rate carries a mathematical bound. On one matched comparison it reached accuracy in the mid-ninety percent range with two data qubits instead of four.
pmc-13424891:
Saldarriaga-Muñoz and colleagues studied 83 patients hospitalized with autoimmune bullous diseases. These are blistering conditions where the immune system attacks the skin. pmc-13425991:

pmc-13426491:

The poll went out to chiefs and staff in wards all through the land, and most of those who were asked took the time to write back in full.
pmc-13427091:

pmc-13427491:

pmc-13427791:

pmc-13427991:

pmc-13428291:

pmc-13430691:

pmc-13430891:

pmc-13431991:

pmc-13432491:

pmc-13433691:

pmc-13436091:
He and colleagues reported a 2026 study on forecasting prostate cancer return after surgery. Doctors still lack sharp tools to tell whose cancer will come back. The team mined single-cell data from tumors that had grown resistant to hormone therapy. They then built a score from pairs of genes rather than single genes.

The final score uses 36 gene pairs and was tested in five outside patient groups. It sorted patients by risk with solid accuracy across all five groups. High-risk tumors showed busy immune surroundings and more gene damage overall. Computer tests pointed to one gene, CKS2, as a driver worth deeper study. Because the score uses gene pairs, it works across testing platforms.
pmc-13436291:
Ni Yan's team built a gated silica nanoparticle in 2026 to deliver curcumin to inflamed joint cells in rheumatoid arthritis. Activated joint lining cells drive inflammation and joint damage, and curcumin fits that biology but dissolves poorly, reaches targets weakly, and spreads without selectivity. The team wrapped hollow silica particles in hyaluronan that opens under acid and oxidative signals, aiming for serum-stable carriage plus CD44-linked uptake by joint cells.

The gated particles held curcumin well and leaked little at neutral pH. They released more under joint-like stress, and in rheumatoid joint cells gave stronger curcumin signal and stronger suppression of growth and TNF-driven inflammation than ungated particles. Arthritis teams get a smart carrier design, still in cell studies, that tackles curcumin's oldest delivery problems.
pmc-13436691:
Rockenbach and colleagues trained a deep learning model in 2026 to predict plant gene activity straight from DNA sequence, then probed what the model had learned. Trained on the start and end control regions of genes in oilseed rape and its relative thale cress, the network forecast activity levels for each gene. The aim was to read gene control rules out of the model rather than assume them in advance.

Predictions matched measured activity across plant varieties. Without ever being shown binding data, the model had picked up the preferred positions of some transcription factor families, the proteins that dock on control regions. It judged a pattern's effect by where the pattern sat, not just its presence. Genes whose activity the model missed most tended to receive extra input from distant or chemical-mark control layers. The authors say such models can guide crop gene engineering.
pmc-13437791:
María Isabel Aguirre and colleagues report a heart tumor in a newborn with no earlier case like it. Myxomas are the commonest primary heart tumors in adults but a rarity in babies, and they usually grow in the right atrium. This male infant suffered an unexplained collapse of heart and breathing during recovery.

A stalked, highly mobile mass hung inside the left atrium from the wall above the appendage. With each beat it slipped through the mitral valve, a ball-valve action that could block blood flow and fling clots loose. Surgeons removed it on day twenty-five through the breastbone with the baby on bypass. Tissue study confirmed a myxoma, and the child went home stable. The authors cannot prove the tumor caused the arrest, yet its motion makes blockage a strong suspect. They urge an early heart scan for any newborn with unexplained collapse.
pmc-13437991:
Ozair Naqvi and colleagues describe United States children infected with COVID-19 and influenza at once, a pairing that stayed rare while flu nearly vanished in the pandemic's first years. Their 2026 study drew on a national bank of health records covering March 2020 to April 2024. Among 1.53 million young patients, 10,277 met the team's definition of co-infection: both viruses found within a week.

Most co-infected children were under twelve. Obesity was their commonest prior condition, ahead of asthma. The youngest children, from birth to age four, carried about triple the risk of a severe or moderate course. Children with two or more prior conditions faced a near-triple risk as well. Loosening or tightening the definition barely moved the pattern, which the authors read as a sturdy finding. They offer their records-based definition as a ready tool for future seasons when both viruses circulate.
pmc-13439791:
Kyle Christopher White's team emulated a trial in 2026 of tight fluid control in very sick patients with sudden kidney injury across twelve Queensland intensive care units. Fluid overload harms kidneys, yet restricting fluids may also starve them, and trial evidence was thin. Over eight thousand patients at high risk of positive fluid balance were modeled with a doubly robust longitudinal estimator, comparing conservative crystalloids, limited nutrition fluids, and diuretics against usual care.

Restrictive care cut fluid balance by over two liters at seventy-two hours and modestly improved kidney rank overall. Effects split by severity: stage one improved while stages two and three worsened, with higher thirty-day mortality in advanced stages. Intensivists get a stage-dependent warning: fluid restriction helps early kidney injury but may harm advanced cases. Small effective samples urge cautious interpretation.
pmc-13439991:
Zubkov and colleagues asked in 2026 whether brain scan data gathered with different quantitative MRI protocols can be pooled to study healthy aging of deep brain structures. Quantitative MRI aims to measure tissue properties, such as myelin content, in units that should not depend on the scanner. In practice the numbers still drift between sites and settings, which threatens pooled studies.

The team merged three datasets from ultra-high-field scanners, one built on one measurement scheme and two on another, and compared age trends with and without pooling. Age-related change in the pooled data ran to a sizable share of lifetime average values. One measure differed more between protocols, while a second stayed steadier. The authors show pooling can add power but also bias results, and they map where each measure is safe to combine.
pmc-13442691:
Jan Stupacher and colleagues test whether company boosts the joy of moving to music in Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Forty people with mild to mid disease tapped to beats of varied rhythmic density, beside 36 peers of like age. Tapping ran in three setups: alone with music, with music plus a visual beat cue, or shared with a helper who tapped along.

Shared tapping lifted the urge to move, felt sync, beat energy, and timing steadiness past music alone. Gains peaked with mid to dense rhythms, and gains ran stronger in patients than in peers. Visual cues changed nothing in this setup. Urge scores also rose with felt closeness to the helper and with trait empathy. The authors back group music work as a low-cost add-on for movement care.
pmc-13443291:
Changyan Yang and colleagues review XPO1, a cell export gate, as a cancer drug target in a 2026 paper. The gate ships tumor guards such as p53 and Rb out of the cell core, where they lose their voice. Many cancers overbuild or overfire the gate, which frees growth and blunts cell death.

Blocker drugs, called SINE compounds, jam the gate and trap guards back in the core. The lead drug, selinexor, has reached clinic use in blood cancers and faces tests in solid tumors. Solo use shows caps, from harm to weak reach. The review weighs paired plans that may lift gains, plus trial paths ahead. The authors frame gate jamming as a young but real arm of cancer care.
pmc-13443791:
Keally Haushalter and coauthors report a 2026 analysis of how shifting food insecurity tracks home food availability in families from TX Sprouts. TX Sprouts is a gardening, cooking, and nutrition trial for mainly Hispanic, low-income pupils in grades 3 to 5. Parents of 839 children reported household insecurity and home stocks of vegetables and sugary drinks at baseline and nine months later.

In the control group, each one-point rise in insecurity linked to fewer vegetables at home, while in the intervention group the same rise linked to more sugary drinks at home. The split analysis followed an interaction between insecurity change and the program for vegetables. The findings suggest garden programs must also buffer families against insecurity shocks, since produce gains alone may not hold.
pmc-13443891:
Vahid Mehrtash and colleagues present a 2026 self-supervised learning method that tells myelodysplastic neoplasms apart from look-alike conditions using only bone marrow biopsy images. Diagnosis today leans on dysplasia spotting that varies between observers, and aspirate smears sometimes fail, so the team trained an image model to capture the morphology that marks the disease.

The model discriminated disease biopsies from mimics accurately, worked across institutions, needed little tissue, and highlighted the key features behind its calls. That interpretability matters in pathology, where a black-box verdict earns little trust. Clinics gain a reproducibility aid for a tricky diagnosis, though prospective trials must confirm performance before routine use.
pmc-13444191:
Jae Hun Kim reviews hyaluronidase as a helper in spine shots and procedures in a 2026 paper. The enzyme chews hyaluronic acid in tissue, which opens paths for injected drugs to spread. Scar and fibrotic tissue in the spine often wall drugs into pockets, a cap this helper may lift.

Studies show better spread of numbing drugs and steroids, with pain and function gains in back shots of three kinds. Gains look clearest in failed back surgery cases, where scar runs thick. Proof for scope-based scar cutting stays mixed, since some gains trace to the cut work alone. Rare allergy shocks mark the main risk. The author casts the enzyme as a support act, not a solo cure, pending strict trials.
pmc-13444491:
Madison Meyer and colleagues report a neuromyelitis optica case that mimicked salt-linked brain harm in a 2026 paper. A 54-year-old woman with high blood pressure and a past gastric bypass came in with numbness, weakness, dizziness, and blurred sight. Her blood sodium sat at a severe low of 115 mmol per liter at that visit.

Care fixed her sodium under close watch, and she went home stable. Weeks later, fresh nerve signs hit, and MRI showed bright marks in both mammillary bodies, neck cord columns, and a spot at C2-C3. Salt-swing harm was the first suspect, given her past low. Deeper checks confirmed neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder instead. The authors note just one past twin case with this mimic shape.
pmc-13445591:
Noriko Kato and colleagues report three patients with Ewing sarcoma of the shoulder blade treated with chemotherapy and carbon ion radiation, rating both cancer control and arm function, published in 2026. The tumor is rare, strikes mostly the young, and seldom starts in the shoulder blade. Heavy particle radiation offers a path that may spare surgery.

The patients were a seventy-five-year-old man, a forty-year-old man, and a thirty-two-year-old woman, treated at two centers in Japan. The two men stayed free of disease two and a half years after treatment, with fair to good shoulder scores. The woman kept fine shoulder motion at three years, though lung spread persisted, and her care included a bout of skin reaction treated with strong pain drugs and steroids.
pmc-13446291:
Karolina Stirblyte and colleagues review how fat handling shapes a rare immune cell's fight against ovarian cancer, in a 2026 paper. The cancer often spreads to a fatty apron in the belly, a rich niche that feeds tumors and dulls immunity. Gamma delta T cells, the focus here, can kill cancer cells without the usual targeting steps, which makes their state in that niche key.

Patient samples show the fatty setting drives these cells to gulp lipids and burn fat for fuel, and long exposure wears their power plants down and raises off-switches. The two main subsets split in habit: one leans on fat burning and can aid tumors, the other on sugar and starves where glucose runs low. The review weighs drug and particle plans to retune the cells.
pmc-13447191:
Nathan Mugenyi and co-authors review drug-resistant infections through a One Health lens in 2026, linking human, animal and environmental health. Resistance harms patients, raises costs and hits low-resource settings hardest. Drivers cross farm, clinic and ecosystem boundaries, so single-sector fixes often fall short.

Literature from 2013 to early 2025 was gathered across several databases plus global reports. Five themes stood out, covering burden, how resistance works, shared drivers, weak tracking and stewardship replies. Misuse of antibiotics in care and farming, poor sanitation and thin lab capacity drove spread, while tracking systems left large gaps. The authors urge joined-up surveillance, wastewater checks and stronger labs in poorer countries as immediate policy steps, warning that delay will deepen the toll.
pmc-13447291:
Qi-ou Chen and colleagues build a personal simulation for night-worn contact lenses that reshape the cornea in 2026 work. Such lenses give clear daytime vision and slow short-sight growth in children, yet standard designs ignore each eye's uneven shape and blinking forces. Roughly a third of wearers get off-centre lenses or fading effect under standard fitting, the authors note.

Real corneal map data fed a patient-specific computer model that includes lopsided anatomy and a refined pressure pattern from the lens. Predicted treatment zones and power change matched clinical measures closely on several accuracy checks. Tests then varied lens zone size and target correction to see how tissue response shifts. The framework aims to support lens choices tuned to the individual eye rather than trial and error alone.
pmc-13447491:
Jing Li and colleagues reanalyse a calligraphy trial in older adults with self-perceived thinking decline in 2026 work. Regular mentally engaging hobbies link to lower dementia risk, and a parent trial showed doubled brush calligraphy practice improved working memory. Whether practice also reshapes two attention and control brain networks was the open question for this secondary look.

One hundred twelve community-dwelling Chinese adults aged fifty-five to seventy-five, all with prior calligraphy experience, were assigned to usual practice or doubled weekly practice for six months. Brain scans at rest measured connection strength within networks before and after. The doubled group gained a stronger link between two named regions inside the salience network, which helps switch attention. No clear change appeared in the executive control network, giving a localised rather than broad effect.
pmc-13447791:
Pasangi Perera and colleagues link partner violence to later drug use across partnership types in a 2026 longitudinal United States study. Violence between partners tracks with harmful drug use, especially in same-sex couples who also face minority stress. A national study following adolescents into adulthood allowed violence reports in the late 2000s to be tied to drug use a decade later.

Over seven thousand participants were analysed, with about a quarter reporting partner violence experience. People who only experienced violence, or both experienced and used it, faced higher drug use risk than those reporting none. Patterns looked similar for same-sex and opposite-sex couples overall, with wide uncertainty in small subgroups. Women who experienced violence showed clearer elevations in risk. Tailored support by gender and partnership type is recommended.
pmc-13448491:
Rui Lv and colleagues study how added organic matter changes the strength and electrical behaviour of loess soil in 2026 laboratory work. Loess in northern China is loose and poor in organic content, yet adding organic material is promoted for carbon storage and soil repair. How much organic matter and water help or harm engineering strength needed controlled testing, with electrical signals tracked during pressing.

Specimens spanning zero to six percent organic matter and a range of water contents were compressed while resistivity was monitored live. Moderate organic additions improved mechanical behaviour, while wetter soil grew weaker throughout. Electrical resistance fell fast as stress rose, then steadied after the elastic stage until failure, when new cracks rerouted current paths. Organic amendment design for loess land can draw on those linked patterns.
pmc-13449191:
Melanie Firestone, Alexandra Edmundson, and Craig Hedberg report in 2026 a survey of how Minnesota consumers handle frozen vegetables and potatoes, foods sold as not ready to eat. Frozen vegetables have been tied to Salmonella and Listeria outbreaks, yet shoppers often see them as safe. The team collected 1,719 completed surveys from adult Minnesota residents at the 2023 state fair, asking what they ate in the past year and how they prepared it.

Most respondents had eaten frozen vegetables, 91.3 percent, and frozen potatoes, 80.1 percent. Even so, 15.7 percent had eaten at least one vegetable type raw, straight from the bag. Leafy greens led at 38.4 percent eaten raw, then carrots at 17.6 percent, while raw frozen potatoes were almost unheard of. Strikingly, over a third of people who said they always follow cooking instructions for leafy greens still ate them raw, flagging where safety messages fail.
pmc-13449491:
Muzaffer Barut and Leyla Sezen Tansi profiled ninety basil lines in 2026 to find top types for drugs and skin care. Basil is prized for its oils and other plant chemicals, but growers need lines that yield well and hold up in a given climate. The team grew the set in the Mediterranean sun over the 2023 and 2024 seasons.

Field plots used a block layout, and lab work measured plant phenols, power to mop up free radicals by two tests, and oil makeup by gas chromatography. The results show which lines pair strong chemistry with steady field yields. Growers can now pick types matched to drug or skin-care use instead of sowing seed of unknown quality.
pmc-13449891:
Voss and colleagues compared three greener routes to methanol in 2026, a key chemical and fuel, using life cycle assessment, cost analysis, and expert scoring for Germany. The routes make methanol from biomass, from waste, or by a power-to-X path that builds it from electricity, water, and captured carbon. Each path differs in energy demand, yield, climate impact, and cost.

Wood and packaging waste feedstocks improved both environmental and cost results, since they reuse carbon already in circulation and avoid landfill. The power-to-X route, by contrast, gave far higher emissions and costs under current conditions, largely due to the price and carbon load of today's electricity supply. Expert scoring kept the same ranking. The authors offer the numbers as timely input for industry and policy choices on cleaning up carbon-heavy sectors.
pmc-13450491:
Harold Nathan Tan and colleagues argue in 2026 that kidney checks used to admit patients to early cancer drug trials need an update. The old Cockcroft-Gault formula, still in wide use, rests on body weight and muscle mass, traits that cancer often changes. A wrong score can shut out a fit patient or let a frail one take a risky dose.

The authors back newer race-free formulas that pair creatinine with cystatin C, a blood marker that is less tied to muscle. Direct measures of kidney function should be kept for cases near a cutoff or where a drug is hard on the kidneys. They also warn that sites with poor lab access need shared labs and referral paths, so entry rules stay fair across regions.
pmc-13450591:
Mingzhi Yu and co-authors build in 2026 a fast way to sift fat bubble recipes that carry gene-silencing RNA into cells. The bubbles, lipid nanoparticles, vary across a huge space of mixes, so hand testing is slow. Their setup pairs tiny fluid channels that make many batches with learning models that guess which mixes will work.

The team made a library of 864 mixes, tested about 200 empty bubbles, and let the models rank the rest by size and spread. Twenty-five picks were loaded with RNA and tested in cells and in mice. Two lipid types silenced the target gene best, and one type gathered most in the lungs, a sign that lab traits alone cannot pick a winner.
pmc-13451791:
Michael Wunderle and a large team scan the eyes in 2026 for hidden nerve and vessel marks of long COVID. The back of the eye gives a painless view of small vessels and nerve layers that mirror the brain. Their group compared patients with lasting post-COVID symptoms to peers who had recovered, and also drew blood marks of vessel strain and swelling.

Eye vessel density did not differ between the groups once age and sex were counted. Yet three nerve layer measures ran thinner in the symptom group, and thinner values tracked heavier symptoms. One swelling signal in blood tied to thinner layers as well. The authors read the pattern as nerve wear, not vessel loss.
pmc-13451891:
Julia Pasqualini Genro and co-authors argue in 2026 that female sex in mental health is more than a risk score entry. A large Brazilian study that tracked suicide bids over fifteen years found female sex among the strongest flags, even with genes, birth facts, and family history counted. World data also place anxiety and deep low mood higher in women.

The piece sets those gaps next to Brazil's toll of gender violence, where most rape victims are girls and femicide hit a record in 2024. Black women bear the largest share of that toll. The authors press for care and policy that treat sex as a lived context shaped by violence and unequal loads, not a bare number.
pmc-13452291:
Li and Dooreemeah published a 2026 case report on a rare kidney placement quirk. In crossed renal ectopia, one kidney sits on the wrong side of the body. In the nonfused form, the two kidneys stay separate rather than joining. Most people with this quirk feel no symptoms at all.

Their patient, a 35-year-old man, came in after an alleged assault. A trauma scan showed no injury but found both kidneys on the right side. The left kidney space sat empty, yet the stray kidney drained to the correct side. Careful scan tracing proved the kidneys had not fused together. Knowing this pattern stops mix-ups with a missing kidney and guides safe surgery. Once doctors know the pattern for sure, most such cases need no treatment at all.
pmc-13452391:
Kavithra Harihararajah and six co-authors review what drug coated balloons do to the fatty plaque inside heart arteries during acute coronary syndrome. That term covers sudden heart events such as heart attacks. Their 2026 review asks whether balloon treatment shrinks or changes plaque rather than leaving a metal stent behind.

The team searched four large databases and kept six studies that used vessel scans to track plaque after treatment. Across those studies, treated arteries showed less plaque area or volume and a wider open channel for blood flow. Some studies also found less fatty core material and lower calcium scores than stent based care. The authors warn that the studies differed a lot in design and measures, so larger trials are still needed.
pmc-13452491:
Kirill K Gubanov and a large team report a surprise: oxygen gas can help, not harm, one class of organic materials that carry electric charge. Left in oxygen, the pair did not lose electrons as feared; its charge sharing grew stronger instead. The team credits oxygen with calming electron trap states, the flaws that normally catch moving charge. Light output from the material tripled, and charge flowed more freely as well. The same lift showed up in other donor and acceptor pairs, which suggests the trick could serve a wide range of organic electronics.
pmc-13454291:
Andrea I Costantino and five colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, what changes in the brain when a novice becomes an expert. Using chess as their test case, the team combined brain scans with pattern analysis methods. They looked at what expert brains encode, how those codes are organized, and where in the brain the work happens.

Three patterns stood out. Skilled players represented high-level relations between pieces more than surface looks. Their brain codes were also more compact and better organized, yet still kept fine detail for judging positions. Activity shifted away from sense-based areas toward front and parietal regions that support general thinking. The authors sum this up as packing richer knowledge into fewer, tidier brain patterns.
pmc-13454491:
Li Chen leads a ten-author team that built, in 2026, a short scale measuring how capable parents feel while their baby is in intensive care. The team drafted 15 items from past research, expert review, and parent focus groups.

The scale was tested on 350 main caregivers across eight units in Suzhou, China. Statistical checks confirmed four parts matching the intended skills. Scores held together well, with total reliability near 0.84 on a standard index. Higher agency lined up modestly with lower parental stress, while links to general health stayed near zero. Parents who had been through the unit before scored higher on talking with staff and on emotional steadiness. The authors offer the scale for family-centered care programs.
pmc-13454691:
Aswin Babu, Ciara Kennedy, Travis Chong, and Jon Spiro present, in 2026, a case where artery spasm, not blockage, stopped a man's heart during the hours after exercise. The patient, aged 51, collapsed with a lethal rhythm and was revived. His case fits MINOCA, a heart attack pattern where the main arteries show no obstruction.

Scans found open arteries and a structurally normal heart, yet a blood marker confirmed fresh heart injury. Full function testing then provoked clear artery spasm meeting all three international criteria for the diagnosis. Treatment tailored to spasm began at once. The authors argue that MINOCA is a working label, not an answer, and that function testing should follow unexplained arrest. They also raise defibrillator fitting for survivors of spasm-related arrest, decided jointly with the patient.
pmc-13454891:
Jasmine L. Hect and six colleagues present, in a 2026 study, rare causal evidence for how the brain sorts voices from other sounds. Most proof in this field only shows correlation. Their chance came from a child patient whose tumor surgery had removed front and middle parts of the left temporal lobe. Two rear hearing areas were spared, with electrodes recording directly from the brain.

One spared area answered voices selectively, while its neighbor answered all sounds without caring about category. During a voice-versus-noise choice task, brief electrical pulses to either area knocked out the child's sorting ability, reversibly, while control sites did nothing. Tracing methods showed the two areas still wired to each other in both directions. The authors conclude that voice recognition needs both areas working together, not either one alone.
pmc-13454991:
Wang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how one small regulatory RNA, miR-200c, steers three different routes of cell death and what that means for disease treatment. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that dial gene activity up or down after genes are read. MiR-200c was first known for its role in cancer spread, but newer work ties it to several death programs in cells.

The review maps how miR-200c influences apoptosis, the tidy self-destruct program; pyroptosis, an inflammatory bursting death; and autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup that can tip into death. For each route it lists the gene targets and signal pathways involved across cancers and other diseases. Because one molecule touches all three programs, the authors discuss miR-200c as a possible drug target and disease marker.
pmc-13455391:
Taqwa Abdeljawad and colleagues track a stubborn hospital germ in Palestine over seven years in a 2026 study. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia resists many antibiotics and threatens intensive care patients, yet local patterns in Palestine were thin. The team reviewed 177 unique isolates from a tertiary hospital between 2018 and 2024, testing three drugs and tracing trends by ward, specimen and prior exposures.

The germ appeared in 1.08 percent of cultures, with no steady yearly trend, and respiratory samples led while over a third came from intensive care settings. Cotrimoxazole and levofloxacin stayed active in about 80.2 and 78.5 percent of isolates, while ceftazidime fared worse, and resistance to all three drugs hit 5.6 percent overall but 21.7 percent in intensive care. Prior antibiotics, COVID-19 and device use each linked with resistance to a specific drug, backing steady surveillance and stewardship.
pmc-13456791:
Wail Alqatta and Wasim Al-Harethee compare, in a 2026 case series, two rare tumors growing beside the aorta, one hormone-active and one silent. Paragangliomas arise from nerve-like tissue and can flood the body with stress hormones. Both patients were men treated with surgical removal.

The first, aged 45, had blood pressure spikes, headaches, and palpitations, and tests confirmed hormone excess. His mass sat at the aortic fork and measured about three centimeters. After drug blockade tamed the hormones, surgeons removed it in 135 minutes with little blood loss, and his symptoms and hormone levels normalized. The second man, aged 52, had vague belly discomfort and normal hormone tests. His five-centimeter tumor came out without blockade in 160 minutes. The authors stress tailoring preparation to whether the tumor secretes.
pmc-13456991:
Xinhua Song and seven colleagues report, in a 2026 case, cat-scratch disease turning up in the brain of an elderly man three months after the scratch. The patient, an 85-year-old East Asian man with heart disease and high blood pressure, first developed abrupt, very high fever. Night delirium with vivid hallucinations followed, then a seizure-like spell and a headache at the back of the head.

Examination found swollen lymph nodes under both arms, while spinal fluid tests for bacteria and fungi came back empty. Gene sequencing of his blood found the culprit, Bartonella henselae, the cat-scratch germ. Antibiotics aimed at it cleared his fever and headache. The authors urge doctors facing fever with delirium to ask about cat contact, even months back, and to start targeted antibiotics early rather than lose days to the search.
pmc-13457191:
Muhuan Liu, Jinglan He, and Jizhen Zhou map two decades of research on macrophages in intervertebral disc degeneration, the disc breakdown behind much low back pain. After cleaning the records, 550 publications remained for analysis with CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and the bibliometrix package. Output surged after 2021, with China and the United States as the largest contributors and limited collaboration between countries. Keyword clusters grouped the field into five areas, from disease mechanisms to clinical diagnostics. Burst terms such as single-cell sequencing, oxidative stress, and injectable hydrogels mark the current frontier, and the authors read the field as shifting toward precise immune-based and regenerative treatments.
pmc-13457391:

Their 2026 study recruited 171 outpatients aged 12 to 19 with depressive disorders and school refusal at one clinic, collecting teenagers' own answers and parents' versions.

Dropping two ill-fitting items left a four-factor structure fitting both informants well, with comparative fit indices of 0.99 for parents and 0.98 for adolescents. Subscale reliability ranged from marginal to good, weakest for one parent-reported factor. Avoidance of unpleasant school situations scored highest in both reports, fitting a depressed sample. Teenagers rated escape from social judgment and pursuit of tangible rewards higher than their parents did; agreement between generations was only fair to good. The authors recommend always gathering both perspectives.
pmc-13458291:
Tao Ren and colleagues measure blood flow in freshly transplanted kidneys using a magnetic resonance technique that needs no injected contrast. Their study scanned 53 recipients two to four weeks after surgery, plus 20 healthy volunteers, with arterial spin labeling MRI, which magnetically tags the blood itself as a tracer.

Cortical flow stepped down in a clean ladder: 389.9 milliliters per 100 grams per minute in healthy kidneys, 295.0 in grafts with good function, and 195.5 in grafts whose filtration rate fell below 60. The three groups differed significantly, and flow correlated moderately with filtration rate across recipients, at R equal to 0.62. The authors present the scan as a repeatable, non-contrast way to quantify graft perfusion early, potentially flagging struggling kidneys before standard markers catch up.
pmc-13459691:
Oluwagbenro O. Adesunloro, Amanda N. Tuckey, Jonathon P. Audia, and Allyson E. Shea argue in a 2026 minireview that amyloid-beta, the protein fragment infamous in Alzheimer disease, may also defend the brain against infection. Plaques built from this fragment have long been read purely as damage. Evidence from clinical reports, animal work, and laboratory studies instead suggests the fragment is produced when microbes invade.

Acting much like an antimicrobial peptide, amyloid-beta can disrupt microbial membranes and trap invaders, while also sending inflammatory signals that rally immune defense. The reviewers gather this evidence to broaden how the molecule is understood. Their framing raises a delicate question for Alzheimer research: blocking a defense molecule could carry costs alongside any benefit.
pmc-13460191:
Zhuqing Zhang and co-authors pooled in 2026 eleven studies to test whether the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio predicts lung inflammation caused by lung cancer treatments. Two hazards were examined: pneumonitis triggered by immune checkpoint drugs and pneumonitis caused by radiation. The combined data covered 2,439 patients, of whom about twelve percent developed one of these lung injuries.

Overall, the blood ratio showed no link with immune pneumonitis of any grade. The picture changed for severe cases, where a high ratio came with nearly eightfold odds of grade three or worse immune pneumonitis. Radiation pneumonitis also tracked with high values, roughly tripling the odds in non-small cell lung cancer. The authors call for more studies before the cheap test guides decisions.
pmc-13461391:
Manfred G. Moertl leads a team that tracked in 2026 how a pregnant woman's autonomic nervous system, the automatic controller of heart and vessels, adapts across the three trimesters. Sixty-seven healthy pregnant women completed a standard testing session each trimester combining rest, paced breathing, and a mental task. Heart rate variability, blood pressure, and the sync between heart and breathing were recorded continuously.

Heart rate climbed across pregnancy and blood pressure dipped mid-pregnancy as expected. Vagal activity, the calming branch's signature, declined steadily, yet the balance between branches stayed level. Responses dulled late in pregnancy: reactions to paced breathing and to mental stress both weakened, and heart-breathing coupling loosened. The authors frame the profile as flexibility narrowing while basic responsiveness survives, offering a healthy reference curve.
pmc-13461591:
Liping Lu and colleagues report a 2026 trial of virtual reality for children with burns during dressing changes and early rehabilitation. Dressing changes hurt and frighten children, and distress can make them resist care. In virtual reality, a headset places the child inside a cartoon world that holds attention away from the procedure. The trial ran in one hospital burn unit in China from 2023 into 2026.

Eighty children who needed repeated dressing changes were split at random into two groups. One group had routine care with standard distraction, while the other wore the headset during care and rehab sessions. The first two dressing changes showed little difference between groups. By the third change, children using virtual reality reported less pain and fear, showed less distress, and cooperated better with dressing and rehab. No serious side effects occurred, though session length and need for extra pain medicine did not change.
pmc-13461791:

The team built the new scale through literature review, expert checks, and a pilot with working professionals, then tested it on two groups of Hungarian university students in sport programs.

A model with one general attitude factor plus the four parts fit the data best, and the full scale scored high on internal consistency. pmc-13462891:
Choi and colleagues in South Korea built in 2026 a fast gene test for the germ that spots strawberry leaves and can halve a crop. The germ is a banned pest in many lands, so nurseries must catch it young. Strain shifts across lands had foiled past tests. The team set the germ's full code against kin germs and pulled out a stretch found in it alone. A primer pair was built on that stretch.

The test lit up for this germ and no close kin. It found the germ at faint loads: a few score gene copies, or a trace of germ mass, in a drop. Best of all, it read germs straight off sick leaves, with no lab clean step. That speed suits border checks and field screens. The team pitches it for watch lists at plant hubs.
pmc-13463091:
Yahua Li and colleagues tested a heat-sensitive liquid plug carrying the drug lobaplatin in 2026 for liver tumours in rabbits. The treatment, called chemoembolization, blocks tumour blood flow while dosing drug locally, but older oily mixes leak drug into the bloodstream. Drug levels inside tumours ran highest with the new plug and lowest with infusion alone. Marker shifts also favoured the new plug, though animal results still need human trials before clinics adopt it.
pmc-13463591:
Patricia Egli leads a team that measured plasma homocysteine in horses with left-sided valve disease. Homocysteine is an amino acid used in human medicine as a sign of blood vessel strain. The team first checked how blood handling and storage change readings from the horse assay.

Readings stayed steady for at least four hours in three tube types, and frozen blood survived up to five thaw cycles. Levels rose slightly with age and with creatinine, a kidney marker. Levels showed no link to heart size, heart function, or how severe the valve leak was. The authors judge the test far less useful for horse heart risk than it is for people.
pmc-13463991:
Guan and colleagues built a machine-learning warning system in 2026 for delirium in intensive care. The target was elderly patients with underactive thyroids, a group at special risk for this sudden confusion. Two large American critical-care databases supplied the data. One trained and tested the model, and the other checked it independently. Candidate variables were sifted down to 13. Nine learning approaches were compared.

On the outside database it scored about 79. The strongest warning signs included consciousness and organ-failure scores. Sedative use, days in intensive care, blood oxygen, calcium, and average blood pressure mattered too. The team wrapped the model in a simple interface. It aims to flag at-risk patients earlier than bedside checks needing patients awake and talking.
pmc-13464291:
Amarpal Karamjit Singh and colleagues report a 2026 pacemaker case that restored natural atrial timing in a 74-year-old man. Sinus node disease and intermittent fibrillation had left him with a long P-wave and first-degree block, and drugs failed to control rate and rhythm. The team implanted a dual-chamber pacemaker with leads at the Bachmann bundle and the left bundle branch.

Capturing the bundle, the heart's preferred bridge between atria, shortened the P-wave and normalised the PR interval, restoring interatrial and atrioventricular synchrony. Conventional appendage pacing cannot match that physiology, the authors argue. Bundle pacing may thus suit patients with sinus disease and atrial rhythm trouble, though wider trials must confirm lasting benefit.
pmc-13464591:
Igor Y. Iskusnykh and three co-authors review redox pairs, matched chemical forms that shuttle electrons, in aging and brain disease. Mitochondria, the cell power units, suffer early and pass the harm onward. Lab strategies to top up the charged forms close the survey as candidate shields for aging brains.
pmc-13465191:
Varaona-Santos and colleagues surveyed women online in 2026 about whether addictive social media use dulls sexual desire. Participants completed validated questionnaires on social media addiction, sexual desire, and depressive symptoms. Questions about age and living arrangements were included. The anonymous study was cross-sectional, recruited through convenience and snowball sampling.

Heavier addiction scores went with lower desire, confirming the core association. The relationship was not simple, though. Age, depressive symptoms, and living with a partner together explained a substantial share of it. Age was the strongest single predictor. Older women reported lower desire than younger women at equal addiction and mood levels. Women living with a partner scored about one and a half points lower on the desire scale than comparable women living apart. The authors urge clinicians to weigh mood and relationship context, not screen time alone.
pmc-13465391:
Yupei Xiang, Bing Fan, and Bo Liu report a belly wall abscess caused by Mycolicibacterium neworleansense, a rare non-tuberculous germ. A seventy-four-year-old man with type 2 diabetes developed the abscess at his long-used insulin injection site on the left abdomen. Such germs usually enter through injury or medical procedures.

Surgeons cut and drained the abscess, and pus cultures grew the slow germ. Gene sequencing plus chemistry tests named the species exactly. Drug tests showed resistance to macrolides and tetracyclines, yet openness to a sulfa drug, shot-based antibiotics, moxifloxacin, and imipenem. Surgery plus the sulfa drug and moxifloxacin cleared the infection fully, a template for like cases.
pmc-13466091:
Carlos A. Amado and colleagues reviewed a mitochondrial microprotein in 2026 as a candidate marker and treatment for inflamed lungs. MOTS-c, encoded inside the mitochondrial genome, steadies metabolism and counters stress, inflammation, and cell death across tissues. The review gathers lab and clinical evidence across acute distress, chronic lung disease, and lung cancer.

Blood levels of MOTS-c fall in acute respiratory distress and in chronic obstructive disease, sleep apnoea, and asthma, while added MOTS-c eased lung injury in animal models. Remote limb preconditioning may protect partly by releasing it, while early lung cancer hints at higher levels that need confirmation. Well-run human trials must test whether raising MOTS-c changes disease course or merely marks it.
pmc-13466291:
Christopher Hale, Zhigang Xu, Prithu Dhar, and Jagannathan Sankar study how heat treatment after rolling, and a zinc addition, change the shaping ability of a magnesium alloy, in a 2026 study. Rolling with mismatched roll speeds refines the alloy's grains and strengthens it, yet leaves a strong crystal alignment that limits bending and stretching. Earlier passes cut thickness by twenty or forty percent at high temperature.

Annealing afterward let new, strain-free grains grow through the metal, nearly completing at the hottest, longest setting tested. Crystal alignment weakened, stress markers fell, and stretch before breaking rose well above the as-rolled level. Electron imaging tracked each stage. The findings guide processors who need magnesium sheet that forms without cracking.
pmc-13466391:
Yun Wang and a large team dissect how a wheat head blight fungus resists a newer fungicide, using gene and chemical profiling together, in a 2026 study. The resistant strain carried paired changes in two subunits of the target enzyme, which kept its energy output and drug resistance stable without visible fitness cost. In the sensitive strain, spraying crashed enzyme activity, energy stores, and toxin output while cell membranes leaked. Wide profiling showed layered defenses beyond the target changes, which the authors map for resistance watchers.
pmc-13466491:
Patryk Jarnot built a search method in 2026 for protein motifs with skewed amino acid mixes, which standard homology tools handle poorly. Such motifs anchor membrane proteins, bind RNA through RGG boxes, and can form prions, yet many were long dismissed and masked in searches. The new method blends three alignment strategies, a motif finder for similar mixes, two-letter filtering, and a fresh alignment score.

Tests against BLAST on membrane domains and RGG boxes raised true positives markedly, with the new score giving the largest gain. Global and global-local alignments also captured all submotifs of a complex polymerase query more often than local alignment alone. Better searches for biased motifs should rescue overlooked domains and sharpen functional annotation across protein families.
pmc-13466691:
Padula and four co-authors linked wildfire smoke to birth defects in this study from twenty twenty-six. About three thousand pregnancies in California's San Joaquin Valley were studied across two national programs. Smoke exposure in the first eight weeks was estimated from fire-related fine particles. Fourteen structural defects were checked against exposure levels.

Higher smoke quartiles raised the odds of several defects. Cleft lip roughly doubled in one exposure band. A heart vessel defect doubled at the highest band. Spina bifida rose consistently across several exposure measures, tripling in the top one. The authors say early-pregnancy smoke may contribute to these defects. They call for confirmation and work on the underlying mechanisms.
pmc-13466791:
Chunmei Wang and colleagues build a six-gene forecast for liver cancer tied to aflatoxin B1, a potent mold toxin in contaminated food, in a 2026 analysis. The toxin is a proven cause of this cancer, above all where diets carry it alongside hepatitis B infection. Gene and clinical records for 377 liver cancer cases came from a public cancer atlas.

Thousands of genes differed between tumor and normal tissue. The team crossed those with predicted toxin targets gathered from three chemical databases, then used network methods to shrink the list to a compact signature. Binding simulations checked how the toxin might grip the signature's proteins. The model aims at prognosis for a cancer subtype that generic tools may fit poorly.
pmc-13466891:
Skowrońska and colleagues report a 2026 study testing a new softener for starch-based films, a candidate material for greener packaging. Plasticizers keep starch films flexible instead of brittle, but common ones soak up moisture eagerly. The salt choline dihydrogencitrate was tried, for the first time, as the only plasticizer in potato starch films at several loadings.

Spectroscopy and X-ray measures showed the salt breaks up starch's crystalline regions, the first job of a true plasticizer. Mechanical and thermal tests confirmed the films grew more flexible, and twenty-five percent by weight gave the best balance of clarity and strength. The films also absorbed less moisture than films made with standard plasticizers. A less thirsty starch film could hold up in humid storage, one of the weak points that has kept starch packaging niche.
pmc-13466991:
Sergiusz Napierała and colleagues build an iron complex whose color shifts with electric voltage, in a 2026 chemistry study. The molecule pairs a stiff light-active backbone with a salen-type ligand holding two iron centers linked by oxygen bridges. Crystal analysis confirmed the paired structure and its slightly distorted geometry.

Earlier iron-salen color changers were single-center and showed limited interplay between their halves. Here the bridge couples the two sides electronically, splitting the ligand's oxidation steps into distinct events that a voltage sweep can read. Spectroscopic tools watched the color and absorption change as the voltage moved, the core test for an electrochromic material.
pmc-13467291:
Aleksander Zelias and a large team review the first years of their robot-assisted heart artery program, comparing early cases with later ones, in a 2026 single-center study. Robotic stenting shields staff from radiation and may sharpen precision, yet switching from hand work brings an undefined learning curve. One hundred two patients treated with a second-generation system between 2021 and early 2024 entered the analysis.

The cohort averaged sixty-eight years and was mostly male. Angiographic success, defined by full flow and a narrow remaining narrowing, reached one hundred percent. Splitting the series into equal early and late halves let the team trace how patient mix, lesion difficulty, and the need for unplanned manual help evolved with practice.
pmc-13467391:
Coppini and colleagues ran a 2026 pilot study tracking saliva microbes in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma, a mouth cancer, before and after tumor removal. Saliva testing is painless, so microbial shifts could one day aid monitoring. Sixteen patients gave samples at both time points, and ten cancer-free people served as a comparison group.

Microbial diversity also fell after the operation. The patients' profiles differed from the healthy group at both points, suggesting disease-linked imbalance. The authors stress the small size and missing surgical details make the results a starting hypothesis, not a clinical tool.
pmc-13467791:
Ioannis Panagiotopoulos, Donald Huisingh, and Emmanuel Koukios review in 2026 how to pretreat tough plant residues so microbes can ferment them into hydrogen fuel. Lignocellulosic biomass, the fibrous leftovers of farming and forestry, must be opened up before its sugars become available. Most pretreatment research chases maximum sugar release, yet a harsher treatment can leave behind a liquid that hydrogen-making microbes cannot use well.

The review judges each pretreatment family by the fermentability of what it produces, not just its sugar yield. Only a few of the well-studied approaches emerge as good candidates for biohydrogen. The best choice also depends on the biomass itself and on what the chosen microbes can eat and tolerate. The authors call for integrated optimization that designs pretreatment around the fermentation that follows it, a shift they argue the field has been slow to make.
pmc-13467991:
Yi-Zhen Gong and colleagues report a prospective study, published in 2026. It tests a simple metabolic index as a survival marker in cancer patients. The index is called TyG-BMI. It combines blood fat and sugar measures with body mass index. It estimates insulin resistance. The team compared it with related indices. They studied 5,221 Chinese patients across several hospitals.

This held especially in oesophageal and colorectal cancers. The index can be calculated from routine tests. It could flag patients needing early nutritional support. Its accuracy alone is modest, the authors note.
pmc-13468391:
Larisa-Mălina Cătăuță and colleagues resolve in 2026 a mismatch between the official quality standard for black cohosh and the chemistry of the plant itself. They were missing from the reference dry extract and other shop extracts, which explains the fingerprint gap: processing changes the profile. Cultivated plants also carried too little of the markers before extraction, though the finished extract met the monograph requirements. The study tells regulators and growers exactly where plant chemistry and the official paperwork diverge.
pmc-13468591:
Jia-Yuan He and Hao Zhang build in 2026 a color-changing sensor for the pollutant 2,4-dichlorophenol out of copper nanosheets coordinated with HEPES, a common laboratory buffer. The sensor read the pollutant linearly across the tested range with a detection limit of 0.3 micromolar, and it was applied to real water samples. The sheets can also help decolorize dyes. pmc-13468691:

pmc-13468891:

Starved to 50 training cases, it still held an area of 0.76, clearly beating comparison models. On an independent external cohort it scored 0.85 area and 0.88 accuracy, suggesting the approach travels across hospitals. The authors pitch it as decision support for personalised lung cancer therapy where annotated data will always be limited.
pmc-13468991:
Liang and colleagues report a 2026 study of rock movement above a longwall coal face at a Chinese mine, where panels of coal are extracted and the roof settles behind the work. From the simulation they built a damage index that quantifies how the rock structure activates as mining advances, and a learning model read the time patterns. pmc-13469691:

The focus was the bacterium's own AmpC enzyme, named EMC-2, which breaks down these drugs.

Reversing single changes confirmed the missing amino acid at position 296 drove much of this wider drug-breaking range.
pmc-13469891:

It highlights studies from 2024 to 2026 using single-cell analysis, spatial mapping, organoids, and trophoblast stem cells to model implantation. No clinical subtypes are established yet, the authors stress, but these tools now let researchers test whether a patient's interface abnormality can be reproduced and corrected in laboratory models.
pmc-13470391:

Main part analysis plus a multi-layer net gave the most stable scores under nested cross-testing, reaching area under the hit-miss curve 0.77 across the ten best species-drug pairs. Best pairs held Candida albicans with micafungin and Candida parapsilosis with fluconazole. Rule-book-based orders could avoid likely tough drugs in about 3 of 10 patients, pending future testing.
pmc-13471291:
Zhang and a large team built a Trojan horse carrier in 2026 riding white blood cells into tumors to deliver a two-in-one immune prodrug. The authors offer the design as an answer to the toxicity-versus-power dilemma stalling STING therapy.
pmc-13471391:

Clinicians saw clear value in the service yet limited testing to patients where they judged the benefit greatest. Planning rarely stretched beyond setting up the research study itself. Sites that reshaped delivery to fit their local routines found adoption easier. Running the service inside a research study, and ordinary workload pressure, both held it back. The authors draw lessons for any wider rollout.
pmc-13472891:

They also lengthened total sleep at one month and at three months. One drug, daridorexant, showed the cleanest safety record. Two others brought more mild side effects than dummy pills, but no rise in grave harm.
pmc-13473291:
Dena K. Plemmons and two colleagues evaluated in 2026 a lab intervention that gets research teams talking deliberately about data handling. The authors argue that giving reasons for choices lets weak reasons be challenged and strong ones ground joint work. The message is that ethical science rests less on written plans than on regular, reasoned conversation about daily work.
pmc-13474491:
Ma and co-authors report burning away an abnormal heart rhythm in a 60-year-old woman whose anatomy was a triple rarity. The authors call for larger series before generalizing.
pmc-13474691:

The field, they conclude, knows how to be present but not yet how to organize.
pmc-13474791:

The authors say the design rules should help build sensitive strip tests for other targets too.
pmc-13474891:
Raagini Jawa and co-authors survey people who use drugs in 2026 about exposure to xylazine, a sedative now mixed into street opioids. Effects and harms were compared by exposure status.

Sedation, blackouts, and wounds were widely reported among the exposed group. Most felt afraid and frustrated, calling xylazine an unwanted contaminant. Cost pressure, withdrawal fear, and lack of other supply kept many from avoiding it. Respondents backed real-time drug checking and safer supply as urgent needs.
pmc-13474991:

pmc-13475691:

Participants had a median age of 66 years, 97 percent needed mechanical ventilation, and 48 percent already had chronic kidney disease when enrolled. Oliguria, meaning very low urine output, triggered therapy in 56 percent of cases. The team compared a modified congestion score against standard scoring to predict recovery and dialysis need.
pmc-13475891:

A hybrid learning model, mixing image-style layers with a memory network that reads sequences both ways, learned to predict force response from the constants. An improved genetic search then worked backward to the constants themselves. Prediction error stayed very small against real test curves. The authors see savings in testing cost and help for designing fruit protection gear.
pmc-13477091:

pmc-13477291:

Among adults who already had a clot, the pattern was also linked to lower death rates. The authors present concentrated exercise as a workable option for busy adults.
pmc-13477691:
