Three databases gave studies on teen girls and women. Each study had to report app use for periods or fertility. Two reviewers pulled facts on their own for contrast. All studies were joined in a narrative summary. A pooled rate used a random-effects model. Use reasons, gains, and privacy worries were logged.
pmc-13478291:
Rui Chai proposed in 2026 a smart system to test and train university students' spoken English, where traditional assessment and scarce personalised practice fall short. The testing arm combines convolutional and recurrent networks with attention-based fusion to score pronunciation, fluency, word use, and coherence from speech.

The training arm uses reinforcement learning to sequence practice to each learner's level. Tests on 4,374 recordings from 486 students showed strong agreement with expert ratings across all four dimensions. Over eight weeks, learners on tuned sequences gained about 2.2 times more than fixed-curriculum learners, with stronger engagement. Broader, longer checks are still needed.
pmc-13478391:
Jie Fang and coauthors published a 2026 methods study making a heat-loving DNA-cutting enzyme work at body-friendly temperatures. The enzyme TtAgo normally needs 65 to 85 degrees Celsius, which limits bedside testing. Adding a DNA building block called dCTP plus a protective binding protein from the same bacterium changed that behavior.

The two additives loosened the enzyme's shape and helped it grab target strands, together enabling strong cutting between 37 and 60 degrees. The team built a one-step test for microRNAs, the tiny RNA markers linked to disease, reaching femtomolar sensitivity within 40 minutes. In a 151-sample clinical group, the test separated liver cancer patients from controls as accurately as the standard laboratory method.
pmc-13478491:
Karina Maciejewska and four colleagues validated in 2026 ultra-short heart rate variability measures from brief ECG clips. Guidelines call for at least five minutes of recording, yet new tools and fast-changing settings push for much shorter windows with no up-to-date rules.

They compared short clips against the five-minute standard in rested, tired, and drowsy volunteers, using correlation tests and Bland-Altman plots. Simple stats and high-frequency power from clips as short as 30 seconds matched well when volunteers were rested and alert, while other frequency measures needed one minute. Longer clips may be needed as fatigue or drowsiness grows, guiding use of short measures in shifting real-world states.
pmc-13479491:
Jie Huang and nine co-authors set out a trial plan to test a tiered care path for cancer pain, guided by live patient reports. Pain is among the most common cancer symptoms and marks worse outlook. The protocol came out in twenty twenty-six.

Care based on live patient reports is seen as the best patient centered model, but trial proof for cancer pain is thin. The trial will enroll over a hundred patients with cancer pain at one hospital. Half get the new path and half get standard care, by lot. In the new path, high pain or mood scores trigger set steps. The study will judge if this watch and respond plan eases pain.
pmc-13479891:
Junfeng Zhang and coauthors published a 2026 study of how inflammation teams up with the Kras mutation to start pancreatic cancer. Pancreatitis is a strong risk factor, and Kras mutations dominate this cancer, yet their interaction was murky. In Kras-mutant mice with pancreatitis, most cell-stress pathways quieted down, while one protein-folding enzyme, ERO1L, rose abnormally.

The chain runs through a disposal protein that Kras suppresses, letting a hypoxia factor accumulate and switch ERO1L on. ERO1L then folds the chemokine CCL2 more efficiently, and that signal draws macrophages into the tissue, building a tumor-friendly crowd. Blocking ERO1L or deleting it only in the pancreas slowed cancer development in the animals. The authors nominate the enzyme as an early intervention point.
pmc-13480091:
Cassandra Hennessy and colleagues present a 2026 methods study on a hidden trap in research that mines health records over time. Routine measures such as weight get logged at every visit, so people with more visits pile up more entries. The team used a landmark design with five years of records and tested nine weight-based measures against ten heart-related outcomes.

The sheer count of weight entries beat every other measure as the strongest predictor for all ten outcomes. Raw weight values, change scores, and body mass index all lost to the visit count. The trap is clear: frequent logging tracks contact with care, which itself tracks illness. Analysts who ignore entry counts may credit a measure with effects that belong to visit patterns. The authors urge anyone using record data to model count variables with care.
pmc-13480191:
Rong Qiu and co-authors present a 2026 study of how bone tissue helps lung cancer spread further. Lung adenocarcinoma often reaches bone, where survival drops below a year for many patients. The team grew cancer cells through three rounds inside bone-like settings to build a hardier line, then traced which bone cells drove the change.

Bone-eating cells called osteoclasts, rather than bone-building cells, boosted the stem-like traits of the cancer cells. Blocking a signal protein or its relay switch removed the boost. A secreted protein named OLFML3 rose with stemness and fed back to raise it further, acting through a growth factor that switched on three core stemness genes. Blood levels of that secreted protein may help flag patients at risk of further spread. The chain of signals offers fresh points where future drugs might cut in.
pmc-13482091:
Melisande Wong and four colleagues showed in 2026 that lentivirus exposure lets a standard DNA fiber assay reveal strand gaps. Tight sister ties normally collapse leading and lagging strands into one fiber, hiding strand-level changes.

Infecting human cell lines with lentivirus before spreading loosened cohesin on new DNA, letting daughter strands part so gaps from faulty Okazaki fragment handling or PrimPol excess became visible. The effect proved transient and independent of viral vectors or genome integration. The tweak turns a routine assay into a simple tool for catching strand replication faults.
pmc-13482291:
Alison Dumont and co-authors present a 2026 cell study on how a protein tug-of-war picks the way breast cancer cells die under spindle-blocking drugs. Such drugs raise NOXA, a protein that muzzles the survival protein MCL-1. The team varied NOXA in cells dosed with a taxane drug plus a blocker of a second survival protein.

Removing NOXA did not save the cells; death merely came later and changed shape. Cells swelled and ballooned through a pore protein called GSDME, a fiery death style steered by caspase enzymes. Fluid around dying cells shifted in inflammatory signals, with three interleukin levels differing by NOXA state. How a tumour dies shapes the immune chatter around it, so tipping the balance may help pair chemotherapy with immune care.
pmc-13482391:
Ziyue Wang and five colleagues built in 2026 a simulation framework for testing organ procurement policy reforms in the United States. Organ procurement links donors, centres, and regulators in one system, yet rules and incentives can drift toward inequity when poorly aligned.

Using centre activity data, they modeled centre responses under the status quo and under a reform regime with equity-weighted incentives. Centre utility drew on volumes, regional traits, and running costs, judged by total welfare and fairness spread. Moderate redesign improved regional fairness with little efficiency loss, giving regulators a clear tool to test reforms before rollout.
pmc-13483591:
Fanfan Li leads a 2026 cancer study on why one class of p53 mutation behaves more aggressively than another. Analysis of large tumor datasets showed that patients whose cancers carry DNA-contact mutations in p53 fare worse than patients with shape-changing mutations. Laboratory work then traced the difference to a specific altered protein, p53-R273H.

The altered protein formed abnormal clumps that trapped BRCA2, a repair protein, and pulled it away from chromosomes. Without BRCA2 in place, tangled DNA-RNA structures called R-loops built up and genome stability suffered. A helper protein named DDX3X proved necessary for clearing those tangles. Blocking DDX3X with a drug strengthened the effect of a PARP inhibitor in mutant cells, suggesting a treatment pairing worth further testing.
pmc-13483691:
Adam Beres tests whether simulator practice can teach medical students an ultrasound view taken from inside the esophagus. Published in 2026, the two-phase study starts with second- and fourth-year students who watched a video, took knowledge and confidence checks, then trained on a live simulator. A larger first-year group later followed the same curriculum.

Knowledge scores jumped by roughly one third in both senior groups after training. Confidence rose across anatomy, general ultrasound, heart ultrasound, and the esophagus-based method itself, with the largest leaps for the specialized method. Fourth-year students showed the steepest confidence gain for that skill. Every participant managed to obtain the required views and name the major structures. Early hands-on simulator exposure looks feasible within crowded curricula.
pmc-13486491:
Al-Barakat and team interviewed tourism instructors about bringing digital tools into English classes for future tour guides. English for specific purposes teaching has long leaned on lectures and textbooks, while the tourism industry itself runs on apps and virtual media. Their 2026 study gathered 65 instructors from guide training institutions and analyzed the interviews for shared themes about technology in language teaching.

Instructors valued simulations, virtual tours, online tests, and interactive platforms as ways to practice real guiding language. They credited the tools with supporting fluency, job-specific vocabulary, confidence, and motivation among learners in the programs described. Digital lessons were also seen as closer to what employers actually expect on the job. Al-Barakat concludes the shift moves classes beyond chalk and talk, though the evidence rests on teacher perceptions rather than measured student gains.
pmc-13486691:
Hosseinkhani and team surveyed 1,250 employees of an Iranian medical university to test whether poor sleep is the hidden bridge between job stress and a worse life. Job stress was scored by the effort-reward imbalance model, which flags people whose hard work goes under-rewarded. Their 2026 analysis combined that score with standard sleep and quality-of-life questionnaires inside a structural model that separates direct from indirect effects.

About 61 percent of employees showed effort-reward imbalance, a clear majority of the workforce surveyed. That group slept worse and scored lower on every quality-of-life domain, from physical health to environment. The modeling showed stress hurt quality of life both directly and through wrecked sleep, especially subjective sleep quality and daytime dysfunction. Reward, feeling valued, protected quality of life most strongly. Hosseinkhani urges employers to fix reward structures and sleep together.
pmc-13487991:
Li Tan, Tian-cheng Jiang, and Zhao-jian Gong test whether a blood protein can predict hidden spread of mouth cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. Patients had early oral squamous cell carcinoma with no sign of neck spread on examination, yet some harbor tiny metastases. The team measured transferrin, a protein that carries iron in blood, before surgery in 386 patients who also had elective neck surgery at a hospital in Changsha, China.

Hidden spread was found in about twenty-seven percent of patients after surgery. Transferrin levels were nearly identical in those with and without spread, and adding the measure did not improve prediction. Tumor grade and depth category remained the useful predictors. The authors conclude transferrin should not guide decisions here.
pmc-13488091:
Ihab Alasasfeh and colleagues report a 2026 emergency case where bedside ultrasound found a torn aorta in a man with belly pain. The 51-year-old patient with hypertension arrived with sudden, severe abdominal pain, a rigid tender abdomen, anemia, and a raised clotting marker. Chest pain, the classic warning sign, was absent, which made the cause easy to miss.

Point-of-care ultrasound, done at the bedside by the treating team, showed a flap inside the aorta. A CT scan with contrast then confirmed a Stanford Type A dissection. The tear ran from the aortic valve down to the leg arteries. It sat in the vessel's first segment, which needs urgent surgery. The authors urge early bedside scanning when suspicion is high.
pmc-13488191:
Yuki Kishino, Yoshiharu Fukuda, Shinya Kiyokawa, and Kaei Hiroi examine how pharmacy counting choices shift an antibiotic stewardship measure in Japan in a 2026 sensitivity analysis. The AWaRe system groups antibiotics by resistance risk, and the Access share shows how much use falls in the safest group. Stomach ulcer bacteria treatment packs combine several drugs in one blister, which can distort routine counts from dispensing data in the city of Nayoro.

Across thirty-three months, removing the pack effect changed the Access share by a small but consistent amount in every month studied. A broader adjustment for similar non-pack regimens was explored as well. The authors recommend stating pack handling openly, since small shifts matter when services are compared closely or judged against targets.
pmc-13488291:
Joaquim Soler and co-authors test pairing two therapies for borderline personality disorder with psychological trauma in a 2026 feasibility trial. Forty-two people, almost all women, first spent six months in group skills training from dialectical behavior therapy, covering mindfulness, emotion control, coping with distress, and people skills. Half then added one-to-one EMDR therapy, which works through painful memories during guided eye movements, while the rest kept up skills training alone.

About sixty-two percent stayed to the end, at similar rates in both arms. Talks afterward suggested the staged plan felt acceptable, and skills work left some people feeling ready for trauma work. Both arms eased borderline symptoms, while only the combined arm clearly cut symptoms of dissociation, a sense of spacing out, in the reported figures.
pmc-13488391:
Dorsch and a team of German materials chemists made in 2026 two new hydrides from CeSi, a cerium silicon compound, by loading it with hydrogen gas. The plain compound holds one spare electron in loose form. Trapping that electron with hydrogen reshaped both its build and its magnetism. The work used heavy hydrogen and neutron beams to see where the light atoms sat, plus computer checks on bonds.

Two forms came out of the pot. One kept the parent frame with hydrogen tucked in its gaps, a fast form on the way. The other, the stable end form, swapped to a new frame with more hydrogen still. Both forms turned ferromagnetic, meaning their tiny magnets line up as one, below a bit above twenty kelvin. That switch point is oddly high for cerium compounds. Their pull strength matched the free cerium ion value near exact.
pmc-13488491:
Larocca and colleagues in Italy built in 2026 two ring shaped molecules that spot metal ions by glow, and tested how they tell metals apart. The rings rest on BINOL, a twisted twin unit long used to grip guests. Metal ions drive much of body work, yet too much of some harms health, so cheap, fast tests have worth. The team made the rings, then read their glow and fine spectra as metals were added.

One ring, the fifth built, gave a two way answer. With silver ions in the mix, its glow fell by about three quarters. With cobalt ions, the glow rose by a like share. No other common metal gave the same split reply. Deep spectra showed the ring bends its frame to fit each guest, a shift that sets the glow change. The authors pitch the ring as a dual sensor for health linked metals.
pmc-13490491:
Martín-Acosta and team measured how many Spanish teenagers follow the full 24-hour movement guidelines, covering activity, screen time, and sleep, and whether fitness explains their math speed. Their 2026 study assessed 578 teens aged eleven to fifteen, testing math fluency and two kinds of fitness, cardiovascular and muscular, then ran mediation analyses on the relationships.

Only about one percent of teens met all three guidelines, while nearly half met none at all in this sample. Teenagers meeting at least two guidelines scored modestly but clearly higher on math fluency than those meeting fewer. Cardiovascular fitness statistically accounted for that advantage in every comparison, acting as the mediator. Muscular fitness played no such role. Martín-Acosta argues schools should promote the combined habit pattern, since fitness carries the benefit into the classroom.
pmc-13490591:
Alzubaidi and team jointly optimized where hovering base stations fly in three dimensions and how they share power among connected devices, aiming at fast yet energy-thrifty 6G downlinks. Hovering stations can reposition over crowds or disasters, but moving and transmitting interact in mathematically nasty ways. Their 2026 framework pairs multiple hovering stations with a sharing scheme where stronger users relay signals for weaker ones, solved by a hybrid of genetic search and wolf-pack-inspired optimization.

Simulations showed the joint framework beating benchmark schemes on both total data rate and total energy efficiency under minimum-rate guarantees for every device. Positioning accounted for where devices cluster on the ground, rather than hovering blindly at fixed points. The hybrid solver converged faster than either parent algorithm alone in the reported runs. Alzubaidi offers the approach for dense Internet-of-Everything deployments in future 6G coverage.
pmc-13491591:
Jin-Gui Bi and four co-authors report a 2026 field and sequencing study of the fall armyworm, an invasive crop pest in western Yunnan, China. The Gaoligong Mountains serve as a cross-border corridor and wintering ground for the moth. Traps tracked adult moths, while metagenomic sequencing profiled the gut microbes of larvae gathered at different sites.

Adults stayed active all year, with numbers peaking from January to May, and southern samples carried the most varied gut microbes. Enterococcus, usually dominant in this pest, was scarce in central and northern samples. At Pianma, near the China-Myanmar border, Providencia dominated instead, alongside extra functional genes and many resistance-linked genes. The authors flag Pianma as a priority site for watching cross-border spread.
pmc-13492991:
Smith and colleagues interviewed twenty patients who had finished physiotherapy for muscle and joint conditions, in a 2026 qualitative study using grounded theory methods. Prescribing exercises usually rests on research and therapist skill, and the patient's side of the process had barely been studied in one-on-one rehab. The talks ran until no new themes appeared.

Smith found patients' accounts sorting into two groups. The why covered education, feedback, and teamwork, which built patients' grasp, trust, and confidence and strengthened the alliance with their therapist. The how covered exercise choice, delivery method, dosage, step-ups, and tools. Running through all of it, and named the core concept, was individualization: programs fitted to the person's goals, skills, other health problems, and life context. Patients' accounts matched what the therapist literature advises, and the authors offer the model as patient-informed guidance for making plans people follow.
pmc-13493191:
Shamsi and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether clonal haematopoiesis, the quiet expansion of blood stem cells carrying acquired mutations, links lupus to early cardiovascular disease. Lupus, a systemic autoimmune condition, is an independent risk factor for heart and vessel disease, above all early artery hardening, and chronic inflammation is the usual explanation. Clonal haematopoiesis likewise drives a pro-inflammatory state and strong cardiovascular risk, and such clones appear enriched in lupus.

The review sets out how the two conditions share immune pathways that could combine or converge, speeding artery damage. Mutant white blood cells of the myeloid line are central to both stories. The authors frame the trio as a triangular inflammatory network and propose clonal haematopoiesis as the missing nexus. Pinning down these links could flag high-risk lupus patients early and open treatment aimed at the clones themselves to cut cardiovascular harm.
pmc-13494391:
Curt G DeGroff writes a 2026 letter to the editor about word choice in color-flow Doppler, the ultrasound method that paints blood flow in colors. His letter responds to a case report that called a checkered color pattern in a lung vein turbulent and linked it to vein narrowing. DeGroff argues the word misleads, since the mosaic pattern on screen does not prove true turbulence in the flow.

He explains that such patterns can arise from smooth flow with speed gradients, from flow that is disturbed but not turbulent, from swirl, or from the machine's own settings and artifacts. True velocity spread within a sampled region is also not the same as turbulence. Since Doppler cannot measure turbulence directly, he suggests disturbed flow as the safer term. The wording matters, because calling a pattern turbulent can push readers toward a narrowing diagnosis the image cannot support.
pmc-13495191:
Shakti Pillay leads a team that built, in a 2026 article, an online course to teach safe transfer of sick newborns between hospitals in South Africa. Newborn deaths run high in Sub-Saharan Africa, partly because transport gear is scarce and the ambulance crews who move babies rarely have newborn training. Specialist retrieval teams are the ideal, but budgets force general crews into the role.

The team shaped a draft course from past studies, chart reviews of local transfers, and talks with experts and learners. Fourteen experts then sorted each topic into core, extended, or advanced tiers across two voting rounds, with a high bar for agreement. The final course stacks three levels in order. Core items, covering basic checks, spotting danger, and when to call for help, won near-unanimous backing. The free online course is built for low-resource settings and leans on growing internet access.
pmc-13495291:
Natalie Bisal and colleagues run, in a 2026 feasibility trial, a digital yoga program built to lift self-care among postgraduate researchers in the United Kingdom. Mental strain runs high in this group, and self-care guards health, yet few programs are theory-based or built with the users. Their seven-week program, Pause Grow Reflect, was co-created on those lines.

Thirty-seven researchers were assigned by lot, two to the program for each one in a control group. Entry, early checks, and liking of the program met the preset bars for a full trial. Staying power, engagement, and later follow-up fell short. Stress hinted at a small edge for the program. Interviews showed burden and time cost were the sore points. The authors call the offer promising and largely workable, provided tweaks lift retention before a large trial tests whether it truly helps.
pmc-13499191:
Naji and a large team present a targeted drug conjugate for high-risk blood cancers. Their 2026 paper describes an antibody-drug conjugate aimed at CCRL2, a surface protein on leukaemia cells, carrying a potent cell-killing payload called a PBD dimer. The target diseases are high-risk myelodysplastic syndromes and acute myeloid leukaemia, including cases with TP53 mutations that resist standard drugs.

The conjugate showed prominent antileukemic activity in laboratory cultures and in animal models, covering the TP53-mutated setting that usually fares worst. Importantly, it caused no significant harm to healthy blood-forming cells in those tests. Mice also showed no major whole-body toxicity at the doses used. The authors position the CCRL2 conjugate as a candidate for patients whose disease lacks good options, with a safety profile that, so far, spares normal marrow.
pmc-13500691:
Yuki Kinishi and colleagues use mice in 2026 to probe how the size of a surgical insult shapes the confused, slowed state that mirrors post-op delirium in patients. Oxidative stress, chemical damage from reactive oxygen, is often blamed for the complication. Three groups received anaesthesia alone, a standard belly operation, or the operation plus a local heat injury, escalating stress step by step. A day later the mice hunted for buried food while blood markers of oxidation and antioxidant defence were measured.

The more invasive the procedure, the longer mice took to find food in the reported results. Oxidation markers climbed steadily as stress rose while the balance of antioxidant power against oxidation fell. Modelling suggested the link between behaviour and oxidative balance shifts with stress level rather than following one simple rule, hinting that heavier operations may need different protective plans than light ones.
pmc-13501691:
Nan Zhang leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 time-course study of how bone marrow stem cells coordinate bone building with blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics. Human marrow stem cells were driven toward bone formation and sampled for RNA sequencing across 504 hours, from the first hour to three weeks. The team mapped genes with enrichment and trend analyses, built co-expression networks to find hub genes, and confirmed signals with gene and protein tests.

Expression unfolded in four stages: adaptation in the first day, proliferation through 72 hours, differentiation control up to 336 hours, and a stable remodelling phase after that. The 72-hour mark stood out as a pivot where bone, vessel, nerve, and lymph programmes couple, with BMP, VEGF, and PPAR pathways switching on. Four gene modules emerged, with hub genes including GDF5, MGP, and PAPPA2. The authors offer the timeline as design guidance for synthetic bone substitutes.
pmc-13501791:
Zizhen Si leads a thirteen-author team with a 2026 study of how methamphetamine damages the brain and entrenches addiction. Using rats that self-administer the drug, hippocampal neurons, and pathway-specific tools, the team followed a quality-control system called chaperone-mediated autophagy, which feeds chosen proteins to lysosomes for disposal. Methamphetamine coerced this machinery into grabbing GPX4, the enzyme that neutralizes oxidized fats, by exposing an unusual recognition tag on the protein.

Losing GPX4 broke glutathione recycling and unleashed ferroptosis, an iron-dependent cell death driven by fat peroxidation, across the hippocampus. Switching off the autophagy pathway in neurons rescued spatial memory and cut compulsive drug seeking, proving the pathway drives the harm rather than merely accompanying it. Blocking drugs aimed at this system eased the damage in early tests. The authors recast addiction's brain injury as hijacked protein housekeeping.
pmc-13502591:
Yulia Pushkar proposes a 2026 mechanism for the most consequential chemistry on Earth: how photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen we breathe. The reaction runs on a manganese-calcium cluster, and researchers have long disputed which two oxygen atoms join to form the O-O bond. Pushkar assigns a bridging oxygen called O3, held near the amino acid histidine 337 by a hydrogen bond, as the exchanging water substrate. A second oxygen, O6, appears at a manganese site during the cycle's S2-to-S3 transition.

Coupling O3 with O6 yields a peroxide intermediate calculated to sit lower in energy than the studied alternative pathway. The protein steers the bond formation through charge control: hydrogen bonding from His337 and an open coordination site favour the new route. The move echoes how globins use a distal histidine to manage oxygen intermediates. Pushkar argues the mechanism fits all data and breaks the field's impasse.
pmc-13503491:
Qi Meng leads the team behind this 2026 trial protocol from China. The plan tests electroacupuncture as an added treatment for organ failure in intensive care patients with sepsis. Sepsis is a harmful body response to infection, and fast repair of organ damage shapes who lives.

Between 154 and 500 patients will be split at random to get real or sham electroacupuncture. Each group gets six sessions of 30 minutes, with the first one done within a day of entry. The main outcome is the change in the SOFA organ score on day seven. The team will also track deaths, days free of the ICU, and days free of organ support to day 28.
pmc-13503791:
Ming Xu and others build a machine learning plan for fracture risk prediction and validate man-made biomedical data. In 2026, the study looks at 169 patient records with age, sex, weight, height, drug standing, and bone mineral density. It compares logit regression, random forest, gradient boosting, support vector machines, and voting ensembles under five-fold cross-validation. Man-made data quality matters because small labeled data sets invite overfitting.

The hard voting ensemble reached 85.8 percent rightness and F1 of 0.822, while logit regression gave the best discrimination with area under the curve of 0.88. Man-made data matched real marginal distributions well but preserved inter-feature correlations weakly. The authors urge rigorous testing before man-made data enters medical machine learning.
pmc-13503991:
Austin Runde and four co-authors told the case of a teen whose blood clotting fault stayed hidden for seventeen years, in a report from twenty twenty-six. The girl, well until then, came to care with blood in her urine and very poor clotting test results. Tests showed no activity of factor seven, a protein the blood needs to clot.

She was given plasma and vitamin K, and her clotting tests soon moved close to normal. Tests ruled out blockers of the factor, which points to a fault she was born with rather than one gained later. Her vitamin K level was also low, which may have made the fault worse. The case shows that even a severe inborn lack of factor seven may cause no bleed at all until well into the teen years.
pmc-13504791:
Jing Qian and three colleagues track how pandemic-era rules reshaped a chlamydial pneumonia in Beijing children, in a 2026 study. The illness is caused by a bacterium that spreads through the air. Strict public health curbs from 2020 onward suppressed many such infections, then release brought rebounds.

Records covered 331 hospitalized children with lab-proven infection from 2017 to 2025. Cases surged in the months after curbs lifted. The typical patient shifted from toddlers to school-age children and teens. Later cases more often carried a second infection, showed denser lung shadows on scans, and needed airway scope checks. Failure to respond to the standard antibiotic class jumped from rare to about a third of cases. The authors call for school-focused prevention.
pmc-13504991:
Tushar Mungle, Vivek Charu, and Philip N Okafor compare hospital outcomes for homeless and housed patients with inflammatory bowel disease, in a 2026 study. Data on this group were nearly absent, though homelessness strains chronic gut care. The bowel diseases covered are Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

Hospital records from four states gave more than one hundred fifteen thousand stays. Homeless patients made up under one percent of stays for each disease. After matching on background traits, death rates and scope use were alike between homeless and housed groups. Surgery rates were alike too, except fewer bowel removals among homeless colitis patients. Clot complications after surgery ran lower for homeless Crohn's patients but higher for homeless colitis patients. The authors report broad parity in hospital care outcomes.
pmc-13507091:
Constantinos Harkos and colleagues build, in 2026 work, a patient-specific model that maps how radiation sensitivity varies inside glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor. Tumor growth squeezes vessels, cuts blood flow, and leaves low-oxygen zones that resist radiation. Their model turns stiffness maps from MR elastography, a scan that measures tissue firmness, into stress and oxygen maps.

Uneven tumor stiffness and stiff tissue near the tumor edge raised stress in simulations. Squeezed vessels then left patches with poor flow and low oxygen, where radiation should work less well. The pipeline links a routine-style scan to expected treatment response. Softening the tumor setting might improve radiation results and help sort patients.
pmc-13507191:
Saroj Khadka and colleagues show, in 2026 work, that sugar import turns down the sticky capsule trait, called mucoidy, in hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae, a bacterium that causes severe infections. The capsule helps the bacterium invade, and its thickness is set by a regulator protein. The team tested whether sugars act as a control signal, separate from their role as food.

Import alone, without sugar burning, suppressed mucoidy across several strains through a known signaling pair that lowered the regulator. Both sticky and non-sticky forms colonized the gut less well than a balanced state in tests of cell binding and gut fitness. Flexible switching, rather than a fixed state, seems key for gut success.
pmc-13507291:
Varunesh Chandra and five colleagues published a soil study in two thousand twenty-six on gas emissions from recycled crop residues. Returning green residues builds soil carbon, but nitrogen-rich material can release ammonia and the potent greenhouse gas nitrous oxide. Placement in the soil may change the balance.

Red clover residue was placed on the surface, layered, or mixed through three contrasting soils in fifty-day lab incubations. Gas fluxes and soil nitrogen were tracked. Nitrous oxide depended strongly on soil and placement; sandy loam emitted most, especially when residue was mixed or layered. Ammonia escaped almost only from surface residue. Emissions exceeded earlier reports for residues. The authors say placement choices matter for climate accounting.
pmc-13508191:
Peng Tong and Na Wang study a long RNA molecule as a possible marker and driver in severe childhood pneumonia, in 2026 work. The study compared 98 children with severe pneumonia against 92 healthy children. Blood levels of the RNA, called LINC01093, and two linked molecules were measured in both groups. The team also built a lab model by exposing lung-related cells to a bacterial toxin. They then silenced the RNA to see whether cell damage eased.

Children with severe pneumonia had higher LINC01093 and higher levels of its target protein, MAPK1. The partner molecule miR-326 ran low in those children. High LINC01093 tracked with worse outlook, and it sorted sick from healthy children fairly well. Silencing it in lab cells raised survival, cut cell death, and lowered inflammation signals. Blocking its partner partly undid that protection, which supports the proposed chain of effects.
pmc-13508291:
Fei Sun and four co-authors report the repair of an unusually long tear in a man's windpipe caused by a breathing tube, in a 2026 case report. The 66-year-old patient was having a stomach procedure under general anesthesia when a sudden air leak appeared twenty minutes after tube placement. A camera check showed a full-thickness tear running nearly the whole chest section of the windpipe. Surgeons combined a neck opening with a camera-guided chest approach to reach both ends.

The chest part was sewn closed after moving a vein aside, and the neck part was repaired through a front opening. The operation had no complications. The breathing tube came out the next day, and the patient went home on day twelve. At three months the windpipe had healed fully with no narrowing. The case offers a template for repairing tears too long for one opening.
pmc-13509291:
Emre Yucel and seven co-authors report real-world results for an antibiotic in hospitalized cystic fibrosis patients, drawn from the SPECTRA study, in 2026 work. Cystic fibrosis brings repeated lung infections and antibiotic exposure, breeding resistant Pseudomonas germs that drive deaths. The drug pair ceftolozane and tazobactam was built for such resistant infections. Records spanned seven countries for adults given the drug for at least forty-eight hours. This subgroup covers sixty-four cystic fibrosis patients treated for one index infection, with data gathered before and after treatment.

Just over half the group carried drug-resistant Pseudomonas. Treatment succeeded in about seventy-eight percent of patients. Success was perfect when the drug came second in line and fell to forty percent when it came sixth or later. Germ clearance was reported in about one in nine patients, and about fourteen percent died in hospital, concentrated in late-line use.
pmc-13509891:
Shengnan Zhou and six co-authors profile neck artery plaques at three stages, from early thickening to plaques at risk of bursting, in 2026 work. Bursting plaques are a key trigger of stroke, yet microbes inside plaques have rarely been mapped across stages. The group read both human gene activity and microbial traces in 48 plaque samples, using strict cleanup steps to guard against contamination in such low-biomass material.

Microbial mixes differed clearly by stage, and 54 human genes tied to tissue reshaping and immune signaling rose step by step. Twenty-one bacterial types appeared enriched in unstable plaques, mostly kinds that live in the mouth or gut. Their predicted functions linked to cell death and inflammatory pathways, and their levels tracked human genes that break down tissue. The authors frame the links as associations that hint at joint host and microbe roles in plaque risk.
pmc-13510091:
Rajashree Patnaik and Yajnavalka Banerjee investigate in 2026 whether a natural fat molecule can quiet inflammation inside cartilage cells, a process tied to osteoarthritis. They focus on factor Xa, a clotting protein that also fires inflammatory signals through a cell receptor called PAR-2.

In lab-grown cartilage cells, factor Xa raised inflammatory messengers, boosted a growth signal pathway, increased tissue-chewing enzymes, and damaged the cells' energy centers. Adding palmitoylcarnitine, the fat molecule that binds factor Xa, blunted all of these effects and restored the energy centers. Silencing the PAR-2 receptor blocked most of the inflammatory response, confirming it as the main route. The authors propose this lipid pathway as a fresh angle on joint inflammation.
pmc-13510391:
Burak Abay, Alp Ozel, Ibrahim Alatas, and Abdullah Eren review early walking outcomes after surgery for clubfoot linked to a spinal birth defect, in 2026 work. The deformity in these children is stiff and often returns, and standard casting had already failed for this group. Records covered 39 children with 55 affected feet who had a release operation on the inner and back parts of the foot. Average age was near four years, and follow-up ran near four years.

Mobility scores improved at walking distances of five, fifty, and five hundred meters after surgery. Gains appeared in each severity band, though children with worse deformity started lower and stayed lower. How well a child moved afterward tied strongly to the spinal level of the defect and to whether thigh muscle strength was kept. The authors say results should be judged against each child's nerve and muscle capacity, not foot shape alone.
pmc-13512291:
Jane Ohia and Juan Cui present a graph-based learning system, named miR-CellMap, that infers how tiny RNA regulators control genes across tumor bulk data and single-cell cancer data, in 2026 work. Most older tools predict targets from sequence alone or from bulk averages, missing how regulation rewires in different cell states. The system builds a mixed graph of microRNAs, genes, and contexts, where a context is one cell or one tumor profile.

Transformer learning on the graph produced regulatory fingerprints, a Bayesian step pruned candidate links, and a scoring layer picked out master regulators plus cooperating target groups. Run on matched single-cell data from a leukemia line and on bulk sets spanning several cancers, the system found repeated and dataset-specific programs, naming regulators from the let-7 family and others. The authors say context-aware maps can expose control switches that bulk tools blur.
pmc-13512591:
Peng and colleagues mapped in 2026 four gene variants in 564 Beijing schoolchildren, as school sports demands in the city rise after 2024 reforms. The variants cover a muscle protein gene tied to sprint and power traits and three folate-processing genes. DNA from saliva was read for every child, with a full success rate, and results were checked against East Asian reference groups.

Peng found all four variants sat in the expected balance for a stable population, and their shares matched East Asian references closely. About a third of children carried the slow-muscle form of the muscle gene in double dose, and a similar share carried the double form of one folate variant. Nearly nine in ten children carried at least two variant copies across the four sites. The sample came from only two schools, so the authors frame it as a baseline, not a citywide picture.
pmc-13514991:
Sun and colleagues explored in 2026 whether CT scan texture analysis can predict Ki-67 in esophageal cancer without a biopsy. Ki-67 is a marker of how fast tumor cells divide, and knowing it helps guide care. Their method, called delta radiomics, compares scan features of the tumor with the patient's own healthy esophagus tissue.

The study covered 59 patients at one center. A random forest model using delta features sorted high from low Ki-67 with moderate accuracy, beating models built on tumor tissue alone or healthy tissue alone. Adding clinical variables did not improve the result. An explanation method highlighted two texture features as most influential. The authors call the work exploratory and say outside validation in more centers is required.
pmc-13515591:
Wang and colleagues built in 2026 a composite coating for pure titanium implants, aiming to fix the metal's poor fit with living bone. Titanium is strong and resists corrosion, but its surface is biologically inert and far stiffer than bone, which slows healing. The team first roughened the metal with micro-arc oxidation, then spin-coated it with a blend of soy protein and two degradable plastics, PLA and PCL.

Wang showed the soy protein made the coating wetter-friendly, rougher, and better stuck to the metal, while tuning how fast it breaks down. The coating's stiffness fell into the range of human bone, and corrosion resistance improved. In lab tests with bone-forming cells, the mix with half soy protein gave the best cell growth, sticking, and bone-building signals. All versions were gentle on blood. The authors offer the coating as a practical route to more active implant surfaces.
pmc-13516091:
Zhaoling Jiang and eight colleagues review antibody-drug conjugates aimed at two tumour targets, HER2 and Trop-2, in a 2026 article. Both proteins sit in excess on many solid tumours and drive growth, spread, and drug resistance. A conjugate couples a homing antibody to a potent cell-killing payload, so the poison lands mainly inside cancer cells. The review lays out how each target works and promotes cancer.

Clinical results then take centre stage across breast, stomach, lung, and bladder cancers. Named drugs such as trastuzumab deruxtecan and sacituzumab govitecan show strong, lasting responses, even in tumours with low HER2 levels and after earlier lines of treatment failed. The authors weigh response data and prospects, then close with the field's open problems, from resistance to side effects. Their verdict: these conjugates are now a real force in precision cancer care, with room to grow.
pmc-13517691:
Thongsriratch and co-authors examine in 2026 a legal problem they call the unmentioned vaccine: lawsuits claiming a clinician never offered, recommended, or documented a preventive vaccine a patient needed. Most vaccine litigation follows bad reactions, but these cases allege harm from silence. The authors conducted a comparative medico-legal review across selected jurisdictions, separating what the law currently requires from the good practice they propose.

They found that patient-centered disclosure duties exist in differing forms, yet vaccine-specific cases are sparse and fact-sensitive, and no universal duty to recommend every vaccine emerges. A strong provider recommendation does raise uptake, but that evidence alone does not create a legal duty. As a proposed remedy, they present a four-step framework: assess, discuss and disclose, recommend or refer, and record and revisit. They stress it is a concept needing validation, especially in lower-income health systems.
pmc-13518891:
Xiaoyi Shao, Hua Li, Qian Ma, and Kai Jin build a 2026 machine learning system that recognizes what participants are doing during hands-on workshops. Action recognition struggles here because activities overlap, class counts are lopsided, and meaning depends on context. Their framework fine-tunes a 3D convolutional network in stages, then adds an unsupervised review.

Training used 208 clips from internal and external datasets, plus public UCF101 material for a side analysis. The tailored 57-class model separated most actions well within its home context, yet similar actions blended and cross-context transfer suffered from merged categories and drift. Shao and colleagues suggest adversarial alignment and pose guidance as next fixes.
pmc-13518991:
Keikavoos Rahmati, Ali A Mohammadi, Vahid Amani, and Mohammad Reza Halvgar report a green, one-pot route in 2026 to new fused-ring compounds built from two familiar drugs, brimonidine and clonidine. Each drug was reacted with azlactones in ethanol with mild acetic acid as catalyst, following a domino addition-then-cyclization path with perfect atom economy and no metals.

Products carried the imidazo[1,2-a]pyrimidine core, a scaffold linked to many drug actions. Surprisingly, brimonidine reactions favored the cis shape while clonidine reactions gave the trans shape across the series. Every compound was new, with structures confirmed by X-ray crystallography and several spectroscopic methods. Rahmati and colleagues highlight the method's simplicity for making drug-like libraries.
pmc-13520291:
Tom L. Osborn and colleagues report in 2026 on low mood and worry among Kenyan high school pupils. Their work tests whether two well known Western questionnaires work well in this setting. The team also counts how many pupils score high, and looks at links with school and social life across three studies run from 2021 to 2023.

The questionnaires went to 7,865 pupils aged 12 to 20 years. About three in ten scored high for low mood. About one in four scored high for worry. Pupils with more support from others felt better. Pupils who felt more in control also felt better. Final-year pupils scored worse, and worry sat at the centre of the symptom web.
pmc-13520491:
Adam Doležal, Van Assche, and Tomáš Doležal analyse a 2024 Czech bill that would regulate all end-of-life practices in one statute. It covers palliative care, stopping life-sustaining treatment, palliative sedation, and assisted death in both its forms. Belgium, whose law shaped the Czech draft, split these across separate statutes. Their 2026 study tests the bill against Belgian practice and European human rights law.

For routine care the bill creates a legal right, names treatment that is medically inadequate as the threshold for limiting care, and wraps decisions in safeguards. These include information, patient participation, ethics committee mediation, and court review. Assisted death requires an incurable illness that cannot be reversed, with unbearable suffering, then passes through staged requests, an outside opinion, and after-the-fact review by a commission. The authors judge the draft a coherent step toward human rights law, with suggestions for refinement.
pmc-13520891:
Lara and colleagues replied in 2026 to a reader's letter about their earlier study of infection outbreaks in Chilean public hospitals from 2017 to 2024. The outbreaks were caused by carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, gut bacteria that resist last-line carbapenem antibiotics. A commenter questioned the bootstrap method, a resampling technique, used to compare median outbreak size and duration between periods.

Lara confirms an error was found on checking, and the reply supplies a corrected table. The difference in median outbreak size between the second and first periods is 3, which is not statistically meaningful, and the gap for the third period is zero. For duration, the middle period differed by about 29 fewer days, also not meaningful. The latest period ran about 66 fewer days than the first, a gap that did reach significance. Outbreak counts and case shares across the periods are also restated.
pmc-13521291:
Du and co-authors identify a gene behind sterile, dying wheat spikelets in this 2026 genetics study. Spikelet degeneration, where the grain-bearing tips of the wheat head die off, sharply limits how much grain a plant can set. The team studied a mutant called ds1. Its head tips degenerated, and its middle spikelets were sterile. They then tracked the cause through the genome.

The mutant's spikes were 17 percent shorter than normal, and grain-bearing spikelets fell by nearly 89 percent compared with ordinary plants in the trial. Mapping placed the cause on chromosome 3BL, in a gene for a cysteine-rich receptor-like kinase that was strongly switched down in dying spikelets. Without it, reactive oxygen built up in anther walls, triggering programmed cell death, and pollen failed to mature, leaving the florets sterile.
pmc-13522091:
Yiming Chen and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on diet, sleep, and lung cancer risk. The Mediterranean diet is rich in vegetables, olive oil, and fish. Diet and sleep have each been tied to cancer risk, but their joint effect on lung cancer was unclear.

The team used the UK Biobank, following 192,034 people for a median of fourteen years. Diet scores and a five-part sleep score were combined into nine pattern levels. Over the follow-up, 1,156 people developed lung cancer. Those in the healthiest diet-sleep group had a forty-three percent lower risk than those in the lowest group. Taking an afternoon nap did not change the diet link. The results support joint lifestyle advice.
pmc-13522491:
Naeimeh Heiranizadeh and co-authors test whether collagen gene activity predicts which early breast lesions will return or become invasive in a 2026 study. The early form, ductal carcinoma in situ, stays inside milk ducts, while the invasive form spreads into nearby tissue. Samples from forty-two patients with recurrence or invasive disease were compared with thirty-two controls whose early lesions did not return.

Four collagen genes were much more active in the case group, with the largest rise near tenfold for one gene. Higher activity was strongest in tumors lacking hormone receptors and in fast-growing subtypes. Accuracy tests gave moderate to good discrimination for each gene. The authors propose collagen profiles as possible markers of risk and as targets for future treatment research.
pmc-13522591:
Chuyu Chen leads a large team examining how a Parkinson-linked protein harms vulnerable dopamine neurons in a 2026 mouse study. Parkinson disease destroys dopamine-producing cells in a midbrain region, and synaptic problems appear long before cells die. Genetic mouse models allowed the team to isolate the most vulnerable neuron subtypes and image their connections at high resolution.

The protein LRRK2 was enriched in vulnerable subtypes, and its disease-causing form disrupted the organization of release sites on their axons. Dopamine release in the striatum fell as a result. Protein analyses showed the mutant increased modification of partner proteins, weakening their link to release machinery. The work frames early synaptic failure as a treatable stage and suggests strategies aimed at release sites.
pmc-13522891:
Lorenz Balcar and colleagues reply to a validation study of risk criteria for liver patients with ascites in a 2026 response. Ascites is fluid buildup caused by severe portal hypertension in cirrhosis. The criteria flag patients with severe ascites and low blood sodium who may benefit from an early shunt procedure that relieves portal pressure. An external group found a similar rate of clinical worsening within a year.

The authors explain why brain dysfunction from liver failure was left out of their model. Patients entered the study at their first ascites episode without overt brain symptoms. The outcome focused on worsening that a shunt could prevent. They argue that shunting may also reduce triggers of brain dysfunction by controlling pressure and fluid. New guidelines and smaller stents should further improve safety, they note.
pmc-13523191:
Kui Ma, Kang Li, Zhe Zhu, and Hui Tian Shao analyze takedown output in professional mixed martial arts in a 2026 retrospective study. Public records covered more than eight thousand UFC bouts from 1997 to 2025, yielding nearly seventeen thousand fighter performances. Takedown density was defined as successful takedowns per minute of fight time, allowing fair comparison across eras and weight classes.

Men's takedown density fell steadily across the period, a trend that held when early years and very short bouts were excluded. Women's density showed no significant trend in the shorter available span. Men's values differed modestly across weight classes, while women's did not. Winners recorded higher takedown density, success rates, and control time than losers. The authors present the benchmarks as descriptive references, not proof that takedowns cause victory.
pmc-13523291:
Aditya Gupta and colleagues identify parasites in the intestines of wild foxes and coyotes in Pennsylvania in a 2026 study. These canids are final hosts for many Sarcocystis species that infect livestock and wildlife, yet the microscopic stages look nearly identical across species. Intestinal scrapings from forty animals sampled in 2024 were examined under the microscope and tested with multi-gene DNA methods.

Parasite stages were found in about half of gray foxes, over a third of red foxes, and more than two thirds of coyotes. DNA testing succeeded in a subset and revealed several species, including one that uses cattle as its intermediate host and burdens cattle production. The results confirm that wild canids spread diverse parasites at the boundary between wildlife and livestock.
pmc-13523791:
Németh and Borondics introduced a new way to take infrared chemical images at nanometer scale without the drift that ruins long readings. Their 2026 methods study tackles nano-FTIR, a technique combining a sharp scanning probe with infrared spectroscopy to identify materials point by point. Heat-driven drift during slow scans normally scrambles where each spectrum belongs, making large high-quality data sets unreliable.

Németh instead scans quickly for position and collects spectral information on a slower step-scan schedule. The topography images then serve as alignment frames to register every spectrum to its true pixel. The result is pixel-perfect alignment across large areas, demonstrated on carbon nanotube plasmon signals across a broad infrared range that other techniques cannot capture. The clean data sets were good enough, for the first time in this technique, to feed into machine learning tools for spotting nanoscale differences in photonic materials.
pmc-13525091:
Svenja Schmidt and four colleagues propose personalized, fortified drinks that astronauts could make in space. Long missions bring health hazards from microgravity and radiation, plus monotonous food that has historically cut calorie intake. Beverages are easy to adjust in composition. Emulsions can also carry fat-soluble ingredients that water-based drinks cannot. The twenty twenty-six paper is a literature review of these ideas.

The authors survey food fortification on Earth and current and developing space food systems. They catalog space health risks that nutrition might soften. Candidate bioactive compounds and micronutrients are matched to those risks. The result is a framework for drinks tailored to individual astronauts, supporting health and food choice on long voyages.
pmc-13525691:
Kan Gao, Feiliang Wang, Lengnan Xu, and Weide Dai compare, in a 2026 retrospective study, two needle treatments for simple kidney cysts in older patients. Sclerotherapy drains a cyst and injects an agent to collapse its wall. One group received a lauromacrogol injection alone, while the other first had the cyst rinsed with 95 percent ethanol.

The study covered 94 patients, average age about seventy, treated under ultrasound guidance between 2019 and 2025 and followed for a year. Cyst volume shrank from an average 113 milliliters to nearly zero in both groups, with resolution and cure rates above 97 percent overall and no significant difference between techniques. Adverse events, however, were far more common with the ethanol rinse, driven by pain and fever. The authors favor injection alone for safety.
pmc-13525891:
France Champenois, Maree Corkeron, and Annette George examine microfossils in an ancient microbial reef in South Australia, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The reef formed during an ice-age gap over half a billion years ago. Layered rock mounds at the site hold many shapes at hand scale.

Fine imaging found streaky and clotted textures, tiny columns, and threads like a known lime microbe. Preserved parts include bacterial sheaths, cell slime, and grain-like cell molds. Early silica coating and clay growth on cell surfaces likely saved the fine detail. The reef builders were a mixed band of thread and round bacteria.
pmc-13526091:
Sobrino-Conde and co-authors test whether two biologically defined types of psychosis also feel different from the inside. Their group had earlier split psychotic disorders into biotype 1, with severe cognitive deficits and brain changes, and biotype 2, with moderate deficits. Anomalous self-experiences, disturbances in the sense of being a self, such as feeling one's thoughts are not one's own, are a schizophrenia theme. Biotype 1 patients, thirty of the group, reported stronger anomalous self-experiences than both healthy controls and biotype 2 patients. That aligned disturbed selfhood with the severe cognitive deficit, structural alterations, and heavier negative symptoms that define that biotype. Biotype 2 patients sat much closer to controls, their difference less pronounced. The authors conclude the biotypes are not just laboratory constructs: they carve psychosis at a joint that patients experience.
pmc-13526791:
Georgaras and colleagues present a 2026 machine learning approach for predicting the atomic structure of twisted layered materials. When two thin sheets are stacked with a slight twist, they form moiré patterns, meaning large repeating patterns with unusual electronic behavior. Standard learned atom models struggle to capture these structures accurately.

Their split model treats forces inside each layer separately from forces between layers, and it improved energy and force predictions about tenfold over standard models. The team also built a new accuracy check based on how stacking arrangements are distributed across a whole moiré pattern, rather than on small test cells alone. Tests on hafnium and gallium sulfide bilayers showed the better structures also gave trustworthy electronic predictions.
pmc-13526891:
Gunasekaran and a large team trace how oxygen-starved tumors spread in this 2026 study of pancreatic cancer, among the most metastatic of malignancies. Low oxygen, or hypoxia, is known to drive both shape-shifting plasticity and chromosomal instability in tumor cells, but how one signal produces both was unclear. The team pinned it on a single epigenetic enzyme, the histone demethylase KDM8.

KDM8 loss in normal oxygen copied hypoxia's effects: sweeping epigenetic changes, rewired gene activity, and defective mitotic spindles that scramble chromosomes. The enzyme's chemical activity was the point, because dead-enzyme versions failed while hypoxia-proof hyperactive variants suppressed metastasis below even normal levels. Blocking this one switch, the authors argue, could restrain pancreatic cancer spread.
pmc-13527291:
Reza Ghorbani and others present, in a 2026 methods study, a joint framework for rebuilding sped-up three-dimensional diffusion MRI acquired in multiple slabs. Scanning slab by slab speeds the scan but leaves visible boundary seams, and undersampling adds artifacts. The model treats image and slab profiles as joint unknowns inside a probability frame. A neural network energy prior, trained on clean diffusion images, guides it, plus a term anchoring profiles to a first estimate. Updates alternate between the image, using a majorize-minimize scheme, and the profiles, using regularized least squares. Across speed factors and slab layouts, the method cut boundary artifacts more than standard correction while keeping consistency and contrast. Shorter scan times could follow.
pmc-13527391:
Hafsa Ali and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, the promise of oxiracetam, a brain drug of the racetam family, for disorders of memory and thinking. Standard drugs for cognitive decline help only modestly and unevenly.
