Lab work credits the drug with several actions: boosting a key memory chemical system, tuning AMPA receptors, aiding the strengthening of connections between neurons, and damping oxidation and inflammation. Trial results in patients are mixed, with some studies showing clear gains and others none over placebo. The safety record looks kind. The authors call the drug promising but unproven, and they ask for large, careful multicenter trials.
pmc-13527891:
Michelle Mai, Colin Rogerson, and Courtney Rowan published a children's intensive care study in two thousand twenty-six on breathing support failure. Children with weak immune systems often get high-flow oxygen through the nose before a breathing tube. Waiting too long to switch raises the risk of death.

The team reviewed ninety-three such patients at one centre. Nearly half went on to need a breathing tube, and deaths clustered in that group. They built a simple score, FLOX, from flow rate, body weight, and oxygen share. Scores at or above a set cut point at the first hours linked to much higher odds of failure. The authors offer the score as an early warning.
pmc-13528091:
Orhan Ay and three colleagues compare waters breaking early in late preterm versus full-term births in a 2026 study. Records covered 646 single pregnancies at one center from 2018 to 2025. The early group, at thirty-four to just under thirty-seven weeks, held 334 cases. The term group held 312. Mothers and babies were compared on many outcomes.

Infection rates in mothers did not differ between groups. Babies told another story. The early group had lower birth weights and far more intensive care stays. About twenty-six percent needed intensive care versus seven percent at term. Breathing problems were also several times more common. Adjustment kept the early group at about five times the odds of intensive care. The authors call late preterm rupture a distinct condition. Careful watchful waiting may suit chosen cases, they suggest.
pmc-13529891:
Sébastien Derégnaucourt and co-authors ask in 2026 whether differences in song structure predict learning ability in zebra finches. Birds came from a colony where males had all learned the same model song, which held cultural background steady. The team built a combined score from song length, syllable counts, and closeness to that model.

Each bird then worked through a foraging task with training, first learning, and a reversal stage where the reward rule changed. Song scores failed to predict success in any stage. The finding fits wider bird work suggesting song quality and general learning skill vary independently.
pmc-13531591:
Laura Anselmi and colleagues priced the funding uplift English general practices need under fairer workload weights. Published in 2026, the cross-sectional study applied updated weights to 6,213 practices with over a thousand patients each, using age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, and twenty long-term conditions. The capitation formula has stood unrevised for over twenty years on crude weights.

Average workload pay stood near ninety-three pounds per patient, ranging higher in deprived areas yet still short of need. Raising every practice to a floor near one hundred two pounds per weighted patient would add about twelve percent to total payments, roughly six hundred seventy-eight million pounds yearly. The authors argue for updated weights plus further fixes for deprived-area underfunding and outcome equity. Readers get a costed case for formula reform.
pmc-13531791:
Mustafa Kurt, Ali Taşdemir, and Merve Gök compare in 2026 death-related feelings between people recovering from opioid addiction and healthy peers. Each group held 86 people, with the patient group in remission on standard medication. Questionnaires measured death anxiety, depression tied to death, suicidal thoughts, impulsivity, and resilience.

Death anxiety itself matched between groups. The patient group scored higher on death-related depression, suicidal thoughts, and impulsivity, with lower resilience. Death-related depression predicted suicidal thoughts, while resilience protected against both thoughts and impulsivity. The authors frame hopelessness about death, not fear of it, as the hidden risk.
pmc-13531891:
Haijing Ma and colleagues track in 2026 the global burden of low back pain blamed on workplace ergonomic strain among people aged 15 to 64. A world disease database supplied disability years and population data from 1990 to 2021. Rates were standardized by age and examined by region, sex, and age band.

The standardized rate fell from about 306 to about 276 disability years per hundred thousand people, though the decline stalled in the last two years studied. Men improved faster, yet women carried higher rates everywhere. Poorer regions and the 50 to 54 age band bore the heaviest load.
pmc-13534791:
William Stokes and nine co-authors compared small blood vessel function in women with and without frequent hot flushes after menopause, in this 2026 study. Hot flushes are already linked to higher blood pressure and weaker function in large vessels, an early step toward artery disease. Whether the smallest vessels are also affected was unknown.

The team studied thirty-four healthy women aged forty-five to seventy, sixteen with at least three flushes a day and eighteen with none. A finger device measured how vessels respond after blood flow is briefly blocked. The flush group scored clearly lower on that response, while blood pressure and heart rate matched the other group. The authors say the weaker small-vessel response may help explain later heart disease risk.
pmc-13536791:
Zhongfei Wang and colleagues compare radiation plans for soft tissue sarcoma in a 2026 dose study using a hybrid platform that combines a standard accelerator with focused gamma rays. Lattice therapy places small high-dose spots inside large tumors while standard doses cover the wider target. Plans for ten cases were built for the hybrid system and for a standard machine, then compared on spot coverage, dose falloff, and healthy tissue exposure.

Hybrid plans delivered higher doses to the high-dose spots and showed steeper falloff beyond them, with lower doses at tumor margins. Exposure to nearby nerves and bones also fell or held steady despite the stronger spot doses. The authors present the hybrid approach as a promising way to sharpen lattice therapy while sparing normal tissue.
pmc-13538591:
Lin Zhang and colleagues build a needle-free screening model for type 2 diabetes in a 2026 methods study. Opportunistic screening using only background, lifestyle, history, and symptom answers could flag cases early without blood tests. A stacked ensemble combined subgroup distance features with mixed sampling to handle skewed classes. Simulations then tested how adjusting changeable habits shifted each person's screening score.

The model caught most true cases, prioritizing sensitivity, yet its overall discrimination stayed modest and false alarms ran high. Adjusting the top three habits captured most of the benefit seen when all six were changed. Score gains concentrated at low decision thresholds. The authors present the tool as a feasible first-pass finder whose habit insights need prospective validation.
pmc-13538791:
Helena W Rodbard and colleagues compare adding weekly semaglutide with reduced basal insulin against simply raising insulin in a 2026 randomized study. A total of 573 adults with type 2 diabetes and overweight on modest basal insulin doses were split between the two strategies for forty weeks. Blood sugar control, weight, insulin dose, and treatment satisfaction led the outcomes.

The add-on strategy beat insulin titration on every front, cutting blood sugar averages further, shedding substantially more weight, and slashing daily insulin needs. Satisfaction scores also favored the add-on arm. Severe low blood sugar episodes fell by more than half, though stomach side effects were far more frequent. The authors present the combination as the stronger path for this group.
pmc-13539891:
Saied Besharaty and five co-authors describe, in a 2026 case report, a benign bone-forming growth sitting in soft tissue of a man's palm rather than on any bone. Osteochondroma is the commonest benign bone tumor, yet a free-standing version in the hypothenar pad of the hand is very unusual.

The patient, a 24-year-old Afghan construction worker, had carried a hard, slowly growing lump for ten years. Imaging showed a well-defined ossified mass detached from bone, and surgeons removed it whole, finding a clotted ulnar artery beside it. Microscopy showed the orderly cartilage cap and mature bone that confirm the diagnosis. Two months later his hand moved fully with no sign of return.
pmc-13540591:
Yulian Xia, Qing He, Yuhui Yao, Lei Yang, Shanshan Zhan, and Shunfeng Mao study faulty peacekeeper cells in type 1 diabetes in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The cells in focus carry a gut-homing tag and should calm immune attack. How well they work in this disease was not clear.

A mouse strain that gets the disease on its own served as the model. Tagged peacekeeper cells were pulled from the spleen and tested for how well they curb fighter cells. A drug that blocks a key immune signal was tried in dishes and in live mice. Treated cells were checked for signal output and calming power, while mice were tracked for blood sugar and pancreas damage.
pmc-13540691:
Novotny and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the many levels of influence on child overweight and obesity in the Pacific Islands. They sorted factors using a social ecological model, which layers influences from the child outward to policy. The review covered studies from the field's start to April 2024. Thirty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria.

Caregiver factors appeared most often, in twenty-two studies, followed by geography and sociocultural factors. Most studies worked at the individual level, then the interpersonal and community levels. No study addressed the policy level at all, a striking gap. Consistent links emerged for modern diets, screen time, mother's body mass index, and public versus private schooling, each tied to higher child weight. The authors map where research clusters and where it is missing for Pacific child health planning.
pmc-13541791:
Ana Torres-Agullo and colleagues apply a data method in a 2026 study. The method is called ROIMCR. It tackles tangled data from a paired instrument setup. Liquid chromatography was paired with ion mobility mass spectrometry. The extra mobility dimension sharpens chemical identification. Its datasets are heavy and full of overlapping signals. Labs need tools that can sort such data fast and still name each part right.

The team worked on standards and plastic leachates. The leachates came from polyethylene plastics. ROIMCR pulled apart overlapping components cleanly. It kept mass accuracy while doing so. It also calculated a size value for each component. Fourteen plastic additives were identified in the polymers. They included phthalates, siloxanes, and phosphates. Such additives can leak out of plastic goods over time.
pmc-13542291:
Ljubiša Bojić and co-authors test AI agents as stand-ins for social media users in this 2026 paper. Pollsters and platforms alike want to forecast how people will react to posts. The team gave language model agents written personas based on real people. They then asked the agents to predict each person's likes, dislikes, comments, and shares.

The study used survey data from 1,511 Serbian participants and twenty-seven different models. Agents scored about seventy-one percent accuracy overall. In head-to-head like-or-dislike tests, their signal beat chance by a modest margin. Simple text-based classifiers still did better. The authors warn that cheap, scalable prediction of reactions deserves watchful governance.
pmc-13542491:
Arianna Rotili, Paolo Palma, and a large team studied immune cells in youth with HIV from birth, in work from twenty twenty-six. Even on good drug care, brief spikes of virus can occur. The team asked if such spikes change how natural killer cells kill, when guided by antibodies. Twenty-two youth were split by their past spike history and checked while the virus was held down.

Youth with HIV showed weaker killing than healthy peers overall. Yet those with more past spikes showed stronger killer-cell response when their own plasma was used. With donor plasma, their cells worked just as well. The team reads past spikes as a kind of training for these cells.
pmc-13543391:
Chunyang Shi and colleagues tested whether three cheap blood numbers can flag first-episode schizophrenia. Published in 2026, the study set 181 drug-free first-episode patients beside 189 healthy controls. Schizophrenia spotting still leans on doctor judgment without measured blood markers, delaying early care.

LHR, NLR, and platelet counts each stood out alone, and together they sorted patients from controls with a score of 0.863. The trio ran higher in patients, hinting at immune upset in acute illness. The authors stress the trio does not prove it can single out this illness alone, and urge head-to-head tests against other acute mind disorders. Readers get a low-cost lead, not a settled test.
pmc-13543491:
Berivan Ece and colleagues published a 2026 protocol for an umbrella review on how nutrients and bioactive food components support brain health across the whole lifespan. Many systematic reviews already examine single nutrients against single outcomes, yet nobody has mapped the whole field at once. Their planned review will search six databases for systematic reviews published from 2016 onward that concern generally healthy people. Each review's quality will be judged with a standard appraisal tool, alongside how much the underlying studies overlap.

Because it is a protocol, no findings are reported yet. The design promises an integrated map: which nutrients have solid review-level backing for which brain outcomes, at which life stages and intake levels. It will also show where backing is thin or duplicated. Such a map would help researchers aim new studies at real gaps and help guideline writers separate well-supported dietary advice from fashion.
pmc-13543591:
Quan-feng Shao and colleagues published a 2026 study building a risk score for triple-negative breast cancer. The score draws on genes tied to low oxygen and lactate metabolism, the conditions created by the Warburg effect inside tumours. This aggressive cancer lacks hormone targets, so prognostic tools matter. Patient data from public databases were mined with regression methods to build a five-gene score, then one gene, COL5A3, was dissected with single-cell data and laboratory experiments.

Patients split by the score differed sharply in survival, mutation patterns, and immune infiltration. COL5A3 stood out as the hub: it marks malignant cells and shapes their surroundings. Experiments showed it promotes cancer progression through a signalling chain running from the receptor DDR1 through FAK into the PI3K and AKT pathway. A collagen gene usually filed under structure, the authors argue, is an active driver and candidate drug target here.
pmc-13545391:
Shangrui Rao and six colleagues published a review in two thousand twenty-six on functional bio-patches used inside the abdomen. Such patches repair tissue and can carry added jobs like fighting infection or releasing drugs. New materials have turned simple patches into multi-use platforms.

The review covers natural, synthetic, and mixed polymers used to build the patches. It then walks through uses in rebuilding the abdominal wall, repairing the gut, restoring the urinary tract, and regrowing blood vessels. The authors close with the hurdles ahead: tuning strength, matching breakdown speed to healing, and adding smart responses. They aim the review at both materials scientists and surgeons.
pmc-13545591:
Yuanyuan Li and colleagues report a cohort study, published in 2026. It was retrospective. It asks whether a heart relaxation measure predicts future heart events. The setting is chronic coronary disease. Peak filling rate measures how fast the heart's main chamber refills. It was measured by SPECT perfusion imaging. The group covered 1,446 patients. Their pumping strength was preserved.

The measure predicted major adverse cardiovascular events in women. This held independently. It did not predict them in men. Both sexes had the same preserved ejection fraction range. Adding relaxation analysis to routine scan reading could sharpen risk estimates for women, the authors argue. One shared threshold for both sexes may miss these differences.
pmc-13546691:
Mayire Aizezi and ten co-authors build a nanoparticle vaccine against the tapeworm behind cystic echinococcosis, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The disease, passed from animals, endangers people and livestock in western China's pastoral areas. Surgery and drugs suffer relapses and side effects.

Their vaccine packs a parasite antigen into biodegradable PLGA particles about four hundred nanometers wide, with high loading and slow release. Immune sentry cells took the particles up and matured. In mice the vaccine lingered in lymph nodes, raised lasting antibody levels above free-antigen and traditional adjuvant groups, and lifted T cell shares. Infected vaccinated mice developed far fewer liver cysts with healthier tissue. Gene profiling showed calmer inflammation.
pmc-13546891:
Marisa Patel, Julia Hanna, Reem Yassine, and Christopher Zarour report blocking a large spleen artery aneurysm in a man with leukemia and low platelets, in a case study from twenty twenty-six. Spleen artery aneurysms are the commonest of their kind in the belly, and those past a few centimeters risk bursting. His blood cancer had also swollen his spleen, which was eating his platelets.

Scans for cancer restaging found the aneurysm grown to about five and a half centimeters. Through a catheter, the team coiled the artery on both sides of the bulge, sealing it off. He received two units of platelets and went home with minimal bleeding and no major problems. The procedure treated both the aneurysm and the platelet drain.
pmc-13547191:
Tetiana Goncharova and colleagues described in 2026 a case where an eye disease disguised itself as a brain and nerve disorder. A 59-year-old woman arrived with swollen optic discs in both eyes, visual field loss, and headache after a flu-like illness. Spinal fluid carried an antibody linked to a recently described brain inflammation, and scans showed white matter changes plus an ovarian growth, all pointing to that brain diagnosis.

Repeated eye imaging over time told another story: the choroid layer thickened and folded, with signs on two kinds of angiography that fit Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, an immune attack on pigmented tissues. Hearing loss in both ears and later pigment loss in the eye supported that reading. The authors stress that follow-up imaging prevents this misdiagnosis.
pmc-13547691:
Sharma, Lokhande, and Vimal report a fast-growing eye socket tumor in a young woman. The patient was 26 and had redness, itching, and a large mass at the inner eye corner. The mass was 4 by 3 cm and pressed on eye muscles. Tissue tests showed nests of small round cells with sudden keratin patches. Stains lit up for NUT protein in the cell nuclei.

Those signs confirmed NUT carcinoma, a rare and harsh cancer. Growths near the tear sac are an odd site for it. Fast growth at the inner eye corner in a young patient should prompt biopsy. Early team care is key once stains confirm the diagnosis.
pmc-13548591:
Jing Li and colleagues translate a job satisfaction scale for labour ward midwives into Chinese and check that it measures soundly, in a 2026 methodological study. China lacked a rigorously validated tool matched to its delivery wards, even as midwifery models change quickly. Working from the Spanish original through its English version, the team followed standard forward and back translation steps, then surveyed 456 midwives across twenty-three hospitals in two provinces.

The finished Chinese scale holds thirty-seven items in five dimensions. Half the sample guided an exploratory analysis and the other half confirmed the structure, which fit the data well. Scores were highly consistent inside the scale and steady when midwives retook it later, and expert ratings of content coverage were near perfect. The authors conclude the scale can reliably gauge satisfaction among Chinese labour ward midwives.
pmc-13548691:
Emelie Mälstam and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six qualitative study of how hospital staff learn Teach-Back, a method for checking patient understanding. Clinicians ask patients to repeat instructions in their own words. Though widely recommended, how professionals actually learn it on the job was little known.

Eighteen professionals and four managers in two settings joined interviews and observed encounters around a training program. Learning proved to be a workplace process at several levels. Personal practice, peer interaction, organizational engagement, and ward conditions all intertwined. Four themes trace that journey, informing how communication training should be embedded.
pmc-13549891:
Ramazan Şimşek studies, in a solo 2026 paper, the hidden curriculum in Turkish children's television. Two public channels share one owner family and one age range but differ in orientation: one is general, the other religion-oriented. The question is how each words the social and emotional skills that children absorb from the shows.

The corpus holds over two hundred thousand words from 24 series and 284 episodes across both channels. Word analyses show the five core skills of the CASEL framework appear at similar rates in both. Value words split more: tradition and care mark the faith channel, while success marks the general one. The sharpest split sits in self-regulation. Faith-framed self-regulation floods the religion channel, while plain self-regulation words run near even. Şimşek calls the pattern partial substitution: the faith framing leads but does not crowd the plain framing out.
pmc-13550491:
Adriano De Marino and colleagues present Selphi, an algorithm that fills in unmeasured spots in a person's genome more accurately than the leading tools, in a 2026 methods paper. Genetic studies genotype only a slice of the genome and impute the rest by matching against reference haplotypes, but rare variants resist because existing methods look through small windows. Selphi searches whole chromosomes for the best matching stretches using a data structure borrowed from text compression, then refines the choice in stages.

Benchmarks on two major reference collections showed higher accuracy than three state-of-the-art programs across ancestry groups and variant frequencies. On UK Biobank data it again led, and the improvement carried through to agreement with full sequencing results and to more accurate polygenic risk scores. Its output plugs straight into standard analysis pipelines.
pmc-13551291:
Viktor A. Wünsch and eleven colleagues build an objective score for difficult facemask ventilation, called MASCAN. Difficult facemask ventilation lacks a robust definition, so clinics and studies spot it inconsistently. Their 2026 study enrolls 400 patients needing tracheal intubation for ear, nose, and throat or maxillofacial surgery. After anesthesia induction, each patient received pressure-controlled facemask ventilation.

An observer checked eight candidate signs, from two-handed grip and jaw thrust to oxygen saturation drops and leak fraction. Difficult ventilation occurred in 43 patients, or 10.8 percent. Five signs survived selection. They were two-handed grip, oral airway use, jaw thrust, tidal volume at or below 2 ml per kg, and oxygen saturation drop of at least 10 percent. The MASCAN model reached an AUROC of 0.96, and the MASCAN score reached 0.94 on the same scale.
pmc-13551791:
Moiz Ahmed Khan, Shajiya Saeed, Ziauddin Afrozuddin, and Wajid Ali Khan published a 2026 study of blood infections in heart patients in Karachi, Pakistan. The team reviewed one year at a large heart center. Staff drew 547 blood cultures from admitted patients in that year. The analysis covered 113 infection cases with named germs. Two inflammation markers were read alongside the cultures.

Gram-negative germs caused nearly two thirds of cases. E. coli was the top single germ. Drug-resistant germs made up about a sixth of the isolates. Both markers ran high in both germ groups, with no firm gap between them. The two markers did track each other closely. The team uses the germ list and resistance rates to guide local care.
pmc-13553291:
Saadoun Salimi and Taha BMJ Ouarda refined how atmospheric rivers are detected over North America, publishing the work in 2026. These narrow corridors of moist air drive floods and much of the West's precipitation, but standard detection thresholds miss slender systems and misjudge strength. Using four decades of ERA5 reanalysis data, the authors weighted moisture-transport measures by tropopause-aware thermodynamics calibrated against balloon soundings.

Checks against soundings and satellite imagery showed better estimates of river strength and shape, plus sharper detection of narrow filaments. Seasonal trends pointed to more river activity in spring, summer, and winter in the east, and in winter and summer in the west. Large-scale climate patterns explained over 45 percent of regional variation, a finding that should sharpen flood forecasts and climate projections.
pmc-13554091:
Supriti Sandhu leads a five-author team testing an old antiviral drug against Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that often resists treatment. The drug, trifluridine, was paired with a standard antibiotic, ciprofloxacin. Tests covered germ strains that still answered to the antibiotic and strains that no longer did. The pair was checked for killing germs, blocking slime layers called biofilms, and harming germ defences.

Together the drugs worked better than either alone, with full teamwork against the sensitive strain. The pair tore germ skins, stirred up harmful oxygen species, and cut the golden pigment that shields the germ. Slime building blocks fell, and genes for gripping surfaces shifted. Under the microscope, treated germs and their films looked bent and broken, laced with debris.
pmc-13555091:
Mathilde Lavigne-Robichaud leads an eight-author team disputing a review's verdict that job strain barely raises heart disease risk in a 2026 letter. The review pooled studies and found a modest risk rise, concluding any true effect is small at most. The letter writers agree that sharper causal reasoning is a worthy goal. They argue, though, that common flaws in the underlying studies push estimates downward.

Exposure measured crudely, over-adjustment for body risk factors, and healthy-worker selection all shrink the pooled figure. Lumping passive jobs into the comparison group blurs it further, and women's later disease onset trims events during working-age follow-up. Lower scores in job-matrix studies may reflect their own bluntness rather than bias in self-reports. Prevention policy, they say, should not rest on the shrunken number.
pmc-13555891:
Shotaro Teruya leads a thirteen-author team tracking shoulder flexibility in college baseball pitchers across four years in a 2026 study. Ten pitchers had preseason checks each year from their first to fourth season. Six standard measures covered rotation and rear shoulder tightness, comparing throwing and non-throwing sides. Only one measure moved with statistical firmness across every check.

Internal rotation in the third position fell steadily, by nearly four degrees per year on average. The decline came from the throwing side alone, while the other side held steady. Other measures showed no meaningful trend, though pitchers varied widely from each other. The authors propose this rotation measure as the marker to watch in long-term shoulder monitoring for pitchers.
pmc-13557091:
Zuzana Dunajová and co-authors show that uneven surfaces help cancer cells spread, in a study from 2026. Most invasion research stresses gene changes inside the tumor. The physical setting around cells also shapes how they move, but it is hard to test in a living tumor.

The team used tiny engineered surfaces with patterns they could tune. Cancer cells on orderly patterns moved as a linked sheet. When the obstacles were placed in a disordered way, the cells broke into single-cell invasion. That shift was as strong as the effect of losing cell-to-cell adhesion. Live imaging and a simple physics model showed two causes: local shape limits at each obstacle, and the cell's summing of disorder over time. The work names broad classes of invasion behavior.
pmc-13558691:
Hui Zhang and four colleagues built in 2026 a risk-aware access control system for the automated lines that manufacture mine ventilation ducting. Static permission lists cannot judge a request whose danger depends on timing, load, and who is asking, and these lines are safety critical. Their framework, HGRAD, draws each access event as a graph linking the user, the exposed interface, the target resource, and a physics-informed risk node, then reads it with a temporal graph network.

Extra machinery audits decisions: an intervention-style filter trims spurious log patterns, adversarial testing hardens the model, and uncertainty estimates temper borderline calls. On a public industrial internet benchmark, the system beat rival baselines in validation and held-out testing. The authors are explicit that this is benchmark proof of concept, since the risk node came from log proxies rather than real mine sensors.
pmc-13558891:
Fitria Fitria and five colleagues examined in 2026 whether eczema severity in adults lines up with measured skin barrier damage and with psychological strain. Atopic dermatitis is known for both a leaky barrier and heavy life impact, yet studies tying barrier readings to mood in the same patients are rare. Their study in Banda Aceh, Indonesia, graded severity with a standard index. Instruments measured water loss through the skin and surface hydration. Validated questionnaires scored anxiety, stress, and quality of life.

Most patients were women and most cases were mild. Severity showed no significant association with any of the five measures, neither in group comparisons nor in correlation analysis, with every trend hovering near zero. The authors close by noting that greater severity may still matter in other respects. Within this mostly mild clinic population, the skin's measured state and the mind's state travelled independently.
pmc-13559191:
Chen, Alvarez Duran, and Lee scan the brains of suggestible people in this 2026 neuroscience study, asking what distinguishes those who readily absorb others' suggestions from those who resist. Forty-two healthy women completed a validated suggestibility scale and were split into high and low groups of twenty-one, then underwent brain imaging at rest and while performing memory and attention tasks.

The highly suggestible group, counterintuitively, showed less interference on the attention task. That implies sharper attentional control. The group also carried more gray matter in two regions. These are the right superior frontal gyrus and left postcentral gyrus. During tasks they activated frontal, parietal, and temporal areas more strongly. At rest, one connection stood out: stronger coupling between a salience network node and a default mode region in the high group. The authors argue suggestibility is a structured neural trait with therapeutic leverage, not mere gullibility.
pmc-13559391:
Dong Eun Kye and colleagues used nationwide Korean health insurance data to test whether inflammatory bowel disease raises the risk of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease, a slow lung infection. Their 2026 retrospective cohort followed 6,869 adults with IBD from 2002 to 2019, matched four-to-one with people without the disease. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis were also examined apart.

Median follow-up stretched past thirteen years. Infection rates came out at 54.82 cases per 100,000 person-years in the IBD group against 43.21 in the matched group, a gap the adjusted models did not find significant. Neither bowel disease subtype showed a raised risk on its own. Competing-risk models told the same story. The authors conclude that, unlike tuberculosis, this mycobacterial lung disease does not appear more often in IBD patients, at least within Korean nationwide records.
pmc-13559591:
Li Yan and colleagues study a newly found mutation in the MUC20 gene, spotted through genetic testing of nine patients with familial adenomatous polyposis, an inherited condition. It seeds the colon with polyps. Their 2026 paper introduces the change, named S671C, into a colorectal cancer cell line using CRISPR editing, then tests the altered cells in dishes and in mice.

Mutant cells grew more slowly, formed fewer colonies, and invaded and migrated far less than their unedited counterparts. More of them died by programmed cell death, and many stalled in the S phase of the cell cycle. Tumors grown in mice were likewise weaker. Sequencing pointed to a reversed epithelial-mesenchymal transition, the shift that makes cancer cells mobile: adhesion proteins rose while invasion enzymes fell. The authors conclude the mutation acts as a brake on colorectal cancer rather than a driver.
pmc-13559991:
Reeves leads a large team studying a gene variant in Alzheimer disease brains, in work from twenty twenty-six. Many Alzheimer brains also hold other lesions, such as TDP-43 clumps. Gene risk may decide which extra lesions appear, but proof has been thin.

The team tested more than two thousand six hundred post mortem brains with a main diagnosis of Alzheimer disease. They checked a variant in the TMEM106B gene and the well known APOE types. Models linked each gene factor to each extra lesion type. The TMEM106B risk variant clustered in cases with one specific pattern. The title claim is selective effect on TDP-43 harm, not on all extra lesions.
pmc-13560391:
Yi Tseng Tsai and ten colleagues compare three statin regimens in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Statins are widely used in this disease, but head-to-head evidence on efficacy, safety, and cost stays thin. Their 2026 retrospective cohort reviews records from a teaching hospital in southern Taiwan. After matching, 729 patients took daily atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, or lovastatin-niacin for six months.

All three regimens cut liver and lipid markers significantly over six months. Lovastatin-niacin cut ALT and AST most, with about 54 percent reaching at least a 30 percent AST drop, against under 30 percent for the statins. ALT response reached about 40 percent versus about 31 percent for the statins. Statins raised HDL cholesterol more, while lovastatin-niacin cut triglycerides and cost less per benefit, with more flushing.
pmc-13562691:
Shuixian Li and nine colleagues hunt for weak points in triple-negative breast cancer, the subtype with the fewest treatment handles. This cancer leans on glutamine, an amino acid, in ways that are still being mapped. The 2026 team mined molecular data, grouped patients by glutamine-related genes, and compared survival and tumour surroundings across groups. One gene stood out: ALDH18A1, which makes an enzyme for building proline. Tumours carried too much of it, and high levels tracked with bigger tumours, spread to lymph nodes, and shorter survival.

Cell experiments showed the gene switching on the AKT/mTOR pathway, speeding cell growth, movement, and invasion while raising proline output. High levels marked tumours that shut immune cells out. A computer screen nominated six compounds that might hit such tumours. The authors propose ALDH18A1 as a warning marker and a drug target for treatment of this hard subtype.
pmc-13563591:
Yu and a team of colleagues examined how two fermentation steps reshape compounds in Tibetan dark tea in twenty twenty-six. Pile-fermentation and golden-flower fermentation are key stages in making this tea. Their combined effect on tea polysaccharides, complex sugars with health effects, was poorly understood.

The team prepared four sugar fractions: neither process, each process alone, and both in sequence. All were acidic, sugar-rich chains with the same building blocks in different ratios. Both steps together gave the lightest chains and the strongest lab effects, including antioxidant action and blocking of fat- and sugar-related enzymes. In tiny worms fed high glucose, the tea sugars cut fat storage, improved movement, and lengthened life. The authors back uses in functional foods.
pmc-13563691:
Ke Liu and three colleagues report results with a skin-flap technique for closing deep pressure ulcers around the buttocks and hip. Such sores, common in people with spinal injuries or long illness, resist grafts and reopen often. Their 2026 series covers 29 patients treated between 2018 and 2021, with ulcers at the tailbone, the sitting bone, and the hip joint area. Dead tissue and sinus tracts were cleaned out first. The repair then slid a flap over the hole, sized about one and a half to two times the defect, and buried its skin-stripped surplus into the cavity to fill dead space.

Twenty-seven flaps healed at the first attempt. Two healed slowly with dressings and further cleaning. Over six to twelve months of follow-up, only one ulcer came back at the same site. The authors call the method simple, safe, and effective, and recommend use for awkward wounds.
pmc-13563791:
Saihao Wang and ten colleagues review methylation of transfer RNA, the adaptor molecules that carry amino acids to the protein-building line. Transfer RNAs are the most decorated RNA species, bearing over a hundred kinds of chemical edits, with about thirteen marks on an average human molecule. Methyl groups are among the commonest and most varied of those edits. The 2026 review gathers what is known about three marks, on adenine, cytosine, and guanine bases, and the enzymes that write and erase them.

Those marks stiffen the molecule's folded shape, keep decoding accurate, and tune how fast proteins are made. Methylation steers the cutting of transfer RNAs into small fragments that regulate genes on their own. When the system slips, disease follows, which is why the review closes on medical stakes. The authors frame tRNA methylation as a control layer, the epitranscriptome, sitting above the genome itself.
pmc-13564091:
Ewa A. Ziółkowska and colleagues write, in a 2026 letter-style report, about gut nerve damage in mice modeling MPS IIIA, a fatal inherited storage disease of childhood. Earlier work by the group found heavy loss of gut neurons in related storage diseases, raising the question of whether bowel problems in these children share one cause.

The team examined the gut nerve network in end-stage MPS IIIA mice to test whether the same degeneration appears there. Framing the question matters because bowel symptoms strongly affect quality of life and may be treatable if their origin is understood. Readers interested in rare childhood diseases get a focused test of whether gut nerve loss is a general feature or disease-specific.
pmc-13564591:
Merve Turan and colleagues test a lung cancer score in a rare prostate cancer type. Their multicentre study from twenty twenty-six covers neuroendocrine prostate cancer in Turkey. This aggressive cancer lacks good prognostic tools. The lung immune index combines inflammation and enzyme markers.

Thirty-four patients from four centres entered the analysis. Most cases arose after standard prostate cancer, some appeared new. Blood data were gathered at three disease milestones. About half the patients scored good on the index at diagnosis. Worse index groups survived much shorter times overall. A lung score may thus help counsel prostate cancer patients. Small numbers mean the finding needs confirmation.
pmc-13564991:
Sibisi and four co-authors turned spent coffee grounds into a browning blocker for apple juice in twenty twenty-six. Cut produce browns when an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, reacts plant compounds with oxygen, hurting looks and appeal. Coffee waste is rich in the same plant compound family.

The team extracted compounds with ultrasound help, then sealed them into microcapsules by freeze-drying with food-grade carriers. Encapsulation topped seventy percent efficiency, and tests confirmed the compounds inside. Ferulic acid was the most abundant find. Added to apple juice, the capsules cut browning and kept the juice lighter over five days of storage. Computer docking showed several coffee flavonoids grip the browning enzyme tightly, explaining the effect. The authors frame the work as early evidence for valorizing coffee waste.
pmc-13566391:
Ayla Tabaksert and co-authors follow, in a 2026 prospective study, fifteen children aged seven to fourteen who received a bone-anchored hearing implant in a single operation. The sound processor was switched on early. Sixteen implants in total were tracked for two years at a university hospital for stability, survival, hearing gain, and skin reactions.

Every implant survived, stability readings rose over time, and hearing thresholds improved compared with the headband device children wore before surgery. Half of the implant sites never had a skin reaction, and the rest had only minor ones that never stopped device use. Families and surgeons get reassuring two-year evidence for a faster route to hearing.
pmc-13568191:
Geneca Henry and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, how young adults experience digital measurement-based care in routine mental health care. In this care style, patients regularly complete set questionnaires about their symptoms on a digital tool, and clinicians watch the scores over time with them. The aim is more responsive, better tuned care. The team spoke with 23 adults aged 18 to 29 at two clinics in southern Alberta, Canada.

Four themes ran through the interviews. The tool itself drew mixed marks for ease of use. Tracking scores helped many reflect on their own shifts in mood. Scores then had to be turned into conversation in the room, a step that worked unevenly. Clinician help proved key. Scores helped most when they were woven into care, not left as homework. The authors urge clinics to plan that weaving in advance.
pmc-13569991:
Lutz, Man, and Chiba-Falek compare brain cell gene activity in Alzheimer's disease and depression in twenty twenty-six. The two conditions share genetic roots. Depression often appears earlier in life, so its biology may preview Alzheimer's changes. The team analysed single nucleus RNA data from human brains.

Patients with Alzheimer's were split by whether they also had depression. Depression linked genes overlapped between Alzheimer's and healthy groups. Shared changes appeared in glutamate neurons and in microglia, the brain's immune cells. One heat shock gene and one energy gene were jointly altered. Female brains showed far more depression linked changes than male brains. Common microglial pathways involved stress and interferon signaling. The authors frame depression as a window on early disease.
pmc-13571291:
Shuhan Liu and co-authors revise a clot-risk score for hospital patients in this 2026 study. The Padua score predicts dangerous blood clots in veins for medical inpatients. The authors adapted it for Chinese patients using local data.

They analyzed 663 internal medicine inpatients to find independent risk factors. Obesity, varicose veins, diabetes, and a D-dimer blood marker each added one point in the new model. A separate group of 414 patients validated the revision. The modified score reached an area under the curve of 0.80, with sensitivity 0.82 at its best cutoff. On most measures it beat the original Padua score. Better risk sorting helps doctors target clot prevention where it counts.
pmc-13571391:
Nisha S Kolhe and four colleagues published this 2026 case report of a single patient, a 65-year-old man whose bypass graft developed a giant pseudoaneurysm, a contained rupture of the graft wall. Vein graft aneurysms complicate only about 0.07 percent of bypass operations but can rupture or compress structures. After eighteen months of worsening chest pressure, angiography and CT imaging revealed a saccular pseudoaneurysm measuring 71 by 45 millimetres in his saphenous vein graft.

Rather than reopening his chest, the heart team treated him through a catheter. Guided by intravascular ultrasound, they deployed covered stents in sequence across the defect, sealing the pseudoaneurysm off while keeping the graft open and flowing. The authors note this is the largest vein graft pseudoaneurysm treated this way. They offer covered stent placement as a minimally invasive alternative to surgery in patients, while acknowledging that management evidence remains thin.
pmc-13572191:
Junyi Tao and colleagues sequence, in a 2026 study, a Salmonella Pullorum strain found in embryos that died before hatching in Yanjin black-bone chickens, a native Yunnan breed. This host-specialized bacterium causes pullorum disease and passes through eggs, killing embryos, yet strains from indigenous breeds were barely characterized.

The complete genome held one chromosome and four small circular plasmids, two of named families, plus hundreds of virulence genes covering secretion, attachment, movement, and immune evasion. Resistance findings mixed one acquired gene with many built-in defenses. In chicks the strain caused depression, white diarrhea, and stunted growth, confirming its harm. Breeders and veterinarians get a reference genome for tracking this egg-borne threat.
pmc-13573991:
Tadesse Billo Reta and a large team probed how strain rules flips in a cobalt oxide film. Strontium cobaltite flips from a low oxygen phase to a high oxygen phase. Such flips draw staff who build circuits and power kits. The 2026 study grew thin films on two base plates, each with distinct strain. Phase field models helped read the flip acts.

Flip speed and form split by path and by base plate. On one plate the shift was sharp and led by fresh seed spots. On the next it spread in an even way from the film face. Models showed oxygen flow in the bulk and at the face, both strain bound, rule the pace. The high oxygen phase felt strain shifts more. The finds give film staff a strain dial for flip speed.
pmc-13574891:
Mohamed Nazem Alibrahim and three colleagues review how doctors define and treat high-risk acute myeloid leukaemia in 2026. This fast-growing blood cancer has poor outcomes when disease is classed as high risk. Older definitions rested mainly on gene and chromosome features seen at diagnosis.

The review argues that risk now shifts during care, shaped by fitness, treatment strength, and leftover disease that tests can still detect. It covers newer risk schemes, targeted drugs, venetoclax-based combinations, and transplant choices. Outcomes stay weak for some groups, notably disease with TP53 changes or relapse after venetoclax. The authors favour plans that adapt as results come in and attack both leukaemia cells and the niches that shelter them.
pmc-13575091:
Michele Musone and a large co-author team review combining two immune treatments for high-risk bladder cancer in 2026. Most bladder cancers are found before they invade muscle. For high-risk cases, BCG placed directly in the bladder is the standard added treatment, yet many patients still relapse.

The review sets out the biology first: BCG primes a strong local immune attack, while checkpoint inhibitor drugs may stop that attack from wearing out. Trial results so far are mixed, with varied responses in early studies of patients whose disease stopped responding to BCG. Recent large trial data for upfront combinations look less clear. pmc-13629891:
Flavio Veiga do Pilar Cobra and a large South American team characterise cemento-ossifying fibroma, a benign jaw tumour, across three countries. Their 2026 multicenter study draws records from eight oral pathology services in Brazil, Colombia, and Venezuela.

One hundred twelve cases were included, with Brazil contributing the largest share. Most patients were female, with a mean age in the mid-thirties. The back of the lower jaw was the most common site. Mixed radiographic patterns were most frequent, and cortical expansion appeared in about half of cases. Complete surgical removal and enucleation with curettage were the commonest treatments. Recurrence occurred in a small share with follow-up.
pmc-13630491:
Jessica Cristiane da Conceição de Andrade and fourteen colleagues test a protein borrowed from a whipworm. The worm is Trichuris trichiura. The question was whether its protein could calm allergic airway disease. Parasitic worms naturally teach the immune system tolerance. Their lab-made protein had already nudged human blood cells toward calmer behaviour. The 2026 letter reports its first animal tests.

In cultured immune cells the protein triggered a mixed signal profile. It leaned toward tolerance and was rich in the calming messenger interleukin-10. In mice made allergic to a tropical dust mite, the protein cut the signals that drive airway allergy. It expanded regulatory T cells. It shifted antibody responses toward a less allergic class. The authors present the molecule as a candidate for allergy therapy. It would work without live infection.
pmc-13632791:
Tarun Ramlogan, Aamir Ali, and Raenelle Ramlogan report a hard diagnostic case: a healthy twenty-year-old woman, pregnant for the first time, developed raised pressure inside the skull. At seventeen weeks she had headaches, light sensitivity, blurred vision, and double vision, with her left eye unable to move outward. Scans ruled out a blocked vein, and a spinal tap showed high opening pressure with normal fluid, after which draining fluid eased her symptoms.

The symptoms returned at twenty weeks, with even higher pressure, and eased again after drainage. She took a pressure-lowering drug, raised in dose late in pregnancy, and delivered by cesarean at thirty-six weeks; her baby did well. Six months later she remained well by phone review, though she missed her last eye check, so final proof of recovery is missing.
pmc-13634191:
Yitagesu Aberra Shibiru and colleagues reported a delayed tumor diagnosis case in 2026. A woman in her early forties had repeated low blood sugar. She also fainted at times. On arrival, her sugar was far below the normal range. Sugar infusion revived her, matching a classic test pattern. For two years she had dizziness, fatigue, and sweating spells. Sweet drinks relieved the spells, and she gained weight. Doctors first blamed a nerve disorder instead. That error delayed the true search.

Blood tests showed very high insulin during a low sugar spell. A scan found a small mass in her pancreas body. No spread was seen. Surgeons removed the tail half of the pancreas and her spleen. Tissue tests confirmed an insulin-making tumor. Her low sugar episodes then stopped fully. The authors urge doctors to consider this tumor early. Basic tests and imaging can secure timely surgery, they say.
pmc-13634391:
Suenaga and coauthors test a score that forecasts outcome after child cardiac arrest. Right forecasts guide care choices and talks with families. The score uses six facts that are easy to get at admission. Past checks used mostly older children, though.

The team reviewed infants and young children in intensive care. Records ran from late 2016 to early 2024. All children had cooling care after their arrest. Scores split children into low, mid, and high risk groups. Brain outcome was the main mark the team checked. Their aim was to prove the score works in the young.
pmc-13634691:
K Kiriki and two colleagues published this 2026 review of ear surgery outcomes in dogs with long-running ear inflammation. The operation, lateral ear canal resection, removes one wall of the ear canal to improve drainage and air flow. It was performed by a single non-specialist surgeon at one primary care clinic between 2016 and 2025. The study covered forty dogs and fifty-eight ears, each followed for at least a year after surgery.

Over a median follow-up of about two and a half years, no ear worsened into end-stage disease or needed the drastic full-removal operation. Serious complications never appeared. Typical ear cleanings per year fell to about a quarter of the pre-surgery level. Itch scores dropped sharply, and owners rated every outcome item highly. The authors argue the operation deserves earlier consideration, in ordinary clinics, rather than last-resort status only.
pmc-13635091:
Simen Rykkje Grønningsæter and colleagues estimated healthy-tissue radiation doses from a first-in-human treatment for cancer spread inside the abdomen. The treatment suspends a short-lived alpha emitter, radium-224, on tiny calcium carbonate particles. Surgeons first removed visible tumors, then the particles were washed into the abdominal cavity two days later. Nine patients with ovarian or colorectal spread took part. Blood samples and camera images tracked where the radioactivity traveled.

Modeling from those measurements put bone surfaces first for dose, then kidneys, then liver, then red bone marrow. Even the highest estimate stayed modest, and camera images showed little activity escaping the abdominal cavity beyond the large intestine. A sensitivity check widened the ranges without changing the overall picture. Combined with clinical reports from the early trials, the authors judge normal tissue doses likely below the levels where complications become probable.
pmc-13638891:
Arne Søraas and sixteen colleagues describe a 2026 pilot study of plasma exchange with young donor plasma in people with early memory problems. The idea borrows from animal work where sharing blood with young animals improved aging bodies and brains.

Twelve patients with mild cognitive impairment and signs of Alzheimer's disease had large volumes of their plasma replaced with plasma from donors aged eighteen to twenty-four. Three treatment schedules were tried. The procedures proved workable, and side effects matched the known risks of plasma exchange. The team says a larger controlled trial should now test whether the treatment helps thinking.
pmc-13639091:
Minh Tri Ho Thanh and eight colleagues published a 2026 cell study on how the protein vimentin helps groups of cells move through collagen. Vimentin is common in connective tissue and cancer cells, yet it seemed to both aid movement and block cells from squeezing through tight spaces.

Working with cell spheroids embedded in collagen networks, the team found vimentin increased collective invasion for fibroblasts and for mixtures with breast cancer cells. The effect depended on enzymes that cut collagen, and imaging plus computer models showed vimentin made spheroids more fluid and contractile. The findings clarify how tissues and tumors spread in three dimensions.
pmc-13645591:
Dorothy Koh and four colleagues develop a teaching framework for special needs dentistry within oral health therapy training. People with disability face worse mouth health and more barriers to dental care than others. The team combined a literature review, mapping of current course content, surveys of students and workers, and a structured expert consensus process. Each phase fed into the framework that follows.

Every phase showed the same gaps: uneven course content, little hands-on practice, and low confidence among students and graduates. Strong interest in more training appeared throughout. The resulting framework sets out ten skill areas, from communication to teamwork and ethical practice, with outcomes split by training level. The authors offer it as a flexible model schools can adopt. They also call for research on how the framework performs once in use.
pmc-13646091:
Paweł Chmara and three colleagues follow 211 patients with cerebral palsy through two years of robot-assisted walking training to see when real gains appear. Participants were mostly children, classed at the three walking levels of motor function. The program ran forty sessions in four sets, with gait checked every six months. Measures covered step pattern quality, step and stride length, speed, and a six-minute walking distance.

Step and stride length improved from the second check onward, speed from the third, and walking distance at every check. By the final round, over half of patients had passed the mark for meaningful change on the main measures. Patients at the lowest walking level gained earliest and most, while middle-level gains arrived later. The authors warn families and clinics that meaningful change takes sustained time, not a short course.
pmc-13648391:
Edwin J. Ovalle and four colleagues test whether a receptor called TIM-4 is required for oral tolerance induced by nanoparticles carrying lysophosphatidylserine, a fat that mimics signals from dying cells. Such particles aim to teach the immune system to accept therapeutic proteins instead of making antibodies against them.

Mice lacking TIM-4 developed tolerance to a model protein delivered by mouth just as well as normal mice, so that receptor is not essential here. Imaging also showed the single-chain particles engaging and travelling through immune cells differently from their double-chain cousins. The authors conclude that chain number, not just the shared head group, shapes how these tolerising particles work.
pmc-13649391:
Yuling Yang and seven colleagues asked if a paired drug plan for sleep during surgery calms the stress response in older patients. The surgery removed part of the food pipe to treat cancer, a major operation. The team looked back at records from 2023 to 2025 at one centre and matched three drug plans in groups of 100 patients each.

The paired plan, using both drugs, showed the smallest rise in the stress hormone cortisol by day three. Pain scores in the first day were also lower than with one drug alone. Scores for thinking decline were a bit lower too, but that gap was not firm. The authors want a larger trial before firm claims.
pmc-13649691:
Zongjun Hu and four colleagues asked if the path of a sugar-and-fat blood score over the first week in intensive care predicts death in heart failure patients. Past work used one reading at entry, which may miss the trend. The team drew on two large United States care databases and grouped score paths for more than 3,600 patients.

Three paths emerged: low, mid, and high. The high path carried the most deaths in both datasets, even after full adjustment for other risks. The mid path showed a weaker link that did not reach firm ground. Repeat checks told the same story. The authors back trend-based reading of this score for the sickest heart patients.
pmc-13649991:
Zhi Gong and eight colleagues build a security system for networks of connected medical devices, where attacks must be caught without gathering patients' raw data in one place. Their system, FedLC-Trans, lets each site train a shared detection model locally and send only model updates to a central server.

The detector mixes light convolutional blocks that scan for local patterns with a transformer part that weighs how features relate, plus an attention step that gathers the most telling signals. Tested across three public hospital-network datasets, the system scored near the top of the accuracy range on each one. The authors are candid about limits: testing ran on a powerful graphics processor rather than small bedside hardware. Training this way reduces data exposure without formally blocking attacks that probe the shared model itself.
pmc-13650691:
Romain Derelle and three colleagues present kamino, a program that builds evolutionary trees straight from proteomes. Proteomes are the full protein sets of organisms, and the program skips the slow clustering and alignment steps that phylogenetics usually demands. Traditional pipelines compare every protein against every other, which becomes punishing as datasets grow.

Kamino works differently: matching regions are spotted through shared sequence fragments flanking variable spots, and shifts in fragment counts pinpoint the variable positions worth extracting into a pseudo-alignment. Trials recovered the known lineages of the tuberculosis bacterium, most curated taxa in a major genome database, and relationships matching published fruit fly and mammal trees. Speed matched genome-based shortcut methods and beat classic marker pipelines by orders of magnitude, with moderate memory needs. The tool, written in Rust and freely released, held up from within-species comparisons to phylum-level spans.
pmc-13652991:
Lin Xie, Chen Zhang, Yonglong Wei, and Wenxiu Ning summarize new work on how the liver regrows after injury, in a commentary published in twenty twenty-six. They discuss a study showing that one zone in the middle of each liver unit holds cells that sense physical force. When tissue stress rises, a force-sensitive channel in those cells opens and lets calcium enter. That signal switches on a gene program that releases a growth-related binding protein, which then prompts nearby cells to divide.

The finding helps explain why regrowth starts in the middle zone of the liver rather than at the edges. The authors note that the pathway can in principle be targeted by drugs, which raises the hope of speeding liver repair. The piece is a short guide to the study and its promise, written for a broad science audience.
pmc-13655991:
Pamela Gaskin and Peter Chami review, in twenty twenty-six, why some people lose little weight on a new class of diabetes and obesity drugs. The drugs mimic gut hormones called incretins, named GLP-1 and GIP. They are a major advance, yet responses vary widely. The review gathers factors tied to low or no response. Higher starting weight, body mass, blood sugar, and insulin resistance all predict poorer response. Gene variants in the GLP-1 receptor gene may also play a role.

Sticking to the drug regimen strongly predicts success, with each extra month linked to more loss. Diet, activity, gut microbes, male sex, and older age also shape outcomes. The authors call for validated predictors to tailor care.
pmc-13669291:
Omar Enríquez-Antonio and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, whether a wild Mexican tomatillo could become a farm crop. The plant, Physalis gracilis, bears sweet orange fruit gathered for home use. For any wild food plant, the first questions are how it breeds and how it performs under care. The team ran crossing tests and a field trial to find out.

Hand crosses showed that all three plant lines studied were fully self-incompatible: each plant needs pollen from another to set seed, though pollen supply itself was not the limit. In open field plots the crop thrived, with about ninety-four percent of plants surviving. The estimated yield ran above eight tonnes per hectare. Fruit size, sweetness, and acidity sat in a pleasing range. The authors name the species a real candidate for open-field growing.
pmc-13674291:
Shalin Feng, Jun Mou, Xiaoqin Wang, and Changping Mu test, in twenty twenty-six, whether C-reactive protein, a blood inflammation marker, causally raises low back pain risk. They used Mendelian randomization, which treats gene variants as natural random assignments. Summary data came from genome-wide studies, with back pain data from FinnGen. Gene instruments were picked at a strict significance threshold. Single-exposure analyses used standard weighted methods. A multi-exposure model adjusted for depression, body mass, and smoking at once.

Genetically higher CRP linked to higher back pain risk. Depression showed no causal link. In the adjusted model, CRP stayed an independent risk factor, and smoking initiation also showed an independent causal effect. Instrument strength was robust. Sensitivity checks supported the findings, the authors report.
pmc-13675491:
Graham Short and co-authors report in 2026 the first proof that ghost pipefishes eat fish. These slender relatives of seahorses were long classed as crustacean specialists. That view rested on just two dietary accounts dating back to the 1960s.

The team scanned preserved museum specimens with micro-CT, an X-ray method that reveals gut contents without cutting the animals open. Inside the type specimen of one species they found two small gobies, swallowed head-first. A second species held fish remains as well, in a specimen collected in 1952. The finds widen the known menu of the whole family and show how museum jars can hold feeding clues for decades.
pmc-13676991:
Mainak Dey and four co-authors report a strain-driven reaction in two thousand twenty-six that builds complex ring systems. Bicyclobutanes are tiny, highly strained rings prized as building blocks. Joining them with indole alcohols could yield rigid frameworks of interest for drug design.

A Lewis acid catalyst drives a formal three-plus-three ring-forming reaction between the two partners. The products are indole-fused bicyclic heptanes rich in three-dimensional character. The reaction runs under mild conditions and tolerates many functional groups. Control tests and calculations support a stepwise path: the acid activates the alcohol, strain release forges a carbon bond, and a ring expansion closes the nitrogen bond. The method gives fast access to complex scaffolds.
pmc-13677691:
Nikhilesh Maity and co-authors present a 2026 model study reworking how ferroelectric and antiferroelectric phase transitions work. Such solids flip electric polarization under temperature or applied fields, and give hallmark hysteresis loops. Older models treat the flips as heat-driven jumps and stay largely qualitative.

The authors instead assume the transitions work by relaxation and need quantum treatment. That flipped pair of starting ideas lets runs built from basic laws match how ferroelectric and antiferroelectric solids act. Lean quantum model work on hysteresis opens better ways to predict how memory and actuator materials will act, for devices built on these switchable crystals.
pmc-13677791:
Plassart and co-authors probe how a polar diatom lives on near-zero light. Arctic diatoms bloom fast when spring light returns. The team grew Fragilariopsis cylindrus across a winter-to-spring light ramp. Cell division stopped at 0.18 micromoles of photons. Photosynthesis electron flow still ran at 0.1 micromoles.

Still cells did not drain their stored reserves. They kept photosynthesis active without growth in that state. Photon capture peaked between 3 and 15 micromoles. Below 1 micromole, that strategy broke down. Cells then burned off energy via quenching paths, a paradox the authors highlight.
pmc-13680091:
Pei Qi, Lizhi Wang, and Wanguo Wang test whether yeast culture in feed eases transportation stress in goats, in work published in 2026. Yeast cultures are known to steady the rumen environment and support immunity. Sixteen goats were split between a basic diet and the same diet plus a small yeast culture supplement.

The trial ran a growth phase, a one-day transport stress, and a recovery feeding phase. Supplemented goats gained more weight per day on less feed. After transport, their rumen and blood profiles showed calmer stress and inflammation markers, and antibody levels held up better. Gut microbe mixes shifted with diet and time in the expected phyla. The authors conclude yeast culture helps goats withstand the physiological strain of transport.
pmc-13681091:
Weigang Tang and co-authors pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, thirteen studies on a small surgical choice: whether to stitch a dialysis catheter in place when it is placed through open surgery. The catheter delivers peritoneal dialysis, and if it wanders from its spot, treatment fails. Fixation promises to hold it, at the price of a longer operation.

Across about twelve hundred seventy-five patients, fixation cut the odds of catheter displacement dramatically, to under a tenth of the unfixed risk. No other complication differed clearly between the groups: blockages without displacement, tissue wrapping, infection, bleeding, infusion pain, and hernia all matched. The fixed operations ran about four minutes longer on average. The authors conclude that fixation buys a large drop in displacement for a small time cost, without raising other harms, and judge it safe and effective for open placement.
pmc-13681691:
W N William and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six randomized trial in advanced head and neck cancer. Patients had cancer that had returned or spread. Standard treatment paired a platinum drug with docetaxel chemotherapy.

One hundred twenty patients were assigned by chance to add erlotinib or a placebo. Erlotinib is a targeted pill taken daily until the cancer grows. The main measure was time before the disease progressed. That time ran longer with erlotinib than with placebo. Side outcomes included survival, tumour shrinkage, and whether rash or markers predicted benefit. Oncologists get controlled evidence on the add-on.
pmc-13682191:
Khadimalah and five co-authors model heat and mass flow of a hybrid nanofluid with machine learning help, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The fluid mixes two kinds of tiny particles in a base liquid. Heat in the solid and liquid parts may sit at different levels, a state called local non-equilibrium. Such flows matter for drug delivery and for blood flow in narrowed arteries.

A math model tracks how radiation and cross-diffusion shape temperature and concentration. Equations are solved with a standard numeric solver in MATLAB. A neural network method is then trained and checked with error and regression scores. As one heat transfer setting rises, solid heat falls while liquid heat rises. The work may aid stent and cooling device design.
pmc-13684391:
Shulin Du, Moyi Zhang, Hao Zheng, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It designs a nanoparticle treatment that strips cancer cells of their main antioxidant shield, glutathione, so two forms of cell death can take hold.

Tumor cells lean on glutathione to survive treatments that would otherwise kill them. The team's particle attacks that shield three ways at once. Iron in the particle converts the antioxidant to a spent form. A sulfur linker drains more of it through chemical exchange. Gold dots choke off the supply of a key building block. With the shield gone, harmful compounds pile up inside the cell. That buildup triggers two death pathways, one driven by sulfur compounds and one by iron and fat peroxides. The paper reports the particle's design, traits, and tumor-fighting tests.
pmc-3313891:
Guyot, Ades, Ouwens, and co-authors present a method for rebuilding survival data from published Kaplan-Meier curves. Trials on time-to-event outcomes usually report only a median time and a hazard ratio. Those summaries are not enough for pooled analysis or for judging cost-effectiveness.

Their enhanced method reconstructs the underlying patient-level pattern from the printed curve, with checks on accuracy. Recovered data let analysts run richer secondary analyses without begging original teams for files. The approach is now widely used in health technology assessment, where survival modelling drives funding decisions.  Health economists adopted the method for models submitted to national appraisal bodies.
pmc-4022491:
Giambartolomei, Vukcevic, Schadt, and their colleagues presented a Bayesian test in 2014 for a key genetics question. Genome-wide studies have found many DNA sites linked to disease and to traits such as blood lipids. The next step is to ask whether two studies point to the same causal variant.

Their test, called colocalisation, checks whether a pair of association studies share a single signal in a region. It works from summary statistics alone, so it does not need each person's raw data. That makes it fast to apply across many published studies. A shared signal hints that two traits may share a biological path worth following up.
pmc-4452191:
Rőszer sought in 2015 to explain the M2 macrophage through its markers and actions. M2 macrophages, also called alternatively activated, are immune cells with wide variety in form. They govern functions where immunity meets tissue balance, metabolism, and hormone signaling.

Today these cells are often identified by the pattern of markers they express. Rőszer reviews those markers and the effector mechanisms, the tools the cells use to calm inflammation and repair tissue. A clearer picture of what defines an M2 cell helps labs compare results across studies. It also matters for diseases where these cells help or harm, from wounds to tumors.
pmc-4665391:
Servant, Varoquaux, Lajoie, and their team presented HiC-Pro in 2015. Hi-C is a method that maps how DNA folds inside the cell by capturing pieces that sit close together. Raw Hi-C data need many processing steps before they become usable contact maps.

HiC-Pro handles the whole job in one flexible pipeline, from raw reads to clean contact maps. It maps reads, keeps only valid ligation products, runs quality controls, and builds maps within and between chromosomes. Three-dimensional genome maps reveal gene control domains and folding changes in disease. A solid pipeline makes those maps reliable enough to compare across studies.
pmc-7080791:
T Rhyker Ranallo-Benavidez, Kamil Jaron, and Michael Schatz presented GenomeScope 2.0 and Smudgeplot in 2020. Before assembling a genome, researchers profile it from raw reads. Counts of short DNA words reveal genome size, variation, and repetitiveness.

The new version handles polyploid genomes, whose multiple chromosome sets confuse older profilers. Smudgeplot adds a visual way to judge ploidy from the same counts. Better profiles prevent wasted assembly effort on misjudged genomes. Plant and animal genome projects, where polyploidy is common, gained a practical standard tool. The tools are distributed freely and have been adopted by several large genome sequencing centers.
pmc-7820391:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Blindness and Vision Impairment Collaborators analyzed in 2020 the causes of blindness and poor vision worldwide, and how they changed over thirty years. Many causes of vision loss can be prevented or treated. At the same time, an aging world population is pushing demand for eye care upward.

The team estimated how common each cause was from 1990 onward, and what share of blindness could have been avoided. They also measured progress against the goals of a long running global initiative for the right to sight. Their findings show where treatment backlogs, such as untreated cataracts, remain largest, giving eye health planners a clear view of unmet need.
pmc-7857391:
Ludovico Cantuti-Castelvetri and co-authors reported in 2020 that a protein called neuropilin-1 helps SARS-CoV-2 enter cells and spread infection. The virus is known to use the ACE2 protein as its main receptor, as did the earlier SARS virus. But the two viruses favor different tissues, which suggested another factor helps decide where the new virus can go.

The team presents evidence that neuropilin-1 acts as such a helper, easing the virus's entry into cells that carry it. That could help explain the virus's reach into tissues such as the upper airways and the brain. Findings like this widen the list of possible drug targets beyond the main doorway.
pmc-8024391:
Robert Sterner and Rosalie Sterner reviewed in 2021 both the promise and the limits of CAR-T cell therapy, a treatment that re-engineers a patient's own immune cells to hunt cancer. The therapy has produced remarkable responses in certain leukemias and lymphomas of B cell origin. Yet many patients still do not benefit, and solid tumors have proved much harder to crack.

The authors catalog the main obstacles, including cancers that escape by losing the target, severe side effects, and the difficulty of making each batch. They then survey strategies under study to overcome those limits, from new target designs to off the shelf cell products. The review gives a balanced measure of a celebrated therapy at a turning point.
poems-pg11091:
John L. Stoddard published this volume of his Poems in 1913 and dedicated it, in Latin, to his dearest wife. Stoddard was famous in America as a travel lecturer, filling halls with lantern-slide journeys to the world's wonders, and his verse carries the same well-traveled, reflective temper. The opening proem sets his modest theme: an old man playing a violin with silent strings, hoping his songs might yet touch a human heart.

Contents show the lecturer's map: the Ring Nebula and the Sphinx, sunset at Interlaken, Corsica, the Venus of Melos, silver herons, and reincarnation. Travel poems alternate with meditations on youth, age, and death. Stoddard knew the poems were a sideline to his lectures. The proem asks only that the dreamer never learn his bow was silent, a disarming frame for a popular performer's private art.
poems-pg12391:
Elizabeth Stoddard published this volume of her Poems in 1895, late in a career spent mostly in the shadow of her novels. Stoddard wrote fiction of unusual psychological force, and her verse shares its weather: compressed, moody lyrics in which months and seasons carry emotional states. Contents begin with the Poet's Secret and move through November, March, August, and October, a calendar of the inner life.

Domestic drama enters in paired pieces, the Wife Speaks and the Husband Speaks, and in the stark title One Morn I Left Him in His Bed. Other poems turn to the sea, the city, and a wolf-tamer, showing her range beyond the lyric of feeling. Stoddard's reputation has grown steadily since her death; this single volume of poems, terse and unsentimental. Is a large part of the reason critics now rank her among the finest American poets of her century.
polish-constitution-3-may-1791:
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth adopted its constitution on 3 May 1791, the first written national constitution in Europe. Reformers in the Great Sejm pushed it through as the Commonwealth weakened and its neighbors circled. The charter was a rescue attempt: strengthen the state before Russia and Prussia could finish dividing it.

The text ends the nobles' right to block all business with a single veto, makes the monarchy hereditary, and gives towns a voice in the state. Catholic faith is kept, with toleration promised to others. Russia answered with invasion, and the partitions wiped Poland from the map within four years. The charter of a nation's last hope, adopted too late, is still honored in Poland's national day.
ponzinibio-de-lamiis-latin-1591:
Gianfrancesco Ponzinibio, a jurist of Piacenza, wrote De lamiis, on witches, early in the sixteenth century. This text comes from the Frankfurt Tractatus duo of 1591, which revived his daring argument. Ponzinibio holds that the witches' flight and sabbath are illusions, not bodily events.

As a lawyer, he attacks the evidence itself. Dreams and torture, he argues, cannot build a capital case. His tract is the daring precursor that Johann Weyer later built upon. Skeptics across Europe cited Ponzinibio as their early authority. The book's courage is plain: a working jurist told the witch courts, in Latin, that their central scene never happened.
prestwich-chalk-plateau-1891:
