Joseph Prestwich, a great English rock scholar, staked his name on the Kent flint claims in this paper of 1891. Benjamin Harrison, a Kent shop man, had found rough flints on the chalk hills that he held to be tools. Prestwich backed him in print, with the talk that came next in full.

The flints, called eoliths, were said to show man at work before the ice age in Britain. Prestwich tells of their beds, depth, and worn forms as proof of true tools, not chance stones. The paper is a grand man's bold bet, held in the full record of its day.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-100:
Volume 100 of Punch, dated April 11, 1891, prints the sixteenth of Mr. Punch's Prize Novels, a burlesque called Germfood by the invented author Mary Morally. Her covering letter, quoted without permission, promises blood, fits, and hysteria in three murderous volumes.

Chapter one opens in a poorer quarter of Paris, whose vagueness the narrator defends against pedants who clamour for accuracy and local colour. The Seine, she warns, shall run red if she chooses. Readers get Punch's mockery of the sensational French-style novel then crowding English shelves, all shrieks and scarlet ribbons.

Leaves from a Candidate's Diary continues in Punch, volume 100, for April 18, 1891. The diarist leaves Billsbury by train carrying two local papers, the Standard and the Radical Meteor, and finds their reports of the same meeting hard to believe as one event.

The Conservative Standard praises the chosen candidate, Richard B. Pattle, for his Oxford honours, his rowing, and his lucrative practice at the Bar. The Meteor calls the meeting an annual farce about who has the money-bags. Readers get electioneering shown from both sides of the press at once.

Punch, volume 100, for April 25, 1891, gives the third of Mr. Punch's Pocket Ibsen pieces: Hedda Gabler, condensed and revised by the paper's own harmless Ibsenite. The drawing room is dressed in black crape, black bombazine, and bouquets of dried grasses.

A posthumous portrait of General Gabler hangs over a black horsehair sofa, a pall rests on the piano, and a cemetery shows through the window. Aunt Julie arrives before breakfast to ask after George and Hedda. Readers get Ibsen's gloom pushed past reason, a hit at the serious drama then thrilling London.

Mr. Punch's Pocket Ibsen reaches its second piece in the number for April 4, 1891: Nora, or the Bird-Cage, a condensed and revised version of Ibsen's famous play. The room is filled with cheap art furniture, chenille monkeys, and Japanese fans.

Nora comes in humming with parcels while a porter carries a Christmas tree after her. She tips him a shilling and eats macaroons. Then Helmer looks in from his manager's room, calls her his little squirrel, and the macaroons are hidden at once. Readers get the doll's-house drama reduced to a bright, biting toy theatre.

Modern Types, written by Mr. Punch's own type writer, reaches number twenty-three in the issue for February 14, 1891: the Tolerated Husband. The essay opens by mocking moralists who praise the pure British hearth against wicked foreign nations.

English wickedness, the writer argues, is merely coarser and duller than the Parisian kind, guttering like a cheap candle beside a steady flame. Divorce court shocks administered by Mr. Justice Butt are quickly forgotten by patriotic readers. Readers get a sly attack on national smugness, dressed as a portrait of one henpecked husband.

Punch, volume 100, for February 21, 1891, prints the thirteenth Prize Novel, Through Space on a Formula, by the invented Rules Spurn. His letter boasts that the tale is about his thousand and first book, though he has lost count.

Spurn promises large numbers of leagues, vastnesses, secrets, and impossible sciences, and denies writing in French since he writes only in English or American. Parody titles riff on famous adventure books of the day. Readers get Punch's hit at the flood of scientific romances and the authors who turned them out by the shelf.

Specimens from Mr. Punch's Scamp-Album reaches number two in the issue for February 28, 1891, with the Literary Ghost. Readers are asked to picture themselves as an elderly lady by her fireside, knitting for a bazaar, when a gentleman without a card is announced.

The maid vouches for him: a perfect gentleman, with a respirator. Blue spectacles and a red nose complete the portrait of the man who writes other people's books for pay. Readers get a rogues' gallery portrait of a trade everyone suspected and few admitted to using, for love or money.

A playlet called The Model Husband Contest opens the pages of Punch for February 7, 1891. At the Galahad-Greens', a wife tells her meek husband that a paper is offering twenty pounds to the wife who makes the best case for her husband as a model.

Cornelia has entered Galahad, not from pride but because the drawing-room carpet is a disgrace and the prize would pay for a new one. She then reads her entry aloud, beginning with his faultless morality. Readers get married life as a prize essay, with love and housekeeping accounts kept in one ledger.

Punch, volume 100, for January 10, 1891, prints the tenth Prize Novel, The Fondman, by the invented Called Abel, author of The Teamster. His letter calls the work a saga and admits he does not know what a saga is.

History be blowed, he writes: mix dates and incidents, fill up with simple human passions, then add a proem and an epilogue with nothing to do with the story. Northern legends and a tale about Mahomet complete the recipe. Readers get Punch's recipe-book mockery of the historical romance trade. All in fun, of course.

Voces Populi visits the Regent Street Tussaud's in Punch for January 17, 1891, reporting talk overheard before the waxworks. A picture at the head shows the paper's sport and art exhibition drawing a badger.

Before the effigy of Dr. Koch, shown examining a test tube, a well-informed visitor explains that he discovered the consumption bacillus, and his friend asks what good it is now he has it. Old ladies with a catalogue study the home life at Sandringham scene. Readers get the crowd at a waxworks thinking aloud, each voice a small comic portrait.

The twelfth Prize Novel fills Punch, volume 100, for January 24, 1891: The Mate of the Marlispike, by the invented Shark Mussell. His letter promises a regular briny ocean story, all storms, thunderclaps, and bellying sails.

Sea slang of the old school is declared played out; the public, he says, requires stories about merchant ships, with hairy villains, tempest-tossed wrecks, human interest, and word-pictures of ships and storms. Parody titles crowd his list of earlier works. Readers get the nautical yarn trade hoisted with its own rigging. Clear the decks, indeed.

Punch opens volume 100 with a calendar for the year, printed in the number dated January 3, 1891. The January page gives thirty-one days of saints, battles, births, and deaths in the paper's compact style.

New Year's Day, Epiphany, the battles of Abydos and Corunna, and the deaths of Pitt and Prescott share the list with sunrise and sunset times. February follows with its own roll of anniversaries. Readers get an almanac page of the kind Victorians pinned up for the year, equal parts history lesson and daily reminder. Such pages were furniture for the year.

Voces Populi reports a row in the pit in Punch for January 31, 1891, subtitled The Obstructive Hat. The scene is a theatre pit during pantomime time, as the overture begins and a family settles into cramped seats.

An overheated matron tells her husband they have done better than expected after the crush, though she thought her ribs gone once. Little Jimmy pipes up that he cannot see, and his mother promises imps dancing and real fire from a pot once the curtain rises. Readers get a working family's night out, told in overheard talk.

Voces Populi goes to a music hall in Punch, volume 100, for June 13, 1891. The house is respectable but not smart, and its better seats are filled with patrons who talk through the acts and applaud everything alike.

The chairman announces the Sisters Silvertwang, character duettists, who sing in praise of nature with a step dance. A white-capped attendant calls out sandwiches at twopence during a pause, and a voluble lady in the shilling stalls tells her companion a story with no reachable point. Readers get the music hall as its audience heard it, talk and all.

Punch for June 20, 1891, pairs a river poem with a bus horse's diary. On the River praises a light canoe, cigarettes, sunshine, a book of verses, and a Thames-side inn as simple joys that suit an idle rhymer.

Then come the memoirs of a bus horse, kept during a social crisis: home late after the last turn, something plainly up, and by Sunday the horses are on strike. The horse cares little for the rights of it, given straw and good feeds. Readers get the omnibus strike of the day retold from the stable.

A Wail from the Tub recalls Sunday, June 14, in Punch for June 27, 1891. Hyde Park fills with a demonstration seeking to extend the Factory Acts to small and unhealthy laundries, with banners, hired bands, and lorries of laundry women in high spirits.

Railway workers, cabmen, tailors, gas stokers, decorators, and carpenters march in, while each platform mostly airs its own grievance and sightseers drift between speeches. Socialists in a corner remember Chicago. Readers get a labour procession drawn with sympathy and comedy in equal parts, from the washerwomen's side of the park.

Voces Populi, under the title Bricks Without Straw, visits a village schoolroom in Punch for June 6, 1891. A juvenile treat is in progress, and a hired magic lantern with slides to last one hour is about to be shown.

The vicar's daughter begs the new curate, Mr. Tootler, to explain the pictures, since the lantern man only manages slides. Tootler, a shy man, admits he knows nothing of Valentine and Orson, the nursery tale chosen for its fine moral. Readers get a kind man's embarrassment turned into gentle village comedy, lantern, slides, children, and all.

The third specimen from Mr. Punch's Scamp-Album appears on March 14, 1891: the Biographer. Readers are asked to imagine themselves a worthy merchant retired to a villa at Norwood, called from watching the sky to meet a gentleman on particular business.

The visitor is a brisk stranger with red whiskers and a flexible mouth, come to write the merchant's life. Experience and practical knowledge are flattered into request. Readers get a portrait of the life-and-times trade, in which any retired tradesman could be talked into print for a price. Vanity supplies the rest.

My Lady, a comic poem, leads the pages of Punch for March 21, 1891. The singer admits his lady is not fair to outward view, and that she flew into a rage on learning this from him.

Yet he calls her divine by her own peculiar line: deeply read, sharp of tongue, feared by tradesmen, and feared by bus conductors for her metallic tones. She goes stridently and contentedly through life, and he marvels that she chose to be his wife. After the poem comes Kensington correspondence on a proposed local railway. Readers get love and alarm in one portrait.

The G.P.O. Cuckoo, a ballad of the post office, appears in Punch for March 28, 1891. A gallant Postmaster arms for the fray and summons his array from north, south, east, and west to defend the department.

An officer rallies the postmen, whose hours are long, against a public that wants boy messengers instead. The papers may rave, the song says, while the office pockets the pence. Raikes, the red knight of the pillar box, stands as the cause's champion. Readers get a labour dispute inside the post office sung as a heroic lay.

Voces Populi remembers a fog in Punch for March 7, 1891, setting its scene on a main road near Hyde Park at eight at night. Nothing can be seen, but horses slipping, wheels grinding, crashes, and strong language can all be heard.

Mrs. Flusters, in a brougham with her husband on the way to dine in Cromwell Road, fears they will be dreadfully late and urges the coachman Peacock to hurry. A blurred shadow on the box answers that the fog is very thick just here. Readers get a London fog as pure talk and noise.

Punch, volume 100, for May 16, 1891, prints the seventeenth Prize Novel, Gasps, by the invented Olph Schreion, author of Screams. His letter explains the freedom of allegory: write something big and vague, with symbols thrown in by the handful.

If the writer reads it next morning and cannot understand it, he may be sure it is an allegory; the public will read in morbid emotions and life problems of its own. No explanation is needed, which saves trouble. Readers get the symbolist tale of the day deflated in its author's own words.

Songs of the Un-Sentimentalist opens the pages of Punch for May 2, 1891, with A Dustman's Silent Tear. The singer confesses that he once stopped his dustman's customary fee in a fit of economic fire, without knowing how the man had offended.

The dustman muttered, turned, and went his way dejected, and the singer vowed never to moisten any eye with grief again. Twice a week after that he hailed the man whether the bin was full or empty, seeking one grateful smile. Readers get a comic ballad of small guilt and large amends.

Mr. Punch's Pocket Ibsen returns on May 23, 1891, with the fourth piece, The Wild Duck, acted at Werle's house in Norway. A brilliant dinner party is in progress, and old Mr. Werle proposes the health of his housekeeper, Mrs. Sörby.

Short-sighted chamberlains drift from the dining room with Hjalmar Ekdal, who writhes shyly under their remarks about the amount they have eaten. The condensed and revised version keeps the solemn manner while cutting the play to pocket size. Readers get another round of Ibsen burlesque, aimed at solemn talk about truth and illusion.

Act three of The Wild Duck, from Mr. Punch's Pocket Ibsen, appears in the number for May 30, 1891. Hjalmar's studio is being tidied by Gina and Hedvig after a photograph has been taken.

Gina explains that a luncheon party with Dr. Relling and Mölvik was cut, since it had little to do with such plot as there is and cutting came cheaper. Hjalmar returns from a walk with Gregers to accuse Gina of having been rather a wild duck before their marriage. Readers get the burlesque's plain-spoken version of Ibsen's great scene of confession.

A first visit to the Naveries leads Punch for May 9, 1891, sending two of Mr. Punch's own men to the Royal Naval Exhibition at Chelsea. They enter with strictly nautical cries about timbers and yard-arms.

The show fills the grounds of the Military Hospital, far larger than the soldierly exhibition of the year before, which had crept in with fear and trembling. This year the Admiralty took what ground it required without comment. Readers get a landsman's tour of the navy's show, full of pride in the sea dogs and jokes about Pimlico gardens.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-volume-101:
The Prince, a letter in mock old style, leads Punch, volume 101, for August 1, 1891. It is addressed by one Nicola Puncio Machiavelli to Vittorio Emanuele, son of Umberto, King of Italy, during the prince's visit to Britain.

Every man, the letter begins, either is a prince or is not one, and the writer offers the fruit of fifty years spent learning men and governments. The young prince is urged to draw advantage for himself and for those he will rule. Readers get Machiavelli's cold counsel dressed for a royal tour, half homage and half warning.

A Terrible Tale, told in verse, heads the pages of Punch for August 15, 1891. The speaker has not left his room for weeks when a burly rough attacks him without a word, tears out his nails, and beats him black and blue.

Only at the end does the joke land: the victim is a carpet, and the attacker a carpet-beater who cleaned him out. After the poem, Leaves from a Candidate's Diary resumes with letters from Billsbury arriving by every post. Readers get a shaggy-dog ballad first and election business after.

The third of The Travelling Companions appears in Punch for August 22, 1891, set on the coach from Braine l'Alleud to Waterloo. Mr. Cyrus K. Trotter and his daughter ride behind with Podbury, while Culchard, not yet on speaking terms, sits up front.

Miss Trotter finds her seat no bed of roses, thanks to a chunk of wood nailed down its middle, and asks why Podbury's friend keeps away from them. Podbury answers awkwardly that Culchard is a queer chap who takes prejudices into his head. Readers get tourists and wounded pride on the road to a battlefield.

Storicules begins in Punch, volume 101, for August 29, 1891, with The Suicide-Advertisement. A shopper at a station machine, choosing between gooseberry nougat and gum caramel, cannot miss the notice for Higlinson's blacking-cream.

The same call meets the eye on hoardings, papers, omnibuses, and leaflets dropped through letter boxes, until importunity pays and the cream is bought. It proves just about as good as any other, yet buying goes on. Readers get a small study of advertising power, told as the first of a set of tiny stories.  It worked on everyone.

Larks for Londoners fills the pages of Punch for August 8, 1891, with letters demanding more free pleasure from the town halls. The first writer accepts free concerts and dances, then asks why billiard tables should not be free as well.

Municipal tobacco, free ale, and wine from the wood follow, all from the rates, which the writer proudly notes he does not pay himself, living in a flat. A second letter insists pleasure should be elevating in kind. Readers get ratepayer politics turned inside out by the people who would spend the money.

Letters to Abstractions reaches number eight in Punch for December 12, 1891, with a letter to Laziness. The writer's heart warms to his subject as he counts a hundred things he ought to be doing instead.

A friend in the wilds of Canada has waited months for an answer and begs for small details of old friends, word of Jack Bumpus's marriage, and any news at all. The unanswered letter does the arguing. Readers get idleness praised and punished in a single page, in the series' mock-solemn style of open letters to things no postman can reach.

Our Booking-Office, the paper's review corner, fills the pages of Punch for December 19, 1891, with Christmas books. The Baron's assistants recommend The Children of Wilton Chase by L. J. Mead and Florence Marryat's tale of adventures in Japan.

Sarah Doudney's Where Two Ways Meet joins the list before the reviewers turn to the festive board, calling readers down to mince pie and plum pudding. Those emblems of good cheer, they note, are themselves down in the mouth. Readers get a Christmas shelf guide with jokes served beside the pudding. All recommended in good faith.

A Queer Christmas Party appears in Punch, volume 101, dated December 26, 1891. The narrator remembers dressing, taking a cab, and dining with a very old friend, yet cannot recall the friend's name or where he lives.

Round the table sit Robert Elsmere, Dorian Gray, Sir Alan Quatermain, the Master of Ballantrae, and Princess Napraxine, heroes and heroines of famous recent novels gathered at one dinner. The account was written down the next day for its strangeness. Readers get a Boxing Day dream in which the year's fiction comes to supper and stays for the evening.

Quite Fabulous, a story of the times dedicated to Professor Munro, leads Punch for December 5, 1891. King Cole, described as a merry old soul, is in truth a tyrant whose subjects labour underground bringing up the black diamonds of the earth.

When the miners complain that sixteen hours are too many, the king grants twelve, then calls them back to demand just as many diamonds as before. The fable turns a coal dispute into a nursery crown. Readers get labour politics in fairy dress, with the moral left plain for any reader of the coal news.

Voces Populi gathers more pot-pourri from the park in Punch for July 11, 1891. Near Cumberland Gate, preachers, reciters, and debaters hold forth behind the rails while small groups discuss something else entirely.

A set debate with a time limit runs between a Parnellite and an Anti-Parnellite under an ornamental chairman. A youthful socialist, working himself to white heat, calls the capitalists greedy gobblers and his well-to-do audience the small fish who let themselves be gobbled, which they accept with perfect gaiety. Readers get Hyde Park oratory as street theatre.

Letters to Abstractions prints its second letter in Punch for July 18, 1891, addressed to Social Ambition. The writer had not meant to write again, but concrete human beings have written to deny that he proved his case.

He answers that he never set out to prove a case, only to enjoy a friendly chat and plead for the class he calls the Dabchicks. Critics complain he talked grandly of queens, dukes, and actresses, then offered one story of a parvenu. Readers get the series defending itself with good humour while the snobbery debate rolls on.

Operatic Notes fills the pages of Punch for July 25, 1891, with a drawing of Amonasro and Aïda trading lines no libretto contains. The black king announces himself as her father; she tells him he ought to be Otello tomorrow night.

The diary for Tuesday, July 14, finds Madame Nordica not at her best as Aïda, lacking colour where the part most needs it, opposite Devoyod's villain of the deepest dye. Trumpets sound husky, as if they had caught cold. Readers get Covent Garden through the paper's own opera glass, affectionate and merciless at once.

Urbi et Orbi opens Punch for July 4, 1891, with Mr. Punch returning thanks for early congratulations on his jubilee. He informs everybody everywhere that the fiftieth anniversary of his natal day falls on July 18, and gives all the world leave to keep it as a whole holiday.

A sketch follows on the Chantrey Bequest, after a member of Parliament proposed that government veto academy purchases it disliked. The President and council of the Royal Academy wait in a studio for government to inspect their latest buy. Readers get the birthday announced and art politics mocked in one number.

Letters to Abstractions turns to Vanity in its sixth letter, printed in Punch on November 14, 1891. The writer pictures Vanity smirking before her constant companion, the abstract mirror, pleased to be the subject of a whole letter.

He warns her the pleasure will fade by the end, since none of her victims like hearing the truth about themselves. Their clouds of offence pass as soon as the truth-teller leaves and the false self recovers. Readers get a moral essay in letter form, sharp about self-love and gentle in its delivery.

Cancel, or Recall fills the pages of Punch for November 21, 1891. The paper takes up a report that the son of the most distinguished Irishman of the century faces forced retirement by age from a large revenue department.

Mr. Punch doubts the sentence has truly been passed, and urges authority to recall it in favour of the son of the Liberator, whose name is also Dan. A headpiece shows the cars prepared for the Welsh Lord Mayor, somehow left out of the procession on the ninth. Readers get Irish loyalty and London pageantry sharing one indignant page.

Letters to Abstractions prints a seventh letter, a second one to Vanity, in Punch for November 28, 1891. The writer describes a letter found innocently on his breakfast table, stamped and addressed in the ordinary way.

Its writer calls him a ridiculous being. She declares his last letter the most absurd thing she ever read, while admitting his story of Hermione Maybloom is absolutely true, since she knew Hermione slightly herself. Readers get Vanity answering back in her own voice, which proves the letter's point better than any argument.  She signs in full.

Only Fancy opens Punch for November 7, 1891, with a telegraphic absurdity from Berlin. Photographers and makers of plaster busts are in crisis because the Emperor keeps changing his appearance from day to day.

Stocks of portraits showing His Majesty with a beard were thrown back on the trades when he shaved it off, and Prussian funds are said to have fallen on the news. A second item grants an opera manager leave to prefix Royal to his house. Readers get foreign courts reduced to coiffure and trade panic, in the paper's driest wire style.

Atropos and the Anthropoids, a dirge at the Zoo, appears in Punch for October 10, 1891. The verses mourn the thinning ranks of the great apes after the deaths of Sally the chimpanzee and George the orang-outang, reported in a daily paper.

One little chimpanzee and one small gibbon remain to cheer the tearful Zoo, the gibbon being advised to write his race's rise and fall. A headpiece dreams of the cyclist centaur of the future on a pneumatic tyre. Readers get animal grief and machine fancy sharing the page, both treated with mock solemnity.

The Automatic Physiognomist, a scene at the German Exhibition, appears in Punch for October 17, 1891. A penny machine promises to reveal character and future from the colour of a customer's hair, and a party of pleasure seekers gathers round it.

Lottie reads the offer aloud and wonders what they will have next, while her admirer marvels how far invention has come since butter-scotch. Aunt Maria calls the thing rubbish and wants to move on toward the band. Readers get fairground science judged by the crowd it hoped to fool, in snatches of overheard talk.

Laissez Faire, an inscription for a free public library, appears in verse in Punch for October 24, 1891. The poem calls the library an institution doomed to scare the devotees of letting things alone, Herbert Spencer named among them.

Free books paid from the rates, the poem argues in the voice of the shocked individualist, mean freedom's ruin. The self-made man and the sweater who sucks wealth from toiling crowds, by contrast, pass as all right. Helping each other is mocked as folly. Readers get the free library fight in sarcastic rhyme, aimed squarely at the doctrine of self-help.

The ninth of The Travelling Companions appears in Punch dated October 3, 1891, set on the Burg terrace at Nuremberg. Podbury sits on a bench grappling with an epitome of Spencer's philosophy.

Reading aloud, he grants that following the divisions of matter to infinity would require infinite time. That time he has not got to spare. Still, he calls the philosophy bally rot he must peg away at to please a certain lady. Then she arrives, with Culchard beside her. Readers get courtship conducted through heavy reading, with jealousy doing the real work on the terrace.

Young Grandolph's Barty, a ballad in stage German dialect, appears in Punch for October 31, 1891. The heading calls it an Afrikander version of the Breitmann ballads, penned in sorrow by a German resident in distant regions.

Grandolph had a party, the song asks, and where is that party now? He fell in love with African gold, rowed with Solly, and split his party in two by secession. Initials stand in for Balfour, Wolff, and Gorst in the mangled verses. Readers get party politics sung as a music-hall lament, dialect and all.

Some Circular Notes reaches chapter four in Punch for September 12, 1891, recording a stay at Reims in telegram-short sentences. The cathedral is seen and pronounced grand, with nothing said about it, since the writer is not making notes for a guidebook.

The hotel's silence suggests a prison on the silent system, relieved by Daubinet singing in the courtyard and shaking hands with everybody on every occasion. Calves, caves, calls, and the start of a drive fill the chapter's own summary. Readers get travel writing stripped to chatter, haste, and one cheerful companion.

Silence and Sleep, lines written at cock-crow, appears in Punch for September 19, 1891. Night broods over hill, meadow, and slow river, while tall poplars stand sentry in a sleeping world.

All who toiled or played through the day rest now, their jests, hoofbeats, mill wheels, and sickles stilled. The speaker too yields, and drifts through silence toward dreamless rest as a tired swimmer floats. A headpiece shows the Daily Graphic weather young woman taking her Sundays out. Readers get a rare straight lyric in the comic paper. The hush holds to the end.

The Waiters' Strike, set at the Naval Exhibition, is sung in Punch dated September 26, 1891. The German waiter, grown fat and proud, throws down his napkin like a challenge and swears he will not wait.

The rebels are said to have lost their place like readers without bookmarks, vanishing from Chelsea in dress suits and disgrace, while murmurings rose in dark public houses. A proverb about striking while the entrée is hot is blamed for misleading them. Readers get a catering walkout at the year's big show turned into ballad justice.

Chapter three of Some Circular Notes appears in Punch for September 5, 1891, bringing the travellers into Reims at ten at night. The town seems in bed and asleep, its few street figures watched by gendarmes.

The party drives under an ancient Roman arch, whose history Daubinet tells vaguely before breaking off, then passes a desolate museum and a brightly lit theatre. The Lion d'Or, its landlady, and its boots await. Readers get the Vacuus Viator abroad again, collecting gloom, legend, and hotel discomfort in shorthand notes.  Night travel tells its own tale.
ripley-compound-of-alchymy-1591:
George Ripley was an English canon and alchemist of the 1400s. His Compound of Alchymy is a poem in twelve gates. The print here is the 1591 dress of the work. It is the chief poem of English alchemy.

Each gate is a step in the Great Work, from first rot to the red stone. Ripley veils his craft in rich signs: kings, beasts, and baths of dew. He warns the false hand and cheers the true son of the art. The poem's fame kept it in print for two hundred years.
russell-studies-scriptures-vol3-1891:
Russell's Thy Kingdom Come, published in 1891, is volume three of Studies in the Scriptures. The book turns from chronology to the papacy, prophecy, and the coming kingdom itself. Russell's followers read it as the sequel that showed what the dates would bring.

He reads the book of Revelation and the parables as a coded history of the church age ending in harvest. The great pyramid of Egypt even enters his argument as a stone witness to the divine plan. The volume deepened the movement's sense of living at the turn of the ages. Russell treats prophecy as a timetable that careful Bible study can read.
russell-thy-kingdom-come-1891:
Charles Taze Russell issued Thy Kingdom Come in 1891 as the third volume of Millennial Dawn. The series, also called Studies in the Scriptures, set out his reading of prophecy. Bible Students, his movement, awaited Christ's kingdom on a dated scheme. This volume carries that scheme toward its climax.

Its Great Pyramid chapters made pyramidology a doctrine of the movement. Russell read the pyramid's passages as a stone calendar of sacred history. Measurements in inches became years in his prophetic sums. The book is a document of record for the Bible Student faith. It is preserved as history, not as endorsement. Its influence built a lasting movement.
saussaye-manual-science-religion-1891:
Pieter Daniel Chantepie de la Saussaye was an Amsterdam professor whose Manual of the Science of Religion, in this 1891 English edition, helped name a field. The science of religion was then new, split between history and philosophy. His manual gave it a method and a map.

De la Saussaye sets out phenomenology, the ordered description of rites, myths, and ideas, before judging any of them. He treats prayer, sacrifice, priesthood, and sacred books as forms that recur across the world. Textbook writers across Europe built on his scheme, and his terms still echo in the field.
sbe-32-vedic-hymns-1-1891:
F. Max Muller gave the Vedic Hymns, Part One, English dress in 1891. The work is Book Thirty-Two of the Sacred Books of the East. The hymns come from the Rig Veda, the most old text of India. Muller spent his life on the Vedas at Oxford.

The hymns here praise the Maruts, the storm gods who ride with Rudra. Rudra, Vayu, and Vata get hymns of their own in the set. Wild winds, rain, and the crash of the storm fill the old songs. Muller's notes weigh each hard word and old rite in the text.
sbe-40-taoist-texts-2-1891:
James Legge gave the Texts of Taoism English dress in the Sacred Books of the East. Book Forty, from 1891, is Part Two of that work. It holds the last books of the Writings of Kwang-dze, known now as Zhuangzi. Zhuangzi is the great wit and sage of the Taoist line.

Books Eighteen to Thirty-Three close the vast, wild text here. Tales of a butterfly dream, a huge fish, and free roams of the mind fill the pages. Zhuangzi mocks stiff rites and the praise of the crowd. Legge's dress was the first full one of the work in English.
schiller-riddles-sphinx-1891:
Writing under the name A. Troglodyte, F. C. S. Schiller issued Riddles of the Sphinx in 1891. The subtitle calls the work a study in the philosophy of evolution. Schiller was a young Oxford thinker at the time. His book fired an early shot in a long campaign.

The riddles are the old puzzles of life: mind, matter, God, and human worth after Darwin. Schiller argues that thought must start from human needs and acts, not from cold abstraction. That stance grew into his humanist form of pragmatism. The book stands as the founding statement of that program. Its bold tone still startles.
schopenhauer-fourfold-root-1891:
Arthur Schopenhauer wrote On the Fourfold Root as his doctoral dissertation in 1813. Mme. Karl Hillebrand translated the German essay into English in 1891. Its subject is the principle of sufficient reason, the rule that everything has a ground. Schopenhauer claimed the rule takes four distinct forms.

He sorts those forms by the kinds of objects minds can know. Causes in nature, grounds of judgment, and motives for action each follow their own version. Sorting them clears up, he thought, much muddle in older philosophy. The essay lays the base for his whole later system. Readers often start his work here.
scientific-american-supplement-no-787-ja: Charles Goodyear is the biography subject of Supplement No. 787, dated New York, January 31, 1891, in Volume XXXI, with the life and discoveries of the inventor of vulcanized India rubber and a portrait in one illustration. Biology gives Andrew Wilson asking whether animals can be separated from plants, a debated point with the bases on which distinctions must be drawn.
scientific-american-supplement-no-794-ma: A new race of dwarf dahlias leads the botany contents of Supplement No. 794, dated New York, March 21, 1891, in Volume XXXI. The plant is called new and of value for flower growers. A portrait of the man who brought it in comes with it, in one picture. Chemistry gives J. Messinger on carbon in organic matter. His piece gives a better method of finding carbon by burning tests, in one picture. Civil engineering gives Professor Karl Pearson's new tool for working up areas and diagrams, in four pictures.
scientific-american-supplement-no-795-ma:
Scientific American Supplement No. 795 reached readers in New York on March 28, 1891, as part of Volume XXXI. The weekly supplement cost five dollars a year, or seven dollars bundled with the main paper, which dated from 1845. Its contents page sorts the issue into headed groups, from poultry keeping to heavy canal machinery.

A report testing two kinds of rations for chickens, backed by data tables, leads the poultry section. Other pieces profile turbine maker N. F. Burnham, name the plant behind Chinese ginger, and map a railway then building through the Andes. Plans to link Chicago with the Mississippi, a dredging machine at work on the Baltic Sea Canal, condenser design, and a Crookes lecture fill the rest.
scientific-american-supplement-no-799-ap:
Supplement No. 799 appeared in New York on April 25, 1891, as part of Volume XXXI. Architecture opens the issue. T. R. Spence discusses marble and mosaic work in a talk first given to a London group of architects, offering practical advice for building designers. A second piece describes a recently finished state hospital in New York, the St. Lawrence Hospital for the Insane, with one illustration.

Botany turns to lavender, tracing its past, its traits, and its uses, with two illustrations. Chemistry offers a precision device that speeds up weighing on a chemist's balance, plus pieces on sunlight spectra and on the varied forms metals can take. Later sections take up water power, with wheels that lift and drive, plus a long lecture by Wm. L. Saunders on making compressed air, shown in 18 illustrations.
scientific-american-supplement-no-803-ma: The great Paris Observatory telescope leads the star study contents of Supplement No. 803, dated New York, May 23, 1891, in Volume XXXI. That piece describes the new telescope lately put in use in Paris. It gives the tool itself and what it can do, in three pictures. Chemistry gives H. Pemberton Jr.'s tool for heating stuff in glass tubes under pressure. The tool is simple and avoids risk of hurt to the user, in two pictures.
scientific-american-supplement-no-810-ju: Cocos Pynaerti, a new dwarf growing palm in one illustration, leads the botany contents of Supplement No. 810, dated New York, July 11, 1891, in Volume XXXII. Chemistry gives Charles A. Kohn on application of electrolysis to quantitative analysis, including applicability of the methods to poison determinations. Civil engineering lists the Kioto-Fu Canal in Japan, connecting the interior of the country with the sea, in three illustrations.
scientific-american-supplement-no-819-se:
Supplement No. 819 appeared in New York on September 12, 1891, as part of Volume XXXII. Astronomy opens the issue with Dr. William Huggins on how the universe took shape and how astronomers now study that question, with one illustration. An electricity piece then explains a large-scale way to split water into hydrogen and oxygen, picturing the gear used in four illustrations.

Mechanical engineering presents a light steam fire engine from England, built for service in India. A medical report by F. A. Burrall recounts a drowning case and a revival, step by step. Metallurgy rounds out the issue with the making of gas cylinders, a sulphuric-acid method for refining silver bullion, and a fresh way to draw metal from stubborn ores.
scientific-american-supplement-no-821-se: The new Labor Exchange in Paris leads Supplement No. 821, dated New York, September 26, 1891, in Volume XXXII, with views of the interior and exterior of the building. Electricity gives S. B. Fowler on construction and maintenance of underground circuits, a comprehensive article discussing devices for protecting underground circuits and methods of inserting cables. Engineering gives railroads to the clouds, sketches of a number of mountain railroads. Marine engineering lists the French armored turret ship Marceau in one engraving, with a full description giving dimensions and cost.
scientific-american-supplement-no-822-oc: The study of mankind leads Supplement No. 822, dated New York, October 3, 1891, in Volume XXXII, reviewing Professor Max Muller's recent address before the British Association. Chemistry gives standards and methods for sugar testing, from a United States tax report, in two pictures. Formation of starch in leaves follows, a study of the work of leaves, in one picture. A. Ganswindt on the water molecule comes next, a piece on how that molecule is built. Civil engineering gives Edward S.
scientific-american-supplement-no-829-no: The sun's motion in space, by A. M. Clerke, leads the astronomy contents of Supplement No. 829, dated New York, November 21, 1891, in Volume XXXII, called a very interesting article on determination of this hitherto uncertain factor. Botany gives W. W. Bailey on hemlock and parsley, the economic botany of the Umbelliferae family. R. A. Weber on raphides, the cause of the acridity of certain plants, follows, covering effects of these crystals on juice from calla and Indian turnip and other plants.
scientific-american-supplement-no-832-de: Old finds at Cadiz lead Supplement No. 832, dated New York, December 12, 1891, in Volume XXXII. The finds are Phenician relics in Spain, with a chance of more big searches in that region, in two pictures. An early horse in America follows. It is a curious find of a native drawing in Nicaragua, in one picture. Star study gives G. E. Lumsden's plea for the common telescope. He cites the growing interest in the field and work done by telescopes of moderate power, with examples from famed observers.
stargate-program-summary-1991:
The Defense Intelligence Agency summed up its psychic spy program in a short paper of May 15, 1991. The STAR GATE Program Summary is the program's own official overview, freed for release years later. STAR GATE was the last name of the long remote viewing effort.

The summary tells what the program sought, how its viewers worked, and what its chiefs claimed for it. Viewers were tasked to describe far and hidden targets by mind alone. The paper is brief, dry, and strange in equal parts. It is the first file to read on the whole remote viewing affair.
tao-te-ching-legge-1891:
James Legge published his complete translation of the Tao Teh King in 1891, as part one of The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East thirty-nine. The Tao Te Ching, ascribed to Lao Tzu, holds eighty-one short chapters of verse-like counsel. It is the founding book of Taoism and one of the most translated texts on earth.

The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao, the book begins, then teaches rule by softness and non-action. Legge adds his introduction and notes, weighing the text's age and meaning with care. His rendering favored exact study over poetic dress. Generations of English students of Chinese thought began with Legge's Lao Tzu. The little book still rewards slow reading.
the-american-missionary-volume-45-no-02-: February 1891, the second number of volume 45, leads with its roll of field workers and money news, then treats teaching of theology, an Indian conference, and the Indian problem. Editors praise open paths for talent and scold bodies that answer to no one. Southern items cover school and church news and Tougaloo University, plus Charleston's Congregational churches. A hospital anchors the women's pages, and letters to the treasurer are printed before the receipts.
the-arena-volume-4-no-19-june-1891: Volume four of The Arena, edited by B. O. Flower and published by the Arena Publishing Company of Boston in 1891, is present as a contents listing. For June 1891 it names The New Columbus by Julian Hawthorne and part one of The Unknown by Camille Flammarion. Julius Chambers writes on the chivalry of the press, Flower himself on society's exiles, and Professor James T. Bixby on evolution and Christianity. Other pieces take up irrigation in the Northwest and neglected crimes. A story is called The Heiress of the Ridge.
the-arena-volume-4-no-20-july-1891:
Number twenty of The Arena, dated July 1891, leads with a signed portrait of Oliver Wendell Holmes and a life study by George Stewart. The study opens on the year 1809, which he calls rich in notable recruits to letters, science, statesmanship, and war. His list runs from Darwin and Gladstone to Tennyson and Holmes.

He, Stewart tells us, was born on August 29 of that year at Cambridge. His father, Dr. Abiel Holmes, had written The American Annals. The son, Stewart promises, would take his place in the front line of poets, thinkers, and essayists. The piece sets Holmes among the giants of his birth year before tracing his own rise.
the-argosy-vol-51-no-1-january-1891: Front matter for volume 51 of The Argosy, edited by Charles W. Wood and covering January to June 1891, is all that is present. Richard Bentley and Son of New Burlington Street, London, publishers in ordinary to Her Majesty, issued the magazine under the motto Laden with Golden Grain. Its leading serial, The Fate of the Hara Diamond, pictured by M. L. Gow, opens with My Arrival at Deepley Walls in the January pages and runs on through The Mistress of Deepley Walls and A Voyage of Discovery.
the-argosy-vol-51-no-2-february-1891: The February number of The Argosy for 1891 survives here only as the bound volume's front pages: volume 51, edited by Charles W. Wood, printed at London by Ogden, Smale and Company for Richard Bentley and Son. The contents trace the serial The Fate of the Hara Diamond, pictured by M. L. Gow, into its February chapters. At Rose Cottage comes chapter five, The Growth of a Mystery chapter six, and Exit Janet Hope chapter seven, before the tale rides north by the Scotch Express.
the-argosy-vol-51-no-3-march-1891: Only the shared front pages of volume 51 stand for the March 1891 Argosy, edited by Charles W. Wood and issued at London by Richard Bentley and Son, publishers in ordinary to Her Majesty. The magazine carries the motto Laden with Golden Grain. In its serial The Fate of the Hara Diamond, pictured by M. L. Gow, the March pages reach chapter nine, set at The Golden Griffin, after the mystery grows at Rose Cottage and Janet Hope makes her exit in the February numbers.
the-argosy-vol-51-no-4-april-1891: April 1891's Argosy is represented by the front pages of its bound half-year, volume 51, running January to June 1891 under editor Charles W. Wood. The London publishers are Richard Bentley and Son of New Burlington Street, and the printer Ogden, Smale and Company of Great Saffron Hill. The contents list the volume's lead serial, The Fate of the Hara Diamond, with pictures by M. L. Gow, from a first arrival at Deepley Walls through Scarsdale Weir and a stop at The Golden Griffin.
the-argosy-vol-51-no-5-may-1891: For May 1891, nothing beyond the volume title pages is present: The Argosy, volume 51, January to June 1891, edited by Charles W. Wood and printed at London for Richard Bentley and Son. The contents for the half-year open with The Fate of the Hara Diamond, pictured by M. L. Gow. Its early chapters bring a narrator to Deepley Walls, meet the mistress of the house, and set out on a voyage of discovery toward Scarsdale Weir.
the-argosy-vol-51-no-6-june-1891: June 1891 closes the half-year bound as volume 51 of The Argosy, and only that volume's front matter is present. Charles W. Wood edited the magazine; Richard Bentley and Son published it at 8 New Burlington Street, London, as publishers in ordinary to Her Majesty. The contents run the lead serial, The Fate of the Hara Diamond with pictures by M. L. Gow, from Deepley Walls and its mistress through Rose Cottage, a growing mystery, and Janet Hope's exit, on to The Golden Griffin.
the-dead-alive-pg7891:
Wilkie Collins opens The Dead Alive at Chapter I, The Sick Man, in a doctor's verdict: heart all right, lungs all right, no organic disease. Philip Lefrank's trouble is overwork, and the remedy is rest. The doctor spoke in Lefrank's chambers in the Temple, half an hour after the young barrister fainted at his desk.

Lefrank explains that he is a junior barrister in good practice, from the Channel Island of Jersey, where his family name was Lefranc before English spelling added the k. Rest, he protests, means ruin in term-time, with the courts sitting and briefs piled on his table. Work, the doctor answers quietly, means death. In court that same day, pressed by senior counsel for facts in his charge, Lefrank finds dates and details mingling in confusion and is led out, terrified.
the-way-of-ambition-pg19491: Robert Hichens's Way of Ambition appears twice in the library in the same Frederick A. Stokes edition of 1913, with illustrations by J. H. Gardner Soper. This record, like its twin, holds the title pages and the start of a contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. A frontispiece caption quotes a question about an extraordinary Cornish genius named Charmian, showing the kind of circle the story moves in. Beyond that, only the bare chapter numbers one and two are visible.
tob-0191:
Max Muller placed his translation of the Upanishads in the Sacred Books of the East, the series he founded and edited. The Upanishads close the Vedas with dialogues on Brahman, the world's ground, and the Self that knows it. Forest sages teach kings and sons in question and answer.

Famous passages ask what the eye cannot see but by which eyes see. Muller's Victorian English is stately and exact. The evidence notes this translation is not on Gutenberg and no text is attached to this entry. The edition's historical place is secure: it carried Hindu philosophy to the general reader of the West.
tob-10091:
Alexander Whyte, a Protestant minister, wrote Santa Teresa as an appreciation rather than a strict biography. Teresa of Avila was the sixteenth-century Spanish nun whose mystical writings and reform of the Carmelite order made her one of Catholicism's most beloved saints. Whyte admired her across a deep church divide.

He dwells on her courage, humor, and practical wisdom as much as on her visions and prayers. Teresa appears as a working reformer who founded convents, handled money and opposition, and still wrote about the inner life with rare clarity. Whyte's warm tribute invites Protestant and general readers to take her seriously.
tob-10791:
Thomas Thomson was a working chemist who wrote in the early 1800s, when the science was still young. His History of Chemistry, in this first volume, runs from the old arts of Egypt and Greece through the phlogiston age to the atomic views of his own day. He knew some of the founders of the new chemistry in person.

Old crafts, alchemy, and early drug lore give way to the study of gases and the fall of phlogiston. The book is dated in spots, as any such tale told from inside must be. Still, it is worth much for its closeness. A science tells its own past while that past is still in living memory.
tob-4191:
Sri Lanka's oldest history comes down in the Dipavamsa, the Chronicle of the Island, kept by Buddhist monks. Hermann Oldenberg edited and translated it in 1879. The verse chronicle tells how the Buddha visited the island, how King Vijaya founded its line, and how the faith took root.

Councils, relics, and the planting of the sacred Bo tree receive careful record. Later chronicles drew on its lists of kings and elders. As the oldest historical record of Buddhism's southern school, the Dipavamsa anchors the island's memory of itself. Verified from the 1919 edition, Oldenberg's version remains the scholar's entry to the chronicle tradition.
tob-4291:
James George Frazer published the first edition of The Golden Bough in 1890, in just two volumes. Volume one opens with a strange scene at Nemi in Italy, where a priest kept guard and could be killed and replaced by his successor. Frazer asks what could explain so grim a custom.

To answer, he gathers cases of magic, taboo, and dying gods from peoples all over the world. He argues that human thought moved from magic toward religion and then science. Shorter than the later twelve-volume edition, the first version states his big idea plainly, and it helped launch the modern study of human cultures.
un-sc-res-1091:
The Council paid tribute to its outgoing Secretary-General on 13 December 1996. Boutros Boutros-Ghali's single five-year term was ending that month. The Council met in closed session for the text. It recognized the central part he had played in guiding the Organization in its Charter duties. His work for peace had spanned the post-Cold War world's first hard years.

The Council acknowledged his contribution to international peace, security, and development. It praised his exceptional efforts to solve problems in the economic, social, and cultural fields. His work to meet humanitarian needs won the same thanks. So did his push for respect for human rights and basic freedoms for all. The Council voiced its deep appreciation for his dedication to the Charter's purposes and principles. It thanked him also for fostering friendly relations among nations. The tribute closed his tenure.
un-sc-res-1191: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1191, adopted on 27 August 1998, is a short procedural text on judges for the war crimes court for the former Yugoslavia. The Council had gathered names put forward for the court by 4 August 1998. It sends nine nominees, from nine different countries, on to the General Assembly. The Assembly then elects from that list under the court's statute.
un-sc-res-1291:
War in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the subject of Resolution 1291 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 24 February 2000. Several African states had troops inside the Congo, and the 1999 Lusaka cease-fire was barely holding.

The text extends and expands the United Nations mission there, called MONUC, to 5,537 troops. MONUC would watch the cease-fire, check violations, and track the pullback of forces. It would help disarm armed groups and back the return of foreign troops to their home countries. The Council also let the mission use force to protect civilians under direct threat of attack.
un-sc-res-1391: The formal record of the Security Council includes the text numbered 1391, catalogued for 1973. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1491: In 2003 the Council voted Resolution 1491 into its official record, and this entry preserves that record through English Wikisource. The document follows the house style of such acts: earlier resolutions recalled, facts noted, then numbered paragraphs that decide the matter. Its value is the primary wording itself, not any summary of it.
un-sc-res-1591:
Darfur sanctions are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1591, adopted in March 2005. Both Sudan's government and rebel groups had broken the cease-fire again and again. Air strikes and village attacks went on, and the Janjaweed militias had not been disarmed. Algeria, China, and Russia abstained.

The text sets up a sanctions committee and a team of four experts based in Addis Ababa. People named by the committee face travel bans and frozen assets worldwide. The named include those who block peace, break the arms embargo, or commit atrocities. The Council also bars attack flights over Darfur and tightens control on arms moving into the region.
un-sc-res-1691:
Security Council Resolution 1691, adopted on June 21, 2006, recommended Montenegro for membership in the United Nations. The catalog year repeats the resolution number and is plainly wrong. Montenegro had voted for independence from its union with Serbia weeks earlier, and its people chose to leave by a narrow margin in a peaceful referendum watched by foreign observers.

The council acted without a dissenting vote, and the General Assembly seated Montenegro on June 28 as the 192nd member state. The short resolution closed the last chapter of the old Yugoslavia's breakup, which had started with wars in the early 1990s. Montenegro's calm path to a seat stood out against that violent past.
un-sc-res-1791:
Burundi's peacebuilding office was extended on 19 December 2007. A government of national unity had formed on 14 November. The Peacebuilding Commission had adopted a strategic framework with Burundi and a way to track it. The last rebel group, the Palipehutu-FNL, still stood outside the peace. Human rights abuses continued to draw concern.

The Council extended BINUB's mandate, as set by resolution 1719 (2006), until 31 December 2008. Burundi's leaders won praise for holding to the peace despite its strains. The FNL was urged to return to the joint verification body and finish the peace process without delay. The South African facilitation and the regional initiative were encouraged to keep pressing the talks. BINUB and the facilitation were told to speed their joint work. The government was urged to press on with governance changes and security reform. The office carried the United Nations role from peacekeeping into peacebuilding.
un-sc-res-1891: Kept under number 1891, a formal Security Council decision is preserved through a Wikisource copy of the UN record. The document's readers in its own day were governments and missions who had to act on it. Its readers now get the same complete text: what the members found, what they decided, and what they asked to be reported.
un-sc-res-191:
Apartheid's own expert report was endorsed on 18 June 1964. Fifty-eight states had brought South Africa's race conflict to the Council in April. The group of experts named under resolution 182 (1963) had reported. Their main finding called for all South Africa's people to be brought into consultation on the country's future. The Council judged the situation a grave disturbance of the peace.

The Council condemned apartheid and the laws behind it, above all the ninety-day detention clause of the General Law Amendment Act. It repeated its urgent appeal for every person jailed or restricted for opposing apartheid to be freed. The experts' recommendations and conclusions were noted, and their main conclusion was endorsed and backed in full. South Africa was invited to accept that conclusion and join the consultations. The Secretary-General had to consider what help the United Nations could give to bring such talks about.
un-sc-res-291:
The end of 1970 brought the Cyprus force its next term, on the advice of a report dated 2 December. The report said the peacekeeping force was still needed to maintain peace on the island. Cyprus's government agreed it should continue beyond 15 December 1970. Resolution 291 was adopted unanimously on 10 December 1970.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They had to keep working together toward the Council's goals, and use the calmer climate on the island well. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 June 1971. The renewal kept the mission in place, as others had done since 1964, while a final settlement remained out of reach.
un-sc-res-391:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was extended in the summer quiet of 15 June 1976. The Secretary-General's report of 5 June held that the force remained essential to the island's calm. Its freedom of movement in the north was still restricted, though talks were mending the problem. Talks between the two communities offered the best hope of a settlement, he judged, if both sides showed flexibility. The parties had agreed to six more months.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964) and its endorsement of the General Assembly's settlement terms. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. Any act that could spoil the search for peace was barred. The stationing of the force in Cyprus was extended for six months, to 15 December 1976. All parties were asked to give the force their fullest cooperation. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and report on the talks.
un-sc-res-91:
Kashmir's mediator resigned and the Council reset its course on 30 March 1951. Sir Owen Dixon had reported on his mission under resolution 80 (1950). India and Pakistan had both restated their wish for a free and impartial plebiscite under United Nations auspices. A plan in Kashmir to call a constituent assembly threatened to prejudge the outcome.

The Council accepted Dixon's resignation at his request, with thanks. It decided to appoint a successor as United Nations representative. The new envoy had to go to the subcontinent, consult both governments, and work for demilitarization of the state. He must report within three months of arrival. If talks failed, the parties were called to accept arbitration on the points still in dispute. The Council also affirmed that a constituent assembly could not settle the state's future, and the military observer group would keep watching the cease-fire.
un-sc-res-991:
El Salvador's civil war had ended, and the Council marked the change in 1995. On 28 April 1995 it paid tribute to ONUSAL, its observer mission there. The country, the text says, had moved from conflict to democracy and peace. The Secretary-General and his representatives had guided the mission. Member states that sent personnel earned thanks. Reports from the mission and its human rights division informed the vote.

The government, the FMLN, and all Salvadorans had to speed up the peace accords. Outstanding promises needed finishing so the gains would last. The Council welcomed their stated commitment to reconciliation. It called on states and world bodies to keep aiding El Salvador. The mission was winding down as a rare success story.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1091, adopted at a closed meeting on 13 December 1996, is the Security Council's farewell tribute to outgoing Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali. It thanks him for guiding the UN, for seeking lasting answers to conflicts worldwide, and for reforms meant to strengthen the UN system. It also honors his work on economic and social problems, aid for people in need, and respect for human rights.

Resolution 1191, adopted on 27 August 1998, is a short procedural text on the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. Recalling the resolutions that created the tribunal and added a third trial chamber, the Council states its decision. It will consider the nominations for the tribunal's judges received by the Secretary-General by 4 August 1998. It then forwards nine nominations to the General Assembly, as the tribunal's Statute requires, for the Assembly's election of the judges.

The war in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement anchor Resolution 1291, adopted on 24 February 2000. The Council backed the deal as the best path to peace and called for all foreign forces to leave in an orderly way. It noted worry over illegal mining of Congo's wealth and over blocked aid access to refugees and displaced people.

The Council extends the UN Organization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, MONUC, until 31 August 2000. It expands it to up to 5,537 military staff, including up to 500 observers. MONUC is to watch the ceasefire, probe breaches, and work with the Joint Military Commission. Within 45 days it must draft a plan covering troop pullback, disarmament of armed groups, and foreign withdrawal. Under Chapter VII it may guard UN staff and sites and shield civilians under direct threat of attack.

At Lebanon's request, UNIFIL is renewed again on 28 January 2002. As in the previous renewal, the force had finished most of its original tasks after Israel's withdrawal. Its remaining work centred on restoring peace and security in the south of the country.

The mandate was extended for six months, until 31 July 2002, and the ongoing reshaping of the force was backed. Lebanon was called on to keep restoring its authority in the south, including through army deployments. The parties were told to ensure the force could move freely across its area, respect the withdrawal line, and show restraint, and violence was condemned.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's multinational stabilization force, SFOR, is renewed on 11 July 2003 for another planned 12 months. The force underpins the 1995 peace agreement, and full support is voiced for the High Representative's continued role. Refugee return across the region is stressed as part of completing the peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized states working through the alliance structure named in the peace agreement to keep SFOR running under unified command. Those states could take all necessary measures to carry out the force's peace-agreement tasks and defend themselves. The situation would be reviewed, and the authorization extended further if the state of the peace required it.

Targeted sanctions on Darfur's spoilers are created by Resolution 1591, adopted in March 2005. Every side had broken the N'Djamena ceasefire and the Abuja protocols: Sudan's air strikes, rebel attacks on villages, and the failure to disarm the Janjaweed all drew blame. The International Commission of Inquiry had reported, and the north-south peace deal risked being undermined by Darfur's war.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets up a Sanctions Committee and a four-member Panel of Experts, based in Addis Ababa, to watch compliance. The Committee will name individuals who block peace, commit atrocities, break the arms embargo, or order offensive military flights. Those named face a travel ban and a freeze of funds and assets, with narrow exemptions for basic and humanitarian needs. Sudan must get Committee approval before moving military equipment into Darfur. It presses all sides back to the Abuja talks, saying there is no military solution.

Montenegro broke away from Serbia in 2006. Its people voted to go their own way. The new state then asked to join the United Nations. Resolution 1691, passed on 22 June 2006, is the Council's reply. The members had read the request with care. They told the General Assembly to admit Montenegro as a member state.

Burundi's peace was young and still frail in December 2007. Resolution 1791, passed on 19 December that year, kept the UN peace team there for one more year. The land had made real strides toward calm. Yet hard tasks stayed on the list. Talks with the last rebel band, the FNL, had to end. Fighters had to lay down their arms for good. The guard forces had to be reshaped. Courts and troops had to learn to guard rights and law. A broad new cabinet had been named that November.

The team, known as BINUB, won a term to the end of 2008. The Council stressed that Burundi's own hands must steer its peace and growth. It cheered a new donor group that lined up aid for the land. It backed the joint plan drawn up by the UN team and the state as well.

Sudan sanctions get their expert panel extended until 15 October 2010 on 13 October 2009. The panel watches the arms embargo and targeted measures tied to Darfur. Commitment to full carrying out of the 2005 north-south peace deal and to a political end to the Darfur conflict, which the 2006 Darfur agreement had failed to deliver, is restated.

The panel is told to report by 31 March 2010 and to coordinate with the joint African Union-United Nations mediation and the Darfur mission, UNAMID. All states and bodies are urged to cooperate with the panel and the sanctions committee. Rebel groups that had stayed out of talks are also pressed to join them at once and constructively, and the sanctions regime stays under active review.

Security Council Resolution 191, adopted on 18 June 1964, deals with apartheid in South Africa. Fifty-eight member states had brought the race conflict to the Council's attention. The Council said apartheid broke the principles of the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It also noted that South Africa had refused to follow earlier resolutions on the subject.

The resolution condemns apartheid and the laws behind it, including the ninety-day detention rule. It urges South Africa to free people jailed for opposing apartheid, spare those sentenced to death, and grant amnesty to detainees and defendants. It also sets up an expert committee to study what measures the Council could take. It asks for an education and training program abroad for South Africans. It repeats the call to stop arms sales to South Africa.

Seven years of Cyprus duty closed with this renewal of December 1970. On the tenth, the Council adopted Resolution 291 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past mid-December.

The text restates the Cyprus decisions, now with Resolution 281 added. It urges the utmost restraint from all parties. It asks for steady joint effort toward the Council's goals. The posting then runs to 15 June 1971. The usual hope closes the text. Progress by then might let the force shrink or withdraw. The mission had begun in 1964 with a three-month term.

Resolution 391, adopted on 15 June 1976, keeps UN peacekeepers in Cyprus for another six months. The Secretary-General reported that the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus was still needed to keep the island quiet and to help the search for a settlement. The force's movement in the north was still limited, and talks between the two communities were the best hope for a lasting deal.

The Council extends the force's stay until 15 December 1976, hoping progress by then might allow it to shrink or leave. It urges both sides to show restraint, stick to past agreements, and keep working toward the Council's goals. It also asks the Secretary-General to keep his good offices mission going and to report back by 30 October 1976.

Belize joined the United Nations through Resolution 491. The Council passed it by a full vote on 23 September 1981. Belize, once called British Honduras, had won its freedom from Britain two days before. Guatemala still claimed its land, so the new state needed friends fast.

The text makes one request: the General Assembly should admit Belize as a member. That step gave the small state the shield of UN membership while the border claim went on. For Belize, this short text carried real weight. A seat in the Assembly was proof to the world, and to its large neighbor, that the new country was here to stay.

Resolution 91, passed on 30 March 1951, resets the UN's work on Kashmir. Eight members backed it, and three did not vote either way. Sir Owen Dixon, sent the year before, had filed his report with no breakthrough. Both India and Pakistan still backed a free vote on Kashmir's fate, held under UN eyes. But a plan to call a law-making body in one part of the state risked fixing the end in advance.

The Council chose a new envoy for India and Pakistan. His charge was to strip troops from the state so the vote could be held. The text warns that a part-state body can not settle Kashmir's fate. Both states were urged to take their last gaps to a judge if the envoy so advised.

El Salvador, not the Golan Heights, closes its UN chapter here. Resolution 991 was adopted unanimously on 28 April 1995. The country had moved from civil war to democracy. ONUSAL, the UN observer mission, had verified the peace accords. Its human rights chief reported on 18 April 1995.

Members paid warm tribute to the mission's work. They urged the government and the FMLN rebels to finish the peace accords' leftover tasks. More outside aid was requested for rebuilding. Then comes the formal ending. ONUSAL's mandate would terminate on 30 April 1995. The resolution reads as a graduation ceremony. A UN success story was being formally signed off.
uslaw-usc-t2-s191:
Section 191 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with oaths given to men who give proof. It sits in Chapter 6, on the ways of work of Congress and its panels, and on probes by them. A set of men are given the power to give the oath to such men. They are the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House. The chair of a joint panel set up by the two Houses is in the list as well. So are the chairs of a panel of the whole and of any panel of either House.

The oath can be given in any case that is under the look of those men or panels. A second part of the section gives a like power to each Member of either House.
volney-ruins-1791: The Ruins, or Meditation on the Revolutions of Empires, Volney's 1791 classic. The empires' ruins. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
waite-the-occult-sciences-1891:
A. E. Waite mapped the whole field of lore in The Occult Sciences, his survey of 1891. One book takes in magic, the great art of gold, and the arts that read fate. Waite sorts high creed from low trick. He gives each art its roots, chief books, and claims in brief.

The survey is calm, fair, and plain in speech. New fans could grasp the whole map from it at once. It is Waite's one tome guide to the field. Few guides of its age hold up so well for a first read. Waite knew the bands and book shops of the field at first hand. That range lets him weigh each art with a calm, fair hand.
walker-pronouncing-1791:
John Walker published his Critical Pronouncing Dictionary in 1791, setting out how English words ought to sound. Walker, once an actor, had become the leading teacher of elocution in London. His book marked the sounds of tens of thousands of words so that any reader could aim at approved speech.

Each entry gives spelling, pronunciation, and meaning, with rules and remarks where usage was in dispute. The dictionary served strivers who knew that accent could open or close doors in British society. For a century it was the authority on respectable pronunciation on both sides of the Atlantic. Its influence lingered in schools and pulpits long after newer guides appeared.
wedekind-spring-awakening-1891:
Frank Wedekind's The Awakening of Spring, a tragedy of childhood, reached English in Francis J. Ziegler's rendering. Brown Brothers of Philadelphia issued the third edition in 1912. Publisher's pages list his other books in English. A proem for prudes, printed before the play, states its thesis without flinching.

To bring up children, boys or girls, kept ignorant of their sexual nature is a fatal error, the proem argues. That error is the drama's whole subject. From its title one might expect a peaceful little idyl of the youth of the year, and no guess could be more wrong. The piece is a tragedy of frightful import. Wedekind wrote the play in German in 1891, as the record name notes. Its schoolboys and girls, kept in the dark by parents and teachers, walk into ruin that knowledge might have spared them.
westermarck-the-history-of-human-marriag:
Edward Westermarck, a Finnish scholar working in England, published this Darwinian history of marriage in 1891. It was a large claim for its time: that marriage and the family rest on instincts shaped by natural selection, not on late invention.

Westermarck argues against the idea that early humans lived without marriage rules. He examines exogamy and the incest taboo, proposing that children raised together lose desire for each other, a claim still debated as the Westermarck effect. His evidence spans animals, early peoples, and civilized law. The book became a standard reference in the study of the family.
wilde-house-pomegranates-1891:
Oscar Wilde wrote these four tales for grown readers, and the set came out in 1891. Its name plays on the rich red fruit of the pomegranate tree. Wilde was then at the height of his fame in the London world of art.

Among the tales stands 'The Fisherman and his Soul,' a long tale of a man and a mermaid. He cuts his soul from his body to wed the maid of the sea, and pays a high price. The set shows Wilde's tale craft at its most rich and grave.
zola-money-1891:
Caxton issued Money at London in 1900, in Vizetelly's English version. Chapter heads run from The Temple of Mammon through Dreams and Schemes. Saccard Makes a Start and The Bank Is Founded follow in order.

Aristide Saccard returns, and this time his weapon is the stock market itself. His Universal Bank turns into a machine for breeding greed in all Paris. Fortunes rise in a morning and vanish by nightfall in the frenzy. A frontispiece shows the ruined Mazaud with a bullet through his head. Furious and prophetic, the 1891 novel reads like later headlines written a full century early.
